Music inspired by the life and message of St Francis of Assisi will be performed at Sofia’s St Joseph Catholic Cathedral on 2 October at 7 pm. Entitled The Legend of St Francis of Assisi, the free concert marks 800 years since the saint’s death.
The performers are sopranо Anastasia Altukhova, mezzo-soprano Gergana Rusekova, flautist Gergana Ivanova, oboist Deyan Ivanov, Stanislava Georgieva on harpsichord and organ, violinists Antoaneta Aleksova and Bozhena Kirkov, violist Rostislava Dimitrova and cellist Vesela Darvarova.
The programme features works by Handel, Bach, Vivaldi, Stradella, Scarlatti, Heinichen, Franck and Liszt.
Admission is free of charge.

ISTRA /Moscow Region/, September 29. /TASS/. Russia-US contacts on the issue of "irritants" will take place soon, with the timing being coordinated, Russian Foreign Minister Sergey Lavrov told reporters on the sidelines of the 23rd annual meeting of the Valdai Discussion Club.
He noted that circumstances would eventually compel the United States to think in terms of multipolarity.
Commenting on Poland’s plans to establish Patriot missile production in the country, Lavrov urged that Russia’s military doctrine be studied closely.
TASS has compiled his key statements.
Contacts with the United States
Circumstances will eventually force the US to think in terms of multipolarity, and this process is only beginning: "I said that circumstances would force them to. But it is only the beginning. Be patient. We have repeatedly outlined, together with the president, all our proposals on how relations should be built on the international stage."
The US is still seeking to promote its own unilateral interests: "The United States is forced to engage with countries such as Russia and China. During these contacts, steps are discussed that will serve the interests of both countries. This is precisely the concept that I would refer to as ‘circumstances forcing them.’"
Russia-US contacts on the issue of "irritants" will take place soon, with the timing currently under coordination: "Not yet. We agreed with [US Secretary of State] Marco Rubio that this would happen. The experts are expected to agree on the specific timing and venue."
Under US President Donald Trump’s administration, Russia has never heard any encouraging signals from the US side regarding the return of diplomatic property: "On this issue, we have never heard any encouraging comments from the US side, with Donald Trump’s administration already in office."
Special military operation
Russia is eliminating threats and destroying the infrastructure of the Nazi Kiev regime in Ukraine: "If you are talking about the destruction of infrastructure used by the Nazi regime, with Western support, to wage war against Russia, then we resort to brute force to suppress this direct threat to us."
EU involvement in military conflict with Russia
European countries are waging a war against Russia and it is beyond any doubt: "Well, if you admit that your weapons are being used against us and we are shooting these weapons down, you may call it whatever you like. However, I have no doubt that this is a war that Europe is waging against us. We have been talking about this for a long time."
Russia’s military doctrine needs to be carefully studied in light of Poland’s plans to establish Patriot missile production in the country and the extent of Europe’s involvement in the conflict in Ukraine: "We have a military doctrine on this matter, which President [of Russia Vladimir Putin] has cited repeatedly. I urge you to study carefully the relevant section of this crucial document."
Germany’s attempts to participate in the Ukrainian settlement
Germany wants to "stay relevant" through its attempts to become involved in resolving the conflict around Ukraine: "It is difficult for me to judge what Germany is seeking. I think one obvious explanation is the basic desire to stay relevant. They believe that things are coming to a head, I am not sure if that is true, when it comes to the Ukrainian crisis."
"The militarization of the European Union, the ever-present incantations about NATO expanding to include the Kiev regime, Russia as an eternal enemy, and the three years that separate it from war with the EU. If the same song is being sung, with the same goal that Mr. [German Foreign Minister Johann] Wadephul himself declared, i.e. repeating these notions behind closed doors without the press in order to force Russia to accept it as the case, then I would call this a fruitless and even harmful undertaking."
It is regrettable that such individuals from the EU and NATO essentially take on "the role of heralding" this European arrangement.

UK to keep national museums free for overseas visitors
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-29
13:25:26 UTC
22:25:26 KST

Aysu Bicer
29 September 2026•Update: 29 September 2026
The UK government has confirmed that national museums in England will continue to offer free admission to all visitors, including overseas tourists.
“Everyone will continue to enjoy universal free admission to our world class national museums in England,” the government said in a statement Tuesday.
Earlier this year, the government had considered introducing admission fees for overseas visitors as a way to boost museum finances but decided against the move.
However, it said charging international visitors could deter domestic audiences and that “the impacts and benefits of charging would not be felt equally across the sector.”
National museums contribute more than £1 billion ($1.3 billion) a year to the UK economy and attract visitors from around the world.
“Seven of the UK’s ten most visited museums are national museums,” the government said.
In 2025, 7.1 million people visited the Natural History Museum, while 6.4 million visited the British Museum.
The government said it would work with Arts Council England and the sector to develop “a long-term strategic plan for the future of museums.”
“Further details will be released in due course,” it added.

America’s Greenland deal has a radioactive backstory
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-29
13:21:36 UTC
22:21:36 KST

America’s Greenland deal has a radioactive backstory
The US, Denmark, and Greenland have signed a new agreement to expand American military activity on the island. Washington calls Greenland vital to its security, but an expanded military presence also raises an older question: What risks does the Arctic island take on in return?
The agreement builds on a defense partnership dating back to 1951. That history includes an episode that brought the risks of Washington’s Cold War strategy into sharp focus: An American mission over Greenland that ended in a nuclear disaster.
The nuclear patrols over Greenland
In the 1960s, in the middle of the Cold War, the US Air Force launched Operation Chrome Dome. This mission implied keeping bombers armed with nuclear weapons on continuous airborne alert, ready to strike the USSR if necessary. If you’ve seen the film ‘Dr. Strangelove’, you’ll remember that Major T.J. ‘King’ Kong’s crew was involved in such a patrol mission.
Theoretically, this strategy was feasible: It would have made it impossible for the USSR to disarm the US with a single blow. However, in practice, as the number of nuclear-armed aircraft patrols increased, so did the number of incidents involving nuclear weapons.
Then-US Secretary of Defense Robert McNamara advocated for ending this program, arguing that Americans had already established an effective early warning system for ballistic missile launches, so the US could take fewer risks and cut costs. However, the Strategic Air Command resisted this idea, fearing it would decrease their importance and result in budget cuts.
A horrific incident occurred in 1966 over Spain when a bomber collided with a refueling tanker aircraft, resulting in several fatalities and nuclear bombs landing on beaches and in the Mediterranean Sea. Despite this incident, the US considered the nuclear threat from the USSR a matter of primary importance, one which justified any security measures.
Eventually, after intense debates, a compromise was reached: The number of patrolling bombers would be reduced, but the airborne patrols would continue.
Thule Air Base in northern Greenland was established in the 1950s. A Mercator projection map gives a distorted sense of distance; in reality, its location was very convenient for potentially launching missiles at the USSR and monitoring missile launches from there. It also provided a convenient vantage point for reconnaissance of the Novaya Zemlya Soviet nuclear test site.
Thus, the US Strategic Air Command built a military base in northern Greenland. The name referred to ‘Ultima Thule’ (farthest Thule) – a mythical island at the edge of the world. The base housed bombers, reconnaissance planes, radar systems, missile launch sites, and early-warning radars. In its most active period, Thule base housed about 10,000 personnel. Additionally, the US launched the highly classified Project Iceworm, which aimed to build a wide network of nuclear missile launch sites concealed in tunnels beneath the ice. One could say Greenland became thoroughly inhabited.
Seven men, four hydrogen bombs, and a fire in the sky
On January 21, 1968, a B-52 bomber rose into the air, carrying four megaton bombs. It took off from New York to visually monitor the nuclear alert system, bearing four thermonuclear bombs, each with a yield exceeding one megaton.
The standard crew consisted of five members; however, a third pilot and a substitute navigator were included on the mission.
Everything started out smoothly. But eventually, the factor of human error came into play.
The third pilot, Major Alfred d’Amario, took aboard a few cloth-covered foam cushions to make his flight more comfortable. He placed the cushions under the instructor navigator’s seat and went to replace co-pilot Leonard Svitenko, who went to take his rest period. The cushions remained in place.
Not long after, the pilots opened an engine bleed valve which channeled hot air from the engine to the heater. Unfortunately, the heater was defective and quickly became dangerously hot.
At some point, the pilots noticed the smell of burning rubber filling the cockpit. While they searched for the source of the burning, a fire had already started onboard. The navigator went looking for the flames, and, on discovering the fire, attempted to extinguish it using two fire extinguishers. However, he was unable to put it out.
Captain Haug, the aircraft commander, requested an emergency landing at the airbase. All the extinguishers had been used, but the fire continued to spread. Smoke thickened to the point that the crew could hardly see each other in the cockpit. Ultimately, as the plane neared Thule Air Base, Haug ordered everyone to abandon it.
Out of the seven crew members, six managed to eject relatively safely. Tragically, co-pilot Leonard Svitenko sustained fatal head injuries while trying to escape.
Haug and d’Amario landed directly on the airbase grounds. The base personnel immediately mobilized to search for the remaining crew. A polar night enveloped Greenland, and the weather was dreadful. A representative of the Royal Greenland Trade Department, Jens Zinglersen, significantly eased the search efforts by contacting local Inuit residents who organized dog sled teams. Thanks to their collective efforts, three other aviators were found – they had landed within a mile and a half of the base and were quickly located.
Gunner Staff Sergeant Calvin Snapp was less fortunate. He ejected first and landed nearly 10 km from the base in -30C degree temperatures. Wrapping himself in his parachute, he waited for help for 21 hours before being rescued by a search team. Miraculously, they found him alive, though severely hypothermic.
But the worst was yet to come. The aircraft carrying thermonuclear munitions was still flying northward and burning up. Finally, it crashed onto the ice about 12 km west of the airbase. There was still plenty of fuel onboard; it ignited on the ice, causing spectacular pyrotechnic effects. The bomb’s non-nuclear explosives detonated, partially melting the ice and scattering radioactive debris everywhere.
There was another poignant detail, however. Greenland belonged to Denmark, which had declared its entire territory a nuclear-free zone. And now, a bomber armed with nuclear weapons had crashed there – though the Danes (at least those who didn’t work in the government) were unaware that there was also radioactive debris all over the ground. The Danish government quickly issued a statement claiming that the aircraft was not in Greenland’s airspace and had only entered it due to an onboard emergency. This was a complete fabrication, but it served as a cover-up for the situation.
The US found itself in a delicate situation that urgently needed fixing.
Cleaning up a nuclear disaster in the Arctic night
The cleanup operation was dubbed Project Crested Ice (or unofficially, ‘Project Doctor Freezelove’). The operation was led by General Richard Overton Hunziker, a seasoned veteran and WWII hero.
A team of scientists, nuclear specialists, and a massive number of troops were dispatched to Greenland. Their mission was to remove all radioactive materials before spring arrived and the contaminated ice would be carried off into the ocean. The polar night brought fierce winds and bitterly cold temperatures, making the task even more challenging.
Radioactive elements were scattered across a 1-mile (1.6 km) by 3-mile (4.8 km) area. In the midst of it was an ice hole measuring 50 meters in diameter. A blackened patch measuring 670 by 120 meters and heavily contaminated with uranium and plutonium was clearly visible from the air.
The US suggested to the Danish authorities that they should just wait for spring when the ice would melt and everything would sink into the Arctic waters. But Denmark was outraged. The Americans were given a choice: Either clean up their mess or close down the Thule base and leave Danish territory.
It must be said that Hunziker and his team worked heroically. They established a small town on the ice, complete with igloos, a power station, a runway, a communications hub, and a decontamination chamber. An icy road connected them to the airbase.
Thousands of people toiled under the harsh conditions, illuminated by floodlights as they cut through the contaminated ice, loaded it onto transports, and hauled it to storage, where it was boxed up in tanks for shipping back to the US. Ice was collected using graders, packed into wooden crates, which were then loaded into steel tanks and onto ships. Debris was recovered manually – some pieces were sizable, but the smallest were no bigger than a battery. Contaminated areas were identified using simple Geiger counters.
The cleanup crew worked with minimal protective clothing. Most people simply wore their regular Arctic expedition clothing.
By mid-September 1968, the operation was officially concluded. In total, 1,700 Danes and 700 Americans participated in it. While the disaster was a stark illustration of the consequences of foolish and irresponsible behavior, the cleanup crew – which braved the harsh cold and literally gathered radioactive waste by hand – accomplished real feats, which, however, remained largely forgotten.
What the ice couldn’t bury
It’s believed that around 93% of the radioactive materials were collected, but some remnants remained on the seabed. One hydrogen bomb likely sank among other debris. Attempts to locate it with a submersible were unsuccessful. A heap of wreckage was discovered on the ocean floor, and somewhere down there, it appears that the remains of the nuclear weapon still lie undisturbed.
In the 1980s and ‘90s, a scandal erupted. Danish cleanup workers launched a legal battle against the American government. Though they lost the case, they succeeded in forcing the release of numerous classified documents. Subsequent investigations revealed that cancer mortality rates among Danish workers involved in the cleanup operation were about one and a half times higher than those of the general population. It also turned out that the health monitoring of the cleanup crews after the incident was inadequate. Ultimately, officials concluded that radiation exposure wasn’t significant and found no link between the increased cancer rate and the 1968 accident.
A heated debate arose around the actions of Danish prime ministers Jens Otto Krag and H. C. Hansen. Krag portrayed himself as a naïve yet honest figure, insisting that he wasn’t aware of aircraft carrying nuclear weapons over Greenland. However, declassified US documents indicated that the Danish government was aware of everything. As for Hansen, he was the one who secretly approved the US to use Thule Air Base as part of its nuclear shield. However, by then, both prime ministers had passed away, and were unable to answer to the population.
After the incident, Operation Chrome Dome was officially shut down. After all, it was the second nuclear disaster in three years, and that was too much even for the ‘hawks’. Secondly, both Russians and Americans already had plenty of missiles, and the use of bombers seemed somewhat archaic. Finally, the USSR and the US initiated another period of détente and developed protocols for handling any accidental incidents involving nuclear weapons. While this didn’t help those who suffered or died from cancer as a result of the accident in Greenland, it did significantly reduce the risk of similar events in the future.

Art Goes Underground in Zaporizhzhia as GOGOLFEST Returns 30 Km From Frontline
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-29
13:19:11 UTC
22:19:11 KST

- Category
- Life in Ukraine
Art Goes Underground in Zaporizhzhia as GOGOLFEST Returns 30 Km From Frontline
The international contemporary art festival GOGOLFEST Pokrova will take place in Zaporizhzhia from October 1 to 4, with most of its program moving underground in response to the security conditions of the frontline city.
Recognized among Europe’s five leading festivals by the EFFE Awards, the event will hold 95% of its program in underground venues to avoid disruptions from air attacks.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
This year’s Zaporizhzhia edition, titled TimeCode, will explore Ukraine’s past, present, and future through a program spanning theater, music, performance, digital art, and public discussions.
At the center of the festival will be Futurum, a large-scale performance directed by Vladyslav Troitskyi that will connect 15 underground schools across Zaporizhzhia through a live digital broadcast.
“Holding the largest contemporary art festival 30 kilometers from the frontline in Zaporizhzhia today means developing practical tools for safe interaction for a new generation instead of allowing Ukrainian cultural life to be paralyzed, as our enemy wants,” GOGOLFEST Program Director Anna Basova said.
She added that the project would create a precedent by connecting the city’s underground educational spaces into a single digital network for one evening. Together with Ukrainian theater director Vladyslav Troitskyi and Ukrainian band DakhaBrakha, children living under the daily threat of Russian attacks will explore a new form of technological art, while the project could serve as a model for safely engaging young audiences in cultural activities in frontline communities.
The festival’s theater program will likewise take place in protected spaces. DakhTrio will present the Ukrainian premiere of the chamber opera Skovoroda. Shevchenko. Stus, which combines academic, folk, and rock influences. According to organizers, most of the compositions based on works by Ukrainian poets Vasyl Stus and Hryhorii Skovoroda will be performed on stage for the first time.
The international program will include Swiss performer Madeleine Bongard’s Be My Margaret! (or in the strangeness of loneliness), a solo production based on interviews with French writer Marguerite Duras. Following 39 performances across Europe in English and French, the production will be presented in Ukrainian for the first time.
The underground music program will focus on contemporary Ukrainian electronic and experimental music. SI Process, the electronic project of drummer and sound producer Stanislav Ivashchenko from the Brave! Factory community, will present a special program adapted to the acoustics of shelters. Ukrainian musician Stas Koroliov and director Anastasiia Vesna will also present a collaborative experimental project combining alternative music, songwriting, and performance.
Beyond its artistic program, GOGOLFEST Pokrova will host discussions and workshops featuring analysts, urban planners, architects, and sociologists. Topics will include the transformation and postwar reconstruction of public spaces in frontline communities, strengthening local communities during crises, and the future of Zaporizhzhia.
The program will also feature The Future. Zaporizhzhia After, a panel bringing together local leaders, architects, and international experts.
The festival comes as Ukrainian cultural projects continue to adapt to the realities of Russia’s full-scale invasion. Ukrainian documentary Landing, which follows a skateboarding community in the frontline city of Okhtyrka, has been selected for the official program of the international SUOMFORNIA film festival in Helsinki, Finland.
The film chronicles the community’s efforts to establish “Krytka,” Okhtyrka’s first indoor skatepark, in 2024 amid the full-scale war.

China's external debt rises in Q2 amid active cross-border trade
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-29
21:19:01 CST
22:19:01 KST

BEIJING, Sept. 29 (Xinhua) -- China's external debt rose in the second quarter of 2026 amid active cross-border trade, while the latest available debt-risk indicators were within internationally recognized safety thresholds.
Outstanding external debt stood at 2.4982 trillion U.S. dollars at the end of June, up 86.1 billion dollars, or 4 percent, from the end of March, data from the State Administration of Foreign Exchange (SAFE) showed on Tuesday.
The increase was mainly driven by relatively active cross-border trade, with both corporate trade credit and intercompany lending rising, said Li Bin, deputy head and spokesperson of SAFE.
Li said China's external debt remained generally stable in the second quarter.
China's goods imports and exports reached 13.61 trillion yuan (about 2.02 trillion U.S. dollars) in the second quarter, up 18.4 percent year on year, the fastest year-on-year growth for any quarter since the third quarter of 2021, according to data from the General Administration of Customs. Trade value in June alone rose 24.2 percent year on year, marking 17 consecutive months of growth.
Yuan-denominated external debt accounted for 56 percent of the total at the end of June, up 1 percentage point from the end of March, while medium- and long-term debt held steady at 41 percent.
SAFE said in July that the share of yuan-denominated external debt had risen while medium- and long-term debt had remained broadly stable at over 40 percent in recent years, with currency and maturity mismatch risks seeing significant declines.
Moderate external borrowing allows Chinese companies and banks to tap both domestic and international markets, diversify financing channels and improve operational efficiency, while risks stemming from excessive debt levels require continued monitoring, SAFE said.
At the end of 2025, China's outstanding external debt was equivalent to 11.9 percent of gross domestic product, below the 20-percent international safety threshold cited by SAFE.
Separate data released on Tuesday showed that China's external financial assets continued to exceed its external liabilities. External financial assets stood at 12.1804 trillion U.S. dollars at the end of June, against liabilities of 8.3555 trillion dollars, leaving net external financial assets of 3.8249 trillion dollars. ■

Libya's High State Council rejects changes to presidential election law as "unconstitutional"
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-29
21:18:53 CST
22:18:53 KST

TRIPOLI, Sept. 29 (Xinhua) -- Libya's High State Council (HSC) has said the House of Representatives (HoR)'s amendments to the presidential election law were "unconstitutional" and called for further institutional consultations on the electoral framework.
The HSC issued a statement on its Facebook page late Monday night detailing its opposition.
The council asserted that any modification to the rules, conditions, and timelines for electoral competition must be carried out through a clear, agreed-upon institutional process.
The move came as the HoR issued Law No. 4 of 2026 on Monday, amending provisions related to the presidential election framework, such as allowing military personnel and dual nationals to run for office under updated terms.
The HSC's stance comes just before the one-month deadline for ratifying the UN-facilitated agreement on presidential and parliamentary elections in Libya.
In April, the United Nations Support Mission in Libya (UNSMIL) began engaging a smaller group of Libyan representatives known as the "4+4" committee, as part of its political roadmap. The discussions focused primarily on resolving disputes over the electoral framework.
In June, the UNSMIL said the participants had reached an understanding on the presidential election law.
On August 30, under UNSMIL facilitation, the 4+4 participants signed an agreement, vowing to restructure the Elections Commission and resolving outstanding legal and constitutional issues affecting presidential and parliamentary elections.
On Spet. 3, the UNSMIL presented the agreement to the HoR and HSC leadership, giving one month to approve it.
The HSC leadership objected to the agreement's existing form, with the dispute focusing on the legal process for approving the electoral rules and the Elections Commission's composition, rather than on the principle of holding elections.
On Sept. 14, the HoR voted unanimously at a session in Benghazi to adopt the 4+4 agreement, saying it was consistent with its existing position on several electoral issues.
Libya has been divided politically and institutionally for years, while the United Nations and Libyan parties have been seeking to reach a consensual framework paving the way for national elections, resolve contentious issues related to the presidential election law, and appoint a new board of the electoral commission to oversee the overall electoral process across the country.
The country's political system remains divided among competing legislative, executive and security institutions. The eastern-based HoR is the country's main legislative body, while the Tripoli-based HSC is a separate consultative institution with an important role in major political and institutional arrangements. The dispute between the two over electoral legislation forms part of a broader division between rival authorities and power centers in western and eastern Libya. ■

Defeat in Nagoya, questions in Tehran: What next for Iran’s U23s?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher

Defeat in Nagoya, questions in Tehran: What next for Iran’s U23s?
TEHRAN - Iran’s U23 football team suffered another major setback at the Asian Games, crashing out of the 2026 tournament in Nagoya after a humiliating 4-1 defeat to North Korea.
The result was more than a disappointing night for Hossein Abdi’s side. It was another warning sign for an Iranian Football Federation that has repeatedly failed to build a clear, long-term plan for one of the country’s most important national teams.
 
 The most worrying aspect is that this was not a squad lacking talent. Several players were regulars for their Persian Gulf Pro League clubs, and the team had been assembled with the stated ambition of using the Asian Games as a step towards the 2028 Olympics. Abdi himself had spoken about the importance of international matches and building chemistry before the tournament.
 
 Yet the team looked increasingly disconnected as the tournament progressed. After a promising opening win, Iran failed to secure qualification against China and then produced a chaotic performance against North Korea. Abdi accepted responsibility and described the result as unacceptable.
 
 That responsibility, however, cannot end with the coach.
 
 Abdi certainly deserves scrutiny. He knew many of these players from their earlier youth-team years and had several preparation camps and overseas training periods. Whatever the logistical difficulties surrounding player availability and preparation, the final performance raised legitimate questions about tactical organization, defensive structure and the team's ability to respond under pressure.
 
 But changing the coach again risks missing the larger issue.
 
 Iran's Football Federation has repeatedly struggled to establish a stable process for selecting U23 coaches and preparing teams well in advance of major tournaments. The pattern has become familiar: a coach is appointed relatively late, preparation is compressed, expectations remain high and, after failure, the entire project starts again with a new name.
 
 Now the federation faces another decision. Names such as Afshin Ghotbi, Farhad Majidi, Yahya Golmohammadi and Mojtaba Hosseini have been mentioned, while the possibility of a foreign coach has also been discussed. Yet the crucial question is not which name appears on the shortlist. It is what criteria and long-term plan will determine the appointment?
 
 Japan will host the 2028 AFC U23 Asian Cup, which will also serve as Asia's qualification tournament for the Los Angeles Olympics. Iran therefore have a clear target and a reasonable amount of time to prepare.
 
 What it needs now is not simply another coach. It needs a defined project: a clear football philosophy, transparent selection criteria, continuity between youth levels, regular international fixtures and measurable objectives.
 
 Otherwise, Iran's U23 team will remain trapped in the same cycle; appoint, prepare, fail, replace and repeat. And another promising generation of players will once again pay the price for a problem that is much bigger than the man standing on the touchline.

CAS launches program for breakthroughs at science frontiers
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-29
21:18:46 CST
22:18:46 KST

BEIJING, Sept. 29 (Xinhua) -- The Chinese Academy of Sciences (CAS) announced on Tuesday the launch of a new program aimed at achieving breakthroughs at the frontiers of science and producing major original research achievements in key fields.
At a press conference held in Beijing, Zhou Qi, CAS vice president, said the program focuses on major scientific questions that will drive a paradigm shift in research and open up new frontiers, harnessing shared access to major scientific infrastructure and AI-empowered scientific research to organize leading talent into systematic, institutionalized research campaigns.
These efforts are designed to support China's pursuit of original, trailblazing breakthroughs on major frontiers of science and in core technologies, Zhou said.
The first batch of 10 projects under the program was unveiled at the media event, targeting research in fields such as the synthesis of new elements, the nature of dark matter and dark energy, microscopic measurement of chemical bonds and the creation of synthetic cells.
Meanwhile, a list of priority areas for the next batch was also released, with key support to be directed toward the fields of physical sciences, life sciences, Earth system sciences, and space sciences.
Wei Zhixiang, director of the Bureau of Basic Science Research of the CAS, said this program will deeply integrate the coordinated use of major scientific facilities with AI empowerment, centering on the directions of "the extremely macroscopic, the extremely microscopic, extreme conditions, and highly convergent interdisciplinary frontiers."
Outstanding scientists from within and beyond the CAS, as well as around the world, are encouraged to join the program and make full use of the large-scale scientific facilities, AI platforms and networks of the CAS, Wei said.
Li Yuhui, deputy director of the Bureau of Basic Science Research of the CAS, said the program will focus on key difficulties in national security, people's health, and major engineering projects, promote breakthroughs in fundamental theory, and encourage scientists to seek new growth areas in the "uncharted territories" at disciplinary boundaries.
The program will use AI to conduct deep mining of massive literature and experimental data, identify key problems approaching the critical point of breakthrough, and then carry out rapid verification through automated experiments by scientific facility clusters.
Yang Weijin, deputy director of the Bureau of Basic Capacity for Science and Technology of the CAS, said major scientific and technological infrastructures can provide ultimate research means for frontier research and for tackling core technologies, and serve as strategic support platforms in the era of big science.
China has deployed 77 major scientific and technological infrastructures. The CAS now operates 43 of them, accounting for 56 percent of the national total, according to Yang. ■

NAGOYA, Japan, Sept. 29 (Xinhua) -- India's Neeru Dhanda made history as the country's first woman to win an Asian Games trap title on Tuesday, while China secured another shooting gold in the women's trap team event at the 2026 Asian Games.
Neeru, 26, entered the women's trap final as the top qualifier after hitting 118 of 125 targets and beating Qatar's Ray Bassil in a shoot-off for first place.
Neeru battled China's Sun Yunong for gold in the final, with the pair tied at 14-14 before Sun missed two targets in the following series. Neeru finished with 28 hits, surpassing the previous Asian record of 24, to take the title.
Sun claimed silver with 26 hits, while Hajar Abdulmalik took bronze.
"Neeru missed, as they all did, but she kept grinding away," coach Peter Wilson said. "We have worked a lot on staying in the present, but the brain likes to trick you into the future."
"I was able to play to my strengths today, but there are still some technical details I need to improve," Sun said. "Overall, I'm fairly satisfied with my performance."
Sun, Liu Shanshan and Zhu Jingyu combined for 346 hits to win the women's trap team title for China. India took silver with 328, while Kuwait claimed bronze with 325.
The victory increased China's shooting gold medal tally to 16, matching its total from the Hangzhou Asian Games.
In the men's trap team event, Kuwait won gold with 355 hits, while Qatar and Kazakhstan took silver and bronze with 349 and 348, respectively. China finished fourth.
Kuwait's 48-year-old Khaled Almudhaf won the men's individual title with 26 hits, one ahead of Chinese Taipei's Yang Kun-Pi. China's Qi Ying took bronze.
It was Almudhaf's first individual gold medal in eight Asian Games appearances.
"I'm an ambassador for older people to see that they can win even at this age," Almudhaf said. "This is a sport where you can shoot when you are older." ■

Unknown Publisher
2026-09-29
21:18:41 CST
22:18:41 KST

URUMQI, Sept. 29 (Xinhua) -- International coffee chain giant Starbucks on Tuesday opened two stores in northwest China's Xinjiang Uygur Autonomous Region, marking its debut in the region and the latest expansion in China, its second-largest market after the United States.
The stores are located in Urumqi, the regional capital -- one in the iconic Grand Bazaar and the other at Urumqi Tianshan International Airport.
The Grand Bazaar flagship store boasts a distinctive design inspired by traditional bazaar canopy silhouettes, with interiors featuring Xinjiang elements like Atlas silk and ethnic musical instruments. Both stores have rolled out locally inspired menus and exclusive drinks, such as the milk-skin-flavored salty milk tea.
"Entering Xinjiang not only marks a further expansion of our store network, but also allows us to engage deeply with this vibrant market and build sincere, lasting connections with our customers there," Molly Liu, chief executive officer of Starbucks China, said in a written statement.
Zhang Yu, an official with the regional administration for market regulation, said Xinjiang has made the "first-store economy" -- a gauge of urban commercial vitality and consumer appeal -- a key lever for boosting domestic demand and consumption.
Zhang added that Xinjiang will continue to improve support policies for first stores, enhance approval efficiency and optimize the business environment.
The openings follow Starbucks' partnership with Chinese venture capital firm Boyu Capital to operate its retail business in China. According to the agreement signed in November last year, Boyu and Starbucks will operate a joint venture with Boyu holding up to a 60-percent interest in Starbucks' retail operations in China, while Starbucks will retain the remaining 40-percent interest in the joint venture, and continue to own the Starbucks brand and license the brand and intellectual property to the new entity.
The latest expansion comes as Starbucks is restructuring its North American business, with the company announcing plans last week to close 250 underperforming coffeehouses in the region.
Starbucks entered the Chinese mainland in January 1999, opening its first store in Beijing. As coffee culture took root and gained popularity, the chain steadily expanded its footprint across China. By Sept. 27, 2026, Starbucks operated 8,342 stores on the Chinese mainland, up 331 from the end of fiscal 2025, according to its fiscal 2026 data.
The Chinese mainland is now Starbucks' second-largest market after the United States, where the company operated 16,933 stores as of June 28, 2026, according to its fiscal 2026 third-quarter results.
Its long-running expansion reflects how foreign brands are seeking opportunities in China's growing consumer market.
The State Administration for Market Regulation said China saw 35,000 newly established foreign-invested enterprises in the first half of 2026, up 7 percent year on year. Separate data from the Ministry of Commerce showed nearly 4,800 foreign-funded enterprises increased investment in China in the first half of 2026. ■

China firmly opposes any action of Philippines to harm China's sovereignty, rights: FM spokesperson

2026-09-29
21:18:40 CST
22:18:40 KST

BEIJING, Sept. 29 (Xinhua) -- China firmly opposes any action of the Philippines that harms China's sovereignty and rights and interests, Chinese foreign ministry spokesperson Guo Jiakun said on Tuesday.
Guo made the remarks at a regular press briefing in response to a query related to a so-called updated "maritime chart" by the Philippine National Maritime Council, which includes islands and reefs in China's Nansha Qundao such as Zhongye Dao and Mahuan Dao.
"Zhongye Dao and Mahuan Dao are part of China's Nansha Qundao and Chinese territory. China has indisputable sovereignty over Nansha Qundao and its adjacent waters," Guo said.
Noting that the scope of Philippine territory is defined by several international treaties, Guo said that China's Nanhai Zhudao, including Nansha Qundao, lie beyond that scope.
The Philippines has illegally occupied several islands and reefs in Nansha Qundao, claimed the so-called "Kalayaan Island Group" beyond its own territory and issued a so-called "maritime chart," which includes relevant islands and reefs of China's Nansha Qundao, Guo said.
"Those actions seriously violate China's territorial sovereignty and the UN Charter and relevant international laws, and are illegal, null and void," he said.
"China firmly opposes any action of the Philippines that harms China's sovereignty and rights and interests. China will continue taking necessary measures to firmly defend its territorial sovereignty and maritime rights and interests in the South China Sea," the spokesperson said. ■

Ukraine’s New Battlefield Robot Drove, Swam and Hauled Ammo for 40 Km on Its First Mission
Ukraine has deployed a domestically produced amphibious unmanned ground vehicle on a frontline logistics mission for the first time, delivering ammunition and supplies across more than 40 kilometers of mixed land and water terrain, the Defense Ministry reported on September 29.
During the mission, Ukrainian troops used the robotic platform to move both ammunition and provisions to forward positions.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
The route stretched more than 40 kilometers and required the system to travel across both dry ground and water.
That capability addresses a persistent logistics problem on parts of the Ukrainian front, where rivers, canals, marshes and other water obstacles can break up supply routes and make conventional ground transport more difficult.
Standard unmanned ground vehicles are not always able to cross such terrain, while aerial delivery is not practical for every type of cargo or mission.
The amphibious UGV is designed to solve that problem with a single platform.
It can move across difficult terrain on land and transition directly into water without requiring a separate transport system or additional vehicle.
Before entering service, the platform spent several months undergoing modifications and testing in cooperation with Ukrainian troops, allowing developers to adapt it to battlefield requirements.
“The Brave1 defense innovation cluster provided grant support for the system, helping bring the solution to practical use,” Ukraine’s Defense Ministry said.
The September mission marked the first known operational use of the Ukrainian-made amphibious UGV for frontline logistics.
Its successful 40-kilometer run suggests Ukraine is continuing to push robotic systems beyond reconnaissance and combat roles and into one of the war’s most dangerous jobs: moving supplies to frontline positions without exposing soldiers to the same level of risk.
Earlier, Ukrainian forces converted a Soviet-era BTR-60 armored personnel carrier into a remotely controlled attack vehicle and used it to destroy fortified Russian positions during offensive operations in eastern Ukraine.

Australian household spending up 6.8 pct in Aug. year on year
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-29
21:18:37 CST
22:18:37 KST

CANBERRA, Sept. 29 (Xinhua) -- Australian household spending was 6.8 percent higher in August than a year earlier, while remaining unchanged from July, official statistics showed on Tuesday.
Household spending rose 1.1 percent in July and 0.9 percent in June, both from the previous month, according to data released by the Australian Bureau of Statistics (ABS).
Recreation and culture spending fell 1.4 percent in August after months of higher spending associated with major sporting events, ABS head of business statistics Tom Lay said in a statement.
Spending on clothing and footwear, recreational goods, food, health and furniture also declined, Lay said.
These falls were offset by a 2.3 percent increase in transport spending, driven by higher fuel spending and new vehicle sales, particularly electric vehicles, as households responded to rising fuel prices, he added.
Fuel spending rose 8.1 percent in August after the full restoration of fuel excise duty on Aug. 3, following temporary relief introduced by the federal government in April, according to the ABS.
Excluding fuel spending, total household spending would have fallen by 0.3 percent in August, the ABS said.
Experimental data showed the volume of fuel spending fell 0.5 percent in August, following a 4.6-percent decline in July, it added. ■

====================================================================================================

China Focus: China brings childcare closer to families
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-29
21:18:25 CST
22:18:25 KST

BEIJING, Sept. 29 (Xinhua) -- As demand for formal childcare continues to grow among Chinese families, young parents are looking for more affordable, convenient and trustworthy services.
China's National Health Commission (NHC) has said efforts are under way to make childcare more accessible, affordable and quality-assured. The country's 15th Five-Year Plan (2026-2030) calls for faster development of affordable childcare, including more publicly provided places and a wider range of services.
For many families, the first hurdle is price. In 2023, childcare cost an average of 1,978 yuan (about 293 U.S. dollars) per child a month nationwide, excluding meals. In first-tier cities, monthly fees topped 5,500 yuan, pricing out many families.
In Baiyin, northwest China's Gansu Province, the city's First People's Hospital runs a childcare center where full-day care costs 750 yuan a month, including three meals and two snacks a day.
Baiyin received 100 million yuan in central government funding in 2024 to support affordable childcare. First-time users can also apply for vouchers allowing their children to try a nearby center free for two weeks.
Similar efforts to lower costs are under way elsewhere. Nine provinces have introduced childcare subsidies since 2021, while 1,315 county-level regions have offered support ranging from construction and operating subsidies to family vouchers. Over the same period, average fees for full-day childcare fell 29 percent nationwide.
Broader family support is also expanding. Since 2025, families have been eligible for 3,600 yuan a year for each child until the age of three. Parents can also deduct 2,000 yuan per child each month from taxable income for children under the age of 3.
Location matters too, especially for families with very young children. Ma Liejian, vice president and member of the Secretariat of the All-China Women's Federation, has called for qualified kindergartens to extend services to younger children and for communities to offer full-day, half-day, hourly and temporary childcare close to home.
In Beijing, 562 public kindergartens have added nursery classes this year, creating more than 10,000 new places for children aged 2 to 3 and giving more families access to childcare closer to home.
Baiyin is following a similar approach. As of April 2025, the city's Baiyin District had 15 registered childcare providers, 13 of them nursery classes in kindergartens, offering a total of 1,360 places.
Changsha, capital of central China's Hunan Province, is building a "15-minute childcare service circle" using community space, kindergarten classrooms and workplace facilities.
Proximity alone, however, does not solve the problem for parents whose working hours fall outside a conventional childcare day. Yang Fan, vice dean of Renmin University of China's School of Population and Health, said more flexible services, including hourly and holiday care, could better meet the needs of parents in flexible employment or shift work.
At a technology park in Shanghai's Yangpu District, an on-site childcare center offers full-day, half-day and hourly care. One project manager said he once booked temporary care through an app just two hours before an unexpected client meeting.
In rural Pingdu in east China's Shandong Province, a childcare center converted from unused village property near agricultural greenhouses operates around the clock, giving farming families an option outside conventional daytime hours.
For parents of very young children, trust can matter just as much as price or convenience.
The same hospital-run center in Baiyin accepts babies as young as three months. Opened in 2021 with 100 places, it has more than 20 certified caregivers. It keeps health records for children and draws on hospital resources for visits by medical experts and multidisciplinary services.
Safety is also receiving greater attention at the national level. A draft law on childcare services, submitted to China's national legislature for a first reading in December 2025, includes provisions governing the licensing of childcare providers, staffing, monitoring and emergency response.
Zhang Li, deputy dean of the Law School at the China University of Political Science and Law, said the proposed licensing system would allow regulators to screen providers before they begin operating. Requirements for public information disclosure, she said, could also improve transparency, help parents better understand the services on offer and strengthen their confidence in sending children to childcare centers.
The draft law's proposal to gradually incorporate inclusive childcare services into the scope of basic public services would strengthen the public-service role of childcare and the government's responsibility for its provision, providing legal support for more stable long-term development, according to He Dan, director of the China Population and Development Research Center under the NHC.
In Baiyin, Guo Jianna and her husband are both busy with work, and all three of their children have spent time at the childcare center run by Baiyin's First People's Hospital.
Shortly before 5 p.m., Xu Xiaoqin, who oversees the center, began getting the children ready for dinner. By the time Guo arrived to pick up her 2-year-old daughter, the girl had eaten and was ready to go home.
"With professional caregivers looking after them, my family and I feel reassured," Guo said. ■

Five arrested after luggage left unattended at railway stations
See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results
Five people have been arrested after four railway stations had to be partly evacuated on Tuesday morning when luggage was left unattended.
Haarlem station and surrounding buildings were closed and cleared after two stray bags were reported at around 10.15am. Some trains were unable to stop at the station.
Luggage was also left standing in Rotterdam, Utrecht and Dordrecht. Police said there was no evidence that the incidents were linked, but they described the situation as “highly unusual”.
Three people were arrested at Haarlem station, while two others were detained at Utrecht Centraal after camera footage showed them acting suspiciously just before they dumped the bags.
In Rotterdam a pedestrian tunnel was evacuated while police checked two abandoned suitcases for possible explosives.
A woman in Rotterdam later came forward to say she had left the bags while she went into the city centre. She was not arrested.
Spokesman Jan Martijn Stout told NOS the incidents appeared to be unconnected, but the suspects were be questioned about why they had left the bags behind.
“Their role is being investigated because it was a significant disruption to public order,” he said.

Ukraine just caught a Geran-5 at 425 km/h—the jet drone that has often outrun Ukrainian interceptor drones since January

Ukraine's air defenders now have purpose-built interceptors for Russia's jet-powered attack drones—weapons whose speed and altitude make them difficult for conventional defenses to catch, Militarnyi reported. A crew from the 1020th Anti-Aircraft Missile and Artillery Regiment downed a Geran-5 over Chernihiv Oblast with a newly delivered interceptor, according to the Serhiy Prytula Foundation.
Russia's long-range drone and missile attacks have become central to its effort to wear down Ukraine's air defenses and grid before winter, and the war in the sky now turns on which side scales its answer faster.
The Chernihiv intercept
The crew, callsign Yastrub (Hawk), made its first successful engagement with the new interceptor, hitting the jet drone at 425 km/h and above 3 km, the foundation said, releasing footage of the strike. The Prytula Foundation supplied the interceptors and said it has contracted several manufacturers to counter the jet threat.
"Our task is to scale this up and strengthen units," it said.
Why it kept slipping through
Russia first used the Geran-5 in January 2026. HUR's own specifications put its warhead at 90 kg, cruise speed at 450–600 km/h, and range at 950 km, with a ceiling of 6 km. That mix of jet speed and high altitude kept it clear of machine guns, shoulder-fired missiles, and the cheap interceptors built to swat slower piston-engine Shaheds.
Ukraine's military intelligence estimates Russian plants now turn out around 3,000 jet-powered Geran-4 and Geran-5 drones a month, according to HUR. A monitoring Telegram channel, Polkovnyk HSh, reports a newer variant that steers by ground imagery instead of satellites, which would blunt jamming—though HUR has not confirmed it and lists no such system among the drone's components. Separately, Russia moved the jet engine inside the fuselage, a change aimed at more speed and range.
After Russia hits Kyiv’s Academy of Sciences with jet-powered drone, the Kremlin says Ukraine must “pay a price”
Where the fight stands
Ukraine intercepts about 55% of Russia's jet drones, against more than 90% of the older models, President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said on 26 September. Since the start of September, Russia had launched more than 2,730 jet drones, and Ukraine had downed or suppressed more than 1,500, he added. Zelenskyy also said Russia plans to spend $12 billion in 2027 on jet drones and loitering munitions alone. Ukraine already has several interceptor prototypes in combat use, and the 1020th crew's kill is one of several jet Geran intercepts Ukrainian units and drone makers have logged this month.

Yemen's health system at 'breaking point': WHO
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-29
13:16:39 UTC
22:16:39 KST

Breadcrumb
Yemen's health system at 'breaking point': World Health Organisation
The renewed fighting in Yemen is pushing the country's health system to "breaking point", the World Health Organisation said Tuesday, warning that diseases like cholera were already circulating widely.
A renewed ground campaign waged by the Iran-backed Houthis against Yemen's Saudi-backed government forces has left hundreds dead and is deepening the country's humanitarian crisis, with at least 145,000 people displaced this month alone, United Nations figures show.
And the country's health system—already weakened by over a decade of civil war—is on the brink.
"Yemen's latest escalation is pushing an already fragile health system towards breaking point," warned Annette Heinzelmann, WHO's emergency director for the eastern Mediterranean region.
Speaking to reporters in Geneva via video link from Cairo, she highlighted how insecurity, damaged infrastructure, displacement of health workers, shortages of medicines and medical supplies and limited access to swathes of Yemen's west coast were preventing many from receiving the services they need.
"Nine health facilities or assets have now been damaged, put out of service, closed or directly attacked" in the hard-hit areas of Taiz, Lahj and Hodeidah, Heinzelmann said.
At the same time, "comprehensive emergency obstetric and newborn care has been suspended in two hospitals in Marib and Ras Al-Arah because staff and operating capacity have been redirected to trauma care for the incoming wounded," she pointed out.
Even before the latest fighting, only around 60 percent of Yemen's health facilities were fully functional, Heinzelmann added.
And the country had been facing high malnutrition and outbreaks of diseases like cholera "already circulating on a large scale", she said.
Since the start of this year, Yemen has tallied nearly 8,000 suspected cholera cases, including 22 deaths, and more than 9,600 dengue cases, including 37 people who had died, according to the WHO.
And "measles is particularly concerning, with more than 22,000 suspected cases and 128 deaths reported this year", Heinzelmann said.
Now, amidst severe overcrowding in some areas, unsanitary conditions and limited healthcare access, the WHO is bracing for more and bigger disease outbreaks.
"When we see population movements, people living in really... an overcrowded setting with limited access to water and safe sanitation, these are factors which can support a wider spread of cholera," Heinzelmann said.
The UN health agency said it had delivered nearly 60 tonnes of medical supplies to 40 facilities across 10 Yemen governorates.
"But several lifesaving supply lines in WHO's Aden warehouse are already at zero stock, including trauma kits and essential medicines," Heinzelmann said, appealing for more funding.
WHO had so far secured only $2 million of the $9 million it needed for its response, she said.

Estonia blames Russia for arson at defence company supplying Ukraine
- Published
Russia was behind an arson attack on an Estonian defence company in the capital Tallinn last month, authorities say.
Prime Minister Kristen Michal said the attack on Milrem Robotics - which supplies Ukraine with unmanned military vehicles - was ordered by Russian special services, but gave no details.
Moscow has been accused of launching sabotage attacks in a number of Nato countries that have been helping Ukraine since Russia launched its full-scale invasion of its neighbour in February 2022.
Russia denies such allegations and has been quick to reject the Estonian accusation, too. But EU countries have rushed to Estonia's support, adding such attacks will not deter them from helping Ukraine.
The attack on Milrem Robotics occurred on the night of 14-15 August.
Estonian Foreign Minister Margus Tsahkna said that, based on information collected by the country's Internal Security Service, "we can conclude with certainty that the arson attack... was an act of sabotage ordered by the special services of the Russian Federation".
Security service chief Margo Palloson told broadcaster ERR that Russia was "constantly planning, looking for opportunities, trying to find people who would carry out attacks", but that last month's arson attack was its first successful attack this year.
The foreign minister said the perpetrators had been arrested and Palloson said they were Latvians who had been living in Russia and taken part in previous attacks. Three suspects were arrested in Latvia and extradited to Estonia earlier this month.
Margus Tsahkna said that "this act of sabotage is part of Russia's broader campaign across Europe, aimed at intimidating us and weakening our support for Ukraine".
French President Emmanuel Macron responded to Estonia's assessment, saying "the multiplication of these hostile acts represents a dangerous escalation by Russia, which will only lead it into a dead end".
He mentioned the incident at Leipzig airport in Germany in August, in which an explosive-laden drone was found near Ukrainian cargo planes.
"Russia needs to know that it will not overcome our unity or our determination to continue supporting Ukraine," Macron added.
An EU spokesman said the 27-member bloc would not cease supporting Ukraine.
Nato chief Mark Rutte urged European governments to stay calm and continue supporting Ukraine.
"Russia continues its reckless campaign of hostile actions against Nato allies. It is trying to weaken our resolve and stop our support for Ukraine. But Russia is failing. It is failing on the battlefield in Ukraine and it is failing to undermine our unity and support for Ukraine," Rutte said.

  - Published2 September
In August alone, Russia was either accused or suspected of the Leipzig airport attack in Germany, a major fire at a warehouse of a defence firm in Bulgaria, a large explosion at a munitions factory outside Rome in Italy, an attempted arson attack on a Ukrainian-owned drone manufacturer in Slovakia, and two suspicious fires in Poland - the latest in a country which has reported several such attacks.
Hybrid warfare or hybrid attacks are loose terms that tend to describe non-military methods, for example cyber-attacks, sabotage or misinformation, designed to exert pressure and destabilise an adversary.
Estonia's internal security service, known as Kapo, said Russia was continuing to look for further opportunities for either sabotage or other hostile acts.
"Individuals recruited for such operations may be misled or manipulated and may be given false or fabricated justifications for their actions in an effort to conceal the involvement of the Russian state," Kapo head Palloson said, external.
Russia always denies involvement in such attacks despite growing evidence to the contrary.
On Tuesday, President Vladimir Putin's spokesman said "such statements are baseless, ill-considered, have absolutely no relation to reality, and lack any form of reasoning".
"We cannot and will not take such statements seriously," Dmitry Peskov said.

Trump and Rubio question U.K. handling of possible plot against air base
Unknown

Trump and Rubio question U.K. handling of possible plot against air base after 5 men released on bail
London — President Trump and Secretary of State Marco Rubio have criticized British counterterror police's handling of a possible plot targeting a U.K. air base used by U.S. forces, with Rubio calling it a "very serious" incident and alleging that it "clearly involved" a foreign actor, and the president suggesting it "might be" Iran.
Five British nationals, all men in their mid-20s, were arrested Sunday morning in an English village near the British air force base RAF Fairford on suspicion of preparing a terrorist act. The base has been used by American bombers to launch attacks on Iran during the seven-month war.
All five men were released on bail Monday, with the head of U.K.'s Counter Terror Policing unit stressing they would remain "subject to stringent conditions on their movement and contact with others" and that they "absolutely remain under investigation as we explore multiple lines of enquiry."
The fact that they were released so quickly and not charged with any suspected crimes, and that authorities did not report finding any explosives or weapons, has fueled speculation, however, that the men may not have been planning to attack the base at all. Some local media outlets have cited U.K. security sources saying the men may just have been looking to steal fuel.
"A very serious thing?"
Reacting to the news in the Oval Office Monday, Mr. Trump said he was "surprised that they released them. I wouldn't have done that."
He said U.S. and British authorities had worked "very closely" on the matter adding: "We know everything about them. We would not have released them."
The president added that the incident "might be" linked to Iran, but when pressed for more information, he replied: "I'd rather not. I mean, I know the answer, I could be very specific, but I'd rather not say. I would not have released them."
Rubio, meanwhile, said Monday that many people following the incident were "disturbed that some of these people have been released on bail."
"What could have happened in the U.K. over the weekend is a very serious situation," Rubio told Fox News, saying it "clearly involves the hands of a foreign actor," without offering any further explanation for the assertion, which went further than British authorities have in characterizing the incident.
"There's a lot more news that'll come out on this in the days to come, but there's only so much I can say right now at this point about it, other than this is a very serious thing," he said.
"Just thieves syphoning fuel?"
Asked about the release of the men, a British legal expert told CBS News Tuesday that it would be "reasonable to release suspects on bail to see where they go and who they talk to."
"It wouldn't be the first time these tactics have been used," said the analyst, who declined to be named. "I don't think the police are being stupid or casual in this."
There has been speculation — not commented on yet directly by British police — that the five men may have been diesel fuel thieves targeting local farms, or perhaps an external fuel supply for the base, for resale. It's a crime that has proliferated in the U.K as the Iran war has driven up diesel and gasoline prices, according to a May report from intelligence agency DeterTech.
Two people described as military sources, speaking Monday to local news outlet Wiltshire 999s, were quoted as saying the suspects were "just thieves syphoning fuel," with barrels and other equipment found in their vehicles.
The British police have said no viable explosive device was discovered in the three vans driven by the men. Images of the police working around those vehicles have shown large, seemingly empty barrels that were removed from at least one truck.
Bad actors working "knowingly or unknowingly" for a foreign state?
Assistant Commissioner Laurence Taylor, head of the London Metropolitan Police's Counter Terror unit, told reporters Monday the incident "may be activity committed by proxies, or individuals either knowingly or unknowingly, working on behalf of a foreign state."
Iranian authorities have warned that any bases used to attack the country would be considered legitimate targets.
Iran has denied any link to the arrests near RAF Fairford. The Iranian Embassy in London said in a statement shared Monday on social media that the regime "categorically rejects and strongly condemns the recent unfounded and malicious speculations published by some British individuals and media outlets attempting to link Iran" to the incident.
Iran has however, like Russia, been accused of using individuals who may be unaware they are even working for a foreign state to conduct sabotage attacks across Western Europe.
The Iran-aligned group Harakat Ashab al-Yamin al-Islamia — or The Islamic Movement of the Companions of the Righteous (IMCR) — has claimed responsibility for several incidents over the past few months, including attacks on synagogues in the Netherlands and Belgium, and multiple attacks on north London's Jewish community.
A representative of the group told told CBS News in March that it would "keep threatening U.S. and Israeli interests worldwide until we've avenged every child in Gaza, Iran, Lebanon, and the resistance nations," and it urged people "to stay away from Zionist and American interests."
In July, the U.K. government said the elite Quds Force of Iran's Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps, "almost certainly directed IMCR attacks across Europe."
Experts have characterized those incidents as part of a growing pattern of Iran and Russia outsourcing sabotage by recruiting sometimes unsuspecting people, often young men, to carry out low-level attacks for financial compensation.
On Tuesday, law enforcement authorities in NATO member Estonia said they had determined an arson attack against a defense industry company in mid-August was a "deliberate and pre-planned act commissioned by Russian security services."

Middle East oil exports rise as LNG traffic through Hormuz picks up
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-29
13:13:17 UTC
22:13:17 KST

Months into the war with Iran, Gulf exporters are finding ways to keep oil and gas moving, but crossing Hormuz remains risky and some customers are still missing contracted cargoes.
Middle East crude oil exports rose in September to their highest monthly level since the Iran war began seven months ago.
Preliminary data from Kpler put regional exports at 16.3 million barrels a day. That was still around 3.2 million barrels a day below the 19.5 million recorded in February.
Saudi Arabia accounted for much of the increase, more than doubling its exports from 2.45 million barrels a day in August to around 5.4 million in September.
Flows through the Strait of Hormuz were projected to reach about 9.7 million barrels a day as Saudi Arabia sent additional crude from its Gulf terminals after attacks damaged its East-West pipeline to the Red Sea. The regional total also includes oil shipped from ports outside the strait.
Several Qatar-linked LNG tankers also crossed Hormuz this month after no visible crossings were recorded in August.
Normal exports have not resumed, however, and QatarEnergy has extended delivery suspensions for some customers in Europe and Asia.
Edison said it had received a new notice from QatarEnergy extending force majeure until early December. Another six LNG cargoes due at Italy’s Adriatic LNG terminal will not be delivered.
That brings the number of missed cargoes since April to 35. Edison has replaced 23 of them, mainly with gas from the United States.
Edison’s 25-year contract with QatarEnergy supplies 6.4 billion cubic metres of gas a year, equal to around 10% of Italy’s total consumption.
Some customers in Pakistan and Bangladesh have also been told that delivery suspensions will continue through November.
Force majeure allows a company to suspend its contractual obligations when events outside its control prevent it from fulfilling them.
The disruption began after joint US-Israeli strikes on Iran on 28 February in the opening salvo of the ongoing war, which has sharply reduced traffic through Hormuz, while both the US and Iran targeted commercial ships in and around the strait.
US President Donald Trump on Saturday rejected an Iranian proposal to reopen Hormuz and end the fighting within seven days. The proposal had been passed to Washington through Qatari mediators, who are continuing to push for talks.
Iranian Parliament Speaker Mohammad Bagher Ghalibaf said no infrastructure in the region would be safe unless Iran’s security was guaranteed, according to state broadcaster IRIB.
“In a region where Iran cannot sell oil, no one else will sell oil either,” he said.
Which LNG tankers crossed Hormuz?
Ship-tracking data from Kpler and LSEG showed GasLog Skagen off Sri Lanka on Sunday carrying LNG from Qatar’s Ras Laffan terminal. It had last been tracked inside the Gulf on 20 September.
Al Ghashamiya delivered a Qatari cargo to India last week, while Shandong Redwood carried LNG to Pakistan. Al Daayen emerged from Hormuz with a shipment bound for China.
An empty Qatar-linked tanker, Al Mafyar, was also tracked entering the strait on 22 September.
The total number of crossings is unclear because some ships turn off their tracking systems as they pass through Hormuz, making them harder to locate.
Qatar exported only 18 LNG cargoes during the first six months of the war, compared with 509 in the same period a year earlier, according to data provider ICIS.
Every LNG tanker leaving Qatar must pass through Hormuz because the country has no alternative export route.
Qatar’s Energy Minister Saad Sherida Al-Kaabi said last week that building a pipeline around the strait would make no economic sense. Such a route would require a new plant outside Qatar to turn piped gas into LNG before it could be loaded onto tankers.
Attacks on Ras Laffan damaged two LNG production units, cutting Qatar’s production capacity by around 17%. Al-Kaabi said repairs would take about three years, but the country’s 12 undamaged units could return to normal operations within weeks once ships could pass through Hormuz safely and regularly.

• Under the Memorandum of Understanding, signed on Tuesday by the culture ministers of Greece and Bulgaria, Athens will receive nearly 50 religious relics that were removed to Bulgaria during World War One.

Demand for UK mortgages slumped to a 32-month low in August as buyers were deterred by rising costs linked to the war in Iran.
Just 54,918 mortgages for new home purchases were approved in August, the Bank of England reported on Tuesday, the lowest monthly total since December 2023.
The data, which is seasonally adjusted, shows the impact of the rise in UK mortgage rates since outbreak of the war in Iran in late February began pushing up the price of oil, and sinking hopes of interest rate cuts.
Simon Gammon, managing partner at Knight Frank Finance, said: “Buying activity weakened through the summer as rising energy prices pushed up borrowing costs. Lending to homebuyers fell 15% in August compared to the same month a year earlier.”
Approvals for remortgaging dipped to about 34,000 in August, from 34,600 in July.
The Bank found that the “effective” interest rate on newly drawn mortgages increased to 4.60% in August, from 4.45% in July. Analysts warned that these rising borrowing costs were taking a toll on activity in the housing sector.
“A further fall in mortgage approvals in August points to affordability pressures continuing to weigh on housing demand, as the shocks from the Iran conflict push up both inflation and mortgage rates,” said Katie Clinton, the head of financial services advisory at KPMG UK.
“Meanwhile, the drop in remortgaging suggests refinancing demand softened, despite many borrowers reaching the end of existing fixed term rates.”
Moneyfacts, the financial product data company, reported that the average five-year fixed mortgage rate hit its highest level since October 2023, at 5.94%, on Tuesday.
Two-year fixed mortgages are the most expensive since July 2024, at 5.93%, according to Moneyfacts.
Paul Dales, the chief UK economist at Capital Economics, warned that prospect of mortgage rates staying above 4.5% for most of 2027 would have a larger influence on activity than the government’s new “Your First Home” scheme for first-time buyers, announced earlier this week.
