‘We Need to Survive’: Zelensky’s Hometown Faces Budget Cuts After Factory Shutdowns
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-29
12:44:29 UTC
21:44:29 KST

When a steel plant stops in Kryvyi Rih, the losses reach far beyond its factory gates. Fewer shifts mean less work for contractors, lower tax receipts for the city and less money for the services residents rely on.
That chain of losses is now forcing the hometown of President Volodymyr Zelensky to cut its municipal budget and postpone some development projects, according to Oleksandr Vilkul, head of Kryvyi Rih’s defense council.
JOIN US ON TELEGRAM
Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official.
However, he said the city would prioritize keeping schools, kindergartens, hospitals, water supplies, and heating systems running.
Vilkul said ArcelorMittal Kryvyi Rih, the Inhulets and Southern mining and processing plants, and the Kryvyi Rih Iron Ore Plant were all idle. Other major businesses were producing at no more than a quarter of their prewar levels leaving many companies that supply or service them without work.
He blamed Russian strikes and difficulties shipping products through ports. The operating status of the other plants was not independently verified.
ArcelorMittal confirmed last week that it could not safely restart its Kryvyi Rih operations. The company said its facilities had been hit four times in five weeks, most recently on Sept. 21.
Five employees were killed and 17 injured in those attacks, with production facilities suffering extensive damages. ArcelorMittal said it would focus on preserving the site so a future restart would remain possible.
Estonia Slams Russian ‘Sabotage’ After Arson Attack on Defense Company
For the city, the immediate concern is both employment and the budget. Vilkul said industrial taxes pay for public-sector wages, infrastructure maintenance, pipe and boiler-house repairs, and social services. He described next year’s budget outlook as poor, though he did not give a figure for the planned cuts or identify which projects would be delayed.
“But this isn’t about development. It’s about survival. Right now, we have to survive,” he said.
Vilkul said municipal utilities had been asked to help displaced industrial workers find jobs. The city’s water and heating companies currently have around 1,000 vacancies between them.

Activist Sarah Cotte vows to support Palestinian resistance
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-29
12:43:15 UTC
21:43:15 KST

Breadcrumb
Activist Sarah Cotte: I will not back down from supporting Palestinian resistance
Sarah Cotte has defied all attempts to deter her from supporting the Palestinian people's right to armed resistance, despite facing nearly three years of legal proceedings that ended with two trials over the same charge: expressing support for Hamas.
Friday, 18 September, marked the end of an ordeal experienced by the young activist, who supports the Palestinian people and opposes Israel and the Zionist movement.
The ordeal began with a campaign led by UK Lawyers for Israel, prompting British police and prosecutors to refer Cotte to the Central Criminal Court, which hears only major criminal cases.
After two trials, jurors acquitted Sarah Cotte , 22, of a charge that could have resulted in a 14-year prison sentence had she been convicted.
In an interview with The New Arab following her acquittal, Cotte said she did not feel a moment of regret despite the suffering she endured.
"I think it was absolutely worth the suffering that I experienced in the context of this case," she said.
She attributed this to being able to "affirm the political point, which is the right to armed resistance and armed struggle".
Despite attempts to portray Palestinian armed resistance negatively throughout the two trials, Cotte insisted that this was "a purely legal issue that should be supported, because oppressed peoples have this right".
A message to Zionists
Cotte criticised what she described as "the self-censorship that we impose on ourselves", as liberals do, in her view, when they "tend to impose censorship on others who express support for armed struggle, and on oppressed peoples so that they are not just victims but freedom fighters".
In this context, the young activist said the prosecution wanted to contribute to a campaign to criminalise those who support fighting for freedom.
She argued it was therefore extremely determined to secure a conviction and to show the rest of the British state, as well as Zionists and others, that it was dealing with pro-Palestine protesters with extreme strictness and severity.
Despite her position in the British state, Cotte praised the judiciary because it still relies on juries in criminal cases, and they had acquitted her twice.
The key point, for her, is that "the jury system works in a way that means a group of your peers, people like you, judge you".
"Most people in this country are horrified by what is happening in Palestine at the hands of the Israeli state, and they feel ashamed of the fact that Britain is complicit in it," she added.
However, she did not rely on this alone during her two trials.
Based on her experience, what also makes a real impression on the public and jurors is "being able to explain your political positions clearly using your own terms and your own language".
One of the lessons Cotte learned from her prosecution was that "regardless of how difficult what the state is trying to do is, when we fight, when we struggle, when we do everything we can, and use politics and our tactics as activists, we can win, and we are winning, and this is not limited to my case alone".
The enemy can be defeated
Another lesson is that, in cases such as defending the right to struggle for freedom, she believes there are no big or small victories.
She said her victory "seems like a small victory", but pointed out that she is one activist among similar people in Britain who are being criminalised.
She considered these victories "very important for giving the movement new energy and raising morale, and showing that the enemy is not too powerful to be defeated and that the enemy cannot crush us and silence us, but that we are capable of responding and confronting it".
Therefore, she explained that "the way I dealt with my case was not centred on me personally so that I could survive but was about being able to share my context, in which I carry out my political activism, and use this case as a platform to speak to people about what I believe in".
Cotte, who is of Ethiopian origin, arrived from France, where she holds citizenship, to Britain to study political economy and philosophy several years ago.
She became political and student activist at the School of Oriental and African Studies (SOAS), University of London, and known, along with many of her colleagues and peers at other universities, for defending the rights of peoples, including the Palestinian people, to fight colonialism, Zionism and occupation.
This brought her into conflict with the authorities and the Israeli lobby in Britain.
Despite what she has been through, she said she would "stay in Britain for a little longer" and does not intend to return to France now.
"I know that if I went back to my country, France, things would be similar, if not worse," she remarked.
She believes there is still an opportunity to continue what she describes as the struggle, saying, "It is important for me to continue fighting against the same people and the same state that I have been fighting."
She will therefore continue "confronting repression and defending, or helping to defend, some of our comrades who are being criminalised" because they want to support the Palestinian people's struggle.
A step to "restore credibility"
Cotte does not expect protests against what she, and many others in Britain, see as British complicity in Israeli crimes to decrease, even after the government of Andy Burnham announced sanctions, which are still being prepared, on "illegal" settlements in Palestine.
She described the language used by the government as "still clearly framed in the context of 'we are committed to Israel's security' and 'we are committed to fighting Israel's enemies who pose an existential threat to it, and this includes Iran, Hezbollah and armed resistance".
While she said she believed the expected sanctions "will, to some extent, have a tangible impact on the illegal settlements", she described them as "part of Britain's broader objective of saving the two-state solution, saving Israel from itself, and trying to save Israel's international reputation".
Regarding the two-state solution, which Britain says it is working to achieve to resolve the conflict between Palestinians and Israel, Cotte described it as "an illusion and a myth that Britain seeks to keep alive".
"We know that Israel will never allow a Palestinian state to be established, and it will always pose a threat to the Palestinian people," she added.
The possible and sustainable solution, which she argues should be fought for, is "one state; one secular, democratic Palestinian state with the right of return" for Palestinians displaced by Israel since its establishment on Palestinian land in 1948.
On domestic politics in Britain, Cotte said the move, namely the announcement of plans to impose sanctions on settlements, also seeks to "restore some credibility to the Labour Party, because this move is actually very electorally popular for the Burnham government".
Since joining SOAS, Cotte has been active in the Revolutionary Communist Group, which she sees as a useful framework for defending those criminalised for defending the rights of the Palestinian people.
In light of her experience, she advised activists, particularly young people, to join political organisations "after establishing their political positions" and not to work alone because she believes that "we can only work collectively".
"The only reason the campaign to defend me worked so well was that it was within a political organisation," referring to the communist group," she said.
She added that "any organisation is a good place to start" active political work and "it enables us to take a very disciplined approach to organising our campaign".
She warned that this approach "means that when the police were harassing us at protests, for example, everyone knew exactly what to do, what to say, what not to say, how to protect each other, and how to respond" to any situation.
Cotte's other advice to young people is: "Get out into the streets. A lot of things happen there; talk to people and meet them."

'I was lured into a trap': Evan Gershkovich on moment that led to 16 months in Russian jail
United Kingdom
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-29
13:43:04 BST
21:43:04 KST

'I was lured into a trap': Evan Gershkovich on moment that led to 16 months in Russian jail
- Published
US journalist Evan Gershkovich has said that he knew he was being set up by Russia when he was arrested by FSB agents and accused of being a spy.
In an interview with Radio 4's Today programme, Gershkovich spoke about the moment he realised he had been "lured into a trap" when masked men surrounded him at a restaurant in 2023, and detained him.
"I'm not interrogated, I'm not tortured… I'm accused of espionage," he said, describing a sense of relief: "They've set me up and fabricated this case so that I can be a valuable hostage - a pawn in a greater game".
Gershkovich, now 34, was sentenced to 16 years in prison, but freed 16 months later as part of a high-profile prisoner swap deal.
Gershkovich had been living in Russia since 2017, and was the Wall Street Journal's foreign correspondent in Moscow when he was arrested - he is now based in Berlin, Germany. He and his employer have always maintained that the charges were false.
On the day he was arrested, Gershkovich was in Yekaterinburg - about 1,600km (1,000 miles) east of Moscow - meeting someone who he thought was a source for a story.
They were sitting in a half-empty dining hall "and a group of about half-dozen masked men marched in and said 'I think we booked that table'." An odd phrase, Gershkovich said, but on reflection it is clever because it "freezes you in place".
The two men stood up and Gershkovich was told he was under arrest by the notorious and powerful FSB, Russia's domestic security service.
"It's at that moment that you realise it's something really serious… When it's the FSB, you know it's been planned."
What about the man he'd been meeting? Gershkovich saw him disappear into the crowd.
Not long after his arrest, the journalist said he realised that the fact he was not being interrogated or tortured - common tactics used by Russia's security service on spies - likely meant that he was being treated more like a commodity, not a true enemy of the state.
"I have this odd moment - a sense of relief flooding over me," he said. "I realised they're not treating me like a real spy. They've set me up and fabricated this case so that I can be a valuable hostage, a pawn in a greater game. That means it will take a while, but I won't be here for 12-20 years."
That realisation helped him stay "stable and disciplined in prison", but also gave him a unique way of predicting what might happen next - and one guess was a prisoner swap.
"I assumed that it would be really loud, that it would cause a global uproar. I mean, it's a foreign correspondent for the Wall Street Journal," he said - and he was right.
Media organisations around the world reported on the case, his face was on a billboard in Times Square and then-US President Joe Biden said he had "no higher priority" than bringing Gershkovich home.
The journalist believed that this was all part of Moscow's plan - to have a high-profile prisoner that it could swap for one of its own - and that was Vadim Krasikov, an assassin who was serving a life sentence in Germany.
"They [Moscow] got away with it in the sense that there were no sanctions imposed. And so they played it really smart, if you think about it cynically."
Gershkovich was held in Moscow's infamous Lefortovo jail, which has held some of the country's most high-profile inmates over the years, including political prisoners and dissidents. During the Great Terror of Joseph Stalin in the 1930s, torture and execution were commonplace.
He described it as a "really isolating experience", in a tiny space.
"That wears on you psychologically," Gershkovich said, but added that he was treated ok: "I was allowed to sleep, the food was fine."
Pictures of Gershkovich smiling at cameras during his court appearances in Moscow were broadcast around the world - and that was deliberate, he said - a way of showing that he was alright.
"I wanted to show people this kind of defiance... We know that this is a fabricated case, and so if this is a game of theatre, let's not let [Moscow] have it play out the way they want it to."
But he stressed that not everyone's time in a Russian prison is like his: "Some people... get tortured. They get broken as human beings, deprived of food, of hot water for showers, told that they're never going to see their families again. I was treated completely differently."
Gershkovich compared his experience to the case of Ukrainian journalist Viktoriia Roshchyna, who died while in Russian captivity in 2024, aged 27. Months later, when her body was finally returned, it reportedly showed signs of torture and her organs had been removed.
Gershkovich knew there was a prisoner swap planned three weeks before it happened - an "excruciating" time, he said, "because now every day is painfully long".
When it finally did happen, on 1 August 2024, it was a moment of "pure joy". But then "the joy fades, the adrenaline subsides, and you're faced with the reality of having to return to normal life again."
Gershkovich said this period was difficult and sometimes overwhelming. He wasn't sleeping, suffered panic attacks in large crowds and had a short temper because he was trying to hold in his emotions.
He has seen therapists who specialise in post-traumatic stress disorder (PTSD), and said writing a book on his ordeal also helped.
And what about a return to Russia? Gershkovich has a deep history with the country - his parents moved to the US from the Soviet Union in the 1970s. He grew up in a Russian-speaking home, with a Russian name, moved there when he was 25 and made many friends, including his Russian girlfriend.
"I would hope to get back one day, but I guess we'll have to see what comes after [Russian President Vladimir] Putin. And it's not completely clear that the next government will be any better."

Battery gold rush: How energy is creating a new market in Italy
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-29
12:42:53 UTC
21:42:53 KST

From paper projects to batteries now online: the energy market is changing and the value of storage is soaring worldwide
Household electricity bills remain high, yet on the wholesale market some operators can even be paid to consume energy. This is one of the paradoxes created by the growth of renewables: sun and wind produce when they can, not when the grid needs them, and in moments of oversupply prices can even turn negative.
This is why huge batteries, BESS (Battery Energy Storage Systems) are needed, able to absorb surplus energy and feed it back into the grid later. Their role is so strategic that it has triggered a genuine gold rush, with Italy in a leading position.
Batteries, 300 GW of connection requests in Italy
By the end of 2025, connection requests for high- and extra-high-voltage storage systems submitted to Terna had reached 300 GW. Yet only 56 GW had received the go-ahead, and just 6.8 GW were ready to start construction.
Storage systems already installed had 7.4 GW of power and 17.9 GWh of capacity. Terna estimates that by 2030 Italy will need around 72 GWh, a figure expected to rise further in scenarios for 2040.
The 300 GW requested therefore are not only projects about to enter into operation: they are also a huge advance booking on the future electricity system.
In her State of the Union address on 16 September, Ursula von der Leyen recalled that in 2025 Europe installed more than 80 GW of new renewable capacity, while a capacity six times greater is still waiting to be connected to the grid. "We must invest faster… speed up grid connections… develop storage", she said.
Germany’s battery rush is even bigger
Germany shows the same dynamic in an even more extreme form. In 2025 alone, grid operators received 18,158 applications for large storage systems, amounting to 573.5 GW.
The connection offers issued covered 54.2 GW; plants actually in operation at medium voltage and above amounted to 3.6 GW.
The Bundesnetzagentur also warns that some of the applications are duplicates: the same developer can submit the same project at several points on the grid and only later decide where to build.
In practice, before the batteries themselves are bought, what is being traded are options.
When the banks arrive: storage turns into an asset class
The story of German company Kyon Energy shows how quickly financing in the sector has changed. In January 2024 TotalEnergies bought it from its three founders, paying 90 million euros up front plus additional earn-outs. Kyon had already developed 770 MW and had a firm pipeline of another 2 GW.
At the time, co-founder Philipp Merk explained that financing large batteries was still difficult: Kyon would initially build with its own capital and seek bank refinancing only once the system was in operation.
Two years on, the picture looks different. In 2026 TotalEnergies sold Allianz Global Investors a 50% stake in eleven Kyon projects, totalling 789 MW and 1,628 MWh; in July a project financing worth around 440 million euros, underwritten by ten financial institutions, was announced.
Structured tolling agreements, effectively leasing out battery capacity, secure a share of contracted revenues and make cash flows more predictable.
The real value can emerge before construction
This is the mechanism also described by Stefano Endrizzi, a partner at MergersCorp, who works on extraordinary finance deals, including in the renewable energy sector.
"How many players have the financial strength to build? Very few, perhaps one in fifty", he notes. Many, however, can secure a plot of land and develop the project "entirely on paper". Value is therefore created even before construction begins.
Large investment funds and energy, engineering and construction companies, EPC contractors, prefer to acquire authorised projects and move straight into the development phase: a practical way of buying time without getting lost in the labyrinth of permitting and bureaucracy.
Italy’s first battery auction attracts a wave of bids
Competition is already visible in Italy. At the first MACSE auction in September 2025, Terna awarded 10 GWh of capacity, all in lithium-ion batteries.
Bids were more than four times higher than the volume on offer and the weighted average price fell to 12,959 euros/MWh per year, compared with a reserve premium of 37,000 euros, a drop of around 65%.
Capital is meanwhile pouring in. In 2025 Modo Energy counted 82 BESS deals in Europe, up from 25 a year earlier, with a disclosed value of 8.6 billion euros. Reported debt rose from 1.4 to 6.1 billion; project finance accounts for half of all transactions.
The clampdown on "phantom projects"
The European Commission has now explicitly acknowledged the problem. In its grid connection guidelines of December 2025 it identifies speculative applications and projects that fail to progress as one of the causes of long queues.
It cites hoarding of grid capacity, multiple applications for the same project and even cases where a connection is blocked with the aim of later selling on the rights.
Among the countermeasures, it proposes criteria linked to project maturity, deadlines, penalties and financial deposits that can be forfeited if the investment does not go ahead.
Italy, new rules to tackle grid saturation
Italy has already begun to adjust course. The Bollette decree of February 2026 introduced a reform to tackle the "virtual saturation" of the grid: capacity will have to be definitively allocated to authorised projects, and some connections obtained by still-immature schemes may lapse.
The implementing decree from MASE was signed on 8 September; the final regulatory step from ARERA is still pending.
The paradox is that the clampdown comes after years in which Brussels and national governments have sought to speed up exactly those procedures which now also need to become more selective.
The RED III directive set shorter deadlines for many permits and provided fast-track lanes for renewables and storage attached to generating plants; in Italy the procedures for stand-alone BESS have also been simplified over time.
Energy projects: simplifying does not mean making everything simple
"It is an enormous amount of work", says Endrizzi. "Even for just 4 or 5 megawatts we are talking about thousands of documents."
Yet the outlay needed to develop a project remains only a fraction of what is required to build the plant itself, while an authorised project can acquire its own value and be sold on.
And here a second paradox emerges. To clear the queues, authorities can demand more substantial financial guarantees and evidence of maturity. But that makes it harder for small developers to hold a position for years, while utilities, funds and large groups have the capital needed.
The fight against speculation can therefore also foster market concentration.
The land rush for renewables, BESS and data centres
The financial race ultimately comes back down to earth. Solar, agrivoltaic, wind power and BESS are all competing for sites and grid connections, while data centres are also rapidly increasing potential demand on the system.
Italy’s CREA estimates the average value of agricultural land in 2024 at around 22,400 euros per hectare and highlights the impact of renewable installations on prices; in some cases it documents photovoltaic offers of about 60,000 euros per hectare.
According to Endrizzi’s experience, farmland in northern Italy that might be worth 15,000-25,000 euros per hectare can, once it becomes attractive for energy development, reach asking prices of around 90,000-100,000.
In the new energy market, the value of land no longer depends solely on what can be grown on it. It also depends on how much energy can flow past it and on the possibility of securing today a foothold in tomorrow’s electricity system.
The language of storage: key definitions
GW (gigawatt) - Measures power, namely how quickly a battery can absorb or release energy.
GWh (gigawatt-hour) - Measures capacity, namely how much energy a battery can store. A system rated at 1 GW that can deliver that power for four hours has a capacity of 4 GWh.
Arbitrage - The mechanism by which you charge a battery when electricity is cheap, or when the price turns negative, and then sell the energy when the price rises.
Merchant - Refers to revenues that are directly exposed to movements in the power market, without a fixed remuneration guaranteed by contract.
Tolling - An operator pays a fee to use battery capacity under contract. The owner thus secures a more predictable revenue component.
Pumped-storage hydropower - A form of storage that uses surplus electricity to pump water uphill from a lower to an upper reservoir. The water can then fall back through the turbines and generate new energy.

Formosa Plastics, Taiwan Pulp plan US chip chemical venture
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-29
12:42:22 UTC
21:42:22 KST

TAIPEI (Taiwan News) — Formosa Plastics Corp. and Taiwan Pulp & Paper Corp. plan to establish a US joint venture producing electronic-grade hydrochloric acid, CTEE reported Tuesday.
The venture, FTA Tech LLC, will build a facility at Formosa Plastics’ existing complex in Texas. Food-grade hydrochloric acid produced there will be further purified for semiconductor manufacturing.
The project aims to establish a local supply chain as semiconductor manufacturers expand production in the US. Formosa Plastics estimated that US demand for electronic-grade hydrochloric acid would grow at a compound annual rate of about 9.5% from 2026 through 2035.
Formosa Plastics and its US subsidiary will each own 25% of the venture, while Taiwan Pulp & Paper will hold the remaining 50%. FTA Tech will have capital of US$38.1 million, while total investment is estimated at US$129 million (NT$4.1 billion). Production is scheduled to begin in December 2028.
Hydrochloric acid is one of several high-purity chemicals used in semiconductor manufacturing, along with hydrofluoric acid, sulfuric acid and hydrogen peroxide. It is used to clean and etch wafers during production, according to Data Bridge.
Formosa Plastics has been expanding its semiconductor materials business through partnerships with Taiwanese specialty chemical companies. It has also teamed up with Chung Hwa Chemical Industrial Works to develop electronic-grade sulfuric acid in Taiwan.

Isamaa head: The state budget one of continued chaos
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-29
12:42:00 UTC
21:42:00 KST

Isamaa head: The state budget one of continued chaos
Opposition Isamaa leader Urmas Reinsalu called the coalition's 2027 budget a continuation of chaos. He said the next government must revise is to cut public sector spending.
"This is a manipulation carried out on paper to create the impression that the state's finances are improving. They are actually getting worse. The documents build in delayed spending and unrealistic revenue expectations," Reinsalu said in a speech after the budget was submitted.
He argued that the government was merely postponing spending and would leave a mess behind for the elections.
"The Reform Party boasts that it has now reduced debt. In reality, the debt burden is growing at an accelerating pace: general government debt is set to rise by 1.9 percent of GDP in 2026, 2.5 percent in 2027 and 4 percent in 2028. Interest costs alone will climb from €272 million in 2026 to €635 million by 2030."
The Isamaa leader called several items included in or omitted from the state budget and the state budget strategy bluffs on paper.
As examples, he cited what he described as an inflated estimate of the maximum potential revenue from renting out prison space and a sharp projected increase in corporate income tax revenue. Meanwhile, he said, the €150 million cost of an explosives plant had been excluded from the budget strategy's balance calculations.
"The shifting of spending between years is a sleight of hand in its own right. Through a supplementary budget for 2026, the government wants to bring forward some spending from 2027 and change the rules for accounting for the purchase of stockpiles. The aim of all this is to make the 2027 budget look healthier."
Reinsalu also claimed that the policy of raising taxes would continue, with increases in fuel and energy excise duties planned in the budget. He objected to what he called the budget's continuing lack of transparency.
"This is illustrated by the billions in previously unspent budget funds and a quarter of a billion euros sitting in SmartCap's account."
The Isamaa leader said a new, expenditure-based budget framework law should be adopted (after Riigikogu elections — ed.) in spring 2027, along with a supplementary budget that cuts spending and reduces government operating costs.
"We must make a real contribution to improving the finances of families with children and reduce the burden of indirect taxes. We must give economic growth a genuine boost."
Isamaa is leading all polls ahead of the 2027 Riigikogu elections.
--
Editor: Urmet Kook, Marcus Turovski

TAIEX retreats as investors rotate between sectors
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-29
12:41:55 UTC
21:41:55 KST

TAIPEI (Taiwan News) — Taiwan’s benchmark stock index fell on Tuesday as investors became more cautious following strong gains last week.
The Taiwan Stock Exchange Capitalization Weighted Index (TAIEX) fell 392.64 points, or 0.82%, to close at 47,631.96. Trading volume remained relatively low at NT$785 billion, according to Taiwan Index Plus and CTEE.
Declines in the market’s largest-cap stocks weighed on the index. TSMC closed unchanged at NT$2,475.
MediaTek lost 7.1% to NT$4,910. Foxconn ended flat at NT$250.5, Delta Electronics fell 3.93% to NT$1,835, and ASE declined 1.72% to NT$687, according to Anue.
High-priced stocks recorded notable declines. Of the 15 stocks trading above NT$3,000 per share, 14 closed lower, with seven falling more than 3%.
Petrochemical stocks were among the stronger-performing sectors, supported by a structural supply shortage in global refining markets and higher oil prices. Formosa Petrochemical gained 8.14%, while Nan Ya Plastics rose 3.78%. Formosa Plastics and Formosa Chemicals and Fiber closed higher.
Power semiconductor stocks also stood out against the broader market after reports that product prices could rise. Phoenix Silicon International and Episil-Precision gained more than 7%, while Mosel Vitelic and Vanguard International Semiconductor rose more than 3%.
Power semiconductors are key components in power conversion, handling functions such as voltage conversion while also protecting circuits against over-voltage. Major international suppliers, including Onsemi and Renesas Electronics, have announced plans to raise prices, benefiting Taiwanese suppliers, according to CTEE, Business Weekly, and MoneyDJ.
Several optoelectronics stocks recorded strong gains. Jochu Technology, Daxin Materials, Aiptek International, Onano Industrial, and General Interface Solution all reached the daily limit. The optoelectronics industry covers a wide range of products that use light and electronic technologies for applications such as light-based data transmission, sensing, and converting light into electrical signals, according to Money Weekly.
In contrast, the custom chip sector, which had performed strongly in recent weeks, saw profit-taking. In addition to MediaTek, Global Unichip fell 7.04%, while Alchip Technologies declined 2.25%.
Analysts said investors are watching oil prices and interest rates, two key international factors. Still, 45 stocks hit the daily limit-up while only two hit the lower limit, suggesting that investors were shifting between sectors rather than broadly reducing their market exposure, according to CTEE.
Analysts also noted that stock purchases made with borrowed funds have grown too quickly in recent weeks, raising the risk of greater short-term volatility. They expect the market to remain volatile at high levels in the near term.
For investment strategies, analysts recommended watching liquid large- and mid-cap AI stocks, as well as thematic stocks backed by earnings. For longer-term sectors, they said investors could continue to monitor TSMC and its advanced packaging and testing supply chain, along with semiconductor equipment, printed circuit boards, optical communications, thermal management, and other core AI-related supply chains.
This information is not intended as personalized financial advice. Investors are encouraged to conduct their own research and analysis before making investment decisions.

Taiwan institute develops AI-powered drone inspection system
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-29
12:41:55 UTC
21:41:55 KST

TAIPEI (Taiwan News) — The Institute for Information Industry has integrated three technologies to improve inspections by drones and other unmanned vehicles, according to a recent press release.
Inspecting large areas such as ports, marine conservation zones and energy facilities can be time-consuming, while remote locations may lack adequate camera and network coverage. The system combines AI-assisted electronic fencing, digital twin technology and resilient networking.
For electronic fencing, coastal cameras use AI to detect and track vessels entering restricted waters, analyze their routes and alert authorities. The system also displays the vessels’ locations and related information on a digital twin platform.
The digital twin synchronizes information about operating areas, vehicles, equipment and network performance. It simulates changing mission requirements and network conditions to help operators adjust communications resources.
For remote connectivity, a resilient network integrates satellite, 5G, Wi-Fi and Ethernet connections. Drone relays and portable private networks can extend coverage to areas that ground equipment cannot reach and maintain communications if one connection fails.
The institute said the system could establish communications within two hours after disasters block roads, compared with more than eight hours for conventional equipment. Related drone systems have been used for inspections, supply deliveries, warehouse inventory, firefighting and biological pest control. The technologies could also support marine conservation, port inspections and energy facilities.

MAC warns China weaponizing Taiwan narratives in cognitive warfare
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-29
12:41:44 UTC
21:41:44 KST

TAIPEI (Taiwan News) — China is weaponizing narratives about Taiwan as part of its cognitive warfare campaign, Mainland Affairs Council Deputy Minister Shen Yu-chung (沈有忠) warned Tuesday.
Speaking at a Chung-Hua Institution for Economic Research forum, Shen said Beijing had used two Trump-Xi summits to promote a framework of “constructive strategic stability” and sought to make Taiwan a foundation of stable US-China relations, Liberty Times reported.
Beijing has also pressed Washington to accept its narrative, but the US has not done so, he said.
Shen said China’s efforts could influence public perceptions of Taiwan’s cross-strait and foreign policies. Beijing’s multifaceted pressure campaign against Taiwan posed the greatest risk to stability in the Taiwan Strait and the wider region, he said.
Although US-China relations and Taiwan-US relations are connected, one cannot be traded for the other, Shen said. Taiwan-US cooperation has grown increasingly close in recent years, with communication remaining smooth.
This showed that continued US dialogue with China had not adversely affected Taiwan-US relations and that cooperation between Taipei and Washington had continued to deepen, he said.
Shen reiterated that the government remained committed to healthy and orderly cross-strait exchanges. He also called on Beijing to engage in dialogue with Taiwan’s democratically elected government on the basis of equality and dignity and without preconditions.

Inflation rises to 4.69 per cent as high fuel prices take their toll
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-29
12:41:23 UTC
21:41:23 KST

Inflation, the figure that reflects the general rise in price levels, has risen further to 4.69 per cent. This rise is largely due to high energy and fuel prices linked to the ongoing war in the Middle East.
Inflation rises to 4.69 per cent as high fuel prices take their toll
From 1.1 per cent in January, via 3.4 per cent in June, to 4.69 per cent in September: inflation continues to rise sharply. The main culprit is the high cost of energy. Energy inflation stood at no less than 24.37 per cent in September (compared with 10.59 per cent in July).
The main factor here is natural gas, the price of which has risen by more than a third year-on-year. The price of heating oil is a fifth higher than a year ago. Compared with a month ago, natural gas has become 6.9 per cent more expensive and electricity 4.2 per cent.
Motor fuels have also become a third more expensive compared with September last year. Diesel has been hit hardest: that fuel now costs 44.1 per cent more than a year ago. For petrol, the increase is 29.1 per cent, and for LPG, 21.2 per cent.
Food slightly cheaper
High energy costs lead to high production costs and may therefore have an impact on food prices in the long term, but this is not yet reflected in the figures. What’s more, food inflation actually fell very slightly in September.
The following items have become cheaper compared to last year: fresh berries, as well as other fruit and vegetables, plant-based milk and cereals. The price of video and audio equipment (televisions, speakers, etc.), power banks and stationery have also fallen.
Loss of purchasing power
Stijn Baert, professor of economics at Ghent University and member of the index committee, warns against a loss in spending power. The index committee includes representatives from both sides of industry. It is where wages and working conditions are discussed as well as the automatic indexation or top-up of Belgian wages and benefits to keep them in line with inflation. Baert argues that whilst wages and benefits are adjusted for inflation, they are not adjusted for the full rise in the cost of living.
“Our wages follow the health index, which excludes unhealthy products such as alcohol, tobacco, petrol and diesel. Health index inflation stands at ‘only’ 4 per cent.”
“If this continues, wages will be adjusted by less than the increase in the cost of living for an average family. So, we will actually lose spending power.”

Russian troops allegedly using civilians as 'human shields' to flee via Kupiansk pipeline, Khartiia Corps says
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-29
12:41:13 UTC
21:41:13 KST

Russian troops using civilians as 'human shields' to flee via Kupiansk pipeline, Khartiia Corps claims
Drone footage allegedly shows Russian troops using civilians, including children and elderly people, as human shields to flee via a gas pipeline in northeastern Kharkiv Oblast amid the Ukrainian push in the Kupiansk sector, Khartiia Corps said on Sept. 29.
Children, elderly people, and a person on crutches walked alongside draft-age men who were likely Russian soldiers wearing civilian clothes, according to Khartiia Corps' drone footage. The group was allegedly led from Kupiansk to the Ostrogozhsk-Shebelinka Gas Pipeline through the contested village of Holubivka near Kupiansk, the unit added.
Khartiia Corps said the group of civilians would have to walk more than 10 kilometers (about six miles) through the pipeline before exiting into a forest, where they would likely be transported to Russian-occupied territory.
The Kyiv Independent could not independently verify the claim.
"The occupiers use this gas pipeline to secretly smuggle their assault troops into (Kupiansk)," Khartiia Corps, part of the National Guard, said in its statement on Facebook.
"Now they are using that same pipeline to abduct civilians."
Khartiia Corps said Ukrainian forces did not launch an attack because doing so would have put civilians at risk.
Throughout the full-scale war, the Russian military has regularly breached international warfare conventions, especially through its indiscriminate attacks on civilian areas and the alleged abduction of civilians from occupied territories.
The Russian military has previously been accused of using civilians as "human shields" in hot spots of the war. In November 2025, the Donetsk Oblast Prosecutors' Office said a Russian commander ordered his soldiers who had entered Pokrovsk to use civilians as "human shields" via radio communications.
There are "several layers" to the Russian tactic, including using civilians as cover while moving through open areas without drone protection, abducting children and elderly people, and potentially using the tactic for propaganda purposes, according to a senior officer at the Corps' headquarters. Khartiia Corps said in its statement that Russian troops were filming the group as it walked.
The source said that while the illegal tactic does not affect the broader picture of the Ukrainian defense in the area, "the overall effect of using pipelines for logistics and human travel is big."
"Russia has been effectively using pipelines in Avdiivka, Sumy, and now in Kupiansk," the source told the Kyiv Independent.
"This literally allows them to teleport close to the front lines)."
Using civilians as cover in combat zones is a serious violation of international humanitarian law (IHL), while the forcible transfer of civilians is also prohibited under the Geneva Conventions. The laws of war also require combatants to distinguish themselves from the civilian population.
Foreign Minister Andrii Sybiha reacted to the video released by Khartiia Corps, calling for what he described as "grave violations of international humanitarian law" to be properly documented and investigated and for those responsible to be held accountable.
"Russia is once again using Ukrainian civilians as instruments of war," Sybiha said in an X post on Sept. 28.
"Civilians cannot be used as instruments of war or forcibly transferred."

Retired Hong Kong woman loses HK$2.9 million in online romance, fake app scam

A retired woman in Hong Kong lost nearly HK$2.9 million (US$369,670) in a romance scam after a fraudster posing as a power company employee won her trust and lured her into a bogus investment scheme.
Police said the case was among at least 18 online romance scams reported in the past week, with total losses nearing HK$7.8 million, according to the force’s CyberDefender social media page.
The 71-year-old retiree met a man on Facebook who claimed to work for a power company.
The pair gradually developed an online romantic relationship, despite never meeting in person.

Nations League: Ukraine–Northern Ireland match preview
Ukraine
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-29

Urial sheep: a vital link in mountain ecosystems

Urial sheep: a vital link in mountain ecosystems
The Shiraz urial sheep is a hybrid of the Armenian mouflon and the Laristan mouflon, inhabiting the highlands and rocky areas of southern Fars Province, particularly Bamu National Park northeast of Shiraz.
Wild sheep are among the key herbivorous mammal species and play a vital structural role in maintaining ecological balance and the long-term stability of mountainous and foothill habitats. A decline or disappearance of these species can disrupt food chains and lead to significant changes in the vegetation cover of their habitats.
Wild sheep also serve as an important link in the transfer of energy from primary producers, such as plants, to secondary consumers, including carnivores. They constitute a major prey base for endangered and threatened species such as the Persian leopard, Asiatic cheetah, wolf, and caracal, making their conservation an important component of maintaining healthy and functioning mountain ecosystems.

The draft budget indicates that Ukraine's own revenues total just 3.2 trillion hryvnias ($71.7 billion). Factoring in revenues from government bond sales, privatization, and grants, this figure reaches 3.7 trillion hryvnias ($82.9 billion). Meanwhile, total expenditures, including public debt service and domestic lending, are projected at 8 trillion hryvnias ($179 billion). With 2027 GDP estimated at 11.144 trillion hryvnias (around $255 billion), the actual deficit that Kiev expects to cover through Western financial aid stands at roughly $96 billion, or 37% of GDP.
The deficit is poised to expand even without accounting for a potential overestimation of next year's GDP growth. In 2026, Ukraine has already amended its budget twice to increase spending. Furthermore, forecasts suggest the country could lose up to 6% of its GDP due to ongoing combat operations. Adjusted for these losses, the real budget deficit could spiral to 40% of GDP.

Supreme Court: Publishing expunged conviction details partly unconstitutional
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-29
12:39:00 UTC
21:39:00 KST

Supreme Court: Publishing expunged conviction details partly unconstitutional
Estonia's Supreme Court has ruled that indefinitely publishing certain expunged drug and arson convictions is unconstitutional, meaning the Riigikogu will have to revisit the legislation.
The Criminal Records Database Act lists offenses for which the names and personal identification codes of convicted people remain publicly available in court rulings online even after their criminal records have been expunged.
As of June 9 this year, the provision affected 8,714 people, including 5,362 convicted of handling a large quantity of drugs, defined as at least 10 doses.
Five people convicted of crimes between 2006 and 2017 asked the court to stop publishing their information. Four had been convicted of drug offenses and one of arson.
The applicants argued that publishing information about expunged convictions harmed their reputations and those of their family members and made it harder for them to support themselves and find work. The Tartu Circuit Court found their requests justified and initiated a constitutional review of the provision.
In two rulings published Tuesday, the Supreme Court emphasized that the constitution allows interference with a person's private life to protect public order and the rights and freedoms of others. "Publishing information about expunged convictions serves the legitimate aim of preventing new serious crimes and protecting other people's fundamental rights," the court said. But it found that indefinitely publishing the information of everyone convicted of a drug offense or arson was neither proportionate nor justified.
The Supreme Court agreed with the circuit court that the drug offenses covered by Section 184 of the Penal Code can vary greatly in severity, depending, for example, on the substance and quantity involved and whether it was supplied to others. Sentences also range widely, from one year to life in prison. In these cases, the applicants received suspended prison sentences close to the minimum and a long time had passed since the offenses, the court noted.
For arson under Section 404, the law provides for a fine or up to five years in prison, meaning the legislature has not classified it as a serious crime. The provision punishes conduct that endangers a person's life or health, even if no actual harm results. It also does not distinguish an isolated act of arson from a pattern of behavior, including pyromania. In this case, the applicant committed the offense in 2006 at age 18 and has not since been convicted of a similar crime.
The Supreme Court said that publishing information about expunged convictions effectively amounts to an additional lifelong social punishment. "It makes it difficult for a person who has served their sentence to reintegrate into society, limiting their opportunities in their private life, work and education. Stigmatizing information may also affect the convicted person's loved ones, including minor children," the court said in a statement.
The Supreme Court therefore declared the Criminal Records Database Act unconstitutional and invalid insofar as it requires information about a person convicted of a drug offense under Section 184(1) or (2) of the Penal Code or arson under Section 404 to remain public in a court ruling after the conviction has been expunged from the criminal records database.
Several ways the Riigikogu can amend the law
The Supreme Court's ruling took effect immediately for the five applicants and for others convicted of the same offenses whose requests to remove their information are currently before the courts. For everyone else with expunged convictions for those offenses, the court delayed the ruling's entry into force by six months to give the Riigikogu time to amend the law.
The Supreme Court explained that publishing information about expunged convictions may still be justified in some drug and arson cases and that lawmakers have several ways to address the issue. For example, they could allow courts to assess whether publication is necessary in each case when a convicted person requests the removal of their information. They could also link publication more broadly to the length of the sentence, whether it was served in prison or other factors indicating the seriousness of the crime or the danger posed by the offender.
The Supreme Court said lawmakers should also avoid creating unnecessary additional work for the courts. Any solution must comply with European Union law.

Australian doctors censored for trying to speak about Gaza
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-29
12:32:13 UTC
21:32:13 KST

Breadcrumb
'We have been silenced': Australia doctors battle censorship on Gaza
Australian doctors are pushing back against a growing pattern of censorship of pro-Palestinian voices in the country’s healthcare system, after hospitals repeatedly cancelled events featuring medical professionals who have worked in Gaza or spoken about the devastation of its healthcare system amid Israel's genocidal war.
There are now calls for an investigation into restrictions on discussions of Palestine in Australian hospitals, with medical professionals warning that the pattern is preventing doctors from sharing first-hand experiences of treating Palestinian children and working inside Gaza’s devastated hospitals.
Perth Children’s Hospital (PCH) cancelled a ‘Children and War’ event just days before it was due to take place on 17 September, after senior management raised concerns about a perceived “pro-Palestinian bias” and discussed preventing Jewish staff from being “upset” by the session, organiser Dr Sue Wareham told The New Arab.
The event was due to feature doctors with experience in Gaza, Afghanistan and Congo discussing the impact of armed conflict on children, but Wareham said Palestine became a central concern behind the hospital’s decision to pull the session.
Wareham, president of the Medical Association for Prevention of War (MAPW) Australia, told TNA that hospital management explicitly cited concerns about Palestine when explaining the cancellation.
“The initial reason I was told (on 12 September) for the cancellation was that there was concern about there being ‘any perception of pro-Palestinian bias’,” Wareham said.
“When I rang the Executive Director of Medical Services on 15 September, she repeated that concern to me and mentioned the need to prevent Jewish staff members being upset by the discussion.”
Emails shared with TNA reveal that PCH Executive Director of Medical Services Dr Clare Matthews reaffirmed her decision to cancel the session in writing on 11 September, while describing it as a “‘not now’, rather than a ‘not ever’ decision”.
Matthews also referred to the need to “address any perception of bias towards a pro-Palestinian position” before holding any future discussion, according to the correspondence.
The hospital has yet to announce another date for the event.
Wareham said Matthews had promised to respond to her concerns in writing but had not done so.
“Dr Matthews said she would reply in writing to my message, but I have not yet received anything in writing from her,” she told TNA.
Doctors push for investigation
Doctors are now pushing for scrutiny of a broader pattern of Palestinian voices and experiences being shut out of Australian healthcare institutions.
Wareham disclosed to TNA that MAPW sent Western Australia Health Minister Meredith Hammat a letter last Thursday raising concerns about PCH’s decision and its implications for medical education about children living through armed conflict.
Wareham described the cancellation as part of “a wider pattern of racism against Palestinian people”.
“The cancellation is a deeply disturbing politicising of the health and welfare of children,” she told TNA.
“When an event is cancelled on the basis of nationality – in this case so that the plight of Palestinian children remains hidden – this is a very dark development for the health professions.”
The session was not exclusively about Palestine. Trauma surgeon Martin Jarmin and general surgeon Dr Farah Abdul Aziz were due to discuss their experiences working or volunteering across conflict zones including Afghanistan and the Democratic Republic of Congo as well as Gaza.
Wareham said organisers wanted to educate hospital staff about the dangers facing children in wars and the ethical responsibilities of medical professionals to protect them.
“One purpose was to alert hospital staff to the dangers faced by children in war zones and our professional and ethical responsibilities to speak out for their protection,” she said.
“An additional purpose was to provide some context for the clinical care of refugee children and adolescents in Australia (of whom there are over 5,000 in Perth alone) to help in their clinical care.”
Emails seen by TNA also detailed the proposed programme for World Patient Safety Day. Dr Mairead Heaney, a Perth-based paediatric anaesthetist and member of Doctors for Palestine, was due to coordinate the session.
Gaza surgeon planned to describe reality inside devastated hospitals
Abdul Aziz, a general surgeon who volunteered in Gaza, told TNA that she planned to show colleagues the severe injuries suffered by Palestinian children and the long-term physical and psychological consequences of Israel’s war.
She intended to “exemplify the cases that the doctors there and the volunteer doctors were dealing with and the injuries sustained by the children with short and long term psychological and physical effects”.
Her presentation would also have given medical staff a first-hand account of working inside Gaza’s devastated healthcare system, where doctors have operated through blackouts, damaged hospitals and acute shortages of basic equipment.
She planned to describe “the conditions that we were operating in, half bombed hospitals, blackouts, damaged equipments, doing bowel surgery with no staplers, minimal equipment and how as doctors we had to go back to basics and operate without our ‘toys’”.
Abdul Aziz also intended to discuss treating patients with multiple traumatic injuries and carrying out damage-control surgery, which she said would have provided valuable clinical education for surgeons attending the event.
Instead, PCH cancelled the session three days before it was due to take place, she said.
“We can’t discuss the medical consequences, treatment, prevention strategy etc. when it comes to Palestinian refugee children as we have been silenced and cancelled every time we try,” Abdul Aziz told TNA.
Gaza healthcare talks repeatedly cancelled
Wareham said PCH was not an isolated case, pointing to previous cancellations at Fiona Stanley Hospital in Murdoch, Western Australia, and the Royal Children’s Hospital in Melbourne involving events where doctors were due to discuss healthcare in Gaza.
“In every case the cancellation has clearly been linked to the inclusion – in panels of diverse speakers with different perspectives – of medical doctors who have spoken out against the catastrophic destruction of health care in Gaza,” Wareham said.
“No other area of healthcare has been subject to such silencing.”
The string of cancellations has fuelled calls for scrutiny over whether Australian medical institutions are disproportionately restricting discussion of Palestinian suffering and the destruction of Gaza’s healthcare system.
MAPW is now pressing for action over the PCH cancellation, while Wareham’s letter to Hammat raises questions about the implications for medical education and healthcare professionals’ ability to discuss the treatment of children affected by war.
The New Arab contacted PCH and Western Australia Health Minister Meredith Hammat for comment but had not received a response at the time of publication.

Stockpiling and calls for military action are among signs of increasing precarity as economy conditions worsen.
Tehran, Iran – Iranians are stocking up on food and medicines as fears grow that the country will face dire shortages as the United States tightens an embargo on the country.
The Iranian government had managed to keep household staples flowing during the early months of the war. But a US naval blockade and pivot to draconian sanctions have led to fears that imports will be limited.
Recommended Stories
list of 3 items
- list 1 of 3Iran touts Hormuz attacks as oil flows increase despite tensions
- list 2 of 3Flights between Iran and Iraq’s Najaf resumes amid US aviation sanctions
- list 3 of 3Iran’s Araghchi meets Qatari mediators as US calls for nuclear talks
More recently, the US announced a ban on Iranian airlines worldwide and is pressing other countries to cut trade ties with Iran in a bid to isolate the country.
Addressing the United Nations General Assembly last week, Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian condemned Washington for its blockade on his country, saying it will prevent food and medicine from reaching the Iranian people.
On Saturday, US President Donald Trump rejected Iran’s offer for a seven-day truce that would see it reopen the Strait of Hormuz in exchange for economic relief and other conditions.
As the war enters its eighth month and hopes for a diplomatic solution dim, Al Jazeera looks at how some Iranians are faring under a US embargo.
Consumers
Tehran’s stores remain stocked, but shoppers are keeping an eye on shop shelves. Their anxiety has deepened since a flurry of social media posts urging people to ensure they have several days of food before a possible new round of fighting with the US.
At one shopping centre, Ali, 51, was loading a trolley packed with rice, flour, pasta, pulses, cooking oil and canned food.
He is stocking up because he is convinced that Iran’s adversary is seeking to “starve” the people to push them to turn on their government.
“This is not a war in the traditional sense. It targets the people to put pressure on the authorities,” he said.
With flights to some nearby countries suspended, imports of certain medicines and mobile phone headsets are hard to find. The prices of those still available in shops have been pushed up.
Haj Pasandideh, a 71-year-old grocer, said he believed warehouses were well-stocked with basic goods at the moment. But the problem lies in the daily price increases due to Iran’s weakening rial, prompting him to bulk-buy goods before the expected hikes.
He sometimes caps cooking oil at one bottle per sale to ensure as many customers can purchase the goods as possible.
Exporters crushed
Farmers are also on edge due to the embargo, unable to ship out their produce and forced to sell to local markets.
The war has worsened the economic situation, even after years of sanctions that have pushed the country from being a regional exporter of agricultural and food products to being one of the region’s main importers.
Mehran, an apple grower, told Al Jazeera that due to the difficulties of exporting, he had sold only a third of this year’s harvest, all of it inside Iran.
Some neighbouring countries have halted trade with Iran in recent months, he said, while trucks now spend days at crossings they once cleared in a day, causing fruit to spoil before it reaches buyers.
“The blockade has not only closed the sea and air but also the land routes but in an undeclared manner,” he said.
Pharmaceutical shortages
The war has also deepened an already-dire shortage of medications. Some pharmacies Al Jazeera visited in southern Tehran had run out of infant formula and dozens of other types of medications.
Although officials have assured Iranians that substitute products were available, pharmacy staff expressed concern about the increasing number of customers searching for infant formula in vain.
“Imported medicines are disappearing fast, and lately people have been coming in to buy certain items before they need them for fear they will run out in future,” Mahsa, a 23-year-old pharmacy assistant, told Al Jazeera.
She said the health authorities had introduced “smart systems” to track the quantity and type of medication each person buys.
Breaking the blockade
The prospect of a prolonged siege and deteriorating economic conditions have driven some Iranians to call for a military solution.
On Tehran’s main thoroughfare, several people told Al Jazeera that another round of fighting with the US was unavoidable. Some urged the government to break the blockade by force before it is tightened further.
Mohsen, a 23-year-old economics student, believes Washington’s goal is to strangle the Iranian economy and the cost will ultimately be felt by Iranian citizens.
Iran possesses many strong cards that it must use to break the air and sea blockade before they develop into a land blockade that would completely choke Tehran, he said.
Alireza Taghavinia, an Iranian international relations expert, told Al Jazeera that the gap between Washington and Tehran was too wide to be bridged. “The siege imposed by force will only be lifted by force,” he said.
In a worst-case scenario, falling living standards could bring protesters onto the streets, he added.
“The enemy is counting on stirring up chaos inside Iran because it believes no military strike will achieve its objectives without internal unrest,” he said.

Who Is Behind the Oleshky Blockade? Investigation Names Russian Commanders and Units

Who Is Behind the Oleshky Blockade? Investigation Names Russian Commanders and Units
Ukrainian investigative journalists have identified two Russian military units and several commanders who may be linked to the blockade of temporarily occupied Oleshky in Ukraine’s Kherson region, where around 2,000 civilians remain with severely restricted access to food, medicine, electricity, and gas.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
According to an investigation by Slidstvo.Info published on September 29, personnel from Russia’s 126th Separate Coastal Defense Brigade of the Black Sea Fleet and the 331st Guards Airborne Regiment are operating in and around the Oleshky community.
The outlet said commanders of the two formations may be connected to the conditions that have prevented regular humanitarian supplies from reaching residents.
Oleshky, located about nine kilometers from the city of Kherson on the Russian-occupied left bank of the Dnipro River, has been under Russian control since the opening days of the full-scale invasion. Its pre-war population of more than 24,000 has fallen to around 2,000, including approximately 50 children, according to regional authorities.
Slidstvo.Info identified the 126th Separate Coastal Defense Brigade as one of the Russian formations currently operating on the Kherson front as part of Russia’s Dnipro grouping of forces.
The brigade is based in Perevalne in temporarily occupied Crimea and was formed in 2014 partly from personnel of Ukraine’s former 36th Coastal Defense Brigade who joined Russian forces following Russia’s occupation of the peninsula.
The investigation found Russian material identifying Colonel Oleg Aleksandrov as commander of the 126th Brigade as of May 2025. However, Slidstvo.Info noted that it could not establish whether he remains in command. An independent OSINT project cited by the outlet currently lists 43-year-old Konstantin Kochetkov as the brigade’s commander.
The second formation identified by investigators is the 331st Guards Airborne Regiment, part of Russia’s 98th Guards Airborne Division. According to Slidstvo.Info, personnel from the regiment are currently deployed in the occupied part of the Kherson region, including around the Oleshky community.
The regiment is commanded by 40-year-old Oleg Morozov, call sign “Kholod,” according to information published by Kostroma regional governor Sergei Sitnikov and cited by the investigation. Morozov was appointed to the position in August 2025 after previously serving as chief of staff and deputy commander of Russia’s 83rd Separate Air Assault Brigade.
The 331st Regiment has operated in Ukraine for years. Slidstvo.Info reported that its personnel were involved in the killing of Ukrainian troops leaving encirclement near Ilovaisk through the so-called “green corridor” in 2014.
The investigation comes as Ukrainian authorities continue to report severe shortages in Oleshky. Ukraine’s Foreign Ministry said in May that Russian forces were blocking evacuations and obstructing deliveries of food, medicine, and other basic supplies to communities on the occupied left bank of the Kherson region.
The ministry said electricity and gas supplies were unavailable and estimated Oleshky’s population had declined from about 24,000 before the full-scale invasion to roughly 2,000.
Ukraine has increasingly relied on drones to deliver supplies across the Dnipro. On September 27, Ukrainian forces delivered approximately four tons of food to 100 locations across Oleshky, according to Kherson Regional Governor Oleksandr Prokudin. The operation involved several Ukrainian military, National Guard, and border guard units.

Russia Ordered Arson Attack on Estonia’s Milrem Robotics Defense Company, Authorities Say

Russia Ordered Arson Attack on Estonia’s Milrem Robotics Defense Company, Authorities Say
Estonia’s Internal Security Service (KAPO) has determined that the arson attack on the Tallinn premises of defense company Milrem Robotics was an act of sabotage commissioned by Russian intelligence services, ERR reported on September 29.
The incident occurred overnight on August 15. Estonian authorities said their conclusion followed an assessment of information gathered during the investigation, which remains ongoing.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
“Today, we can say with complete confidence that the arson at Milrem in Estonia on the night of August 15 was an act of sabotage commissioned by Russian intelligence services. The Internal Security Service reached this conclusion after a thorough assessment of the information collected,” Estonian Prime Minister Kristen Michal said.
Investigators are continuing to establish the full circumstances of the incident. Preliminary information had previously indicated that the arson was commissioned, while suspects in the case have since been detained and remanded in custody.
According to KAPO, the attack forms part of a broader Russian campaign in Europe aimed at intimidating Ukraine’s allies and reducing their support for Kyiv.
Estonian security officials warned that the threat of further provocations and attempted acts of sabotage linked to Russia remains.
“Russian intelligence services continue recruitment and influence attempts in Europe, including for the purpose of carrying out sabotage. Defense industry organizations and companies that contribute to supporting Ukraine are at increased risk. The Internal Security Service recommends that they strengthen physical and cyber protection measures,” KAPO said.
Estonian security services said they continue to closely monitor Russian activities and cooperate with domestic companies and international partners in response to potential threats.
Milrem Robotics, which is majority-owned by UAE-based defense group EDGE, is an Estonian company specializing in autonomous and unmanned ground vehicles.
The company has supplied unmanned ground systems to Ukraine for missions including battlefield logistics, reconnaissance, and explosive ordnance disposal. In June, Milrem Robotics opened a production line in the Netherlands, where Dutch funding is supporting the production of 100 additional vehicles for Ukraine.
The findings come as Estonia continues to strengthen its defense infrastructure. A planned military base in the eastern border city of Narva is expected to cost slightly more than €20 million (approximately $23 million), with completion now scheduled for summer 2028. The revised timeline puts the project about six months behind the original schedule.

Ukraine’s FREYJA Interceptor Missile Gets New Dual-Mode Seeker
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-29
12:31:02 UTC
21:31:02 KST

- Category
- War in Ukraine
Ukraine’s FREYJA Interceptor Missile Gets New Dual-Mode Seeker
Ukrainian missile maker Fire Point has updated its FP-7.x Freyja interceptor with a combined infrared and radar seeker, Defence Blog reported on September 28, citing the company’s official X account.
The revised specification replaces the infrared-only seeker previously described for the missile.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
Defence Blog reported that Fire Point published the updated specification card on X but did not explain the change or identify the supplier of the radar component.
Fire Point had presented the Freyja project in August with an imaging infrared seeker designed to track a target’s heat signature. A combined seeker can use both infrared emissions and radar reflections during the terminal phase of an interception, the report noted.
The dual-mode approach can help maintain tracking when one sensor is affected by weather, decoys, or the target’s design. According to Defence Blog, the seeker is mounted in the missile’s nose and guides the interceptor during the final stage of flight.
The FP-7.x is listed as 7.25 meters long and 0.53 meters in diameter. Its top speed is between 1,500 and 2,000 meters per second, equivalent to roughly 5,400 to 7,200 kilometers per hour.
The missile carries a fragmentation warhead designed to detonate near the target and scatter metal fragments. It uses inertial guidance and receives radio course corrections from the ground while in flight.
Fire Point’s August presentation listed Russia’s Iskander-M ballistic missile at about 2,100 meters per second at the end of powered flight, Defence Blog wrote.
The comparison places the current FP-7.x close to the speed range of one of Russia’s main short-range ballistic missile systems.
The FP-7.x is being developed as the interceptor for Freyja, a pan-European ballistic missile defense project intended to provide a cheaper alternative to the US-made Patriot system. Ukraine and nine other European countries signed a declaration launching the initiative on July 13, Defence Blog reported.
Fire Point serves as the project’s main system integrator and has agreements with 13 European defense companies. Partners include Hensoldt, Thales, Diehl Defence, Saab, Kongsberg, Leonardo, MBDA, and Safran, covering radars, guidance systems, seekers, and command-and-control equipment.
According to Defence Blog, Fire Point was founded in Kyiv in 2022 and is best known for its FP-1 long-range attack drones and FP-5 Flamingo cruise missile. The FP-7.x is a faster derivative of the company’s FP-7 ground-attack ballistic missile.
Fire Point has indicated that the FP-7 design drew on Soviet-era S-300 and S-400 interceptor concepts. The company also uses composite materials in the airframe to reduce production costs, the report noted.
Fire Point chief executive Iryna Terekh told Janes in July that the current FP-7.x uses a blast-fragmentation warhead. Defence Blog reported that Terekh described the configuration as having a low chance of destroying the payload of an incoming ballistic missile.
The company plans to develop the missile into a hit-to-kill interceptor that destroys its target through direct impact. Terekh also indicated that the FP-7.x could eventually reach about 2,200 meters per second as development progresses.
Fire Point wants each interceptor to cost less than $1.14 million and aims to produce 2,000 missiles per year, according to Defence Blog. The company presents the system as a lower-cost alternative to Patriot interceptors, which remain in limited global supply.
Ukraine continues to rely heavily on Patriot systems to counter Russian ballistic missiles. Defence Blog noted that Fire Point hopes to have the first FP-7.x interceptors ready by the end of 2026 if European partners deliver the remaining components.
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy previously revealed that Ukraine expects the first FREYJA air defense system to be ready by the end of 2026.

Norway Pledges $12M to Help Return Deported Ukrainian Children, Detainees and POWs

- Category

Norway Pledges $12M to Help Return Deported Ukrainian Children, Detainees and POWs
Norway announced nearly $12 million in new humanitarian funding on September 29 for deported Ukrainian children, unlawfully detained civilians, and prisoners of war.
The Norwegian government stated that the funding will be channeled through UNICEF and the International Committee of the Red Cross (ICRC).
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
The package was announced in connection with the international conference “Pathways to Peace: Returning Ukrainian Children, Detained Civilians, and Prisoners of War,” held in Toronto on September 28 and 29 and co-hosted by Norway, Canada, and Ukraine.
“These funds will help trace missing persons, support efforts to bring more people home, and assist with rehabilitation and reintegration of those affected by the war,” Norwegian Foreign Minister Espen Barth Eide said.
Norway earmarked NOK 15 million, about $1.6 million, for UNICEF’s work to reintegrate children who have returned to Ukraine and trace those who remain missing.
The funding is part of Norway’s broader NOK 132 million, about $13.8 million, contribution to UNICEF’s humanitarian program in Ukraine.
Another NOK 10 million, about $1 million, will go to the ICRC’s Central Tracing Agency Bureau, while NOK 90 million, about $9.4 million, will support the organization’s wider humanitarian operations in Ukraine.
State Secretary Eivind Vad Petersson is leading the Norwegian delegation at the Toronto conference and will moderate a panel discussion on Ukrainian civilians unlawfully detained in Russia.
The Norwegian government said many Ukrainian children remain in Russia after being unlawfully deported or forcibly transferred, while an unknown number of Ukrainian civilians are also being unlawfully detained.
According to the government, detained civilians and prisoners of war are being held in extremely difficult conditions, while many families have no information about the whereabouts of their relatives.
Norway cited reports that detained Ukrainian civilians have been subjected to isolation, torture, and other forms of inhuman or degrading treatment, while often being denied adequate healthcare, sufficient food, and access to legal representation.
Since 2022, Norway has provided more than NOK 1 billion, about $104 million, to UNICEF’s work in Ukraine. Around NOK 80 million, about $8.3 million, has been earmarked specifically for efforts involving unlawfully deported and forcibly transferred Ukrainian children.
Norway has also provided more than NOK 1 billion to the ICRC since 2022, including NOK 40 million, about $4.2 million, for its Central Tracing Agency Bureau.
Oslo said it will use the Toronto conference to draw greater international attention to the situation of detained Ukrainian civilians and strengthen international efforts to return children, civilians, and prisoners of war.
The Norwegian package follows similar Western commitments to the return of Ukrainian children taken by Russia.
On September 24, the US State Department announced $27 million to trace, return, and reintegrate Ukrainian children, with $12 million approved for programs assisting returnees and $15 million submitted for consideration.
The funding was revealed at a UN General Assembly side event on deported and forcibly displaced children. More than 2,100 children have been returned under the Bring Kids Back UA initiative, including 150 since the start of 2026.

What trap? US-China relations show conflict is far from inevitable

The term is widely used in commentaries on US-China relations. Frictions get written off as “inevitable” regardless of what actually happened. Both sides are, for now, choosing the diplomatic equivalent of indicating before they change lanes.
Any analysis about power transition has to start with power itself, so here is where the two superpowers stand at the moment. By market exchange rates, the US economy was worth about US$30.6 trillion in 2025 against China’s US$19.4 trillion, putting China’s economy at roughly 63 per cent of the size of the US.
