SpaceX's Starship engine failure could cause problem for NASA's 2028 moon mission objectives
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-29
12:29:52 UTC
21:29:52 KST

The Starship engine failure that nearly foiled the orbital debut of SpaceX's next-generation spacecraft on its 14th uncrewed test flight may complicate NASA's ability to meet its time frame for astronaut missions to the moon.
Starship, designed in part to carry large payloads to space, is one of two vehicles vying to become the first craft that NASA will use as early as 2028 to land humans on the moon and bring them safely home, a feat last achieved in 1972 at the end of the Apollo era.
While Starship accomplished a number of key objectives in its latest test launch from Texas on Monday, the mission was cut short by several hours after a malfunction of its propulsion system.
Despite the unexpected shutdown of one of its three main Raptor engines following Starship separation from its lower-stage booster rocket, flight controllers proceeded with sending the spacecraft to orbit for its first-ever commercial satellite deployment.
Determining what caused the engine glitch remains critical to SpaceX's bottom line. But the stakes are potentially higher for NASA, as a Starship moon-landing vehicle would rely on the same engine system for transporting astronauts through space to and from the lunar surface.
How big a blow to Starship's development progress the engine snafu becomes depends on whether it turns out to be "a one-off failure of a single part" or points to a larger design problem that requires upgrades "across the fleet," said Dean Sladen, an aerospace engineer for Accu Components.
"Any engine fix that holds up the next flights, including the planned attempt to catch the ship with the launch tower's arms (after re-entry), eats into that schedule," he said.
NASA and SpaceX did not immediately respond to Reuters requests for comment.
'The real pressure is the moon'
A longer delay would pose not only a greater setback to SpaceX's commercial ambitions to rapidly expand its Starlink broadband satellite network, but its pivotal role in NASA's Artemis moon program.
"The real pressure is the moon. NASA needs Starship for Artemis III," an Earth-orbit test mission targeted as soon as next summer as a rehearsal flight for the program's actual first crewed lunar landing, Sladen said.
Raptor engine and propulsion-system issues have contributed to several previous Starship setbacks, including an engine that failed to ignite as planned during Starship's 12th flight in May. The methane-fueled engines are among the most complex and expensive components on the rocket.
During some previous flights, SpaceX scrubbed plans to test-ignite the Raptor engine in space. But all of the engines successfully fired during ascent on Starship's 13th flight in July.
SpaceX, the newly public venture founded by Elon Musk near Los Angeles in 2002, is competing with Blue Origin, the rival rocket company from fellow entrepreneur Jeff Bezos, to usher in an era of lunar exploration under NASA's Artemis program.
While SpaceX was originally contracted to provide the first crewed lunar lander for Artemis, the head of the US space agency, Jared Isaacman, said in April that NASA would go with whichever lander was ready to fly first. NASA saw the added competition as healthy for progress in light of mounting delays in Starship's test flight program.
NASA hopes to return to the moon's surface by 2028
NASA officially aims to return astronauts to the moon's surface by 2028 - a target widely seen as overly ambitious - to get there ahead of China, which plans a crewed lunar landing by 2030.
A functioning lunar landing craft also will be needed for the precursor Artemis III mission, as early as summer 2027, to test rendezvous and docking maneuvers in low Earth orbit.
SpaceX is developing a Human Landing System based on its Starship vessel, a towering stainless-steel vehicle far larger than any moon lander built before. Blue Origin is building its own Blue Moon lander, relying on a more traditional design philosophy.
If ready, both landers are likely to participate in the Artemis III mission, demonstrating orbital maneuvers using their in-space engines.
Isaacman went public with the competing lander strategy days after completion of NASA's Artemis II mission sending astronauts around the moon and back in what was the first crewed launch of NASA's Space Launch System rocket, built by Boeing and Northrop Grumman, and the Orion capsule, made by Lockheed Martin.

Israel should stop treating the Kurds as a temporary ally - opinion
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-29
12:29:23 UTC
21:29:23 KST

Foreign Minister Gideon Sa’ar delivered a timely and important message at the first Kurdish-Jewish Conference in London on September 6. He has once again clarified that Israel recognizes the Kurdish historical and ongoing predicament in the Middle East.
Sa’ar went beyond recognition and pointed out that the Kurdish-Jewish relationship in the Middle East is strategic.
His remark highlighted not only the Kurdish-Jewish relationship but also the Kurdish-Jewish alliance, neither invented nor merely a political construct, but a natural alliance rooted in the close ties between the Kurdish and Jewish peoples since the first Jewish deportation by the Assyrians around 720 BCE to Northern Mesopotamia, in contemporary Kurdistan.
This historical Jewish deportation overlaps with the beginning of the Kurdish calendar around 650 BCE.
This encounter laid the foundation for a Kurdish-Jewish relationship that is deeply rooted in the history and collective memory of both peoples.
To honor these close Kurdish-Jewish ties, Kurdish people hope that Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu, as head of the cabinet and ultimate executive authority, will directly echo and institutionalize Sa’ar’s stance to build genuine, lasting trust among the Kurdish people.
Subsequently, Kurdish-Jewish solidarity can move decisively beyond an era in which Kurdish aspirations were treated as convenient rhetorical leverage against Ankara and Tehran rather than as the basis for enduring strategic commitments.
With the belief in this ancient relationship, Kurdish and Jewish academics, civil society representatives, and diaspora activists convened to discuss the shared challenges they face both in their homelands and across the diaspora. The Kurds welcomed the conference and warmly embraced Sa’ar’s message.
Similarly, Israeli media extensively reported on the gathering and its objectives. The conference underscored the strategic relationship between two indigenous peoples of the Middle East and their shared concerns regarding threats emanating from the Sunni and Shi’ite axes.
The strongest headwinds came, unsurprisingly, from the Turkish media and nationalist supporters of the self-appointed monarch Reza Pahlavi, who have circulated distorted narratives about the Kurdish people and their political movements.
These narratives target a people already enduring daily atrocities at the hands of the IRGC and the wider militarized forces of the Mullah regime.
The Kurdish people are a nation of over 50 million whose ancestral homeland was unjustly partitioned between the Iranian Safavid and Ottoman empires in 1639, and later between Arab states and Turkey following the post-World War I settlement of the Middle East in the 1920s.
The Kurds are an indigenous people with their own distinct language, history, culture, and territory, forming an ethnic peoplehood that is neither Turkish, Arab, nor Persian. As a separate nation with its own distinct identity, language, culture, and deep historical roots, the Kurdish people possess every legitimate right to demand full statehood.
Within this framework, self-determination and separatism remain their natural, inherent right under the principle of indigenous sovereignty. The Kurds have been denied their nation-state and, consequently, have suffered multiple genocides, ethnic cleansing, and forced displacement under successive Muslim regimes in Tehran, Ankara, Damascus, and Baghdad.
This history is inseparable from the contemporary debate over Iran. The divisive and accusatory rhetoric of contemporary monarchists recalls, in the eyes of many Kurds, the denial and repressive policies of the grandfather Reza Shah Pahlavi, following the collapse of the Qajar Empire in 1925.
Kurdish demand for recognition
The Pahlavi dynasty pursued a centralized Persian nationalist project that marginalized minority identities, including those of Kurds and Jews. Kurdish demands for recognition of their cultural and linguistic identities were denied.
Kurds were misrepresented as “mountainous Iranian people,” a policy that nationalist Turks adapted earlier in constructing a hegemonized Turkish national state. As part of these measures, Kurdish elites and leaders, including Simko Agha, were assassinated while Kurdish political movements were suppressed.
Jews endured a similar fate under the repression of the Pahlavi era. Jewish leaders suffered a similar fate: as part of Pahlavi’s nationalistic project, Shmuel Haim, a prominent Jewish leader and head of the Iranian Zionist organization, was arrested and executed in 1931 for allegedly promoting Zionist activities and encouraging Jewish emigration to Jerusalem.
The Pahlavi regime’s systematic repression and authoritarian policies toward minority communities had a lasting impact. In 1946, the government of Mohammad Reza Pahlavi, the father of the current self-appointed Reza Pahlavi, crushed the short-lived Kurdistan Republic in Mahabad and executed its principal leaders.
The Pahlavi regime continued a repressive and authoritarian policy toward diverse minority communities, including the Kurds, which resulted in the emergence of the current Mullah regime in 1979. The Kurds have again remained a primary target of the new Mullah regime, facing daily executions and repression.
Kurdish leaders and activists have been executed in Iran and assassinated abroad, including in Vienna and Berlin. The regime continually scapegoats Kurds, justifying state crimes by alleging collaboration with Mossad.
The state murder of the Kurdish woman Jina Amini in the custody of Iran’s morality police became a defining example of severe repression against the Kurds. Since the February 28 war within Iran and across Iraqi Kurdistan, the regime has killed over 100 Kurdish people, mostly civilians, and wounded more than 1,000.
While Kurds face extreme atrocities by the Mullah regime, monarchist supporters of Reza Pahlavi attack Kurds in the diaspora and on social media, weaponizing accusations of separatism to delegitimize Kurdish autonomy.
However, they deliberately obscure a vital reality: although national self-determination and statehood remain their fundamental right, Kurdish leadership has actively chosen to pursue a democratic, decentralized, and federal Iran.
Members of the Kurdish coalition, including PDK-I, PJAK, Komala, and PAK, have voluntarily set aside unilateral separation to offer a shared future rooted in regional autonomy, civic equality, and collective liberation.
Similarly, at a Moshe Dayan Center panel, representatives of all Kurdish parties declared their readiness to cooperate with transformative forces, including Israel and the US, on regime change and democratization.
The accusations of separatism and attacks on Sa’ar are calculated attempts by Reza Pahlavi’s followers to create a rift between Kurds and Israel, undermining the forces actively resisting the regime. This divisive, chauvinistic policy fractures opposition solidarity, protects the Mullah regime from imminent collapse, and undermines those fighting for freedom.
Yet Sa’ar’s message in London was significant precisely because it recognizes the reality that Kurds and Jews, two peoples with ancient roots in the Middle East, have common interests in defending their identity, security, and peaceful future.
Strengthening the Kurdish-Jewish relationship is strategically important in confronting the challenges posed by authoritarianism and repression in the region.
The writer is a researcher at the Kurdish Forum at the Moshe Dayan Center for Middle Eastern and African Studies at Tel Aviv University. X: @dagweysi

Yashar party leader Gadi Eisenkot responded to Netanyahu's comments later on Tuesday, stating in a post on X/Twitter that "opposition leader Yair Lapid must be briefed immediately" if the security threats are found to be legitimate.
"This is necessary to ensure that this is indeed a genuine threat and not a political maneuver intended to undermine the electoral process," Eisenkot, the leading candidate to replace Netanyahu as prime minister, added.
"Israel’s security must never be conflated with the election campaign," Eisenkot emphasized. "Not even for appearances’ sake."
Lapid issued an official response to the Prime Minister's Office (PMO) following Netanyahu's remarks, demanding an urgent security briefing and noting the opposition leader's desire to understand the threat and the prime minister's preparations to address it.

Pentagon breach exposed data on over 3 million people – media
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-29
12:28:09 UTC
21:28:09 KST

Pentagon breach exposed data on over 3 million people – media
A Pentagon personnel system breach has reportedly exposed sensitive data on more than three million people, including military personnel and their families, several media outlets have reported, citing US defense officials. The disclosure follows a separate breach of the FBI’s jobs website.
The Defense Manpower Data Center (DMDC) system was reportedly accessed by a small number of unauthorized users between October 2025 and July 2026, affecting some 2.76 million living people and another 294,000 who are deceased, unidentified Pentagon officials have told CNN and ABC News.
According to them, the exposed files include Social Security numbers and other personal details, as well as information about military jobs and occupational specialties.
DMDC maintains more than 60 million records overall, including on active-duty and reserve troops, civilian employees, contractors, retirees, veterans, and military family members.
The leak was initially reported by the Military Times last week citing an internal breach notice received by one of the affected individuals. The publication said two unnamed defense officials had confirmed the authenticity of the letter.
Heads up! This is coming down. pic.twitter.com/nKawhTNX5h
— U.S Army WTF! moments (@usawtfm) September 22, 2026
According to the notice, DMDC said that a “security vulnerability” in a file-sharing system allowed unauthorized users to gain access to unencrypted personal information. The system was said to have been patched “immediately” after it was discovered – nearly nine months after the unauthorized access began.
The notice offered affected individuals a year of free credit monitoring services.
However, the Pentagon has not yet officially confirmed the breach, nor commented on who was behind the intrusion or what they did with the information they accessed.
Meanwhile, the FBI is dealing with an unrelated breach claim involving its recruitment website. Last week, the hacking group ShinyHunters claimed it had stolen personal data on nearly all FBI agents, their spouses, and job applicants.
The group said that the attack was “not financially motivated” and instead of a ransom, demanded that the FBI remove a cybersecurity advisory published in May that ShinyHunters says contains false allegations about them.
The FBI has said it is investigating and has notified employees, but has not yet established where the breach occurred or confirmed the scale of the theft.

Swiss archaeologists redraw Roman maps after drought discoveries
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-29
12:27:53 UTC
21:27:53 KST

Swiss archaeologists redraw Roman maps after drought discoveries
AVENCHES, Switzerland, Sept 29 - Archaeologists are redrawing Roman maps of Switzerland after traces of long-buried ruins emerged as the country endured the hottest summer on record.
Drought can reveal hidden archaeological sites through "parch marks" created when vegetation above them withers, one of several effects of this year's heatwaves, which also exposed World War Two wrecks on river beds.
Alerted by a history enthusiast, archaeologists in the Swiss canton of Vaud used a drone to take daily images of fields around Aventicum, the former capital of Roman Helvetia, founded 2,000 years ago after Julius Caesar defeated local tribes. It is now the site of the small town of Avenches.
"These are the richest discoveries made there in the last 50 years, at least over the last two generations of archaeologists," said Jordan Anastassov, archaeologist for Vaud.
The images revealed traces of thermal baths, houses, roads and a possible temple that were previously unknown or dimly understood, many in never-before-excavated areas of the city, which thrived under Roman rule before gradually fading as Germanic incursions increased from the third century onward.
The team of five archaeologists superimposed the discoveries onto maps in purple, filling blank spaces and correcting mistaken markings.
"We are now asking really interesting questions we wouldn't otherwise be asking," said archaeologist Hugo Amoroso.
Some of the traces captured from June to August vanished after mowing and with lower temperatures, but the perimeter of a new pool in the baths is still visible in a partially withered alfalfa field as unseasonably warm weather has persisted in September.
Other buried historical remains have emerged elsewhere in Switzerland and Europe, but many are harder to interpret because they are isolated and lack dedicated researchers.
The Swiss archaeologists will present their findings to peers and may conduct targeted digs later.
"We aren't going to wish for droughts," said Pierre Blanc, director of excavations for the site. "But we're going to make the most of this and keep looking." REUTERS

Economic Watch: Multinationals double down on R&D in China to serve global markets
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-29
20:27:43 CST
21:27:43 KST

CHONGQING, Sept. 29 (Xinhua) -- As foreign companies race to deepen their R&D footprint in China, tech firm HP has opened a new AI innovation center in southwest China's Chongqing Municipality, underscoring a broader shift from manufacturing to locally rooted research and development with global reach.
"Manufacturing was the starting point of our partnership. Innovation is its future," said Jonathan Jennings, HP's global chief procurement officer.
HP's launch of the new China AI innovation center reflects a wider trend among foreign companies operating in China. For decades, the country was best known as the world's factory, where global manufacturers built vast production lines to serve overseas markets. Now, many multinationals are moving research, design and product development closer to Chinese customers, suppliers and engineers, embedding innovation in China to serve global markets.
The scale of this shift is visible in data. Figures released by the Ministry of Commerce show that by the end of March 2026, Beijing was home to 332 foreign-funded R&D centers, with 55 added this year. Shanghai hosted 647, with 15 new ones established in the same period.
A recent survey of multinational executives in China revealed that 42 percent of companies plan to invest in China-based R&D that serves global markets over the next two years.
"Many multinationals' manufacturing bases in China are being upgraded into sources of innovation," said He Yadong, spokesperson for the Ministry of Commerce, citing recent R&D investments by companies such as AstraZeneca, Philips and Schneider Electric.
For many executives, the main reason is speed. Chinese customers, supply chains and engineering teams allow new products to move from concept to market far faster than in many other regions.
"Our customers in China adopt new technologies in about 12 to 14 months, while it can take three to four years elsewhere," said Jerome Dorlack, president and CEO of Adient, a global leader in automotive seating. The company operates three global technology centers in China, including the largest one located in Chongqing.
The talent pool in China is another draw. "China has long emphasized university education for scientists and engineers, and the new generation of Chinese engineers and scientists has a strong mathematical foundation while becoming increasingly creative," said Michael Mertin, CEO of AT&S AG, an Austrian manufacturing company.
This talent advantage is now feeding into artificial intelligence (AI), which has become a focus for foreign companies in China. HP's Chongqing center is developing AI-powered inspection systems, while Adient is using AI vision to identify production defects earlier in the process.
The global reach of China-based R&D is already taking shape. Audi's innovation center in China is engineering luxury vehicles that could feed into Audi's global product portfolio, while Valeo is leveraging its R&D centers in China to deepen local innovation and export self-developed core new-energy technologies worldwide.
Policy support is reinforcing this trend. China's 15th Five-Year Plan (2026-2030) calls for attracting more foreign companies to establish regional headquarters and R&D centers, with many cities rolling out measures to support these efforts.
"The concentration of foreign R&D centers in China shows the country is moving up the value chain and global production networks are being redrawn," said Wang Lei, a professor at the School of Government of Beijing Normal University. "Deeper integration between foreign and local innovation will raise productivity, strengthen China's role in global innovation, and pave the way for shared growth." ■

Major water conservancy project begins power generation in China's Xinjiang
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-29
20:27:35 CST
21:27:35 KST

URUMQI, Sept. 29 (Xinhua) -- The first batch of generating units of the Dashixia Water Conservancy Project in northwest China's Xinjiang Uygur Autonomous Region was connected to the grid for power generation on Tuesday, its constructor said.
Located in Wensu Grand Canyon in Xinjiang's Aksu Prefecture, the 247-meter-high dam of this water conservancy hub is currently the world's highest concrete-faced sand-gravel dam, according to the constructor, China Gezhouba Group Co., Ltd.
When fully operational, the hub can generate over 1.89 billion kilowatt-hours of electricity annually, capable of meeting the electricity needs of approximately 600,000 households.
It will also channel 3.42 billion cubic meters of water to the Tarim River each year, easing water shortages on more than 6.8 million mu (about 453,333 hectares) of farmland, while significantly boosting flood control capacity and greatly advancing agricultural modernization in southern Xinjiang.
During the construction process, blockchain technologies were applied to collect concrete data and manage transportation, making project quality controllable and traceable, noted Song Xiaojian, the project manager.
To mitigate the impact of the project on fish, the constructor also invested 65 million yuan (around 9.64 million U.S. dollars) in various ecological protection measures, which went into operation ahead of schedule, according to Yang Yanling, who is with the project's quality and environmental protection department.
So far, a total of 141,000 fish have been released through artificial propagation, Yang added. ■

TEKNOFEST Southeast to open Wednesday in Türkiye's Sanliurfa
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-29
12:27:19 UTC
21:27:19 KST

Rauf Maltas, Cebrail Caymaz and Gizem Nisa Demir
29 September 2026•Update: 29 September 2026
The world's largest aviation, space and technology festival, TEKNOFEST, will open its doors to visitors Wednesday at Sanliurfa GAP Airport in Türkiye under the name TEKNOFEST Southeast, with the five-day event expected to feature air shows, technology competitions, exhibitions and educational activities.
The festival, which has welcomed nearly 12 million visitors since its launch, will be held from Sept. 30 to Oct. 4 in Sanliurfa, a southeastern province of Türkiye.
Anadolu is the festival's "Global Communications Partner."
Organized under the leadership of the Turkish Industry and Technology Ministry, the T3 Foundation, and Defense Technologies Engineering and Trade Inc. (STM), the festival will cover an area of 191,000 square meters at Sanliurfa GAP Airport.
Air shows, exhibitions and activities for all ages
TEKNOFEST Southeast will bring together activities for visitors of all ages throughout the five-day event.
The festival will feature air shows by Türkiye’s leading aviation and defense platforms, including SOLOTURK and the Turkish Stars, as well as fighter aircraft.
Visitors will also have the opportunity to see ATAK helicopters, HURKUS, ANKA, Bayraktar TB2, Bayraktar TB3, and Bayraktar AKINCI, alongside land and naval vehicles.
The program will include concerts, stage performances, exhibitions, educational workshops, simulation areas, a planetarium, science shows, the TEKNOFEST Time Tunnel, displays of domestically developed land, naval and air vehicles, trade fair activities and special first-flight experiences for students.
More than 1.6M contestants applied from 99 countries
TEKNOFEST Southeast will feature technology competitions aimed at supporting technological development in critical fields, with teams that advance through the preliminary stages receiving financial and other forms of support.
More than 1.6 million contestants and hundreds of thousands of teams applied to the technology competitions held as part of TEKNOFEST Southeast. Of more than 730,000 teams that applied, 2,000 advanced to the finals.
Successful contestants will receive more than 100 million Turkish liras in total support.
Applications to this year's TEKNOFEST Technology Competitions came from 99 countries, including the US, France, China and Japan.
Eleven new categories were added, including 5G, the Artificial Intelligence and Smart Road Safety Competition, the Technological Applications in Combating Addiction Competition and the Electronic Warfare Competition.
Finals of 14 technology competitions to be held in Sanliurfa
The finals of technology competitions in 14 categories will be held in Sanliurfa as part of TEKNOFEST Southeast.
These include the Technological Applications in Combating Addiction Competition, organized by the Turkish Green Crescent Society; the Blockchain Competition, organized by the Scientific and Technological Research Council of Türkiye (TUBITAK); the Steel Dome Air Defense Systems Competition and Mobile Satellite Terminal Competition, organized by ASELSAN; the Financial Technologies Competition, organized in cooperation with Takasbank and the Central Bank of the Republic of Türkiye; the HackMasters Southeast Competition, organized by the Cybersecurity Presidency; the International Invention Competition under ISIF, organized by the Turkish Patent and Trademark Office; the Mining Technologies Competition, organized by Turkish Gold Inc.; the Architectural and Visual Design Competition, organized by KUME Foundation; the 3T in Oncology Competition, organized by Cansagligi; the Agricultural Technologies Competition, organized by Bilişim Vadisi and TUME; the TEKNOFEST Drone Championship and World Drone Cup, organized by STM; and the TEKNOFEST Robolig Competition, organized by the T3 Foundation.
Online registration required
Admission to TEKNOFEST Southeast is free, but visitors must register online to enter the festival grounds.
Visitor entry and exit will be available between 9 am and 7 pm local time each day. Organizers recommend using public transportation to reach the festival area for faster and easier access.
Further information about TEKNOFEST Southeast and visitor registration is available at www.teknofest.org.

Source: Ukrainska Pravda; Free Media Awards 2026

Quote from Tkach: "I am proud to be Ukrainian and honoured to live and work at this defining time for our country.

Quote from Tkach: "Ukrainian journalists, working every day under fire even far from the front line, report not only on Russian crimes, sanctions violations and Kremlin criminals who sometimes still feel at home in the civilised world. Ukrainian journalists do not slide into propaganda; they shine a bright ray of light on the corridors and offices of the Ukrainian government. We point out mistakes, expose conspiracies in the interests of private individuals, and talk about abuses of power – so that mistakes can be corrected, the government serves exclusively in the interests of the people, and our country becomes stronger in the fight for freedom."
Details: Tkach noted that over the past four years, UP's investigative department has tracked down more than 10 former top officials, MPs and government-linked individuals in various countries who fled Ukraine and were hiding from justice. At least as many officials, he added, have resigned following UP investigations.
He also revealed that he currently has victim status in 13 criminal proceedings concerning obstruction of journalists' lawful professional activities.
"The last time I was threatened with murder because of my professional activities was a year ago. The latest attack on our film crew took place two months ago. And you know what I have to tell you today? We are preparing new material!" Tkach said.
He concluded his speech by saying that Ukraine's struggle is taking place on two levels simultaneously.
Quote from Tkach: "Ukraine is not only fighting the Russian aggressor externally – Ukraine is fighting corruption internally, preserving democracy as a reliable weapon against dictatorships."
Background:
- The Free Media Awards were established by the Norwegian Fritt Ord Foundation and the German Zeit Stiftung Bucerius to support independent journalism in Eastern and Central Europe.
- The award organisers commended Tkach for his investigations into corruption and abuse of power, his reports on government contracts and defence procurement, the privileged status of wealthy individuals, and the lifestyles of the Ukrainian elite abroad since the start of the Russian invasion. The jury also praised his investigations into covert Russian influence in Western countries.
- The Fritt Ord Foundation emphasised that Tkach's work demonstrates that investigative journalism in wartime is "not only possible, but absolutely crucial".

Sudan has called for international action against foreign parties supporting the paramilitary Rapid Support Forces (RSF) opposing the government, and accused the UN Security Council of failing to identify and condemn the group’s sponsors.
Sudanese Foreign Minister Mohieldin Salim Ahmed Ibrahim made the appeal at the UN General Assembly in New York on Monday, saying external support for the RSF was prolonging the war.
“Pressure must be exerted on the regional sponsors and certain neighboring states,” Ibrahim said.
The foreign minister accused unnamed countries of allowing weapons and supplies to reach the RSF through their territory and enabling attacks by the paramilitary group and mercenaries to be launched from outside Sudan’s borders. He also claimed hospitals had been established in neighboring states to treat wounded RSF fighters.
Ibrahim said the UN Security Council had failed to identify and condemn the RSF’s sponsors, which he accused of recruiting foreign mercenaries, providing political backing to the paramilitary group and financing media platforms spreading what he described as “disinformation” against the Sudanese Armed Forces (SAF).
Sudan has previously accused the United Arab Emirates (UAE) of providing military support to the RSF, allegations Abu Dhabi has repeatedly denied. Khartoum has also accused neighboring Ethiopia of allowing its territory to be used for drone attacks against Sudan, a claim Addis Ababa has rejected.
The accusations come weeks after a UN fact-finding mission found reasonable grounds to believe that a transnational network had supplied the RSF with weapons, logistics, training and foreign personnel. Investigators identified private entities and intermediaries operating from countries including the UAE, with transit routes through Chad, southeastern Libya and Somalia.
Ibrahim said peace would require the RSF to be disarmed and its weapons to remain under the control of state institutions. He also called for attacks on civilians and infrastructure to end.
Sudan plunged into a civil war three years ago after a struggle for power broke out between the SAF and the RSF.
Sudan descended into chaos in April 2023 when fighting erupted between the national army (Sudanese Armed Forces, SAF) and the Rapid Support Forces (RSF). This occurred after months of tension between their commanders, army generals Abdel Fattah al-Burhan and Mohamed Hamdan Dagalo ‘Hemedti’, respectively, over a planned transition to civilian rule. What began in the capital, Khartoum, as a power struggle has devastated the country, killing tens of thousands and displacing millions.
Regional and international peace efforts, including African Union mediation and Saudi–US talks in Jeddah, have repeatedly stalled. Sudanese officials have named Colombians and Ukrainians among mercenaries backing the RSF against the army. Officials have also accused Ukraine and the United Arab Emirates of involvement and recently claimed the European Union has an “incomplete understanding of the complex situation” in the country.
Khartoum has also accused authorities in neighboring Kenya of backing the RSF and has broken ties with the East African grouping IGAD amid mistrust of regional mediation. In July, TASIS, a political coalition aligned with the paramilitary, announced the formation of a rival government months after its members signed a charter in Nairobi. It named Gen. Dagalo as chairman of a 15-member presidential council, a move rejected by the UN and AU.
The RSF was originally established by the Sudanese government under former President Omar al-Bashir in 2013, drawing heavily on the Janjaweed militias that Khartoum had used to fight rebels in Darfur. Its status was later formalized by law before tensions with the regular army erupted into open warfare.
Diplomatic efforts to end the war have intensified on the sidelines of the UN General Assembly in New York. Russian Foreign Minister Sergey Lavrov discussed ways to resolve the conflict with his Sudanese counterpart last week, while the African Union and the US called for an immediate humanitarian truce followed by a durable ceasefire and a Sudanese-led political process.
Washington does not regard either side as representing legitimate constitutional rule in Sudan. Khartoum strongly rejected the US position, calling for respect for the country’s sovereignty and national institutions and warning against legitimizing the RSF through force.

Inflation in Spain surges to 4.9% in September on higher fuel prices
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-29
12:24:00 UTC
21:24:00 KST

Inflation in Spain climbed 0.6% in September to 4.9%, driven by higher fuel prices, lubricants and package holidays. Core inflation rose 0.2% to 3.1%.
Inflation in Spain jumped to 4.9% in September, six tenths of a point higher than in August, driven mainly by the rising cost of fuel and lubricants for vehicles, according to the flash estimate of the Consumer Price Index (CPI) published on Tuesday by the National Statistics Institute (INE).
INE explains that fuel prices rose again in September, in contrast with the fall recorded in the same month of 2025, which contributed to the sharp rebound in inflation.
The movement in package holidays also had an impact as their prices fell by less than what they did a year earlier.
The surge takes inflation to its highest level since February 2023, when it reached 6%. By category, energy products posted an increase of 21.6%, while unprocessed food went up by 5.8% and services by 3.9%.
Core inflation, which excludes unprocessed food and energy products, rose by two tenths and stood at 3.1%, according to the INE.
In September, consumer prices increased by 0.3% compared with August, the biggest rise in the monthly rate for this month since 2021. This is the eighth consecutive month with a positive monthly rate, following the 0.4% fall recorded in January.
The Harmonised Index of Consumer Prices (HICP), used for European comparisons, pushed its annual rate up by four tenths, to 5%, while the core inflation rate for this indicator stood at 3.2%.
The figure released on Tuesday is provisional. The INE will publish the final September reading on 14 October.

Swiss allocate funding for research into cultural artefacts

Swiss allocate funding for research into cultural artefacts
The Swiss government has provided just under CHF2 million ($2.4 million) in funding for research into the provenance of cultural artefacts from colonial and archaeological contexts, as well as from the field of Nazi-looted art.
The aim is to enable institutions to gain new insights into the provenance of their collections.
Funding for the 26 projects from 2027 to 2028 was awarded following a public call for proposals, the Federal Office of Culture announced on Tuesday. A total of 30 applications were received by the authority. The open call for proposals was also intended to reach out to institutions that have had little experience with genealogical research to date.
In addition to in-depth individual studies, the government also funds projects that lay systematic foundations. These include the cataloguing and digitisation of archives to make them accessible for research. Other projects carry out systematic initial assessments of entire collections.
More
Human remains in museum depots force Swiss to confront colonial legacy
Focus on colonial contexts
According to the press release, one focus of the funded projects is on examining collections from colonial contexts. The aim is to lay the groundwork for further investigations and potential dialogues regarding repatriation. Several projects are being carried out in collaboration with partner institutions and communities of origin.
The Natural History Museum in Basel, for example, is investigating the provenance of 189 Indonesian human remains in collaboration with an Indonesian university. A joint project involving nine Swiss museums, including the Museum der Kulturen Basel and the Bern Historical Museum, is researching over 6,300 artefacts from Cameroon.
More
Why are human remains from the colonial era stored in Swiss museums?
Another key area is research into Nazi-looted art, the Federal Office of Culture noted. Several art museums are carrying out projects on works with unclear provenance during the Nazi era. At the Kunstmuseum Basel, for example, the provenance of 336 drawings dating from 1933 to 1945, which may have a problematic provenance, is being investigated in greater depth.
This funding forms part of the 2025–2028 Culture Programme and is based on the Cultural Promotion Act.

The horseshoe alliance: How America’s hard-left, far-right are converging on key issues
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-29
12:22:45 UTC
21:22:45 KST

The political divide in a deeply polarised American society is becoming increasingly blurred as the country heads to crucial midterm elections that could impact the balance of power in Congress.
Progressive lawmakers with positions typically associated with the hard-left end of the political spectrum now find themselves in agreement with far-right commentators on a range of issues that have otherwise divided US society for decades.
Be it Israel’s genocidal war on Gaza, unconditional military aid to Tel Aviv, yet another US war in the Middle East, the unrestrained power of AI platforms, or the accountability of those involved in Jeffrey Epstein’s paedophilia ring, the two opposite sides of the US political spectrum have taken increasingly identical positions.
The convergence of the ideological opposites has a textbook name: the horseshoe alliance.
It’s a theory derived from the U-shaped horseshoe – where the hard-left and the far-right bend toward each other and, on some key issues, stand closer to one another, far away from the political centre.
The so-called horseshoe alliance in the US is most visible on the issue of Israel’s relentless war in Gaza.
A Pew poll found earlier this year that six in every 10 Americans held an unfavourable view of Israel, including large majorities of Democrats and a rising share of Republicans under the age of 50.
Similarly, a Gallup poll showed that more Americans now sympathised with Palestinians than with Israelis – a first since the polling firm began asking this question in 2001.
Josef Gregory Mahoney, a professor of politics and international relations at East China Normal University in Shanghai, explains the shift through the prism of religion.
“What leads an American Catholic, an American Protestant, an American Jew, or an agnostic or atheist to support or oppose genocide in Gaza can be influenced by personal perspectives on religion,” he tells TRT World.
He says that political commentator Tucker Carlson – who has gained a massive following in the Global South because of his highly critical view of Israel and its expansionist policies – is an Episcopalian Christian who “publicly lauds Catholicism”.
“Both churches, distinct from white evangelicals, have expressed reservations about what Israel has done in Gaza,” he says.
Some American Jews object “either from similar moral concerns” or because they worry that Zionist excesses undermine Israel’s long-term security, he says.
“Most Americans are not that different from each other. It’s often the case that identity politics plays up those differences in extreme ways,” he says.
Douglas Rossinow, a history professor at Metro State University in Minnesota, says the political shift is generational, but other factors have also contributed to it.
Older members of the Democratic Party have indeed changed their view of Israel, he tells TRT World.
“For the Democrats, it is the party elites versus the party supporters on a popular level where Israel/Palestine is concerned,” he says.
That shift in public sentiment has finally reached Congress. In July, the House of Representatives rejected an amendment by Congressman Thomas Massie of Kentucky to end $3.3 billion in aid to Israel.
The move failed, but as many as 104 Democrats voted for the cut – a nearly three-fold increase from only 37 Democrats who backed a similar effort only two years ago.
According to Mahoney, the political overlap matters because it punctures the old claim that criticism of Israel’s war is a “fringe” position.
But he warns that the shift should not be construed as a new policy altogether.
“MAGA as a governing project is not an anti-Zionist project,” he says, while referring to the make-America-great-again movement that helped bring the Republican Party to power.
“Parts of it will still arm Israel… Other parts will say America First and mean: stop writing the cheques,” he says.
“Palestine should treat the second group as a tactical opening, not as a comrade,” he adds.
Rossinow says the future of US-Israel relations remains uncertain despite the emerging horseshoe alliance.
More important than any left-right partnership is the “broader alienation” of the general public from Israel, he notes.
“The Republicans have not faced as serious a backlash on this issue from primary voters yet, despite the prominence of Tucker (Carlson) and (Steve) Bannon,” he says, while referring to the two far-right pundits, who have railed against Israeli premier Benjamin Netanyahu for influencing US foreign policy.
Iran war: A betrayal of America First?
The Iran war is another flashpoint where the far-right and hard-left seem to be converging.
Isolationist voices on the Republican right have called the war a betrayal of “America First” because they believe Washington acted solely to protect Israeli interests.
On the left, anti-war progressives have opposed it as another imperial project meant to reorganise countries thousands of miles away.
Polls show the war is unpopular with a majority of Americans and especially with younger Republican voters.
But Mahoney warns against confusing this phenomenon with any well-thought-out strategy.
“They share a refusal to open another expensive war, while the domestic order is already straining,” he notes.
The overlapping positions in the two camps can “cancel a march to Tehran in a given month”, but are not enough to lift sanctions or produce a permanent settlement.
Rossinow describes the Iran war as one more source of “bitter disillusionment” among MAGA supporters, who had believed earlier Republican promises of non-intervention in the Middle East.
“The war against Iran was another betrayal,” he says.
United against AI oligarchs
The newest meeting point for the far-right and hard-left in the US is Big Tech.
Bannon, the far-right strategist, and Senator Bernie Sanders, a self-declared democratic socialist, spoke back-to-back at the same Washington conference on September 15 to condemn AI “oligarchs” and demand tighter control of the emerging technology.
They did not endorse one another’s programmes, even though each of them criticised the same AI platforms.
For Mahoney, Sanders’s position on AI is framed around “class and accountability” questions.
But Bannon’s scepticism of AI platforms is based on his views about “sovereignty and anti-oligarchy”, Mahoney says.
“They are not building a joint programme. They are hitting the same firms because those firms now sit on labour, information, and the means of political speech,” he says.
More than an electoral tactic?
Is the horseshoe alliance part of a tactical restructuring in the run-up to the mid-term elections?
Mahoney disagrees, saying it is not merely a midterm tactic.
“Tactics are there – they always are – but they are not what produced the overlap,” he says.
“There is no joint party, no shared theory of the state, no common programme for Palestine, Iran, or the dollar,” he notes.
What exists is a “conjunctural convergence” that can be “electorally useful” in 2026.
“It is not an electoral invention,” he says.
Rather, the overlap has imperial and fiscal roots.
“The US is having more difficulty sustaining imperial prerogative and paying off the domestic coalition that used to receive the spoils,” he notes.
When that happens, the opposing wings of the political spectrum discover that they can speak on the same stage “without first becoming friends”.
Rossinow says he is sceptical that the shift will last long.
That’s because the patterns of partisanship for party establishments are deeply ingrained, he says.
“Most of those on the US left do not want a left-right alliance,” he says, adding that cooperation on non-intervention, Epstein files, and even AI remains possible.
“But this will be sporadic,” he adds.
For the Global South, Mahoney’s advice is straightforward: do not mistake a crack in the US consensus for a new policy.
“Some Americans notice the moral obscenity. Some notice the fiscal and military overstretch. A few notice both. That is the horseshoe,” he says.
The horseshoe can constrain the worst impulses of the centre, he notes.
However, the horseshoe alliance cannot end Zionism as a political project, or defend Iran, he insists.
“Those remain tasks for the peoples actually under the bombs and the sanctions,” he says.

Uzbekistan’s $1.4b food market awaits Iran

Yet Iran’s share of this market remains limited, and economic actors believe that expanding Iran’s food industry exports to Tashkent requires resolving financial and transportation obstacles and gaining a more accurate understanding of the market.

Among these, food products and live animals, with a share of about $1.4 billion, were one of the main import groups. Notably, imports in this group grew by 45.9% compared with the same period last year.
These figures show that Uzbekistan’s food market is not merely a domestic consumer market; given the country’s population of more than 37 million and its position as one of Central Asia’s trade hubs, it could become more important for regional food exporters.

French hard-right leader accuses opponents of 'total war' after claims of antisemitism

French hard-right leader accuses opponents of 'total war' after claims of antisemitism
- Published
The president of France's hard-right National Rally (RN), Jordan Bardella, has said he will sue for libel after a report published antisemitic comments that it alleged he had made as a young activist.
The Mediapart website released what it said was the result of "several months" of investigation into "dozens of written conversations" Bardella allegedly had in 2013.
With seven months to go before France's presidential elections, Bardella condemned "the beginnings of a total war" aimed at destabilising his party, and RN presidential candidate Marine Le Pen said she had total confidence in him.
The alleged remarks included blatantly antisemitic tropes, and Bardella said they were an attempt to destroy his political career.
Mediapart did not produce screen-grabs of any of the alleged remarks. It said it had "independently authenticated" the conversations, which came from "a bigger documentary base corroborated by witness statements".
But Bardella, 31 – who is a likely prime minister if Le Pen wins the presidential election – said the allegations were a fabrication aimed at derailing the RN's increasingly confident bid for power.
"Everything is going to be done to destabilise the campaign," he told CNews television on Monday night. "Either Mediapart is running this operation itself, or it is being manipulated by interested parties.
"Of course I have instructed my lawyer to sue for libel."
Le Pen said the alleged remarks "seem so weird that they can only be a forgery – one of those dirty tricks for which Mediapart appears to hold the secret".
Among the statements that Mediapart alleges Bardella made when he was 17 or 18 are: "All the banks are owned by Jews"; "The Jew has to dominate other people, crush them and rob them"; and "What they want is a new world order dominated by Israel, with of course Jerusalem as its capital."
Mediapart is an avowedly leftwing website which has exposed a number of scandals over the years, though its targets have been politicians of all stripes.
The French hard right is riding higher than ever in pre-election polls, with the latest this week, from Toluna-Harris, showing Le Pen a clear victor over whatever rival she faces in the crucial second round in May.
According to the survey, Le Pen would pick up 35-36% of the vote in the multi-candidate first round. Her likely opponent in the two-way run-off would be Jean-Luc Mélenchon of the radical left who she would eradicate with 69% of the vote.
But in a stark warning for the political establishment, the poll showed that she would also easily beat the most popular centrist candidate Edouard Philippe, with a score of 57%.
On Sunday the RN received another boost when results of a partial election for the upper house of parliament, the Senate, produced for the first time enough seats for the party to form an official group.
Under Marine Le Pen, daughter of the historic party founder Jean-Marie Le Pen, the RN has made huge efforts to distance itself from the French far-right's antisemitic roots.
Last year Bardella was the first senior figure from the party to be invited to Israel, for a conference on antisemitism.
Today the party regards militant Islam as a pre-eminent threat – a position it shares with many Jews. The RN even styles itself as a "shield for the Jewish community".
The alleged comments from Bardella throw back to a current of far-right thinking that Mediapart says has never been eradicated but only covered up in the new-look party.
Leftwing politicians called on Bardella to resign, and the head of the Jewish umbrella organisation Crif, Yonathan Arfi, said the alleged comments "were an illustration of the limits of the RN's clean-up act".
But RN deputy Jean-Philippe Tanguy said the source of the allegations was disaffected members of the party who had been expelled years ago because of their antisemitic ideas.
"From what I know, it is the antisemitic rabble that were so bravely purged by Marine Le Pen. At the start of the 2010s, they were numerous and well-organised, but they were defeated. These people have always had it in for us."

Iran-Belarus trade reaches $76m in 2025
TEHRAN- On the eve of the Iran-Belarus Joint Economic Committee, the Director General of the Central Asia, Caucasus and Russia Office of the Iran Trade Promotion Organization announced: The value of trade exchanges between Iran and Belarus in 2025 amounted to $76 million.
According to IRNA, citing the Iran Trade Promotion Organization, Mehdi Babaei stated that agricultural and petrochemical products had the largest share in Iran’s exports to Belarus, and added: The 19th meeting of the Iran-Belarus Joint Economic Cooperation Committee will be held with the participation of Seyed Mohammad Atabak, Minister of Industry, Mining and Trade, and the Minister of Industry of the Republic of Belarus.
Babaei considered the holding of joint committees as a foundation for strengthening and expanding mutual cooperation between the two countries and added: At this meeting, emphasis will be placed on developing cooperation in the fields of trade and industry, agriculture, investment, health and pharmaceuticals, as well as strengthening interaction between the private sectors of the two countries, with the aim of expanding Iran-Belarus economic and trade relations as much as possible.
According to him, at the end of this meeting, a memorandum of understanding on cooperation between the industry ministers of the two countries will be signed. Also, meeting with the Prime Minister and officials of the Republic of Belarus and the opening of Iran’s dedicated trade pavilion with the member states of the Eurasian Economic Union at the “InnoProm Belarus” exhibition are among the other programs planned within the framework of this meeting.
Back in mid-August, Iran’s Deputy Agriculture Minister for planning and Economy Affairs met with the Minister of Agriculture and Food of Belarus, emphasizing the development of bilateral cooperation in the fields of agricultural fertilizers, machinery, and joint investment.
According to Mehr News Agency, Akbar Fathi, Iran’s Deputy Agriculture Minister for planning and Economy Affairs, met and held talks with Yuri Gorlov, Minister of Agriculture and Food of the Republic of Belarus, on the sidelines of the 7th meeting of the Policy Council of Agriculture and Industry of the Eurasian Economic Union, held in Almaty, Kazakhstan.
During the meeting, the capacities and areas for developing agricultural and economic cooperation between the Islamic Republic of Iran and the Republic of Belarus were reviewed, and both sides emphasized the need to strengthen bilateral interactions and utilize existing capacities to develop trade and investment in the agricultural sector.
One of the main axes of the negotiations was the continuation and development of cooperation between the two countries in the supply and trade of potash and phosphate fertilizers. In this regard, existing capacities for expanding trade cooperation, as well as examining areas for joint investment in the production and supply of agricultural inputs, were taken into consideration.
The Iranian side, referring to the importance of sustainable supply of inputs needed by the agricultural sector, emphasized the use of capacities of EAEU member states to diversify input supply sources and develop long-term cooperation.
Also during this meeting, capacities for joint cooperation in the field of agricultural machinery and equipment were discussed and exchanged.
Both sides emphasized identifying the capacities of manufacturing companies and private sector activists of the two countries and paving the way for the development of exchanges, technology transfer, and joint investments in the field of agricultural machinery and equipment.
The development of trade in agricultural and food products between Iran and Belarus was another focus of this meeting. Within this framework, existing capacities for increasing trade exchanges in the fields of poultry meat, dairy products, and various fruits were reviewed, and the need to facilitate trade and create suitable grounds for greater presence of producers and exporters of the two countries in each other's markets was emphasized.
Also, the issue of developing trade relations and utilizing the capacities of existing agreements and mechanisms to increase the volume of agricultural and food product exchanges between the two countries was taken into consideration.
At the end of this meeting, both sides emphasized the continuation of consultations and follow-up on the issues raised with the aim of developing joint investments, increasing agricultural trade, strengthening cooperation in the field of inputs and agricultural machinery, and creating new opportunities for private sector cooperation.
The meeting was held within the framework of the programs of the 7th Policy Council of Agriculture and Industry of the Eurasian Economic Union and in line with strengthening the agricultural diplomacy of the Islamic Republic of Iran and developing economic interactions with the member states of this union.

21:17:23 KST

‘KEEP OU-’: Banksy’s powerful anti-Brexit installation to go up for sale
Titled “Keep Ou T” and currently displayed ahead of Phillips' Frieze Week Modern & Contemporary Art Auctions in London, the artwork dates from 2019 and goes under the hammer next month.
It's no stretch to assume that world famous and apparently “unmasked” British street artist Banksy is no fan of Brexit.
In May 2017, Banksy painted a massive mural in the port town of Dover - Britain's main gateway to continental Europe - showing a workman on a ladder using a hammer and chisel to chip away one of the twelve gold stars on the European Union flag.
Now, one of the artist’s other anti-Brexit installations is soon heading to auction in London.
Titled “Keep Ou T” and currently displayed ahead of Phillips' Frieze Week Modern & Contemporary Art Auctions in London, the artwork dates from 2019 and is expected to fetch up to €2.1 million.
The words “KEEP OUT” are painted onto the repurposed shuttered gate of an EU arrivals gate from Heathrow airport. Except the ‘T’ is missing. One of Banksy’s signature rats can be seen using the ‘T’ as a tool to crack the padlock at the bottom of the closed border gate.
Banksy’s “Keep Ou T” seems to express the artist’s disdain towards Britain’s decision to leave the EU and the piece shares a similar sentiment to that of his 2018 artwork titled “Vote To Love”, which had a heart-shaped balloon over a UKIP 'Vote Leave' placard.
At the time, “Vote To Love” was priced at £350 million – a taunt aimed at Boris Johnson's infamous Leave Campaign bus which pledged to save the same amount for the NHS post-Brexit. A decal on the side of the bus made the false claim / pledge: "We send the EU £350 million a week, let's fund our NHS instead". The bus became one of the most prominent symbols of the Leave Campaign and the £350m figure was widely disputed, including by both the UK Statistics Authority and the Institute for Fiscal Studies.
“Keep Ou T” is estimated to sell for £1.2 million - £1.8 million (€1.4m - €2.1m). The auction takes place 15 October in London.

Netherlands demands hundreds of billions in EU budget cuts
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-29
12:15:57 UTC
21:15:57 KST

Netherlands demands hundreds of billions in EU budget cuts
See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results
The Dutch government has co-signed a letter to the EU presidency demanding the bloc’s next budget, which is set every seven years, be dramatically scaled back.
Prime minister Rob Jetten’s minority coalition is one of six so-called “frugal” governments, whose countries pay more into the EU budget than they get back.
The European Commission has proposed an almost €2 trillion budget for the 2028-2034 period, which governs spending on everything from agriculture to defence and funding for poorer regions.
Along with Germany, Sweden, Denmark, Austria, and Finland, the Netherlands is now pressing for a cut of several hundred billion euros from the proposals.
The letter, which has not been made public but has been seen by major news outlets, states: “Our six countries alone finance almost 40% of all Member States’ contributions. While net contributors as a whole are in the minority, they shoulder around three-quarters of the total financing burden.”
An almost €2 trillion budget would represent a 60% nominal increase in the size of the current budget, which, they argue, is “simply not realistic.”
Divisions
 There are 17 other countries, including Spain and Italy, who are insisting on protections for impoverished regions and struggling sectors like agriculture, and want the overall budget raised above €2 trillion.
The Commission has also suggested creating new EU-wide taxes, including a levy on large companies and a tobacco excise duty, to raise capital and ease the burden on countries like the Netherlands. In June, the Cypriot presidency proposed a 2% cut to the Commission’s plan, which the six considered far too small.
Negotiators want to get a deal done by the end of the year, before elections in France, Italy, Spain and Poland complicate the talks. All 27 member states must agree to the budget.
But according to the Financial Times, a diplomat from one of the six countries said there would be no deal this year unless the budget was cut by hundreds of billions of euros.
Ireland, which currently holds the rotating EU presidency, is due to present a new compromise text in the coming days, ahead of a summit of EU leaders on October 15 and 16. European Council president António Costa will meet Jetten in the Netherlands on October 9 to discuss the budget.
Jetten’s shift
 The letter marks a U-turn for Jetten, whose D66 party went into the 2025 election calling for a European budget twice its current size, financed by new EU-level taxes. The same manifesto proposed €750 to €800 billion a year in extra European investment, paid for with joint borrowing.
In office with his minority coalition, Jetten has taken a different line. At an informal EU summit in Cyprus in April, he rejected the €2 trillion proposal, telling reporters the Dutch contribution would “explode” under the plan, according to De Telegraaf. In June he told NOS the Commission’s proposal was “simply not good enough”.
A big part of the reason is money – at the moment, the Netherlands gets a discount on its EU bill. Brussels wants to end that discount, which would cost the Dutch around €2 billion more a year. In total, the plans would add up to €5.4 billion a year to what the Netherlands pays the EU, according to the Court of Audit, the government’s spending watchdog.

Exclusive: EU-wide digital levy might generate up to €25bn annually for next budget
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-29
12:15:32 UTC
21:15:32 KST

The European Parliament's proposed digital levy could raise up to €25bn a year for the next EU budget, five times the Commission's estimate, according to figures shared exclusively with Euronews by MEP Danuše Nerudová.
A digital levy proposed by the European Parliament to help fund the EU's next long-term budget could raise up to €25bn a year, according to leading MEP Danuše Nerudová.
The new estimates put the yield of the Parliament's proposed EU-level taxes far above what the European Commission originally calculated.
Talks are at a crunch point. EU countries are scrambling to agree the next Multiannual Financial Framework (MFF) by the end of the year, and new "own resources" flowing directly into EU coffers remain a key flashpoint.
"We need new own resources to cover the repayment of the joint debt and to fund new priorities in the EU budget," Nerudová (Czechia/EPP) told Euronews.
She asked Parliament's services to assess how much the proposed EU-wide taxes on online gambling, digital services and crypto assets could raise. Their findings differ sharply from the Commission's.
According to the Parliament's estimates, seen exclusively by Euronews, the digital levy could raise up to €25.2bn a year, five times the Commission's figure.
"The European Parliament is calculating with a much broader tax base than the Commission. The tech space also covers, for example, streaming and data processing services, which the Commission completely omitted," Nerudová said.
The Parliament's proposal widens the levy's scope well beyond advertising and intermediation services and raises the rate from 3% to 5%. The Commission's estimate was based on existing digital services taxes in France, Spain and Italy.
"This is a very conservative estimate, even though it's much higher than the Commission's proposal. But the huge difference is the tax base we are using in our estimates," Nerudová continued.
Several member states, meanwhile, have expressed scepticism about a digital levy over "geopolitical concerns", namely the risk that the US government could retaliate with new trade measures.
"These reactions are coming even without the digital levy. We have a lot of tech giants here, running their business all around Europe without paying a fair share. This is the tool to tax those companies, which are not on the same level playing field as the European ones," Nerudová said.
"This is the right tool to raise money for the EU budget in a sustainable way," she added.
The Parliament's estimate for online gambling is more than double the Commission's, at €3.9bn against €1.9bn. It also puts the yield of a capital gains tax on crypto assets at €3bn, compared with the Commission's €2.4bn.
The tax on online gambling faces stark resistance from Malta, home to the European headquarters of many online betting operators.
The capital gains tax on crypto assets is generally regarded favourably, but also as very difficult to implement, as it would be easy to circumvent and subject to the volatility of this market.
Asked whether the Commission could implement the taxes in time for the start of the next budget period in 2028, Nerudová said negotiations were already behind schedule.
"The crypto asset tax might be complicated, but a digital levy is quite easy to implement at EU level," she said.

Spain announces new housing measures after protests over 87-year-old woman's eviction
- Published
Spain's coalition government has approved new housing measures following protests over the country's housing crisis, sparked by the eviction of an 87-year-old woman from her home in Madrid last week.
Ministers met on Tuesday to discuss the proposals, which include a potential ban on evictions until 2030, Health Minister Mónica García said.
She said the measures would bring relief to more than five million people - but opposition politician Míriam Nogueras said the agreement left "small landlords out in the cold".
The new housing measures need to be approved in parliament, where the leftist coalition government lacks a majority.
García said other measures agreed upon on Tuesday included the rolling over of contracts until 2028; stricter regulation of short-term and room rentals; and banning the purchase of housing by investment firms.
"It is time to intervene in the speculative housing market and start striking a balance between ordinary citizens and vulture funds," García said.
Referencing the protests, she added: "Thanks to the mobilisations and the encampments. Without you, this would not have been possible."
But Nogueras, spokeswoman for the pro-Catalan independence party Junts, said: "We all agreed that evictions - where the property is owned by a fund, a vulture fund, run by someone managing millions of euros - obviously need to be stopped."
"Lumping together in this category those who have invested their savings in a flat, a restaurant or a property - putting them all in the same basket - is a mistake," she told Spanish public broadcaster RTVE.
The minority government, which is made up of the ruling Socialists and the junior partners Sumar, has 30 days from the decree's publication to reach an agreement in parliament. Congress will vote on the proposals on Friday.
Housing Minister Isabel Rodríguez urged political parties to support the proposals - which will be presented in the form of two separate bills - after the eviction of 87-year-old Maricarmen Abascal last week.

Ahead of the government's announcement, the lawyer for Maricarmen, who has become a symbol of Spain's housing crisis, said she would be allowed to return to her home after reaching a deal with the company that owns it on Monday.
Abascal, who was admitted to hospital after being forcibly removed from the apartment on a stretcher, was unable to attend the meeting and is yet to sign the deal.
In the north-eastern city of Zaragoza, another woman's eviction was temporarily suspended on Tuesday, the European Pressphoto Agency reported.
Esmeralda Tejero, 51, has lived in a flat in the city for eight years with her 11-year-old daughter, but stopped paying her rent some time ago as she could not afford it on top of her daily living costs, she told Catalan newspaper el Periódico on Monday.
Protests calling for housing relief measures broke out last week in Madrid and have spread to other cities including Barcelona, Seville, Malaga and Cadiz.
Thousands marched through the capital on Saturday demanding stronger protection for tenants in the face of a housing shortage and soaring rents.
They have warned that they would continue to protest if the government did not meet their demands.
The Bank of Spain estimates the country is short of 700,000 homes, based on the gap between demand and new construction.
House prices have risen by 12.2% in the past year, according to figures for the second quarter of 2026 from national statistics institute INE.
The shortage in rental housing means that costs rose by 8.5% in 2025, according to real estate firm Idealista, with Madrid alone seeing an increase of 9.7% in rents. It said Barcelona and Madrid were Spain's most expensive cities to rent a home, at €23.8 per square metre and €22.7 per square metre respectively.

Private sector’s 5 demands for expansion of export
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-29
12:13:08 UTC
21:13:08 KST

Private sector’s 5 demands for expansion of export
TEHRAN- A member of the Iran Chamber of Commerce, emphasizing that the main problem of Iran’s exports is not a lack of production capacity, deemed it necessary to reform trade processes, reduce transaction costs, and create infrastructure for a sustainable presence in foreign markets.
Shahla Amouri, President of the Ahvaz Chamber of Commerce, Industries, Mines and Agriculture, said that the problem of Iran’s exports is not a lack of production capacity; the problem is the inability to convert this capacity into a sustainable presence in the market. An economy that has supply capacity—from energy and raw materials to industrial and agricultural products—can use foreign trade for growth when an Iranian firm can deliver its product to the customer at a predictable cost, through a clear process, and in competitive time. The gap between these two points is where a significant part of Iran’s economic advantages is eroded.
Between producing a good and selling it sustainably in a foreign market lies a chain of decisions and processes: from financing and regulations to transportation, standards, insurance, market information, and distribution networks. Weakness in any link destroys part of the advantage created at the production stage.
In today’s trade, a foreign customer does not buy only goods; they also buy reliability. Continuous supply, consistent quality, on-time delivery, predictable prices, and after-sales services are part of the value of a transaction. Therefore, successful export is not the result of a single deal; it is the result of building trust and continuity in a trade relationship.
Khuzestan is a clear example of this reality. Having ports, a land border with Iraq, access to open waters, and diverse industrial and agricultural capacities has placed this province in a position where it can be one of the drivers of the country’s regional trade. But geography becomes an economic advantage only when infrastructure and trade governance can turn this capacity into an efficient path for firm activity.
Meanwhile, one of the less-seen issues is the difference between “the possibility of accessing the market” and “the ability to remain in the market.” The initial presence of a good in a foreign market may be formed by a single deal, but its continuation depends on understanding consumer behavior, standards, competitors’ prices, distribution channels, import regulations, and supplier credibility. Many small and medium-sized firms do not have regular and usable access to this information.
For this reason, trade development policy must move beyond providing general information and toward trade intelligence. A firm must know, in each target market, what product with what specifications, through what route, and to which customers can be offered. This information must be up-to-date, practical, and convertible into an economic decision.
On the other hand, the country’s foreign trade structure still faces a multiplicity of processes and scattered responsibilities. In a single chain, an exporter encounters multiple institutions and regulations, while the performance of these institutions has not always been designed around a common goal. The result is increased friction along a path that should be predictable for firms.
To reform this situation, five actions must be pursued as a single package: First, reducing administrative friction by integrating systems, exchanging information among agencies, and eliminating parallel controls; second, managing trade time and cost by setting specific indicators for core processes and continuously measuring performance; third, creating shared services for small and medium-sized firms in cargo consolidation, warehousing, packaging, transportation, and specialized consulting; fourth, launching a market intelligence system in border provinces to provide up-to-date information on demand, regulations, competitors, and distribution networks; and fifth, creating a clear mechanism for resolving trade problems by designating the responsible agency, a response deadline, and an evaluable result.
These five axes are in fact five links in a single reform: simplifying the path, reducing transaction costs, enabling the presence of small firms, gaining a more accurate understanding of the market, and turning unresolved issues into cases with a designated responsible party and timeframe.

In a decisive move that signals a new phase in regional economic integration, Iran and the Republic of Azerbaijan are rapidly expanding their bilateral trade and transit cooperation through a series of high-level agreements, infrastructure projects, and customs facilitation measures. The momentum, driven by political will at the highest levels and supported by tangible results at border crossings, positions the two neighbors as strategic partners in connecting the Caucasus, Central Asia, and the Persian Gulf.
At the heart of this economic rapprochement lies the Bileh Savar border crossing in Iran's northwestern Ardabil Province—a 24/7 customs post that has emerged as a vital artery for trade. Over the past year alone, the crossing recorded $268 million in exports, demonstrating its growing capacity to handle increased commercial volumes. This figure is particularly noteworthy given that the period coincided with external pressures and regional instability, underscoring the resilience of Iran's border economy and its ability to maintain trade flows even under challenging circumstances.
