Two former Hungarian ministers detained over suspected bribery and misuse of public funds
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-29
12:09:56 UTC
21:09:56 KST

Two ministers in Viktor Orbán’s former far-right government suspected separately of misusing millions of euros of public funds and taking millions more in bribes have been detained, hours after Hungarian MPs voted to lift their immunity.
Prosecutors said on Tuesday that Balázs Hankó, Orbán’s culture minister and still an MP in the former prime minister’s nationalist Fidesz party, was taken into custody late on Monday. Hankó is suspected of misappropriation of funds. He has denied any wrongdoing.
Miklós Seszták, an MP from Fidesz ally KDNP who served as minister for national development between 2014 and 2018, was also detained on Monday as part of an investigation into alleged bribery. He too has denied wrongdoing.
“Yesterday was an important day,” said Hungary’s prime minister, Péter Magyar on Tuesday. His Tisza party swept to victory in April elections promising to investigate alleged corruption and abuse of office during Orbán’s 16-year rule.
“After decades of lies, for the first time, many millions of Hungarians could experience what real regime change and equality before the law really mean, Magyar said on social media. “Hungary is no longer a country without consequences.”
The arrests came hours after Hungary’s parliament on Monday voted to suspend Hankó and Seszták’s immunity – but also that of Magyar, who had asked for his to be lifted so he could clear himself of what he called a “character assassination”.
The graft investigations into the Orbán-era ministers are the first against senior figures in the former government. Magyar, meanwhile, is accused of snatching a phone from a man filming him in a nightclub in 2024 and throwing it into the Danube River.
The prime minister has denied his conduct amounted to theft and called the case, which involves a damages claim of €300 (£260), a “sham”. He said he took responsibility for his actions but denied committing a crime and criticised prosecutors for “conflating” the ex-ministers’ corruption cases with “an attempted political character assassination”.
Magyar has repeatedly said that in recent years corruption and misuse of public funds have cost Hungary between 8% and 10% of its GDP under successive governments led by Orbán, who has repeatedly denied allowing rampant corruption and outright theft of public money during more than a decade and half in power.
Prosecutors allege Hankó oversaw the criminal misuse of 17.3bn forints (€47m) of public funds from Hungary’s national cultural fund (NKA), channelling the money to artists and groups with ties to Fidesz and financing its 2026 election campaign.
“My conscience is clear, this is a political show trial,” Hankó said in a live video broadcast on Orbán’s Facebook page shortly before his arrest.
In July, police raided the Fidesz offices and seized the party’s internet servers in connection with alleged “misappropriation and other criminal offences” at the NKA, prompting Orbán to accuse authorities of conducting a sham investigation in order to render his party “legally unviable”.
Prosecutors also suspect Seszták of accepting more than 12bn forints (€32.6m) in bribes and kickbacks connected to vehicle procurements under Hungary’s state bus company, as well as to public construction projects. The case centres on the purchase of secondhand buses at allegedly inflated prices.
Separately, Hungary’s national asset protection and recovery office, the anti-corruption body established by Magyar’s government as part of his anti-graft drive, on Monday announced the first four cases it intends to tackle.
The first concerned “selling political connections to obtain residence permits for employment”, the body said in a statement, and the second case is about alleged corruption involving local council expenditure on park maintenance and public catering.
The third case involved “a state-owned company and state investments” and has links to Dániel Jellinek, a real estate mogul and one of Hungary’s wealthiest businessmen, the statement said.
The real estate firm that Jellinek heads has said he will cooperate fully with the authorities. “Our firm position is that Mr Jellinek has not committed any offence in connection with the matter. We are confident that the investigation will confirm this and that the proceedings against him will soon be discontinued,” it said in a statement this month.
The fourth concerned “seemingly unjustified propaganda and event costs” at the sovereignty protection office, an Orbán-era body set up to monitor what Fidesz alleged was “undue political interference” by foreign entities in Hungary, and abolished by Magyar’s government in June.

Greece: Asylum seekers with rejected claims must leave the EU as soon as possible
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-29
12:08:27 UTC
21:08:27 KST

Greece is leading a group of five European Union countries seeking to send asylum seekers – whose claims have been rejected and who therefore have no right to remain in the bloc – to third countries, such as Rwanda, starting next year, reports Politico.
Greek Migration Minister Athanasios Plevris indicated that the group of five nations—Greece, Denmark, Austria, Germany, and the Netherlands—aims to launch a pilot project as early as the first half of 2027 to send asylum seekers with rejected claims to specific countries outside the EU. He added that the project should be fully operational by the second half of the year, coinciding with the time Greece assumes the EU presidency. The plan is being developed as Europe continues its efforts to manage a decade-long migration crisis—one that has fueled support for far-right, populist political forces across the continent.
Plevris emphasized that the plan does not involve the creation of “return centers,” but rather entails designating specific countries to which asylum seekers can go. He stated that there is no talk of asylum seeker centers in the sense of sending people to closed camps in third countries. If an asylum seeker’s application is rejected, the individual would be able to either return to their country of origin or go to a third country outside the EU.
Two EU diplomats, speaking on condition of anonymity, said that the first agreement would be with Rwanda. Uzbekistan and Uganda are also being considered as potential destination countries.
Plevris noted that
the countries being considered as options for sending asylum seekers already have large migrant populations
and possess the facilities to accommodate these individuals. The EU nations developing the plan are reportedly open to whatever format the host countries prefer.
Rwanda has long been a focus of migration plans. In 2022, the UK announced a controversial, multi-million-pound agreement with Kigali to send asylum seekers who were not permitted to remain in the UK there. After years of legal battles, the plan was abandoned. The timeline proposed by Plevris is ambitious, given that several key aspects of the agreement remain unresolved. The Minister stated that representatives of the group of countries are currently consulting with relevant organizations to establish oversight procedures ensuring that the human rights of asylum seekers are respected in third countries. He added that, naturally, this mandate would not be delegated to others; while the plan’s proponents seek the involvement and expertise of international organizations, the responsibility will rest jointly with all five nations.
The funding required for the plan will also come from the five participating countries; Plevris noted that they aim for a financially realistic project, though the group would eventually like to see active involvement from the European Commission. He acknowledged that the plan does not entail transferring large numbers of asylum seekers to third countries; rather,
it is a means of increasing pressure to boost the number of voluntary returns.
During a meeting with EU interior ministers on the 1st of October, Plevris will also present Greece’s plan for addressing acute migratory pressure, which includes the option to temporarily suspend the acceptance of asylum applications from new migrants. He stated that migration within the EU would only function effectively if migration flows were managed, adding that the bloc requires mechanisms to handle emergency situations.
Greece frequently faces criticism regarding violations of EU regulations and the turning back of illegal migrants. The minister maintained that Greece guards its borders in accordance with international law and will offer no apologies for doing so.
Plevris, who holds strong views on migration issues, has also expressed support for and admiration of US President Donald Trump’s approach to the problem. He further confirmed that the EU is investigating the use of bloc funds for the construction of migrant camps in Greece; data and audit information had been requested and provided by the Greek side, but no further action is currently taking place.

Following a Russian strike on its building, the National Academy of Sciences of Ukraine (NASU) has appealed to the global scientific and academic community, calling for concrete actions and urging against the resumption of cooperation with Russian state scientific institutions.
"On September 28, 2026, Russia launched a direct strike using a jet-powered drone against the Presidium building of the National Academy of Sciences of Ukraine in central Kyiv. This day will forever remain one of the most tragic in the Academy's history, which spans more than a century. The Russian strike claimed the lives of two people. The National Academy of Sciences of Ukraine extends its deepest condolences to their families and loved ones. The entire academic community shares in this loss. The Presidium building sustained significant damage. Fire engulfed the upper floors; people were cut off by the flames and forced to escape through the windows," the NASU statement reads.
The Academy views the strike as an attack on science itself and on the country's intellectual potential.
The Academy emphasizes that international solidarity with Ukrainian science must be backed by concrete decisions today; therefore, it is calling upon the global scientific and academic community to take specific actions.
"Science cannot exist in a vacuum of moral responsibility. There can be no 'routine scientific cooperation' with a state that kills people and destroys the scientific institutions of another country... We call upon academies of sciences, universities, research centers, scientific foundations, international scientific organizations, and publishers not to resume or legitimize institutional cooperation with Russian state scientific and educational entities while Russia wages an aggressive war against Ukraine," the statement reads.
It emphasizes that Russian state scientific institutions, supporting the aggression, cannot return to the international scientific community as if nothing had happened.
"There can be no 'science above politics' when science itself has come under armed attack. There can be no normalization where terror continues and accountability is absent. We call upon the global scientific community to stand united," the NASU added.

A journalist has been crowned king of Uganda’s Tooro Kingdom, becoming the 13th monarch of the Batooro people in a ceremony marking the end of a succession dispute.
Edward Rukidi Kijanangoma succeeded King Oyo Nyimba Kabamba Iguru Rukidi IV, whose death last month from cancer at age 34 triggered a feud after his mother said a previously undisclosed son was entitled to the throne.

Uganda is a constitutional republic governed by an elected president, but four pre-colonial kingdoms remain influential symbols of identity and heritage despite not having political power.
A 21-member committee from the royal Babiito clan selected Kijanangoma, 56, who is Oyo Nyimba’s cousin.
Kijanangoma took the royal name Edward Rukidi Nyabongo I in a traditional ceremony that included the slaughter of a bull and sprinkling of a hen’s blood in Tooro’s capital, Fort Portal.
Nyabongo I walked to Karuziika Palace from midnight to 3am on Tuesday (21:00 GMT on Monday to 00:00 GMT on Tuesday) before taking part in a mock battle for the crown.
Former colleagues of Nyabongo I at the state broadcaster UBC, where he worked as a news anchor and editor, described him as humble and down to earth.
The selection of Nyabongo I as king was widely contested because he wasn’t in the direct line of succession, and the coronation took place despite objections from Oyo Nyimba’s mother, Best Kemigisa, and sister, Princess Ruth Komuntale.
They say the late king left behind a young son and a will naming him as his heir. The claim to the throne has led to increasing disquiet within the community on the selection of Nyabongo I.
The reason for Kemigisa’s withholding of the identity of the heir remains unclear.
Critics said, however, that Oyo’s alleged child would have to have been introduced to the kingdom’s elders when his father was still alive to become a legitimate heir, if he even exists at all.

Iran, WHO join efforts to eliminate human rabies by 2030
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-29
12:07:23 UTC
21:07:23 KST

Iran, WHO join efforts to eliminate human rabies by 2030
TEHRAN – The National Plan for the Elimination of Human Rabies 2026–2030 was formally countersigned at a seminar marking World Rabies Day, hosted by the Ministry of Health and Medical Education's Centre for Communicable Disease Control.
The initiative aims to strengthen national efforts to prevent and ultimately eliminate human rabies through coordinated measures in disease surveillance, prevention, public awareness, and timely access to post-exposure treatment.
Speaking at the event, Dr Jean Jabbour, WHO Representative in the Islamic Republic of Iran, emphasized the need for collaboration across human health, veterinary services, municipalities, communities and other sectors through a One Health approach. He also highlighted timely care after animal bites and dog vaccination as essential measures to prevent rabies deaths
Achieving the goal of zero human deaths from rabies by 2030 requires enhancing collaborations among the health system, veterinary, municipalities, and local communities within the framework of the “One Health” approach, Jabbour stated.
Dog bites contribute to 99 percent of human rabies cases. Despite being fatal, rabies is entirely preventable. However, no single organization can defeat the disease on its own, the health ministry’s website quoted Jabbour as saying.
The official made the remarks on the occasion of World Rabies Day, which is marked on September 28 every year.
Highlighting this year’s World Rabies Day theme, ‘Stronger Together’, he noted that rabies elimination needs ongoing multi-sectoral cooperation among physicians, veterinarians, health staff, municipalities, and local communities.
Referring to the number of animal bites in the country, he said over the past two decades there has been a fivefold increase in the number of reported cases. More than 441,000 individuals bitten by animals were referred to medical centers in the past Iranian year (March 2025 – March 2026). Twenty of them lost their lives, and it could have been prevented. Eleven individuals died without receiving any treatment.
The statistics indicate that, in addition to prompt presentation of the bitten person to medical centers, timely and appropriate post-exposure care and the raise of public awareness are critical, and every case of animal bite must be treated as a medical emergency. When a person is bitten or scratched by an animal, even if the bite looks small, they have to visit a healthcare provider right away, he added.
Noting that approximately four out of every five confirmed rabies deaths in Iran are due to dog bites, Jabbour stated that stray dogs alone account for more than half of these cases, while the rest are attributed to wild animals, including wolves and foxes.
The official underlined the role of One Health strategies for rabies control, including constant vaccination of dogs, effective management of stray dogs, and the promotion of close cooperation among the human health, environmental health, and veterinary sectors, he added.
Lauding the adopted measures in the country, Jabbour said some 729 rabies prevention and treatment centers are operating across the country, and post-exposure care services are provided in all provinces.
Around one million doses of human rabies vaccine and 180,000 vials of anti-rabies serum are procured for the national program, annually; Pasteur Institute of Iran helps diagnose confirmed cases of rabies as well as train physicians and health workers.
The official went on to say that the development of a national strategic document for rabies eradication is also a significant step toward aligning Iran with the global goal of “zero human deaths from dog-mediated rabies by 2030”, adding that the WHO is committed to supporting Iran, through technical assistance and collaboration, in achieving the goal.
Why “Stronger Together”?
The 2026 theme, ‘Stronger Together’, highlights a simple truth: rabies elimination is only possible when we work together.
Expand access to life-saving dog vaccinations.
 
 Improve rabies surveillance and reporting systems.
 
 Strengthen public awareness and education.
 
 Support policies that protect both people and animals.
 
 Build sustainable community-led solutions.
 
 Rabies elimination depends on connected systems. Stronger partnerships create stronger outcomes!
We all have a role to play
From local communities and veterinary professionals to governments, healthcare workers, educators, and global partners, we all have role to play in making a world free from rabies a reality.
Communities: Communities are often the first line of defense against rabies. Education, awareness, and responsible animal care help prevent cases before they happen.
Veterinary Professionals: Mass dog vaccination remains the most effective way to stop rabies at its source.
Healthcare Workers: Timely treatment and accurate diagnosis save lives.
Governments and Policymakers: Strong legislation, investment, and national coordination are essential for long-term progress.
Global Partners: Collaboration across sectors helps share resources, expertise, and solutions that accelerate impact.
One Health in action
Rabies elimination depends on interconnected action. Education, vaccination, surveillance, and legislation cannot work in isolation, they must function as part of one coordinated system.
World Rabies Day 2026 reinforces the importance of a One Health approach, recognizing the connection between human, animal, and environmental health.

Hackers have stolen personal data from 150,000 members of the Jims fitness chain. Parent company Colruyt has confirmed the breach. The data theft dates back to this summer, but its true scale has only now become clear. The chain is now trying to warn all members about potential phishing messages.
Data breach at Colruyt’s Jims fitness chain much larger than thought
Initially, a “malicious party” was said to have been able to download customer data from “a limited group of customers” between 13 and 20 July.
The company added that the accounts affected had since been reset and given extra security measures. Colruyt also reportedly had the fraudulent email addresses and domain names used in the phishing attacks blocked.
Hack larger than anticipated
It is now the end of September, and Colruyt has reluctantly had to admit that it had underestimated the scale of the data breach. That “limited group of customers” turns out to consist of some 150,000 members from 31 of the 85 Jims fitness clubs in Belgium.
Their names, addresses, dates of birth, email addresses, membership details and, in certain cases, bank account numbers may have been stolen. The stolen data is already being offered for sale on the dark web. No passwords or health data have been leaked. Furthermore, data from other Colruyt systems is not believed to be affected.
“The Belgian Data Protection Authority was informed within the applicable timeframes, in accordance with legal obligations,” said Colruyt spokesperson Hanne Poppe. “We are also closely monitoring the situation with all parties involved, including the police, with whom we have lodged a formal complaint.”
Warning email on the way
Jims’ members are also due to receive an email today explaining the potential impact of the data breach. In it, Colruyt warns, amongst other things, about malicious emails or text messages.
“As the data in question was made available online, there is a risk that third parties may attempt to use it for fraudulent purposes, such as phishing via email, text message or telephone. As an active member of Jims, we advise you to be particularly vigilant regarding messages referring to your membership, payments, direct debits, refunds or changes to your account.”

EU announces 5 steps to counter illegal migration and disinformation
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-29
12:06:00 UTC
21:06:00 KST

EU announces 5 steps to counter illegal migration and disinformation
Ukrinform reports this, citing the European Commission’s press service.
The plan’s main initiatives include digitizing border monitoring, stepping up efforts to counter disinformation and introducing tougher measures against human trafficking networks.
The plan proposes expanding the mandate of the European Border and Coast Guard Agency (Frontex) to monitor social media in order to improve its operational response. Member states are to immediately transmit data on any changes at the borders to EUROSUR.
To counter the spread of fake news and disinformation that fuel migration flows, special initiatives for harmonized responses (GARRI) will be established. A flexible system for applying the Digital Services Act (DSA) is also being developed to engage with major online platforms, search engines and partner countries.
The plan calls for the swift adoption of a new sanctions regime targeting individuals involved in migrant smuggling. At the same time, the European Parliament is urged to agree on a position on the updated Directive on combating the facilitation of unauthorized entry, transit and residence and to expand Europol’s mandate.
The EU is expected to step up cooperation with online platforms, banks and digital payment providers to identify and track illicit money transfers by organizers of illegal migration routes. In parallel, the European Centre against Migrant Smuggling at Europol will be strengthened.
The plan provides for the use of trade, visa policy and development assistance as leverage to encourage countries of origin to take back their citizens. It also envisages fully digitizing procedures for returning irregular migrants and increasing Frontex’s involvement in these processes.
Implementation of the five-point plan is expected to be coordinated among the European Commission, EU justice and home affairs agencies and member states following discussions at the October meeting of the Council of the EU.
As previously reported, the EU is considering setting target dates for completing key stages of accession negotiations with Montenegro, Ukraine, Moldova and Albania.

Poland recovers looted painting that once hung in SS officers’ club in occupied Warsaw
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-29
12:04:58 UTC
21:04:58 KST

Keep our news free from ads and paywalls by making a donation to support our work!
Notes from Poland is run by a small editorial team and is published by an independent, non-profit foundation that is funded through donations from our readers. We cannot do what we do without your support.
A Polish painting looted by Nazi Germany during World War Two, and which once hung in an SS officers’ club, has been returned by its owner, who donated it to the National Museum in Warsaw.
“History is coming home,” said culture minister Marta Cienkowska, celebrating the return of Alfred Wierusz-Kowalski’s Winter – Napoleon’s Retreat from Moscow, which she described as “one of the most significant wartime losses in Polish painting”.
Her ministry is responsible for seeking the return of tens of thousands of artworks and other cultural items that were looted during the war and remain missing.
Kolejny sukces restytucyjny! Odzyskaliśmy jedną z cenniejszych i najbardziej znanych strat wojennych malarstwa polskiego. Obraz „Zima – Odwrót Napoleona spod Moskwy” Alfreda Wierusza-Kowalskiego trafił dziś do zbiorów Muzeum Narodowego w Warszawie.

— Ministerstwo Kultury i Dziedzictwa Narodowego (@kultura_gov_pl) September 28, 2026
Wierusz-Kowalski, who was active in the late 19th and early 20th centuries, was a renowned realist painter whose work often featured animals alongside people. His Winter – Napoleon’s Retreat from Moscow had, by the 1930s, become part of the collection of Andrzej Rotwand, a wealthy banker and industrialist.
In June 1939, it was featured in an exhibition organised by the Society for the Encouragement of Fine Arts in Warsaw, which occupied the building that is now the famous Zachęta National Gallery of Art.
However, the exhibition was brought to an abrupt end when Nazi Germany invaded Poland on 1 September 1939. The works on display, along with other items from the gallery, were seized by the occupiers, with many used to decorate the offices and apartments of German officials.
Winter – Napoleon’s Retreat from Moscow was displayed in a club for high-ranking SS and police officers located in Warsaw’s Blanka Palace. The same building also housed Warsaw’s German-installed commissioner, Helmut Otto, and mayor, Ludwig Leist.
No information has been released as to the fate of the painting in the immediate aftermath of the war. However, it eventually came into the possession of Ewa Tsonis, who has now handed it back.
Speaking at a ceremony in the National Museum in Warsaw, Tsonis said that her late father, Michał Stefan Koryzna, had purchased the painting in the 1960s from Desa, a major gallery and auction house, in the city of Kraków.
“I grew up with this painting. It was greatly appreciated and loved in our family,” she said. However, after recently conducting research into the painting’s history, she became aware of its provenance and notified the culture ministry.
Experts from the National Museum in Warsaw confirmed the identity of the painting, which remains in good condition and in its original frame. Tsonis then donated the work to the museum.
“Restitution is not possible without the cooperation of many people and institutions – both on the side of the state and on the part of the owners of the works,” said Cienkowska, who thanked Tsonis for her “incredibly responsible and civic-minded attitude”.
“Such attitudes are still rare but, because we constantly talk about restitution – we search for lost works and strive to recover them – we are increasingly approached by people who own lost objects and feel a sense of responsibility for cultural heritage.”
Cienkowska noted that the culture ministry has so far secured the return of over 920 works, with around 200 more restitution cases currently underway in 18 countries.
Germany has agreed to return to Poland a collection of 73 medieval documents that were looted during WWII.
The culture minister has hailed it as "the most important and valuable return of stolen cultural heritage in modern Polish history" https://t.co/GxHQ8A0jyr
— Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) December 1, 2025
However, that is still just a small fraction of the over 60,000 missing items listed in the ministry’s database of missing works, which includes seven further paintings by Wierusz-Kowalski.
Two other works from Rotwand’s collection – Italian Woman by Anna Bilińska and Mother with Children by Kazimierz Alchimowicz – were also hung in the SS officers’ club during the war and today remain missing.
Poland has in recent years stepped up efforts to secure the return of historical and cultural items looted during the German and Soviet occupations.
In 2022, it appealed to UNESCO for help in securing the return of cultural items that remain missing after being looted by Nazi Germany. It also launched a campaign seeking the return of thousands of items that ended up in Russia after the war.

Ehsan Qaboul, head of the Ministry of Science, Research and Technology’s Center for International Scientific Cooperation, said Iran is firmly committed to expanding ties with Russia, outlining the next steps by Tehran and Moscow to strengthen bilateral cooperation, including the formation of the joint science and technology commission.
Qaboul added that the Minister of Science, Research and Technology is scheduled to travel to Moscow within the next three months to finalize the document on international scientific cooperation between Iran and Russia.
He also announced plans for 500 cooperation programs with Russian universities and scientific institutions.
The programs include holding 100 joint educational courses involving Russian professors, enabling 100 doctoral and master’s students to choose a second academic supervisor from among professors at
Russian universities, and organizing 100 technology events aimed at expanding bilateral cooperation from science and education into the technology sector.
Qaboul further said that 100 joint cultural events with Russian universities and academic and educational institutions, as well as 100 scholarships for Russian students, are also among the planned initiatives. The scholarships will give priority to students seeking to study Persian language and literature.

For his part, Jalali highlighted the Comprehensive Strategic Partnership between Iran and Russia and emphasized the need to boost ties in scientific, technical, and cultural fields.
In February, Yevgeny Primakov, the head of the Russian Federal Agency for the Commonwealth of Independent States, Compatriots Living Abroad, and International Humanitarian Cooperation, voiced his country’s interest in expanding scientific and academic ties with Iran to further technological cooperation between the two countries.
“The main objective of the organization is to lay the basis for developing joint efforts with the University of Gilan. We look forward to recognizing the capacities of the two sides, and exploring ways to implement the collaborations more effectively,” IRNA quoted Primakov as saying.
The official went on to say that scientific ties will lead to the development of joint projects, the exchange of professors and students, and the establishment of collaborative research networks.

Spain agrees on measures to fix housing crisis, ban eviction
September 29, 2026
Spain's coalition government on Tuesday said it has agreed new measures to tackle the country's housing crisis after the forceful removal of an 87-year-old pensioner from her apartment in Madrid last week, sparked nationwide solidarity protests.
Spanish Health Minister Monica Garcia said the housing legislation includes a ban on evictions until 2030, tighter rules for short-term rentals and a two-year extension for existing leases.
"It's time to intervene in the speculative housing market and begin to rebalance the scales between citizens and vulture funds," Garcia, who belongs to the leftist government's junior coalition partner Sumar, wrote in a post on X.
Legislation still needs to pass through parliament
The Spanish government, led by Prime Minister Pedro Sanchez and his ministers, approved the measures after a meeting.
But since Sanchez leads a minority government, he is still dependent on votes from a number of other parties in parliament before the bill is set in law.
Sanchez's ruling Socialists were engaged in talks with coalition partners Sumar and others up to Tuesday.
Socialist Housing Minister Isabel Rodriguez is scheduled to address a press conference later on Tuesday.
A case that triggered mass protests in Spain
Images and videos last week that showed Maria del Carmen Abascal — known by her nickname Maricarmen — escorted out of her apartment by riot police officers touched a nerve among Spaniards who've long called for a solution to the housing crisis in the country.
Maricarmen's father had first rented the property in 1956 in Madrid's Retiro neighborhood and she continued as the tenant after her parents died.
Spanish newspaper El Pais reported that Maricarmen had rented the apartment from a private landlord until 2018, after which a real estate company acquired the property and took over its management.
According to the newspaper, the legal dispute between Maricarmen and the real estate company lasted eight years and their latest attempt to evict her from the apartment marked their fourth attempt to do so.
The issue placed Spain's housing market in the spotlight where many long-term tenants have been priced out of their apartments due to an affordability crisis and a shortage of homes in Europe's fourth-largest economy.
Protesters rallied around Maricarmen's cause, especially because pictures of her being taken out of her apartment building and into an ambulance were vividly present across social media.
She is a wheelchair user too.
People then hit the streets of Madrid in the thousands on Saturday, with many having ended their protest by setting up tents in Madrid's historic Puerta del Sol plaza at the end of the night.
More people, including multigenerational families, joined Sunday.
Maricarmen to return home because of 'social mobilization,' lawyer says
Maricarmen's lawyer on Monday said that she was going to be able to return home, calling the victory a "result of the social mobilization."
"If this agreement we have reached is signed, it will obviously be a better and happier outcome for everyone," Abascal's lawyer Beatriz Duro told reporters.
"Hopefully this agreement, this different way of ending this type of situation, which is unfortunately experienced every day in this country, helps to change the paradigm when it comes to housing in general," Duro said.

Why are garlic presses so out of fashion? | Kitchen aide
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-29
12:00:50 UTC
21:00:50 KST

Why are garlic presses suddenly a no-no? Recipes now stipulate grating instead, but who wants lumps of garlic in their dinner?
Sally, by email
  People sure do love to hate on the garlic press, not that that’s anything new: in her aptly titled essay Garlic Presses Are Utterly Useless, Elizabeth David called them “both ridiculous and pathetic”, while Anthony Bourdain wrote in Kitchen Confidential: “I don’t know what that junk is that squeezes out the ends of those things, but it ain’t garlic.” Fighting talk, indeed.
Christina Soteriou, recipe writer at Ottolenghi Inc and author of Big Veg Energy, however, takes a more balanced approach: “A garlic press is not necessarily a no-no, and there can definitely be a time and a place for it,” she says. “It’s definitely quicker [than chopping], but I’d use it only when said garlic is going into a sauce, stew or braise.” Which is to say, in a dish where those lumps that concern Sally will cook down and dissolve almost entirely.
For Jenny Chandler, author of The Capsule Kitchen, meanwhile, there’s no “abhorrence and disgust at the idea of anybody using a garlic press, it just seems to add extra work to your cooking”. First, you’ve got to fumble around in a drawer to find it, then “half the garlic just squeezes up around the sides of the press, so I’ve got to do it twice to get all the garlic out”. That’s especially irksome given that Chandler is more often than not crushing multiple cloves. “So, in the time it takes me to locate my press and load it with, say, four cloves, I could have just crushed them with a bit of salt on a board under a heavy blade,” she says. And you’ll sure need extra time for cleaning the damned thing, Chandler adds: “That’s an absolute pain.”
Soteriou usually minces her garlic with flaky sea salt “for the absolute best garlic flavour”, otherwise she “almost always” uses a Microplane grater or pestle and mortar. “The flavour is more consistent and mellow,” she explains. “Without getting too science-y, a pestle gently breaks down the garlic cells and releases a rounder, more even flavour, whereas a garlic press gives a slightly more bitter and uneven flavour because of how the cells are sharply broken down.” A Microplane falls somewhere between the two, and of course doing that by hand can be a sticky business. “People think a garlic press stops you from getting garlicky fingertips,” Chandler says, but there’s another solution: “When I worked on a boat many years ago, the owner gave me a bar of stainless-steel soap, which turned out to be miraculous at getting rid of garlic smells.” The sulphur compounds in garlic bind to the metal molecules and wash away under water, and the same works if you brush those garlicky digits against a stainless-steel sink.
As with most things in life, Sally should just do her, though Soteriou does suggest sticking to one rule: “A garlic press for anything that’s going to be slow-cooked, and a Microplane, pestle and mortar, or minced for anything where it will be raw or cooked very quickly.” Just “never, ever buy ready-crushed garlic”, Chandler says. “That’s another business altogether and it tastes awful.”

How gold surpassed cocaine as Peru’s most profitable criminal industry
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-29
12:00:50 UTC
21:00:50 KST

“Halt, stop right there,” shouts a Peruvian Navy Seal, firing warning shots into the air. But the fleeing man pays no attention, scrambling up to the rim of a football pitch-sized crater and disappearing into the dense rainforest as the commandos give chase, swearing and shooting.
Meanwhile, other marines set dynamite charges on a makeshift wooden raft that floats in the crater, which is essentially an enormous pit of opaque, stagnant water. The raft has a diesel-fuelled suction pump motor with thick plastic tubing used to suck up and sift through river sediment for tiny particles of gold.
Soon after, a mushroom of orange and black fumes envelops the trees – and seconds later comes the sound of the explosion, shattering the peace of the Tambopata National Reserve, one of Peru’s most prized Amazon parks.
Located in the south-eastern Madre de Dios region, the reserve is visited by about 40,000 tourists a year, many of whom stay in luxurious ecolodges further down the Malinowski River that marks the Tambopata park’s northern border. But today eight patrols are moving along the river, by helicopter or boat – and every few hundred metres they encounter more evidence of illegal gold mining, operations that have laid waste to more than 500 hectares of the park’s rainforest in the last year, according to satellite mapping data from Amazon Conservation. In total, more than 140,000 hectares have been lost to mining in Madre de Dios – a shocking 97.5% of the total deforestation caused by mining in Peru’s Amazon rainforest, an area twice the size of the US state of California.
Military crackdowns on illegal mining in the Amazon are not new in Peru. But the skyrocketing international price of gold has caused this destructive activity to spread, empowering local gangs and attracting transnational organised crime. “Dirty” gold has become the country’s most profitable illicit industry, even surpassing drug trafficking in the world’s second-biggest producer of cocaine after Colombia.
“Gold prices have risen,” said Gen Víctor Cotrina, the military commander of Madre de Dios, who is leading the crackdown on illegal gold mining. “That’s why, if a miner’s motor is destroyed, he’ll replace it quickly because gold is at its peak price; the very next day he’s back to his mining activities. He’s back at work again.”
For troops used to combating drug trafficking by targeting well-hidden plantations of coca, which is used to make cocaine, the fight against illegal gold presents new challenges as the end product is not an illicit drug but a legally traded commodity, Cotrina said. “The difference is that an open-pit mining operation doesn’t require covert operations, whereas drug trafficking does.” He said previous anti-mining crackdowns had been ineffective due to corruption and patchy enforcement. But now, with “aerial surveillance and military personnel who are available 24/7 to conduct patrols, we are determined to eliminate mining in this region”.
According to Peru’s financial supervisory body, illegal gold mining is the top illicit finance threat to the country. For the first time, the illegal trade surpassed the legal production of gold in the first half of this year, according to the Peruvian Economics Institute think tank, which estimates it could reach as much as $18 billion in value by the end of 2026. The country’s Financial Investigation Unit found that illegal mining accounted for nearly 60% of all investigations in terms of value between 2021 and 2025 – far higher than drug trafficking (8%) or tax crimes (4%).
The evidence is not difficult to find or destroy. Behind the wall of green that marks the edge of the reserve, troops and environmental prosecutors set ablaze a network of well-supplied mining camps, built with timber and blue tarpaulins and stocked with food and beer. In one location they find a jungle brothel with wooden tables, a bar counter, a stereo and a giant teddy bear, a shower still wet with beauty products inside. A lone cockerel crows as the abandoned camps go up in flames.
But during four days of operations in late August, prosecutors arrested just a handful of suspects. Two women had been left behind by the fleeing miners: Andrea, 30, wept as she begged the officers not to arrest her, explaining she was a single mother who had been working as a cook and could find no other work to support a sick mother and two children. Liz Compi, 20, was found sitting on a boat with her one-year-old son. She said she had taken the job as a cook for $450 a month after being abandoned by her partner and sacked from a previous job.
Authorities took both women back to the city and released them. Ronal Flores, a deputy prosecutor for Peru’s Office of the attorney Ggeneral who helped to rescue Compi, said it was pointless to arrest most workers at the camps as they tended to have no knowledge of the workings of the much bigger illicit enterprise. Many are left behind to sink motors in the river to avoid detection; even hours later, the machines can be winched up with pulleys and put back to work.
“In these places, the big fish – the owners – are rarely caught. It’s usually the low-level operatives who we find,” said Flores, a short, energetic man with a black moustache who led the operations on behalf of the Public Prosecutor’s Office backed by the US non-profit Global Conservation. He admitted that they could only slow the pace of the rainforest’s destruction, but that the state agencies lacked the budget to maintain the intensity of raids, even though the military destroyed and seized an estimated $500m in machinery, supplies and illegal dredgers, according to government figures.
Flores said the raids had destroyed about 150 mining barges and motors in the Amazon park, but that was “nothing compared to the magnitude of the damage being caused within the reserve”.
A single mining dredger, operating 24 hours a day, can produce as much as 50 grams of gold – which, with the price of gold at more than $4,650 a troy ounce in late August (having peaked at roughly $5,600 an ounce in late January), could fetch more than $6,000 in Madre de Dios.
Since the beginning of Covid-19 pandemic, the price of gold has tripled. Tens of thousands of miners have poured into protected Amazon parks and Indigenous reserves, stripping away vast tracts of rainforest and leaving behind a denuded, pocked terrain, stagnant pools and disrupted river courses. Mercury is the cheapest and easiest way to extract gold because it binds with the particles in the river sediment. As a result, an estimated 180 tonnes of the toxic metal contaminates Peru’s waterways every year, poisoning wildlife and damaging human health, particularly among Indigenous communities that depend principally on freshwater fish as their main protein source.
The latest raids, dubbed Operación Mercurio II, follow on from an earlier iteration, Operación Mercurio, which began in 2019 and achieved a 62% overall reduction in illegal mining deforestation, including a 92% drop in the most critical illegal hub, La Pampa. But the miners returned to La Pampa and deforestation surged, while extortion and hired killings spiralled as a local gang, Los Guardianes de la Trocha, took control of the $1bn trade.
The dirty gold departs Peru as contraband to Bolivia and Brazil, but much of it is laundered into the legal trade via a controversial registration system called Reinfo. The system, in theory, should bring informal miners into the legal economy, but critics say it allows them to continue working without environmental permits and laundering illegal gold through formal companies. The trade is so lucrative that members of Congress have backed five repeated extensions of Reinfo, despite pushes to reform or eliminate the registry.
“The government’s response is moving very slowly,” said Flores after another day of relatively fruitless jungle raids, destroying camps that are likely to spring back up soon after. “Meanwhile, illegal mining operates 24 hours a day. The miners measure time in grams, not minutes, so we need to rethink how we investigate mining,” he said. “Unfortunately, as we can see today, they are getting the better of us.”

Stop shaming people for using AI. Start organizing to prevent our obsolescence | Garrison Lovely
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-29
12:00:50 UTC
21:00:50 KST

I don’t need to tell you that people hate AI. The list of grievances is long: slop, cheating, bias, enfeeblement, electricity bills, environmental destruction, exploitation, theft, cybercrime, doom. But resistance to the technology has often taken the form of shaming people for personally using it, with precious little organizing against the companies building the machines. This is perplexing, given that those companies are attempting to render us obsolete.
The executives may contest this framing, offering some bromides about how AI will augment human work or how we’ll simply find new jobs to do. But their clear goals are to create systems that so clearly surpass our abilities that we will have little hope of competing.
OpenAI defines its north star of artificial general intelligence (AGI) as “a highly autonomous system that outperforms humans at most economically valuable work”. And the Anthropic CEO, Dario Amodei, writes: “AI isn’t a substitute for specific human jobs but rather a general labor substitute for humans.”
The industry’s ultimate ambition, what it calls AGI, is better understood as a universal labor-replacing machine. These systems would be able to do any work a human could do from a remote desk – leaving livelihoods safe to the extent a human touch is preferred, a physical presence is required, or the jobs themselves are legally protected.
You may doubt that the industry will ever succeed in its perverse quest, but we should agree that it shouldn’t even be allowed to try.
We should freeze frontier AI development – that is, the effort to build AGI, and only resume the work when there is strong public buy-in and broad scientific consensus that it will be done safely and controllably.
But realizing this commonsense ideal will require us to get organized enough to overcome the richest industry in history. And that means changing the way we think about AI.
In many corners of the internet, especially on the left, people pride themselves on never touching the stuff – while simultaneously making bold, deeply mistaken claims about its nature and capabilities.
I understand the reluctance to give these companies your money, your data, your attention. But using what is increasingly an indispensable technology is not an endorsement of the industry building it, any more so than using Instagram to advocate for aggressive regulations on social media would be an endorsement of Mark Zuckerberg’s toxic empire.
Moreover, the people using AI are going to outcompete the ones who don’t, bending the world in their preferred direction, while forming a deeper understanding of the technology itself. Bosses will use Claude Code to replace workers, while the leftist policy analyst Matt Bruenig is having it build a publicly accessible, automatically updating database of National Labor Relations Board decisions. If you’re serious about your mission, you should use whichever tools work best.
Most importantly, anyone not seriously engaging with what the technology can already do – and might soon do – is ceding their seat at the table. Sixty-nine active members of Congress have publicly used terms like artificial superintelligence, the Singularity and AI existential risk. If certain techies are the only people willing to acknowledge that the technology’s capabilities have dramatically improved and could pose a species-level threat in the future, that’s who concerned policymakers will disproportionately listen to.
The left’s lack of engagement here is a real loss. Even non-leftists recognize it. Joshua Achiam, then OpenAI’s chief futurist, declared: “The left has completely abdicated their role in this discussion. A decade from now, this will be understood on the left to have been a generational mistake; perhaps even more than merely generational.”
Dean Ball, who led the authorship of Trump’s AI action plan before becoming an executive at OpenAI, declared: “Joshua is right.”
You may be suspicious of political adversaries wishing you were more present in the arena, but they recognize that – on the technology’s current course – this is an all-hands-on-deck situation. Indeed, we all need to reckon with the industry’s race to replace us, but we especially need – and especially don’t have – the left. We need organizers. We need people who can’t help but think about power to teach the ones who never learned to. We need ambition. We need people who believe that better worlds are possible.
The popularity of stigmatizing individual AI usage has been a gift to the industry, fracturing would-be opponents and activating our identities as consumers. BP had to pay an ad agency to popularize the “carbon footprint” to shift the blame for climate change to individuals. When we think as consumers, the goal becomes minimizing our own complicity. We should instead think as citizens: how do we democratically govern this technology in the public interest?
Right now, AI is being governed by unelected, unaccountable tech billionaires, subject to intense pressures from shareholders and the Trump administration. To have any hope of changing this intolerable status quo, we’ll need to build a movement powerful enough to defeat the richest industry in history.
In March, when I finished writing Obsolete, the book this piece draws from, I predicted:
 It won’t be easy, but the ingredients are there for a mass movement unlike any the world has ever seen. Everyone has a stake in how AI develops – a reality that will become increasingly indisputable as the technology eats ever more of the world.
Since then, the dangers have appeared faster than I expected, but public awareness has grown even faster – making me feel more optimistic than ever. The AI story was never going to have a happy ending without deep and sustained engagement from the world, not just the tiny handful of people racing to build our replacements.
The big question is whether we can channel this new wave of concern into effective advocacy. Personally, I think the most promising place to start is at Irreplaceable.org. (I serve on the non-profit board and am donating my share of the book’s royalties to Irreplaceable.) Founded by veterans of the climate movement, Irreplaceable aims to meet people where they are, organize their anger into political power, and build a coalition strong enough to win democratic control over AI. The non-profit is organizing a national walkout to Freeze AI on 20 October. Anyone can join one near them or host their own.
I have no illusions that a day of walkouts will solve our AI problems. But it will bring together people with shared concerns, and some of them will become the friendships that sustain successful movements. Most of all, we’ll need to keep our eye on the ball: the companies trying to render us obsolete, not the friends and neighbors using their products.
- 
  Garrison Lovely is a freelance journalist, the author of Obsolete: The AI Industry’s Trillion-Dollar Race to Replace Us – and How to Stop It (Nation Books, 29 September), and the co-host of the podcast Organize Against the Machine

Brain structure linked to how well patients respond to an antidepressant, small study finds
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-29
12:00:49 UTC
21:00:49 KST

An exploratory study of people with major depressive disorder found that the shape and structure of several regions of the brain’s outer layer, measured before treatment began, were associated with how much patients’ symptoms improved over about eight weeks of taking the antidepressant vortioxetine. The regions included areas of the frontal lobes involved in emotion regulation and planning, visual areas at the back of the brain, and the insula, a region involved in emotional awareness and in sensing the body’s internal state. The paper was published in BMC Psychiatry.
Major depressive disorder (MDD) is a common and often recurring psychiatric condition that can substantially impair everyday functioning and quality of life. Although many antidepressant medications are available, only about one-third of patients achieve remission, meaning their symptoms largely resolve, after their first treatment. People differ considerably in how well they respond to antidepressants, making it difficult to know in advance which treatment will work best for a particular patient.
Researchers are therefore trying to identify characteristics that might help predict treatment response and support more personalized approaches to care. Clinical factors such as the initial severity of depression, duration of illness, anxiety symptoms, and early improvement during treatment have all been linked to later outcomes.
Yingna Li and colleagues at Beijing HuiLongGuan Hospital in China used high-resolution structural magnetic resonance imaging, which captures the brain’s anatomy rather than its activity, along with a technique called surface-based morphometry, to explore whether features of the cortex, the brain’s wrinkled outer layer, could help predict improvement in depressive symptoms after antidepressant treatment.
They also wanted to know whether cognitive improvement is associated with these brain characteristics. The researchers were particularly interested in memory performance. They noted that cognitive problems are common in depression and sometimes persist even after mood symptoms improve. Because cognitive impairments can negatively affect the lives of depressed individuals, finding ways to predict their recovery is also an important goal.
The researchers initially recruited 34 adults between the ages of 18 and 50 who met diagnostic criteria for major depressive disorder, along with 26 healthy individuals for comparison who were matched with the depressed participants on age and sex. All of the patients had experienced at least one previous depressive episode and had not taken antidepressants in the eight weeks before enrolling. Four participants with depression and three healthy participants were excluded because of poor-quality brain scans, mostly due to excessive head movement, and 10 more participants with depression did not return for the follow-up visit. As a result, all analyses were performed on 22 participants with depression and 21 healthy participants.
All participants with depression took a daily 10-milligram dose of vortioxetine. Before and after treatment, they were assessed with the 17-item Hamilton Rating Scale for Depression and the Hamilton Anxiety Rating Scale, two clinician-administered measures of symptom severity, and completed the Repeatable Battery for the Assessment of Neuropsychological Status, a set of brief tests of memory, attention, language, and visual-spatial skills. On average, participants’ depression scores fell from about 27 to about 8 over the course of treatment.
Participants with depression had brain scans at the start of the study and again about eight weeks later, after treatment, while healthy participants were scanned once. However, this study analyzed only the scans taken at the start, because the goal was to see whether brain features measured before treatment were linked to later improvement.
The researchers used these scans to measure four features of the cortical surface: cortical thickness; the gyrification index, which reflects how much of the cortex is tucked into folds rather than exposed at the surface; sulcus depth, the depth of the grooves between folds; and fractal dimension, a measure of how complex and irregular the folding pattern is.
Compared with healthy participants, those with depression showed less folding in the right insula.
Among participants with depression, higher fractal dimension, indicating more complex folding, in the left superior frontal cortex, the right rostral middle frontal cortex, and the right lateral occipital cortex was associated with greater symptom improvement. The two frontal regions are part of the prefrontal cortex, which is involved in emotion regulation and executive control, while the lateral occipital cortex is a visual area. Greater cortical thickness in the insula on both sides of the brain and in the left pericalcarine cortex, part of the primary visual cortex, was also linked to greater improvement.
In contrast, lower fractal dimension in the left cuneus, another visual region, and less folding (a lower gyrification index) in the left lateral occipital cortex were associated with greater improvement. Several of these associations, including those involving the insula and the right lateral occipital cortex, concerned improvement in anxiety scores rather than depression scores.
On the cognitive side, shallower grooves (lower sulcus depth) in the left lateral occipital cortex were associated with greater improvement in delayed memory, the ability to recall information after some time has passed since it was first learned.
To check whether these associations might hold up beyond the specific people studied, the researchers used a technique called leave-one-out cross-validation, in which a statistical model is built using all but one participant and then used to predict the remaining participant’s outcome, with the process repeated for everyone.
In these tests, which also accounted for participants’ age and sex, fractal dimension of the left cuneus was associated with changes in depression scores, though this result was only borderline statistically significant, and fractal dimension of the left superior frontal cortex was associated with changes in anxiety scores. The link between sulcus depth in the left lateral occipital cortex and delayed memory did not reach statistical significance in this test.
“Baseline cortical morphometric features were associated with clinical and cognitive changes following antidepressant treatment in MDD [major depressive disorder],” the study authors concluded. They also added that “these findings are preliminary and should be interpreted with caution, pending replication in independent cohorts.”
The study contributes to the scientific understanding of the links between the brain’s structure and the course of depression during treatment. However, it should be noted that the study was conducted on a very small sample of participants, and the authors acknowledge that because many separate analyses were run, some associations may be false positives and their strength is likely overestimated. Results of larger studies may differ.
All patients received the same drug, so the findings may not apply to other antidepressants, and participants were relatively young. There was also no placebo group, so the study cannot separate improvement caused by the medication from improvement that might have happened for other reasons. Additionally, the design of the study does not allow any causal inferences to be derived from the results.
The paper “Baseline cortical structural features are associated with depressive and cognitive improvement in major depressive disorder” was authored by Yingna Li, Shuping Tian, Siyan Zan, Ruonan Du, Wenzhou Liang, Liying Zhao, and Zhiren Wang.

The night sky is getting 10% brighter every year. We’re forgetting what darkness feels like
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-29
12:00:49 UTC
21:00:49 KST

Every night, I can turn off the lights in my room – but I can’t do anything about the outdoor lights in the walkway or parking lot that leak through the curtains. Living in Portland, where the night is still illuminated by street lights, porch lights and parking lot glare, I forgot what it actually feels like to sleep in darkness.
I was excited when I realized my travels to a residency in south-east Oregon would show me a sky I hadn’t experienced in decades. In the Oregon outback, part of the International Dark Sky Places network, I would be surrounded by 2.5m acres of unpolluted night in every direction.
I sent out a note to the other residents asking if anyone wanted to look at the stars with me. Everyone said yes. Thirty minutes after sunset, we trekked through the tall grass and out on to the dry lakebed. Those of us with headlamps set them on red so we wouldn’t destroy our night vision. We laid down our blankets and looked at the night sky together. There, just over the hills, was Venus. Vega shone overhead. So did numerous satellites which we could tell weren’t natural by their movement. They were so bright my eye was constantly drawn to them.
As it got darker, more stars and constellations seemed to materialize: Ursa Major and Minor, Cygnus, Cassiopeia. By the time the Milky Way appeared, a band of light rising out of the night, we fell silent. We saw one shooting star and then another. I lay on my blanket and looked up until I felt small.
Every year, the night sky is becoming 10% brighter. Eighty per cent of people live under light-polluted skies. And while the UN declared a healthy environment – clean air, clean water – to be a human right, I believe we also all have a right to darkness as well.
This doesn’t mean turning off every streetlamp. But do we really need bright white floodlights at the front of every garage? Replacing lights with ones that are bright enough to do the job – and no brighter – might make it so I wouldn’t have to get in my car and drive for hours to see the night sky as it actually shines above us.
To preserve the darkness would mean rules and enforcement around the warmth of the lights, where they point, and how bright they can be. It would mean not putting in three lights when one would do. If we recognized that darkness is something we need, we’d become more careful about chasing it away.
Some communities have already done this. Flagstaff, Arizona, was the first city to have outdoor lighting rules, adding them in 1958. In 2001, Flagstaff became the first recognized Dark Sky City. Their rules regulate how much light can be used, what type, and where it can shine.
Other cities and towns in the US and abroad have followed. New York state is now considering a Dark Skies Protection Act, which would add restrictions on outdoor lighting – including some that would affect the city that never sleeps. All it takes to preserve the night near you is the desire to protect it with a new zoning law or, perhaps, a rule for how bright car headlights can be.
Access to darkness is about more than stargazing. The night is its own habitat. Artificial lights confuse animals who use the moon to navigate, whether they’re baby sea turtles navigating toward a parking lot instead of the ocean or moths who fly in circles around a lightbulb. Lightning bugs and frogs need darkness to complete their courtship rituals. Migrating birds get thrown off course by the bright lights of big cities.
But the effects of light pollution linger even after it’s daylight again, becoming visible. Research has shown light pollution is breaking the relationship between plants and pollinators, changing the time of year trees break into flower, and disrupting circadian rhythms for all living creatures. This includes humans. Whether it’s artificial lights indoors or creeping in through the window at night, studies have found that we need darkness in order to rest, recover and stay healthy.
Most light pollution comes from street lights, buildings, parking lots and sports courts left lit all night but increasingly there’s a threat of light pollution coming from the sky itself. Even if the rules of the Dark Sky Sanctuary let me see the Milky Way that night on the lake, it couldn’t stop the growing number of satellites from mixing in with the starry night.
Dark-friendly practices such as making sure nightlights are targeted and shielded won’t do anything about the more than 11,000 Starlink satellites currently in orbit, or a company who wants to provide artificial sunlight on demand, using satellites to illuminate areas of the Earth as large as three miles. Things we launch into space aren’t required to have an environmental review even when they affect life back on Earth.
The stars hold our history. They have been maps, calendars, omens and landmarks. When it was dark, the constellations helped people find their way home. Now the night sky is an attraction people travel to. In our urbanizing world, the night sky is out of reach for those who don’t have the time or resources to find it.
Darkness is becoming another luxury, but it can belong to all of us again. A right to darkness doesn’t mean every city would look like the rural Oregon outback but it might make a few more stars visible after dark, let a few more creatures rest, give all of us a reason to look up again – no matter where we are.

DOE announces deadline for National Environmental Award
TEHRAN – The Department of Environment (DOE) has set November 6 as the deadline for submitting entries for the 14th National Environmental Award, which will be held this year under the theme “Healthy Environment, Sustainable Future,”.
The award aims to develop the culture for environmental conservation, promote environmental values, identify successful people and effective methods, encourage creativity, support innovative environmental solutions, and raise public participation, doe.ir reported.
The projects that focus on preventing pollution and environmental degradation while lowering costs, safeguarding and restoring endangered plant and animal species or a valuable habitat that is facing degradation, conducting studies on effective strategies for preserving the environment, enhancing environmental awareness, and implementing measures to prevent incidents arising from environmental crises are among the projects to receive the award.
‘Environmental protection is a pillar of national and social security’
In September, President Masoud Pezeshkian described environmental protection as a key pillar of the country’s national and social security, stressing that the preservation of natural resources must be addressed within this framework.
Speaking at a meeting with environmental experts on September 3rd, Pezeshkian said the government was prepared to create the necessary conditions for using the plans, ideas and initiatives put forward by environmental activists and specialists.
He added that the government would support scientific and practical solutions for addressing the country’s real environmental challenges, IRNA reported.
Pezeshkian emphasized that tackling environmental problems requires close cooperation among the government, universities, the private sector, civil society organizations and the public.
“This shared capacity must be used to move toward sustainable governance, balanced development and the protection of the country’s resources for future generations,” he said.
The president also identified education and public awareness as key elements in reforming consumption patterns and protecting the environment.
“If we invest in properly educating the next generation, we are in fact investing in the future of the country,” Pezeshkian said.
He warned that without educating children and teenagers from an early age about environmental protection, efficient use of water and electricity, energy management and social responsibility toward natural resources, future generations could repeat patterns of environmental degradation, even if significant resources are spent on environmental protection today.
Pezeshkian stressed that environmental awareness should begin at school, saying that teaching students how to use water, electricity, gas, and other natural resources responsibly should be incorporated into the educational and developmental process.
Other issues raised during the meeting included prioritizing the reuse and recycling of water, strengthening the role of environmental experts in agriculture and water-use efficiency, preventing excessive extraction of mineral resources, and making greater use of universities in addressing environmental challenges.
In June, the head of the Department of Environment (DOE), Shina Ansari, elaborated on different measures taken to address environmental challenges, saying that national security cannot be realized without paying attention to the environment.
Environmental degradation, air and soil pollution, and the destruction of protected areas have shown that environmental security is directly tied to national security, she noted.
Over the past Iranian year (March 2025 –March 2026), apart from environmental challenges like drought, climate change, and dust storms, the country went through complicated situations experiencing the irreparable harms caused by the two imposed wars (the 12-day war in June last year, and the recent 40-day war) on civilian, cultural, and environmental infrastructures, Ansari said.
“Despite all these challenges, the Department of Environment has stood by the people and the country, striving to mitigate the adverse impacts and strengthen national security.”
The national resilience depends on environmental security. Without clean water, air, fertile soil, and sustainable biodiversity, it is impossible to talk about sustainable security, Ansari added.

Argentina demands UK halt Falklands oil project
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-29
12:00:39 UTC
21:00:39 KST

Argentina demands UK halt Falklands oil project
Argentinian President Javier Milei has demanded that Britain cease oil exploration near the disputed Falkland Islands, threatening legal action if London fails to comply.
Buenos Aires maintains that the South Atlantic archipelago, which it calls the Malvinas, is part of its territory, despite it being administered by the UK since 1833.
The two countries fought a brief war over the territory in 1982 after Argentine forces seized the islands and Britain sent a naval task force to retake them. In a 2013 referendum, Falkland Islanders overwhelmingly voted to remain a British overseas territory, a vote Buenos Aires does not recognize as resolving the sovereignty dispute.
Milei said in a post on X on Monday that he had given instructions to the Foreign Ministry and legal experts “to initiate international arbitration against the UK for the illegal plundering of our resources through the Sea Lion Project.”
“If in 2 weeks the UK does not halt the illegitimate exploitation, we will go to the International Tribunal for the Law of the Sea (ITLOS),” he warned.
The Sea Lion oil field lies around 220 km (137 miles) north of the Falkland Islands and is estimated to hold around 1.7 billion barrels of oil. British company Rockhopper and Israeli firm Navitas, which are developing the $2.2 billion project, are planning to begin drilling on site in early 2028.
ITLOS is an independent court established under the 1982 UN Convention on the Law of the Sea. Decisions by the Hamburg-based tribunal are legally binding, although it lacks the means to make countries comply with them.
The British government has said it fully supports the companies involved in the Sea Lion project, insisting that the people of the Falklands have the “right to develop their natural resources as they see fit.” Rockhopper and Navitas also previously shrugged off Argentina’s complaints about the project, arguing that they are operating under a valid license issued by the UK.
Earlier in September, Buenos Aires initiated sanctions proceedings against 60 people and companies over being involved in oil exploration near the Falklands.
The Argentinean government has doubled down on its claim to the islands after US President Donald Trump, who previously called Milei his “favorite president,” said in late August that Washington’s longstanding neutral stance on the status of the Falklands was under review.
Milei dedicated most of his speech at the UN General Assembly in New York last week to the Falklands, saying that Argentina could “take matters into our own hands” if the global body fails to act against the Sea Lion Project.
UK Defense Secretary Wes Streeting responded by accusing the Argentinean leader of reciting the “same old bogus propaganda” and insisting that Britain has “the ability to defend” the Falklands militarily.

Hong Kong firms lag mainland China on AI adoption amid legacy-system burden: Accenture

Hong Kong businesses are lagging behind their mainland Chinese peers in adopting artificial intelligence, as entrenched legacy systems and a risk-averse corporate mindset slow the city’s digital transition, according to a senior executive at consultancy Accenture.

Millions of Americans Live in a County Without a Surgeon
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-29
12:00:05 UTC
21:00:05 KST

In medical emergencies, time matters. Seeing a surgeon soon after your appendix has ruptured or you’ve been in a car accident can mean the difference between life and death.
But more than a third of U.S. counties have no general surgeons, according to a new analysis published Sept. 28 in the Journal of the American College of Surgeons.
While many people assume that surgeons primarily perform elective procedures, many surgeons in rural communities serve multiple roles, says Dr. Thomas Tsai, medical director for health policy research at the American College of Surgeons and a co-author of the study. In that way, “access to surgeons is the keystone for the broader rural health care ecosystem,” he says.
The study provides yet another data point that rural health care is in trouble in the U.S. It found that 38% of counties in the U.S.—home to roughly 15 million Americans—have no general surgeons, and 30% of counties have no surgeon across 12 different specialties. Even many rural counties with hospitals, which are often called critical access hospitals, have no full-time surgeon.
“The question is, what kind of surgical care is being deferred? How far are people being transferred to receive the care that they need? What does that represent in terms of a burden to patients? And what does this mean in terms of costs to the health care system?” Tsai says.
The lack of surgeons in rural areas could worsen as H.R. 1, also known as the One Big Beautiful Bill Act, is implemented across the country. It includes cuts to Medicaid and is projected to force many hospitals to close.
Overall, access to surgeons was unequal throughout the country: surgeon supply in some specialties was 12 times higher in some regions than others. Rochester, Minn., where the Mayo Clinic is located, has 250 surgeons per 100,000 people, while Harlingen, Texas has just 20.
Part of the problem is that training isn’t keeping pace with demand, especially as the country ages and needs more medical procedures, Tsai says. In other research, the American College of Surgeons recently projected that the U.S. would face a shortage of nearly 28,000 surgeons by 2038.
But there also needs to be more training for surgeons in rural areas so that they create roots there, which will make them more likely to stay in places far from the big cities where training mostly occurs, says Tsai.
Some other solutions could potentially help improve surgical care in rural areas. Doctors in other countries are experimenting with doing robotic surgeries through telehealth, for instance, but regulatory barriers in the U.S. have prevented that here, he says. By comparison, rural areas can access primary care relatively easily, he says, through telehealth and advanced practice providers. What they often can’t access, he says, is specialty care like surgery.
“As the population ages and patients have more and more complex conditions, what they will need increasingly is actual access to surgeons and surgical specialists to address their surgical issues,” he says.

DRC: Early access to care and oxygen decisive for Ebola patients’ survival – WHO

Unknown Publisher
