====================================================================================================

From forests to towns: What is behind Russia’s bear encounters?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-29
11:47:28 UTC
20:47:28 KST

Bear attacks have killed six people in Russia’s Siberian region of Krasnoyarsk this month alone. In neighboring Khakassia, bears approached the town of Abaza last week from so many directions that a senior regional official described it as “effectively under siege.”
Three bears were killed during an operation to drive them away from an area near the town bridge, Khakassia’s deputy head Dmitry Buchenik said last Wednesday. Across Siberia and Russia’s Far East, attacks have left 17 people dead in recent months, according to state news agency Tass.
Russia is home to the world’s largest brown bear population, and the animal has long been one of its most recognizable symbols. But for communities reporting bears near homes, roads and tourist routes, that familiar presence is becoming an immediate concern.
In Krasnoyarsk, investigators are examining whether officials ignored repeated warnings before the fatal attacks. In Tomsk, authorities have restricted forest excursions and tourist gatherings until at least Nov. 1.
The encounters have drawn attention to what is bringing bears closer to people and how to prevent attacks.
A wildlife specialist points to shortages of food before winter, while Russia’s Natural Resources Ministry warns that garbage and deliberate feeding can erode the animals’ natural wariness of humans.
The ministry also urges caution in judging the scale of the problem: encounters are difficult to count, and videos now circulate far beyond the communities where they happen.
Mikhail Krechmar, a specialist in conflicts between large animals and humans, told Anadolu that heightened bear activity was being observed in populated parts of Siberia, including southern Krasnoyarsk, Tuva, Khakassia, Irkutsk and Buryatia.
“All these areas have had a very poor crop of their main fattening foods – nuts and acorns. Without them, bears cannot settle into their dens for the winter, and this is why there has been a mass movement of bears toward human settlements,” he said.
Krechmar said such episodes occur in cycles, with earlier reports describing similar conditions.
“The last time we saw the highest number of bear attacks on people and the highest number of bears coming into human settlements was in 2014, and that figure has not yet been exceeded. There was an absolutely similar situation in 1962. I read the old reports, and I can see that exactly the same thing was happening,” he said.
The Natural Resources Ministry said between 20 and 30 bear attacks are officially recorded each year, identifying 2014 as an exceptional year.
“The only anomalous spike occurred in 2014, when 166 cases were recorded,” it told Anadolu.
The ministry said encounters were harder to document than attacks. People may not realize a bear has approached at night, while those who spot one in the wilderness may tell friends or relatives without notifying officials.
“Videos recorded during such incidents now spread rapidly through the internet and social media, creating the impression that they are happening everywhere,” it added.
While shortages can push bears out of the forest, food around settlements can give them a reason to return.
“We are dealing with unsanitary conditions in settlements and garbage dumps, as well as with people behaving very inappropriately toward bears – trying to feed them and then being attacked by the bears because they do not understand these nuances,” Krechmar said.
The ministry said expanding economic and tourism activity was making food waste increasingly accessible to bears. It warned particularly about animals that have “grown up around garbage dumps.”
“A mother bear brings her cubs to feed near people. This is how feeding preferences develop, and the animal eventually stops eating other types of food,” it said.
According to the ministry, Russia had 307,900 brown bears in 2026, with the largest populations concentrated in Siberia and the Far East.
But the size of that population does not directly determine the danger to people, it stressed. Numbers vary considerably between regions, and an animal’s familiarity with humans is a crucial factor.
“The dangerous bears are those that are not afraid of people – for example, animals that have grown up around garbage dumps, feed on food waste near tourist bases and settlements, or have been deliberately fed by people,” it said.
Krechmar cautioned against attributing every attack to human behavior, however.
Bears are predators, he said, and an encounter can be dangerous even when people have not tried to attract them.
He estimates that between 30 and 80 people are killed in bear attacks each year.
“It may seem like a small figure, but in reality it is a very, very significant number,” he said. 
 
For Svetlana Sidyakina, the encounter came during a vacation near Lake Lama on the Putorana Plateau in north-central Russia.
She and her husband had gone into the tundra to pick berries. She was gathering fruit while he walked nearby.
“My husband spotted the bear. There were bushes there, and apparently we disturbed it. It rose onto its hind legs and stood up from behind the bushes. When my husband saw it, he immediately shouted, ‘Sveta, run!’” she told Anadolu.
Sidyakina said she was so frightened that she could barely turn her head toward the animal, seeing it only out of the corner of her eye.
“And I just ran – I ran at such a speed that nobody expected from me. My husband later said that I simply jumped over every obstacle in my path like some kind of professional athlete,” she said.
At first, she did not know where to go. Her husband’s shouting alerted friends waiting on the lakeshore, who began firing shots into the air. She used the sound to find her bearings. 
 
In Krasnoyarsk, the question facing investigators is whether authorities could have prevented fatal encounters.
Residents submitted more than 120 reports of bears entering populated areas across more than 15 districts, including the regional capital, according to the Investigative Committee’s branch covering Krasnoyarsk and Khakassia.
Despite those warnings, investigators alleged, local authorities failed to take measures to regulate the bear population or prevent the animals from approaching inhabited areas.
A criminal investigation into alleged negligence is underway.
“The investigation will include a legal assessment of the actions taken by officials responsible for responding to the presence of bears in inhabited areas,” the committee said.
The Natural Resources Ministry said regional authorities are responsible for preventing attacks and regulating bear populations when they pose a threat to people.
Hunting is one mechanism used to control numbers, with regions setting annual quotas based on population estimates, it said. Authorities can also introduce heightened-alert regimes and fines for feeding wild animals.
The ministry said it was gathering proposals from the regions on further changes to legislation.
Krechmar urged residents in affected parts of southern Siberia, where he described the situation as an “emergency,” to stay out of the taiga unless absolutely necessary.
“Not every encounter will end in an attack, but every encounter with a bear is dangerous. I emphasize – every one,” he said.
“A bear that is hungry, that has not eaten for two or three days and sees no prospects of finding food in the future is deadly dangerous, and cannot be scared away,” he added.
For authorities, however, a bear’s appearance near a settlement does not automatically mean it must be removed, the ministry said. The response should depend on its behavior, proximity to people and whether there is an immediate threat.
“The animal can be scared away if it is not showing aggression, retains its natural wariness of humans and has not become accustomed to the same ‘easy food’ it gets because of people,” it said.
That distinction puts food waste and feeding at the center of efforts to prevent further encounters.
For people who do encounter a bear, Krechmar’s recommendations ranged from quietly withdrawing to trying to frighten the animal away, depending on the circumstances.
In areas without a “bear alert,” he advised moving quietly out of the animal’s sight, then allowing it time to leave before departing the area.
“If a bear is coming toward you, try to scare it with your voice. Of course, bears may eat us if the opportunity arises, but humans are not their usual food,” he said.
He recommended carrying a whistle when hiking or picking mushrooms and berries, and suggested that a loud horn could also help scare a bear away.
“Take it and blow it. There is also such a thing as a pneumatic horn, which is very useful because it produces extremely harsh, unpleasant sounds. You can also download some particularly loud, awful modern music onto your smartphone and play it to the bear,” he said.
He also suggested holding a jacket above one’s head to appear larger, saying bears’ poor eyesight could make the sudden change confusing enough to drive them away.
“If the bear has already charged and is directly attacking, then, if you have time, fall to the ground, pull your legs toward your stomach, cover your head with your hands, expose your back to it and pray,” he said.

European Travel Commission CEO: 'Climate change is the biggest threat to tourism right now'
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-29
11:46:47 UTC
20:46:47 KST

While Europe remains the world’s tourism playground, Eduardo Santander of the European Travel Commission told Euronews that the continent needs to coordinate better to tackle climate challenges and congestion.
With Europe being the most visited continent in the world, how can tourism flows be managed in a way that supports local communities while also adapting to the challenges of climate change?
Speaking at the Euronews Travel & Tourism Summit in Brussels, Eduardo Santander, CEO and Executive Director at the European Travel Commission (ETC), described the continent as becoming a “museum or attraction park” for the world’s travellers.
“There’s nothing wrong” with that, he said, adding that an attraction park or museum can be a “perfect place to be” when it is “well organised” and “well managed”.
In the latest edition of the World Economic Forum’s Travel & Tourism Development Index (TTDI) published in September, European countries accounted for seven of the world’s top 10 countries for tourism, with Spain ranking in third.
This popularity comes with significant economic weight. Tourism accounts for 10% of Europe’s economy, Santander said, adding that in some markets, the tourism industry is "instrumental", including in his native Spain, where it accounts for 10% of GDP. In other markets, he added, this figure jumps to as much as 15% or even 20%.
As such, the ETC chief said that tourism infrastructures, such as accommodation and transport, deserve greater investment, especially as the continent looks to bolster productivity in industries such as the chemical and automotive sectors.
Rather than overtourism itself, he said congestion is a more pressing challenge – ranging from services at airports to ground transportation and bottlenecks at Europe’s popular attractions.
Climate change reshaping the industry
Aside from congestion and pressures on local communities, Santander also explained that “climate change is the biggest threat to tourism right now, by far”.
“We see that trains cannot run sometimes because the rails are expanded because of the heat. We saw this at the cruise lines on the European rivers – they couldn’t run because it was too dry,” Santander said.
“We see resilience becoming one of the engines of European tourism. We have to become even more resilient to whatever is next.”
Here, he highlighted the rise of the “coolcations” trend attracting travellers of the world. Summer of 2026 saw travellers look beyond the usual Mediterranean destinations amid scorching heat waves, in search of cooler escapes.
“We have to prepare for that in a much more coordinated and comprehensive way,” he added.

Ukrainian farmers as of Sept 29 had harvested 34.3 million tonnes of grain and pulses from 7.1 million hectares, or 61% of the projected area, the press service of the Ministry of Agrarian Policy and Food reported.
The average yield of grain and pulses was 4.82 tonnes per hectare.
The harvest of wheat, barley and peas has been completed. Farmers harvested 26 million tonnes of wheat from 5.11 million hectares at an average yield of 5.08 tonnes per hectare, 6.6 million tonnes of barley from 1.48 million hectares (4.46 tonnes per hectare), and 812,300 tonnes of peas from 301,900 hectares (2.69 tonnes per hectare).
Corn harvesting has yielded 789,000 tonnes from 153,300 hectares at a yield of 5.15 tonnes per hectare, millet 75,400 tonnes from 32,800 hectares (2.3 tonnes per hectare), and buckwheat 44,700 tonnes from 34,700 hectares (1.3 tonnes per hectare).
The largest volumes of grain and pulses were harvested by farmers in Odesa region, at 5.6 million tonnes, Dnipropetrovsk region, at 2.76 million tonnes, and Mykolaiv region, at 2.65 million tonnes.
Meanwhile, farmers have harvested more than 8.4 million tonnes of oilseeds. Rapeseed harvesting has been completed, with 3.87 million tonnes harvested from 1.33 million hectares at an average yield of 2.91 tonnes per hectare. Sunflower harvesting has yielded 3.36 million tonnes from 1.66 million hectares (2.03 tonnes per hectare), and soybeans 1.22 million tonnes from 571,400 hectares (2.13 tonnes per hectare).
Sugar beet harvesting is under way, with 296,500 tonnes dug from 5,800 hectares at an average yield of 51.12 tonnes per hectare.

Search for dozens of missing college students in Mexico leads to human remains, 17 new suspects
Twelve years after the disappearance of dozens of Mexican students from a rural university, allegedly at the hands of drug traffickers and police, authorities said Monday they had identified 17 new suspects.
Thousands of people attended an annual march on Saturday in Mexico City to demand justice for 43 young men who were studying to be rural teachers in Ayotzinapa, in the violence-hit state of Guerrero. The students were traveling from Guerrero to a protest in Mexico City on Sept. 26, 2014, when police stopped them in the town of Iguala.
The investigation suggests the police handed the students over to a local cartel. In 2024, an alleged leader of the Guerreros Unidos cartel was arrested in connection with the case.
Dozens of arrests have been made but so far no one has been convicted in an affair that traumatized Mexico and stained the country's reputation.
Only three bodies have been recovered.
Mauricio Pazaran, the special prosecutor in charge of the investigation, said a new analysis of phone calls made on the night of the students' disappearance led to the arrests of the 17 new suspects.
He said the analysis revealed communications between public officials, police officers, individuals linked to organized crime groups, and private citizens.
He added that at a funeral home, investigators found an illegally obtained weapon, a bone and unregistered bone fragments and teeth.
He said a public employee and a municipal police officer had used the cellphones of two students days after their disappearance.
One of the new witnesses "participated directly in the events, but was a minor at the time," he added.
The minor, who was arrested in April, is a member of the Guerreros Unidos cartel, the prosecutor said.
He said a total of 168 people are being prosecuted in the case, 130 of whom were in pretrial detention.
In August, a former governor was arrested for ordering the deletion of security camera footage in Iguala on the night of the disappearances.
Last year, authorities arrested a former senior judge in connection with the case. Lambertina Galeana is accused of helping to conceal videos that allegedly showed the incident unfolding, officials said.
The state's former attorney general was also arrested in 2022 in connection with the case.
Authorities have been able to identify burned bone fragments of only a few of the 43 missing students. The work largely involves searching for clandestine body dumping grounds in rural, isolated parts of the state where drug cartels are active.
 Mexico has been plagued by cartel violence that has killed or left missing over half a million people in just a few decades, according to the government's estimates.

A year ago Andy Burnham had a tough business reception at Labour’s party conference. The then mayor of Greater Manchester, with clear ambitions to replace Keir Starmer, had rattled the City of London with his comment that Britain should be less “in hock” to bond markets.
Returning to the annual gathering in Liverpool a year later as prime minister, the mood is different. Labour is pushing to repair relations with corporate Britain and reassure City bond traders against a jittery backdrop amid the Middle East war.
At a private reception on Monday night hosted by the Confederation of British Industry (CBI), HSBC and National Grid, John Healey told executives the government would do “our bit” to support firms struggling with rising costs. The chancellor said his budget next month would also have fiscal discipline at its core.
“I very much welcome the chance as chancellor to work with you,” he said.
Over bottled beer and glasses of wine overlooking the River Mersey, one executive praised the chancellor: “Can I just say, bloody wonderful speech of yours at conference today. Really determined to achieve success; it went down very well.”
For most bosses, however, there is a caveat: the 28 October budget. Labour gained a reputation after its return to government in 2024 for love-bombing bosses before then raising taxes on firms.
“Ask us on 29 October [how business feels]” said the CBI chief executive, Rain Newton-Smith.
She said that while Burnham appeared to be in listening mode, Labour faced difficult decisions at next month’s budget.
“When you get a change [of administration], you’re sort of changing mid-flight, and that allows you to think what was working, what wasn’t. Without denigrating the previous [administration], they’ve sort of said, ‘“Look, we need to get change, but also, how can we be responsive?’”
In previous years there had been a clamour among businesses to attend Labour’s annual conference – held for three years running in Liverpool – to the point it was jokingly dubbed the “Davos on the Mersey”, referring to the annual gathering of the global elite in the Swiss ski resort.
Starmer had run a strategy before his landslide election victory to win corporate endorsements to burnish Labour’s credentials in City boardrooms. But within his first months in office relations had soured, after Rachel Reeves sprung £40bn of tax increases – centred squarely on employers – in her first budget.
This year, delegates said there appeared to be fewer top bosses at Labour’s “business day”, where executives paid £6,000 a ticket to attend an exclusive breakfast reception hosted by the business secretary, Jonathan Reynolds, followed by a “fireside chat” with Burnham.
However, corporate Britain was still evident en masse, with companies including Mastercard, HSBC and Heathrow among those paying thousands to sponsor fringe sessions and private networking events.
After smaller sessions focusing on policy, executives were ushered into the main auditorium to hear the chancellor’s speech, including Paul Thwaite, the chief executive of NatWest, and the bosses of the “B5” group of leading business trade bodies.
In the auditorium the chancellor gave little away about the budget, despite striking a markedly different tone to Burnham’s “in hock” comment from a year earlier – insisting that he and the prime minister were “in lockstep” in their commitment to balance the books.
“There is nothing progressive about losing control because it’s always working people who pay for it,” he said.
Shevaun Haviland, the director general of the British Chambers of Commerce, said Healey’s speech was “significant” because the chancellor had acknowledged that private enterprise was vital for helping the UK economy to grow.
However, she warned that companies still faced severe headwinds. “[The government’s] strategy is unlikely to succeed while the everyday cost of doing business is still soaring. Firms are being asked to invest while facing a tsunami of rising costs from employment, energy and business rates,” she said.
Lobbyists said there appeared to have been a concerted effort to ensure senior ministers spent time with business leaders and to match them more directly with the relevant sector.
One external affairs chief at a FTSE 250 retailer noted a marked shift in willingness to listen to business concerns, highlighting the work of the prime minister’s special adviser for business relations, James Carroll.
Varun Chandra, who had been Starmer’s chief business investment and trade adviser and who stayed on under Burnham, was also orchestrating meetings at the private CBI reception on Monday night.
One minister said the business leaders they had met in Liverpool welcomed the renewed sense of optimism projected by the new government – in contrast to what some saw as Starmer’s downbeat attitude.
Businesses have welcomed individual initiatives, such as Burnham’s tax cut for pubs and clubs; but are yet to understand what “Manchesterism” might mean if applied UK-wide – and remain concerned about the possibility of tax rises in next month’s budget.
Steve Rigby, the chief executive of the family-owned property and technology company Rigby Group, said Labour’s approach to business had improved from two years ago, but he was reserving judgment until the budget in a month.
“The PM and Jonathan Reynolds are visible and engaged, whether they are listening to our concerns will become clear in the budget,” he said. “You can buy tickets to get into the right rooms, where proper access [to the politicians] is possible – but you have to work hard to get it.
“Really we are in a holding pattern until the budget. The signs are good – we like the boring, no-leaks approach from Healey [so far]. However, businesses have absorbed about as many tax rises as they can, which is what the main focus will be over the next month.”

Rights groups warn Spain’s planned Ceuta deportation decree threatens asylum protections
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-29
11:42:40 UTC
20:42:40 KST

Alyssa Mcmurtry
29 September 2026•Update: 29 September 2026
Human rights organizations on Tuesday urged Spain to abandon a proposed decree to accelerate deportations from Ceuta, warning that it would undermine asylum protections.
In a joint statement, organizations including Oxfam and the Spanish Commission for Refugees said the proposal would create an "exception to the right to asylum based on place and time."
The government has been preparing the measure following a mass crossing into Ceuta in late July, when nearly 80,000 people crossed into the small Spanish African enclave.
El Pais newspaper reported Saturday that officials were aiming to bring the proposal before the Cabinet on Tuesday, although the text remained under development.
According to the newspaper, the Interior Ministry-backed proposal would shorten administrative and judicial procedures to speed up asylum decisions and returns to Morocco.
More than 10,000 migrants remained in Ceuta, according to government figures cited by El Pais.
The organizations warned that the draft would allow some asylum-seekers to be removed before decisions on their applications and restrict their ability to invoke protection against being returned to danger.
They said this threatened the principle of non-refoulement, which protects people from being sent to countries where their lives or physical safety would be at risk.
The groups also criticized a provision under which asylum applications would be ruled inadmissible if submitted more than seven days after notification of a return, expulsion or refusal-of-entry order.
People could miss that deadline because they lacked information about asylum or faced difficulties accessing initial screening procedures, the organizations said.
They also warned that a proposed five-calendar-day deadline for appealing unfavorable decisions would undermine access to legal assistance.
They said it would leave insufficient time to appoint a lawyer, examine the case file and consult the applicant with an interpreter where necessary.
The statement also criticized the removal of safeguards involving the UN refugee agency's role in assessing applications.
The groups urged the government to withdraw the proposal and honor its commitment to implement the EU's migration and asylum pact in the least harmful way possible for asylum rights.

Stevia instead of tobacco – potential alternative for the Eastern Rhodopes
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-29
11:42:24 UTC
20:42:24 KST

Article
Stevia instead of tobacco – potential alternative for the Eastern Rhodopes
Tuesday 29 September 2026 13:15
Tuesday, 29 September 2026, 13:15
PHOTO Yordan Yovkov High School - Kardzhali
Font size
The land in the Eastern Rhodopes has never been easy to cultivate - characterized by steep slopes and small, fragmented fields, its soil has still managed to sustain the local population for centuries. Livelihoods in this region of Bulgaria have long been tied primarily to agriculture and livestock farming, with tobacco holding a special place among the crops grown there.
For decades, tobacco farming was a way of life for entire families and villages. The work began before sunrise every day and continued for months. Today, however, tobacco fields in the Eastern Rhodopes are far less numerous and this traditional livelihood is gradually giving way to other sources of income - such as aromatic and oil-bearing herbs, fruit growing, organic farming, and more.
PHOTO xnews.bg
The first experiment with growing stevia in the Eastern Rhodopes has already taken place, yielding promising results. This herbaceous plant, used as a natural sugar substitute due to its sweet leaves, originates from South America, but in recent years it has also been considered a potential alternative crop, including for regions where traditional tobacco cultivation is gradually losing ground.
Observations by a team from the Yordan Yovkov High School in Kardzhali, the Agricultural Institute in Shumen, and the Agricultural Experimental Station in the Eastern Rhodopes indicate that the plant thrives under local climatic conditions and may have potential as an alternative agricultural crop.
PHOTO xnews.bg
The experiment started after the success of students from the "Yordan Yovkov" School in Kardzhali, who, under the guidance of senior biology and health education teacher Vanya Encheva, grew stevia from seed. In April, the Agricultural Institute in Shumen provided 16 plants of the patented Bulgarian variety "Stella." Approximately 30 plants of the wild variety, cultivated by the students, were also planted in the experimental field.
For seven months, the plants were cultivated at the Agricultural Experimental Station in Dzhebel under the supervision of Chief Assistant Professor Dr. Elitsa Atanasova and her team. The experiment demonstrated that stevia thrives without the use of chemicals against diseases and pests and tolerates local conditions, including drought.
PHOTO xnews.bg
The results are particularly impressive for the "Stella" variety, which demonstrates significantly higher productivity compared to wild stevia. The plants have developed vigorously, exhibiting substantial weight and extensive branching. According to Vanya Encheva, this difference was expected given that the variety was created for higher yields, yet the magnitude of the result exceeded initial expectations.
PHOTO kardjalinews.bg
The experiment will last at least three years. The next important stage is to determine whether stevia can survive the winter under local conditions and be cultivated as a perennial crop. Winters in the Eastern Rhodopes are generally milder but quite variable due to the terrain and the influence of warmer air from the south. Relatively little snow falls in the lower areas and the snow cover is short-lived.
The results of the agricultural experiment are already attracting interest outside the scientific and educational environment, with inquiries for the purchase of produce. However, the current crop is experimental and not intended for sale. Part of it will be donated to an endocrinology hospital department and the students are also preparing a stevia recipe book.
PHOTO kardjalinews.bg
The team is also planning new partnerships, including with the Trakia University - Stara Zagora. The goal is to link the accumulated scientific and practical experience with entrepreneurship and the possibilities of developing a new agricultural product.
The first year of the experiment shows that stevia adapts well to the conditions of the Eastern Rhodopes and the "Stella" variety demonstrates high productivity. The results are to be followed up over the next two years to determine whether the plant can become a sustainable alternative to the region's traditional tobacco cultivation.

To the people voting for Nigel Farage: is this really the finger you want on the red button? | Marina Hyde
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-29
11:42:24 UTC
20:42:24 KST

Another week, another chance for Nigel Farage to demonstrate his literally hysterical leadership inabilities. For a guy who supposedly valorises the wartime British spirit, Nigel would genuinely have had to have been interned during that conflict on account of his serial predilection for spreading panic and unverified information at any given chance. The weekend incident near RAF Fairford was simply the latest in a long line of occasions that make you suspect the poster on the wall at Reform HQ reads simply: “Lose Cool and Start Shitposting.”
Despite its popularity now, the famous “Keep Calm and Carry On” poster from the second world war was almost certainly never displayed in that conflict. Although more than 2m copies of it were printed, it was in fact held in reserve in case a really serious crisis hit. Which, when you consider even the blitz apparently didn’t clear the bar, it is almost impossible to conceive of in our era where comparatively minuscule incidents force certain party leaders into more than 24 hours of madly irresponsible and emotional online incontinence.
Many of you may find you have a low tolerance for shrieks of “We have the right to know absolutely everything, immediately!” from a congenitally secretive guy who notoriously declined to declare the £5m he was given from a Thai-based crypto-billionaire and, since that weird “gift” has been uncovered, has been in a prolonged tantrum that has caused him to snap at any attempts to discover more about what might have motivated it. “None of your business,” ran one particularly ill-judged attempt by Farage to put the issue to bed. “What’s it got to do with you?”
I do find my finger hovering over the “What’s it got to do with you?’ button with increasing regularity when Farage appears on screen to insert himself into moments of obviously active sensitivity. The clearly nuanced and potentially complex Fairford investigation – still ongoing, despite the release on bail of the five men arrested – was a case in point, although on Monday Nigel did attempt to set it out in a madly precipitous video on what he called “the Fairford plot”, captioned: “Fairford proves my point on Iran and the IRGC.” Does it? OK, thanks Jack Ryan.
Anyone who judges that this intemperate psychological liability should have access to the nuclear codes and other top-level information must have a subconscious wish for their answer to the question “where do you see yourself in five years’ time?” to be “living in Britain’s catacombs and distilling drinking water from my own urine”. It’s unclear whether a Prime Minister Farage would just bottle everything or shoot first and ask questions later, but the most likely metaphorical outcome in any given scenario may well be him shooting the wrong person first, then refusing to answer questions later.
Furthermore, as always with Nigel, it’s worth highlighting his insistence on rising to only the occasions from which he feels he might personally benefit. And so it is that he will have an awful lot to say about the horrific murder of Henry Nowak, but nothing or next to about those of Jo Cox or Sarah Everard. Whatever may or may not have happened at Fairford feeds into what we have to call, with heavy irony, his two-tier approach to public life. After all, for a guy who supposedly worries about illegal activity that could bear the hallmarks of foreign sponsorship, Farage strangely didn’t have a lot to say about the Ukrainian and Romanian nationals who were recruited via a Russian-speaking pseudonymous Telegram user to commit arson on property connected to Keir Starmer and on a car he had previously owned, back when Starmer was prime minister. Even after they were found guilty, the Reform leader didn’t seem to find this sort of darkly intriguing activity worthy of comment. Things he did find worthy of comment that same month included disputes over flying the St George’s cross flag and AI scam videos.
The thing about attaining the very highest office in the land is that you have to be prime minister of all the things, all the time. It is difficult to see how someone as cynically selective as Farage could somehow become the sort of leader able to speak for a nation. Or, just as importantly, the sort of leader able to realise when it’s time to shut up for a nation.
Far more troubling still is the gathering sense that Farage is too mentally weak for the role, and would go to pieces in very short order once plunged into the realities of life in Downing Street. Perhaps his declining poll ratings mean worrying may be unnecessary. But he’s increasingly a set of walking psychological red flags: emotional, quick to temper, incapable of rising above the self-serving.
Amazing that there is a psychological screening test to determine whether you are up to appearing on a reality TV show these days, but you could ascend to the office of prime minister without submitting to anything similar. At least 20% of would-be Big Brother contestants are deemed mentally unfit to participate during the casting process each year. And looking at the five main party leaders this week, you’d think a similar percentage had the potential to absolutely implode were they to enter the Downing Street house. Perhaps our politics needs new duty-of-care guidelines, so that the office of British prime minister is psychologically guardrailed to the same level as, say, a dating show like Love is Blind.

Israel bans Arab parties from election: What you need to know
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-29
11:42:00 UTC
20:42:00 KST

Why and how is Israel banning Arab parties from election?
September 29, 2026
With less than a month until the Israeli elections, a move from the country's Central Elections Committee (CEC) to bar all Arab parties from running has ignited a debate about the relationship between security, national identity and democratic representation in Israel.
Should the bans remain in place when Israel goes to the polls on October 27, Arab citizens of Israel, who make up about a fifth of the country's population, will find themselves without their most likely source of representation in the Israeli parliament, the Knesset.
However, the decision is not final, and the Supreme Court could overrule it in the coming days.
Which Arab parties have been banned from the election?
Perhaps the most high-profile party to be banned is Ra'am, otherwise known as The United Arab List. The party currently holds five of the 120 seats in the Knesset and takes a conservative, Islamic position. Earlier this year it announced that it would allow Jewish candidates to stand for the party, with former Israeli police commissioner and deputy minister of national security, Yoav Segalovitz, set to run if the party is permitted.
The ban also applies to The Joint List, a coalition of three parties — Hadash (a left-wing Jewish-Arab party), Ta'al (an Arab nationalist party) and Balad (a Palestinian nationalist party).
The alliance was formed in part to avoid splitting votes and to ensure the parties clear Israel's 3.25% electoral threshold. Together, Hadash and Ta'al currently hold five Knesset seats, while Balad has no representation in the outgoing parliament. In recent polls, the parties jointly hold at least seven seats.
The CEC also banned two individual candidates from the joint list. These were the chairman of Balad, Sami Abu Shehadeh, a Palestinian-Israeli politician and former member of the Knesset (MK), and Ofer Cassif, a Jewish lawmaker and current MK for Hadash.
The CEC comprises representatives from the outgoing parliament, meaning Likud is well represented. It reportedly voted 18-5 to bar Ra'am and the Joint List on Wednesday. The following day, the committee rejected a petition against National Security Minister Itamar Ben-Gvir's Otzma Yehudit party. Ben-Gvir recently drew criticism from Germany and many other countries for saying that he thinks "targeted killings should be carried out in Gaza" regardless of whether those people posed an immediate threat.
While a representative of the Supreme Court chairs the Central Elections Committee, the court will ultimately decide the ban after the Adalah rights group confirmed it would appeal on behalf of the parties.
Why are these parties banned?
Right-wing parties such as Benjamin Netanyahu's Likud and Otzma Yehudit started petitions to ban these parties and individuals. A stipulation in the Knesset's basic law bans candidates who show "negation of the existence of the State of Israel as a Jewish and democratic state," "incitement to racism" or "support for armed struggle by a hostile state or a terrorist organization against the State of Israel."
Supporters of the bans argued that some of the parties' leaders had made statements or engaged in conduct that crossed those legal boundaries. In Ra'am's case, petitioners cited alleged connections between organizations linked to the party and bodies connected to Hamas, as well as statements by Mansour Abbas that they claimed reflected contradictory messages to Hebrew- and Arabic-speaking audiences.
Petitions against Sami Abu Shehadeh and Ofer Cassif similarly relied on past statements and writings that opponents argued amounted to support for positions that undermine the existence of Israel as a Jewish state.
What is the response of those banned?
Ra'am and the Joint List strongly reject the allegations.
Ra'am argues that petitioners failed to provide the clear and convincing evidence required under Israeli law. The party points to Mansour Abbas' condemnation of the October 7 attacks and his efforts on behalf of Israeli hostages as evidence that it does not support terrorism.
The rights organization Adalah, which is representing the parties, said "the CEC conducted an illegitimate political process aimed at persecuting ideas the majority does not accept, and it ended with the disqualification of all Palestinian representation in the Israeli Knesset."
The Joint List said the move amounted to an attempt to disenfranchise more than a million Arab citizens and accused the government of seeking to suppress Arab political participation.
Cassif struck a similar tone on X, when he called the decision "another nail in the coffin of the remnants of democracy" in Israel.
Has this happened before?
Not on this scale. While Israel's election authorities have previously attempted to disqualify Arab parties and candidates, the exclusion of all major Arab-led electoral lists at the same time would be unprecedented.
Balad, in particular, has been previously banned, before a Supreme Court ruling allowed the party to run after all. This happened in 2022, 2019, 2009 and 2003, often unanimously. Cassif's ban in 2019 was also overturned.
Since a 1985 legal amendment allowed such challenges from the committee, the Supreme Court has upheld only one such decision — against the ultra-nationalist Orthodox Jewish party Kach in 1988.
What has the reaction been to the banning of Arab parties from the Israeli election?
Many supporters of the bans argue that the October 7 attack and subsequent war in Gaza changed the political context.
They contend that statements or activities that may previously have been tolerated should be viewed more seriously after the Hamas-led attack and during an ongoing regional conflict.
Ahead of the CEC decision, Netanyahu's Likud party spelled out its backing for a ban. "There is no room in the Knesset for those who harm IDF soldiers and are unable to say that Hamas and Hezbollah are terrorist organizations," said a party statement.
Netanyahu is wanted by the International Criminal Court (ICC) on charges of war crimes and crimes against humanity in Gaza following October 7, 2023.
Responses from the Israeli center, meanwhile, have been divided.
Some centrist politicians have supported disqualifying specific candidates, while expressing concerns over excluding entire party lists representing a substantial minority of Israeli citizens.
Perhaps crucially, Israel's legal establishment has so far not endorsed the disqualifications. The office of Attorney General Gali Baharav-Miara reportedly concluded that the evidence against Ra'am and the Joint List did not satisfy the legal requirements for exclusion, although it did support the ban of Balad chairman Sami Abu Shehadeh.
Much of the media reaction has been scathing, with an opinion piece in the Jerusalem Post reading: "Israel has spent decades proudly calling itself the only democracy in the Middle East. Attempting to exclude the political representatives of Arab citizens, who make up roughly a fifth of Israeli society, is dangerous and fundamentally undemocratic."
Meanwhile, the Times of Israel lamented the CEC's back-and-forth banning process, saying that it's a "safe bet that on October 27, voters will be able to cast ballots for the Joint List and Ra'am," before adding that: "Given the unsuccessful track record of these disqualifications, coalition politicians may have been willing to play fast and lose with democratic rights in order to throw some red meat to their base and delegitimize the Arab parties — all while counting on the Supreme Court to maintain the status quo."

Swiss politicians back pay cap for health insurance bosses
The Swiss House of Representatives has approved a bill to cap the remuneration of senior executives at health insurance companies. Senior executives’ salaries are to be based on the maximum amount for the highest pay band in the federal administration.
The parliamentary initiative was adopted on Tuesday by 157 votes to 27, with eight abstentions. The motion now goes to the Senate.
The salary cap is to be adjusted in line with inflation and take into account both the number of insured people and the average total costs per insured person.
To verify compliance with this rule, the draft bill would require basic health insurers to publish the remuneration and level of employment of all members of their management and administrative bodies, naming each individual member.

Jewish dreidels, an icon, and a 19th-century cross — an attempt was made to take cultural valuables out of Ukraine
Ukraine
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-29
14:39:36 EEST
20:39:36 KST

Jewish dreidels, an icon, and a 19th-century cross — an attempt was made to take cultural valuables out of Ukraine
Kyiv • UNN
Kyiv customs officers confiscated 19th-century cultural valuables bound for the United States and Estonia. No permits for their export were provided.
Kyiv customs officers prevented the export of 19th-century cultural valuables from Ukraine—dreidels, an antique icon and a cross. An expert examination confirmed that the items are cultural valuables. The State Customs Service of Ukraine reports this, UNN writes.
The dreidels and cross, which were headed to the United States, and the icon, which was headed to Estonia, were discovered during customs control of international postal shipments. Given their signs of antiquity, customs officers sent them to the National Museum of the History of Ukraine for an expert examination to determine whether they belonged to cultural valuables
According to the experts’ conclusion, the three small spinning tops are dreidels, traditional to Jewish culture. They are an attribute of an ancient game that children play during the celebration of Hanukkah. The sides of the dreidels bear Hebrew letters that form the phrase "A great miracle happened there."
The history of this game is connected with events in the 2nd century BCE. In 167 BCE, the Syrian king Antiochus significantly restricted the rights of Jews to observe religious commandments and banned the study of the Torah. Jews were forced to study it secretly, hiding in caves. According to tradition, children were left near the entrance and, upon noticing guards approaching, began playing noisily with dreidels so that the adults would have time to hide the Torah scrolls.
The discovered dreidels are of archaeological origin. Similar items are represented in Ukraine’s museum collections only to a very limited extent.
The metal icon of the Holy Mother of God "Joy of All Who Sorrow" is an example of 19th-century Old Believer cast-copper artwork. Such icons were worn as amulets or hung near the head of sick people.
The eight-pointed cross that was discovered is an altar crucifix. Such crosses became an obligatory attribute of priests, who put them on during ordination.
Under current Ukrainian legislation, permits are required to export cultural valuables abroad. No such documents were provided to the customs officers.

Türkiye plans to digitally archive centuries-old Turkish music
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-29
11:38:23 UTC
20:38:23 KST

Türkiye is preparing a digital archive of centuries-old musical works, historical scores and performance recordings that will be made freely accessible to the public in 2027.
The project, led by the Culture and Tourism Ministry’s General Directorate of Fine Arts, will bring together scores from the Seljuk and Ottoman periods, along with religious hymns, gazels, concert recordings and stage performances.
The archive aims to give musicians, researchers and the wider public access to Türkiye’s musical heritage through a single online platform.
Omer Faruk Belviranli, director general of Fine Arts, said that the directorate oversees 29 orchestras, choirs and musical ensembles, including six state symphony orchestras and the State Polyphonic Choir. Other ensembles specialise in traditional Turkish music, folk music, folk dances and music from different regions.
Archiving performances
A separate project is also under way to digitally record artistic productions by the directorate’s ensembles.
“Works we produce must definitely be recorded. If it is visual, there must be a video recording; if it is audio, they must definitely be recorded through the YouTube channel,” Belviranli said.
He said 15 of the directorate’s 29 units have professional recording studios and that an existing archive of performances will be transferred to an online platform.
“We currently have an archive. All that remains is to bring this archive to life and transfer it to the YouTube channel, or whichever channel we will publish it on, in accordance with our minister’s instructions,” he said.
The digital archive will also include historical musical notation reflecting centuries of Turkish musical tradition.
“Turkish music is a sea,” Belviranli said. “We have in our possession, in the form of an archive, very special scores inherited from the 700-800-year-old Seljuk and Ottoman tradition to the present day, Hamparsum notation, scores written in Ottoman Turkish and many more.”
Hamparsum notation is a historical system developed during the Ottoman period to record Turkish music.
“We will definitely transfer all of these to the archive and make them available to those interested,” he said. “We will create a digital sea that our listeners can access free of charge, where everyone interested can see everything with one click and gain access to the details of the archive.”
Belviranli said an exact number of works could not yet be given, but the archive would cover the programmes of the directorate’s 29 units and eventually include tens of thousands of works.
He said the recordings would allow people to study individual pieces and performances, while stressing that digital access would not replace the experience of attending a live concert.
“Music lovers will be able to listen to the concerts digitally through our archive, but being at concerts is like watching the same match. Watching it on television and going to the stadium to watch it are very different,” he said. “Being able to feel that atmosphere, that spirit, is very important.”
The directorate also plans to continue sending musical ensembles abroad. Belviranli said it had received requests from at least 42 countries for performances marking October 29, Türkiye’s Republic Day.
He said foreign audiences accounted for nearly 80 percent of spectators at some overseas programmes, particularly those featuring traditional music, whirling dervish performances, Turkish World music and folk dances.
“We are striving to be a bridge carrying the past into the future,” Belviranli said.

PARIS, Sept. 29 (Xinhua) -- France's public debt rose by 59.6 billion euros (67.7 billion U.S. dollars) in the second quarter of 2026 from the previous quarter, reaching 3.59 trillion euros (4.08 trillion dollars), or 119 percent of gross domestic product (GDP), the French National Institute of Statistics and Economic Studies (Insee) said Tuesday.

Under the Maastricht Treaty, which entered into force on Nov. 1, 1993, member states adopting the euro are required to keep their public budget deficit below 3 percent of GDP and public debt below 60 percent of GDP.
According to data released by the French Ministry of Economy and Finance on Sept. 19, the country's public debt will continue to rise, reaching 119.3 percent of GDP in 2026, and is projected to rise further to 121.7 percent in 2027, more than double the European Union's 60-percent limit. ■

Tuesday, 29 September 2026, 11:36

From 1988 to 2024, Bulgaria’s population fell from 8.9 million to 6.4 million. Rural areas are losing population twice as fast as urban areas. This is the finding of a World Bank report, funded by the EU to assess Bulgaria’s National Strategy for Demographic Development, BTA reported.
The populations of Plovdiv, Varna and Burgas, the country’s second-, third- and fourth-largest cities, remained broadly stable between 2001 and 2024, changing by no more than 5%. Sofia’s population has grown by around 10%.
Against the backdrop of this unfavorable trend, the analysis also identifies significant opportunities, noting that Bulgarians today are healthier and better educated than ever, economic activity is at its highest level since the late 1990s, emigration has slowed, and more Bulgarians are returning to the country.

While waging all-out war on Ukraine, Russia keeps probing Europe with drones and sabotage that stop just short of open attack. Its small Baltic neighbors are already preparing their people for a possible invasion, and American soldiers on their soil have long been the clearest sign that attacking them means fighting the US. With Washington weighing a pullback and telling Europe to fend for itself, each US unit that stays on Russia's doorstep carries more weight than its size.
"There will be fewer US troops in Europe"
Nausėda spoke in an interview with LNK television on 28 September.
"There will be fewer US troops in Europe. This is partly related to what US President Donald Trump says, to the signals the US administration is sending us that Europe must take on more responsibility itself," he said.
Europe must do more for itself, and it is already doing so, Nausėda added. The US presence in Lithuania matters not only for its military power but also for deterrence, he argued.
"The presence of these troops is precisely what reduces the likelihood of military conflict or military aggression," he told LNK, ELTA reported.
"The heavy battalion will be here"
Nausėda called the decision a kind of encouragement for Lithuania. "As the overall number of US troops in Europe decreases, in Lithuania that number will at least remain, will not decrease, and perhaps will even be slightly larger," he said. "In any case, the heavy battalion will be here."
The battalion will keep its Abrams tanks, but an engineer battalion will replace the artillery battalion, Nausėda said on LRT's Savaitė program. The rotation will again last nine months. The Americans will number roughly as before, over 1,000, Defense Minister Robertas Kaunas said.
Estonia has also secured the return of US troops, at least temporarily, LRT noted.
Trump announces 5,000 US troops to Poland — one week after US froze scheduled combat-team rotation and amid Russia’s threat
More than 1,000 US troops began leaving Lithuania when their rotation ended in early June, and no replacement arrived, LRT said. It was the country's first gap in the US presence since 2020. American heavy battalions have rotated through Lithuania since 2019.
The Pentagon is weighing a withdrawal of about 25,000 US troops from Europe, and possibly as many as 40,000, NBC News reported, adding that no final decision had been made. About 80,000 US troops are now stationed on the continent. Germany, Italy, and Spain would likely be among the countries most affected.

BEIJING, Sept. 29 (Xinhua) -- China's service sector has maintained strong growth momentum this year, contributing 66.1 percent to the country's economic growth in the first half (H1) of 2026, up 5.9 percentage points from the same period a year earlier, the National Development and Reform Commission (NDRC) said on Tuesday.
Since April, the business activity expectations index for the service sector has remained above 55 percent for five consecutive months, well clear of the 50-percent threshold that separates expansion from contraction, according to Li Chunfang, an NDRC official.
The sector has maintained positive momentum, underpinned by supportive policy expectations, growing market confidence, resilient consumption and vibrant opening up, Li noted at a press conference.
Following the release of a State Council guideline in April aimed at expanding the capacity and improving the quality of the service sector, the NDRC and 40 other government departments identified 131 key tasks for 2026 and 2027.
Over the past six months, relevant authorities have rolled out 81 supporting measures, while more than 60 percent of the key tasks have seen notable progress. A total of 27 provincial-level regions have also convened meetings or issued policy documents to promote development in the service sector.
With services now forming the bedrock of the Chinese economy, the country has elevated this sector's strategic importance to new heights.
In April, China held a conference focused on the service industry, the first of its kind at the national level, indicating a stronger policy focus on the development of a sector serving as both the largest pillar of China's economy and a major source of employment.
Official data showed China's service sector had surpassed 80 trillion yuan (about 11.87 trillion U.S. dollars) in added value last year, making up 57.7 percent of the country's GDP.
During Tuesday's press conference, Li said China is stepping up efforts to deepen the integration of advanced manufacturing and modern services. Building on two rounds of national pilot programs launched since 2020, authorities are guiding local governments in carrying out a new round of pilot projects to promote closer integration between the two sectors.
Financial support has continued to expand. By the end of the second quarter of 2026, outstanding medium- and long-term loans to the service sector in domestic and foreign currencies stood at 76.22 trillion yuan, up 6.4 percent year on year, and 1.3 percentage points faster than overall loan growth, the People's Bank of China revealed.
Authorities are also seeking to make better use of existing land and buildings for development of the service sector, and cultivate more internationally competitive "China Services" brands.
Li said China will continue to strengthen resource support, improve policy measures, and accelerate their implementation to further expand the capacity and enhance the quality of its service sector. ■

20:36:10 KST

by Xu Shumin, Liang Jiajun
HONG KONG, Sept. 29 (Xinhua) -- While Hong Kong is globally renowned for its towering skyscrapers and relentless urban tempo, a growing legion of paddlers heading out into the dawn sees a different face of the metropolis.
For the paddlers, the city is defined by maritime routes threading from Deep Water Bay to Sai Kung and Lamma Island, nurtured by a vibrant network of clubs and enthusiasts dedicated to outrigger canoeing.
In late August, a 43-member Hong Kong delegation returned from the 2026 International Va'a Federation (IVF) World Sprint Championships in Singapore -- a testament to how the sport has evolved from a niche weekend pastime into a sophisticated, competitive discipline on the international stage.
Originating in the Polynesian islands and also known as the Hawaiian canoe, the craft features an outrigger float (ama) attached to the main hull via lateral spars (iako), creating a distinctive, wave-resistant structure.
Paddlers sit single-file in the slender craft, paddling rhythmically on one side before switching. Once an indispensable means of survival for island traversal and open-ocean fishing, it has evolved into a dynamic global water sport.
Watch a six-person canoe (OC6) slice through the foam, and the precision borders on telepathic. At the core of the frenzy is a simple, clipped bark: "Hut!" Calling the rhythm from seat three is 63-year-old Martha Levin. With every cue, all six paddlers cleanly alternate sides in lockstep, setting the vessel's trim and cadence.
Born in Hong Kong, Levin spent years abroad before returning in 1995. Seeking a way back to the emotional fabric of her hometown, she threw herself into water sports at the Victoria Recreation Club, where she now serves as chair.
"I was captivated during a race in Hawaii, looking out at hundreds of boats taking to the ocean alongside leaping dolphins," Levin recalled, her eyes brightening. "Right then, I was hooked. I was completely in love with the sport."
To Levin, Hong Kong's waters offer a diverse year-round training ground: calm, warm waters in the summer contrast with winter swells that can surge up to two meters. "Hong Kong is really my home," she said. "It feels like a way of life to come back here to the team, the camaraderie."
In Levin's eyes, outrigger canoeing is never a solo pursuit. In the same vessel, young corporate professionals in their 20s paddle shoulder-to-shoulder with mothers in their 50s; broad-shouldered powerhouses sit alongside petite teammates whose endurance keeps the rhythm steady. Each must juggle demanding careers, family commitments, and intensive regimens.
"It's more than just me, so everyone makes the effort to show up on time," she noted.
This distribution of power in a six-seater is almost constitutional. Seat three is the metronome, responsible for the switch commands, while seat six, the steersperson at the stern, reads the sea, sets the strategy, and commands the boat's overall course.
Steering from the stern is Alex Miranda, a native of Brazil who now serves as the paddle sports head coach at the Royal Hong Kong Yacht Club. Now in his 50s, Miranda remains a fixture across diverse maritime communities and disciplines.
For him, stepping into a canoe represents a deliberate return to nature and community. "You get really focused and all the distractions of everyday life just kind of clear out," he said.
On the open water, there is no margin for complacency. Paddlers must remain hyper-focused, continuously synchronizing their strokes, assessing the hull's trim, and reading changes in the wind and swell. To accommodate varying goals, the club runs structured programs on Tuesdays, Wednesdays, Thursdays, and Saturdays catering to all age brackets.
Miranda and his peers also look beyond local shores, aiming to expand outrigger canoeing into other cities across the Guangdong-Hong Kong-Macao Greater Bay Area. "The Greater Bay Area already has good paddlers coming from the tradition of dragon boating, so they can combine that with outrigger paddling and try something slightly different to grow the sport," Miranda said.
While the sport once drew predominantly middle-aged participants, Miranda has noticed an influx of younger faces filling the docks.
Take Tommy Yiu, a 31-year-old local resident, who cut his teeth on university dragon boating before crossing over to outrigger canoeing in 2024 on a colleague's whim.
Unpredictable weather and shifting currents frequently threaten to throw a canoe off course. Once accustomed to tackling problems single-handedly, Yiu found that battling adversity on the sea taught him humility and team trust. "Survival and speed only come when you surrender your ego and trust your crew entirely," he reflected.
"The moment you set foot inside the boat, your pedigree, your job title, your socio-economic status -- it all evaporates," said 50-year-old crew member Wang Xiaoxin. "Everyone is reduced to the same basic weight, pulling toward the exact same marker."
A mainlander relocating to Hong Kong, Wang found herself in an emotional low two years ago. Multiple sports failed to lift her spirits until her husband recommended outrigger canoeing. The expansive horizon and welcoming community won her over on her very first outing, anchoring her immediately.
"I was an incurable late-riser," she laughed. "Now, dragging myself out of bed at 5 a.m. is second nature, purely because of the camaraderie of my teammates," she said. Recalling her first Round the Island race in Hong Kong, she remembered encountering towering waves near Po Toi Island. Relying purely on mutual trust, the crew persevered through the chop and crossed the finish line.
As a professional jewelry designer, Wang discovered that the resilience she gained on the water seamlessly translated into her daily craft. The rigorous mindfulness required during dawn paddles mirrors the stillness and precision demanded when handcrafting delicate jewelry, the two disciplines feeding into one another.
At the World Championships in Singapore, Wang saw competitors with disabilities racing flat out, and paddlers in their late 70s cutting through the water. "It made me embrace the passage of time and realize that we should never place limits on our lives," she said.
As the session winds down, paddlers rinse the salt from their skin, change into work attire, and disperse into the glass towers in town, the workshops of industrial estates, and lecture halls.
Hong Kong will always have its gleaming skyline, but just beyond the shore, there are waves, winds, and fellow paddlers moving forward as one. ■
