NATO responses to Russian attacks will not always be public or tit-for-tat – Rutte
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-29
11:11:00 UTC
20:11:00 KST

NATO responses to Russian attacks will not always be public or tit-for-tat – Rutte
Rutte said this during a joint press conference with Lithuanian Prime Minister Mindaūgas Sinkevičius at NATO headquarters in Brussels, according to Ukrinform.
“When it comes to the word ‘hybrid,’ I have said many times that it sounds a bit soft and innocent. In the end, we are talking about gray-zone tactics: these can be drones, sabotage or even cyberattacks,” Rutte said.
At the same time, he stressed that NATO has all the necessary response options on the table.
“You will not always see them publicly. They will not always be symmetrical. It will not always be tit-for-tat, but we have the response options we need,” the secretary general said.
He cited a symmetrical action as an example: when an undersea cable between Finland and Estonia was cut in late 2025, NATO launched Operation Baltic Sentry to protect critical undersea infrastructure.
As an example of an asymmetric response, Rutte mentioned the actions of allies such as Sweden, the United Kingdom, Belgium and France aimed at making it more difficult for Russia’s “shadow fleet” to operate, so that “these rusty tankers do not generate profits for Russia.”
At the same time, Rutte advocated a measured approach in responding to Russian provocations, saying that NATO must bear in mind that it is dealing with the Kremlin leader, who has already sacrificed the lives of up to 1.2 million of his own servicemen in a “completely unprovoked war.”
“So there is a certain need for restraint here, but at the same time, we need to continue investing in defense, as the Lithuanian government and other NATO countries are doing,” Rutte said, urging allies to continue strengthening the Alliance.
He also welcomed the recent interception of a drone over Lithuania by Italian fighter jets as part of an air defense mission.
Another element of the response to Russia’s actions is continued support for Ukraine, the secretary general stressed.
“The best response to any Russian action in this gray zone is to increase, not decrease, support for Ukraine. Because ultimately, their goal is to divide us, make us lose focus on Ukraine and start having discussions among ourselves about what is happening, why it is happening, and how these events are connected,” Rutte explained.
“Our message to Moscow is clear. We will do more for Ukraine, not less,” the secretary general concluded.
As previously reported by Ukrinform, Supreme Allied Commander Europe General Alexus Grynkewich said that the allies had stepped up intelligence sharing in response to a wave of acts of sabotage and other incidents likely linked to Russia, and called for calm amid threats from Moscow.

INTERVIEW – As Merz loses ground, could Germany see a 'chancellor swap'?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-29
11:10:23 UTC
20:10:23 KST

- Snap elections would amount to 'political suicide' for CDU/CSU and SPD, and no senior conservative appears ready to take over amid unpopular reforms, Muno says
- Growing distrust of established parties and economic anxiety are driving voters toward right-wing AfD and eroding faith in democracy, expert war
Chancellor Friedrich Merz’s crushing defeats in recent state elections have raised fresh questions in Germany about his political future and the survival of his coalition government.
A recent YouGov poll found that 48% of Germans do not expect Merz to remain chancellor through the end of the year, while a separate survey for news channel n-tv showed 55% want him to resign.
But Wolfgang Muno, a professor of comparative politics at Germany's University of Rostock, said Merz is unlikely to step down anytime soon despite growing pressure, and that coalition partners have little appetite for early federal elections.
“A snap election would be more or less political suicide for Chancellor Merz’s Christian Democrats (CDU/CSU) and their coalition partner, the Social Democrats, as both are polling below their results in the last federal election,” he told Anadolu.
The Christian Democrats’ record losses in three federal states this month have fueled speculation about a “chancellor swap,” in which the CDU/CSU would nominate a new candidate and elect a successor in the federal parliament without calling new elections.
Muno, who closely follows German domestic politics, described that scenario as unrealistic in the short term, saying no senior conservative appears ready to take over while the government is pushing through unpopular reforms.
“I don’t see any candidate who is willing to do so. Neither North Rhine-Westphalia’s premier Hendrik Wuest nor Bavarian premier Markus Soeder said they would be willing to step in,” he said, referring to the two popular figures widely mentioned as possible successors.
Even if conservative lawmakers united behind a new candidate, Muno argued, a leadership change would do little to address Germany’s deeper problems.
The election results, he said, reflect widespread public frustration that Merz’s resignation alone cannot resolve.
CDU’s heavy defeat, right-wing AfD’s rise
This month, Merz’s CDU suffered heavy losses in state elections in Saxony-Anhalt, Mecklenburg-Vorpommern and Berlin.
The anti-immigrant AfD won by a wide margin in the two eastern states, while in the Berlin city-state election the CDU was overtaken by the socialist Left Party.
Surveys suggested that while state-level concerns – such as local economic conditions, public services and infrastructure – played a role, many voters also used the elections to voice their discontent with the Merz government.
The right-wing AfD made unprecedented gains, particularly in the east, winning 38.2% in Mecklenburg-Vorpommern and about 43.8% in Saxony-Anhalt.
Muno said AfD’s surge cannot be explained solely by voters with extremist views or concerns about immigration, stressing that the party has also attracted people who feel alienated from the established parties and are looking for an alternative.
“We have a higher and higher level of mistrust in established political parties,” he said.
“They (voters) are drawn to right-wing populist politicians who say: ‘Those politicians in Berlin, the elites, do not care about you; they do not make policy for you,’” he added.
Economic worries and a steady stream of crisis narratives are deepening that sense of alienation, Muno said, pointing to the economic downturn, the energy crisis, and fears of rising gas prices ahead of winter.
Lower-income groups in particular see the government’s planned changes, especially to pensions and health care, as socially unfair, Muno said.
“They say people with lower income have to suffer from cuts, but people with higher income do not suffer the same way,” he said.
- Declining confidence in democratic system
Muno warned that while the AfD’s surge is concerning, an even greater danger is the steady erosion of public confidence in democracy, especially in the eastern states.
“I would say we are losing many people … because they don’t believe in democracy anymore,” he said.
He stressed that senior AfD figures’ understanding of democracy fundamentally conflicts with a liberal, pluralist system, saying the party seeks to curb the independence of the judiciary and media freedom and abandon the principle of equal rights for all.
“In the view of the AfD, there are different groups of people, and especially immigrants should not have the same rights as the people they consider to be Germans by blood,” he said.
“That’s their basic idea, and this is why it’s also a danger for democracy itself.”
In May 2025, Germany’s domestic intelligence agency, the Federal Office for the Protection of the Constitution (BfV), classified the AfD as a “confirmed right-wing extremist” organization. The party is contesting the designation in court.
Muno pointed to surveys on attitudes toward democracy in the two eastern states where the AfD won this month’s elections.
In Mecklenburg-Vorpommern, three-quarters of people no longer see democracy as the better political system, he said, while in Saxony-Anhalt more than half of respondents said they would prefer “only one strong party” deciding and representing the people.
 
Need for tangible results, positive narrative
Muno also highlighted another weakness behind the mainstream parties’ poor performance.
They have focused too much on crisis talk, he said, reinforcing the AfD’s narrative that Germany faces constant problems and that nothing is going well.
To win back disillusioned voters, he said, Merz’s conservative CDU/CSU alliance and their Social Democrat coalition partners must first deliver concrete results people can feel in their daily lives.
Just as important, Muno argued, mainstream politicians need a positive narrative for overcoming socioeconomic concerns – one that builds trust and addresses people’s fears.
Otherwise, he warned, more people will begin to question the value of democracy itself.
“If democracy is not able to deliver social benefits and economic benefits, then the people say, what’s the sense of democracy? I can vote, but I don’t have enough to pay my rent, to pay for my gasoline,” he said.
“People fear their income is falling and their wealth is shrinking, and this is a very dangerous situation,” Muno warned, adding that if voters no longer see democracy delivering a stable living, more of them will simply stop believing in it.

Israel's Health Ministry shuts down Tel Aviv private hospital
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-29
11:08:16 UTC
20:08:16 KST

A private hospital in northern Tel Aviv was shut down on Monday after a surprise inspection uncovered serious deficiencies, a statement by the Health Ministry said.
Medical operations at the Medica private hospital were suspended after inspectors found that staff were performing procedures beyond the scope of their professional qualifications and posing an immediate risk to patients, the Health Ministry said.
According to the ministry, additional grave deficiencies included the facility's work processes and staff's ongoing violations of mandatory regulations.
The management of the Medica network, its owners and board of directors will be summoned to a hearing at the Health Ministry. It is also considering taking personal measures against staff members who performed medical procedures beyond the scope of their professional authority.
The latest findings follow serious deficiencies uncovered during a surprise inspection last July at another Medica private clinic in Tel Aviv called Medica Raphael.
Following those findings, the ministry ordered the immediate suspension of operations in the facility's operating rooms. According to the ministry, activity at Medica Raphael is being resumed gradually.
"Thousands of surgeries are performed every month at Medica Tel Aviv by some of Israel's leading physicians, and we operate according to the highest medical and safety standards," a statement by the Medica private hospital said.
"The Health Ministry made a sweeping decision based on random findings. We will respond to the Health Ministry through the appropriate channels," the statement added.
Israel's health care system comprises public, semi-public and private providers, with the latter growing considerably in recent years.
The state-financed health maintenance organizations (kupot holim) operate most primary and family medicine clinics, either directly or through contracts with privately operated clinics.
However, a report published in 2023 found that more than one million Israelis – 12 percent of the entire population – have had to forgo medical services in 2021 or 2022 because they couldn't afford the copayments.
Moreover, 35 percent of Israelis said they gave up on doing medical tests or treatments through the health maintenance organizations because of the long wait times. Of these, 51 percent then turned to more expensive private clinics.
As a result, Israel's private health care sector has expanded significantly in recent years. One important driver has been the growth of voluntary health insurance, which can provide access to private providers, a wider choice of physicians and faster access to some services.
An OECD report from 2023 noted that more than 80 percent of Israelis now have some form of voluntary health insurance, making Israel one of the countries with the highest rates of supplementary health-insurance coverage.

Iraq: US troops withdraw from their Iraqi US-led Operation Inherent Resolve mission against ISIS after 12 years as Baghdad delays militia disarmament
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-29
11:08:00 UTC
20:08:00 KST

Iraq: US withdrawal leaves security questions
September 29, 2026
For Iraq's government in Baghdad, September 30, 2026, marks the end of an era. "October 1 will be a new day in the course of the Iraqi state, with the country free of any foreign military presence and the completion of national sovereignty over its territory," Iraq's Prime Minister Ali al-Zaidi said in a statement.
The occasion will be celebrated as "Independence Day" with four official public holidays.
By Wednesday, the United States will have completed the withdrawal of its remaining 2,500 troops from Iraqi territory according to a 2024 agreement. Their departure concludes 12 years of the US-led Operation Inherent Resolve mission against the Islamic State group, or ISIS, which at the time was advancing across the country and in neighboring Syria.
The withdrawal also marks the end of more than two decades of US military involvement in Iraq. Following the US invasion in 2003, US forces withdrew in 2011 and returned in 2014 to fight the Islamic State group. The withdrawal also follows the broader US strategy of reducing its military presence in the Middle East.
However, the US withdrawal does not mean an end to all foreign military deployments in Iraq. Turkey still has troops in Iraq, even though Ankara said earlier this week that it would gradually hand over a military base in northern Iraq to Baghdad.
"In 2024, Baghdad and Washington agreed to what they called a normalized relationship," Renad Mansour, deputy director for the Middle East and North Africa program and director of the Iraq Initiative at the London-based think tank Chatham House, told DW. "For Baghdad, the political aim will be now to make clear that Iraq wants to remain an ally of the US," he said.
In his view, Iraqi Prime Minister Ali al-Zaidi is concerned that Washington could start viewing Iraq and its Iran-backed non-state militias as too close to Iran, given that the US and Israel are at war with Iran.
Baghdad extends disarmament deadline
Initially, Baghdad had linked the end of the US military mission to the disarmament of Iraq's numerous armed groups and militias. The plan also included bringing these paramilitary groups under state control.
Iraqi Prime Minister Ali al-Zaidi said last week that the new deadline was June 30, 2027. The revised plan includes a 90-day period during which armed groups would refrain from attacks in exchange for assurances that US forces would not target them, followed by a gradual handover of weapons that is due to be completed by June 30, 2027.
Yet not all armed groups are likely to follow this plan as several powerful armed groups have rejected disarmament or demanded conditions that could delay the process.
"The hardest-line armed groups — Kata'ib Hezbollah, Harakat al-Nujaba and Kata'ib Sayyid al-Shuhada — have so far given no indication that they are prepared to surrender their weapons to the state and integrate into Iraq's armed forces," Alina L. Romanowski, distinguished fellow with the Scowcroft Middle East Security Initiative at the Atlantic Council's Middle East program, said.
Renad Mansour told DW that he was not surprised by the extension of the deadline. Iraq's political landscape has been highly fragmented since the US invasion that toppled Saddam Hussein in April 2003. There have been more than eight years of war, the rise and fall of ISIS, and the US withdrawal in 2011 and return in 2014. "Many political movements are associated with armed organizations, so it is hard to see a revolution in the security sector happening any time soon," he told DW, predicting that "even next year, many armed groups will continue to remain free of the central government."
What does this mean for Iraq's minorities?
The withdrawal of US troops also includes the departure of military personnel and the removal of US air defense systems in Erbil, the capital of the semi-autonomous Kurdistan Region in northern Iraq. Kurdish Prime Minister Masrour Barzani has already called on Baghdad for protection against missile and drone attacks from Iran. Since the beginning of the US-Israeli war with Iran in February, attacks by Iraq's Iran-backed armed groups on US-linked targets in Erbil have been on the rise, while Iranian attacks on infrastructure belonging to Iranian Kurdish opposition groups in Iraq have also increased.
On Monday, Kurdish officials in Erbil said that three drones targeted a camp affiliated with Iran's Kurdish opposition. Local officials said the drones were Iranian-made, but responsibility for the attack was not independently confirmed.
Yerevan Saeed, a nonresident senior fellow with the Iraq Initiative at the Atlantic Council and the director of the Global Kurdish Initiative for Peace at American University, is concerned that Iraq's vulnerable ethnic and religious minorities, such as Christians and Yazidis, as well as Kurdish communities, could be left more exposed from October 1, 2026, onward. "The withdrawal signals the end of an era in which foreign boots provided a buffer against central and regional predation," he said.
Chatham House's Mansour, meanwhile, notes that US-Iraqi ties will not end on September 30, but rather shift toward "other arenas, including economic ties rather than having a security-focused relationship."
In July, US Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth said after meeting with Iraqi Prime Minister al-Zaidi, that they had discussed how a sovereign, stable and strong Iraq would pave the way for mutually beneficial commercial and defense cooperation.
However, in the statement following the meeting, Hegseth added that "building a normal US-Iraq bilateral defense relationship requires a secure environment free from terrorist coercion."

Why has a Cornell rape investigation been reopened?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-29
11:08:00 UTC
20:08:00 KST

Why has a Cornell rape investigation been reopened?
Former student at Ivy League university files a lawsuit alleging she was drugged and raped at a fraternity house in 2024.
New York state prosecutors have reopened a case involving an alleged gang rape at Cornell University after a woman filed a civil lawsuit accusing the school and law enforcement officials of not doing enough.
According to court documents filed in the lawsuit on September 16, which include screenshots of a group chat purportedly between members of the university fraternity at the centre of the allegations, the woman, referred to as Jane Doe, alleged she was drugged and raped at the fraternity house in 2024.
The case has sparked anger on social media directed at Cornell and the District Attorney’s Office in Tompkins County, New York, over their handling of the allegations.
On Monday, District Attorney Matthew Van Houten said in a statement that while at the time of the assault his office had found that evidence from the complainant’s initial statement did not meet the legal threshold to bring charges, he would now let a grand jury decide.
“Once we determine the appropriate charges, the case will be prosecuted in the most objective and impartial means available – by testimony to the Tompkins County grand jury,” Van Houten said.
Here’s what we know about the case:
What’s the case about?
According to the 101-page lawsuit, the complainant visited a friend at the Chi Phi fraternity house at Cornell University in Ithaca, New York, on October 19, 2024, while she was already intoxicated after drinking at a local, off-campus bar.
She stated that two members of the house propositioned her to sleep with both of them and later pressured her into taking ketamine and smoking marijuana.
Doe, 20 at the time, alleged she was then raped by seven men at the Chi Phi fraternity house over the course of seven hours before blacking out about 5:45am.
She said in the lawsuit that because she was under the influence, there was no way she was able to provide consent.
Doe added that although she reported the incident to the university’s police department on November 8, 2024, prosecutors filed no criminal charges.
In a statement to US broadcaster CBS News on Monday, Doe’s lawyer, Thomas Giuffra, said she went to the police because she believed she was the “victim of a crime”.
“Other than her initial contact with Cornell Police, she was not contacted by investigators from the Tompkins County District Attorney’s Office or any investigators trained in interviewing rape survivors,” Giuffra said.
He added that Cornell expelled two fraternity members after an internal review of the allegations, but five others received lesser repercussions, including suspensions, workshops and essay assignments.
“Not one of these guys was arrested. Not one. That I can tell you for a fact,” Giuffra told CBS New York, adding that Doe dropped out of school after her ordeal.
The lawsuit names Matthew Ingalls, Johnathan Newell, Winston Lee, Gillio Lopes, Diego Sarabia, Scott Norris and Scott Kretzschmar as the men in question.
It also names Cornell; the Chi Phi fraternity; Doe’s sorority, Delta Delta Delta; the off-campus bar; and the seven men as defendants and accuses them of breach of contract, negligence and violations of state law.
Doe is seeking monetary damages, including compensatory and punitive damages. The lawsuit did not specify how much Doe was asking for.
What was the group chat about?
The lawsuit includes images of a group chat on Snapchat among members of the fraternity in which one person alerted others crudely that they could sleep with the victim for “free”.
An image of the group chat shows a message from one person who wrote: “I f****** love Chi Phi.”
Kretzschmar, a then-fraternity member, allegedly sent two responses in the Snapchat group but has denied involvement.
Have any of the defendants responded?
Yes. Kretzschmar’s attorney, Jeremy Saland, told CBS News that the messages were inappropriate but were not evidence of sexual assault.
“This is a situation where there was an ugly Snapchat – ugly, period. … But that doesn’t make my client a rapist, and it certainly doesn’t make anyone a sex offender,” Saland said.
He added that his client had briefly entered the room where Doe was but did not touch her “in any way, shape or form” and left quickly afterwards.
Regarding the accusation of ketamine use, Saland said Kretzschmar took a hair follicle test that found he did not have the drug in his system, adding that no one has contacted him about a renewed investigation.
“We are available to present exonerating evidence. I just hope the right thing is eventually done, this case is closed and my client can live his life and not be subject to this selfish, repugnant, vile claim by this woman about him,” he added.
Meanwhile, Andrew Miltenberg, an attorney representing Lopes, also told CBS New York that his client “unequivocally denies the allegations against him”.
What has the university said?
In a statement published on Monday, Cornell said it supports the district attorney’s decision to have Doe’s story heard by a grand jury.
It explained that the university initially conducted its own investigation into the allegations over several months and sent the matter to a hearing in which a panel of trained faculty and staff heard evidence from Doe and the defendants.
“At its conclusion, the hearing panel issued a range of sanctions, which included expulsions and suspensions from Cornell. None of the individuals charged were offered the opportunity to write essays as a sole consequence of their involvement,” the statement read, adding that Chi Phi fraternity was closed in 2024 and remains barred from campus.
“Any suggestion that the university did not impose consequential punishments for those involved is false. A continuation of the false narrative that there were minimal consequences in this case is irresponsible, will make survivors feel less safe and supported, and will perpetuate the underreporting of sexual assault,” it added.
What has the district attorney said?
According to Van Houten’s statement on Monday, in Doe’s initial statement in November 2024, she did not allege that she was drugged against her will or gang-raped.
“On the contrary, Jane Doe’s statement described her participation in drug use and sexual conduct as voluntary, conscious and consensual. My office obviously did not and could not have based our November 2024 decision on the allegations in a civil lawsuit that would not be filed until nearly two years later,” he said.
“I recognise the reality that it can take years of therapy and healing for victims of sexual assaults to fully process and understand what happened to them. Seeking justice sometimes requires us to reconsider or reopen cases when we are provided with additional evidence,” the statement added.
Van Houten said a female senior prosecutor from his office who has significant experience in prosecuting sex crimes and has been involved in conducting jury trials in college sexual assault cases will prepare the case for the grand jury.
How common is sexual assault on university campuses in the US?
According to the Association of American Universities Campus Climate Survey in 2019, the overall rate of nonconsensual sexual contact by physical force or an inability to consent among women attending universities in the United States was 13 percent.
Among undergraduate women, the rate was 26.4 percent, or roughly one in four students. For undergraduate men, it was 6.9 percent.
Among postgraduate female students, 10.8 percent reported sexual contact by physical force or an inability to consent.

Ireland lost to Israel

Ireland lost to Israel when they stepped on the pitch
But the Irish team can still redeem itself.
For the past few months, Irish Sport for Palestine (ISFP), which I am part of, has been campaigning for Ireland to boycott its football matches against Israel. We believe playing against Israel legitimises a genocidal regime and gives cover for international law violations, apartheid and war crimes.
On Sunday, the match between the two teams went ahead in an almost empty stadium in Hungary. Regardless of the final score (3-0) in Ireland’s favour, they lost the minute they stepped on the pitch to play Israel. They lost because they went against the majority of the Irish people who do not want these matches to be played. They lost because they succumbed to pressure to normalise genocide.
A February poll showed that 76 percent of respondents did not want the team to play Israel. In a survey of professional football players in the Irish men’s and women’s leagues also conducted in February, 63 percent said Ireland should not play Israel.
The very spirit of Ireland, including Irish sport, is rooted in anticolonial resistance, so why should Irish football help legitimise a settler-colonial project?
One player, Gavin Bazunu, embodied that spirit with his courageous and principled decision to boycott the match. Instead of following his lead and taking into account the sentiments among other players and the Irish public, the leadership of the Football Association of Ireland (FAI) deliberately created confusion around hypothetical sanctions. It also sought to use a communication with the Palestinian Football Association, which has long called for FIFA and UEFA to suspend Israel, as a form of tacit approval.
In the end, instead of taking responsibility for the decision, the FAI leadership decided to hide behind the players on the national team and have them vote on whether they should play. The players should have never been put in that position.
Ultimately, the power and the blame lie with the FAI as well as UEFA and the Irish government, where there has been a total absence of leadership at every level. Decision-makers at the top of the FAI have consistently proven themselves to be dishonest and untrustworthy.
Last November, 93 percent of FAI members voted in favour of its board formally requesting Israel’s removal from UEFA. This was based on Israeli violations of statutes relating to illegal settlement clubs and antiracism policies.
Why, then, did the FAI leadership insist on playing this game? Why did it not reflect the wishes of FAI members and the Irish public? Why did it not protect Irish players? Why did it not stand up to UEFA like other federations have done in the past?
Israel lost the match on Sunday, but they triumphed on the pitch. They use these sporting moments to weaponise their Zionist propaganda and let violence spill into sport. Whether it’s the Israel Football Association and its intimidating behaviour, players and their military-style celebrations or the Israeli fans with their military chants and racist insults, they are all given full permission to turn the sporting arena into a battleground.
A match that proceeded with heavy security in a so-called neutral venue with barely any fans or media broadcasting should indicate how far outside the realm of normality this is. Yet, as long as Israel remains in sporting competition, this is the reality that sport will continue to operate in.
Decision-makers said playing the match was a win for football and for keeping politics out of sport. This is the lie they need to maintain to protect their interests and the status quo. This is the excuse UEFA hides behind for not removing Israel even though there are clear legal grounds to do so as well as their own precedents.
Meanwhile, the FAI is telling us how courageous the players who took to the field were and how their pre-match protests were acts of solidarity that will raise awareness.
Don’t fall for it. Words and symbolic gestures are hollow without principled action to back them up. We have come too far as a movement, and any action less than boycotting the match is unacceptable.
The institutional rot of sporting organisations like the FAI means a system overhaul can’t come quickly enough. The FAI completely threw its players and coaching staff under the bus. It gave a masterclass in what not to do, but its president, Paul Cooke, still believes it has all been handled “as well as could be expected”.
This is the kind of entitlement that comes with a historic lack of accountability from within the FAI, and as expected, there are widespread calls for the FAI board’s resignation.
There are also calls on the Irish government to provide clarity on its role in all of this too as it continually speaks out of both sides of its mouth on all issues relating to Palestine.
The Irish people are angry, and rightfully so, but this isn’t over; it is still Stop The Game. Anger will fuel us but hope will sustain us. There is another chance for Irish football to do the right thing on October 4 when the second fixture is supposed to take place in Serbia.
It is not an exaggeration to say the potential impact of this moment could be seismic. Not playing the game would be the most sporting thing the Irish players could do. It would be celebrated as one of our country’s greatest sporting victories.

Germany and five other EU countries are demanding a substantial cut to the 2028–2034 budget. They also want to change spending priorities.

Details
The letter, dated September 28 and obtained by the publication, was another attempt by the frugal camp to cut the EU’s next long-term budget — the Multiannual Financial Framework (MFF). We are entering a decisive phase of the negotiations, during which we must determine the overall size of the MFF and decide which areas need to be financed as a priority
It was signed by German Federal Chancellor Friedrich Merz, Austrian Federal Chancellor Christian Stocker, and Prime Ministers Mette Frederiksen (Denmark), Rob Jetten (the Netherlands), Petteri Orpo (Finland), and Ulf Kristersson (Sweden).

Violence, Israeli settlement make life ‘intolerable’ for Palestinians in West Bank: Red Cross
Unknown
Unknown Publisher

Mohammad Sio
29 September 2026•Update: 29 September 2026
Violence, movement restrictions and accelerating Israeli settlement expansion are making living conditions increasingly “intolerable” for Palestinian civilians in the occupied West Bank, the International Committee of the Red Cross said Tuesday.
The ICRC said dozens of Palestinians have been killed, hundreds injured and many more displaced this year, while homes and property have been damaged or destroyed, leaving families without shelter or livelihoods.
“The frequent and severe violence must be brought to an end,” said Julien Lerisson, head of the ICRC delegation for Israel and the Palestinian occupied territories.
“(Israeli) authorities have a responsibility to protect the population from violence, including when that violence is inflicted by settlers. What international humanitarian law says on the protection of private and public property, and on the population’s access to essential services, must be respected,” he added.
The ICRC said the humanitarian impact of the violence, including loss of life and serious injuries, is “overwhelming.”
It warned that movement restrictions are preventing patients from reaching health care, children from attending school and people from accessing their homes and livelihoods.
The restrictions are pushing families and entire communities into “increasingly intolerable conditions in which to live,” the organization said.
The ICRC said ambulances are sometimes held for hours at checkpoints and roadblocks or forced to take longer routes to avoid road closures and violence, making it harder for first responders to reach people in need.
It said that “Israel has a right to take measures to ensure its own security. However, as the occupying power in the West Bank it also has a responsibility towards Palestinians, who are protected persons under international humanitarian law.”
The occupying power is required to treat protected persons humanely at all times, protect them from acts or threats of violence and make every effort to restore and maintain public order and civil life, the ICRC said.
“Upholding international humanitarian law and respecting obligations under the law of occupation are necessary steps towards restoring the safety and dignity of the population,” Lerisson said.
“This means protecting civilians from violence and ceasing the expansion of civilian settlements,” he added.
The statement comes amid an escalation in violence by Israeli occupiers in the occupied West Bank, alongside tighter restrictions on Palestinian movement and illegal settlement expansion.
According to the Palestinian Colonization and Wall Resistance Commission, Israeli occupiers carried out 628 attacks against Palestinians and their property across the West Bank, including occupied East Jerusalem, in August.
In June, 14 UN special rapporteurs warned that the sharp rise in “settler terror” with state support and complicity in the occupied Palestinian territory posed an existential threat to Palestinian communities.
Since the start of Israel’s genocide on Gaza in October 2023, Israeli forces and occupiers have intensified attacks across the West Bank, killing 1,206 Palestinians, injuring around 13,350 others, and detaining more than 24,600, according to Palestinian figures.

We start with calls for a nationwide high school blockade in France this Tuesday. It comes as the public sector also goes on strike. In other news in France, the investigative website Mediapart has published revelations of alleged anti-Semitic comments made by Jordan Bardella, the French far-right leader. He is the man tipped to become prime minister if Marine Le Pen wins the presidential election next year. He has also been at the forefront of the far-right National Rally party's image rebranding. Mediapart accuses him of making anti-Semitic comments a decade ago, at the beginning of his political career when he was a young far-right activist. The website accuses him of "obsessional anti-Semitism". Bardella has angrily denied the comments, saying he was a minor in 2013 when the alleged comments were made. The Washington Post turns its attention to artificial intelligence and specifically how data centers are changing landscapes. In an interactive article, the paper looks at how AI data centres are transforming American landscapes – farmlands and desert are now teeming with the structures. What was once a warehouse surrounding by farmland today houses the US's largest operating data centre, Elon Musk's Colossus 2. This transformation is taking place across the US.
Finally, call it the hunk shortage! The nationwide search to find the Mister who will represent England at the Mister World pageant has so far proven fruitless – just seven candidates signed up. Ahead of the October 7 final, organisers are getting desperate. They sent Miss England to a beach in the hopes of drawing some candidates – and are even asking Miss England semi-finalists to nominate their boyfriends or brothers! Where have all the hunks gone, the Guardian wonders!

In February 1934, Austria descended into civil war, pitting the Austrofascist regime of dictatorial chancellor Engelbert Dollfuss against the weak Social Democratic Party. The regime put down the left's resistance in a few short, bloody days; the Social Democrats were subsequently outlawed. Bruno Kreisky – the man who would become Austria's first and only Jewish chancellor in 1970 – then faced a choice: head into exile, or stay and join the resistance. It was a decision that would shape the rest of his life.

Gujarat HC rejects Kejriwal's appeal  in PM Modi's degree case, told to pay Rs 25,000

Aam Aadmi Party National Convenor Arvind Kejriwal speaks during an interview session. (ANI Photo)
NEW DELHI: Gujarat high court on Tuesday rejected Aam Aadmi Party (AAP) convenor Arvind Kejriwal’s appeal in the case related to Prime Minister Narendra Modi’s academic degree.A division bench of Chief Justice Sunita Agarwal and Justice DN Ray upheld the single judge’s order. It also retained the Rs 25,000 cost imposed on Kejriwal.The single judge had quashed a 2016 Central Information Commission (CIC) directive asking Gujarat University to disclose details of PM Modi’s degree."In the totality of facts and circumstances of the present case, no error on any of the submissions of the appellant hearing can be found in the judgment impugned. The appeal stands dismissed accordingly with no further order as to cost," the high court said.Kejriwal’s counsel, Abhishek Manu Singhvi, challenged the basis for imposing the cost.He argued that his client had not "persisted" in seeking PM Modi’s degree, as observed by the single judge.Singhvi also said the CIC had initiated the proceedings on its own and named Kejriwal as a respondent based on a letter, not a formal application.The counsel further argued that if the degree was available online, it should fall within the scope of the Right to Information (RTI) Act.
He said the cause of action would then cease to exist.Gujarat University had told the single judge that the degree was already available online. However, Kejriwal’s lawyers later argued in a review petition that it had never been uploaded. The single judge rejected that plea.Solicitor General Tushar Mehta, appearing for Gujarat University, argued that Kejriwal had pursued the case relentlessly and held press conferences to defame the institution.Mehta urged the high court to impose costs on Kejriwal for filing the appeal. He said this would help prevent misuse of the RTI Act and stop government officials from spending working hours on requests that did not serve the law’s purpose.In 2016, Kejriwal wrote to the CIC, saying he had no objection to government records about him being made public. He also questioned why the commission wanted to "hide" information about PM Modi’s educational qualifications.Based on the letter, the then CIC, M Sridhar Acharyulu, directed Delhi University and Gujarat University in April 2016 to provide information about PM Modi’s degrees to Kejriwal.The universities challenged the order in the high court. Three months later, the court stayed the CIC directive.
In May 2016, then Gujarat University vice-chancellor MN Patel said PM Modi had completed his MA in Political Science in 1983, securing 62.3 per cent as an external student.Gujarat University later published the degree on its website and challenged the CIC order in the high court.On March 31, 2023, a single-judge bench quashed the CIC directive. It also imposed a cost of Rs 25,000 on Kejriwal and criticised his approach to the RTI proceedings as casual.The bench also pulled up the CIC for what it described as "judicial activism". Kejriwal then challenged the order before the division bench.

In final election fight, Brazil's Lula carries hopes of Latin America's receding left
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-29
11:03:08 UTC
20:03:08 KST

In final election fight, Brazil's Lula carries hopes of Latin America's receding left
BRASILIA, Sept 29 - When Brazilian President Luiz Inacio Lula da Silva addressed the United Nations General Assembly in New York this month, he used one of the world's biggest diplomatic stages to deliver a message that has come to define what is likely the final presidential campaign of his decades-long career.
"Brazil does not fit into anyone's backyard," he said to applause, seeming to portray Sunday's vote in the largest Latin American country as part of a wider battle against undemocratic forces as he warned of "foreign interference" in this year's race.
After a wave of right-wing election victories swept Latin America in recent years, aided by the return of an emboldened Trump administration in Washington, many progressives view his reelection bid against Senator Flavio Bolsonaro, son of former far-right President Jair Bolsonaro, as a potential turning point that could help reverse the region's conservative drift.
Lula has sought to portray Senator Bolsonaro, whom he has called a "nobody" in campaign speeches, as a stand-in for a broader right-wing movement, sharing images linking the senator to Argentina's President Javier Milei, Israel's Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu, and US President Donald Trump.
Yet Lula enters the campaign's closing stretch about even with Senator Flavio Bolsonaro, running in place of his father, who was arrested for leading a failed coup after losing to Lula in 2022.
Despite success with falling inequality and unemployment, Lula's government still struggles with voter frustration with rising living costs, and it has not overcome the polarization that has gripped the country for nearly a decade.
The international interest in the race was evident during Lula's New York visit, where he met US progressives, Mayor Zohran Mamdani and Senator Bernie Sanders. Latin American social media users have also been following the campaign intensely.
“There is a perception among international observers that Brazil is not merely electing a president. Given the country’s influence, it is helping to determine which political camp will emerge stronger in the next phase of a global struggle between democracy and authoritarianism," said Paulo Abrao, executive director of the progressive think tank Washington Brazil Office.
One person close to the president said that several leaders who were at the UN told the Brazilian delegation that they "are watching us with concern about which Brazil we will have after these elections."
'AS LONG AS I AM ALIVE'
Lula's 2023 return to power capped a dramatic comeback.
After leaving office 12 years earlier with an 87% approval rating, Lula saw the wave of optimism that had brought his party to power in 2002 largely replaced by a wave of hatred.
In 2016, he became the main target in a sprawling corruption investigation as Brazil descended into turmoil, including the impeachment of his successor, former President Dilma Rousseff.
Lula spent 580 days in prison before his conviction was overturned because of flaws in the investigations and legal proceedings.
The arrest stopped him from running against Jair Bolsonaro, a former army captain who rose to power in 2018 vowing to undo much of what progressives had achieved since the end of military rule in the 1980s.
Still, Lula remained a symbol for much of the global left, attracting visitors that ranged from former Uruguayan President Pepe Mujica to the philosopher Noam Chomsky.
He returned to office convinced that Brazil stood on the front line of a broader struggle against a global right-wing movement.
The January 8, 2023, attacks by Bolsonaro supporters on government buildings in Brasilia, days after his inauguration, only reinforced that belief for many.
"As long as I am alive, the far right will not return to power in this country," he has repeatedly said while promoting his campaign.
REGIONAL STAKES
While Lula has strengthened ties with China, revived Brazil's leadership role in the BRICS bloc of emerging nations and expanded engagement with Europe, recent right-wing victories in South America, and a confrontational relationship with the Trump administration, have left him increasingly isolated in the Western Hemisphere.
Some Brazilian diplomats say Washington views Brazil as the last major obstacle to a sweep of Trump-aligned governments across Latin America, after recent victories in Chile, Colombia, Honduras and Peru, and an unprecedented expansion of US power in Venezuela after its military intervention.
In Washington, progressives view Lula as a "beacon of hope," said Alex Main of the Center for Economic and Policy Research, a left-leaning think tank.
In neighboring Argentina, opponents of libertarian President Javier Milei see Lula's possible reelection as a potential boost ahead of next year's vote.
"If Lula wins, it will create a countercurrent to what has been taking hold in the region and show there is resistance to these right-wing winds," said Santiago Cafiero, a congressman and former foreign minister.
Diplomats from liberal governments in Europe and other regions, who have been supportive of Brazil's progressive climate initiatives, are also watching closely.
"If human rights are being violated in a pretty big way or if the Amazon is being deforested in a big way, then it's going to be much more difficult for us to engage with Brazil," said a European ambassador, who asked not to be named.
FEARS OF INTERFERENCE
Brazil's resistance to Trump and his tariffs appears to have benefited Lula among some voters, lifting his approval ratings as some progressives dubbed Flavio Bolsonaro as "Tariflavio," pointing to the senator's recent visit to the US to win Trump's support.
But in recent weeks, Lula's allies have voiced concerns that the Trump administration might refuse to recognize election results if he wins, arguing attempts to interfere are already underway.
They point to US Secretary of State Marco Rubio's remarks blaming Lula for the failure of trade negotiations that led to higher US tariffs on Brazilian goods, and a failed effort to send US officials to Brazil on a mission to "discuss electoral integrity," according to the US State Department.
Before the 2022 election, former President Joe Biden sent his Central Intelligence Agency director to tell former President Bolsonaro not to mess with elections, sources told Reuters at the time, and made sure the US was among the first countries to recognize the result.
Last week, 31 Democrats in Congress, including US Representative Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez, urged Rubio to respect Brazil's election result.
In a letter, they expressed "grave concern" over a "sustained, multifaceted campaign of interference and destabilization in Brazil."
The State Department did not respond to a request for comment but has denied previous accusations from Lula's government of election interference. REUTERS

Cuba's top trade official says US impeding reforms, denies talks with Trump associates
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-29
11:02:57 UTC
20:02:57 KST

Cuba's top trade official says US impeding reforms, denies talks with Trump associates
HAVANA, Sept 29 - Cuba's top trade official dismissed reports that companies linked to US President Donald Trump had come to Cuba this year to talk business, while calling the US trade embargo the biggest impediment to the roll-out of historic free-market reforms.
Cuban foreign trade and deputy prime minister Oscar Perez-Oliva Fraga said neither he nor any other Cuban official had met with representatives from Trump-tied businesses.
"I have no knowledge of any company directly linked to President Trump having made contact with Cuba," Perez-Oliva told Reuters in a wide-ranging interview in his ninth-story Havana office, fronting the Straits of Florida.
Under increased pressure from the Trump administration, including renewed sanctions that have hit its economy hard, Cuba in June unveiled unprecedented free-market reforms that, if fully implemented, would represent the biggest change to the island's socialist economy since former president Fidel Castro took control in 1959.
But, said Perez-Oliva, to make further progress, Washington must ease up on the sanctions, which include an oil blockade imposed in January that all but eliminated imports from Mexico, Venezuela and other former top fuel suppliers.
"It is not our policy to prohibit US companies from investing in Cuba, trading with Cuba, or conducting business of any kind with Cuba," Perez-Oliva said. "What prevents this possibility is the existence of the trade embargo."
Washington says the island's reforms do not go far enough and has called for "free and fair" elections.
Trump associates have been linked with potential business opportunities in Cuba over the years. In 2016, Trump's business associates visited Cuba and met with top tourism officials to discuss opportunities, according to minutes viewed by Reuters of those meetings.
PLAYING FAVORITES
Trump administration policies have skewed some sectors of Cuba's economy in favor of US investors, Perez-Oliva told Reuters.
"On the one hand, international companies — Cuba's traditional partners worldwide — are being threatened and urged to halt economic and commercial relations with our country," he said. "On the other, efforts are being made to boost the activities of US companies."
He pointed to a US State department policy that has allowed US companies to export fuel to the Cuban private sector, which he criticized as an effort to attempt to return Cuba to colonial-era dependence on the United States.
"(The policy) is aimed at forcing Cuba's economic dependence," said Perez-Oliva, whose maternal grandmother, Angela Castro, was an elder sister of former Cuban president Fidel Castro. "We will never again be a colony of any country."
Cuba's government has shown little sign of crumbling, despite severe economic hardship and Trump's repeated promises it would soon collapse.
WHAT'S NEXT
The stalemate has left investors of all nationalities in the lurch, Perez-Oliva said.
Canada's Sherritt International suspended direct participation in a nickel and cobalt mining joint venture with the Cuban government following a Trump administration executive order in May that threatened sanctions on mining-related businesses in Cuba.
Australia's Antilles Gold, which holds a copper and gold mine in Cuba, is also considering its next move, the minister said.
US investors have shown interest in both companies but have yet to receive permits exempting them from US sanctions, according to media reports.
"Neither Antilles Gold nor Sherritt has withdrawn (from Cuba)," Perez-Oliva said. "In light of these sanctions, these companies are evaluating alternatives to determine how to continue their operations."
Neither Antilles Gold nor Sherritt immediately responded to requests for comment.
Perez-Oliva said he would keep working to improve Cuba's economy and attract foreign investment.
The 55-year-old dismissed persistent rumors that he was being groomed as Cuba's next president.
"I have no aspirations in that regard," Perez-Oliva said. "I am simply a public servant, and I will work wherever I am needed, without aspiring to any particular position." REUTERS

Animal rights campaigners win case against Swiss egg advert

Animal rights campaigners win case against Swiss egg advert
The Swiss Fair Trading Commission has criticised an advert by Suisse Garantie for eggs. The claim that the eggs mostly come from “small flocks” is misleading, it ruled. Several animal welfare organisations had previously lodged complaints.
In fact, around 65% of laying hens in Switzerland are kept on farms with more than 4,000 birds; 80% of the birds are kept in flocks of more than 2,000. Animal welfare organisations have criticised this, arguing that it far exceeds the natural flock size of around 30 hens.
The fair trading commission has now agreed with them and upheld the complaint in its entirety. The commission recommends that Suisse Garantie refrain from using the disputed advertising claim in future, the animal welfare platform “Werbemist” said on Tuesday.
More
How well are Swiss animals protected?
False impression suggested
Suisse Garantie’s promotional video from February 2026 stated that Swiss eggs mostly came from family farms “with small flocks, animal-friendly housing and the best care”.
“This statement suggests a particularly animal-friendly and small-scale production method. Yet Swiss laying hens, too, predominantly live in factory farming conditions,” the animal welfare organisations wrote in response.
More
Swiss government scrambles to deal with egg shortage
The advert also glossed over the conditions in other respects. Most laying hens suffer from painful sternum fractures and are killed after only about a year when their egg-laying performance declines. Despite the commission’s decision, the advert remains online. The animal welfare organisations called on Suisse Garantie to remove the advert immediately.
The “Werbemist” platform is a project run by the Association Against Animal-Harmful Advertising and has been online since April 2026. It analyses advertising content that glosses over conditions in animal husbandry. The association is supported by the animal welfare organisations Animal Rights Switzerland, Sentience, the Foundation for Animals in Law and Tier im Fokus.

====================================================================================================

Taylor Swift fans lower climate concerns to justify star’s carbon footprint
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-29
11:00:49 UTC
20:00:49 KST

Young adults who consider themselves devoted fans of pop star Taylor Swift may lower their own environmental concerns to justify the singer’s high carbon dioxide emissions. When confronted with news about the excessive pollution generated by her private jet, highly identified fans tend to rationalize the behavior, which correlates with a decrease in their personal intentions to engage in climate-friendly actions. These findings were published in the journal Psychology of Popular Media.
Young adults belonging to Generation Z, people born between 1995 and 2012, are known for their high levels of environmental awareness. Many individuals in this demographic express deep anxiety about global warming and actively engage in climate advocacy. At the same time, this generation came of age alongside the explosion of social media and celebrity culture.
A tension arises when a beloved public figure engages in actions that harm the environment. In 2022, data tracking private jet flights named Taylor Swift the biggest celebrity emitter of carbon dioxide. Carbon dioxide is a greenhouse gas that traps heat in the atmosphere and acts as a primary driver of global climate change. Swift’s private jet use produced about 1,185 times more carbon pollution than the average person generates in a year.
Researchers wanted to understand how young, climate-conscious fans process information that puts their fandom in direct conflict with their environmental values. The research team included Leah Dajches of New Mexico State University, Taylor A. Foerster of Oregon State University, Juliana L. Barbati of the Union of Concerned Scientists, and Jessica Gall Myrick of Good Pug Media. They focused on a psychological process known as moral reasoning.
Moral reasoning refers to the mental strategies people use to resolve the discomfort they feel when someone they admire violates a social or ethical norm. One strategy is called decoupling, where a person separates their judgment of the bad behavior from their appreciation of the celebrity’s professional work. A person using this strategy might condemn a star’s pollution but continue to stream their music.
Another strategy is rationalization, which involves making excuses for the behavior or convincing oneself that the actions are not actually that bad. The researchers proposed that people with a strong fan identity would be highly motivated to use these strategies. Fan identity goes beyond simply enjoying a musician’s work; it involves feeling a sense of belonging to a broader social community of supporters. When a celebrity at the center of that community does something wrong, fans may feel a personal need to protect the group’s reputation.
To test this dynamic, the researchers recruited about 1,000 undergraduate students from two public universities in the United States. They filtered the group to include only adults between the ages of 18 and 29. The participants began by completing a survey that measured their level of Taylor Swift fan identity, answering questions about how much they liked her and how often they engaged with her fan community.
The study participants were then randomly assigned to read one of three mock news articles. The first article discussed the massive carbon footprints of celebrities in general. The second article covered the exact same topic but explicitly named Taylor Swift in the headline and included specific data about her private jet emissions. The third article was a control story about an unrelated topic, such as multitasking or common air travel questions.
After reading their assigned article, the participants completed another series of questionnaires. These surveys asked them to rate their agreement with statements representing different moral reasoning strategies. For example, a rationalization statement read, “High CO2 emissions are not as bad as some other things celebrities do.” Another statement measuring decoupling read, “A celebrity’s CO2 emissions do not change my assessment of them as an artist.”
Finally, the participants answered questions to measure their personal concern about carbon dioxide emissions. They were also asked to rate their intentions to engage in climate-friendly behaviors. For instance, they indicated their agreement with statements about taking steps to reduce their own contribution to global warming.
The researchers found that merely reading about Swift’s carbon emissions did not automatically change a person’s environmental views across the entire group. Differences in environmental concern between the three article conditions were not statistically significant on their own. The outcomes depended heavily on how strongly a participant identified as a fan of the pop star.
High-level Swift fans who read the article specifically highlighting her emissions reported the highest levels of rationalization. When these devoted fans read about Swift’s environmental impact, they were much more likely to justify or excuse the behavior compared to high-level fans who only read about the carbon footprints of general celebrities. This psychological defense mechanism had a ripple effect on their broader views.
Engaging in rationalization was linked to lower overall concern about carbon dioxide emissions. It also predicted a decrease in the participants’ stated intentions to engage in environmentally friendly behaviors. By making excuses for the pop star to protect their fan identity, the individuals ultimately weakened their own pro-environmental attitudes.
The data showed that having a strong fan identity was directly associated with higher environmental concerns. The act of rationalizing the celebrity’s specific transgression reduced those pro-environmental attitudes. The fans effectively prioritized their psychological connection to the celebrity over their climate values.
The study relies on a specific demographic, which limits how broadly the conclusions can be applied. The participant pool consisted mostly of white, heterosexual, cisgender women who attended college and leaned politically Democratic. People from different age groups, educational backgrounds, or political affiliations might process celebrity transgressions using entirely different psychological mechanisms.
The researchers also noted that they could not reliably measure one specific type of moral reasoning, known as coupling. Coupling happens when a person allows a celebrity’s bad behavior to permanently ruin their opinion of the star’s professional work. Because the survey questions designed to measure this strategy did not yield reliable data, the researchers had to exclude it from their final analysis.
The experiment focused exclusively on Taylor Swift, meaning the results might not hold true for fans of other public figures or different types of media personalities. The study also did not measure whether participants already knew about the singer’s private jet usage before taking the survey. Prior knowledge could have influenced how strongly the mock news articles affected their responses.
Future investigations could explore how different types of fandoms, such as sports enthusiasts or political followers, react to environmental scandals. Researchers might also track people over a longer period to see if the drop in environmental concern is temporary or if excusing a celebrity’s pollution leads to lasting changes in personal habits.
The study, ““Don’t Blame Me”: Testing the Effects of Taylor Swift Fan Identity on Emerging Adults’ Moral Reasoning Strategies and Environmental Cognitions,” was authored by Leah Dajches, Taylor A. Foerster, Juliana L. Barbati, and Jessica Gall Myrick.

Did Israel just move to completely erase the idea of Palestine?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-29
10:59:28 UTC
19:59:28 KST

Israel has issued an unprecedented order seizing privately owned Palestinian land for illegal settlement infrastructure in a part of the occupied West Bank designated for Palestinian civil and security administration, a senior UN official has warned.
Briefing the Security Council on Monday, Ramiz Alakbarov, the UN’s acting special coordinator for the Middle East peace process, said the order targeted land near Qabatiya, south of Jenin, to build a road connecting Noa and Emek Dotan, two of 34 recently approved illegal Israeli settlements.
“This marks the first reported seizure of Area A land explicitly for settlement infrastructure,” he said.
Security Council Resolution 2334, adopted in 2016, declares Israeli settlements in occupied Palestinian territory, including occupied East Jerusalem, illegal and demands an immediate and complete halt to all settlement activity.
Delivering the UN secretary-general’s 39th report on the implementation of the resolution, Alakbarov warned that continued illegal settlement expansion threatened the viability of an independent, sovereign and contiguous Palestinian state.
“The rapidly expanding settlement footprint, including outposts, is taking place in conjunction with a rise in settler attacks,” Alakbarov said.
“These developments are in breach of international law, further entrenching the unlawful Israeli occupation and undermining the right of the Palestinian people to self-determination,” he added.
The significance of the Qabatiya order extends beyond the road itself. It takes land for illegal Israeli settlement infrastructure inside territory assigned to Palestinian administration under the Oslo framework, further eroding the territorial basis for Palestinian self-government and a future state.
Why Area A matters
Under the 1995 Oslo II Accord, the occupied West Bank was divided into Areas A, B and C, with different arrangements for Palestinian and Israeli control.
Area A was placed under Palestinian civil and internal security administration. Area B has Palestinian civil administration and Israeli security control, while Area C, covering roughly 60 percent of the territory, remains under full Israeli control.
Alakbarov described the new Israeli order as the first reported seizure of Area A land explicitly for settlement infrastructure. Under the Oslo framework, Area A is designated for Palestinian civil and internal security administration.
Israel’s far-right Finance Minister Bezalel Smotrich has openly called for taking over the Palestinian territory as mandated under the accords.
“In any case, Oslo is null and void. In any case, Areas A and B are also ours,” he said on September 8.
National Security Minister Itamar Ben-Gvir has also backed scrapping the Oslo Accords, with his Jewish Power party introducing legislation seeking their annulment.
Ben-Gvir described the accords as “one of the greatest mistakes in the country’s history”, according to an analysis published by Anadolu, and called for that mistake to be reversed.
Connecting settlements, fragmenting Palestine
The Qabatiya road order comes amid a wider expansion of illegal settlements and their infrastructure.
According to the figures presented in Alakbarov’s briefing, Israeli authorities approved 8,085 illegal settlement units in the occupied West Bank and occupied East Jerusalem during the reporting period, which ran from June 13 to September 18.
Separately, Israeli authorities published construction tenders for nearly 2,240 units in Area C, including 1,234 in the “E1 corridor” near occupied East Jerusalem.
Alakbarov described E1 as an “existential threat” to a viable Palestinian state and warned that continuing “creeping annexation” violated international law.
The location explains the stakes. E1 occupies one of the last geographical links between Ramallah in the north and Bethlehem in the south.
Increasingly fragmented land
Alakbarov warned that the project would effectively sever the connection between the northern and southern West Bank and further isolate East Jerusalem from the rest of the territory.
Smotrich has explicitly presented illegal settlement construction as a means of defeating Palestinian statehood.
“This reality definitively buries the idea of a Palestinian state,” he said when announcing the controversial E1 plan in August 2025.
He described illegal Israeli settlement homes, neighbourhoods and roads as Israel’s rebuke to the countries seeking to recognise Palestine.
Experts warn that as illegal Israeli settlements become more connected, the land available for a Palestinian state becomes increasingly fragmented.
Villages emptied as settlements expand
Alakbarov also linked settlement expansion to attacks by illegal settlers and the displacement of Palestinian communities.
Sustained illegal settler violence completely emptied three Palestinian villages, bringing the number of depopulated rural communities to 49 since January 2023, according to the figures presented in the briefing.
Israeli authorities also demolished or seized 536 Palestinian properties in the occupied West Bank, including occupied East Jerusalem, displacing 736 people, among them 347 children, according to the figures.
Alakbarov said Israeli building permits were nearly impossible for Palestinians to obtain.
Meanwhile, more than 33,000 Palestinian residents of the Jenin, Tulkarem and Nur Shams refugee camps remained displaced following Israeli military offensive.
“I’m deeply concerned by the scale of displacement of Palestinians in the West Bank, where entire communities have been displaced, some multiple times, which may raise concerns about ethnic cleansing,” Alakbarov said.
‘Palestine cannot be erased or ignored'
Palestine’s UN envoy Riyad Mansour told the council that illegal annexation was already unfolding through land seizures and illegal settlement expansion.
He warned that construction tenders in the “E1 corridor” were part of an effort to destroy the prospect of Palestinian statehood, while moves to weaken the Palestinian Authority risked facilitating further displacement.
Mansour urged governments to impose consequences on those sustaining the occupation, including through financial and commercial relationships.
“The time has come to move from statements to measures, from condemnation to accountability, and from declarations of solidarity to implementation,” he said.
Despite the expanding illegal settlements, Mansour insisted that international support had demonstrated that Palestine could not be erased or ignored, and that Palestinians’ rights could not be extinguished by Israeli occupation or illegal annexation.

Destroying the Islamic Republic is not the same as saving Iran - opinion
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-29
10:58:30 UTC
19:58:30 KST

Israeli Foreign Minister Gideon Sa’ar’s video message to a Jewish-Kurdish conference in London was notable for one line in particular. He described the Kurds as a people spread across four countries who have “not yet achieved political independence,” and argued for stronger ties between Jews and Kurds.
Nothing is surprising about Israel seeking closer relations with Kurdish communities, and Sa’ar was speaking about Kurds across four countries, not specifically about Iran. But that distinction does not survive the journey.
In Iran, and among Iranians abroad, a senior Israeli official raising Kurdish political independence while the Islamic Republic is under attack is heard as a statement about Iran. It is heard that way because the argument that Israel’s interest lies in encouraging Iran’s ethnic and regional movements surfaces regularly in Israeli strategic commentary.
The timing therefore matters. As the Islamic Republic comes under growing military, economic, and domestic pressure, Israel faces a broader question than how far it can weaken Tehran: does it want to weaken the regime, or weaken Iran itself?
One possible strategy is to reduce the Iranian state’s capacity so severely that the Islamic Republic can no longer project power across the region. From that perspective, stronger ethnic and regional movements can look useful. They tie down the center and reduce Tehran’s ability to rebuild the networks that have threatened Israel for decades. That logic is understandable. It is also risky.
Weak states do not simply become weak adversaries. In the Middle East, the collapse of central authority has often created space for militias, foreign intervention, and conflicts that are much harder to contain. Iran is not Syria or Libya.
It has close to 90 million people, sits across several strategic corridors, and borders Turkey, Iraq, Armenia, Azerbaijan, Turkmenistan, Afghanistan, and Pakistan. A fragmented Iran would not necessarily be a safer Iran. It could be the beginning of several new conflicts at once.
There is another path: maintain pressure on the Islamic Republic while making clear that the objective is not the dismemberment of Iran. That means supporting the possibility of political change without trying to design Iran’s future from outside. Regime change and state collapse are not the same thing.
This matters because something unusual has happened in the relationship between Israelis and Iranians. For decades, the Islamic Republic tried to make hostility toward Israel part of Iran’s political identity. Yet among parts of Iranian society, especially in the Iranian diaspora, the opposite has happened. Demonstrations have displayed the Lion and Sun flag alongside Israeli, American, and host-country flags.
Inside Iran, the security apparatus is widely experienced as an instrument of domestic repression rather than national defense, and blows against it are not universally mourned, but even celebrated. On the Israeli side, there has been a noticeable effort to distinguish between Iran and the Islamic Republic, with public messages of solidarity directed at Iranians themselves.
None of this should be romanticized. It does not mean that Iranians broadly support Israel, nor that a future democratic Iran would automatically become an Israeli ally. Public attitudes can change quickly, especially during war. But four decades of interstate hostility have not produced equivalent hostility between the two societies.
If Israel comes to be seen as supporting the breakup of Iran, this opening could close quickly. Many Iranians who strongly oppose the Islamic Republic are just as strongly attached to the country’s territorial integrity. Kurdish, Arab, Baluch, and other opposition movements are part of Iran’s political landscape, but separatist groups have not demonstrated broad national support and cannot redraw Iran’s borders without major and sustained outside backing.
The regional consequences would also be serious. Turkey, Iraq, and Pakistan all have their own minority and territorial concerns. None would look casually at a process of fragmentation next door. What begins as a way to weaken Tehran could draw neighboring states, local armed groups, and outside powers into a much less predictable conflict.
Israel therefore has to think beyond the immediate military balance. Is the long-term goal an Iran too weak to pose a threat, or an Iran whose political transformation removes the basis for that threat?
Liberation and reconstruction, and which is more difficult
The second outcome is harder, and Israel cannot produce it; Iran’s political future will ultimately be decided by Iranians. But a territorially intact, post-Islamic Republic Iran moving toward a secular liberal democracy and a less confrontational foreign policy is not implausible. If it happens, the consequences for regional politics would be enormous.
The Abraham Accords showed how quickly supposedly fixed alignments can shift. A future rapprochement between Iran and Israel, sometimes imagined as a “Cyrus Accord,” would go much further. It would reconnect two ancient civilizations with a long historical relationship and reshape the strategic balance of the Middle East.
In the Book of Ezra, Cyrus the Great is remembered not simply for allowing the Jews to leave Babylon, but for enabling their return to Jerusalem and the rebuilding of the temple. Israeli leaders have often invoked that history when speaking about Iran, usually casting Cyrus as the foreign liberator.
The analogy is being run backward. Cyrus is remembered not for dismantling a state but for restoring a people’s political existence and underwriting its rebuilding. Liberation and reconstruction are different political problems, and the second is the harder one.
Israel may be able to help weaken the Islamic Republic. What follows is another matter. If its strategy contributes to the collapse of the Iranian state itself, it may trade one dangerous enemy for a generation of instability.
If it distinguishes clearly between the regime and the country, it can help preserve something far more valuable: the possibility that today’s adversary could, one day, become a strategic partner.
The writer is an associate professor of International Relations at Leiden University in the Netherlands, specializing in political conflict, violence, and Middle East politics.

More than 100 students are now enrolled in the Jewish program at Baku’s School No. 46, with the community reporting steady growth in recent years.

The program has been headed since 2008 by Rabbi Zamir Isayev, head of Baku’s Sephardic Jewish community, who recently celebrated his 45th birthday.
To mark the occasion, members of the community gathered with Isayev in a sukkah in Baku, joined by representatives of the Azerbaijani authorities.
Letter from chairman of Azerbaijan’s State Committee on Affairs with Religious Associations

The letter referred to tolerance, multiculturalism and interfaith dialogue as priorities of state policy under President Ilham Aliyev.
For Isayev, however, the most important story remains the school itself.
Growth reflects desire for strong Jewish identities
He says the rise in enrollment is about much more than crossing the 100-student mark. Each additional child represents another family choosing Jewish education and another part of the next generation growing up connected to its history, tradition and community.
The growth also reflects the confidence of Jewish families in maintaining a strong Jewish identity while remaining fully integrated into Azerbaijani society.
Alongside his work as a rabbi and educator, Isayev has become increasingly active internationally. Still, Isayev says education remains the heart of his work.
For Baku’s Jewish community, the need for more classroom space is a welcome sign: the community is not only preserving its institutions, but continuing to build for the next generation.
