AI: Concern as Germany plans to double data center capacity
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-29
10:00:00 UTC
19:00:00 KST

AI: Germany plans to double data center capacity
September 29, 2026
The digital future is here, and it is unfolding in the town of Dietzenbach.
Google, EdgeConnex, and Maincubes, two US tech companies and one German, have each reserved a spot for a data center in the small town near Frankfurt am Main.
Dietzenbach is a logistics hub near Frankfurt's airport, and home to 35,000 people.
The Frankfurt region, the center of Germany's financial industry, is one of the most attractive locations for digital cloud operators worldwide, and as demand for computing capacity continues to grow, more centers are planned for the region.
Locals worry about electricity and water usage
However, the news of plans for a fourth mega data center has been met with resistance by locals. The stacks of tens of thousands of computers in a data center need a high supply of energy to run around the clock. They radiate large amounts of heat and need cooling, which requires huge quantities of water.
The people of Dietzenbach DW met were worried about their water and electricity bills rising, as well as a higher temperature in their town.
"We want to know two things: What are the benefits for the local community here in Dietzenbach? And what are the environmental impacts?" said Dietzenbach resident Wilhelm Sauer, pointing at the four imposing chimneys rising from the EdgeConnex data center.
He and the other local activists believe that the toll the data centers will take on regional resources may not be offset by the limited number of new jobs announced.
Dietzenbach's mayor, Dieter Lang of the center-left Social Democratic Party (SPD), however, is optimistic. He predicted that around 100 "high-value jobs" would come to his town through the Google data center.
He also expects it will benefit his city's coffers: "We expect a substantial tax contribution," Lang told DW.
But Tara Merk, researcher on Community Data Centers at the Weizenbaum Institute, is skeptical: She believes Germany can probably expect little revenue from data centers operated by US companies, "because the profits may be taxed elsewhere."
"Especially thinking about big tech companies — they're not going to be doing their taxes in Dietzenbach," she told DW.
Data centers and lack of information
In August 2026, the German government launched a data centers registry listing energy consumption, water consumption, and energy efficiency measures for the data centers that are already operating.
But the list includes only around 300 data centers, far fewer than the estimated 2,000 data centers the government says are running across the country.
"Some companies report their smaller projects but not the big ones," Werner Neumann, board member of the environmental group BUND, told DW.
There is no official overview of how many data centers are being built or where. The civil society project Heisse Luft (Hot Air) has decided to fill these information gap, and has developed an online map of the planned data centers across Germany. The map is updated every day with information based on crowdsourcing from local communities.
"Theoretically, we should have access to this information," Tiziana von Witzleben, co-founder of the Heisse Luft initiative, told DW. "Maybe the German government doesn't have the capacity to [collect this information] and share it. But I believe it is on purpose, particularly [on the part of] big players like Google and Amazon. [They] are known to be very secretive about what they do. Because they know that if they tell people, they will get a lot of protest."
Unlike in the US, where a nationwide movement mobilized protests all over the country, protests against data centers in Germany remain a local community phenomenon.
In February, the local council of Groß-Gerau in the Frankfurt region voted against a €2.5-billion ($2.8-billion) data center proposed by a US operator, at least partly as a result of massive protests from the residents wary of heat waste, the daily Frankfurter Allgemeine Zeitung reported.
In Maintal, another town in the region, an EdgeConnex mega data center faced intense protest against its plans to build its own gas-fired power plant. The €1-billion project is now searching for power alternatives in a region which is already hitting its grid limits.
The race for computational power
Germany is the largest data center market in Europe, both by capacity and number of sites, and the Frankfurt/Rhine-Main region, which includes Dietzenbach, holds over a third of the country's total data center capacity.
Its proximity to the Commercial Internet Exchange (DE-CIX) infrastructure in Frankfurt makes the region attractive for digital cloud operators.
To achieve its strategic goal of doubling data center capacity by 2030, the federal government, a coalition of the center-right Christian Democratic Union (CDU) and the SPD, has proposed amending the Energy Efficiency Act (EnEfG) that regulates energy consumption and climate protection.
The environmentalist Green Party questions whether the targets are based on real demand. The socialist Left Party, on the other hand, is skeptical of the expansion as a whole. Both parties oppose the government's plans to relax the rules to attract more data centers.
On the opposite end of the political spectrum, the far-right Alternative for Germany (AfD) supports the expansion of data centers but criticizes the law promoting the use of renewable energy to power them.
Why are energy efficiency amendments controversial?
The proposed amendment would push back the deadline for operators to achieve renewable energy targets, and would relax requirements for the reuse of heat waste.
Despite this plan, Tara Merk still considers the push for energy-efficient data centers in Germany to be a progressive example in the global context.
But she is critical of the parts of the law that would give companies the right to declare that the data on the amount of water and electricity they use are trade secrets.
"This proposed amendment shifts the regulatory landscape very much in favor of operators," she told DW. "Having good data is needed to regulate, intervene, and build trust and acceptance within local communities."
"I think [lack of transparency] is ultimately going to foster more antagonism between data centers and local communities, making it harder for operators to expand or even keep their existing sites running the way they are," Merk warned.
Algorithm Watch, an AI watchdog, argued in a public statement that the legal changes the government is proposing are not about cutting bureaucracy, but more about appeasing US tech giants Microsoft, Google, and Vantage.
"German and European operators mostly have no problem with the current rules," Algorithm Watch said. "The amendments run counter to the government's own aim of strengthening German/European firms."
This summer, the watchdog launched a campaign and collected 150,000 signatures against the amendments to the law, calling for the public reporting obligations of data centers to be retained.
The amendments were presented to the Bundestag in September. If the new law passes, the government hopes it will take effect in January.
Edited by Rina Goldenberg

With bans and taunts, Trump escalates his assault on the media
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-29
10:00:00 UTC
19:00:00 KST

With bans and taunts, Trump escalates his assault on the media
-    Click here to listen to this article
-   Share via
See more from the L.A. Times in Google Search. Set us as preferred
- Despite a federal judge’s order, President Trump has refused to resume full access to CNN, dismissing its reporters as ‘fake news.’
- Five times in the last two months, the president has sneered at and insulted female reporters.
WASHINGTON — Under a light rain on Sunday at the Australian ambassador’s residence in Washington, CNN hosted its third annual tennis tournament, the Kangaroo Cup, pitting Beltway journalists against administration officials. The event aims to inject some levity into an historically adversarial relationship, reminding both sides of the spirit of the game. Themed drinks and tennis whites set the tone.
White House officials played with grace. But the mood this year was altogether different down Pennsylvania Avenue. Despite a federal judge demanding the administration reverse course on President Trump’s punitive actions toward his disfavored news outlets — CNN, MS NOW and Politico — he has refused to resume full access to the storied cable news channel, dismissing its reporters as “fake news.”
It is only the latest attack on press freedom by a president whose drive to punish critics and exert influence over the media appears to be growing.
During last week’s lavish state visit for Xi Jinping, Trump praised China for having “the friendliest press corps” and dismissed their repression of speech, despite the World Press Freedom Index ranking China among the world’s worst offenders — at the bottom of the list, alongside North Korea and Eritrea — for restrictions on journalists.
Five times in the last two months, the president has sneered at and insulted female reporters, mocking their appearance or dismissing their credentials.
The White House has signaled that CNN will be left off Air Force One for President Trump’s Saturday trip, the latest media restriction from the administration in an ongoing dispute with 1st Amendment implications.
He has declined to name a successor for his former press secretary, Karoline Leavitt, whose final news conference, on Aug. 27, was one of only a handful of briefings held throughout the summer. His administration launched its own streaming service last week, called Trump TV, in an attempt to circumvent traditional cable news. And on Monday, he posted renderings of the White House briefing room reconverted to its former use as a presidential pool and spa.
Trump’s escalating attacks on the press come just weeks before the midterm elections, as former officials and election experts warn the administration could seek to undermine confidence in the results. They also come at a precarious moment for public trust in the media, with more Americans saying limits on the press can be justified to combat misinformation.
A Pew Research Center survey released earlier this month found that 73% of Americans regard a free press as “very” or “extremely” important to society. Yet the country remains deeply divided over whether journalists should be barred from reporting “inaccurate” information, with a majority, 53%, supporting limits in some circumstances — even if it means the government itself would have the final say in determining what is true.
Trump’s attempt to bar three outlets from the White House grounds came just three days after the Pew poll was released.
“Plenty of presidents have complained about the press before. And presidents have restricted certain forms of press access or press action during wartime,” said Peter Kastor, chair of the History Department at Washington University in St. Louis. “In the moment — and especially afterward — Americans condemned this as antithetical to the constitutional protections for press freedom and the national commitment to an open democracy.
“What I find most striking about Trump’s press action is that he has made it unabashedly personal,” Kastor added. “He doesn’t like the way media outlets are covering him, so he is going to punish them.”
President Nixon famously limited White House access for the Washington Post over its coverage of the Watergate scandal. But he never attempted to bar press credentials completely — and ultimately authorized the conversion of the pool facility into the briefing room that exists today.
Other presidents have jostled with the press. President Obama was accused of limiting access to independent photojournalists, and famously favored nontraditional media outlets at the advent of the social media age. President George W. Bush limited his personal interactions with the press and curtailed access to government records.
Federal court judge calls the ban unconstitutional and rejects the White House argument that the action was done in the name of national security.
Thomas Jefferson, the nation’s third president, once stated he “deplored” the “putrid state into which our newspapers have passed, and the malignity, the vulgarity, and mendacious spirit of those who write for them.”
Yet, “it is however an evil for which there is no remedy,” he also said. “Our liberty depends on the freedom of the press, and that cannot be limited without being lost.”
Trump’s particular style — as a showman and his own spokesman — makes his relationship with the media innately personal, said Andrew Rudalevige, a professor of government at Bowdoin College and author of “The New Imperial Presidency.”
“Presidents almost always feel that bad press is a feature of their staff’s poor communication of their policies — not that the policies themselves are unpopular or ill-advised,” Rudalevige said.
“Since President Trump does so much of his communication, though, this deflection is less available,” he added, and “thus the problem is with the press itself, not the policy or its purveyor.”
CNN’s legal fight continues, even after securing temporary reprieve from a judicial restraining order. So does the Associated Press’ lawsuit over the administration’s effort last year to punish the wire service for refusing to adopt Trump’s preferred name, “Gulf of America,” for the internationally recognized Gulf of Mexico.
While he keeps losing in court on 1st Amendment grounds, the president keeps testing new limits, looking for what will stick.
On the tennis court Sunday, at least, his administration won.

A few years back, I posted about the “Daily Logic” and “Daily Semantics” project of Josh Dever, professor of philosophy at the University of Texas at Austin.
The projects offer up mini-lessons in logic or semantics that anyone can subscribe to.
At the time, Professor Dever wrote, “The idea of each is that each day you get sent a little, roughly 200 word bite in the relevant area, so that you can gradually and painlessly(-ish) build up real expertise.”

The lessons are pitched at roughly the “grad student new to the area” level.

Beats 360 Review: Customizable, Stylish, and Fun
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-29
10:00:00 UTC
19:00:00 KST

Easily swappable ear cups and headband. Multiple cushion color and fabric options. Water-resistant. 32 hours of battery life with ANC.
TIRED
Lackluster midrange sound. No wired listening. Strong clamping makes for uncomfortable everyday wear.
The Beats 360, I'll admit, didn't click for me until I started thinking of them as over-ear workout headphones. As everyday headphones, I had a tough time ranking these, given the competition, but as gym cans, the Beats 360 are stellar.
It took me a while to come to this conclusion because working out with over-ear headphones has always kind of sucked. They shift around a lot, get warm and sweaty around your ears, and are way, way heavier than earbuds. That last part might not seem like a big deal, but if you’re running a half-marathon, a half-pound weight on top of your head starts to get annoying fast. This stigma made me ignore this attribute about the Beats 360 at first.
Still, the number of people I see working out (and running) with Apple AirPods Max, one of the heaviest popular over-ear headphones around, shows the demand is there. And the Beats 360 fulfill that niche brilliantly, with a secure fit, IPX4-rated water resistance, and swappable cushioning. They may not be the best over-ear headphones for other things (like high-resolution audio), but it’s hard to knock them when they get their main thing (customizable over-ear workout headphones) right.
From Gym to Street

The Beats 360 are, first and foremost, fun headphones. That may not sound like much, but it’s a rarity in the sea of same-y over-ear headphones I’ve reviewed. The 360 have a slim, smooth design that’s appealing, with a soft-touch finish and an adjustable headband with smooth, telescoping metal (similar to AirPods Max or Sonos Ace Ultra).
The main draw of the 360s is the swappable headband and ear cups. With a slight downward pull, the headband comes off, and the ear cups do the same with a satisfying twist. In the box, you get a cushion set (headband and two ear cups) color-matched to the headphones, but mixing and matching colors is a big part of the 360's appeal (and its marketing).
This video is about My MovieVideo: Harry Rabinowitz
Making them easy to remove also makes them easier to clean and replace—a headache with most other headphones—and I consider that crucial for anything I’m going to exercise with.
The cushions come in two fabric options: Performance Knit, a mesh-like fabric that’s decently breathable and durable, and UltraPlush, a much softer, faux-leather style material akin to what you’d find on other premium over-ear cans from Bose, Sony, and Sonos.
The Performance Knit ear cups are better for working out—they feel more breathable, especially when I start to sweat. For everyday listening, though, the UltraPlush is much softer and more comfortable over time.
Video: Harry Rabinowitz
To be clear, the Beats 360 didn’t make me suddenly love working out with over-ear headphones. I still think wireless workout earbuds, like Beats’ own Powerbeats Pro 2, are the way to go, but the 360s are absolutely better than other over-ear options. The clamping force is strong enough that the headphones stay secure for most (but not all) exercises, without feeling so strong that they’re uncomfortable. Bicycle kicks and sprints still caused them to shift around a bit, unsurprisingly.
On the scale, the 360 are a middleweight. They are heavier than Sony and Bose over-ear headphones, but lighter than the AirPods Max. It's a good balance. Could they be a little lighter? Sure. Do they feel super heavy? Not really.
I appreciate the physical button controls, especially when working out. I do wish the buttons were a little more distinct and easy to recognize by feel alone. Things like a small tactile dot on the volume up button or a slight divot between the volume up and down would go a long way to helping me distinguish the all-smooth buttons.
I found myself swapping to the UltraPlush cushions whenever I wasn’t working out, and I started calling this “normal mode” and the Performance Knit setup “sport mode." In everyday use, the slightly strong clamping force of the 360s switches from a pro to a con—they get uncomfortable to wear after a few hours of office work.
Noise-canceling and transparency are highlights here. While not as strong as flagship headphones from Sony or Bose, the Beats 360 are close enough, and the ANC plus natural sound isolation did a good job shushing coworkers, cafés, the office cafeteria, and crowded New York City subway cars. With ANC enabled, you get 32 hours of battery life, which is very strong.
Connectivity is also simple and easy. Like other recent Beats headphones, the 360s pair instantly with Apple devices, and they support Apple device swapping, Apple Find My, and Siri. On Android, you get fast pairing, Google’s Find Hub, voice assistant with a button press, a few other Google/Android audio switching features, and the stand-alone Beats app. There's no wired connectivity, which is fine, since a cord is the last thing you want to deal with while exercising.
It’s only when I listen to my favorite playlist in the comfort of my office that the 360s' biggest weakness reared its ugly head: sound quality. Simply put: They sound OK, but not for headphones that cost $350. Unfortunately, they do not sound nearly as good as the $300 Sony WH-1000XM4C, $350 Sonos Ace, or $370 Bose QuietComfort Headphones (2nd Gen).
The first time I listened to music with the Beats 360 (after testing the Bose QC for weeks), I literally yelled, “Where are the mids?!” Listening on the Beats 360 feels like someone scooped out the midrange—guitars and vocals in certain genres seem weak or lost. On cheaper headphones, this wouldn’t be something I would harp on much, but for a $350 flagship headphone, it’s a miss, especially when the 360s get so much else right. Simply put, I won’t be reaching for the Beats 360 when I want to get lost in my favorite album or soundtrack.
Reliable Workout Buddy
I can see the Beats 360 doing very well for the gym. At $350, they're pricey but significantly less expensive than Apple AirPods Max, making them a good alternative for Apple users. To be fair, the Bose QuietComfort Ultra (2nd Gen) and Sony WH-1000XM6 are also cheaper than AirPods Max and provide better sound quality than the 360s, but lack the fitness chops. The removable ear cups and headband are downright fun, and mixing and matching colors is a breath of fresh air in headphone land.
These are not the best-sounding over-ear headphones out there. They aren’t best in class at any one metric, actually. But the 360 are an intentional trade-off—OK everyday performance for superior workout performance. If that compromise is where the Beats 360 want to hang their hat, they’ve got next to no over-ear headphones putting up a good fight in the workout space.
Personally, I almost always wear wireless earbuds or open earbuds when I work out. I still find them vastly more comfortable and more convenient for the job. But that’s just me. And if the Beats 360 finally get people to stop wearing AirPods Max to run in, I’m rooting for them.

AI: Concern as Germany plans to double data center capacity

AI: Germany plans to double data center capacity
September 29, 2026
The digital future is here, and it is unfolding in the town of Dietzenbach.
Google, EdgeConnex, and Maincubes, two US tech companies and one German, have each reserved a spot for a data center in the small town near Frankfurt am Main.
Dietzenbach is a logistics hub near Frankfurt's airport, and home to 35,000 people.
The Frankfurt region, the center of Germany's financial industry, is one of the most attractive locations for digital cloud operators worldwide, and as demand for computing capacity continues to grow, more centers are planned for the region.
Locals worry about electricity and water usage
However, the news of plans for a fourth mega data center has been met with resistance by locals. The stacks of tens of thousands of computers in a data center need a high supply of energy to run around the clock. They radiate large amounts of heat and need cooling, which requires huge quantities of water.
The people of Dietzenbach DW met were worried about their water and electricity bills rising, as well as a higher temperature in their town.
"We want to know two things: What are the benefits for the local community here in Dietzenbach? And what are the environmental impacts?" said Dietzenbach resident Wilhelm Sauer, pointing at the four imposing chimneys rising from the EdgeConnex data center.
He and the other local activists believe that the toll the data centers will take on regional resources may not be offset by the limited number of new jobs announced.
Dietzenbach's mayor, Dieter Lang of the center-left Social Democratic Party (SPD), however, is optimistic. He predicted that around 100 "high-value jobs" would come to his town through the Google data center.
He also expects it will benefit his city's coffers: "We expect a substantial tax contribution," Lang told DW.
But Tara Merk, researcher on Community Data Centers at the Weizenbaum Institute, is skeptical: She believes Germany can probably expect little revenue from data centers operated by US companies, "because the profits may be taxed elsewhere."
"Especially thinking about big tech companies — they're not going to be doing their taxes in Dietzenbach," she told DW.
Data centers and lack of information
In August 2026, the German government launched a data centers registry listing energy consumption, water consumption, and energy efficiency measures for the data centers that are already operating.
But the list includes only around 300 data centers, far fewer than the estimated 2,000 data centers the government says are running across the country.
"Some companies report their smaller projects but not the big ones," Werner Neumann, board member of the environmental group BUND, told DW.
There is no official overview of how many data centers are being built or where. The civil society project Heisse Luft (Hot Air) has decided to fill these information gap, and has developed an online map of the planned data centers across Germany. The map is updated every day with information based on crowdsourcing from local communities.
"Theoretically, we should have access to this information," Tiziana von Witzleben, co-founder of the Heisse Luft initiative, told DW. "Maybe the German government doesn't have the capacity to [collect this information] and share it. But I believe it is on purpose, particularly [on the part of] big players like Google and Amazon. [They] are known to be very secretive about what they do. Because they know that if they tell people, they will get a lot of protest."
Unlike in the US, where a nationwide movement mobilized protests all over the country, protests against data centers in Germany remain a local community phenomenon.
In February, the local council of Groß-Gerau in the Frankfurt region voted against a €2.5-billion ($2.8-billion) data center proposed by a US operator, at least partly as a result of massive protests from the residents wary of heat waste, the daily Frankfurter Allgemeine Zeitung reported.
In Maintal, another town in the region, an EdgeConnex mega data center faced intense protest against its plans to build its own gas-fired power plant. The €1-billion project is now searching for power alternatives in a region which is already hitting its grid limits.
The race for computational power
Germany is the largest data center market in Europe, both by capacity and number of sites, and the Frankfurt/Rhine-Main region, which includes Dietzenbach, holds over a third of the country's total data center capacity.
Its proximity to the Commercial Internet Exchange (DE-CIX) infrastructure in Frankfurt makes the region attractive for digital cloud operators.
To achieve its strategic goal of doubling data center capacity by 2030, the federal government, a coalition of the center-right Christian Democratic Union (CDU) and the SPD, has proposed amending the Energy Efficiency Act (EnEfG) that regulates energy consumption and climate protection.
The environmentalist Green Party questions whether the targets are based on real demand. The socialist Left Party, on the other hand, is skeptical of the expansion as a whole. Both parties oppose the government's plans to relax the rules to attract more data centers.
On the opposite end of the political spectrum, the far-right Alternative for Germany (AfD) supports the expansion of data centers but criticizes the law promoting the use of renewable energy to power them.
Why are energy efficiency amendments controversial?
The proposed amendment would push back the deadline for operators to achieve renewable energy targets, and would relax requirements for the reuse of heat waste.
Despite this plan, Tara Merk still considers the push for energy-efficient data centers in Germany to be a progressive example in the global context.
But she is critical of the parts of the law that would give companies the right to declare that the data on the amount of water and electricity they use are trade secrets.
"This proposed amendment shifts the regulatory landscape very much in favor of operators," she told DW. "Having good data is needed to regulate, intervene, and build trust and acceptance within local communities."
"I think [lack of transparency] is ultimately going to foster more antagonism between data centers and local communities, making it harder for operators to expand or even keep their existing sites running the way they are," Merk warned.
Algorithm Watch, an AI watchdog, argued in a public statement that the legal changes the government is proposing are not about cutting bureaucracy, but more about appeasing US tech giants Microsoft, Google, and Vantage.
"German and European operators mostly have no problem with the current rules," Algorithm Watch said. "The amendments run counter to the government's own aim of strengthening German/European firms."
This summer, the watchdog launched a campaign and collected 150,000 signatures against the amendments to the law, calling for the public reporting obligations of data centers to be retained.
The amendments were presented to the Bundestag in September. If the new law passes, the government hopes it will take effect in January.
Edited by Rina Goldenberg

Press review: EU fails to boost Ukraine aid as pro-Western politician takes Serbia's helm
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-29
10:00:00 UTC
19:00:00 KST

MOSCOW, September 29. /TASS/. The EU is struggling to fulfill its stated objective of providing Kiev with interceptors for its Patriot systems; the US Republicans are highly likely to face a major defeat in the November congressional elections; and a pro-Western politician has temporarily assumed power in Serbia, while the former president prepares to become prime minister. These stories topped Tuesday’s newspaper headlines across Russia.
Izvestia: EU unable to urgently increase military support for Ukraine
The EU will not be able to provide Kiev with the interceptors it needs for its Patriot systems. The few missiles currently available are needed by Greece, Spain, and the US, and, according to media reports, the EU is refusing to transfer them to Ukraine. At a meeting in Brussels on September 28, EU defense and foreign ministers were unable to reach an agreement on transferring this type of ammunition to Kiev, EU foreign policy chief Kaja Kallas acknowledged. However, experts believe the European Commission may personally press countries that possess the weapons Kiev needs. The EU could indeed exert pressure on certain countries, including Greece, to transfer interceptor missiles to Ukraine, Luxembourgish European Parliament lawmaker Fernand Kartheiser told Izvestia. However, he noted that the West has only a small number of them left due to the conflict in the Middle East. "Ukraine will no longer receive significant quantities of missiles and will not be able to produce enough of them on its own - if it is even capable of manufacturing them at all. It will remain vulnerable to air attacks. Its logistical and economic infrastructure could be systematically destroyed with minimal resistance," Kartheiser emphasized. The main problem for the EU is that it lacks sufficient interceptors for air defense, long-range strike capabilities, and intelligence and targeting data, Pavel Anisimov, deputy director of the International Relations and Political Science Institute at the Russian State University for the Humanities, pointed out.
According to him, some of the most scarce systems are those for the US Patriot system. Therefore, Brussels continues to purchase American weapons for Ukraine while simultaneously attempting to reduce its dependence on a single supplier by jointly developing more affordable missile and air defense systems. In turn, Moscow Pedagogical State University’s History and Politics Institute Deputy Director Vladimir Shapovalov stressed that Brussels will most likely continue to look for missiles for air defense. However, only a few countries, including Germany, Poland, and the Baltic and Scandinavian states, will meet European demands, the expert noted.
Meanwhile, the rest will attempt to block this decision so as not to weaken their own military capabilities. EU countries have long since abandoned a common stance on Ukraine: Bulgaria, Hungary, and Slovakia have officially refused to supply Kiev with weapons.
Vedomosti: Donald Trump's party very likely to suffer crushing defeat in November elections
US President Donald Trump’s fellow Republicans are bound to lose their majority in the House of Representatives following the November 3 election, and the possibility of them losing their majority in the Senate seems plausible as well, Charlie Cook, founder of the Cook Political Report, one of the most authoritative political rating aggregators in the US, stressed.
Historically, the president’s party has almost always lost House of Representatives seats in midterm elections while retaining its Senate positions. However, there have been instances when the president’s allies lost their majorities in both chambers following midterms: in 1918, 1946, 1954, 1994, and 2006. Even if the president’s party loses only the House, it will likely hamper most of the administration’s major initiatives and reforms since that is where all tax and budget legislation starts.
The Republicans’ chances there are limited both by Trump’s unpopularity and by the low approval ratings of the party’s candidates, political scientist and American studies expert Malek Dudakov told Vedomosti, recalling that according to the Real Clear Politics aggregator, only 38.7% of citizens support the president. The expert noted that the Republicans’ main problem is the economy and their inability to explain to voters how they intend to fix it. "There is very little time left before the election, and it is unlikely that the Republican Party will be able to change the situation in its favor in that time," Dudakov said.
The Republicans’ impending defeat in the House of Representatives is a predictable outcome, Pavel Koshkin, a senior researcher at the US and Canadian Studies Institute of the Russian Academy of Sciences, noted. However, there is another important aspect: whether the Republicans, even while in the minority, will be able to occasionally thwart the Democrats’ agenda following the election. According to the expert, if the margin of seats is small, this will certainly happen, just as the Democrats are doing now. "It seems to me that the Democrats are unlikely to win by a large margin. In addition to taking control of the House of Representatives, they may gain a small majority in the Senate. Therefore, Trump will retain his leverage," Koshkin stressed.
Nezavisimaya Gazeta: Pro-Western politician temporarily assumes power in Serbia
Aleksandar Vucic, who served as Serbia’s president for nine years, has resigned. This marks the beginning of a political maneuver that, if successful, will allow him to assume the role of prime minister and remain in power. Ana Brnabic will serve as acting president at least until the parliamentary elections on October 25. She is a close ally of Vucic. However, unlike him, Brnabic has criticized Russia for its policies toward Ukraine. She also has a reputation as a staunch supporter of closer ties with the EU.
Vucic’s term was officially set to expire in May 2027. After that, he would have lost the opportunity to remain in power. The country’s constitution prohibits him from running for a third term. Therefore, the former president will attempt to return to the prime minister’s office, which he held from 2014 to 2017.
Vucic may well be successful in carrying out this political maneuver, Yakov Smirnov, a research fellow at the Europe Institute under the Russian Academy of Sciences, told Nezavisimaya Gazeta. "Vucic’s chances of winning the election and becoming prime minister are very high. His electorate remains loyal to him, and the fragmented opposition parties have failed in recent years to put forward a clear candidate capable of unseating the former president and his party in the election," he noted.
As for Brnabic, her political views will not prevent her from pursuing the former president’s political agenda. "Brnabic is the ideal candidate for Vucic as acting president. She lacks significant political autonomy, and she is not very popular in Serbia. None of the political players in Serbia or abroad regard her as a serious figure. This is because she is, in a political sense, entirely Vucic’s creation, possessing agency only within the framework of the political system under Vucic’s control," the expert explained.
Rossiyskaya Gazeta: Reasons behind OpenAI's decision to pause training of AI models
OpenAI, one of the leaders in the modern AI industry, has temporarily suspended the training of new models following a series of incidents involving unpredictable behavior by its AI agents and promises to resume training after implementing additional security measures. These incidents are not isolated glitches but rather systemic issues with the controllability of autonomous AI agents - programs that independently set subgoals and determine how to achieve them without step-by-step human supervision.
OpenAI and its rival AI company Anthropic are currently working with independent security experts to investigate tens of thousands of incidents in which their models carried out problematic actions, such as bypassing content filters, creating third-party message boards, escaping isolated test environments, hijacking websites, and attempting to circumvent control systems through self-prompting.
Some experts view OpenAI's situation primarily as a PR stunt. "For OpenAI, this high-profile pause addresses several problems at once. The narrative is that their models are so powerful that they have to be shut down. You couldn’t ask for better publicity. At the same time, the company appears more responsible in the eyes of regulators just as the US is debating regulations for the industry," Oleg Rogov, head of a group at the AIRI Institute, told Rossiyskaya Gazeta.
Meanwhile, Pro-Vision Communications CEO Vladimir Vinogradov believes OpenAI’s decision marks the industry's first "digital psychotherapy" session. "The companies pushed the big red button. Amid the arms race, they paused due to the unpredictable actions of the agents. For the global AI industry as a whole, this signals the end of the venture capitalist-driven era of chaos. Now, investors will demand security protocols and log audits, and the race for speed will give way to a race for predictability," he pointed out.
According to experts in the Russian AI sector, these turbulent developments will only indirectly impact the industry. "Neither OpenAI nor Anthropic officially operates in Russia, and a few months’ pause won’t close the gap between Russian AI models and industry leaders. But there will definitely be some impact. Russian companies that are deploying agents have received a ready-made checklist of what could go wrong: bypassing filters, escaping an isolated environment, and unauthorized data collection. This means that, from day one, an agent should be given exactly as much access as the task requires," Alexander Danilov, founder and CEO of Nodul, a platform for creating AI agents, stressed.
Kommersant: Decline in gold prices due to concerns over persistently high oil prices
Gold prices tumbled by more than 3% at the start of the week, falling below $4,150 per ounce. This decline was driven by speculative trading amid surging oil prices and anticipation of a potential Federal Reserve rate increase in October. Meanwhile, strategic investors, concerned about the US government’s lack of fiscal discipline, continue to boost their portfolios’ gold holdings. As a result, gold ETF holdings exceeded 3,130 metric tons, marking the highest level since early March.
Last weekend, US President Donald Trump announced that he was rejecting Iran’s proposal to open the Strait of Hormuz and cease hostilities. As a result, on Monday, the price of the nearest Brent crude oil futures contract climbed by 4.3% to $108.8 per barrel. "Hopes for a rapid recovery in supplies have faded, and oil prices have risen again. This is currently a negative signal for gold, as high energy prices fuel accelerating inflation and increase the likelihood that the Federal Reserve System will have to tighten monetary policy more aggressively," Freedom Global analyst Vladimir Chernov told Kommersant.
At the same time, the price drop is occurring against a backdrop of persistently high demand from professional investors. According to Bloomberg, the total assets of gold exchange-traded funds (ETFs) rose by 8.8 metric tons last Friday, reaching 3,133.6 metric tons. Over the course of a month, these assets grew by nearly 66 tons, returning to levels seen in early March. Inflows into gold ETFs follow a different logic, as they reflect the behavior of strategic investors who take long-term positions, experts pointed out. "Strategic investors continue to buy gold as a hedge against geopolitical fragmentation, rising government debt, the risk of a loss of confidence in fiat currencies, and to further diversify their reserves," independent portfolio manager Alyona Nikolayeva emphasized.
However, such purchases alone cannot trigger an immediate price reversal. Therefore, according to Chernov, with oil prices high, the price of gold could well decline to the 4,000-4,100 dollars per ounce range. A more significant drop would require further deterioration in expectations regarding the Federal Reserve System’s interest rates, as well as an escalation in the Persian Gulf region. "The shipping agreement is more likely to support gold prices by lowering rate expectations than to cause prices to plummet due to the disappearance of the geopolitical premium. In August, signs of progress in the Strait of Hormuz gave the metal its strongest daily gain since February," Alina Poptsova, a stock market analyst at Alfa-Capital Asset Management, noted.

'I'd rather die here than in Africa': Migrants describe violent deportation flight
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-29
10:00:00 UTC
19:00:00 KST

-    Click here to listen to this article
-   Share via
See more from the L.A. Times in Google Search. Set us as preferred
- Migrants deported from the U.S. describe being shot at with pepper balls and forcibly restrained during a flight to the Central African Republic.
- More than 25,000 people have been expelled under a Trump administration program sending asylum seekers and others to ‘third countries’ where they have no ties.
- ‘They sent me to a failed state,’ said a Cuban man now stuck in Bangui, the troubled capital of the Central African Republic.
On a tarmac in Texas, federal agents repeatedly ordered a group of shackled immigrants off a bus and onto an airplane that they had heard was destined for Africa.
Many complied, but some men refused. They had sought protection in the U.S. after fleeing repressive governments and asked to speak to lawyers before being deported to a faraway continent.
“Tell us where you’re taking us,” Kenis Adalberto López, a 44-year-old from Nicaragua, said he told immigration agents through tears. “I’d rather die here than in Africa.”
Eventually, an agent boarded the bus and fired pepper balls at the men, according to interviews with three of them. López, who was hit twice in the chest with projectiles, said he was strapped to a stretcher and carried onto the plane, where he was restrained for the roughly 24-hour journey to Bangui, the capital of the Central African Republic.
More than 25,000 people have been expelled from the U.S. under a Trump administration program to deport asylum seekers and other migrants to “third countries” where they have no ties.
A federal appeals court ordered a pause on the program last week, saying the government failed to give migrants “a meaningful opportunity” to challenge their deportations to third countries. The Trump administration vowed to take the case to the Supreme Court, with Atty. Gen. Todd Blanche describing the program as “an entirely legal and invaluable tool to stem the tide of illegal immigration.”
The administration has routinely said that its enforcement operations are carried out in compliance with federal law and that detainees are treated humanely.
The Aug. 29 deportation of López and 42 others to Bangui highlights the sometimes violent tactics that officials have used to force detainees onto flights out of the U.S. — and the perils that await them once they land.
López and others recounted their journey in phone interviews from Africa.
The plane carried migrants from several countries, including Iran, Bangladesh and Afghanistan. Human rights lawyers say that many of them, including an Afghan man whose brothers worked with the U.S. military, had no criminal records and had been granted a special protection that barred them from being returned to their home countries because they had proved to a judge that they faced possible torture there.
-   Share via
Two of the men who resisted boarding the plane were kept in full-body restraint suits resembling straitjackets for much of the flight, according to witnesses. All of the deportees were shackled at the ankles and wrists while in the air.
After stops in two other African countries, the plane touched down in the Central African Republic, one of the world’s poorest nations and the site of an ongoing civil war between Muslim and Christian rebels that has claimed tens of thousands of lives over the last 15 years. The primary languages are Sango and French.
The migrants were given shots for yellow fever and taken to a housing complex, where they remain today, monitored at all times by armed guards.
Bangui, which sits across a wide river from the Democratic Republic of Congo, is battling a recent cholera outbreak and faces water shortages and power outages.
Crime is rampant, with the U.S. government itself warning Americans not to visit the Central African Republic because of “unrest, crime, kidnapping, landmines, health issues and terrorism.”
Three flights carrying U.S. deportees have arrived there since June, according to human rights groups tracking the issue. Many complain that U.S. immigration agents confiscated their identity documents upon detention and never returned them, making it all but impossible to leave the country. Their immigration status in the Central African Republic is unclear.
Two men who arrived on a July 31 flight recounted being kidnapped on the street by armed men who they believe were police officers.
Yasmani Moreno said he and the other detainee each had to pay the equivalent of $100 to be released.
Moreno, 31, who arrived in Florida on a raft from Cuba in 2016, was initially allowed to stay in the U.S. under the “wet foot, dry foot” policy, which until 2017 let Cubans who reached U.S. soil remain in the country. His temporary permit expired before he obtained a green card.
He has documented his time in Africa extensively on TikTok, taking his followers for walks along Bangui’s muddy streets. “They sent me to a failed state,” he said in an interview.
After decades of coups and strife, government forces have sought to disband many militia groups there, sometimes with the help of mercenaries with the Wagner Group, a Russia-based military contractor accused of human rights abuses. International experts have denounced President Faustin-Archange Touadera’s repression of the opposition and push to eliminate term limits as worrisome turns toward autocracy.
For deportees who came to the U.S. after fleeing authoritarian countries, an unknown future in another undemocratic nation is frightening.
Luis Hernández, 38, escaped Nicaragua after he marched in 2018 pro-democracy protests that were violently suppressed by the left-wing Sandinista government. He asked for political asylum at the U.S. border. A judge denied his request, but granted him protection from deportation under the international Convention Against Torture. For years, he led a quiet life working as a waiter in hotels in Washington, D.C.
In the past, people with such protection were generally allowed to stay and work in the U.S. indefinitely.
But in February, Hernández went to a regular immigration check-in and was detained. He was held in jails across the U.S., he said, until he was taken by bus to the tarmac in Texas on Aug. 28.
President Trump, in his push to expel 1 million people annually, has vastly expanded the pool of migrants eligible for deportation, with asylum seekers and people who a judge said may be tortured upon return now making up a growing share of detainees.
The U.S. has earmarked around half a billion dollars in aid to third countries who agree to take deportees, according to an investigation by the nonprofit journalism consortium Forbidden Stories, which found that in some cases, deportees sent to third countries were later returned against their will to their home nations.
“This is a deliberate attempt by the Trump administration to place refugees whom the U.S. government has determined need protection directly in harm’s way,” said Savi Arvey, director of policy for refugee and immigrant rights at Human Rights First.
Hernández said he was never notified that he was going to be sent to Africa — but that he and fellow deportees had heard rumors about flights there and suspected their fate when they saw the size of the plane they were being ordered to board. He said he was struck twice in the back and once in the knee with canisters containing pepper spray after he resisted boarding; pains from the blows persist.
After arriving in Bangui, he said, he went days without eating and sleeping, and suffered what he described as a mental breakdown.
“This is inhuman,” he said. “It’s psychological violence.”
He is worried in particular about ties between the Central African Republic and Russia, which is an ally of Nicaragua’s Sandinista government.
Sandinista operatives are suspected in a series of shootings, abductions and killings of Nicaraguan exiles in Costa Rica in recent years. Hernández wonders whether he is safe.
He has been following the news in the U.S. — including the recent appeals court ruling against the third country deportation program. His lawyer has urged him to look for another country that might grant him political asylum, but Hernández still holds out hope that the U.S. will welcome him back.
“There will be justice,” he said. “There’s still a democracy there.”
Linthicum reported from Mexico City. Special correspondent Ismael López in Jacksonville, Fla., contributed to this report.

His mom was detained by ICE. Two months later, he died by suicide
-    Click here to listen to this article
-   Share via
See more from the L.A. Times in Google Search. Set us as preferred
- Samuel Gonzalez Terrones, 21, died by suicide two months after ICE detained his mother.
- Samuel had been diagnosed with depression and schizophrenia. His family says he grew increasingly despondent as his mother remained in custody.
- A federal judge later ruled Minerva Terrones Dominguez’s detention unlawful and ordered her release, but without Samuel she no longer qualifies for the immigration relief her lawyers had pursued.
In May, when Samuel Gonzalez Terrones was diagnosed with depression and schizophrenia, he started seeing a therapist and taking medication that he hoped would finally alleviate the dark thoughts that had begun creeping up so frequently he would sometimes seek help by calling the police on himself.
A month later, his mom, Minerva Terrones Dominguez, 54, had just hopped off a bus on her way to a grocery store in San Bernardino when immigration agents arrested her for being in the country illegally. While she languished in detention, the family said, Samuel grew increasingly despondent.
To help pay for an immigration lawyer, his siblings and dad had taken up extra shifts at their jobs. But because Samuel’s condition meant he couldn’t hold a steady job, he spent more and more time alone at home in Rialto.
“My mom was the one who would take care of him when he would have those bad thoughts,” said his older sister Sari Gonzalez, 32. “Everybody would be at work or at school, so my mom was the only one that would be here to calm him down, to say, ‘Your siblings will be here in a bit, just wait.’”
The lawyer, Arturo Burga, had figured out a way to free Minerva from detention and allow her to stay permanently in the U.S. The legal pathway, called cancellation of removal, hinged on proving that her deportation would cause extreme hardship to a U.S. citizen: Samuel.
They never got to file the paperwork.
At 3:55 a.m. on Aug. 12, San Bernardino police responded to a railroad crossing. Samuel was pronounced dead at the scene, according to a San Bernardino County coroner’s news release. He was 21.
In a letter Samuel wrote before his death, an excerpt of which was shared with The Times, he talked about his mother’s detention. He said her being taken away by Immigration and Customs Enforcement made him feel like he’d hit “one last wall.”
“To the ICE agent who took away my mother: I hope it was worth it,” Samuel wrote. “I can’t handle anymore injustices in this world.”
Suicide prevention and crisis counseling resources
If you or someone you know is struggling with suicidal thoughts, seek help from a professional or call 988. The nationwide three-digit mental health crisis hotline will connect callers with trained mental health counselors. Or text “HOME” to 741741 in the U.S. and Canada to reach the Crisis Text Line.
Motivations for suicide are often complex and unknowable, and it’s unclear how the Trump administration’s aggressive immigration policies may have moved an immigrant or family member to harm themselves. But immigrant advocates say they have heard of such deaths.
This month, a 20-year-old Haitian man in Springfield, Ohio, walked into oncoming traffic after the Trump administration ended his Temporary Protected Status and ICE fitted him with an ankle monitor.
In May, the Associated Press found that at least 10 detainees had died by suicide since President Trump took office — a pace that far exceeds the growth in the detainee population.
ICE did not respond to requests for comment.
Samuel’s family describes him, the second youngest of seven siblings, as a caring and generous person who, at his best, was quick to laugh, loved chocolate conchas and video games, and dreamed of becoming a graphic designer.
He kept a dark aesthetic, with a lip piercing and nails frequently painted black or red. But he also had a lighter side, Sari said, as evidenced by the Hannah Montana stickers decorating his bedroom wall.
When the siblings were younger, they worked out together and would challenge each other to see how many pull-ups they could do. They liked hanging out at a skate park, laughing as he guided Sari’s small dog, Polar, down a rail on a board.
His mental health struggles started in 2021, when he was a freshman at Cajon High School. Little by little, he lost his passion for the gym, Sari said, and everything else.
Sari said she and her siblings each played a different role in helping Samuel through his struggles. He and his younger sister played video games. Sari would talk to him about adulthood. Their older brother would take him to church. On good days, their father would bring him along to landscaping jobs.
“He really did try to get better,” she said. “He held on for a really long time, and I’m proud of him for being so strong.”
The day Minerva was detained, Samuel and Sari were at home.
According to a federal court petition seeking Minerva’s release from ICE custody, federal agents stopped her, said she “looked like someone” they were seeking and mocked her when they found her EBT card while searching her belongings.
Minerva has lived in the U.S. for 33 years, had never been arrested or convicted of a crime and had never been in removal proceedings, according to her lawyer.
Sari said an ICE agent called her and said she had an hour to pick up her mother’s things from the agency’s local office and to say goodbye before ICE moved her to a detention center.
Samuel was inconsolable. “I’ve never seen him cry like that,” Sari said.
Sari took up extra hours at the plastics factory where she works as a machine operator. On Sundays, her only day off each week, she would take Samuel and their youngest sister to visit their mom at the Adelanto ICE Processing Center. The drive was 45 minutes without traffic, but they’d always arrive three hours early to join other families on the wait list to see loved ones.
On the way to the facility, Samuel was visibly happy. But on the way home, Sari said, all would be crying.
The extra expense of legal representation left the family struggling to pay for bills and food. In the evenings, Samuel stopping spending time with his siblings and retreated to his bedroom.
Burga, the lawyer, alerted ICE of Samuel’s death via email and requested Minerva’s emergency release under humanitarian grounds. He said the ICE deportation officer who replied struck a softer tone than usual, offering sincere condolences to the family.
“Our office was devastated,” said Amber Burga, executive director of the law firm. “I thought to myself, it takes somebody committing suicide for them to have compassion.”
Sari waited two weeks to tell Minerva. She waited, in part, because her mom had an upcoming court hearing and she didn’t want grief to cloud her thinking.
Sari was given 10 minutes in a visitation room to break the news about Samuel’s death to her mother.
“It was just me, my aunt and the officer who was watching,” she said. “When I told her, they wouldn’t even let me hug her while my mom was crying. They told me, ‘You can’t hug her. You can’t touch her.’”
Three days later, on Aug. 31, a federal judge — who didn’t know about Samuel’s death — issued an order granting her petition for release from detention, finding that she had been held illegally “based solely on DHS’s mistake.”
In her ruling, U.S. District Judge Brianna Fuller Mircheff wrote that when Minerva was detained, another federal judge had already declared it unlawful for Homeland Security to require mandatory detention for people who, like her, had entered the U.S. illegally.
Minerva had been arrested without a warrant, and an immigration judge had not determined whether she was a flight risk or a danger to the public.
Referring to Minerva and similar cases, Mircheff wrote, “Hundreds, if not thousands of individuals were held without process that was owed to them.”
Lawyers for the federal government had argued that Minerva could simply wait until she had been detained for six months, at which point she’d be entitled to a bond hearing, court records show. That suggestion didn’t fly with Mircheff, either.
“It is beyond cruel to suggest that this Court would let her sit in custody another four months,” she wrote.
Minerva is still in deportation proceedings. Without Samuel, she no longer qualifies for the legal pathway her lawyers had built a case around. Sari said she’s now considering joining the U.S. military to access the immigration benefits available for undocumented parents of enlisted members.
The family started a fundraiser to cover the cost of Samuel’s funeral.
Samuel’s parents, siblings, and a few dozen other family members and friends arrived on Sept. 22 at noon to bury him at the Rialto Park Cemetery. Each person held a white, long-stemmed rose.
Sari sobbed. Minerva looked on at the black casket holding her youngest boy, the goofball who loved his family, the one who had longed for her support while she was detained.
Times staff photographer Gina Ferazzi contributed to this report.

With bans and taunts, Trump escalates his assault on the media
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-29
10:00:00 UTC
19:00:00 KST

With bans and taunts, Trump escalates his assault on the media
-    Click here to listen to this article
-   Share via
See more from the L.A. Times in Google Search. Set us as preferred
- Despite a federal judge’s order, President Trump has refused to resume full access to CNN, dismissing its reporters as ‘fake news.’
- Five times in the last two months, the president has sneered at and insulted female reporters.
WASHINGTON — Under a light rain on Sunday at the Australian ambassador’s residence in Washington, CNN hosted its third annual tennis tournament, the Kangaroo Cup, pitting Beltway journalists against administration officials. The event aims to inject some levity into an historically adversarial relationship, reminding both sides of the spirit of the game. Themed drinks and tennis whites set the tone.
White House officials played with grace. But the mood this year was altogether different down Pennsylvania Avenue. Despite a federal judge demanding the administration reverse course on President Trump’s punitive actions toward his disfavored news outlets — CNN, MS NOW and Politico — he has refused to resume full access to the storied cable news channel, dismissing its reporters as “fake news.”
It is only the latest attack on press freedom by a president whose drive to punish critics and exert influence over the media appears to be growing.
During last week’s lavish state visit for Xi Jinping, Trump praised China for having “the friendliest press corps” and dismissed their repression of speech, despite the World Press Freedom Index ranking China among the world’s worst offenders — at the bottom of the list, alongside North Korea and Eritrea — for restrictions on journalists.
Five times in the last two months, the president has sneered at and insulted female reporters, mocking their appearance or dismissing their credentials.
The White House has signaled that CNN will be left off Air Force One for President Trump’s Saturday trip, the latest media restriction from the administration in an ongoing dispute with 1st Amendment implications.
He has declined to name a successor for his former press secretary, Karoline Leavitt, whose final news conference, on Aug. 27, was one of only a handful of briefings held throughout the summer. His administration launched its own streaming service last week, called Trump TV, in an attempt to circumvent traditional cable news. And on Monday, he posted renderings of the White House briefing room reconverted to its former use as a presidential pool and spa.
Trump’s escalating attacks on the press come just weeks before the midterm elections, as former officials and election experts warn the administration could seek to undermine confidence in the results. They also come at a precarious moment for public trust in the media, with more Americans saying limits on the press can be justified to combat misinformation.
A Pew Research Center survey released earlier this month found that 73% of Americans regard a free press as “very” or “extremely” important to society. Yet the country remains deeply divided over whether journalists should be barred from reporting “inaccurate” information, with a majority, 53%, supporting limits in some circumstances — even if it means the government itself would have the final say in determining what is true.
Trump’s attempt to bar three outlets from the White House grounds came just three days after the Pew poll was released.
“Plenty of presidents have complained about the press before. And presidents have restricted certain forms of press access or press action during wartime,” said Peter Kastor, chair of the History Department at Washington University in St. Louis. “In the moment — and especially afterward — Americans condemned this as antithetical to the constitutional protections for press freedom and the national commitment to an open democracy.
“What I find most striking about Trump’s press action is that he has made it unabashedly personal,” Kastor added. “He doesn’t like the way media outlets are covering him, so he is going to punish them.”
President Nixon famously limited White House access for the Washington Post over its coverage of the Watergate scandal. But he never attempted to bar press credentials completely — and ultimately authorized the conversion of the pool facility into the briefing room that exists today.
Other presidents have jostled with the press. President Obama was accused of limiting access to independent photojournalists, and famously favored nontraditional media outlets at the advent of the social media age. President George W. Bush limited his personal interactions with the press and curtailed access to government records.
Federal court judge calls the ban unconstitutional and rejects the White House argument that the action was done in the name of national security.
Thomas Jefferson, the nation’s third president, once stated he “deplored” the “putrid state into which our newspapers have passed, and the malignity, the vulgarity, and mendacious spirit of those who write for them.”
Yet, “it is however an evil for which there is no remedy,” he also said. “Our liberty depends on the freedom of the press, and that cannot be limited without being lost.”
Trump’s particular style — as a showman and his own spokesman — makes his relationship with the media innately personal, said Andrew Rudalevige, a professor of government at Bowdoin College and author of “The New Imperial Presidency.”
“Presidents almost always feel that bad press is a feature of their staff’s poor communication of their policies — not that the policies themselves are unpopular or ill-advised,” Rudalevige said.
“Since President Trump does so much of his communication, though, this deflection is less available,” he added, and “thus the problem is with the press itself, not the policy or its purveyor.”
CNN’s legal fight continues, even after securing temporary reprieve from a judicial restraining order. So does the Associated Press’ lawsuit over the administration’s effort last year to punish the wire service for refusing to adopt Trump’s preferred name, “Gulf of America,” for the internationally recognized Gulf of Mexico.
While he keeps losing in court on 1st Amendment grounds, the president keeps testing new limits, looking for what will stick.
On the tennis court Sunday, at least, his administration won.

            TEHRAN – Mahsa Beheshti from Iran won a bronze medal in weightlifting in the 2026 Asian Games on Tuesday.
Beheshti, 17-year-old, achieved a snatch of 113kg, clean and jerk of 146kg, and a total of 259kg in the women's 86kg category.
Wu Yan of China won the gold medal with a snatch of 124kg, clean and jerk of 149kg, and a total of 273kg.
Bahrain’s Alina Marushchak claimed the silver medal with a snatch of 124kg, clean and jerk of 148kg, and a total of 272kg.
Reyhaneh Karimi from Iran had previously won the bronze medal in the women’s 77kg category.

Iran warns no regional oil is safe as IRGC touts new weapons
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-29
09:59:37 UTC
18:59:37 KST

Parliament speaker Ghalibaf said if Iran cannot sell oil, "no one in the region will sell oil," as the IRGC called Trump "a big liar," said US bases were the "only source of insecurity" in the region and warned new weapons were being prepared for the battlefield.
Any obstruction to Iran's energy exports would have consequences for the entire region, Iran's parliament speaker Mohammad Bagher Ghalibaf said on Tuesday, as the IRGC launched a public attack on US President Donald Trump and said it was preparing new weapons for the battlefield.
"If Iran cannot sell its oil, no one in the region will sell oil, and if our security is not guaranteed, no infrastructure will be safe," Ghalibaf said in an online parliamentary session, cautioning Washington against "miscalculations".
"The Iranian people must never be frightened by blockade and threats. If the American enemy's decision-making machine fails to grasp this fundamental reality, it will remain trapped in a cycle of receiving heavy blows from the Iranian nation," Ghalibaf said.
IRGC spokesman Hossein Mohebi, speaking at a press conference with foreign media on Tuesday, called Trump "a big liar" and said US forces must leave the Middle East and that Tehran was continuously producing new weapons.
"We are constantly designing new weapons, upgrading existing ones and mass-producing armaments to defend ourselves," Mohebi said.
"If the confrontations take on a different shape, we will certainly bring new weapons into the field."
Ebrahim Azizi, head of parliament's National Security Committee, has separately said Iran is fully prepared for a conflict more intense than what he described as the "40-day war".
IRGC blasts US military bases as 'only source of insecurity'
On regional relations, Mohebi said US military bases were "the only source of insecurity" in the region and pointed to "long-standing bonds" with 15 neighbouring countries.
Since the US-Israeli strikes on Iran in late February in the opening salvo of the war, Tehran's retaliatory actions — including strikes on the territory of its neighbours, disruption of shipping and the closure of the Strait of Hormuz — have strained those relationships.
Iranian officials have insisted their targets are solely US military assets. Anwar Gargash, diplomatic adviser to the president of the United Arab Emirates, said recently in Dubai that while relations with Tehran should continue, trust damaged by attacks in the Gulf would take years to rebuild.
On nuclear matters, Mohebi rejected claims that Iran is weeks away from building a nuclear weapon, calling them "the same lie that has been propagated for 25 years."
The IAEA has not reached an agreement with Tehran on redeploying inspectors or resuming monitoring.
Since Mojtaba Khamenei was selected as the Islamic Republic's new ayatollah, voices within Iran's political establishment have increasingly raised the possibility of a review of the country's nuclear doctrine, a development that has drawn international concern.

Government plans DKK 22 billion extra for defense in 2027
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-29
09:58:49 UTC
18:58:49 KST

Eight Danish municipalities did not meet the required staffing ratio in kindergartens in 2025, according to figures published Monday by Statistics Denmark.
The municipalities are Ringsted, Odder, Holstebro, Ikast-Brande, Struer, Brønderslev, Rebild and Thisted.
Under the political requirement, there must be at least one pedagogical staff member for every six children in kindergartens. In 2024, 14 municipalities failed to meet the requirement.
The trade union BUPL, which represents pedagogues working in Danish children’s institutions, noted that more municipalities now meet the requirement than before.
“Staffing ratios have improved, and that is an important first step to ensure the quality in our daycare institutions,” BUPL chairperson Elisa Rimpler said.
“But we are not at the finish line at all when it comes to giving children the quality they are entitled to.”
Since 2024, there has also been a requirement of at least one employee for every three children in nurseries.
Five municipalities failed to meet that requirement last year: Bornholm, Holstebro, Ikast-Brande, Thisted and Rebild.
Rimpler said the figures were not good enough and called on municipalities to increase their efforts.
“There is a need to build on top of this, because in many places the staffing ratios on paper are experienced as very far from reality,” she said.
“Both because managers, long-term sick employees, and pedagogues employed to support individual children are counted, and because many of the extra employees do not have the necessary professional qualifications.”
According to BUPL, the law does not require the employees counted in the staffing ratios to have professional training.
The union said the share of pedagogues among staff was 57% in 2019, compared with 50.6% last year.
Children, Elderly and Housing Minister Jacob Mark of the Socialist People’s Party, SF, said it was serious when municipalities failed to meet the legal requirement.
He said the minimum staffing ratios were working because more nurseries and kindergartens were getting more staff around children and nationwide cuts to staffing had stopped.
“But, as I also see, there are eight municipalities that do not meet the minimum staffing ratios. That is completely unacceptable. I am going to intervene against that,” the minister said.
Mark also criticized the practice of counting managers and long-term sick employees in the staffing figures. He said managers are not with children all the time, while long-term sick employees are not with them at all.
According to Mark, municipalities “just” need to hire more pedagogical staff.
The minister said he will send a letter to the eight municipalities that do not meet the requirements. The same municipalities will also face scrutiny from Ankestyrelsen, Denmark’s public authority for supervising municipalities and other public bodies.
Ankestyrelsen can impose a range of sanctions after assessing why a municipality is not complying with the law, including advisory opinions and fines.
“Now they have had four years. Now they must reach the finish line with those minimum staffing ratios,” Mark said.

Amsterdam man arrested over links to ShinyHunters hacking group
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-29
09:58:49 UTC
18:58:49 KST

Amsterdam man arrested over links to ShinyHunters hacking group
See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results
A 24-year-old man from Amsterdam has been arrested on suspicion of involvement with the hacking group ShinyHunters, which has been behind a number of large-scale attacks on Dutch businesses in the past year.
Police said on social media that he was arrested this month and will appear in court in Rotterdam on Wednesday.
Sources told broadcaster NOS that the suspect is Pepijn van der S., who was sentenced to four years in prison in 2023 for extortion, money laundering and hacking. He was released this year.
Van der S. reportedly has a background in legitimate cybersecurity, having worked for Amsterdam-based security firm Hadrian. He also carried out ethical hacking research with the Dutch Institute for Vulnerability Disclosure. At the same time, he was leaking data stolen from clients and other companies, the court found in 2023.
ShinyHunters was responsible for an attack on Dutch telecoms provider Odido earlier this year, in which millions of customers had their personal data stolen. After the company refused to pay a ransom, the group posted much of the data on the dark web.
The hackers were also behind an attack on Canvas, an online learning platform used by students, after which its parent company paid a ransom to prevent further disruption.
Last week, ShinyHunters also claimed to have accessed the details of thousands of employees at the FBI, the US federal law enforcement agency. The FBI said an investigation was underway.

MADRID, Sept. 29 (Xinhua) -- Mallorca goalkeeper Ivan Cuellar is in hospital after suffering a serious head injury in an accident at the club's training ground.

Asian Games | China loses to DPRK 2-0 in women's football semifinal
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-29
17:58:36 CST
18:58:36 KST

SHIZUOKA, Japan, Sept. 29 (Xinhua) -- China lost 2-0 to DPR Korea in the women's football semifinal at the Aichi-Nagoya Asian Games here on Tuesday.
China reached the last four after a 1-0 extra-time win over Vietnam in the quarterfinals, and head coach Ante Milicic made several changes to its line-up for the semifinal, with Zhang Linyan and Li Qingtong sidelined by injury and Wang Yanwen suspended after accumulating yellow cards.
DPR Korea threatened early, hitting the crossbar in the third minute when Myong Yu Jong's shot from the right rebounded after a cutback. Heavy rain made the remainder of the first half cagey. China's first effort on goal came only in first-half stoppage time, when Shao Ziqin nodded over.
China almost took the lead shortly after the restart. In the 47th minute Wang Shuang's free kick found Zhang Chengxue, who beat the offside trap and headed toward goal, but DPR Korean keeper Yu Son Gum saved and Zhang's follow-up narrowly missed.
DPR Korea was awarded a free kick from a similar position six minutes later. Under pressure in the box, China defender Yao Wei inadvertently headed the ball into her own net to hand DPR Korea a 1-0 lead.
China coach Milicic brought on striker Yuan Cong as he sought to bolster the attack, but pushing forward left space at the back and DPR Korea increasingly controlled the game. They made the advantage safe in the 79th minute when a partially cleared corner fell to Myong, who was unmarked and fired into the far corner.
DPR Korea finished with 10 shots, five on target, while China managed only five shots with one on target.
"We always knew it was going to be a difficult game against a strong opponent in difficult conditions. I thought we defended well," Milicic said after the match. "Unfortunately, we conceded an own goal. We probably didn't have enough depth in our team to get back into the game."
Milicic said China's missing players had made the task more difficult, noting that the squad had been reduced from 26 players at the Asian Cup to 23 at the Asian Games.
"Without Zhang Linyan, Wang Yanwen, and Li Qingtong, missing three players is a lot," he said. "If you are going to compete against DPR Korea, you have to be at your best."
Milicic also attributed the result to details in set pieces.

DPR Korea, who thrashed Chinese Taipei 5-1 to make the semis, will face the winner of Japan and South Korea in the final. China will play for the bronze medal on Friday against the loser of the two sides.
"We need to be disappointed tonight, but tomorrow morning we have to wake up and put this game behind us," Milicic said. "We only have two days of recovery, so we need to move on quickly, learn from this game and freshen up." ■
