Expert: Russia clearly has the upper hand in the air in Ukraine
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-29
09:16:00 UTC
18:16:00 KST

Expert: Russia clearly has the upper hand in the air in Ukraine
Ukraine faces a difficult winter as Russian air attacks intensify and shortages of Patriot interceptor missiles leave it struggling to protect civilian infrastructure, Marko Mihkelson tells ERR in an interview.
How would you assess Ukraine's situation right now?
Ukraine is certainly heading into a very difficult fall and winter. Daily news from across the country shows that Russia has launched a massive campaign of aerial terror against all of Ukraine.
The targets include the capital and many other Ukrainian cities, all the way to the western border. As Ukrainian intelligence has determined in recent days, Russia's aim is to completely destroy Ukraine's civilian infrastructure capacity to withstand the winter. It is targeting energy supplies, data centers, water supplies and sewage systems. As we saw in the recent attacks on Kyiv where hospitals and buildings belonging to the Academy of Sciences were hit, the targets are wide-ranging.
A clear problem for Ukraine right now is its limited air defense capability, specifically because it is short of interceptor missiles for Patriot systems. Another major problem is the jet-powered Geran-5 drones Russia is using with Chinese support. They are being used extensively and causing a great deal of destruction.
What can Ukraine do to defend itself in the current situation?
It is certainly crucial to obtain the air defense weapons it needs from allies and partners as quickly as possible, above all interceptor missiles for Patriot systems from the United States and other allied and partner countries that have them in storage.
The other issue is the need to develop a capability to intercept jet-powered drones as quickly as possible. Several projects are underway, but Ukraine currently has no working solution.
How long could that development take?
When I met Robert Brovdi, commander of Ukraine's Unmanned Systems Forces, in September, he said it could take three to four months. That is, of course, a fairly critical period for Ukraine. Those interception systems will certainly be developed, but for now Russia has a clear advantage in the air.
The shortage of Patriot systems has been known about for a long time. How could the situation be resolved and are there ways to do it?
There are faster and slower solutions. President Volodymyr Zelenskyy also raised the possibility of producing Patriot systems in Ukraine under license when he met Donald Trump in the United States. But it would take years before production delivered any real benefit.
Right now, it is vital that the United States and everyone else able to produce interceptor missiles increase their production capacity. Even more important is a contribution from countries that already have the missiles in storage. Greece and some other countries, for example, should either sell or give them to Ukraine. We see every day that Russian attacks on civilians are intensifying and Russia hopes to bring Ukraine to its knees over the winter. As Ukrainians have repeatedly shown over the years, they will not give up, however hard things get.
The subject of trilateral talks has come up again recently. Why now?
It has always been there in the background. The United States, and the current administration in particular, wants to see this war end through negotiations. At the same time, we heard very clearly from Russian Foreign Minister Sergei Lavrov's remarks at the U.N. General Assembly that Russia's aim is to bring the war to a victorious conclusion. It expects the war and its military operations to achieve all its objectives.
Even Lavrov's meeting with the German foreign minister, the first in many years, was in fact a mockery on Russia's part. Russia essentially said outright that it was unwilling to negotiate on those terms. Russia demands Ukraine's capitulation and hopes to achieve it by force if words are not enough.
Fortunately, we are also seeing positive news from the front, particularly recently around Lyman, where Ukraine's Third Army Corps is carrying out a highly successful operation called Vivaldi. It has liberated nearly 200 square kilometers of Ukrainian territory in recent weeks.
The rotation of U.S. troops in the Baltic states will continue. That is certainly good news for us, but why was the decision made now?
I think it is good that the decision came before the Pentagon's final analysis and decision on the overall deployment of troops in Europe, which are still expected. There has been discussion and speculation that as many as 25,000 U.S. troops could leave Europe.
The decisions to increase the presence in Poland and resume rotations in Estonia and Lithuania — with a helicopter unit also coming to Latvia — are certainly very positive and timely for us. That is especially true at a time when speculation about possible Russian action against NATO is spreading almost daily on social media around the world.
To what extent might the sharper threat assessments recently seen in Western media have helped prompt the decision?
For us, the threat assessment has not changed in any way over the past few weeks. Possible patterns of provocative Russian behavior, such as false flag attacks using drones, were already known in the spring when U.S. intelligence made the information more widely available.
I think this reflects good work by our diplomats and, of course, Estonia's contribution to developing its independent defense capability — that same 5 percent of GDP. Our good partners Latvia, Lithuania and Poland are contributing as well. In doing so, we show that we are staunch allies of the United States. It is clear, however, that we must keep the United States' overall strategic approach to conventional defense in Europe in mind. European countries themselves certainly need to contribute substantially more.
There will certainly be some redeployment within Europe. How much hope is there that we might get additional troops?
I think the presence itself is what matters. Importantly, all the allies we have in Estonia — the United Kingdom, France and the United States — are nuclear powers and very important partners in NATO. Their activities under NATO's defense plans, together with our own military units and brigades, must provide the clearest possible deterrent to the adversary, Russia. It is also important that the units stationed here, regardless of their size, have every opportunity to carry out the exercises they need to be ready for combat.
Will U.S. units be combat-ready when they come to Estonia?
The units I have met at Nursipalu in the past have always said that, if necessary, they would be ready to defend Estonia that very day.
At the same time, looking at the U.N. General Assembly, there were some conflicting signals from the other side. The G20 invitation and the sanctions on Belarus are examples. What is the U.S. trying to say with these decisions and what is its goal?
Sometimes it is hard to understand what lies behind particular tactical steps. As we discussed earlier, the current U.S. administration wants, one way or another, to find a path toward restoring relations with Russia.
It is Russia that does not want to restore relations in a way that would ultimately be acceptable to the Americans and their allies. Russia continues its massive war of aggression and is escalating its acts of terror in NATO member states. In this situation, we should not expect that there is some purely diplomatic move, as yet undiscovered, that could stop the war or restore relations.
That cannot be achieved without putting pressure on Russia. I believe the United States has also come to understand this in one way or another, particularly considering the sanctions legislation signed by Trump that was finally passed by Congress after many months. Of course, we would like to see the United States act more forcefully to pressure Russia.
How would you assess relations between the U.S. and Europe right now?
How should I put it? There has not been much new lately; if anything, there have been some more positive developments. At the U.N. General Assembly, a solution was found to the U.S.-Greenland issue, which had been a source of concern for some time. Fortunately, the sound and skillful diplomacy of Denmark and its partners, and ultimately the United States as well, led to an agreement.
It essentially returned matters to the same framework that Denmark and the United States have operated within for the past half-century. So that is largely positive news. The more serious question is how the planned changes to troop deployments in Europe might affect the broader strategic picture, as well as Europe's own conventional defense and deterrence capabilities.
It is very important to continue working closely with our American partners and allies on this. Whatever steps they take must not diminish Europe's and NATO's ability to deter Russia.
--
Editor: Marcus Turovski, Johanna Alvin
Source: "Välisilm"

Germany’s potential next leader holds talks in Türkiye
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-29
09:14:53 UTC
18:14:53 KST

Hendrik Wüst, the premier of Germany’s most populous state and the country’s potential next leader, has begun his three-day visit to Türkiye on Sept. 28. (AA Photo)
Hendrik Wüst, the premier of Germany’s most populous state and the country’s potential next leader, has called for a “new chapter” in ties with Türkiye as he began a three-day visit to the country on Sept. 28.
Wüst, the conservative premier of North Rhine-Westphalia, arrived in the Turkish capital Ankara with a large delegation that included senior business representatives.
He was received by President Recep Tayyip Erdoğan shortly after landing.
The visit comes as Germany and Türkiye mark the 65th anniversary of the 1961 labor recruitment agreement that brought Turkish “guest workers” to West Germany.
Around 3 million people of Turkish origin currently live in Germany, according to the country’s Federal Statistical Office, with slightly more than half holding German citizenship.
Wüst highlighted the strong links between Türkiye and North Rhine-Westphalia, noting that roughly one-third of Germany’s population of Turkish origin lives in the state.
“They are naturally part of our state,” Wüst said, becoming the first premier of North Rhine-Westphalia to make an official visit to Türkiye.
The 51-year-old politician has repeatedly rejected speculation that he could seek to replace Chancellor Friedrich Merz, whose government has come under pressure.
“I want to remain premier of North Rhine-Westphalia,” Wüst told German broadcaster ZDF before departing for Türkiye, adding that his priority was to help “get the federal government firing on all cylinders again.”
During his first day in Ankara, Wüst was scheduled to visit a Henkel facility belonging to the Düsseldorf-based company before paying his respects at the mausoleum of Mustafa Kemal Atatürk, the founder of modern Türkiye.
He was also due to meet Turkish business representatives.
On Sept. 29, Wüst is expected to hold political meetings in Ankara before traveling to Istanbul.
His Istanbul program includes a business conference and a ceremony honoring former Germany football captain İlkay Gündoğan with an award recognizing tolerance and intercultural reconciliation.
Speaking ahead of the trip, Wüst said he wanted to concentrate on areas where Germany and Türkiye could deepen cooperation, arguing that difficult issues could be addressed more effectively through a close partnership.
“No [German] region is as closely connected to Türkiye, socially and economically, as North Rhine-Westphalia,” he said.

OCCRP Partner Siraj Wins 2026 Samir Kassir Award
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-29
09:14:00 UTC
18:14:00 KST

The Samir Kassir Award for Freedom of the Press has named Ali Al-Ibrahim, co-director of OCCRP member center Siraj, and Syrian investigative journalist Mais Katt as joint winners in its investigative reporting category. The award recognizes their September 2025 cross-border investigative project, “Syria’s Stolen Children: How the Assad Regime Turned Detainees’ Children into Hostages Between Intelligence Agencies and Orphanages.”
Published a year ago following the fall of Bashar al-Assad in late 2024, the investigation documents how officials from al-Assad’s security services abducted hundreds of Syrian children of political detainees and hid them inside children’s charities in order to coerce and intimidate their families. The investigation exposed the complicity of several care institutions, including facilities run by the major European charity SOS Children’s Villages, whose leadership knew about the abuses for years and remained silent.
The Samir Kassir Award, which has been presented by the E.U. since 2006, selected the investigation from 194 submissions across 11 countries in North Africa, the Middle East and the Gulf.

Andriy Shevchenko celebrates his 50th birthday: the journey from &quot;Dynamo&quot; to the UAF
Ukraine
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-29
12:13:53 EEST
18:13:53 KST

Andriy Shevchenko celebrates his 50th birthday: the journey from "Dynamo" to the UAF
Kyiv • UNN
Andriy Shevchenko is celebrating his 50th birthday. The Ballon d’Or winner has gone from "Dynamo" and "Milan" to becoming president of the UAF.
Today, September 29, Andriy Shevchenko, president of the Ukrainian Association of Football, former player for "Dynamo," "Milan," and "Chelsea," former forward of the Ukraine national team, Ballon d'Or winner, and former head coach of the national team, celebrates his 50th birthday, reports UNN.
Details
Andriy Shevchenko's football career began in 1992 in Kyiv, where he moved with his family from the village of Dvirkivshchyna in the Kyiv region. Interestingly, Andriy's parents were skeptical of their son's passion, while his father, who was a warrant officer, wanted his son to become a military man as well. However, Andriy's first coach, Oleksandr Shpakov, managed to convince his parents.
Andriy Shevchenko made his first appearance in senior football in the 1992/93 season. With 12 goals, he became the top scorer for first-league team "Dynamo-2." He was then invited to Ukraine's youth national team and made his debut in the top division—he first came on as a substitute on November 8, 1994 (in a match against "Shakhtar"). At that time, "Dynamo" was coached by Jozsef Szabo.
Shevchenko truly made a name for himself in the 1997/1998 and 1998/1999 seasons.
In the 1997/1998 season, "Dynamo" defeated Catalan club "Barcelona" twice in the Champions League group stage, with an aggregate score of 7:0; in the second match, Shevchenko scored a hat trick.
The following season, Kyiv's "Dynamo" reached the Champions League semifinals after defeating formidable Madrid side "Real" in the quarterfinals. The first match took place in Madrid, and it was Shevchenko who opened the scoring—after a pass from Rebrov, he burst toward the Spaniards' goal at fantastic speed and scored past Bodo Illgner. The match ended in a 1:1 draw. In the match in Kyiv, Andriy Shevchenko opened the scoring by following up on his own missed penalty, then finished off "Real" with a second goal—2:0.
In the summer of 1999, Italy's "Milan" paid $25 million for Andriy, and "Sheva" spent what were probably the best years of his career there. An interesting fact is that the money received for Shevchenko made it possible to build "Dynamo's" modern training base in Koncha-Zaspa. New buildings were constructed, a medical and rehabilitation center was established, and indoor arenas and high-quality pitches were added, creating European-level infrastructure.
August 29, 1999—his Serie A debut in the match "Lecce" - Milan" (2:2). In his very first season, he became Serie A's top scorer, scoring 24 goals in 32 league matches and finishing ahead of such goal scorers as Batistuta (23 goals) and Crespo (22).
Overall, Shevchenko ranks second on "Milan's" all-time top scorers' list, with 174 goals to his name.
At "Milan," the Ukrainian became Serie A's top scorer twice, won the Italian championship and the Champions League, and in 2004 received the "Ballon d'Or."
Interestingly, his transfer to "Milan" could have fallen through because of a possible kidnapping.
In 1999, while the player was arranging his transfer to "Milan," the Security Service of Ukraine intercepted phone conversations among criminal kingpins. They discussed a plan to kidnap Shevchenko for ransom. Ultimately, the footballer was provided with additional security, thwarting the criminals' plan.
At "Milan," Shevchenko also became the first Ukrainian in history to win the Champions League, doing so in the 2002/2003 season by converting the decisive penalty in the match against "Juventus."
Incidentally, Shevchenko's teammates at "Milan" were surprised by his culinary preferences.
In one interview, Andriy Shevchenko said that when he first brought a piece of Ukrainian salo to "Milan's" training ground, some of the guys were frightened.
"Honestly. Someone even thought it was a drug. At the time, I simply did not understand that Italians had never seen pork fat in their lives. Just as there is never any snow in Africa on the equator, they had never seen it either. I remember cutting off the first very thin slice and offering it to Maldini. He refused. So I put the pork fat on bread and started chewing. You should have seen Paolo’s eyes—and those of the entire group—at that moment. And how do you think it ended? Every time I later returned to Italy, I had to bring half a bag of pork fat for the "Milan" players, they loved it so much. There were so many orders that I regretted having so recklessly arrived at the "Milan" training base with Ukrainian drugs," Shevchenko recalled.
In the mid-2000s, Italy’s "Serie A" began to be rocked by turmoil. The reason was corruption scandals, in which Shevchenko’s "Milan" was also involved. While the trials and investigations were ongoing, Shevchenko moved to London’s "Chelsea," for which 30.8 million British pounds (about 45 million euros) was paid. Thus, the Ukrainian became the most expensive transfer in the history of British football and entered the top ten most expensive transfers of all time.
There is also another version of the reason for "Sheva’s" move to "Chelsea." Andriy’s wife, Kristen Pazik, wanted to live in London, where she would have had more opportunities for a career in the fashion business.
Shevchenko’s career in London frankly did not work out, in particular because of constant injuries, and after a loan spell at "Milan," Shevchenko returned to his home club, "Dynamo," in 2009.
In the first match after his return, at the packed Valeriy Lobanovskyi Stadium, in the match between "Dynamo" and "Metalurh Donetsk," Shevchenko came on as a substitute for Denys Harmash, and in the second minute of added time, Shevchenko converted a penalty.
After Euro 2012, hosted at home, in which the Ukrainian national team participated for the first time, Shevchenko ended his career. It should be noted that in the first match against Sweden, it was Shevchenko’s brace that secured the national team’s first-ever victory at the European Championships, scoring his 47th and 48th goals, which made him the national team’s top scorer. However, Andriy Yarmolenko is close behind "Sheva," with 47 goals to his name.
After ending his career, Shevchenko became the coach of the Ukrainian national team, with which he reached the quarterfinals of Euro 2020, defeating Sweden in the round of 16, this time as a coach. The legendary phrase, "Malinovskyi, Zinchenko, cross, shot, goal," has been forever etched in the memories of fans.
On January 25, 2024, Andriy Shevchenko was unanimously elected president of the Ukrainian Association of Football, replacing Andriy Pavelko, who is implicated in a case involving a scheme to withdraw nearly UAH 295 million in Federation funds through controlled commercial entities.
Congratulations to Andriy Mykolayovych on his anniversary. We wish him strong health, family warmth, strength, inspiration, and new achievements for the benefit of Ukrainian football.

Almost 4,500 civilians evacuated from combat zone in DPR, senior Russian senator says
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-29
09:13:24 UTC
18:13:24 KST

MOSCOW, September 29. /TASS/. Some 4,500 civilians were evacuated from the combat zone in the Donetsk People’s Republic (DPR) as it was liberated from Ukrainian troops, Natalya Nikonorova, deputy head of the Federation Council Committee on International Affairs, told TASS.
"As many as 4,459 people have been evacuated [from the combat zone in the DPR], including 971 in the Konstantinovka direction. Thirty temporary accommodation centers for 2,574 people have been set up, where 1,721 evacuated citizens, including 89 low-mobility people and 52 children, have been accommodated," the senior Russian senator said.
According to her, temporary accommodation centers have been established across 17 municipalities in the DPR.
From September 23 to September 27, 2022, the DPR and the Lugansk People’s Republic (LPR) as well as the Kherson Region and the Zaporozhye Region held a referendum where the majority of voters opted to join Russia. On September 30, Russian President Vladimir Putin and the heads of the four regions signed treaties on their accession to Russia. On October 4, 2022, Putin signed laws on the ratification of these treaties. A year later, on September 28, 2023, the Russian president signed a law declaring September 30 as Day of Reunification of the Donetsk and Lugansk People’s Republics, and the Zaporozhye and Kherson Regions with Russia.

Amsterdam wants simpler rules to get asylum seekers working
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-29
09:13:15 UTC
18:13:15 KST

Amsterdam wants simpler rules to get asylum seekers working
See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results
Amsterdam is making a scheme to help asylum seekers find paid work a permanent fixture, after a pilot involving over 1,000 refugees managed to get 332 of them into jobs in just over 18 months.
The city council is also calling on the national government to make it easier for employers to hire asylum seekers, by scrapping the work permit they currently need.
“It is important that asylum seekers get the chance to work while their application is still being processed,” work and income chief Sofyan Mbarki said in a statement. “Work gives people self-esteem and an income, and it helps them integrate quickly.”
Participants were recruited at three locations: the Willinklaan refugee centre and the emergency shelters at the A&O Hostel in Zuidoost and on board the MS Galaxy, a cruise ship that is being temporarily used to house asylum seekers.
National plans
 Mbarki said the results backed up last week’s advice by the socio-economic council, which said councils should be legally required to help newcomers find work that matches their skills.
He also welcomed plans by work and participation minister Thierry Aartsen (VVD) to have councils help 75,000 more people into work, but said councils would need funding from The Hague to do it.
Drop-out risk
 The pilot officially ends this year but will continue for another 4 years, as set out in the city’s coalition agreement.
The evaluation, by urban research institute Platform31, found that work gave participants more financial stability and helped their language skills. Employers described them as motivated and keen to learn.
It also recommended more aftercare and job coaching in the first months, to reduce the number of people who drop out of jobs after being placed.
Amsterdam wants the work permit (tewerkstellingsvergunning) replaced with a simple obligation to notify the UWV, the system already used for displaced Ukrainians in the Netherlands.

Iran parliament speaker warns no one in region will sell oil if Tehran cannot
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-29
09:12:50 UTC
18:12:50 KST

Mohammad Sio
29 September 2026•Update: 29 September 2026
Iranian Parliament Speaker Mohammad Bagher Qalibaf warned Tuesday that no country in the region would be able to sell oil if Iran were prevented from doing so, according to the state-run IRNA news agency.
“The US and other countries should know, as we have said, that in a region where we cannot sell oil, no one will sell oil,” Qalibaf said.
His warning comes as Iran faces severe restrictions on its oil exports amid the ongoing conflict with Washington and US sanctions.
Iran’s Central Bank governor said in August that the country’s oil exports had fallen to zero, saying Tehran was no longer exporting crude because of the war and sanctions.
The US military, meanwhile, said on Sept. 19 that more than 1 billion barrels of crude oil had passed through the Strait of Hormuz in recent months with US military assistance, while claiming Iran had exported “zero barrels” under what Washington calls its “ironclad blockade.”
“If our security is not guaranteed, no infrastructure will be safe,” Ghalibaf said.
Earlier this month, Qalibaf warned that US energy infrastructure and assets around the Gulf and the Strait of Hormuz could face Iranian retaliation if Washington attacked Iran’s oil and gas facilities.
Qalibaf also referred to recent remarks by US President Donald Trump concerning the Strait of Hormuz and the passage of vessels through the waterway, describing them as a repetition of earlier US claims.
Trump on Saturday rejected an Iranian proposal to reopen the Strait of Hormuz to normal commercial traffic within seven days, saying Tehran’s conditions were unacceptable and claiming Washington already had “total control” of the waterway.
Under Tehran’s proposal, Washington would release frozen Iranian assets, lift oil sanctions and end the US naval blockade on Iranian ports, after which Iran would move to reopen the strait and talks on a final agreement would begin.
Iran has kept the Strait of Hormuz restricted while demanding that Washington fulfill commitments under a June memorandum of understanding. Iran says that the waterway will not fully reopen until Iran’s conditions are met and US commitments are implemented.
On Monday, Iranian Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi said that Qatari mediators will present the US with new ideas discussed with Tehran on how to meet Iran’s conditions for reopening the Strait of Hormuz.
Qalibaf also warned Washington against further pressure on Tehran, saying Iran will not retreat in the face of what he described as “air or commercial blockades.”
His comments come as Washington has expanded economic pressure beyond Iran’s oil and maritime sectors to civil aviation.
“The leaders of the White House should know that Iran, a wise nation that has made history, will never retreat because of lines being drawn, speeches, or air or commercial blockades,” Qalibaf said.
He added that Iran’s response to “any threat or adventurism” would be “regrettable and swift.”
In February, the US and Israel launched a war against Iran, which responded with attacks on Israel and US targets in the region before a ceasefire agreement was reached in April.
Washington and Tehran later signed a memorandum of understanding in June concerning freedom of navigation in the Strait of Hormuz, but implementation stalled over disagreements related to security in the strategic waterway as tensions continue to escalate between the two sides.

Putin Adds 15,500 Active Troops to Russia’s Military, Raising Force to 1.55 Million
Russian leader Vladimir Putin has issued a new executive order adding 15,500 active service members to the Russian Armed Forces, setting the total military headcount at 2,441,630 individuals, which includes 1,550,500 active military personnel.
Prior to this change, the total military headcount stood at 2,426,130 positions, with 1,535,000 active service members, according to The Moscow Times on September 28.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
This decision marks the fourth time this year and the seventh time since Russia’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine that the Kremlin has expanded its authorized military strength.
This recent adjustment follows a decree signed in late July, which added 25,000 active troops to establish dedicated military construction units, The Moscow Times reported.
Earlier in the year, a June 12 presidential order raised the number of active troops to 1,510,000, bringing total military personnel to 2,399,130. That followed a March adjustment that set the overall military workforce at 2,391,770, including 1,502,640 active soldiers.
According to draft budget projections for 2027, defense allocations could rise to 17.1 trillion rubles ($223.6 billion), accounting for 35% of all federal expenditure.
Russia has already begun an additional mobilization effort, Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy stated during his evening address. Ukrainian intelligence previously reported that Russian forces plan to mobilize 300,000 personnel this year.
The expansion also involves an influx of foreign soldiers. Specifically, 8,000 North Korean troops are already on Russian territory, with an additional 10,000 set to deploy. According to the president, in exchange for this troop deployment and with Russian technical support, Shahed drone production has been established inside North Korea.
President Volodymyr Zelenskyy announced that Russia has started additional mobilization efforts, planning to draft 300,000 troops alongside deploying 18,000 North Korean soldiers.
Previously, it was reported that Russia may be preparing a new wave of mobilization. Ongoing heavy losses and a stalled offensive have fueled expectations in Moscow that a large-scale conscription drive could be launched later this year.
According to these reports, the resulting pressure is already being felt within military enlistment offices.

We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.

Easy Targets Are Mostly Gone as EU Faces Internal Trade-Offs Over Russian Sanctions

Easy Targets Are Mostly Gone as EU Faces Internal Trade-Offs Over Russian Sanctions
European Union sanctions against Russia are increasingly influenced by the national interests of individual member states.
Governments now frequently use negotiations over sanctions lists to secure political concessions on separate issues, as reported by Euractiv.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
Last week, EU countries agreed to extend sanctions against figures close to the Kremlin in exchange for removing Russian oligarchs Alisher Usmanov and Mikhail Fridman from the bloc’s blacklists.
This decision raised concerns among several European diplomats, who pointed out that member states are increasingly using sanctions as leverage to secure foreign policy goals.
According to Philipp Lausberg, a senior analyst at the European Policy Centre, EU sanctions against Russia have shifted since 2022 from energy security concerns to economic, corporate, and foreign policy interests, Euractiv reported.
He noted that "the easy targets are mostly gone," as earlier sanctions packages already addressed oil, gas, raw materials, export controls, and financial measures.
European officials are now left to target entities that support shadow fleets, financial structures, cryptocurrency platforms, and companies in third countries that help Russia circumvent export restrictions.
However, these operations are significantly harder to block. Experts note that technological restrictions and export prohibitions remain among the most effective tools available to the European Union.
Previously, European Union diplomats hit a deadlock over renewing sanctions on nearly 3,000 Russian targets after France joined Slovakia in demanding the removal of billionaire Alisher Usmanov.
France cited national security and efforts to free its citizens detained in Azerbaijan, while Luxembourg pushed to delist billionaire Mikhail Fridman, forcing the EU to agree to a one-week extension to avoid the regime's expiration.

Raising $178 Billion for Defense, Russia Sets Its Biggest Military Budget Since 2022
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-29
09:11:23 UTC
18:11:23 KST

- Category
- War in Ukraine
Raising $178 Billion for Defense, Russia Sets Its Biggest Military Budget Since 2022
Russia is preparing to increase its defense expenditures to 17.1 trillion rubles ($178 billion) in 2027, according to Reuters.
This planned allocation represents a 27% increase compared to the initial target of 13.5 trillion rubles ($140.5 billion) and marks the highest defense outlay since the beginning of Russia’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
Over the next three years, total military spending is projected to reach 50 trillion rubles ($520.4 billion).
For 2026, the previous plan set defense expenditures at 12.1 trillion rubles ($125.9 billion), though actual spending details remain classified, with additional defense-related funds potentially allocated under non-military budget categories.
Alongside higher military allocations, official estimates indicate a growing fiscal gap.
The federal budget deficit forecast for 2026 has been adjusted upward to 3.2% of gross domestic product, doubling the previous 1.6% estimate, while total budget expenditures in 2026 are expected to expand by 13.2% to 48.6 trillion rubles ($505.8 billion), equivalent to 20.9% of GDP, Reuters reports.
In the first nine months of 2025, Russia spent $146.4 billion from its budget on military expenditures—four times more than it had in 2021—which accounted for 39% of total government spending.
As military costs rose, civilian spending shrank, and the current budget allocated just 25.1% to social needs, marking the lowest level in two decades.
In total, the state directed $522 billion in taxpayer funds toward the war effort between 2022 and 2025, an amount that could have otherwise financed the entire higher education system for 24 years or supported federal healthcare for 22 years.

Frugal countries pile on pressure to shrink EU budget
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-29
09:09:57 UTC
18:09:57 KST

Six "frugal" EU leaders have stepped up pressure on the Irish presidency to slash the next long-term budget by "several hundred billion euros" in its new compromise text.
The leaders of six "frugal" net contributors to the EU budget have written to the Irish presidency, stepping up their push for a lower overall figure in its upcoming compromise proposal.
The letter, dated 28 September and seen by Euronews, is the latest attempt by the frugal camp to shrink the EU's next long-term budget, the Multiannual Financial Framework (MFF). Talks have entered a crunch phase, with a deal targeted by the end of the year.
"We are now entering the decisive phase of the negotiations, in which we must determine the overall size of the MFF and decide which areas should be prioritised for funding," the document reads.
It is signed by German Chancellor Friedrich Merz, Austrian Chancellor Christian Stocker and Prime Ministers Mette Frederiksen of Denmark, Rob Jetten of the Netherlands, Petteri Orpo of Finland and Ulf Kristersson of Sweden.
It is addressed to Irish Prime Minister Micheál Martin, whose country holds the rotating presidency of the Council of the European Union. Dublin is due to present a new compromise text in the coming days, ahead of a European Council summit on 15-16 October.
"If the Irish negotiating box is to serve as the basis for further discussions, it must set out an overall volume that can realistically be financed by those who carry the main financial burden. This issue cannot be postponed," the letter reads.
In June, the Cypriot presidency proposed a 2% cut to the European Commission's proposed MFF for 2028-2034, worth nearly €2 trillion. The six countries considered the reduction far too small to win their support.
"Almost every EU member state is making painful efforts to consolidate its public finances. There will be no European sovereignty without sound public finances," the letter continues. "The European Commission has proposed a nominal increase of around 60%. That is simply not realistic."
The frugal countries are also pushing to change what the money is spent on. They want to shift funding away from traditional policies such as cohesion and agriculture towards "modern" priorities.
"The funding should be focused on common investment in security and defence, competitiveness, innovation and the fight against irregular migration," the text says.
The letter repeats the message the six leaders delivered in Berlin on 27 August, when they asked for cuts of "several hundred billion euros" without settling on a precise figure.
"We would like to reiterate that the MFF negotiations are characterised by a fundamental asymmetry: our six countries alone finance almost 40% of all member states' contributions," the letter reads.
They also criticised as "out of step with the times" the Commission's plan to increase staffing at the EU institutions while most public administrations face cuts, a view shared by most member states.
"The Commission's proposal will need to be reduced by several hundred billion euros. All headings will have to contribute to these savings," the letter adds.

World Bank outlines ways to address the demographic crisis

Tuesday 29 September 2026 11:36
Tuesday, 29 September 2026, 11:36
PHOTO archive
Font size
From 1988 to 2024, Bulgaria’s population fell from 8.9 million to 6.4 million. Rural areas are losing population twice as fast as urban areas. This is the finding of a World Bank report, funded by the EU to assess Bulgaria’s National Strategy for Demographic Development, BTA reported.
The populations of Plovdiv, Varna and Burgas, the country’s second-, third- and fourth-largest cities, remained broadly stable between 2001 and 2024, changing by no more than 5%. Sofia’s population has grown by around 10%.
Against the backdrop of this unfavorable trend, the analysis also identifies significant opportunities, noting that Bulgarians today are healthier and better educated than ever, economic activity is at its highest level since the late 1990s, emigration has slowed, and more Bulgarians are returning to the country.

He added that the agreement was the result of intensive negotiations between Bulgaria and Greece. “On Saturday, October 3, at 12:30 p.m., I invite all Bulgarians to Battenberg Square, in front of the Royal Palace in Sofia, to welcome the remains together and pay tribute to the great Bulgarian ruler”, Rumen Radev said, as quoted by BTA.

The Greek Orthodox Church has also expressed its position on the return of the tsar’s remains, according to the report cited by Bulgarian online media.
As a military commander and later as ruler, Tsar Samuil defended Bulgarian lands for 43 years against the Byzantine Empire’s invasion, which lasted for half a century. He died on October 6, 1014, in Prespa.

Honeywell gets $25.6M for nuclear-tough navigation gyro
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-29
09:08:21 UTC
18:08:21 KST

- The U.S. Air Force Research Laboratory awarded Honeywell $25.6 million to mature a compact, radiation-hardened strategic gyroscope, with work due by July 2029.
- The contract follows a $41.6 million laboratory award in 2020 for Honeywell to design a Compact Strategic-Grade Gyroscope.
The U.S. Air Force Research Laboratory has awarded Honeywell Aerospace $25.6 million to keep developing a small, radiation-hardened gyroscope accurate enough for “strategic” use, the class of navigation sensor that has to work in space and survive the effects of a nuclear environment.
The cost-plus-fixed-fee contract covers what the Pentagon calls the compact strategic gyroscope maturation project, the U.S. Department of War said. Honeywell will do the work in Clearwater, Florida, and is expected to finish by July 1, 2029. The laboratory’s office at Kirtland Air Force Base, New Mexico, is managing the contract.
Combined with accelerometers in an inertial navigation system, it lets a missile, satellite, ship or aircraft work out where it is and which way it is pointing without GPS or any other outside signal. “Strategic-grade” refers to the most accurate class of these sensors, used where drift has to stay extremely low for long periods, such as in ballistic missile guidance and satellite pointing. Radiation hardening means the sensor and its electronics are built to keep working when hit by the radiation found in space or produced by a nuclear blast.
The notice does not say which weapon or spacecraft the gyroscope is intended for.
The award builds on earlier Air Force Research Laboratory work with the same company. In early 2020, the laboratory’s Space Vehicles Directorate at Kirtland gave Honeywell a $41.6 million contract to design a Compact Strategic-Grade Gyroscope, Military & Aerospace Electronics reported. That five-year effort, carried out at Honeywell’s Phoenix site, called for building and testing four prototypes, refining the design into six strategic-grade units, developing a radiation-hardened custom chip and software for the gyro, flying it on an experimental satellite for a one-year mission in low Earth orbit, and laying out a path toward a gyroscope that could keep operating through the radiation and electromagnetic pulse of nuclear explosions. The earlier contract was scheduled to run through August 2025.
The Department of War did not say how much of the first project’s goals were met or whether the space flight took place. The new work is described as “maturation,” which in defense research usually means taking a design that has been shown to work and making it more reliable, easier to build and closer to use in a real system.
The contract was competitively awarded, and the government received two offers. Only $500,000 in fiscal 2026 research and development money was committed at the time of award, with the rest of the $25.6 million to be added in later years.
Honeywell’s Clearwater site is one of the company’s main centers for navigation and inertial sensor work. The notice did not name the second bidder.

The two-day summit, hosted under the American G20 presidency, will gather trade ministers at a time when world trade is navigating fragmentation risks and geopolitical tensions.
The agenda will focus on combating the weaponization of food supplies via coercive trade decisions, eliminating forced labor within global supply chains and addressing structural production overcapacity.

Genes may influence fruit, vegetable intake: twin study
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-29
17:07:28 CST
18:07:28 KST

SYDNEY, Sept. 29 (Xinhua) -- An international twin study found that genetic differences contribute to fruit and vegetable intake, highlighting the complex mix of biological, social and environmental factors that shape people's diets.
The research challenges the idea that healthy eating is simply a matter of willpower, finding that genetics may help explain why some people find it easier than others to maintain healthy dietary habits, according to a statement released Tuesday by the Center for Healthy Brain Ageing (CHeBA) at Australia's University of New South Wales.
The study, published in Behavior Genetics, examined 5,789 twins aged 45 to 90 from four international community-based studies.
Researchers estimated that fruit consumption was 25 percent heritable and vegetable consumption 17 percent heritable, meaning genetic differences accounted for about one-quarter of the variation between individuals in fruit intake and around one-sixth of the variation in vegetable intake.
"Dietary behavior is far more complex than people think," said lead author Annabel Matison, a postdoctoral research fellow at the CHeBA, adding, "Genetics is one of many factors that may contribute to what we eat, alongside food availability, culture, cost, personal preferences and our individual life experiences."
However, the findings showed that genetic influence should not be viewed as "genetic destiny," noting that most of the variation in dietary intake was attributable to non-genetic influences.
The study also found a positive genetic correlation between fruit and vegetable intake, suggesting some genetic factors influencing fruit consumption may also influence vegetable consumption. ■

Türkiye must take center stage as global trade routes shift, sector body says

2026-09-29
09:05:14 UTC
18:05:14 KST

Gokhan Ergocun
29 September 2026•Update: 29 September 2026
The Foreign Economic Relations Board of Türkiye (DEIK) report revealed that China shifts its trade routes to alternative markets, creating new opportunities for Türkiye amid changing global trade balances.
 
DEIK prepared an analysis covering the transformation in Chinese foreign trade and its possible consequences for Türkiye after the US implemented additional customs tariffs.
 
The document showed that China's export share to the US decreased to 11.14% in 2025 from 14.68% in 2024.
 
DEIK Chair Nail Olpak stated on Tuesday that protectionist policies in global trade reshaped global routes instead of just affecting two countries.
 
Olpak noted that the decline in the US market drove China to create new trade channels across a wide geography from Association of Southeast Asian Nations (ASEAN) to Africa.
 
China increased its exports to Africa by 25.9%, the Middle East by 9.7% and the EU by 8.6% in the 2024-2025 period, he said.
 
The analysis highlighted Nigeria in Africa, the UAE in the Middle East and Germany in the EU as prominent markets for China.
 
The president mentioned that Türkiye must closely monitor the geographic diversification in Chinese exports.
He stated that China heavily targeted Africa, the Middle East and Europe to compensate for its loss in the US market.
Olpak added that these regions represent areas where the Turkish business world traditionally maintains a strong presence or aims to expand.
The report indicated that the production capacity, geographic location and logistics advantages of Türkiye provide significant benefits during this global trade restructuring.
Chinese exports to Germany, the largest export market for Türkiye, increased by 10.55% during the 2024-2025 period.
The existing data showed that the rise of China in the German market did not pose a direct threat to Türkiye yet.
The DEIK report warned that Türkiye should closely monitor the increasing competition in the African and Middle Eastern markets.
China exported goods worth $20 billion to Egypt in 2025, while Turkish exports to the country stood at $4 billion.
 
Olpak stressed that Türkiye established multi-dimensional relations in Africa involving contracting, investments and industrial cooperation beyond simple price competition.
Chinese exports to the UAE surged to $72.9 billion in 2025, whereas Türkiye recorded $9.3 billion in exports to the same market.
 
He urged Turkish companies to focus on greater value-added production, stronger brands and innovation against China's strong position in electrical devices.
The president highlighted that global trade started to experience a rising competition of trust alongside the traditional price and technology rivalry.
 
Olpak concluded that Türkiye aimed to become a reliable partner that takes a proactive position in the new trade architecture instead of just watching the changes.

Earlier this month the business, which is jointly owned by Liberty Global and Telefonica, reportedly kicked off a £600m cost-cutting programme including job cuts as it looks to deal with a £22bn debt pile.
A spokesman for VMO2 confirmed Bertram’s departure, saying:
“Jo has held a number of executive positions during her time within the company and played a pivotal role in the completion of the merger between O2 Business and Daisy Group, successfully leading integration activity during the first year of the new business.
We’d like to thank Jo for her leadership and significant contribution during her time at the company.”
UK mortgage rates are unlikely to drop back unless energy prices fall, warns SimonGammon, managing partner at KnightFrankFinance:
“Buying activity weakened through the summer as rising energy prices pushed up borrowing costs. Lending to homebuyers fell 15% in August compared to the same month a year earlier. At the time, leading fixed rates were edging closer to 4.5% – they’ve since risen to 4.8%.
“The large lenders are doing business with very thin margins in an attempt to retain market share, which leaves them vulnerable to swap rate volatility. Without a sustained fall in energy prices, leading fixed rates are likely to remain around 4.5% through the autumn selling season, which will keep a lid on activity.
“The government’s announcement of a first-time buyer support scheme will provide a boost to sentiment, particularly in more affordable parts of the country, but mortgage rates remain the bigger constraint. A meaningful recovery in transaction volumes is likely to require a sustained improvement in borrowing costs.”
UK pays highest yield since 1999 at 10-year bond auction
Newsflash: Britain’s government has paid the highest interest rate since 1999 on a sale of 10-year bonds this morning.
An £4.25bn auction of a new UK gilt maturing in 2036 has just concluded, with bond investors successfully demanding an average yield of 5.383% when bidding to buy the debt.
That’s the highest yield, or interest rate, since September 1999, Reuters reports.
The auction, held by the DebtManagementOffice, received bids for more than three times as much debt as was for sale, showing investors were still keen to buy UK debt, but at a price….
This results follows months of turmoil in the government bond markets, driven by inflation fears, which has driven up the yield on debt traded between bond investors.
Today’s auction highlights that those moves have real implications for the government, as higher bond yields push up the cost of servicing the national debt.
The fall in mortgage approvals last month shows that higher borrowing costs are taking a toll on activity in the housing sector, reports PaulDales, chief UK economist at Capital Economics.
Dales told clients:
Even though the Bank of England has not (yet) raised interest rates, the further fall in mortgage approvals from 56,000 in July to 54,900 in August (the lowest since December 2023) shows that the sharp rise in mortgage rates is restraining activity.
At face, value, that’s consistent with house price inflation slowing from 1.7% in August to around 0% in six months’ time.
Higher borrowing costs and continued macroeconomic uncertainty are “slamming the brakes on the mortgage market”, warns Richard Pinch, senior director at banking and credit advisory consultancy Broadstone.
“Despite some of the green shoots of economic recovery we have seen through the year, affordability pressures are clearly still biting as households head towards another challenging winter.
“The sharp rise in consumer credit borrowing, particularly on credit cards, suggests more households are leaning on credit to absorb everyday cost pressures.
“For lenders, the priority must be to identify signs of financial strain as early as possible and ensure borrowers have access to appropriate support and flexibility before temporary affordability pressures become more serious.”

UK's biggest AI supercomputer may have to wait until 2030s for enough power
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-29
09:01:26 UTC
18:01:26 KST

The UK start-up says the data centre could eventually expand from 50 to 90 megawatts of power — enough, if used continuously, to consume as much electricity in a year as about 315,000 typical UK homes, based on 2026 figures from UK energy regulator Ofgem.
The launch of the United Kingdom’s largest planned AI supercomputer, due to open next year, could be delayed until the 2030s because of problems securing enough electricity.
The project was announced as part of the first tech deal between the United Kingdom and the United States, as Britain pushes to expand its artificial intelligence (AI) industry.
The site is being developed in Loughton, east of London, by UK-based start-up Nscale, which counts US chipmaker Nvidia among its investors.
In 2025, Nscale announced plans to install around 23,000 Nvidia AI chips in the data centre and link them together to form what it says will be the UK’s largest AI supercomputer. That computing power is intended to support Microsoft’s Azure cloud services.
However, UK Power Networks (UKPN), the company that will connect the site to the local power grid, has told Nscale that the grid will not be able to supply enough electricity to the site until the early to mid-2030s, according to UK AI industry newsletter The Morning Intelligence.
In an interview with the newsletter, UKPN pointed to work needed on the wider national transmission network.
National Grid, which maintains that network in England and Wales, said it was working with the national system operator NESO and local network operators to speed up connections.
Nscale is looking at generating power on-site and is speaking to UK Power Networks about ways to accelerate the connection, the Morning Intelligence added.
Soaring data centre electricity consumption in Europe
The UK start-up says the data centre could eventually expand from 50 to 90 megawatts of power — enough, if used continuously, to consume as much electricity in a year as about 315,000 typical UK homes, based on 2026 figures from UK energy regulator Ofgem.
The Loughton site is part of Nscale’s wider plan to install nearly 59,000 Nvidia AI chips across data centres in the UK.
Across Europe, demand for data centres is growing while authorities are tightening rules for new data centres amid growing pressure on electricity grids.
Data centre electricity consumption across Europe is projected to rise from 96 terawatt-hours in 2024 to 236 terawatt-hours by 2035, according to UK-based energy think tank Ember.
Earlier this month, Scotland halted new hyperscale AI data centre approvals amid concerns over whether the country’s energy grid can cope with rapidly rising demand.
Amsterdam has restricted new data centres and expansions over concerns about space and power, while a bill proposed by Denmark’s government in August would give large electricity users, including data centres, a lower priority for grid connections.

On the rocks? Scotch distilleries pause production as unsold ‘whisky loch’ grows
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-29
09:01:00 UTC
18:01:00 KST

Obscured by the Scottish countryside on the outskirts of Kirkcaldy, Cluny bond is, in effect, a small town built to store whisky. By the time the latest set of warehouses are finished on the former opencast coal mine, Diageo’s 220-hectare (544-acre) maturation campus will be able to store almost 3m casks of Scotch. The drinks multinational needs the space.
After a 15-year boom turbocharged by the Covid-19 pandemic, demand for Scotch whisky has slumped around the world. Distilleries have paused production across Scotland to avoid adding to the glut of supply, known as a “whisky loch” – the equivalent of a “wine lake”.
Last week, the community-owned GlenWyvis Distillery in the Highlands announced it would appoint administrators following sustained financial pressure in the whisky market. On Monday, workers at Cameronbridge, Diageo’s largest distillery, a short drive from Cluny bond, began strike action in opposition to the company’s plans to cut hundreds of jobs across its Scottish operation.
Diageo produces about one in three bottles of Scotch globally, including popular brands such as Johnnie Walker. Dozens of Scotland’s 156 active distilleries are rumoured to be up for sale.
“Strangely, Scotch has had a really good time since the 2008 financial crisis,” said industry veteran Nick Morgan. “But people have stopped buying at the crazy rates they had been.
“People who bought whisky in the pandemic because they had nothing else to do realised they probably had enough at home for two or three years. There’s increased awareness of health issues, many are choosing to drink less, and booze got very expensive during the good years for the business.”
Fluctuations in Scotch whisky’s £5.36bn export market have proven particularly hard to navigate. By law, the drink must be matured for a minimum of three years in an oak cask in Scotland, with high-end speciality Scotch being aged in barrels for up to 40 years. Such lengthy maturation periods, used to create a wide range of flavour profiles from sweet to sulphurous, can make it hard to plan production.
Despite Donald Trump’s decision to remove duties on Scotch exports to the US after the King and Queen’s state visit to the White House earlier this year, the industry had already suffered a significant hit. The US president’s “liberation day” tariffs in April 2025 resulted in a 15% fall in Scotch exports to the US, according to the Scotch Whisky Association.
Demand in France – until recently the largest market by volume – has fallen, while the market in China has never really taken off as hoped. Optimists point to early signs of a tentative recovery, however, with the industry returning to growth in the first half of this year. Exports to India in particular have surged – but have not yet offset declines elsewhere.
The downturn is by no means limited to Scotch, either. Many drinks manufacturers are experiencing a post-pandemic slump, with five of the biggest publicly listed alcohol producers sitting on a record $22bn of aging spirits, according to the Financial Times.
Holyrood Distillery, in the shadow of Arthur’s Seat in Edinburgh, is among those to have paused production while its owners wait out the difficult period. Its bulbous copper stills, which would usually be hard at work producing single-malt Scotch, sit idle. Co-founder Rob Carpenter says he does not know when that will change.
“Anecdotally, my understanding is that the industry might be producing around a third of its normal level right now,” he said. “No one has a crystal ball, so nobody knows what is going to happen 10 years from now. You try to anticipate where things are going to be. It is a curse of the industry in a sense.”
Unlike many of its rivals, Holyrood Distillery benefits from tourists visiting the Scottish capital. About 40,000 people each year tour the stone building, which is almost 200 years old and used to support the Innocent railway. The tours account for around half of the company’s current revenue.
“It is not really that people have stopped drinking spirits,” Carpenter added. “[But] consumers are nervous. We all see what’s happening in the world. There is not a lot of predictability in things right now, and people are just being careful with what they spend their money on. This is a luxury spirit.”
The current industry downturn is not new. In the 1980s, the Scotch whisky industry faced a similar mixture of weak demand and chronic oversupply, causing a flurry of distillery closures across Scotland. The rise of Japanese whisky producers, a global economic downturn, and overconfidence from a 1970s boom drove a prolonged bust.
Today, few think the latest slump is the beginning of a permanent change in the industry’s fortunes. When Holyrood Distillery opens for tours, visitors file in, scanning through the single malts on the shelves.
“Whisky is a waiting game,” said Morgan, who charted Johnnie Walker’s 200-year history in a 2020 book. “If you look at the data on sales, every time you have one of these downturns, it comes back higher. At the moment, the business is in the trough. I can pretty much assure you in five years time, when demand really cranks up again, they’ll find they haven’t got enough whisky, and they’ll have to switch everything on.”

Murdered for their eyes: people with albinism living in terror in Madagascar
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-29
09:00:59 UTC
18:00:59 KST

Not long after midnight in late May this year, three men barged through the door of the small room where Nicole Soalala lived with her family on the outskirts of Toliara, a coastal city in the south of Madagascar. Her husband got up to ask what they wanted, but they attacked him with a piece of wood and an axe.
Soalala, 32, grabbed her youngest child, Landricia – an 18-month-old girl with albinism – and hoisted her on to her back, holding her there with a piece of fabric she started to wrap around herself. Her eldest daughter, 15, hid under the table with her other two children, aged six and three.
As Soalala’s husband lay on the floor on the verge of losing consciousness, the attackers turned their attention to her. “I felt that I was the one they were coming for and I waited to die,” she says. “But then the one with the axe suddenly started trying to pull my child away from me.”
Soalala tugged on the fabric, pressing her daughter closer to her body. “Let the child go,” said the man. Soalala pulled tighter still. “Let the child go, or we will kill you,” he repeated. Losing patience, the men wrenched away the little girl and ran.
She chased after them, screaming for help and crying. “My heart hurt me so much that I couldn’t stand it and my legs gave up on me,” she says. She collapsed about 100 metres down the dirt road, outside the large faded red gates of a school.
Days later, Landricia’s decapitated body was discovered at the home of a witch-doctor. Her head was found wrapped in plastic bags in a suitcase at another property a couple of kilometres away from where she was taken.
Landricia is among 13 people with albinism who have been killed in the country this year, according to Albinos Madagascar, an organisation set up in 2022 to advocate for people with the condition. Every one of them was beheaded. All but three of the victims were children, ranging from nine months old to 14 years. According to the association, this is already the worst year on record for killings of people with albinism in Madagascar.
“The situation is very critical, very cruel.” says Fulgence Soja, the association’s president, who lives with albinism himself. “There are a lot of big problems facing us, and we feel really unsafe.”
Albinism is an inherited genetic condition that reduces the amount of melanin pigment formed in the skin, hair and eyes and occurs in all ethnic groups. It often leads to poor vision and heightens the risk of skin cancer.
In sub-Saharan Africa, the prevalence of albinism is the highest worldwide, affecting more than one in 4,000 people in some countries, according to the World Health Organization.
People living with the condition face severe threats, including ritual killings, rape and mutilation, in several African countries. These attacks are driven by harmful superstitions that their body parts bring wealth, political success and good luck.
In Madagascar, the eyes of a person with albinism are particularly sought after. Children are targeted because of beliefs suggesting their innocence will make any potion made from their body parts more powerful. They are also vulnerable and easier to kidnap.
Nobody will talk openly about what goes on, but everyone is aware. Witch-doctors the Guardian spoke to denied all knowledge of any beliefs surrounding people with albinism, or what they might be “used for”. They, and others, say these beliefs must come from “outside”.
This level of brutality against people with albinism is said to be a recent phenomenon in Madagascar. Soja remembers first hearing about a beheading of someone with albinism in 2017. Muluka-Anne Mitti-Drummond, the UN independent expert on albinism, started receiving reports of killings in Madagascar in 2021.
“We had recorded more than 28 cases of attacks between late 2020 and 2022; the majority were against children. I was very concerned,” she says. She visited the following year and compiled a report on what was happening.
Mitti-Drummond found that profiles of attackers varied, and included relatives of victims, community members, people who travelled from other regions, and dahalos (cattle raiders). “Most perpetrators are acting with the intent of selling body parts or exploiting a person with albinism for financial means,” she wrote. “In many cases, only the middleperson is caught, while the masterminds of the attacks remain unknown.”
Life-altering sums of money are paid to those willing to kill a child with albinism and procure their eyes. Often entire networks are involved, and violence is said to increase in the run-up to elections. Sources told the Guardian that, because of this and the expense, high-powered people, including senior politicians and business people, were probably ordering some of the killings.
Madagascar is one of the poorest nations on Earth with about 80% of its population living on less than $2.15 (£1.60) a day. Since it gained independence from France in 1958, the country has experienced bouts of political instability, disputed elections and violent coups. In October 2025, youth-led protests toppled president Andry Rajoelina, and Col Michael Randrianirina declared himself head of a transitional government for what he said would last 18 to 24 months.
The country is also among the most vulnerable to the climate crisis, with drought, floods and cyclones causing death, displacement, and damage to crops and infrastructure. A lean season and El Niño threaten to push the south into emergency conditions this year, with high levels of food insecurity and malnutrition.
Sabina Lauber, a senior human rights adviser to the UN in Madagascar, believes it is this that is driving people to target individuals with albinism. “Madagascar is one of the very few countries in the world where every development and wellbeing indicator has decreased over the last 10 years,” she says. “At the same time, the population has dramatically increased and so there is a level of desperation for survival. People are turning to harmful practices to address the problem.”
In the hours after Soalala’s daughter was taken, a phone and a flip-flop were found in the courtyard outside. They had been left behind by the attackers and were taken away by the police for investigation.
Soalala divided her time between searching for Landricia alone and with members of the police and her wider family and visiting her husband, Mario William Solovenin, in hospital. It was a few days before she remembered where she had seen one of the attackers before.
About three months earlier, she says she and Solovenin had taken Landricia to hospital to treat sunburn on her shoulders. On the way they met a man that Solovenin knew through his work as a rickshaw driver. That man later came by the house, which the family now believe was to scout out their home.
Soalala told this to the police, who went to arrest him. He gave up the names of his accomplices. Chantal Rasoavahininoro, Soalala’s cousin who also lives in Toliara and acted as an intermediary between authorities and the family, says the men were tortured to extract confessions and information as to where Landricia’s body was.
When Soalala was told her daughter had been beheaded, she was inconsolable, says Rasoavahininoro. “Her first question was, ‘Are the eyes there?’” she says. “She almost went mad, she lost her mind.”
Four months on, a team of lawyers representing the family is in the preliminary stages of putting a case together. According to one of the team, Arlette Rafanomadio, 18 people, including two women, have now been arrested and are being held in custody.
One is a Sri Lankan national involved in mining.
Madagascar has a wealth of natural resources, including gold, manganese and copper. The island produces at least 40% of the world’s sapphires, alongside rubies, emeralds and semi-precious quartz. Tohovery Razakamanana, a UN human rights officer, says a significant proportion of attacks against people with albinism have occurred in or near mining areas, particularly mines for precious stones and gold. He also notes that while these attacks used to be concentrated in certain areas of the south, widely seen to be poorer and with higher levels of food insecurity, they are now happening all over Madagascar.
“To get back to the very beginning,” he says, “it all started in the deep south. Then we observed some cases in the south-east, south-west, midwest, and then in the north. But rarely in the capital and surrounding districts.”
While data collection has been poor, making it difficult to determine the origins and extent of attacks against people with albinism, human rights organisations say the situation this year is particularly worrying because of the geographical spread and grisly nature of the killings. People in cities are now being targeted rather than just those in remote rural areas.
An atmosphere of terror now exists for people with albinism and their families. Odette, 20, lives in a city in northern Madagascar where it is hot year round. She doesn’t understand why she is a varira (the Malagasy word for someone with albinism), but she knows her eyesight is blurry and that she burns easily. She squints as she struggles to see, there are sores all over her arms and legs and her lips are cracked and swollen from the sun.
In February, her cousin Marcellin, 14, who also had albinism, was murdered. She remembers him as a cheerful and talkative boy, who used to come round asking for soap.
Marcellin was beheaded and his body left under a mango tree across the dirt track from the wooden property where he lived with his older sister and her family. His head has never been found.
When the Guardian visited, two young girls sat behind a table under the same mango tree selling vegetables. The tyre Marcellin was sitting on outside his front door when he was snatched is still there. According to Soja, four people linked to a local politician have been arrested.
Odette has a three-year-old son and struggles to make money; she earns about 3,000 ariary (50p) a day from working in the fields and doing odd jobs. She is not with the father of her child. When she told him she was pregnant he didn’t stick around. She says: “He told me, ‘I love the colour of your skin, but I’m not going to be with you, because you’re varira.’”
One evening about a month ago, she was at the home she rented with her son when she heard a group of men approach and bang on the door. She ran to her mother’s house. After that, she decided to move in with her wider family and now sleeps sharing a mattress with about a dozen people in a small mud hut with a straw roof overlooking a patch of water not far from the city centre.
“I am a varira like Marcellin, so I’m really scared,” she says. “The house is not a good one, it’s not secure. I worry that there aren’t enough people here and that if someone comes, they will murder me.”
About 90 miles (150km) west, nine-year-old Veroline and her younger brother play outside the mayor’s house in a village near a Unesco-recognised national park where tourists go to see lemurs and other wildlife.
Both children have albinism. Three members of the armed forces watch over them; one carries a shotgun, another wears a handgun at his side.
They are here, living under the mayor’s protection, because in May, their older brother, Rakotombelo, 14, was killed. Veroline was sleeping in the same room when some men crashed through the wooden door. It remains broken to this day. She has very few memories of that night, other than her aunt telling her to run. Her father, who lives in a nearby town, says she told him she hid under a cart parked outside, against the wall of the house. “Some people came and I found out they were enemies,” she says. “I saw them carrying my brother. I told them, ‘Why are you doing that? Is he a child you gave birth to that you can do that to him?’”
Her aunt, Rasoa, and her husband were held hostage by two men in the next room. “They carried knives and said ‘Don’t move, or we will kill you’,” says Rasoa. When they left, she screamed until neighbours came. It was then that she realised her nephew’s head had been cut off. His body had been left, and the wall was covered in blood. “What happened was scandalous,” she says. “I was so sad because he was like my child. Even now, I’m devastated that a child I raised was violated like that.”
While she was at Rakotombelo’s funeral a couple of days later, there was a secret ballot held among the villagers to determine who they suspected had committed the murder. Fourteen people were arrested and are being detained, according to Francois Xavier Zaranaina, the mayor. Rasoa’s husband is one of them. “We don’t have any proof, but all I can say is that some of them might have done it, some of them probably didn’t do it, but because of various rumours and conflicts, those people were arrested,” says Zaranaina.
He has heard the superstitions about the eyes of people with albinism and suspects that is why Rakotombelo, who he says was good at football, was killed. He is eager for Veroline and her brother to no longer be his responsibility, particularly as the killers may come back. “They are burdens,” he says.
The killings have become an issue of national concern. The president has deployed his personal guard to hunt down perpetrators, and the first lady has promised to open a centre in the south where people with albinism can seek refuge.
On 4 August, a video was posted on the president’s Facebook page showing the alleged perpetrators behind the murder of a child with albinism who were caught in a sting operation; among the accomplices were the child’s grandfather and police officers. Two days later, the president wrote in a post accompanied by photos: “Because I heard that there are still people threatening to kill this albino child and her mother, I have decided that the family will be brought up to [the capital] Antananarivo immediately, and I will personally take full responsibility for their lives!” The Guardian could not independently verify the information in the posts, or the videos.
UN experts and local advocates emphasise that addressing the crisis facing people with albinism in Madagascar requires collaboration. Soja, who is now advising the president on the issue, wants a national action plan that addresses security, education and health “so that we can live like everyone else”.
Before that, he says: “The priority is to stop [the killings] because any solution for people of albinism to be able to educate themselves and go to work, depends on that.”
Razakamanana at the UN says a lack of accurate data remains a stumbling block. He is urging the government to conduct a census to determine how many people with albinism there are in the country.
Much needs to be done in terms of raising awareness, he adds. “Even educated people in the capital are not aware [that albinism is a genetic condition]. We have to start with awareness-raising campaigns and education.”
Four months on from the murder of baby Landricia in Toliara, Soalala and her husband’s grief is still raw. They look broken, weary and like every last drop of joy has been drained from them. Tears form in Soalala’s eyes as she talks about what her daughter was like. Landricia had a reddish tint to her hair with chocolate-coloured eyes. “She took after her father, and was a calm and happy child,” she says.
Soalala still cries often and so does her eldest daughter. Her youngest remaining child, Patricia, who also has albinism, often asks where nanke (an affectionate Malagasy term for a younger sibling) is. “I tell her she is dead, I don’t want to lie. I also tell her I don’t want to talk about it,” says Soalala.
When Patricia was born, Soalala says people in the community warned her: “The child has albinism. Be careful, protect her because she might get stolen.” For that reason, Soalala doesn’t work and rarely goes out, preferring to keep her children hidden. The family relies on her husband’s daily income of about 6,000 ariary (£1) from driving a rickshaw.
The family lives in a constant state of anxiety and terror. As Patricia starts to cry and demands attention from her mother, Soalala says: “I can’t sleep at night because I’m so scared and anxious. The evil people might still be seeking this child.”
