Anthony Rogers HM Chief Inspector of the Crown Prosecution Service
HMCPSI - The Military Court Service, August 2026
Organisation
The MCS is independent of the Service chains of command and is staffed by civil servants employed by the Ministry of Defence (MOD) working from both court centres.
To ensure independence, the Director MCS is appointed by the Defence Council as the Court Administration Officer (CAO). The CAO has a legislated function to give notice of court proceedings and to specify lay members of the court (equivalent to jury selection).
The Court Martial Appeal Court recently clarified the respective roles of the Judge Advocate and the CAO in relation to the constitution of the Court Martial, concluding that the Judge Advocate’s role is to give direction on the composition category, while the CAO is responsible for specifying individual members. These duties are conducted in accordance with the Armed Forces Act 2006 and related Statutory Instruments.
The CAO is a permanent member of both the Service Justice Board (SJB) and the Service Justice Executive Group (SJEG).
The Director MCS operates from the Bulford Court Centre supported by a Senior Management Team and a Court Administration Unit. Each Court Centre has a dedicated Court Officer who is directly responsible for the management of court proceedings, liaison with the Judiciary and court listings.
The current Director of the Military Court Service is Mr Cleaven Faulkner JP:
Military Court Service Strategic Plan 2026-2030
The Strategic Plan, owned by the Director of the Military Court Service (MCS), sets the direction for MCS personnel and partners in delivering Military Court business.
The Service Justice System is a vital public service relied upon by hundreds of victims, witnesses, families, and defendants across the UK and overseas to deliver justice outcomes that matter.
Building on the achievements of the past four years, this plan provides a clear roadmap for delivering an operating model centred on timely, impartial, and efficient administration of Service court proceedings. It aims to strengthen confidence in a justice system that is fair, effective, and accessible to all who depend upon it.
The strategy drives a culture of continuous improvement and ongoing modernisation of our court processes. It recognises the value of embracing technology‑based systems that enhance efficiency, reduce duplication and bureaucracy, and improve integration with our partners and stakeholders. These reforms lay the groundwork for MCS to deliver a new fully integrated Military Court Listing System (MCLS), with its incumbent in‑court digital case management system, Case Center.
Following significant investment in recent years, the MCS is now well placed to consolidate progress, continue to adopt innovative technologies and ensure that the Services have a modern, effective court system that works in the interests of all Service personnel and their families. Looking ahead to 2030, the strategy identifies the areas in which the MCS will continue to modernise and transform, ensuring best value for money and delivering an increasingly efficient and effective criminal court service for the Royal Navy, the Army, and the Royal Air Force.
Through this modernisation, we aim to build greater confidence in and respect for the Service Justice System. We are committed to continue our work in building a leading‑edge service that is open, inclusive, and innovative. Success will be delivered through the professionalism, dedication, and integrity of our people, who work every day to uphold the principles of justice.
Military Court Centres
There are two permanent court centres in the UK. Bulford, Wiltshire and Catterick, North Yorkshire.
A view of the Bulford Military Court Centre
A view of the Catterick Court (BSL Version)
Military Court Centre information and images of our court rooms.
Due to the draw down of British Forces Germany, the permanent court centre at Sennelager has been converted for other use but has been retained as a Court Martial location should one be required. MCS have a permanent Court Martial capability at Episkopi, Cyprus.
The court system is entirely portable, with the ability for MCS to convene trials outside of the MCCs anywhere in the UK or elsewhere. The most recent examples have included Nightingale Courts at Tidworth and Catterick and overseas in Cyprus, Germany and Gibraltar.
MCS have invested in the latest Digital Audio Recording (DAR) technology to meet legal compliance for the recording of proceedings. The capability covers both the four fixed courts and two portable recording equipment sets. The Service Courts have the latest Digital Evidential Presentation System and now have the capability to support the pre-recording of evidence from victims of serious sexual assault (Section 28).
The Service Courts have a state-of-the-art case management system called Case Center. This product is the latest version of the Crown Court system, Caselines and has been operational since September 2023. MCS are moving towards completing the last element of its digital transformation program with Board members using laptops to view evidence, via the Case Center Jury Portal, during proceedings.
Procedure
The Deputy Director MCS oversees the delivery of the MCS assize programme. Cases are listed within ‘assize sessions’, held at the Military Court Centres run by MCS staff. However, a particularly lengthy or complex Court Martial or Service Civilian Court case may be listed as a ‘stand-alone’ outside the assize sessions. Where possible the volume of cases is equally split between both Court Centres.
At the listing phase of case management, the Court officer will work with the resident Judge Advocate to appoint a Judge Advocate to each case.
The MCS policy is to list a case for an initial hearing within 42 days after receipt of directional papers from the Service Prosecuting Authority.
How we select a Court Martial Board
Our Operating procedure for selecting Court Martial Boards
.
On 1 January 2023 legislation delivered changes to the constitution of a Court Martial board. The changes required the CAO to specify Court Martial boards with at least one man and one woman (so far as is reasonably practicable) and to specify an increase from five lay members to six, for proceedings of a prescribed description. Specification of the OR7 rank from the nominated pool of lay members may now also be permitted under the act.
‘OR7 rank’ means any of the following— chief petty officer, staff corporal, staff sergeant, colour sergeant, Royal Marines, flight sergeant, chief technician.

The Military Court Service case management system, Case Center (formerly Caselines)
The Military Court Service partners with Thomson Reuters using Case Center. The application streamlines the way the courts prepare, manage, and present digital cases within a centralised cloud-based solution.
The court will manage proceedings by sending and sharing case materials from any device, keeping all parties in sync as they prepare for a hearing. In a hearing, purpose-built presentation tools streamlines proceedings so parties can direct others to the right document in a timely manner.

After you enter your details and the role you will be performing within the Service Justice System you will be registered and ready to be invited to your allocated cases.

Once you have been verified by the Military Court Service either directly with the court, or with the Armed Forces Criminal legal Aid Authority, you will be invited to the case. This process mirrors that applied by the Ministry of Justice in the use for the Digital Case System (DCS).

Court Martial and Summary Appeal Court Guidance
Guides are issued under the authority of the Judge Advocate General and the Director of the Military Court Service jointly as an aid to those who practise in the Service Justice System, and it is to be used in all hearings. Volume 1 provides information about procedure generally and it deals with all types of proceedings in the Court Martial as well as in the Summary Appeal Court. Volume 2 provides information specifically for members of boards.
Guidance on practice, procedure and sentencing is issued by the Judge Advocate General.

Apply for a transcript of a Service Court hearing
Service Court hearings are always recorded. You can apply for a transcript of a Service Court hearing. The court can refuse to provide part or all of a transcript (for example, if details of the hearing are confidential).
If you wish to apply for a transcript you may download and fill in a .
Once completed, email your application to mcs-group@mod.gov.uk.
Transcripts may attract a financial cost unless you are a party to proceedings.
Sentencing remarks in the Court Martial
Transcripts of the judge advocate’s sentencing remarks in cases heard after 1 January 2025 in which the sentence includes dismissal from His Majesty’s Service will be considered for publication by the Judge Advocate General. If published, transcripts will remain on the page for up to 12 months from the date of conviction.

Remote observation of Service Court proceedings
Open justice has been a fundamental principle for centuries. The principle is a broad one, but at its core has always been a right of access to a public hearing. Historically, this has meant access for reporters and other members of the public to the court or other room in which the hearing takes place.
The primary legislation is contained in section 85A of the Courts Act 2003 as inserted by section 198 of the Police, Crime, Sentencing and Courts Act 2022. The regime is implemented by the Remote Observation and Recording (Courts and Tribunals) Regulations 2022. The power is to “direct that images or sounds of the proceedings be transmitted electronically”. It is to be exercised “for the purpose of enabling persons not taking part in the proceedings to watch or listen to” them. It is not designed for those taking part in the proceedings.
Any person wishing to make an application to the Military Court Service to request permission for the remote observation of a hearing can do so:
Applicants must ensure the court are given at least 3 clear working days to process applications.

Taiwan reports 12.3% drop in road deaths
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-29
08:39:16 UTC
17:39:16 KST

TAIPEI (Taiwan News) — Taiwan recorded 1,569 road deaths from January through July, down 12.3% from the same period in the government’s 2023 baseline year, the Ministry of Transportation and Communications said Tuesday in a press release.
The ministry said all major road safety indicators had improved from the baseline, although elderly road deaths remained a concern. Wu Tung-ling (吳東凌), director-general of the Department of Railways, Highways, and Road Safety, said motorcycle fatalities fell by 206, or 18.1%, while pedestrian deaths declined by 18, or 9%, and deaths involving drunk driving fell by 82, or 54.3%, per CNA.
Compared with the same period last year, however, deaths among people aged 65 and older increased by 33, or about 5%, to 697. Wu said the increase was concentrated in Taoyuan, Taichung, and Hualien County.
Motorcycle crashes accounted for about half of the elderly deaths in those three localities, with many occurring when riders turned left at intersections. Pedestrian incidents accounted for about 20%, with many occurring while people were crossing roads.
The ministry designated 2023 as its baseline year because that marked the beginning of a four-year road safety improvement plan. Compared with the 2023 baseline, elderly road deaths fell by 22, or 3.1%.
Wu warned that data from previous years showed elderly road deaths tended to increase during the fourth quarter. He attributed the trend to larger temperature differences between day and night, shorter daylight hours in autumn and winter, and age-related declines in physical function.
Wu urged older people to take extra care when traveling early in the morning or at night and to wear brightly colored clothing or reflective accessories to make themselves more visible.
The ministry expanded its definition of drug-impaired driving incidents in July. Previously, the statistics counted only cases in which the party considered primarily responsible was impaired. They now also include cases in which another party was impaired and committed a traffic violation.
From January through June, 23 deaths were recorded in incidents involving drug-impaired driving, followed by seven in July alone. Officials said the revised definition was intended to present a more complete picture of such incidents and help police assess enforcement measures.

DPP’s Chen Ting-fei hopes to become Tainan’s first female mayor
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-29
08:39:08 UTC
17:39:08 KST

TAIPEI (Taiwan News) — DPP Tainan mayoral candidate Chen Ting-fei (陳亭妃) hopes to become the city’s first female mayor, drawing on her grassroots support and decades of political experience.
Born in Tainan’s West Central District, Chen’s political career began early, per Storm Media. At age 7, she campaigned for her father, Chen Chia-chao (陳佳照), a participant in the Tangwai movement.
After winning the election, Chen Chia-chao initially tried to steer his daughter away from politics before eventually accepting her decision and fully supporting her political career, per FTNN. Chen Ting-fei’s first foray into electoral politics came in 1998, when she followed in her father's footsteps and defeated her KMT rival, Hsieh Lung-chieh (謝龍介), in a city council election through one of the seats reserved for women.
The two would face each other in four subsequent elections, with Chen receiving more votes than Hsieh in each contest, per Tai Sounds. In 2016, she received more than twice as many votes as Hsieh.
After losing the DPP’s mayoral primary to then-lawmaker Huang Wei-che (黃偉哲), Chen launched a second bid for the party’s mayoral nomination, this time against lawmaker Lin Chun-hsien (林俊憲), per NOWNews. Chen defeated Lin, a member of the New Tide faction, attributing her victory to grassroots support built through years of public service and determination, per Newtalk.
Speaking about the type of administration she would build, Chen said she would serve as a bridge between Tainan and the central government while taking a proactive approach to addressing issues as they arise, per Newtalk. Noting the Cabinet’s Thursday meetings with special municipality mayors, Chen said she would have Tainan’s city government hold an internal meeting on Wednesdays to determine the city’s agenda for the following day’s meeting with the central government, per Newtalk.
Regarding her vision for the city, Chen proposed seven major agendas for Tainan, per Newtalk. They include narrowing the development gap between areas north and south of the Zengwen River, upgrading agricultural infrastructure, improving the city’s social welfare system, and investing in road and rail networks.
Chen said developing refrigeration systems, domestic and export marketing networks, and a natural disaster damage reporting system would empower farmers and fishers. On social welfare, She said she would compare the benefits provided by Tainan with the average offerings of the other five special municipalities.
Chen said that if Tainan falls behind, her administration would work to improve the city’s benefits. She emphasized that her approach would focus on addressing deficiencies in Tainan’s existing system rather than making political promises that might not be fulfilled, per Mirror Media.
Discussing Tainan’s industries, Chen said her plan would focus on three key sites: the Floral Industry Innovation Center in Houbi District, the Shalun Smart Green Energy Science City, and the Southern Taiwan Science Park, per Mirror Media. Noting that Tainan was once the most important city in Taiwan, Chen said investments in agriculture, semiconductors, and medical technology could help restore the city’s former prominence.

Russia plans record $200 billion military budget for 2027
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-29
08:39:08 UTC
17:39:08 KST

- Russia plans record defense spending of 17.1 trillion rubles in 2027, about 27% above its earlier plan, government documents seen by Reuters show.
- Moscow now expects a 2026 federal budget deficit of 3.2% of GDP, double its earlier forecast.
Russia plans to spend a record 17.1 trillion rubles ($201 billion) on its military in 2027, while its budget deficit this year is now expected to reach double the government’s earlier forecast, according to government documents seen by Reuters.
The defense figure is about 27% higher than the 13.5 trillion rubles Moscow had previously penciled in for 2027 and the largest since Russia launched its full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022, Reuters reported Sept. 28. The documents show total defense spending of about 50 trillion rubles ($592 billion) over the next three years. The government is expected to send the draft budget to parliament by Oct. 1.
For 2026, the government had planned to spend 12.1 trillion rubles on defense, but the actual figure is classified and will not be published. Economist Janis Kluge of the German Institute for International and Security Affairs noted on X that the Finance Ministry had originally intended to cut defense spending slightly this year.
The government now expects the 2026 federal deficit to reach 3.2% of gross domestic product, up from its earlier estimate of 1.6%. Total spending this year is set to rise 13.2% to 48.6 trillion rubles, or 20.9% of GDP, while the forecast for oil and gas revenue, long the backbone of Russia’s budget, was cut to 7.6 trillion rubles from 8.9 trillion.
Kluge said the federal figure does not tell the whole story, because it leaves out Russia’s regional budgets and possibly its social security funds. He estimated the consolidated deficit across all levels of government will be close to 4% of GDP. Regional budgets were slightly in surplus on average as of Aug. 1, he said, but a sharp drop of about 0.7% of GDP is expected at the end of the year, pushing them into deficit.
Moscow plans to cover the gap by borrowing more and dipping into savings. Net borrowing this year will rise 26% to 5 trillion rubles, and the government will take 459 billion rubles, about 11% of the liquid assets in its National Wealth Fund, to reduce the deficit. State debt is projected to climb to 21.7% of GDP in 2027 from 19.9% this year, above the 20% level Russian authorities have described as safe.
The government has also announced tax increases for 2027, including a new windfall tax on metals and mining companies expected to raise about 200 billion rubles a year.
Defense is set to take about 35% of Russia’s total federal spending in 2027, according to figures cited by The Moscow Times and the Kyiv Post. Combined with national security spending, which covers the Interior Ministry, the National Guard and the security services, the total reaches 21.4 trillion rubles, or 43.9% of the budget.

Lai approval remains at 51.4%, highest since April 2025
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-29
08:39:04 UTC
17:39:04 KST

TAIPEI (Taiwan News) — President Lai Ching-te’s (賴清德) approval rating remained at 51.4% in a poll released Tuesday, maintaining its highest level since April 2025.
The latest survey by the Taipei Trust in Democracy Association put Lai’s trust rating at 51.2%, up 1.3 percentage points from August and above 50% for the first time since April 2025. His disapproval rating fell 1.2 percentage points to 41.1%, per Newtalk.
The share of respondents who said they did not trust Lai dropped 3.8 percentage points to 35.7%, the lowest level recorded since December 2024.
In Taipei, 58.4% of respondents said they trusted Lai, the highest among the regions surveyed. The figure was 58.1% in Kaohsiung and Pingtung, 56% in Taichung, Changhua, and Nantou, and 52.6% in Yunlin, Chiayi, and Tainan, per SETN.
The survey also asked respondents how they viewed the three major political parties. The DPP’s favorability rating rose 0.6 percentage points from August to 47.4%. The KMT’s rating fell 1.5 percentage points to 26.4%, while the TPP’s declined 1 percentage point to 21.6%.
Overall, 47.4% of respondents viewed the economy favorably and 45.2% viewed it unfavorably, per NOWNews.
The Taipei mayoral race drew the most attention among local elections, with 40.6% of respondents saying they were following it. A separate poll released by the association last week found incumbent Mayor Chiang Wan-an (蔣萬安) and DPP candidate Puma Shen (沈伯洋) in a tight race.
The latest telephone survey questioned 1,075 people aged 20 and older nationwide from Sept. 21 to 23, including 698 by landline and 377 by mobile phone. It had a margin of error of 3 percentage points at a 95% confidence level.

Early voting ahead of Latvia’s 15th Saeima election draws higher-than-expected turnout – first figures revealed
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-29
08:38:57 UTC
17:38:57 KST

Early voting ahead of Latvia’s 15th Saeima election began on Monday without any significant incidents, while voter activity was slightly higher than expected, Central Election Commission (CVK) Chairman Māris Zviedris told LETA.
Zviedris said the election process had generally proceeded as planned, although minor delays were observed at some polling stations as staff familiarised themselves with the new procedures and their details.
“I would say everything is within the normal range. There have been minor delays at polling stations as staff become familiar with the process and understand all its nuances, but that is natural and within acceptable limits,” Zviedris said.
According to him, the CVK has so far received no reports of serious incidents or problems requiring special attention.
Commenting on voter turnout, the CVK chairman said the figures indicate that the public has been successfully informed about the possibility of casting a vote for safekeeping ahead of election day.
“It is positive that turnout is slightly higher than expected,”
Zviedris said, adding that the CVK hopes more convenient voting options will also encourage overall voter participation in the 15th Saeima election.
Zviedris said delays by some polling stations in submitting voter turnout data should not be regarded as a serious problem. In most cases, they are related to clarifying data and carrying out additional checks in the voter register.
The CVK chairman said polling station staff are paying particular attention to preventing incorrect entries and ensuring that voters cannot be marked in the system more than once. If an incorrect entry is identified, it is corrected after the polling station closes.
As previously reported, nearly 26,000 people cast their votes on the first day of early voting ahead of the 15th Saeima election, representing 1.67% of Latvia’s 1,557,615 eligible voters, according to data compiled by the CVK.
In the previous Saeima election, 11,316 voters, or 0.73% of eligible voters, cast their ballots for safekeeping on the first day. At that time, however, this was possible at only 66 polling stations and over a three-day period.
The State Digital Development Agency previously confirmed that the Election Platform operated stably and as planned on the first day of voting, while CERT.LV detected no cybersecurity incidents related to the election process.
The official election day is Saturday. Until then, voters can cast their ballots for safekeeping on every working day this week at any of the 933 polling stations across Latvia.

In addition to its existing major customer, three other semiconductor companies are certifying Chung Hwa Chemical’s production lines for advanced processes.
Electronic-grade chemicals accounted for more than 40% of the company’s revenue in the second quarter. Shrinking semiconductor process nodes and rising demand for high-purity cleaning chemicals are driving rapid growth in the electronic-grade sulfuric acid market. Taiwan’s consumption is estimated to rise from 30 million kilograms per month last year to 60 million kilograms by 2027.
Beyond semiconductor chemicals, the company is expanding into higher-value specialty chemical applications, including materials for high-frequency electronics and other industrial uses. Its high-frequency resin materials have entered small-scale trial production, while the company has also secured a tender to supply specialty chemicals for defense applications.

Faisal Mahmud
29 September 2026•Update: 29 September 2026
Chinese drugmaker Hengrui Pharma said Tuesday it has agreed to license global rights to an experimental weight-loss drug to Denmark’s Novo Nordisk in a deal potentially worth up to $2.6 billion.
The drug, HRS-1596, is a Phase I-ready GLP-1/GIP dual receptor agonist designed for once-weekly oral dosing, Hengrui said in a statement.
Under the agreement, Novo will receive exclusive rights to develop, manufacture and commercialize the drug globally, excluding mainland China, Hong Kong, Macao and Taiwan.
Hengrui will receive $300 million upfront and could receive additional development, regulatory and commercial milestone payments, bringing the potential deal value to $2.6 billion. It is also eligible for royalties on net sales.
HRS-1596 is designed to reduce weight and improve blood sugar control through mechanisms including appetite suppression, stimulation of insulin secretion and improved insulin sensitivity.
Hengrui said the drug has potential applications in obesity, type 2 diabetes and other metabolic diseases.
Chinese authorities have approved Hengrui to begin Phase I clinical trials of HRS-1596 for weight management and type 2 diabetes.
Novo, maker of obesity drug Wegovy and diabetes treatment Ozempic, has been expanding its pipeline of oral treatments for obesity and other cardiometabolic diseases. Its Wegovy pill was approved by the US Food and Drug Administration for weight management in 2025.
The Hengrui deal remains subject to US antitrust clearance and other customary conditions and is expected to close in the fourth quarter of 2026.

Electric bikes overtake ‘ordinary’ bikes
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-29
08:37:51 UTC
17:37:51 KST

More electric bikes are now being sold than ordinary bikes, and 45 per cent of households in Flanders already own an electric bike according to figures from Fietsberaad, the advisory body on cycling policy. In terms of the total number of journeys, the electric bike is already more important than public transport. Moreover, users are getting younger and younger.
Fietsberaad, the knowledge and advisory body for cycling policy in Flanders, has highlighted the importance of the electric bike in a new report. It analysed figures and graphs from various travel behaviour surveys that have been carried out annually in Flanders since 2015. Its annual FietsDNA survey also provided insights.
The rise of the electric bike is undeniable and is particularly clear when we look at the ‘modal split’ – that is, the distribution of journeys across the various modes of transport used: car, bicycle, public transport or on foot.
Whereas in 2015 Flemings made less than one per cent of journeys by electric bike, last year this figure had already risen to over 7 per cent. The total number of cycle journeys, both electric and non-electric, has risen from 12 to 20 per cent over that period.
‘That increase can be attributed entirely to electric bikes,’ says Wout Baert of Fietsberaad, ‘as the number of journeys made by conventional bicycle remained virtually unchanged during that period.’
It becomes even clearer when we factor in the figures for journeys by public transport. Journeys by train, tram, bus and underground account for less than 5 per cent in the latest survey, whilst we already make 7 per cent of our journeys by electric bike. In Flanders the electric bike is outperforming public transport as a whole.
Increasingly a trend among young adults
Ten years ago, it was mainly people aged 55 and over who rode electric bikes, but in the most recent surveys we see the average age of e-bike riders falling.
In the 35 to 44 age group, the majority of cycle journeys are made by electric bike (54.7 per cent). This age group already covers 70 per cent of all the kilometres they cycle by electric bike.
In the younger group, aged 28 to 35, we are already seeing 21 per cent of journeys made by electric bike. More than half of the kilometres cycled (52 per cent) in this group are already covered on an electric bike.
Commuting
If we look solely at commuting, the latest report from 2025 shows that 22 per cent of journeys to and from work are already made by bicycle. Of that 22 per cent, just over 12 per cent are made on electric bikes and nearly 10 per cent on conventional bikes. Electric bikes have therefore become more important for commuting than conventional bikes.
“The many options for leasing a bicycle through work contribute to this, and people can choose from a range of electric lease bikes: speed pedelecs, cargo bikes, as well as fat bikes with thick tyres. It is worth noting here that the range – or the number of kilometres a person can travel – increases significantly with an electric bicycle.”

Iranian airliner with passengers on board seized at Istanbul over €3-million debt
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-29
08:37:00 UTC
17:37:00 KST

Bailiffs boarded the Caspian Airlines Boeing 737 as passengers sat ready for departure and served a €3 million debt order before it could take off. The seizure came days after US secondary sanctions on Iran's aviation sector took effect, halving international flights at Tehran's main airport.
A Caspian Airlines Boeing 737 was seized at Istanbul Airport on Monday by court-ordered enforcement officers acting on a debt claim of approximately €3 million, stranding passengers who had already boarded a flight bound for Iran.
Lawyers and bailiffs representing the creditor, aviation representation and supervision company ACM Temsil Gözetim, arrived at the aircraft — registered EP-KPB — as it was ready for departure and served the seizure order before it could take off, according to Anadolu Agency.
Passengers and cabin crew were removed from the aircraft and returned to the terminal.
Caspian Airlines is a Tehran-based carrier founded in 1993 and operating as part of Iran's state aviation group. It flies Boeing 737s on domestic and international routes, including to Istanbul.
Iranian carriers have faced chronic difficulties maintaining their fleets and meeting financial obligations to foreign counterparts as a result of decades of US sanctions, which restrict access to aircraft, spare parts, maintenance services and international financial systems.
The war between the US and Iran that began in February has compounded those pressures, with Iranian airspace repeatedly disrupted and international routes curtailed.
The seizure came days after sweeping US secondary sanctions on Iran's aviation sector took effect last Wednesday.
The US Treasury had sanctioned 27 Iranian airlines and nine associated service providers on 8 September under its Operation Economic Outcast, warning that foreign airports, fuel suppliers, ground handlers and ticketing companies that continued servicing Iranian carriers would themselves face sanctions and risk being cut off from the US dollar system.
The secondary sanctions triggered a rapid contraction of Iranian aviation internationally, with flights by Iranian carriers suspended in Iraq, the UAE, Azerbaijan and Oman.
In turn, Iran's largest private carrier Mahan Air suspended flights to Turkey and Oman.
Lufthansa and Austrian Airlines suspended their own routes to Iran through 24 October. Qatar Airways suspended services citing airspace restrictions. China, Russia and Pakistan have continued to maintain flights to and from Iran.
Daily international flights at Tehran's main airport fell from 80 to 90 before the sanctions to around 41 by Monday, according to tracking data.
Tehran has filed formal complaints with the UN, the International Civil Aviation Organisation and the International Court of Justice.
Turkey has not formally barred Iranian carriers, which is why Caspian Airlines was still operating the Istanbul route at the time of the seizure.

Attorney-General pushes for Israel's Supreme Court to ban leader of Arab party Balad from election
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-29
08:35:56 UTC
17:35:56 KST

Attorney-General Gali Baharav-Miara has asked the Supreme Court to approve the disqualification of Balad chairman Sami Abu Shehadeh from the upcoming election, according to a position filed on Tuesday.
The Justice Ministry announced the position in the names of Baharav-Miara and chief prosecutor Amit Aisman.
In the filing, submitted ahead of Thursday’s hearings on candidate and party disqualifications, the attorney-general asserted that Abu Shehadeh meets the legal threshold for disqualification, specifically on the grounds that he supported an armed struggle by a terrorist organization against the State of Israel.
The Supreme Court is reviewing the Central Elections Committee’s September 23 decision to disqualify Abu Shehadeh, as required before the disqualification of an individual candidate can become final.
Disqualification of Abu Shehadeh on the grounds of Basic Law
At the heart of the matter is Section 7A of Basic Law: The Knesset. It establishes three grounds for disqualifying a candidate or electoral list: negating Israel’s existence as a Jewish and democratic state; incitement to racism; and supporting an armed struggle by an enemy state or terrorist organization against Israel.
The Elections Committee disqualified Abu Shehadeh on the first and third grounds. Baharav-Miara, however, asked the court to approve his disqualification only on the armed-struggle ground and to overturn the committee’s decision concerning Israel’s existence as a Jewish and democratic state.
The filing centered on an Arabic-language article Abu Shehadeh published on two news sites on October 8, 2023, while the Hamas-led attack was still underway.
“The article Abu Shehadeh published on October 8, 2023 - one day after the murderous terrorist attack began, and while it was still underway - expresses a position of support for the armed struggle of the Hamas terrorist organization against the State of Israel,” reads a statement on behalf of Baharav-Miara and Aisman.
According to the filing, the article described the attack as a historic military, political and strategic event and argued that, if the small and besieged Gaza Strip could achieve intelligence concealment and operational surprise, others could do so.
The attorney-general argued that, because of its content, context and timing, the article constituted an exceptionally grave piece of evidence that could independently satisfy the normally stringent legal threshold for disqualification.
The filing also cited a social-media post showing three men whom the disqualification application identified as terrorists, accompanied by words of respect and appreciation.
Abu Shehadeh denied supporting armed struggle when he appeared by video at the Elections Committee hearing. He condemned the October 7 attack and said his political path was democratic and nonviolent. He argued that the article was intended as political analysis and as a call to move the struggle from the military arena to the political and diplomatic arenas.
He also acknowledged that the article should not have been written in the form in which it appeared.
A-G says explanations 'unconvincing'
The attorney-general’s filing said those subsequent explanations were partial and unconvincing and did not address the central allegations, including the article’s timing, its failure to condemn the attack and its discussion of the operational lessons others could draw from it.
The new position goes further than Baharav-Miara’s submission before the Elections Committee hearing. At that stage, representatives of her office said the article appeared to provide a basis for the armed-struggle allegation and that the committee should consider the request seriously after hearing Abu Shehadeh’s response, but stopped short of expressly recommending his disqualification.
During the committee hearing, a representative of the attorney-general said there was a basis for the request. After considering Abu Shehadeh’s affidavit and oral explanations, the attorney-general is now explicitly asking the Supreme Court to approve the disqualification on that ground.
Adalah – The Legal Center for Arab Minority Rights in Israel, which represents Abu Shehadeh, said in response: “The Attorney General is engaging in blatant discrimination between Jewish and Arab political candidates.”
It continued, “By her logic, those who called for genocide in Gaza and incited hate crimes and pogroms in the West Bank are free to run in the elections, while an Arab candidate is barred over a single article, which did not include any call for violence.”
Adalah noted that Abu Shehadeh cited his “repeated, explicit condemnations” of the October 7 attack, and that he “stated unequivocally that he opposes violence and armed struggle.”
The application was filed by Otzma Yehudit and its chairman, National Security Minister Itamar Ben-Gvir. Abu Shehadeh is running in third place on the Joint List.
Ben-Gvir welcomed the position, saying, “Even the attorney-general and the state attorney cannot deny the evidence we presented against Sami Abu Shehadeh.” He criticized the attorney-general’s office for not gathering the material itself and credited attorney David Bavli, No. 11 on Otzma Yehudit’s electoral list, with compiling it.
Committee representatives voted 30-4 to disqualify him. Committee chairman Supreme Court Justice Noam Sohlberg also voted on the armed-struggle ground, bringing the tally on that ground to 31-4.
The court will review Abu Shehadeh’s disqualification before the same nine-justice panel that will subsequently hear challenges concerning the disqualifications of MK Ofer Cassif and the Joint List.

Kyiv • UNN

Anthropic warns potential investors about the risks associated with developing advanced artificial intelligence. Among them, the company cites the possibility that AI could pose catastrophic or existential risks to humanity. Reuters reports, UNN relays.
Details
In the IPO prospectus reviewed by Reuters, the company said its models may exhibit what is known as "self-preservation behavior." This includes possible "resistance to shutdown," "concealing or manipulating information," and behavior "resembling blackmail."
"Our development of highly advanced models, platforms, and applications, as well as the expansion of their use cases, may further increase the risk that our models will cause harm," Anthropic said in a statement.
According to available information, the company also noted that during training, models sometimes acquire unexpected capabilities that may remain undetected until they are deployed. According to the prospectus, this could lead to serious safety incidents.
OpenAI canceled the launch of a new AI model due to safety concerns29.09.26, 09:47 • 1840 views
"Although public companies regularly disclose to investors the risks associated with their products, few, if any, have issued warnings that their technology could potentially lead to the extinction of humanity. Anthropic has emphasized both the transformative potential of artificial intelligence, as well as industrialization and electricity, and the irreversible harm it could cause if mishandled," the publication writes.
Moreover, according to available information, Anthropic safety researcher Evan Hubinger estimated at more than 10% the probability that artificial intelligence could kill people within the next decade.
"The company, which positions itself as a safety-first artificial intelligence lab, devoted approximately 80 pages of the 261-page main section of its offering prospectus to outlining risk factors—nearly twice as many as the 48 pages it used to describe its business," the publication writes.
Meanwhile, SpaceX, which owns xAI, devoted only about 38 pages out of the 277 pages of the main text of its offering prospectus to risk factors.
"The models’ potential awareness of our evaluation efforts creates a significant limitation on our ability to assess model safety," Anthropic’s offering prospectus states.

Argentina's Milei threatens UK with international legal action over Falkland Islands oil project
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-29
08:32:00 UTC
17:32:00 KST

Argentina threatens UK legal action over Falklands oil
September 29, 2026
Argentine President Javier Milei on Monday gave the United Kingdom two weeks to halt an oil project near the Falkland Islands or face international legal action.
The potentially lucrative project has intensified the long-running sovereignty dispute as the islands prepare for oil production that could transform their small economy.
What has Argentina threatened to do?
Milei said Argentina would take the dispute to the International Tribunal for the Law of the Sea in Hamburg if the UK did not halt the Sea Lion project within two weeks.
"I instructed the Foreign Ministry and our legal teams to initiate arbitration proceedings against the United Kingdom for the illegal sacking of our resources through the Sea Lion Project in the North Falklands Basin," Milei wrote on X.
"If within two weeks the United Kingdom does not stop the illegitimate exploitation, we will go to the International Tribunal for the Law of the Sea," he added.
Argentina argues that Britain's authorization of oil exploration violates a UN resolution calling on both sides to refrain from unilateral actions while their sovereignty dispute remains unresolved.
Milei has also threatened to bar companies involved in unauthorized oil exploration around the Falklands from operating in Argentina's oil and mining sectors.
His government has sent Argentina's Congress a bill proposing prison terms of up to 20 years for extracting resources around the islands without Argentine authorization.
Argentine authorities say they are investigating at least 60 companies and executives for possible violations.
What is the Sea Lion oil project?
Sea Lion is a major offshore oil field around 220 kilometers (137 miles) north of the Falkland Islands.
The project is being developed by Israel's Navitas Petroleum and Britain's Rockhopper Exploration under licenses issued by the Falkland Islands authorities.
Oil production is expected to begin in 2028.
The companies have rejected Argentina's objections, saying they hold valid licenses for the project.
The UK has also defended the right of the Falkland Islanders to develop their natural resources.
Why are the Falkland Islands disputed?
The Falkland Islands have been under British control since 1833, but Argentina claims sovereignty over the archipelago, which it calls the Malvinas.
Argentina invaded the islands in 1982, triggering a 10-week war with the UK.
The conflict killed 649 Argentine military personnel, 255 British service members and three islanders before British forces retook the territory.
The UK says the islanders have the right to determine their own future.
In a 2013 referendum, 99.8% of voters backed remaining a British Overseas Territory, with turnout of about 92%.
Argentina rejects the referendum and maintains its sovereignty claim.

Raytheon to build record numbers of AMRAAM missiles
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-29
08:31:04 UTC
17:31:04 KST

- The U.S. Air Force awarded Raytheon a multi-year AMRAAM contract worth up to $20.7 billion, running through June 2033.
- The deal includes foreign military sales to 16 countries and follows a February agreement to build at least 1,900 AMRAAMs a year.
The U.S. Air Force has awarded Raytheon a multi-year contract worth up to $20.7 billion to build AMRAAM air-to-air missiles, a deal the company says will push production of the weapon to record levels.
The award, announced Sept. 25 by the U.S. Department of War, covers complete missiles, spare guidance sections and related work, and runs through June 30, 2033. Raytheon will build the missiles in Tucson, Arizona. The contract does not say how many missiles it will buy.
The AMRAAM, short for Advanced Medium-Range Air-to-Air Missile and also known as the AIM-120, is a radar-guided missile fighter jets use to shoot down enemy aircraft beyond visual range. Now in its fifth generation, it is carried on 14 aircraft and ground platforms and fielded by 44 countries, and has recorded more than 7,000 successful live firings in tests and combat, Raytheon said. It is also the main interceptor for NASAMS, the ground-based air defense system Norway and Raytheon developed together, which Ukraine uses against Russian cruise missiles and drones.
Raytheon described the deal as a five-year multi-year contract with two option years, awarded under the Department of War’s “Arsenal of Freedom” push to expand munitions production. Multi-year contracts let the Pentagon buy several years’ worth of weapons at once, which gives manufacturers the confidence to invest in factories and suppliers and usually lowers the price per missile.
The award follows a framework agreement Raytheon and the Department of War signed on Feb. 4, 2026, under which the company committed to producing at least 1,900 AMRAAMs a year. That agreement was one of five covering Tomahawk cruise missiles, AMRAAM and three Standard Missile interceptor variants. RTX, Raytheon’s parent company, said it nearly doubled AMRAAM output in 2025 compared with 2024 and is working with small and mid-sized suppliers across the country, as well as exploring co-production with international partners, to raise it further.
Much of the demand comes from abroad. The contract includes foreign military sales to 16 countries: Australia, Belgium, Canada, the Czech Republic, Denmark, Finland, Germany, Italy, Japan, Kuwait, the Netherlands, Norway, Poland, Sweden, Taiwan and the United Kingdom.
The contract is a sole-source award, meaning Raytheon did not compete for it, and part of it is an undefinitized contract action. That lets work begin before the government and the company agree on final prices and terms, up to a set ceiling, in this case $20.7 billion.
Only a small share of the money has been committed so far. The Department of War obligated $85,715 in fiscal 2026 U.S. Air Force weapons procurement funds and about $154.3 million in foreign military sales funds at the time of award. The rest will be released as the contract is finalized and future budgets are approved.
The Air Force Life Cycle Management Center at Robins Air Force Base, Georgia, manages the contract.

UNGA 81: Five key takeaways from general debate
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-29
08:30:40 UTC
17:30:40 KST

UNGA 81: Five key takeaways from general debate
UN Secretary-General Antonio Guterres warns the future will be shaped by four tests: AI, climate change, war and inequality.
The 81st United Nations General Assembly (UNGA) concluded on Monday with artificial intelligence (AI), the Israel-Palestine conflict and the US-Israel war on Iran dominating world leaders’ addresses during the general debate.
UN Secretary-General Antonio Guterres, in his final address before his term ends, warned that the future of the world would be shaped by four tests: AI, climate change, wars and inequality.
Recommended Stories
list of 3 items
- list 1 of 3Turkiye calls for UN Security Council veto to end: Could it happen?
- list 2 of 3Jerusalem Daily: violence continues as the world watches the UNGA
- list 3 of 3German, Russian foreign ministers hold rare talks amid rising tensions
“Across all four tests, the decisive issue is power. Power over force, money, energy, technology, rules and the future. That is why the UN Charter – and the work of the United Nations – matter more than ever,” Guterres said.
Speeches ranged from calls to reform the UN to appeals for upholding international law, as the global body has been undermined by the unilateral foreign policy pushed by United States President Donald Trump.
Here are the biggest takeaways from this year’s summit:
Palestine
The situation in Palestine was a key issue among members amid Israel’s ongoing genocidal war on Gaza despite the so-called “ceasefire” and escalating settler pogroms in the occupied West Bank.
France, Canada, Iraq, the United Kingdom and others called for Palestinian sovereignty during their speeches.
“What credibility do we have if we continue to remain inactive in the face of Gaza,” French President Emmanuel Macron said in his address.
“Some boast of a supposed peace, but this peace hasn’t reopened humanitarian routes for a single second,” he said, adding: “Must we stand by and watch this spectacle that shames us all?”
Macron, British Prime Minister Andy Burnham, his Canadian counterpart Mark Carney and Saudi Foreign Minister Prince Faisal bin Farhan Al Saud chaired a meeting at the UNGA on Palestinian statehood, which is being actively undermined by Israel. Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu’s government has accelerated construction of illegal settlements and provided impunity to settlers in the occupied territory.
At the same time, the US-led Board of Peace unveiled a 66-project reconstruction blueprint with proposed funding of $2.4bn for the Gaza Strip on the sidelines of the UNGA.
However, the board’s plan excludes the UN agency for Palestinian refugees (UNRWA), saying it has no role in the future of Gaza. The decision was described by Palestinian political analyst and playwright Ahmed Najar to Al Jazeera as aligned with Israeli efforts to “marginalise and ultimately dismantle the agency, removing it not only from Gaza’s present but from its future”.
Dozens of delegates left the hall in protest as Netanyahu delivered his speech, in which he declared that Israeli forces would continue fighting against Hamas and Iran.
Trump defends military action on Venezuela, Iran
In his address, Trump emphasised that while others spoke of peace, he “made peace”.
Trump defended his actions in abducting the then-Venezuelan President Nicolas Maduro in January and said, since his military operation, hundreds of political prisoners had been freed in the South American country and that Caracas had signed the largest oil deal in history last month, covering “65 billion barrels of oil, which will benefit both Venezuela and the United States enormously and help drive down the cost of energy all over the world”.
“It was perhaps the biggest deal ever made. To the victor belong the spoils – you’ve all heard that,” Trump boasted.
Trump reiterated that he would never allow Tehran to have nuclear weapons and that the 12-day war in July 2025 had “obliterated their nuclear programme beneath mountains of rubble” as the ongoing US-Israel war on Iran had sunk “159 ships of their navy” to the bottom of the sea.
“I have a big decision to make – will a deal be made with Iran that lets them rebuild and create a far greater country than it ever was before … or do I annihilate the Islamic Republic and do it quickly, never giving them a chance to kill and destroy people and countries again,” he said, adding: “I believe we make a deal right after the elections.”
Popular Iranian officials
During sideline talks and one-on-one meetings, Iranian officials were in demand.
In his speech to delegates, President Masoud Pezeshkian emphasised that Iran had only “defended ourselves” amid attacks on his country and killings of Supreme Leader Ayatollah Ali Khamenei, scientists and children.
“We are not terrorists, our innocent people have been the targets of cowardly attacks and aggressions imposed upon our country,” he said.
Pezeshkian added Iran would not accept that peaceful nuclear technology is held exclusively in the hands of a few countries.
“We will not bow our head and give up the right that is inherently ours,” he said.
Meanwhile, on the sidelines of the summit, Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi met his counterparts from India, Qatar, Turkiye, Pakistan, Ukraine and other countries.
He also met US Special Envoy Steve Witkoff and Trump’s son-in-law Jared Kushner in a four-hour meeting mediated by Qatar.
AI dominance
World leaders used their time at the podium to call for a global approach to using AI as interest in the technology grows, but fears that it could escalate if unchecked are also growing.
In his address, Finnish President Alexander Stubb said AI was the “most consequential technology in the history of mankind”.
“It will impact science, the economy, politics, security, and the very essence of our humanity. Humans can and should be in the driver’s seat. We have a choice: we can compete, cooperate or slow down. For me, cooperation is the best way forward,” he said.
While discussions are moving away from a good-versus-bad dichotomy, officials disagreed on approaches.
While Guterres and the European Union called for safety standards and international rules, Trump said AI innovation should not be constrained by international regulation, adding that the US should control its AI sector.
Xi skips the UNGA
Chinese President Xi Jinping skipped the UNGA despite being in the US for a summit with Trump. He sent Vice President Han Zheng to attend.
Xi rarely attends the UNGA. He had sent Premier Li Qiang in his place last year. In 2024, Foreign Minister Wang Yi attended the annual gathering.
Without mentioning Iran in his address, Han reiterated Beijing’s position that “sovereignty and security of countries in the Middle East, including the Gulf, should be respected”.
“China calls for advancing the governance of the West Bank and the post-conflict reconstruction of Gaza in accordance with the principle of the Palestinians governing Palestine. It also calls for bringing the Palestinian question back onto the right track of the two-state solution at an early date,” he said.
Han also called for a “people-centred approach and develop AI for the positive and for good, narrow the digital divide, and promote development that is universally beneficial”.

"It's one that clearly involves the hands of a foreign actor," Rubio told Sean Hannity on broadcaster Fox News in an interview Monday, adding that he would not go into further detail.
The release of the five—all London-based Britons in their mid-20s—came as British Prime Minister Andy Burnham announced an emergency meeting of top officials to ensure they have "the full picture".

Here's what we know so far:
Counter-terror probe
UK counter-terror police are leading the investigation after authorities received reports Sunday of three "suspicious" white vans near the airbase, which has been used by the United States to bomb Iran.
Police said in their latest update Monday that the five men held, who all live in inner London boroughs, were being released on bail.
"This does not mean the investigation is over," Assistant Commissioner Laurence Taylor, the head of Counter Terrorism Policing, said, adding the five would be subject to "stringent" bail conditions.
He said officers were "considering this from every possible angle, including that this may be activity committed by proxies, or individuals either knowingly or unknowingly, working on behalf of a foreign state".
The men were arrested on suspicion of explosives offences and "preparation of a terrorist act" under UK anti-terrorism laws, according to police.
They had been travelling in the three suspect vehicles, which have since been subject to "extensive examination, with the support of military assets and forensic experts".
Bomb-disposal team
Authorities have not confirmed details of the threat but bomb-disposal experts were seen working at the scene.

Iran denies involvement

US Secretary of State Marco Rubio said the incident "clearly involves the hands of a foreign actor", without giving further details.
Iran's embassy in London said on X that it "categorically rejects and strongly condemns" the "unfounded and malicious speculations" that Tehran was involved.
US bombers
Britain gave the United States permission in March to use Fairford for "specific defensive operations into Iran" to destroy Iranian missiles at source.
US bombers and other planes have since been seen taking off and landing from the base—the only one on Britain's mainland used for this purpose.
Residents in the rural Cotswolds area surrounding Fairford said the site, which hosts a range of US military equipment and personnel, had seen increased activity and security in recent months.
Authorities evacuated around 85 households from the village early on Sunday, and they were allowed to return home the next day.

Russia to increase military spending in 2027 – Reuters
Russia plans to spend US$202.58 billion on defence in 2027, which is approximately 27% more than previously budgeted.
Source: Reuters
Details: Russia plans to spend RUB 17.1 trillion (approximately US$202.58 billion) on defence, a 27% increase over the RUB 13.5 trillion (US$159 billion) projected in the initial budget plan.
It is noted that this represents the highest figure since the start of the full-scale war in Ukraine in 2022.
This data is according to Russian government documents reviewed by Reuters on Monday 28 September.
According to these documents, total defence expenditures over the next three years will reach RUB 50 trillion (US$589.6 billion). For 2026, the Russian government previously planned defence spending of RUB 12.1 trillion (US$142 billion), though the actual amount is classified and will not be disclosed. A portion of military spending may also be reflected under other sections of the budget.
The documents also reveal that the Russian government raised its 2026 budget deficit forecast to 3.2% of gross domestic product, up from the previous estimate of 1.6% of GDP. Overall budget expenditures in 2026 are set to rise by 13.2% to RUB 48.6 trillion (US$573 billion) or 20.9% of GDP.
Furthermore, the obtained documents indicate that a new windfall tax on metallurgical and mining companies is expected to bring Russia approximately RUB 200 billion (US$2.3 billion) annually.
Background: Kremlin ruler Vladimir Putin signed a decree increasing the official number of personnel in the Russian Armed Forces to 2,441,630.

OpenAI apologises to Australia over unauthorised government website access
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-29
08:28:42 UTC
17:28:42 KST

OpenAI apologised to Australia on Tuesday after revealing that its artificial intelligence models accessed government websites without authorisation during internal training and evaluation.
“In June, during internal training and evaluation our models accessed Australian government websites in ways they were not authorised to,” the company said.
“We also should have handled our response better. We are sorry and working to do better in the future.”
The company said it identified the activity in mid-August while reviewing earlier training and evaluation work following a separate incident involving AI research platform Hugging Face.
The apology came five days after Australian Prime Minister Anthony Albanese disclosed the Medicare portal incident in New York on the sidelines of the UN General Assembly.
Albanese said on September 24 that an OpenAI agent had gained unauthorised access to Services Australia’s Medicare Statistics Reporting Service.
The agent accessed public and non-public files, prompting a forensic investigation with assistance from the Australian Signals Directorate.
Australian officials said the portal contains aggregate Medicare statistics and is separate from systems handling individual Medicare claims and personal information.
OpenAI said its review identified activity involving four Australian government organisations: Services Australia, the NSW Bureau of Crime Statistics and Research, the Victorian Department of Health and the Australian Institute of Health and Welfare.
At Services Australia, an experimental internal model had been assigned a research task concerning government spending per person on medicines for skin conditions in Victorian communities.
Australian task force to be established
OpenAI said the model struggled to obtain the information and then took unauthorised actions that allowed it to access material beyond what was publicly available.
The company said the model examined technical information and source code and accessed internal files, credentials and aggregate statistics.
However, OpenAI said its review found no evidence that individual patient or client records were accessed.
“We did not intend for this activity to occur, and the access to the service and follow-on activity should not have happened,” it said.
OpenAI said its models also accessed systems operated by the other three agencies but did not access individual crime records, medical records or identifiable survey responses.
The company said it has strengthened safeguards, including additional network restrictions and monitoring.
It also pledged technical support for affected agencies and assistance in strengthening Australia’s cyber defences.
OpenAI said it will establish an Australian task force with independent experts to develop recommendations on AI-related cybersecurity and improve coordination between AI developers and governments.
Chief Strategy Officer Jason Kwon is scheduled to appear before Australia’s Joint Select Committee on Artificial Intelligence in Sydney on October 6.

After the latest rise, Australia's rates are topped by this one country
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-29
08:28:36 UTC
17:28:36 KST

IN BRIEF
- Australia's cash rate is now one of the highest in the world, but lower than Iceland's.
- Experts say Iceland's dramatic rate is the product of over two decades of financial instability.
Australia has the second-highest interest rate among comparable economies after the Reserve Bank hiked rates to a 15-year high on Tuesday.
Taking the crown is Iceland, where the cash rate currently sits at 8 per cent — the highest of the 41 advanced economies as defined by the International Monetary Fund.
The Central Bank of Iceland set the historic rate in August, claiming the increase was "driven mainly by hikes in public levies and price increases caused by the war in the Middle East".
Similarly, the Reserve Bank of Australia (RBA) cited higher energy and fuel prices and the Middle East conflict as reasons for Australia's hike from 4.35 per cent to 4.6 per cent.
Treasurer Jim Chalmers denied a fair comparison could be made between Australia and Iceland's interest rates.
News that makes sense
Your trusted source for staying up-to-date with the world around you. Get free daily news updates and analysis, straight to your inbox.
"If you want to make a comparison with other countries and other economies, you need to acknowledge that growth here is faster than a lot of other economies," he said on Tuesday following the RBA announcement.
Chalmers said Australia currently has fast economic and employment growth, low debt and an economy "equal to the US".
"We've got a lot going for us in Australia, but we've got a lot coming at us from around the world as well — that's clear in the Reserve Bank's Statement," he said.
"We take all of those challenges very seriously. When you compare us to the world, there are some things that we are doing much better than the rest of the world."
Iceland, a small island nation that sits between Greenland and Norway in the Atlantic Ocean, has a population of almost 397,000 — almost 100,000 less than the ACT.
As of August, the national inflation rate was 5.6 per cent.
"While it does have considerable supplies of renewable geothermal energy ... it's reliant on transporting almost everything other than the food it can grow for itself," independent economist Saul Eslake told SBS News.
"It's very exposed to the increases in energy prices that we have seen since the outbreak of the conflict in the Middle East."
Eslake explained that Iceland's high interest rate can be attributed to a "fairly tumultuous" 25 years.
"It had an enormous boom in the lead-up to the global financial crisis of 2007/8. But then, Iceland faced the collapse of its banking system and house prices, and large parts of its economy."
He said Iceland had one of the most traumatic experiences of any country during the global financial crisis.
"That left Iceland more vulnerable than other economies might be to the kind of shocks that we've seen this year."
He said one of the major mistakes the Central Bank of Iceland made was decreasing interest rates as inflation unexpectedly rose after the COVID-19 pandemic.
"They pushed up their cash rate to 11 per cent in the aftermath of the COVID pandemic because inflation rose more than almost any other country," he said.
"They then cut interest rates in 2023, and cut them back down to 9.25 per cent in 2025 — only to find that inflation didn't fall, it rose again.
This followed further interest rate rises to tackle inflation.
Eslake said the RBA made the same mistake in 2025 when it didn't increase interest rates and so, in the face of rising inflation, was forced to increase rates in February this year.
In August, Iceland's government held a referendum on negotiating membership in the European Union, which would include replacing its Króna currency with the euro, and potentially easing financial pressure.
The European Central Bank interest rate is 2.25 per cent compared to Iceland's 8 per cent.
"It would not solve Iceland's structural faults, but it could become a catalyst to a more healthy economy," Vilhjalmur Hilmarsson, chief economist at Icelandic labour union Viska, told the Agence France-Presse news agency.
However, Iceland voted 52.8 per cent against the referendum's proposal. Instead, the nation's government will focus on strengthening its ties with the EU through the European Economic Area Agreement, which it shares with Norway and Liechtenstein.
Eslake was unsurprised by the verdict, believing Iceland a proud nation.
"Clearly, Icelanders value their independence," he said.
As for Australia, Eslake said Tuesday's interest rate hike was "entirely expected".
"It flows from the stronger-than-expected inflation data that we've seen over the past couple of months. It flows from the fact that most indicators for economic activity have been a little stronger than expected," he said.
"As the Reserve Bank board said today, it also reflects the renewed increases in energy prices as a result of the ongoing impasse or conflict in the Middle East, which is not looking likely to last much longer than anticipated."
Eslake said it isn't a fair or appropriate comparison to link Australia and Iceland.
"We are very different countries, with very different trading relationships and very different economic structures as well as being very different in scale and scope," he said.
However, the economist warned that both Iceland's Central Bank and the RBA should be more careful when betting on falling inflation.
"You don't want to be in an embarrassing position to reverse the interest rate cuts that you've previously instituted," he said.
"You have to have good reason to be confident you're on top of the inflation problem you're seeking to solve before cutting interest rates."
— With additional reporting from Agence France Presse.

India needs heritage zones, not heritage islands
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-29
08:27:27 UTC
17:27:27 KST

At the end of August this year, the Prime Minister visited Uzbekistan. Had his visit been a trifle longer and encompassed the Registan complex in Samarkand, he may have come across an interesting feature in the madrasas that constitute the complex. Within each madrasa, the cells where students once lived are now shops for handicrafts, bridging the gap between architectural history and living heritage. The marketplace does not just bring alive the otherwise passive monument, it also creates a ‘heritage zone’ compelling visitors to spend more time and adds to the local economy. This phenomenon of creating heritage zones, common in that country, is something India would do well to learn from.A visitor to the Qutab Minar complex in Delhi, also a UNESCO World Heritage site like the Registan Square, sees a set of magnificent monuments. However, the place gives no clue about the larger heritage ecosystem that lies just beyond the walls of the Qutab complex. And importantly, the opportunity to create a showcase of living heritage too has been missed.
Sharing a wall with the Qutab complex is Mehrauli Archaeological Park, dotted with tombs, mosques, a magnificent stepwell, stables, cupolas as well as some British era structures.
On the other side of the complex lies Mehrauli village, with more tombs, a dargah, the Zafar Mahal, another stepwell and a tiny World War I marker. Nothing in the Qutab complex indicates the existence of this larger heritage universe.Nor is there any mention of the superb Dastkar Haat, a short drive away. In March this year, the Haat saw a major fire that destroyed over forty shops and caused losses of several crore. To anyone who has visited the place, it is apparent that the Haat suffers from a lack of space. On the other side, the Mehrauli Archaeological Park, spread over 200 acres, lacks publicity and footfalls. The back wall of the park is broken and serves as a thoroughfare for people in Mehrauli village. After dark come the unsavoury elements. An uncovered drain flows through a part of the park. The logical solution would be to marry the two spaces.Imagine a scenario where visitors had an option to exit – or enter - the Qutab complex into the Archaeological Park, in one corner of which the Dastkar Haat is relocated. Currently the park has a solitary café. Create more such cafes and even fine dining areas, as well as an amphitheatre enabling cultural performances and open-air exhibitions.
AdvantagesThe biggest plus is to create urban spaces in and around hitherto neglected heritage zones that ensure:
Higher footfalls in the heritage zone itself, which would especially benefit less-known monuments.
Optimal utilization of space in the heritage zone, bringing in new audiences causing benefits to both the monument’s eyeballs as well as the Haat.
Seamless cultural connection between handicrafts and heritage zones building a multi-sensory journey encompassing architecture, craft and culture.
Ensures neglected parts of a large heritage zone are spruced up and not left to be covered by vegetation or intruded by anti-social elements.
Creates economic opportunities, both to the artisans and to the agency managing the monument. A revenue sharing arrangement could be explored.
ChallengesThe Dastkar Haat is a creation of a non-profit society which runs for the welfare of artisans, in partnership with Delhi Tourism. The latter reports to the Delhi State Government while the Delhi Development Authority – which controls the park – is under the Central Government’s Ministry of Housing and Urban Affairs. The monuments are with the Archaeological Survey of India (ASI), under the jurisdiction of the Central Government’s Ministry of Culture. Imagine the sheer number of bureaucrats involved and the resultant turf war. Adding to the confusion are some madrasas, supposedly under the umbrella of the Waqf Board, which are functioning out of monuments.The suggestion of bringing a Haat into the vicinity of a space that has the Jamali-Kamali mosque, Balban’s tomb and the Rajaon-ki-Baoli would instantly anger heritage hardliners, not to mention ASI officials.
Process
Curation of such a zone will need to be pioneered by the Union Ministry of Culture, bringing in subject matter experts from the private sector or non-for-profit bodies such as the Indian National Trust for Art and Cultural Heritage (INTACH).
Monitoring the heritage zone to ensure the monument stays untouched is a task for the ASI, of or state department, if it is a state managed monument.
Pan-India modelThis model ‘heritage zone’ already exists in Sunder Nursery and begs to be implemented in sites across India. The nursery was once a mere offshoot of the Humayun’s Tomb complex, drawing in only flora and heritage afficionados.
Today, it is a magnificent cultural hub.Imagine the Tughlakabad Fort as a place for musical evenings instead of being overgrown with scrub. Imagine if the National Crafts Museum were not in isolation in a corner of Bharat Mandapam but within the Purana Qila complex. Imagine if the neglected spaces near Ujjain’s Kaliyadeh Palace were leveraged to create a crafts bazaar. Imagine if Chhattisgarh’s tribal art, crafts and cuisine were to be given a space – even on a seasonal basis – at the heritage hub of Sirpur. Imagine!(The author is a heritage enthusiast)

Teknofest to bring technology, aviation to southeastern Türkiye
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-29
08:27:13 UTC
17:27:13 KST

Stands have been set up at GAP Airport as part of TEKNOFEST Southeast, which will be held in Şanlıurfa from Sept. 30 to Oct. 4. (AA Photo)
Türkiye’s major aerospace and technology festival Teknofest will bring exhibitions, technology competitions, educational workshops and air shows to the southeastern province of Şanlıurfa from Sept. 30 to Oct. 4.
Organized by the Industry and Technology Ministry and the Turkish Technology Team (T3) Foundation, the festival will be held at an area established at GAP Airport.
The event will combine modern technology with Şanlıurfa’s ancient heritage. The province is home to Göbeklitepe, one of the world’s oldest known monumental sites, and is known in Türkiye as the “city of prophets” because of its long-standing religious and historical associations.
Visitors will be able to see a range of Turkish aerospace and defense platforms, including the Bayraktar KIZILELMA, KAAN, Bayraktar TB3, HÜRJET, Bayraktar AKINCI and Bayraktar TB2, as well as various aircraft and land vehicles.
Air demonstrations will be among the festival’s main attractions from Sept. 30 to Oct. 3. Visitors will see flight performances by the Bayraktar AKINCI, Bayraktar TB3, Bayraktar TB2 AI, AKSUNGUR, T-129 ATAK and T-70, alongside performances by the Turkish Stars aerobatic team with NF-5 aircraft and SOLOTÜRK with F-16s.
The program will also feature military helicopter formations, a special-forces demonstration, parachute and paramotor shows, as well as various stage performances.
A HÜRJET and KAAN musical and an NSosyal trivia competition will accompany a concert by Turkish singer Semicenk. The festival will conclude on Oct. 4 with a closing ceremony and awards presentation.
TEKNOFEST Güneydoğu will offer a range of interactive attractions, including a planetarium, a Göbeklitepe Experience Area, the “Journey of Materials” and Hezarfen Experience Areas, and a HÜRJET Experience Area.
Visitors will also be able to explore the Çelik Kubbe (Steel Dome) digital experience area, an ASELSAN land vehicles exhibition and a Turkish Land Forces vehicles exhibition.
The festival will host workshops focused on science and technology. Technology competitions will cover areas including agricultural technology, artificial intelligence, blockchain, financial technologies, mining, air defense systems, robotics, satellite terminals and drone technology.
International events such as the World Drone Cup and HackMasters Güneydoğu will also take place.
Science shows, technology-themed activities for children and a theater production will provide programs for visitors of different ages throughout the five-day festival.
