NDIS advocates are pushing for alternatives to group homes
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-29
08:26:20 UTC
17:26:20 KST

The government wants to cut NDIS costs, advocates are pushing for alternatives to group homes
Jason Toppin's group home is more than a roof over his head.
"This place means a lot to me. It's a part of me that no one can take away," said the 47-year-old, who lives with a vision impairment and intellectual disability.
"This is my happy place."
He's firm friends with the four men he's shared the house with for 12 years. They all have similar disabilities and are of similar ages.
Most evenings they settle in to watch TV together. Friday nights they get takeaway and they visit their local milk bar on the weekends.
The home is run by St John of God Accord and is funded by each resident's National Disability Insurance Scheme (NDIS) plan, which also pays for the support they receive to cook, get out into the community and have supervision overnight.
"It's very warming, family-like and the staff do a good job here," Jason said.
Currently, group homes like Jason's are the main accommodation option for people with disability but not every group home is as happy.
The federal government is looking to reduce the cost of the NDIS by $36 billion over the next four years and disability advocates believe it's an opportunity to consider alternative living plans.
The Disability Royal Commission heard evidence of violence, abuse and neglect in group homes. In its final report, a majority of commissioners recommended group homes be phased out.
Professor Christine Bigby of LaTrobe University, who has worked in intellectual disability research for three decades, said group homes themselves are not the problem.
"Time and time again we come back to what's the housing model … and if we get that right, everything else will follow," she told 7.30.
"That's actually not the case. The most important thing is the quality of support."
Within the NDIS, Supported Independent Living funding assists people with high significant needs living in accommodation settings, usually group homes.
This form of support currently costs the scheme $16.6 billion a year, around 10 per cent of which pays for overnight stays.
Advocates say alternative approaches to supported living could be cheaper and better for residents.
"There are people currently living in group homes that could be living more in the community and could be living more cost-effectively," said Jess Walker from the Summer Foundation, an advocacy body focused on alternative housing models.
"Group homes ... have been the default option available for people with disability, and what we need to see is a growing of alternative options so people have choice about how and where they live."
A different path to independence
One of those options is a disability housing model called Individualised Living Arrangements (ILA).
It allows someone with mild to moderate support needs to achieve independence by living with a flatmate — not a carer — in a regular property in the community.
Meghan Kyne is one of nearly 500 Australians who have chosen the model. She lives with an intellectual disability, and speaks fondly of her flatmate Isabel Hankey, who she's been sharing a house with for the last three years.
"Isabel is a cool person and a wonderful person," Meghan said.
The two share the bills and chores, have long chats over dinner and look out for each other when they're unwell.
"[Meghan's] a really considerate housemate," Isabel said.
"It's a lovely arrangement."
Isabel's rent is subsidised in exchange for this companionship, having someone in the house overnight and informal guidance such as prompts with daily tasks.
Meghan also has separate NDIS funding for support workers to assist her with other tasks, including preparing meals, doing laundry or grocery shopping.
The arrangement has an added informal support benefit: all the people Meghan has gotten to know in the community check in on her and help her live an independent life.
Meghan's service provider says the average annual cost of the 21 homes it oversees is just less than $170,000. One-to-three support in a group home would be more than $230,000 per person.
Housing arrangements like Meghan's are overseen by a service provider, which finds appropriate housemates using a rigorous vetting process involving police and other checks.
The provider also organises rental agreements and assigns a staff member to keep an eye on things.
Despite the cost benefit of the arrangement, the NDIS is funding fewer participants to take up what it calls "individualised living options" — down from 623 people in 2024 to 482 earlier this year.
In the first quarter of 2024-25, more than 1,600 people were given funding for the initial planning stages of the arrangement. But in the last quarter of 2025-26, funding to explore the model was given to only 338 people.
'Life-changing' flexibility
Katie Ferguson, who lives with a physical disability, has chosen to live on her own so she can manage her own schedule and decide who to have around her.
"When you live by yourself, you've got total freedom of when you work, when you come home, who you talk to," she said.
To make that possible, she uses a drop-in and on-call service run by not-for-profit Mobile Attendant Care Service (MACS).
Every evening, support workers fan out across Brisbane and the Gold Coast to around 70 clients who only need assistance for between 15 minutes and an hour.
They arrive at Ms Ferguson's home between 11pm and 1am so she can be hoisted into bed from her wheelchair.
Ms Ferguson also uses MACS in case she needs additional support during the night. All up, it costs the NDIS about $51,000 a year.
If she paid for support workers to sleep over, the cost would more than double to almost $114,000 annually.
MACS general manager Alison Herring says the flexibility is life-changing for their customers, and she would like to see the mobile service made available nationally.
"Our support model stretches the funding a lot further," Ms Herring said.
"We're able to just bill the customers for the time of support that they're receiving, which makes it much more cost-effective for them."
But any move towards tightening the disability housing market and directing NDIS participants to large, established housing providers would make that challenging.
Supporting a solution
The federal government is currently considering whether to adopt an approach to disability housing that could see it play a more active role in how it's planned, funded and monitored.
Disability Minister Mark Butler told 7.30 he only wants a pool of approved providers to offer services in supported living arrangements to remove poor-quality operators from the system.
But the government made no mention of any of the alternatives to group homes when it asked the disability community for their input.
Mr Butler said he thought alternative models would have been a "significant issue raised".
Under the NDIS, organisations providing support to people living in disability accommodation must be registered and undergo independent auditing.
Mr Butler said more was needed to ensure providers offering SIL services were looking after people properly.
"What we want to do … is to provide participants with choice but from a panel of providers in their community who we have confidence are providing the right level of service,"
"I don't think you can say that confidently about all SIL services."
According to Professor Bigby, having a panel of providers was an opportunity to improve the quality of supports.
"It would make for a much more organised, controlled market and a market that might meet people's needs," Professor Bigby said.
"You could have a panel where you would not be able to get on that panel unless you could demonstrate you met criteria for quality in an observable way."
The NDIS was intended to give participants choice, creating an open market for services.
Mr Butler acknowledged the SIL market was not working as effectively as it could be and said there is a "tension" between making choice and control possible while maintaining high-quality services.
"The central philosophy here is choice and control, and that as much as anything, should include living options," he said.
Professor Bigby said alternatives to group homes represent a "leap into the unknown".
As she sees it, alternatives to group homes are geared towards people with relatively low support needs and are usually overseen by resourceful relatives, which not everyone has.
"It also raises a question about actually who's exercising choice and control," she said.

Trump was asked by reporters about comments by David Perdue, the U.S. ambassador to China, who said on “Fox News Sunday” that Trump had raised selling weapons to Beijing during his recent meeting with Xi, The Hill reported.
“I never heard of that one,” Trump said. “I don’t have to ask him. You mean we’re going to sell? I think he probably was talking about that.”
In his Sunday interview with host Shannon Bream, Perdue said Trump had played down U.S. arms sales to Taiwan in his talks with Xi by describing them as one of many weapons deals the United States makes with other countries.
“President Trump continues to say, ‘Hey, we sell arms to other people around the world,'” Perdue said.
Bream pointed to concerns from lawmakers in both parties about delays in delivering weapons and aid to Taiwan, which China claims as its territory and has threatened to take by force. Perdue rejected the suggestion that Washington had slowed arms shipments to Taiwan to keep Xi happy. He said Trump “is as strong on Taiwan as I’ve ever seen anybody” and that the two leaders would return to the subject of U.S. arms sales to Taiwan in future talks.
Selling weapons to China would run against long-standing U.S. policy. The United States has banned arms sales to China since the 1989 Tiananmen Square crackdown, and the Taiwan Relations Act of 1979 commits Washington to providing Taiwan with weapons for its self-defense. The United States does not formally recognize Taiwan as a country, and past administrations have avoided saying whether U.S. forces would defend the island if China attacked.
Trump gave his meeting with Xi a glowing review on Monday. “I would rate it at 12,” he said, on a scale of 10, describing the talks as “very respectful, very good, great meeting.”
He has confirmed he will meet Xi twice more before the end of the year: at the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation summit in China in November and at the Group of 20 summit in Miami in December.
In November 2025, Trump warned in a “60 Minutes” interview with CBS News that China would face “consequences” if it invaded Taiwan. Pressed by Norah O’Donnell on what those consequences would be, he declined to say, adding that “the other side knows.”

An index value above 100 indicates an optimistic outlook about the general economic situation, while a value below 100 signals a pessimistic perspective.

Russia has quietly started a new round of mobilization and plans to bring in more North Korean troops, Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said. He cited a new report from Ukraine's military intelligence. The same day, the Kremlin published a decree enlarging Russia's army for the fourth time this year.
Russia widens recruitment at home and abroad
Zelenskyy spoke in his evening address on 28 September, after a briefing from Ukraine's military intelligence (HUR).
"In effect, the Russians have already begun additional mobilization—they are increasing the number of people they recruit through various means," he said.
Moscow also plans to recruit more foreigners, Zelenskyy said. He urged the governments of countries whose citizens Russia recruits to counter it, and said Kyiv would inform each of them.
Ukraine says Russia has been losing soldiers faster than contract recruitment replaces them. If so, an unannounced call-up lets the Kremlin refill its ranks without a formal draft. ISW says Putin may hold off on such a draft until he sees whether his strikes work. Ukrainian intelligence had expected Russia to announce a mass mobilization after this month's State Duma elections.
More than 8,000 North Koreans in Russia, 10,000 more in preparation
More than 8,000 North Korean troops are currently on Russian territory, Zelenskyy said. Pyongyang is selecting another 10,000 for training and deployment to Russia, he added.
Russia is paying, among other things, with technology, according to Zelenskyy. North Korea has launched production of Shahed-type attack drones with Russian technical support, he said.
That is a step beyond what Kyiv reported in June 2025. Moscow and Pyongyang had then only agreed to start preparing such production. In August, Zelenskyy warned that Russia could receive up to 50,000 North Korean troops.
North Korean missile unit deploys to Russia for ballistic strikes on Ukraine, Kyiv says
Kremlin raises the army's size again
Putin's decree sets the authorized strength of Russia's armed forces at 2,441,630, including 1,550,500 military personnel, Vedomosti reported. The decree gives no reason.
The order adds 15,500 troops and is the fourth such increase this year, Euronews said. Since March, the combined increase has reached 47,860 soldiers. Putin's 2022 "partial mobilization" decree also remains in force, the outlet noted.
Russia could open northern front by February if it orders new mobilization, Ukraine intel says
Moscow keeps denying a call-up
In early September, Putin claimed that reports of a coming mobilization were "complete nonsense" and "an information attack on Russia." Russian officials gave similar assurances days before the 2022 call-up.
Ukraine's military and foreign intelligence had earlier said that Russia's General Staff prepared a scenario to mobilize 600,000 people over 2026 and 2027, 300,000 each year.

Hackers gained access to the data of nearly 3 million people at the Pentagon - media
Kyiv • UNN
A breach of the Pentagon's database exposed the Social Security numbers and service records of 2.76 million living people and 294,000 deceased people. There is currently no evidence of misuse of the information.
The confidential data of nearly 3 million Americans, Social Security numbers, and information about the positions of military and civilian employees were exposed in a hacking attack on the U.S. Department of Defense. This was reported by ABC News, according to UNN.
Details
According to the publication, as a result of a breach of the Pentagon’s extensive personnel database, confidential information about many service members was exposed, including Social Security numbers and details about their positions.
"The scale and sensitivity of the disclosed information could raise national security concerns, particularly because the files contained details about the work performed by military and civilian employees," the publication writes.
According to the available information, the leak concerns 2.76 million living people and another 294,000 deceased individuals.
"The information system of the Department of Defense’s Defense Manpower Data Center (DMDC) experienced unauthorized access to the personal data of a small number of unauthorized users between October 2025 and July 2026. After the breach was discovered, the DMDC immediately remedied the vulnerability," an official said.
As the publication writes, the DMDC stores data on service members, reservists, civilian employees, contractors, retirees, veterans, and their family members. In total, the system contains more than 60 million records.
At the same time, according to the publication, the Department of Defense said it currently has no evidence that the exposed information was improperly used. Those affected are being offered personal data protection services and credit monitoring.

Burnham to signal willingness to look at scrapping pension triple lock to fund social care
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-29
08:22:55 UTC
17:22:55 KST

Andy Burnham will signal he is prepared to look at scrapping the pensions triple lock to fund a national care service, telling the Labour conference he will be willing to make difficult arguments to tackle the UK’s intractable issues such as social care.
Government sources have suggested the prime minister will signal his willingness to review the policy but stop short of a pledge to scrap it altogether. The Unite general secretary, Sharon Graham, said the move would be “electoral suicide”, with an end to the triple lock likely to be attacked by the Conservaties and Reform.
In his speech, he will promise “an honest conversation” with the public, saying: “Hope comes from honesty and from saying the things politicians usually avoid.”
Graham said Burnham had not committed to scrapping the policy, which ensures the state pension increases annually by either inflation, average wage growth or 2.5% – whichever is highest.
“When we met with Andy this week, it certainly wasn’t mentioned,” she told BBC Radio 4’s Today programme. “But I do think that it’s important that Labour make sure that working-class people know that they’re on their side, and this would be a direction of travel that would say the opposite to that.”
Asked whether the lock should be overhauled to fund social care, Graham said: “What I understood the national care service to be was a universal benefit: everybody paid in and everybody gets out, and that is what actually the principle of that is.
“Going to a group of people who are getting around £12,500 a year in order to pay for it, to take away their security, is wrong. I think it’s morally wrong.”
Labour’s deputy leader, Lucy Powell, said the party remained committed to the triple lock, which was in its manifesto. “The triple lock has really delivered for pensioners, in this country, over the course of this parliament,” she told Sky News.
“I think we’re going to see [the] state pension rising by about £2,000 a year, significantly, and that’s really important so pensioners … can know that their income is secure and will continue to rise over the course of this parliament.
“I don’t know what Andy’s going to say about that today, but I know that what he’s talking about is this big conversation about solving these big problems, but being really honest with people that they come at a cost.
“They do come at a cost. You can’t just solve the social care crisis without having the big conversations about how you’re going to do this.”
The housing secretary Angela Rayner said Burham would start a “brave” conversation on the funding of social care. “I think he’s absolutely right to start the conversation,” Rayner told Sky.
“We’ve got a prime minister who said, I am okay with burning through all my political capital to the point where it might finish me off, on the basis of my legacy will be something better and different.”
Having ousted Keir Starmer from office, Burnham has spent much of his first few weeks promising a radical shift in tone and policy.
He will tell the conference on Tuesday: “We can’t carry on as we are. Politics as usual has taken Britain backwards. More of the same isn’t good enough and isn’t going to get us where we need to be.”
Though the conference has been upbeat, Burnham will tell Labour delegates he wants to strike a serious tone with his speech and address some of the most intractable issues in British politics, such as social care, energy costs and youth inactivity.
In the speech, the prime minister will say that he will resist “the usual tub-thumping conference speech … the patriot in me tells me something very different is needed”.
He will say “everyone wants less drift and more direction” and that he will “answer that call” today. His offer – expected to contain a number of new policies – will be “a more serious prospectus for Britain than people have been offered in a generation”.
“I accept people will not agree with every part of it, but I believe it can turn Britain around,” he will say.

Fighting in Ethiopia intensifies: What’s the latest?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-29
08:19:23 UTC
17:19:23 KST

Fighting in Ethiopia intensifies: What’s the latest?
Ethiopia’s government and allies claim capture of key town that could pave way for federal forces to push towards Tigray’s capital, Mekelle.
Government forces and their allies in Ethiopia say they had taken control of a strategic town in the conflict-hit northern region of Tigray after days of fighting with rebel forces across multiple fronts.
The Tigray Peace Force, an armed group composed of Tigrayan fighters aligned with the federal government, said in a statement on Facebook that they had captured the town of Alamata with the national army.
Recommended Stories
list of 3 items
- list 1 of 3Is Ethiopia on the verge of another civil war as fighting erupts in Tigray?
- list 2 of 3Ethiopia’s Fano fighters claim capture of army vehicles and weapons
- list 3 of 3EU unlocks humanitarian aid for crises worldwide
Fighting has intensified across northern Ethiopia in the past week amid renewed hostilities between the federal government of Prime Minister Abiy Ahmed and the Tigray People’s Liberation Front (TPLF) and its allies, shattering the fragile Pretoria Agreement, a peace deal signed in November 2022.
In the previous fighting from 2020 to 2022, hundreds of thousands of people were killed and millions displaced.
Here is what you need to know about the latest developments:
What is the latest with the fighting?
On Monday, the Tigray Peace Force said its fighters had captured Alamata, a strategic town about 120km (75 miles) south of Tigray’s capital, Mekelle. Video verified by the Reuters news agency showed soldiers walking through Alamata carrying Ethiopian flags.
Two diplomatic sources also told Reuters the town had fallen while a source linked to opposition forces said they were retreating.
The latest fighting erupted last week when Tigrayan rebel forces launched a major offensive, seizing three airports in Tigray and pushing into the neighbouring Afar and Amhara regions. The TPLF says it is fighting a “defensive war”, accusing federal forces of attacks using drones and heavy artillery.
Federal government forces and their allies have since counterattacked.
The headquarters of Tigrai TV, seen as the key outlet for the rebel authorities in Mekelle, was hit by a drone on Sunday.
Where is the fighting taking place?
The fighting has occurred on several fronts across northern Ethiopia, stretching across Tigray, Amhara and Afar.
Alamata is particularly important because it sits near Tigray’s southern border with Amhara and serves as a supply hub for troops, fuel and food. Its capture could allow federal forces to push north towards Mekelle.
A military source told Al Jazeera that government forces had already advanced and were heading towards or surrounding the Tigrayan capital.
Meanwhile, TPLF forces seized Erebti, a strategically important town in the Afar region, over the weekend, according to an Ethiopian commander who spoke to The Associated Press news agency on condition of anonymity.
The Tigray Peace Force also acknowledged that Erebti had fallen to the TPLF but disputed reports that the takeover followed intense fighting, according to AP.
The offensive in Afar could threaten supply routes from Djibouti, through which most Ethiopian imports, including fuel, pass.
The fighting in Afar also comes amid allegations of direct Eritrean involvement. Al Jazeera’s Taha Tawakul, reporting from Afar, said its governor told Al Jazeera that Eritrean forces were participating in the fighting, controlled more than two-thirds of the region and were moving to cut the road linking Djibouti and Eritrea.
“The situation is, therefore, extremely dangerous, and perhaps in the coming hours, the federal government will intervene alongside the Afar regional government,” Tawakul reported.
The Eritrean government has yet to respond to the governor’s allegations.
Fighting has also spread into Amhara, including around North Wollo. The Ethiopian military said about 270 Tigrayan fighters have been killed and more than 200 wounded there.
What is the humanitarian situation on the ground?
The fighting is already taking a devastating humanitarian toll.
Doctors Without Borders, also known by its French acronym MSF, on Monday said there had been a surge in the number of wounded in the north.
The number of patients in the Korem and Alamata hospitals rose from about 180 to more than 420 in 48 hours. MSF said 300 wounded had arrived at Suhul Hospital last week.
Internet and phone networks have also been disrupted in Tigray.
The cofounder of the Afar Pastoralist Development Association, Valerie Browning, told AP that about 150,000 people had been displaced since the latest fighting began.
Who are the actors involved?
At the centre of the conflict are Abiy’s government and the TPLF, which dominated Ethiopian politics for nearly three decades before Abiy came to power in 2018.
War broke out in November 2020 between the TPLF and federal forces.
The two-year conflict took a devastating human toll. Former Nigerian President and African Union mediator Olusegun Obasanjo estimated that 600,000 people were killed although other assessments have given different death tolls.
Days before the latest offensive, the TPLF joined six other armed groups to form the Ethiopian Peoples’ Forces Alliance for Survival, which said it wants to remove Abiy’s government and establish a transitional administration.
The coalition includes the Oromo Liberation Army and the Amhara Fano National Movement, bringing together groups that have previously fought one another.
The conflict also risks drawing in Ethiopia’s neighbours. Ethiopia’s army chief, Field Marshal Berhanu Jula, has accused Eritrea of supporting the opposition and alleged that Sudan and Egypt are also providing backing.
Eritrea and Sudan have denied the allegations. Egypt’s Ministry of Foreign Affairs spokesperson Nader Zaki told Reuters that its policy was based on “full respect for the sovereignty, unity and territorial integrity of states”.
In a post on X, Sudan described the accusations by Ethiopia’s government as “baseless and unfounded”, asserting that they lacked any “foundation or evidence”.

Poland has in recent years detained, charged and in some cases convicted dozens of agents accused of carrying out espionage, sabotage and other so-called “hybrid actions” on behalf of Russia and its ally Belarus.
Many such actions have been carried out not by trained operatives sent to Poland, but by so-called “disposable agents”, often immigrants and refugees from Ukraine and Belarus already in Poland, who are hired through Telegram and paid in cryptocurrency to carry out acts of sabotage and espionage.
A report by the International Centre for Counter-Terrorism published earlier this year found that Poland was the “primary focus” of Russia’s growing campaign of sabotage in Europe.

The Bulgarian National Radio Symphony Orchestra has been named this year’s recipient of the Academician Marin Goleminov National Award, Kyustendil Mayor Ognyan Atanasov announced during a ceremony in the city.
The renowned composer’s granddaughter, Lilia Goleminova, said the award was presented to the BNR Symphony Orchestra for the mark it has left on Bulgarian history by recording Bulgarian music. She added that, for the third consecutive season, every concert by the Symphony Orchestra has featured a Bulgarian work. Goleminova told the audience that there had never been a year with so much debate before the winners were selected in both the main category and the accompanying category, BTA reported.

UK: US government questions bail for Fairford base suspects
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-29
08:17:00 UTC
17:17:00 KST

UK: US government questions bail for Fairford base suspects
September 29, 2026
The US government has described the security alert over the weekend at the RAF Fairford base in southern England as a "very serious situation," thanking UK authorities for their cooperation.
But President Donald Trump and Secretary of State Marco Rubio also both questioned the move to grant the five suspects bail under strict conditions as investigations against them continue.
RAF Fairford is a major military air field fairly close to the south coast of England. It's a rare European base from which the US operates heavy bombers, with the range to reach Iran amid the current conflict in the Gulf.
What did Rubio and Trump say about the case?
Marco Rubio said in an interview with Fox News that while there was much he could not say on air for now, the security scare during which five young men were detained constituted a very serious situation.
"It's one that clearly involves the hand of a foreign actor. I won't get into great detail about that yet," he said, without mentioning Iran until a later point in the interview in a more hypothetical context.
"I think it ties us to the reality here, and that is we are dealing with elements in the world, and in the case of Iran, for example, who have openly threatened to attack American interests globally," Rubio said.
The Iranian Embassy in London, meanwhile, said that it "categorically rejects and strongly condemns the recent unfounded and malicious speculations" of Iranian involvement.
Rubio also echoed President Donald Trump in saying that "a lot of people are disturbed by the news that some of these people have released on bail."
Trump had mentioned the issue in comments to reporters in the White House earlier on Monday.
"I will tell you, I would have said, 'Don't let them have bail.' I'm surprised that they released them. I wouldn't have done that," he said.
What have British investigators said about the case?
Five men in their 20s, all from the London area and with British citizenship, were arrested on Sunday in the vicinity of the air base, which is in a rural area roughly two hours' drive west of the capital. They were wearing face coverings.
Police seized three "suspicious" white vans and evacuated around 85 households in the vicinity, bringing in bomb disposal teams.
Locals were able to return home on Monday, and preliminary reports from the British Press Association and others suggested the materials in the vehicles were not viable explosives, but counterterrorism and explosives experts continued to examine the scene.
The head of UK Counter Terrorism Policing, Assistant Commissioner Laurence Taylor, acknowledged the "significant interest in whether the current geopolitical context has a bearing on this incident," and said investigators were considering "every possible angle."
One of these angles, he said, was the possibility "that this may be actively committed by proxies or individuals either knowingly or unknowingly working on behalf of a foreign state."
Taylor said that the men had been released under stringent conditions, and that granting them bail did not in any way signify an end to investigations against them.
Defense Secretary Wes Streeting said that decisions like granting bail were operational matters for police and prosecutors, not politicians.
Prime Minister Andy Burnham chaired a security meeting known as Cobra, after the secure Cabinet Office Briefing Room A that hosts such sessions, on Monday evening.
What is RAF Fairford?
RAF Fairford is a large military airbase not far north of Swindon in Gloucestershire, west of London.
It's a base for US heavy bombers in Europe and has been used as a launch point for operations involving long-range B-52s in a series of conflicts in recent decades including both Iraq wars, the NATO bombing of the former Yugoslavia, and most recently in a limited capacity in Iran this year.
Residents in the Cotswolds region had noted an increased security presence and activity at the base amid the conflict, as is often observable around such bases during such periods.
Because of the longstanding close military ties — and very often infrastructure set up during World War II when Nazi Germany occupied much of Europe — southern England is home to a string of airbases also used by the US military.

Since March 2022, following Russia’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine, more than one thousand companies have exited the Russian market by selling or transferring management to local managers.

Russia Rejects Black Sea Grain Truce as Ukraine Warns Exports Could Stay Critical for Months
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-29
08:16:26 UTC
17:16:26 KST

Russia has rejected all proposals for a new Black Sea grain deal that would allow Ukraine to resume large-scale agricultural exports by sea.
Russia and Ukraine together account for roughly a quarter of global grain exports, making disruptions in the Black Sea a major concern for global food markets.
JOIN US ON TELEGRAM
Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official.
Countries that have tried to mediate between Kyiv and Moscow informed Ukraine that the Kremlin had rejected the options discussed, Ukraine’s Agriculture Minister Taras Vysotskyi told Bloomberg.
“All possible rounds of negotiations have been tried, but without success,” he said, adding that there are no signs of a Black Sea grain truce being reached in the coming months.
“Unfortunately, it is difficult to imagine any possible solutions to this issue in the coming months,” Vysotskyi said. “We really need to prepare for the situation to remain as critical as it is now.”
Ukrainian agricultural exports have already fallen sharply. Ukraine shipped just 1.13 million tons of wheat, corn, barley, and sunflower oil in August, compared with 2.6 million tons a year earlier, according to Trade Data Monitor.
The figure has only been lower once since Russia launched its full-scale invasion – in April 2022, when Russian naval forces had blocked Ukraine’s Black Sea ports and alternative land routes to Europe were still being established.
A year-long Black Sea grain deal brokered by Turkey and the UN in July 2022 allowed Ukrainian agricultural exports to resume by sea. Russia later withdrew from the agreement.
Russia Plans Record 17.1 Trillion-Ruble Defense Budget as War Costs Deepen Fiscal Strain
Turkey has again been trying to revive an arrangement. During a meeting with Russian President Vladimir Putin in Kyrgyzstan in early September, Turkish President Recep Tayyip Erdogan said the issue needed to be resolved as the damage caused by the disruption continued to grow.
Egyptian President Abdel Fattah el-Sisi has also urged Putin to help stabilize the situation and maintain uninterrupted grain supplies from Russia and Ukraine.
Black Sea flows hit long-term lows
The latest export data show how severely Black Sea trade has deteriorated.
Andrey Sizov, director of agricultural consultancy SovEcon, estimates that Russia exported 1.8 million tons of wheat in September, while Ukraine exported around 900,000 tons.
That puts combined Russian and Ukrainian wheat exports at roughly 2.7 million tons – 60% below last year and the lowest level since the 2010-11 season.
Sizov said grain prices have recently fallen on expectations of progress toward a new deal, even as actual Black Sea flows remain at long-term lows.
The disruption could be difficult for other grain-producing regions to compensate for quickly.
Agriculture generates more than half of Ukraine’s export revenue. Kyiv is increasing shipments through alternative routes, but Vysotskyi said those routes can handle no more than about half of traditional export volumes.
As a result, around 30 million tons of agricultural products are expected to remain unexported from Ukraine this season, he said.
Russia faces its own export disruption
Russia is also struggling with disruptions to its grain exports after Ukrainian forces began targeting Russian ports in the Azov and Black seas in July.
Around 80% of Russia’s grain exports pass through those ports. Ukrainian drone attacks have damaged grain terminals and more than 100 vessels, according to the Russian figures cited in the report.
SovEcon estimates that Russian grain exports fell to a 16-year low in August and September, running at roughly one-third of last year’s level.
The Russian Grain Union estimates that weekly wheat exports have fallen fourfold to around 347,000 tons.
Amid the disruption, Putin has ordered the Russian government to begin purchasing grain from farmers for the state intervention fund, according to Interfax.
Russian Agriculture Minister Oksana Lut said authorities could purchase between 1 million and 3 million tons of grain to support producers.
The federal intervention fund held around 3.7 million tons of grain in August, while the most recent state purchasing auctions were held in the first half of 2024.
The move came after Communist Party leader Gennady Zyuganov warned that without urgent government purchases at a “reasonable” price, Russia’s next planting campaign and harvest could be put at risk.
Russia’s state grain intervention mechanism, introduced in 2001, is designed to support farmers when supplies are excessive by purchasing grain for state reserves and selling it when supplies are tight.

Lithuania and Poland Map Out Emergency Routes as Tensions Mount Near Kaliningrad
Lithuania and Poland are structuring joint contingency plans to evacuate civilians in the event of potential Russian military aggression, as reported by The Telegraph.
Additionally, Lithuania plans to close its borders to civil servants and individuals subject to military mobilization in the event of war with Russia.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
According to reports regarding the country's contingency plans, this measure aims to prevent government officials and draft-eligible citizens from fleeing if military hostilities break out while authorities manage civilian evacuations across the Suwalki Gap.
Preparations focus on the Suwalki Gap, a strategic 100-kilometer stretch of border connecting Lithuania and Poland while separating Belarus from Russia's Kaliningrad enclave.
To test these measures, approximately 20 Polish personnel have joined local exercises alongside roughly 3,000 Lithuanian emergency workers and 1,000 volunteers, according to The Telegraph.
Concerns stem from Western intelligence assessments regarding potential further military escalation by Moscow, leading officials in Vilnius and Warsaw to establish operational frameworks for a wartime scenario.
The Suwalki Gap remains recognized as one of the most exposed areas along NATO’s eastern flank, according to The Telegraph. Bilateral efforts center on coordinating transit corridors, regional infrastructure, and general logistics.
The overarching framework is designed so that emergency movement routes could also accommodate civilian evacuations from Estonia and Latvia if the security situation demands it.
"Vilnius and Warsaw are also working on a bilateral agreement that should become the basis for implementing these plans," said Vilmantas Vitkauskas, head of Lithuania's National Crisis Management Center, according to The Telegraph.
Lithuania has also developed a comprehensive population evacuation plan in the event of a military threat.
As part of those preparations, Poland’s Podlaskie Voivodeship is coordinating arrangements to serve as a transit corridor for residents evacuating from the Baltic states.

China urges the Philippines to stop playing up South China Sea issue in multilateral fora
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-29
16:15:09 CST
17:15:09 KST

UNITED NATIONS, Sept. 29 (Xinhua) -- A Chinese envoy said Monday that the Philippines should stop playing up the South China Sea issue in multilateral fora and should, instead, return to the bilateral track.
In exercising the right of reply at the General Debate of the 81st session of the UN General Assembly, Sun Lei, China's deputy permanent representative to the United Nations, said that with regard to the Philippine statement delivered at the debate on Saturday, China has consistently maintained that the United Nations is not the appropriate forum to discuss the South China Sea issue.
However, he said, China finds it necessary to issue a solemn response to the relevant erroneous claims by the Philippines.
China's position on the so-called "South China Sea arbitration" has been consistent and clear, Sun said. The Philippines' unilateral initiation of arbitration violates fundamental principles of international law, including state consent and pacta sunt servanda, and contravenes the United Nations Convention on the Law of the Sea, he added.
The "arbitral tribunal" exceeded its authority and abused its jurisdiction. The so-called "award" it rendered is illegal, null and void. China neither accepts nor recognizes the "award," and opposes and will never accept any claim or action arising from it, said Sun.
This is both to safeguard China's own territorial and maritime rights and interests and to uphold the international maritime rule of law and a fair and equitable international maritime order, he said.
The Philippine attempt to play up the 10th anniversary of the so-called "award" is utterly meaningless. The fact is that the "award" has not only failed to resolve the maritime issues between China and the Philippines, but has also exacerbated regional tensions, becoming a stumbling block to China-Philippines relations and to peace and stability in the South China Sea, he said.
China does not accept any imposed solution with respect to territorial issues and maritime delimitation disputes, and remains committed to resolving the disputes through negotiation and consultation with countries directly concerned. China will continue to work with members of the Association of Southeast Asian Nations to jointly safeguard peace and stability in the South China Sea, he said.
China urges the Philippines to stop playing up the issue in multilateral fora, return as soon as possible to the right track of bilateral consultations, work with China to manage South China Sea disputes, and work together to safeguard peace and stability in the South China Sea, said Sun. ■

Thousands of drivers strike in the Philippines over rising fuel prices
Transport workers blame US-Israel war on Iran for rising fuel prices as government offers free rides for commuters.
Public transport drivers strike in Manila over soaring fuel prices
Thousands of drivers of informal public transport vehicles have stopped work in the Philippines in protest against rising fuel prices, prompting the government to deploy police officers and buses to help stranded commuters.
The two-day strike, organised by Piston, a transport workers’ union, began on Tuesday.
Recommended Stories
list of 3 items
- list 1 of 3Philippine president declares energy emergency as impact of Iran war felt
- list 2 of 3Photos: Manila’s streets empty as fuel prices surge amid Hormuz crisis
- list 3 of 3Philippine transport strikers say Marcos Jr failing to control oil prices
Protesters want fuel prices cut to 55 pesos ($0.88) a litre, the level before the United States and Israel launched their war against Iran in February. Organisers said that at least 70,000 drivers and operators would take part in the strike.
National police spokesman Allen Rae Co said officials had monitored 11 rallies involving 275 people in Manila and that the strike had not caused a significant disruption in the capital region.
He said 8,643 police personnel were deployed to assist commuters and maintain peace and order.
US-Israel war on Iran
The Department of Transportation said it would provide free rides to passengers on Tuesday.
In the southeastern Bicol region, the authorities sent buses to help affected commuters, the state-run Philippine News Agency reported.
Piston has blamed the US-Israel war on Iran for the rising prices. “Fuel prices will continue to rise as long as the US persists in waging war,” it said in a social media post.
It accused President Ferdinand Marcos Jr’s government and the US of making drivers suffer through the oil crisis.
Another group, Manibela, earlier staged a strike on Monday, demanding relief from rising fuel costs and the removal of the value-added tax and excise tax on fuel.
It suspended the strike on Tuesday to hold a dialogue with the Land Transportation Office. Drivers and operators “can no longer shoulder the burden of the continuous rise in fuel prices”, the group said in a statement.
The Philippines most recently increased fuel prices on August 25. The move was attributed to geopolitical conflicts and hostilities in the Middle East, which have disrupted shipping lanes such as the Strait of Hormuz and reduced global oil supplies.
In March, the country declared a national energy emergency over the price increases, becoming the first in the world to do so.
The Philippines relies heavily on imported oil, which pushes up consumer inflation and transportation and logistics costs, and cuts into the take-home pay of drivers and low-income households.
‘Bleeding communities’
The Land Transportation Franchising and Regulatory Board, which regulates public transport, called the fare increase a reasonable adjustment.
“Rising fuel prices significantly impact not only operators but also the workers who rely on the continuous and stable operation of public utility vehicles for their livelihood,” the agency said in a statement.
Al Jazeera’s Jamila Alindogan, reporting from Manila, said drivers in the city have seen their daily wages drop from $10 per day at the beginning of the year to less than $5 now.
“Many here say the inflation is actually bleeding communities,” she said.
“The prices of goods are also steadily increasing, and it’s a crisis that’s being felt by millions of Filipinos across the country. And although the war in Iran and the events in the Middle East have actually triggered this crisis, many Filipinos say the government can no longer use that excuse for its inability to respond to the major economic needs of millions of Filipinos,” she added.

Swiss Senate gives clear backing to EU treaty package
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-29
08:13:00 UTC
17:13:00 KST

Swiss Senate gives clear backing to EU treaty package
Following a debate lasting several hours, the Swiss Senate has voted in favour of the EU treaty package in principle – by a clear margin of 29 votes to 15. The details of the so-called Bilateral Agreements III can now be discussed.
From 2:38pm on Monday afternoon, the cards were laid on the table in the Senate regarding the EU dossier. As expected, the debate on whether to proceed was long and lively. The speeches from both sides made the implications of the treaties with the EU clear.
At 8:41pm, at the end of the general debate, only the seven-member Swiss People’s Party group as a whole, along with four German-speaking members each from the Centre Party and Radical-Liberal groups, voted against proceeding with the bill. The entire seven-member Social Democratic Party group, the three Greens, the Green Liberals representative, as well as ten members of the Centre Party group and eight members of the Radical-Liberal group voted in favour of the package in principle.
The result came as no surprise. The lines had already been drawn before the parliamentary debate: the right-wing Swiss People’s Party is fundamentally opposed to the entire package. The other parties, as well as the social partners and business organisations, support the bilateral approach in principle, but subject to certain conditions.
More
The Swiss-EU bilateral treaty updates, explained
A long-negotiated compromise
More than half of the members of the Senate took the floor during the over five-hour debate on the motion to proceed. Afterwards, Foreign Minister Ignazio Cassis, Economics Minister Guy Parmelin and Justice Minister Beat Jans delivered their combined one-hour case for the EU treaties.
The government’s package is the result of a long-negotiated compromise between political parties, cantons and social partners, said Senator Carlo Sommaruga from the left-wing Social Democratic Party and chair of the Senates’ Foreign Affairs Committee. Rejecting the treaty package would lead to an erosion of the existing agreements, he said.
Opponents in the Senate warned against voting yes to the treaty package, arguing it would weaken popular rights and place Switzerland under the jurisdiction of the EU. Members of the Swiss People’s Party also criticised the fact that the treaty package with the EU would once again significantly boost immigration into Switzerland.
For years, Switzerland’s largest party has been campaigning against the further development of relations with the EU, referring to it as a “treaty of submission”. However, there are also critics among centrist parties and within the Radical-Liberal Party, as the opening debate in the Senate once again revealed. For the majority, however, the advantages outweighed the disadvantages.
Debate set to continue for hours
The details of the comprehensive proposal are now set to be debated, likely until Wednesday evening. Among the contentious issues are the referendum question, wage protection, and the provisions on immigration, dynamic adoption of EU law, state aid, and education and research.
The package of agreements was negotiated between Bern and Brussels from March to December 2024. It comprises 94 EU legal acts, 18 agreements and protocols, and two joint declarations. The majority of the agreements were signed in Brussels on March 2, 2026, by Parmelin, who holds the rotating Swiss presidency this year, and the President of the European Commission, Ursula von der Leyen.

‘A false problem’: Italy’s Muslims question Meloni’s burqa ban
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-29
08:11:27 UTC
17:11:27 KST

‘A false problem’: Italy’s Muslims question Meloni’s burqa ban
As the prime minister attempts to stave off a far-right challenger, a small minority of Muslims are being targeted.
Milan, Italy – In Milan’s al-Wahid mosque, tucked in a peaceful inner courtyard within the bustling Navigli district, worshippers attending Friday prayers were perplexed by the Italian government’s recent decision to ban the burqa and niqab in schools.
Mulayka Laura Enriello, a 58-year-old high school maths teacher, said that while some schoolgirls wear a headscarf, she had never in her career seen students wear face-covering garments.
Recommended Stories
list of 3 items
- list 1 of 3‘Offer he can’t refuse’: Is Italy’s mafia law breaking crime or families?
- list 2 of 3Italy’s Meloni slams protesters following clashes in Bologna
- list 3 of 3Italy suspends free movement with Spain: Is Schengen in crisis after Ceuta?
“Those girls who want to wear a (hijab) to school do so, no one bothers them, neither teacher nor student,” she told Al Jazeera.
Prime Minister Giorgia Meloni outlined the proposed ban on Sunday during a rally of her nationalist conservative Brothers of Italy (FdI) party, pitching it as a move towards gender equality.
“You must go to school with your face uncovered,” said Meloni. “And in Italy no one, in the name of a real or supposed tradition, can decide that a young woman must hide herself.”
The state-run Ansa news agency has reported that as few as 500 to 600 female students currently wear a full-face covering.
Enriello said the proposal feels inhumane.
“If a girl shows up at school wearing a burqa, I can’t tell her to go home,” she said. “I have to treat her as a minor who probably thinks she is doing something good.”
The mosque’s imam, Yahya Pallavicini, said the ban raised a “false problem”, focusing public attention on a garment used by a small minority and warps the “perception” of Islam.
“This is an attempt to present a unified model of society, a society that is white supremacist and if something is different it is caricatured by the specious use of the burqa,” he told Al Jazeera.
The plan is an example of “intellectual dishonesty” being used to malign a small segment of Muslim society that is less palatable to the Italian public, added Pallavicini, who is also the vice president of the Italian Islamic Religious Community.
Political symbol to critique Islam
Meloni’s party is not alone in framing garments worn by some Muslims as contrary to Western secular values.
Female activists from the French far-right group Collectif Nemesis staged a theatrical protest at the annual rally held by Italy’s populist League party in Pontida last week, in which they removed full-face coverings on stage as the crowd shouted “liberta” (“freedom”).
Renata Pepicelli, professor of Islamic Studies at the University of Pisa, said the stunt was reminiscent of the French colonial authorities in Algeria in 1958, when groups of Algerian women removed and burned their veils – at times under coercion – in a show of alliance with Paris.
The veil is still a “battlefield” and its removal symbolises social predominance, she said.
“The ban that Meloni decided to put forward must be ascribed to this climate,” she told Al Jazeera.
The decree, however, refrains from openly mentioning burqas and niqabs but instead forbids participation at school with a full-face covering and “in any other modality that prevents identification”.
Nico Tonti, a researcher in the department of legal studies at the University of Bologna, said that while the directive has taken effect, Parliament can scrutinise its “proportionality” to its stated objectives and its compatibility with religious freedom rights.
Tonti added that Italian law has so far prohibited wearing items in public that make personal identification difficult, except for a “valid reason”.
“This clause has been at the centre of the debate between religious freedom and public order,” he told Al Jazeera. “Over the years, jurisprudence has progressively recognised religious observance as a valid reason to exclude the conduct from prosecution.”
Challenge from the right
Observers say the timing suggests political calculations behind the ban.
With the campaign for the 2027 elections under way, Meloni faces a challenge from her right as the National Future party of former general Roberto Vannacci gains ground, reaching eight percent in public opinion surveys since its creation in February.
Lorenzo Castellani, professor of History of Political Institutions at LUISS University, said the prime minister is attempting to project a more hardline, nationalist direction.
“Meloni is approving this legislation to give a strong signal to right-wing voters, for whom security and immigration are among the main concerns,” he told Al Jazeera.
Castellani predicted that Meloni would bet on three topics in her electoral campaign – immigration, security and political stability.
“The first two allow her to speak to her electorate without leaving Vannacci to take the lead on identity issues,” the analyst said.
“The third is what makes her proposal different, presenting herself not only as a capable leader who can respond to certain demands, but also as the head of a government that can bring them forward.”
While Italy is famed for political instability, Meloni leads the country’s longest-lasting government since World War II, overtaking Silvio Berlusconi’s record of 1,412 consecutive days in power earlier this month.
Castellani predicted that Meloni would attempt to bank that result in the next elections. “She will try to link immigration and security to [the third] topic: government continuity.”

Russia's agricultural exports to Uzbekistan surge nearly 1.5-fold in January-August

Unknown Publisher

MOSCOW, September 29. /TASS/. Russia increased its agricultural exports to Uzbekistan by 46% in volume and 36% in value terms during the first eight months of 2026, reaching approximately 930,000 tonnes worth $916 million, the Agroexport federal center reported on Tuesday.
"According to expert estimates, Russia supplied Uzbekistan with around 930,000 tonnes of agricultural products valued at $916 million between January and August 2026. Compared to the same period last year, exports grew by 46% in volume and 36% in value," the statement said.
The top five agricultural commodities exported during this period included sugar (293,000 tonnes), soybean cake and meal (211,000 tonnes), wheat (over 71,000 tonnes), non-alcoholic beverages (over 41,000 tonnes), and sunflower oil (over 31,500 tonnes).
Agroexport noted that Russia achieved record-high export figures for the January-August period in both volume and value terms. The growth was primarily driven by shipments of sugar, soybean cake, and meal.
The center added that Russia's annual agricultural exports to Uzbekistan have consistently exceeded $1 billion since 2024.

Is ditching of plans for Antwerp University’s Bioscape research campus a missed opportunity?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-29
08:10:51 UTC
17:10:51 KST

The Bioscape research campus in Edegem, near Antwerp University is not going ahead after all. Planning permission was revoked in August and now investors are pulling out reports daily Gazet van Antwerpen. The university has confirmed the news. “Young researchers will now have to develop their medicines and therapies elsewhere,” the university says. Employers’ organisation Voka Antwerp-Waasland is disappointed hundreds of jobs will be lost.
Is ditching of plans for Antwerp University’s Bioscape research campus a missed opportunity?
Bioscape was to be a large research campus comprising several buildings in Edegem, on land owned by the university. It was intended to provide space for young researchers from the pharmaceutical and biotechnology sectors, close to the university and Antwerp University Hospital.
However, the planning permission process has been dragging on for some time. At the end of August, the planning appeals council revoked the planning permission following complaints from local residents concerned about heavy traffic and parking problems. The council also felt that the impact on traffic had not been adequately assessed.
The fact that the Bioscape research campus will not be built is a missed opportunity for Antwerp University says Johan Wets, sociologist and migration specialist at HIVA, the research institute for Labour and Society at Leuven University. “On the one hand, students will not be able to specialise further; on the other, fewer people from abroad will be attracted to the university,” says Wets.
“Young researchers may now leave Antwerp and perhaps even go abroad” the university claimed following the news that Bioscape will not be going ahead after all.
Here young researchers from the pharmaceutical and biotechnology sectors were to be provided with facilities close to the university and Antwerp University Hospital.
Less interest from abroad
Migration specialist Johan Wets does not wish to speak of a ‘brain drain’. A brain drain refers to the departure of highly educated and talented individuals to other regions or countries to work there. “The project has not been realised, so it is difficult to use that term,” says Wets. “But it is certainly a missed opportunity.”
“Highly qualified people could have developed further in their discipline,” Wets continues. “That opportunity for new specialisations is disappearing. In addition, fewer people will come here from abroad. International researchers could have filled 500 jobs.”
Added value for businesses
“Missed business opportunities, missed employment, missed research and innovation,” says a disappointed Bart Van Meerbergen of Vaccinopolis, a specialised clinical research facility at Antwerp University dedicated to researching infectious diseases and testing new vaccines and treatments. For many years he worked at a company based at Bioscape in Ghent and is a strong advocate a similar project in Edegem, where Vaccinopolis is also based.
At Vaccinopolis, there is extensive collaboration with companies in the pharmaceutical sector. “If those companies were to want to set up in Antwerp, it would have been a major advantage for them to be able to do so at Bioscape, as it is close to Vaccinopolis, Antwerp University and Antwerp University Hospital,” says Van Meerbergen. “Some companies wanted to relocate part of their operations here.”
A dilemma like the one faced by nurses in Kenya
Migration expert Johan Wets compares the situation to that of nurses in Kenya who cannot find work in their own country and therefore move to the United Kingdom. “They do not leave Kenya because there is no need for nurses, but because there are insufficient resources for the medical sector,” explains Wets.
‘So, whilst there may be enough qualified people here to take on a job as a researcher, there are no opportunities for them to do so. In that case, there are two possibilities: they move away, or they look for a job in another sector.’

Lindt to cut prices as chocolate demand weakens in key markets
- Lindt plans to cut chocolate prices starting January due to weak demand and subdued consumer confidence in key European markets like Germany, Switzerland, and Austria.
- The company lowered its 2026 organic sales growth forecast to 0%-2%, causing its shares to drop sharply, reflecting doubts about volume recovery and pricing power.
- Lindt expects positive volume growth in 2027 from easing cocoa costs and increased brand investments, and plans to invest in ice-cream equipment to adapt to hotter summers.
AI generated
ZURICH – Lindt plans to lower prices for its chocolate products after it pared back its sales-growth guidance for a second time in 2026, citing subdued consumer confidence.
The Swiss company is cutting prices for its Christmas offerings and plans to lower them across the board starting from January, chief executive officer Adalbert Lechner said on Sept 29 on a media call.
Lindt earlier revised its full-year 2026 outlook for organic sales growth to a range of 0%-2%, down from 4-6% previously, having already trimmed it in March.
The shares slumped as much as 8% in early trading in Zurich, the biggest intraday decline since the March guidance revision. They were down by more than a quarter in 2026 through the close on Sept 28 due to doubts about a recovery in volumes.
The confectionary maker has been grappling with tepid demand in Germany, Switzerland and Austria, as well as increased price sensitivity among customers. A heat wave also weighed on sales in Europe across the chocolate industry during the summer months.
“A second cut within six months dents Lindt’s reputation for reliable guidance, a key support for its premium valuation,” Vontobel analyst Jean-Philippe Bertschy wrote in a note.
“Pricing power, long Lindt’s trump card, is now being tested.”
Lindt, or Chocoladefabriken Lindt & Spruengli AG, expects “positive volume growth” in 2027 thanks to easing cocoa prices and increased brand investments, Lechner said.
“With our hedging strategy, we did not benefit in a big way from lower cocoa prices this year, but we will see a positive impact next year that allows us to do lower price points,” he told reporters.
Lower prices introduced in August in some of its key markets had already shown “that there is a direct link to volume development”, he added.
Lindt is planning to ramp up investments in ice-cream equipment for its stores and is considering offering cooled products, he said, warning that “we have to prepare for hotter temperatures in any summer”. BLOOMBERG

SDE deputy chair: Government's tax break for the well-to-do root of state budget woes
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-29
08:04:00 UTC
17:04:00 KST

SDE deputy chair: Government's tax break for the well-to-do root of state budget woes
Social Democratic Party Deputy Chair Riina Sikkut said abolishing Estonia's income "tax hump" was the root of the budget's problems, tying the government's hands.
"Because the nearly €800 million cost of abolishing the 'tax hump' (Estonia's progressive basic exemption reduction scheme, which was replaced with a flat €700 exemption for everyone — ed.) and canceling the income tax increase was covered with borrowed money, the government's hands are tied. That was its own decision and unfortunately it means teachers, rescue workers, healthcare workers and specialized care services are paying for the tax cut. Social Democrats consider that deeply unfair," Sikkut told ETV Tuesday morning.
She said the government had tried to keep the deficit within 4 percent through accounting measures, bringing some spending forward into this year and postponing other costs, including construction of Rail Baltica.
"Government members probably felt they had achieved some kind of mathematically optimal result. But looking at it from the outside and from the opposition, no one can praise this budget."
Sikkut said she would not support bargaining over the budget. There is therefore no prospect of the Social Democrats helping the government push it through in exchange for measures they favored.
"Ultimately, this isn't about individual budget lines. If you've started making a Napoleon cake according to a recipe, you can't take cinnamon rolls out of the oven after the Riigikogu has considered it."
Sikkut said her greatest concern was healthcare, particularly specialized care. The Supreme Court has ruled that two-year waits for people with mental disabilities are unacceptable, she said, but the new state budget provides no funding to address the problem and comply with the ruling.
"Because the root of the whole problem — abolishing the 'tax hump' — lies in last year, the opposition cannot change anything now either. We have to say honestly that a solution will come after next March's elections. The hope that a government with a five-month horizon will make farsighted decisions with long-term effects will not be realized."
Sikkut said she was convinced the state budget would be revised after the Riigikogu elections.
She also pointed to the country's growing debt burden, saying the state had no control over rising interest rates.
"A few years ago, interest payments on loans were €20 million to €30 million, which is already a large sum. Now they are €200 million to €300 million and in four years they will exceed €600 million. With €600 million, we could solve the funding problems in healthcare and specialized care, as well as the pay problems facing teachers, police officers and rescue workers. Instead, we will be paying that interest in the future because we have been able to borrow until now."
She noted that the European Central Bank and the U.S. Federal Reserve were already signaling interest rate increases.
"We have no control over that and will simply pay a bigger bill in the future. So experts' advice to bring spending or debt growth under control quickly is not some abstract concern. Eventually, those interest costs will limit what we can do next year and the year after in areas where the problems are acute."
Sikkut said finding the right balance would therefore be a major challenge for the next government. She added that borrowing to cover recurring expenses, such as pensions or salaries, would be a mistake.
"Yes, you can borrow for investments. But we must cover recurring expenses with recurring revenue, whether that comes from state fees, taxes, environmental charges and so on. No other country has found another formula."

The fires caused extensive damage to the two homes while the attack spread panic among residents, the sources told Anadolu.
According to the sources, Israeli forces provided protection to the settlers and sent additional military reinforcements to the area.
Israeli forces also compelled members of the Tubasi family to evacuate their homes again at gunpoint, the sources were quoted as saying.
In a statement, the Israeli military said more than 100 settlers rioted in Jalud overnight, preventing Israeli forces from facilitating the return of a displaced Palestinian family to their home by blocking roads, setting tyres on fire and throwing stones at security forces.
“Soldiers and Israel Border Police forces operated in the area of Jalud to disperse Israeli rioters and protect the residents of the area, as the return of a Palestinian family to their home in the area had been coordinated,” a statement said.
“Due to the violence, the mission to return the family to their home was not completed,” the military added.
Homeowner Mahmoud Tubasi told Anadolu that the family returned under the court order but found extensive destruction caused by settlers who had taken over the property and prevented its owners from accessing it.
The settlers returned during the night and set the house on fire, destroying it and rendering it uninhabitable, he added.
The Tubasi family was forced to leave their homes in Jalud in July after repeated harassment and violence by settlers.
Israeli violence against Palestinians in the West Bank has been steadily growing since the eruption of Israel’s genocidal war on Gaza in October 2023, but the pogroms have intensified significantly this year.
The United Nations Office for the Coordination of Humanitarian Affairs recorded more than 1,330 settler-related attacks on Palestinians in the West Bank from January to late July, averaging six a day and representing the fastest pace in about 20 years.
Settler groups, often supported or protected by Israeli soldiers, have attacked Palestinians in several ways, including shooting them, besieging homes and engaging in other forms of communal violence that experts have described as pogroms.
Israeli settlements built on occupied Palestinian land are illegal under international law.
Israeli raids continue
In a separate attack on Tuesday, Israeli settlers assaulted an elderly Palestinian woman after breaking into her home in Qaryut, south of Nablus, local sources told Anadolu.
A video filmed by volunteer medic Bashar al-Qaryuti showed the woman suffered bruises to her hand and head.
She said a group of settlers broke down the door of the house and assaulted the woman.
In al-Mughayyir, northeast of Ramallah in the central West Bank, Israeli settlers attacked Palestinian homes and property as Israeli army forces raided the village and detained a young man.
The attack targeted three homes while the assailants set fire to another home belonging to a Palestinian detainee, witnesses told Anadolu.
“The frequent and severe violence must be brought to an end,” Julien Lerisson, the head of the International Committee of the Red Cross’s delegation for Israel and the occupied territory, said on Monday about the rising settler activity.
“Authorities have a responsibility to protect the population from violence, including when that violence is inflicted by settlers. What international humanitarian law says on the protection of private and public property and on the population’s access to essential services must be respected,” he said.
In August, US Ambassador to Israel Mike Huckabee described Israeli settlers involved in violence against Palestinians in the occupied West Bank as “terrorists”, warning that such acts cause serious damage to Israel’s image.
In June, 14 UN special rapporteurs warned that the sharp rise in “settler terror” with state support and complicity in occupied Palestinian territory posed an existential threat to Palestinian communities.

HAIKOU /China/, September 26. /TASS/. The city of Sanya on the southern coast of China’s Hainan Island has established mechanisms to help local companies rapidly enter international markets, Hainan Daily reported.

On June 30, it established a dedicated service platform to facilitate and strengthen ties between Hainan-based companies and their overseas partners.

According to the newspaper, an increasing number of companies are seeking to use the institutional advantages of the Hainan Free Trade Port to enter international markets, including through Sanya’s CBD. Statistics show that it registered 32 new projects involving outbound direct investment in January-August, accounting for more than 86% of the city’s total during the period. The amount of registered Chinese investment capital exceeded $167 million. The number of such projects is expected to continue growing rapidly.

More people dying from falls, 21 a day on average: CBS
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-29
08:00:33 UTC
17:00:33 KST

More people dying from falls, 21 a day on average: CBS
See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results
The number of people who died after an accidental fall in the Netherlands rose again last year, to 7,810 – an average of 21 per day – according to new figures from national statistics office CBS.
The figure is 480 more than in 2024, and falls are the most common non-natural cause of death in the Netherlands, CBS said.
The numbers cover people who trip, slip or fall and die within 30 days. Falls involving a vehicle, such as a bike or mobility scooter, are counted as traffic accidents and are not included.
Most victims are elderly: 79% were 80 or older and just 2% were under 60. Women accounted for 60% of deaths among people in their eighties and 72% among the over-90s.
The rise is not only down to the ageing population. Even when adjusted for age and population growth, the death rate from falls has gone up every year for the past 15 years. The CBS reported a similar increase two years ago.
The sharpest rise is among women aged 90 and over. In 2025, 2.1% of all women in that age group died after a fall, compared with 1% in 2016.
More fatal falls happen in winter than in summer – over the past five years, 28% of fatal falls among men and 27% among women took place in winter, compared with 22% and 23% in summer.
Of the 7,330 people who died after a fall in 2024, some 5,000 were receiving long-term care, most of them living in care institutions. Falls caused 7.7% of all deaths in care institutions that year.
The figures were published to coincide with fall prevention week, run by the health ministry and safety organisation VeiligheidNL.

Sunken American frigate will become a reef off Scotland
United Kingdom
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-29
09:00:20 BST
17:00:20 KST

The decommissioned frigate USS Klakring, sunk by British and American forces off the Hebrides this month, will become a natural reef on the seabed, and the environmental approvals were obtained before the exercise took place, the officer who commanded it has said.
Captain Kelechi Ndukwe, commander of Task Force 65 at Naval Station Rota in Spain, was asked at a media roundtable what happens to the wreck and who carries responsibility for it. “For the environmental side, it was all done during the course of the planning. It was approved by the EPA in advance, and it’ll become a natural reef. It’s sunk in a deep, deep valley there, right off the Hebrides,” he said.
The ship went down on 21 September, some 150 nautical miles offshore of the Hebrides range, during an exercise that ran from 14 to 25 September, as we reported. The hull was engaged with the SM-6, the Mark 48 Advanced Capability Torpedo, the Naval Strike Missile and Sea Venom, fired by USS Paul Ignatius, the submarine USS Massachusetts, the Type 23 frigate HMS Portland and aircraft of both air forces.
The choice of an American hull drew attention when the tow was first reported, given that the Royal Navy has been disposing of Type 23 frigates at a steady rate and sending them abroad for scrapping. Asked why a ship had been towed across the Atlantic rather than a British vessel used, Ndukwe described a cost-sharing arrangement agreed between the two governments. “Speaking specifically to towing the ship, that was part of the agreement between the two navies and the departments of defense, was that we would pay for the tow of the ship across, and then the Royal Navy or the UK would pay for the range, so that was planned into the whole exercise,” he said.
Klakring was an Oliver Hazard Perry-class frigate, decommissioned in 2013 and laid up at the Philadelphia Naval Inactive Ship Maintenance Facility until she was towed down the Delaware River on 12 August for the Atlantic crossing, making first for Campbeltown.
Sinking exercises are the standard means of disposing of a hull that has no further sale, museum or training value, and the practice is regulated. Vessels used as targets are stripped of fuel, oils and hazardous materials beforehand under a general permit issued by the United States Environmental Protection Agency, which also sets a minimum water depth and a minimum distance from land for the sinking. Wrecks sunk in this way have in some cases been surveyed years later and found to support marine growth, which is where the natural reef description comes from.
Sensors fitted to the frigate before the exercise recorded the effects of each weapon as it struck, and the captain said that data would be analysed over the coming months alongside battle damage assessment shared between the two navies. He described the North Atlantic weather as having presented obstacles during the serial, while saying that all primary objectives were met and the ship sank without difficulty.
Planning has already started on a further iteration of Atlantic Thunder, which Ndukwe said the two navies aim to run in 2028.

Global investors are turning to China again in search of alternatives to crowded US asset markets, with Pimco seeing Chinese bonds as one of the safest ways to diversify portfolios after sentiment towards the world’s second-largest economy “flipped 180 degrees”.
The US-based asset manager, which oversaw more than US$2 trillion in assets by the end of June, had been pointing its clients, particularly those outside the United States, towards Chinese offshore bonds, according to its president, Christian Stracke, because it was one way to reduce concentrations in US dollar and equity assets after years of strong gains in the American market.

“It’s not always that people are worried about the US. It’s just that their portfolios, because the US has done so well, have become very exposed to the US dollar, to the US equities market.”

A sequel at Sycamore Gap: Felled ‘Robin Hood’ tree sprouts new hope
