A sequel at Sycamore Gap: Felled ‘Robin Hood’ tree sprouts new hope
- The iconic Sycamore Gap tree, felled by vandals in 2023, is sprouting new growth nearly 1m tall, giving hope for its recovery.
- The National Trust has taken special measures like reducing soil compaction and limiting human disturbance to help the tree regrow.
- The vandals were sentenced to over four years in prison for damaging the tree and the adjacent 2,000-year-old Hadrian's Wall.
AI generated
An iconic tree beside an ancient Roman wall with a supporting role in a Hollywood blockbuster is showing signs of life, three years after two attention-seeking pranksters reduced it to a stump.
A thick ring of new shoots nearly 1m tall has been seen around the Sycamore Gap tree, which found global fame when it was featured in the 1991 film Robin Hood: Prince Of Thieves, starring Kevin Costner.
The tree, in Northumberland, England, was cut down by Daniel Graham and Adam Carruthers on Sept 28, 2023.
This act of malicious mischief sparked outrage from many fans of the tree, which is believed to be at least 120 years old when it was felled.
Britain’s National Trust, which owns the site, fenced the stump off, hoping it might grow back.
Now, Andrew Poad, general manager for the charity, which owns the site, said the growth has left him “filled with hope”.
“These flourishing shoots are really encouraging and show that the special measures we’ve taken, including reducing soil compaction around the roots and limiting human disturbance, are paying off,” he told British newspaper Metro.
“We’re grateful to all the visitors who, through the care they are taking, are supporting our efforts to protect the tree and give it the best possible chance to thrive,” Poad added.
Planted in the late 1800s at the centre of a dramatic dip beside Hadrian’s Wall, the Sycamore Gap tree became a favourite subject and destination for photographers, artists and sightseers.
In the late hours between Sept 27 and Sept 28, 2023, Graham and Carruthers drove to the tree and cut it down with a chainsaw before taking a section of it back to Carlisle, a city in northern England, according to court records.
As public grief and anger spread the following day, the pair exchanged messages revelling in the reaction, according to prosecutors.
The fallen tree also damaged Hadrian’s Wall, built by the Romans nearly 2,000 years ago to mark the northernmost edge of their empire.
Prosecutor Richard Wright said during the trial that Graham and Carruthers had been on a “moronic mission” to commit “mindless vandalism”.
Graham, a groundworker from near Carlisle, and Carruthers, a mechanic from Wigton, never explained their motive and sought to blame each other during their trial.
The two men, who were 39 and 32 at the time, were sentenced in July 2025 to four years and three months in prison for criminal damage to the tree and wall.

UN: 8.3 mln refugees at risk due to ‘severe’ funding cuts
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-29
07:58:33 UTC
16:58:33 KST

Displaced Sudanese children who have returned from Ethiopia gather amid tents fortified against heavy rain by sandbags, in a camp run by the United Nations Refugee Agency (UNHCR) in Sudan's border town of Gallabat on September 4, 2024. (AFP File Photo)
Nearly 8.3 million refugees and other forcibly displaced people face losing vital assistance from UNHCR, the U.N.’s refugee agency warned on Sept. 29, as protection services crumble due to “severe” funding cuts.
“UNHCR’s ability to protect and assist refugees, internally displaced people (IDPs) and stateless people is being eroded by a sustained and worsening funding shortfall,” the agency said in a report detailing the human cost of budget cuts.
The agency said its available funding had fallen from $5.2 billion in 2024 to $3.9 billion in 2025, while the number of people it is mandated to protect is hovering around historically high levels.
UNHCR said it needed $8.5 billion this year to protect refugees, but by the end of July had received only 32 percent of that amount ($2.7 billion).
This means nearly 8.3 million forcibly displaced people are “at risk of losing access to UNHCR assistance,” the agency said.
“Continued severe funding cuts are pushing refugee support and protection structures towards breaking point in the world’s main displacement situations,” it added.
UNHCR said it had undertaken reforms and prioritization measures to protect its most critical work, but said the scale and persistence of the shortfall meant that even its highest-priority work was now being affected.
“Protection cannot be reduced indefinitely without systems collapsing,” said Dominique Hyde, UNHCR’s external relations chief.
“Below a certain threshold, services do not simply reach fewer people; they can stop functioning altogether, leaving those most at risk without the protection they need.”
The agency said that in Chad, 319,000 refugees faced registration delays, leaving them without the documentation to access services, while around 233,000 children could lose child protection services.
In Ethiopia, child protection coverage in some areas has diminished by up to 85 percent.
And in Sudan, tens of thousands of survivors of sexual violence and children at serious risk could lose access to critical protection services, the agency warned.
When registration stops or child protection services disappear, “the very risks that people fled, violence, exploitation and abuse, reappear in displacement,” warned Hyde.
Some 117.8 million people worldwide were forcibly displaced from their homes at the end of 2025, according to UNHCR, down from 2024’s record 123.2 million.
Of those 117.8 million, 35.6 million were refugees under UNHCR’s mandate, with two-thirds coming from Venezuela, Ukraine, Syria, Afghanistan and Sudan.
UNHCR shed nearly 5,000 jobs in 2025, more than a quarter of its workforce. The United States, traditionally the world’s top donor, has heavily slashed foreign aid, while other major donors have been tightening their belts.
The Geneva-based agency said funding cuts were undermining its efforts to help people move away from reliance on aid.
In Iraq, up to 350,000 refugees and asylum seekers risk losing access to economic inclusion opportunities, it said.

====================================================================================================

New pharaohs: How Egypt combines high tourism numbers with the world’s largest population of political prisoners
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-29
07:56:36 UTC
16:56:36 KST

The Arab Republic of Egypt is expected to set two new world records by the end of 2026: for the number of tourists it attracts and for the number of political prisoners it locks up. Until recently, Egypt had trailed Syria in the latter ranking; however, after the fall of the Assad regime and the release of tens of thousands of Syrian prisoners of conscience, the Egyptians seized the lead, surpassing even the misanthropic regimes of Myanmar and Iran. Meanwhile, most foreigners visiting the Pyramids or spending a few days at an Egyptian resort never stay long enough to notice that the regime in Cairo rules by repression, fear, propaganda, and the personality cult of usurper president Abdel Fattah el-Sisi.
In the winter of 2011, amidst the Arab Spring protests, the streets of Cairo were patrolled not only by the army and police but also by Bedouins from neighboring Giza. On Feb. 2 of that year, armed with sharpened sticks, stones, and rebar, they staged a bloody attack on the protest camp. Eleven people were killed and several hundred wounded.
Later, the attackers explained to journalists that because of the revolution, tourists had almost stopped coming to the Egyptian capital. As a result, the Bedouins, who made their living giving tourists camel and mule rides along the roads of the world’s most famous necropolis, were left without income and could no longer support their families or feed their animals. The Bedouins hoped that breaking up the protest on Tahrir Square would calm things down and bring tourists back to the pyramids at Giza.
“Virginity tests” for protesters
At around the same time, the military was setting up torture chambers and special “medical rooms” in the famous Egyptian Museum — just a few hundred meters from the main revolutionary camp on Tahrir Square. At the Museum, intelligence officers carried out so-called “virginity tests” — sexualized violence against female protesters, who were forced to undergo gynecological examinations in public.
State propaganda at the time claimed that the women taking part in the revolution were all, without exception, prostitutes, and that the “virginity tests” were meant to prove this. But the public did not believe the state-sponsored stories, so the authorities tried to walk it back — claimed the tests were carried out solely to confirm that the detainees had not been subjected to sexual violence by soldiers or police, arguing that the revolutionaries were making baseless accusations of rape against security forces and that it was necessary to prove those accusations false.
The job of saying so publicly went to one of the generals leading the crackdown on the protests: Abdel Fattah el-Sisi. This was the first time many Western journalists heard his name.
According to one theory, it was el-Sisi himself who allowed the armed Bedouins onto Tahrir Square, since at the time he headed the country’s branch of military intelligence, which was responsible for carrying out acts of sabotage and provocation, among other things. However, it has never been definitively proven that el-Sisi personally issued the order.
What is not disputed is the fact that, in 2011, the general failed to live up to the expectations that then-President Hosni Mubarak had placed on him — he was unable to crush the revolution, which toppled the regime and led to Egypt’s first-ever democratic presidential election. But Mohamed Morsi, the Muslim Brotherhood Islamist who won that vote, saw a kindred spirit in the relatively young (he was 56 in 2011) and conspicuously devout general. It was Morsi who appointed el-Sisi as commander-in-chief of the armed forces.
Just two years later, in 2013, el-Sisi would “repay” Morsi for that trust by overthrowing him and sending him to prison for life. The list of charges against Morsi was seemingly endless, but at the top of it was treason. Egypt’s first — and, so far, only — democratically elected president died behind bars in 2019.
El-Sisi, who took Morsi’s seat soon after his overthrow, presented himself as the savior of the nation. According to the military command’s version of events, he had saved Egypt from Islamist terrorists who had propelled their own man, Morsi, into power. Ever since, Abdel Fattah el-Sisi has ruled the country through propaganda about “revolutionary prostitutes,” mockery of the opposition, and outright violence.
Brother against “Brother”
On Aug. 14, 2026, the World Coalition of Egyptians Abroad published an appeal to the authorities in Cairo calling for the release of political prisoners and an investigation into the circumstances under which thousands of people had been jailed for their personal views. The appeal was backed by the Association of Families of Egyptian Political Prisoners and by the International Association of Families of Political Prisoners, which was founded in London that very week.
The date was not chosen at random. It was on Aug. 14, 2013, that Mohamed Morsi’s rule in the country came to an end. That July, Morsi and his entourage were taken into custody by soldiers under el-Sisi’s command. State television ran round-the-clock footage of the arrests of the country’s top officials and their supporters, captioned: “Egypt is fighting terrorism.” The deposed president was declared an agent of Hamas and Hezbollah, and his followers were branded accomplices of terrorists. Those followers had set up a protest camp on Rabaa Square, demanding the president’s release.
On Aug. 14, the military destroyed the camp with extraordinary brutality. At dawn, soldiers opened fire with automatic weapons against the sleeping camp residents. Armored vehicles and bulldozers were then sent in to raze the protesters’ tent city. At least 817 people died that day (Egyptian authorities themselves acknowledged 638 deaths). Thousands ended up behind bars. They were later joined by tens of thousands more, detained in raids on opposition party headquarters, in apartments, and in mosques.
Most of those arrested 13 years ago remain behind bars, many still awaiting trial. The Morsi supporters rounded up in the summer and fall of 2013 are the demographic that makes Egypt the world leader in political prisoners.
The Morsi supporters rounded up in 2013 made Egypt the world leader in political prisoners
Still, new prisoners are constantly being added as Egyptian authorities wage a genuine war on those they deem to be religious extremists (above all, followers of the Muslim Brotherhood movement, which Morsi himself came from). Every year, hundreds more people are put behind bars, often on unfounded charges of terrorism or espionage. According to human rights organizations, Egypt holds between 50,000 and 70,000 political prisoners.
For years, Egypt was second on the list of countries with the largest numbers of political prisoners — behind only Bashar al-Assad’s Syria, which had sent more than 130,000 people to prison on political grounds. However, after Assad’s overthrow in 2024, the new authorities in Damascus emptied entire prison complexes, granting Egypt the lead in this shameful contest.
Incidentally, Egypt also has prison compounds built specifically for political prisoners. The most notorious is Scorpion Prison, which holds 2,000 people and was specifically designed so that sunlight never reaches the cells. But deprivation of vitamin D is just one — and probably the most innocuous — form of torture faced by its inmates.
Human rights reports state that Egypt’s political prison complexes are overcrowded and lack adequate medical care. Poor food, non-functioning ventilation, and prison staff brutality often lead to mass hunger strikes and suicide attempts. Among those who have tried to take their own lives because of abuse suffered in confinement was Mohamed Morsi’s nephew, arrested in 2022 without any justification.
Not all political prisoners in the country are Islamists. The prisons also hold members of democratic movements who actively opposed Mohamed Morsi and staged mass protests against the unconstitutional actions of Egypt’s first popularly elected president. In 2013, they demanded that Morsi abandon his attempts to appropriate parliamentary powers for himself.
Paradoxically, it was the actions of democratic groups like the April 6 Youth Movement that gave el-Sisi a pretext to arrest Morsi and take his place. As a result, in 2013–2014 many of these democrats ended up behind bars, charged with participating in the activities of banned parties and movements. Thousands of detainees remain in prison to this day.
Man of the hour
It was also in 2013–2014 that it became clear el-Sisi was preparing for a long personalist rule. The new authorities set about building the aforementioned prison complexes (officially called “correction and rehabilitation centers”), which were clearly intended for political opponents. Sure enough, dissidents began to be arrested en masse based on even the slightest suspicion of disloyalty.
Then a campaign was launched to transform the little-known figure of el-Sisi into Egypt’s leading man — an irreplaceable, wise ruler without whom the country would be doomed to collapse. The construction of the general’s personality cult began before his presidency — even before he announced his intention to run for the top office. Just days after the Rabaa massacre, the streets of Cairo and other cities were decorated with giant portraits of el-Sisi bearing captions like “Conqueror of terrorism” or even “Lion of the nation.” Street vendors — whether picking up on the trend or acting on direct orders from the military — pulled T-shirts and other souvenirs commemorating the 2011 revolution from their stalls. New merchandise soon appeared in its place — this time bearing the portrait of the “savior general.”
The biggest musical hit in the summer of 2013 was a song by pop artist (and head of the musicians’ union) Mostafa Kamel, glorifying the heroism of the army and el-Sisi personally. The general is never named in the song — instead, it features an anonymous “hero” who “will sacrifice everything for the homeland.” Still, to make sure everyone understood exactly who was being described, the music video for the song cuts to el-Sisi every few seconds. As of today, 13 years after its release, the video has 38 million views.
In state and semi-state media, el-Sisi was called “blessed” and “long-awaited.” His looks were compared to the pharaohs of antiquity — his strength to Greek gods and heroes. Within a matter of weeks, a petition calling on el-Sisi to run for president gathered millions of signatures.
Over the years since Mohamed Morsi’s overthrow, his successor’s personality cult has evolved further. The Sisi-mania of 2013–2014, which at times took on comical forms, is now tightly controlled. Stories about saving the homeland and heroic battles against terrorists have given way to reports that presidential oversight is doing wonders for the economy, that from the very start of his rule el-Sisi has shown a “modern vision of statehood,” and that he governs Egypt skillfully and confidently, with the full approval of all Egyptians.
In state propaganda, the president remains, as ever, Egypt’s sole hope and mainstay. However, today, el-Sisi is portrayed less like a military superman and more like a merely visionary official. After all, the state no longer dares to irritate people with fairy-tale stories about an all-powerful el-Sisi at a time when Egypt is going through one of the most severe economic crises in its modern history.
Old friends, new enemies
El-Sisi has tried-and-tested methods for dealing with those unhappy with his presidency: torture, blackmail, intimidation. He has used this arsenal even against people who considered themselves the president’s associates and allies.
In 2018, a military tribunal sent Egypt’s former chief of staff Sami Anan to prison for announcing his readiness to run against el-Sisi, who was then seeking a second term. Anan spent nearly two years behind bars on charges of violating military statutes, and since his release has led a quiet life, making no attempt to return to politics.
Another prominent military figure, Air Marshal Ahmed Shafik, made it to the second round of the country’s first-ever democratic election in 2012, losing to Morsi by just a few percentage points. In 2018, Shafik withdrew his candidacy after Morsi’s people showed him documents allegedly proving his involvement in Mubarak-era corruption schemes. The compromising material also included several intimate videos of the marshal, filmed by hidden cameras installed in his bedroom.
However, these methods have not helped shore up el-Sisi’s popularity — a fact that presents a major challenge for the general-president. In 2023, on the eve of el-Sisi’s reelection to a third term, protests swept across Egypt, with participants demanding the president’s resignation and even burning posters bearing his photo. People were driven to protest by inflation, unemployment, and the authorities’ indifference to the fate of their neighbors in the Gaza Strip, who had become hostages of the war between Israel and Hamas.
People were driven to protest by inflation, unemployment, and the authorities’ indifference to the fate of fellow believers in the Gaza Strip
In the past three years, these problems have only gotten worse, and people blame the person who holds the most power in the country — the president — for the catastrophic rise in prices, for the state’s default on its social obligations, and for its foreign-policy failures. In this context, el-Sisi is changing both his propaganda narratives and his strategy for political survival. No longer a president backed by mass popular support, he now leads a clique of people strong and influential enough to keep the army and security services, if not the public, under his control.
The people in uniform have become the regime’s true mainstay. El-Sisi has not merely preserved the economic system formed under Mubarak, in which the military plays a key role across a whole range of sectors — construction, banking, telecommunications, and insurance among them. He has literally turned officers into the country’s economic elite. Companies run by military officers get priority in the allocation of state contracts. They have access to preferential loans. And state auditors give them the benefit of the doubt. In addition, an abundance of free labor — conscript soldiers — makes officers’ construction firms far more profitable than those that actually have to pay wages to their workers.
On top of that, under el-Sisi officers have gained effective immunity from prosecution, pensions far higher than those for civilians, and priority access to senior government posts after leaving the service.
City of dreams
El-Sisi and his inner circle understand that if a new popular revolution were to break out — one resembling the uprising that toppled Mubarak in 2011 — they would not stand a chance against it. Western analysts put the probability of mass protests breaking out in Egypt before the end of this year at 15–20%, and even in the more-than-likely event the regime makes it to January, nothing suggests public discontent will subside anytime soon — not with the currency devaluing at a near-record pace and modest economic growth failing to lift living standards or wages.
The situation has not yet ripened into an open revolt, but much could change in the easily foreseeable future. Through manipulation of the constitution, el-Sisi has not only secured the ability to run for president an unlimited number of times, but has also extended the length of a presidential term from four to six years. The next election is due to take place in Egypt in 2030, and by then el-Sisi is supposed to move — along with his government, parliament, and security agency — to an entirely new city currently being built in the desert 45 kilometers from Cairo.
This city is still unnamed — in official documents it is called the New Administrative Capital. Officially, it is being built to relieve overcrowded Cairo and free the city of smog and endless traffic jams. But the new capital has several features that indirectly underscore the authorities’ fear of a new revolution.
For one, the city under construction has no separate neighborhoods planned for the middle class or workers (the main actors of the 2011 revolution). It has no narrow streets (only wide avenues that cannot be barricaded). Every square and plaza is designed so that any crowd gathering there could be dispersed with machine-gun fire from the roofs of nearby buildings (which are all linked by underground passages). And on top of all that, the new capital has no public transit links to Cairo or other cities.
The new nameless city will have no narrow streets — only wide avenues that cannot be barricaded
In other words, Egypt is building a new “Tahrir-proof” capital — in part with money from foreign tourists. That same money also goes toward building prisons for political prisoners, funding propaganda, and paying the salaries of security officers who blackmail and intimidate dissidents.
One could say that Egypt’s two records — for tourists and for political prisoners — are interconnected. The more people come to Egypt, and the more money they spend, the bigger the budgets available to the military and security services that guard Abdel Fattah el-Sisi’s regime.

OpenAI apologizes to Australia over unauthorized AI access to government websites
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-29
07:56:28 UTC
16:56:28 KST

Rabia Ali
29 September 2026•Update: 29 September 2026
OpenAI apologized to Australia on Tuesday after revealing that its artificial intelligence models accessed government websites without authorization during internal training and evaluation.
“In June, during internal training and evaluation our models accessed Australian government websites in ways they were not authorised to,” the company said.
“We also should have handled our response better. We are sorry and working to do better in the future.”
The company said it identified the activity in mid-August while reviewing earlier training and evaluation work following a separate incident involving AI research platform Hugging Face.
The apology came five days after Australian Prime Minister Anthony Albanese disclosed the Medicare portal incident in New York on the sidelines of the UN General Assembly.
Albanese said Sept. 24 that an OpenAI agent had gained unauthorized access to Services Australia’s Medicare Statistics Reporting Service.
The agent accessed public and non-public files, prompting a forensic investigation with assistance from the Australian Signals Directorate.
Australian officials said the portal contains aggregate Medicare statistics and is separate from systems handling individual Medicare claims and personal information.
OpenAI said its review identified activity involving four Australian government organizations: Services Australia, the NSW Bureau of Crime Statistics and Research, the Victorian Department of Health and the Australian Institute of Health and Welfare.
At Services Australia, an experimental internal model had been assigned a research task concerning government spending per person on medicines for skin conditions in Victorian communities.
OpenAI said the model encountered difficulties obtaining the information and then took unauthorized actions that allowed it to access material beyond what was publicly available.
The company said the model examined technical information and source code and accessed internal files, credentials and aggregate statistics.
However, OpenAI said its review found no evidence that individual patient or client records were accessed.
“We did not intend for this activity to occur, and the access to the service and follow-on activity should not have happened,” it said.
OpenAI said its models also accessed systems operated by the other three agencies but did not access individual crime records, medical records or identifiable survey responses.
The company said it has strengthened safeguards, including additional network restrictions and monitoring.
It also pledged technical support for affected agencies and assistance in strengthening Australia’s cyber defenses.
OpenAI said it will establish an Australian task force with independent experts to develop recommendations on AI-related cybersecurity and improve coordination between AI developers and governments.
Chief Strategy Officer Jason Kwon is scheduled to appear before Australia’s Joint Select Committee on Artificial Intelligence in Sydney on Oct. 6.

Delhi HC quashes FSSAI order directing Red Bull to drop 'energy drink' label
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-29
07:56:16 UTC
16:56:16 KST

The court set said the decision was taken “without affording any opportunity” to the company to present its views.
NEW DELHI: Delhi high court on Tuesday quashed an order issued by the Food Safety and Standards Authority of India (FSSAI) directing Austrian beverage maker Red Bull to stop using the “energy drink” descriptor on its cans.The court set aside the June 30, 2026 order, saying that the regulator had taken the decision “without affording any opportunity” to the company to present its views.The order came after Red Bull challenged the FSSAI directive, which required the company to remove the “energy drink” descriptor from its range of caffeinated beverages.Red Bull had approached the Delhi HC on Monday, challenging the FSSAI order issued by an Assistant Director on June 30. The company said it had been selling its products in India since 2002 using the “energy drink” descriptor.During Monday's hearing, Justice Amit Mahajan sought clarity from FSSAI on whether Red Bull had been issued a show-cause notice and given an opportunity to explain its position before the order was passed.The court also questioned the need for immediate action without first hearing the company and asked FSSAI to take instructions on the matter.
No interim protection was granted to Red Bull during Monday’s proceedings.Red Bull also challenged a July 17 communication issued by FSSAI to food safety authorities across states and Union Territories, directing them to take action against allegedly non-compliant products.According to the company’s petition, the June 30 direction was issued without prior notice or an opportunity of hearing. Red Bull further claimed that the July communication led to enforcement action, including the seizure of its products at various locations across the country.The company has questioned the basis for the change in FSSAI’s position, citing a March 2024 advisory which, according to its petition, had clarified that the expression “energy drink” could be used for products falling under the relevant food categories applicable to caffeinated beverages.
Earlier in June, India directed makers of high-caffeine beverages sold as “energy drinks” to stop using the description, rejecting efforts to stall the move in a market expected to be worth $1.6 billion by 2028, Reuters reported.Red Bull’s India unit had said the “abrupt prohibition” of the label, without any change to the underlying product standard, “introduces substantial regulatory uncertainty and adversely affects” its existing and planned commercial investments.Energy drinks have faced scrutiny from regulators in several countries over concerns about their high caffeine, sugar and taurine content. England is also set to ban the sale of energy drinks to children under 16 from April next year.

UK Government confirms free entry to national museums will continue
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-29
07:54:25 UTC
16:54:25 KST

The UK government says national museums will remain free for all, ending months of speculation that international visitors could be charged to enter institutions.
UK Culture Secretary Lisa Nandy has confirmed the UK’s national museums will remain free and open for all.
Nandy confirmed universal free entry would be maintained for the 15 institutions sponsored directly by the Department for Digital, Culture, Media and Sport (DCMS) - institutions like the Tate, the National Portrait Gallery, National Museums Liverpool and the British Museum – which currently displays the Bayeux Tapestry.
“Our museums are the places that light up the world,” Nandy said. “They remind of us our shared history and enable us to step outside the confines of our lives. There is something incredibly special about that. That’s why they must be free, forever, for everyone to access. I’m delighted that we’re continuing that transformative policy pioneered by the last Labour government, opening up access to our excellent museums for generations.”
The policy of universal free entry came into effect on 1 December 2001 in the UK and will celebrate its 25th anniversary later this year.
Nandy’s confirmation at an event hosted by Art Fund and The Cultural Policy Unit at Tate Liverpool during yesterday’s Labour conference follows increased debate about whether national museums should introduce entry fees for international visitors.
Mayor of London Lord Sadiq Khan had opposed government plans to consider charging international visitors, saying that free museums and galleries were a "fundamental" part of London life.
Following Nandy’s announcement, Director of the Cultural Policy Unit Alison Cole hailed free entry “one of the landmark cultural policies of our time”, saying: “It is wonderful that the Government has recognised not only its economic merits, but also its power to express our values and shape how we engage with the world.”
Gabriele Finaldi, the director of London’s National Gallery, said: “Free entry to national museums is one of the UK’s greatest cultural assets: it enables millions to visit, enjoy and learn. Thanks to free entry our museums are a deeply integral part of national life and free entry to museums is widely admired among our museum peers internationally.”
Research shows visitors to the 15 national museums in the UK have risen by 96 per cent since the policy of universal free entry came into effect in 2001 - from nearly 22.8 million in 1999 to just under 44.7 million in 2025/26.
Conversely, any adult visitor from outside the European Union, Iceland, Liechtenstein and Norway now has to pay €32 to enter the Louvre. The price hike – which represents a 45% increase – came into effect in January and has sparked debate about “dual pricing”.
The Louvre said the new rate will help fund investments under its “Louvre – New Renaissance” modernisation project and could bring in an additional €15 to €20 million a year.
Elsewhere in France, the Palace of Versailles, the Paris National Opera and the Château de Chambord in the Loire area have also upped their prices for non-European visitors.
French researcher Patrick Poncet previously drew a parallel between the French decision and Donald Trump’s “America First” policy, under which his administration raised the entry fee for foreign tourists in US national parks by $100, effective 1 January 2026.
The French policy is “symptomatic of the return, as elsewhere in the world, of unbridled nationalism”, Poncet wrote in the newspaper Le Monde.

Germany news: Merz revolts over EU budget, report says

Germany news: Merz revolts over EU budget, report says
Published September 29, 2026last updated September 29, 2026

Germany warns Slovakia against doubting NATO defense
German Foreign Minister Johann Wadephul has indirectly criticized Slovakia's stance on Russia's war in Ukraine, warning that doubts about NATO deterrence could endanger the entire alliance.
"The greatest threat to freedom on our continent comes from Moscow. The greatest danger to Europe is Putin's belligerent imperialism," Wadephul said during talks with Slovak Foreign Minister Juraj Blanar in Bratislava.
"Questioning these facts is not only lacking in solidarity, it would be irresponsible," he added. Wadephul said countries that doubted NATO's deterrence created risks for themselves and weakened security guarantees for all allies.
Slovakia's left-nationalist Prime Minister Robert Fico has increasingly accused Western countries of escalating tensions with Moscow and questioned the policies of both NATO and the European Union.
Fico recently said he would prefer Slovakia to be neutral and expressed doubt that NATO allies would send troops to defend the country in an emergency. However, he acknowledged that Slovakia remained bound by its NATO membership.
Merz calls teachers Germany's most important profession
German Chancellor Friedrich Merz has praised teachers as "the most important professional group in our country" at the German School Award ceremony in Berlin.
"I speak as a father and grandfather: We entrust you with the most valuable thing we have. Our children," Merz said.
Against the backdrop of Germany's weak results in the PISA international education assessment, Merz said ensuring that young people receive a good education was "one of the most important, if not the most important, tasks facing our society."
The chancellor admitted that he "rarely felt like" going to school as a child but said the ceremony had encouraged him to visit schools more frequently.
The €100,000 ($114,000) top prize went to the Bertha von Suttner Comprehensive School in the central state of Hesse, for its data-driven teaching model and personal support for pupils.
The jury said dedicated departments at the school evaluate data and use the findings to improve lessons. Students also have designated staff members who serve as permanent points of contact.
Only 15% of pupils arrive with a recommendation to attend a gymnasium, Germany's academically oriented secondary school. However, two-thirds later obtain the Abitur qualification needed to enter university, according to the jury.
Ukrainian defense minister cancels trip to Germany amid intensifying Russian strikes
Ukrainian defense minister has canceled his trip to Germany on Tuesday as Russia hammers the country withround-the-clock drone attacks to wear down its capital and the economy.
Yevgeniy Khmara was scheduled to meet his German counterpart Boris Pistorius at a time when Ukraine has been pushing for allies to step up military and financial aid ahead of winter.
At least nine people were killed across the country on Monday when Moscow's forces pounded apartment buildings, offices as well as a building of the National Academy of Sciences of Ukraine in downtown Kyiv.
The AFP news agency cited an unnamed source telling it that Khmara had canceled trips to both Germany and Norway "due to the situation in Ukraine and intensification of Russian attacks, which requires rapid attention."
Patricia Schlesinger: Ex-RBB director's trial date set for November 10
The former director of Berlin-based broadcaster RBB (Rundfunk Berlin-Brandenburg) is to stand trial in connection with allegations of financial mismanagement and misuse of company resources that emerged when she was heading the channel in 2022.
The public prosecutor's office filed criminal charges against Patricia Schlesinger and three others last year in December.
The Berlin regional court on Tuesday accepted that indictment, meaning that it believes the case has enough weight to move to trial.
The trial, which is scheduled to begin on November 10, is set to see 56 hearing days because the trial is likely going to be a complex one.
The case is a very high-profile one because it involves someone who was at the helm of Germany's public broadcasting system as Schlesinger was also the director of ARD, the powerful association of the country's nine regional stations.
Schlesinger has denied all allegations. "Ms. Schlesinger based all her decisions as director solely on the interests of RBB. We will fully refute the accusations," her lawyer Oliver Sahan told German press agency DPA.
The trial ends at the end of June 2027, a spokesperson for the Berlin court told reporters.
Germany intends to block sale of Hamburg logistics firm to China's Cosco
The German government intends to block the sale of logistics firm Zippel to Chinese state-owned group Cosco over security risks, the Handelsblatt newspaper reported.
The newspaper cited a restricted government memo that mentioned security and strategic risks that could come with the planned deal.
Cosco, which is one of the world's largest container shipping companies, last year announced that it would like to acquire an 80% stake in Zippel. It already has a minority stake in Hamburg's port terminal.
Zippel, a traditional German company based in Hamburg, the country's largest port city, arranges transportation of freight and cargo.
A number of ministries have been in favor of blocking the deal.
A final decision has yet to be made.
CDU struggles: A trip to Sardinia and a beach chair at the chancellery
The center-right Christian Democratic Union (CDU) led by Chancellor Friedrich Merz's party has seen better days: Most recently, it suffered unprecedented defeats in state elections in Saxony-Anhalt, Mecklenburg-Western Pomerania, and Berlin. At this time of voter disenchantment, two prominent CDU politicians have come under fire on social media: Jens Spahn and Philipp Amthor have been facing accusation of being out of touch and self-absorbed.
A few weeks ago, Spahn resigned from his powerful position as parliamentary group leader of the CDU and CSU bloc in the Bundestag after Spahn had announced that had become a parent with the help of a surrogate mother in the United States. He was accused of hypocrisy because surrogacy is banned in Germany and the CDU and Spahn himself had repeatedly voted to uphold this ban.
Spahn was then given a seat on the influential Budget Committee. He called in sick for a meeting, but at the same time the tabloid BILD published a photograph of him vacationing in Sardinia with his young son. Spahn immediately resigned that post as well.
The CDU's Philipp Amthor has only recently become Minister of State for Federal-State Cooperation in the Chancellor’s Office. There, he placed a beach chair on the balcony of his new office and proudly showed it to a TV reporter. As a reminder: His party has just been voted out of the state parliament in his home state of Mecklenburg-Western Pomerania on the Baltic Sea coast. But that didn't seem to have dampened the minister's good spirits.
Once again, social media reactions were fierce: This time with criticism of the young government official’s alleged arrogance. Amthor swiftly had the beach chair removed.
As the German saying goes, "Wer den Schaden hat, braucht für den Spott nicht zu Sorgen" (He who suffers the loss need not worry about the ridicule). That is seen to apply quite accurately to the CDU at the moment.
NRW premier Hendrik Wüst's trip to Turkey: What's on the itinerary
Hendrik Wüst is and remains Germany’s "reserve chancellor." Following his meeting with President Recep Tayyip Erdogan, the premier of the country's most populous state, North Rhine-Westphalia (NRW), will meet with three additional ministers: Foreign Minister Hakan Fidan, Finance Minister Mehmet Simsek, and Industry Minister Mehmet Fatih Kacir. A travel itinerary befitting a true statesman.
Without a doubt, NRW — home to one-third of the three million people of Turkish descent in Germany and with a trade volume exceeding ten billion euros — is the most important German state for Turkey.
But the personnel debates within Chancellor Merz’s conservative CDU party, to which Wüst also belongs, are also drawing attention here. These meetings are proof that here, too, people are betting on Wüst as a future chancellor.
During his trip, Wüst also struck a self-critical tone regarding Germany's history with racism and xenophobia. For too long, he said, Germany has viewed the many people of Turkish descent “occasionally as a problem”— the very same people who have helped Germany achieve its prosperity.
Coalition talks underway in Mecklenburg-Western Pomerania
Coalition talks are underway in the northeastern German state of Mecklenburg-Western Pomerania.
The Social Democrats (SPD) are meant to meet with the Green Party to talk about forming a government. The SPD met with the socialist Left Party yesterday too.
A coalition between the Social Democrats, the Greens, and the Left Party is the only viable option in the state to keep the far-right Alternative for Germany (AfD) out of the math.
The AfD won the contest in Mecklenburg-Western Pomerania with 38.2% of the vote but has no option to govern the state since none of the other parties will work with it.
The SPD, which has long governed the state, finished second with 35.5% of the vote.
Merz threatens to withhold approval for EU budget, FT reports
German Chancellor Friedrich Merz and his counterparts from five other nations have threatened to withhold their approval to a seven-year European Union budget proposal unless it were slashed by billions of euros as they've demanded for.
Merz and leaders from the Netherlands, Sweden, Denmark, Austria and Finland have signed a letter to make clear their wish to have the proposed budget trimmed by billions of euros or see it blocked, according to the Financial Times.
The budget for 2028-2034 was outlined by the European Commission last year and needs to be approved by all EU countries.
The proposed budget was set at nearly €2 trillion ($2.33 trillion) and parties involved are hoping to reach an agreement by the end of 2026.
The proposed amount is significantly higher than the current one set at between 2021 and 2027.
Merz earlier this month said cuts should apply across all policy areas and rejected relying on further joint EU borrowing to bridge the gap.
"Excessive debt threatens our sovereignty and our capacity to act," Merz said earlier this month, adding that governments had the "admittedly painful task" of setting priorities.
The German leader has called for the bloc's next budget to shift spending toward competitiveness and defense, arguing that a "20th-century budget" could not address current challenges.
The EU budget is funded primarily through contributions from member states, either in the form of national contributions calculated on the basis of gross national income or as a percentage linked to national VAT revenues.
As the EU's largest economy, Germany contributes the largest amount in absolute terms.

Floods kill more than 100 in Thailand and India, affect millions
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-29
07:52:38 UTC
16:52:38 KST

More than 100 people have been killed as heavy rains and flooding battered parts of Thailand and India, affecting millions of people, local authorities and media reported on Tuesday.
In Thailand, flooding has killed 23 people and affected more than 2.6 million across 29 provinces and the capital Bangkok, The Nation reported, citing the Department of Disaster Prevention and Mitigation.
Four people died in Bangkok, eight in Samut Prakan, which lies between the capital and the sea, and six in Sa Kaeo, an eastern province, it said.
The remaining deaths were recorded in Chanthaburi, southeast of Bangkok, Ayutthaya and Saraburi, two provinces to the north of the capital.
The department’s latest report, issued at 6am on Tuesday (2300GMT on Monday), said flooding remained in 167 districts, 890 subdistricts and 5,077 villages, affecting 940,300 households.
Water levels were rising in 14 provinces, stable in six provinces and Bangkok, and receding in nine others, according to the department.
Bangkok has been among the worst-hit areas after days of intense rainfall inundated roads and residential neighbourhoods. Local authorities continued pumping water from affected areas as rainfall eased.
September is the peak of Thailand's rainy season, but many Bangkok residents said this year's floods seemed worse than previous ones.
Scientists warn the intensity and frequency of extreme weather events will increase as global warming accelerates because of fossil fuel emissions.

MOSCOW, September 29. /TASS/. A detachment of the Russian Navy’s Northern Fleet ships entered the Kara Sea through the Shokalsky Strait, the fleet’s press service reported.
This occurred for the first time in the history of the Russian Navy, it said.
"A detachment of ships and auxiliary vessels of the Northern Fleet, under the command of the fleet’s Deputy Commander Vice Admiral Oleg Golubev, has for the first time in the history of the Russian Navy passed through the Shokalsky Strait, which separates the October Revolution Island from Bolshevik Island in the Severnaya Zemlya Archipelago, and entered the waters of the Kara Sea," the statement reads.
The Northern Fleet’s press service reported that while passing through the strait, a training alert was issued on the ships to boost combat readiness for navigating the narrow passage. They noted that the crew of a Ka-29 helicopter was deployed from the ice-class patrol ship Ivan Papanin, after which it carried out ice reconnaissance along the route.
"Passage through the strait was conducted in difficult ice conditions," the fleet reported. Nevertheless, the ship crews maintained navigational safety, maneuvering with varying courses and speeds to safely avoid icebergs.
"While transiting the strait, the Northern Fleet sailors evaluated the suitability of the new navigation area for operations by Russian Navy ships," the fleet’s press service concluded.
Long-distance Arctic deployment
The long-distance deployment of the Northern Fleet’s detachment of warships and auxiliary vessels across the Arctic Ocean is being conducted under the command of Deputy Commander of the Northern Fleet Vice Admiral Oleg Golubev. The task force includes the ice-class patrol ship Ivan Papanin, the large landing ship Kondopoga, the rescue tug Pamir, and the ocean-going tanker Sergey Osipov.
The Arctic deployment of the Northern Fleet’s ships is being conducted to protect Russia’s maritime navigation and economic activities in the Arctic.

Over 100 Jewish rioters storm West Bank village, torch home of a Palestinian family trying to return
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-29
07:50:55 UTC
16:50:55 KST

More than 100 Israeli rioters descended overnight on the Palestinian village of Jalud near Nablus as Israeli forces attempted to return a Palestinian family to the home it had left after months of repeated harassment, according to the IDF and police. Rioters blocked roads, set tires and Palestinian property on fire and threw stones at security forces, leaving three Border Police officers lightly injured.
The Tubasi family left its home in Jalud in July after months of harassment by extremist settlers. Ahead of the family’s attempted return, messages circulated in Hilltop Youth groups calling on supporters to come to the area and prevent it.
The IDF said the operation to return the family was ultimately abandoned because of the violence.
“More than 100 Israeli rioters were present in the village, blocking roads, setting tires on fire and throwing stones at security forces,” the military said. “The rioters also set fire to Palestinian buildings in the village, torched vehicles and other property.”
Three Border Police officers were lightly injured in the clashes, and a security-force vehicle was damaged. The military said riot-control measures were used against the crowd.
Three Israeli suspects were arrested. Two, aged 15 and 17, were detained by IDF troops and transferred to police, while an 18-year-old Jerusalem resident was later arrested after police said they found balaclavas and a club inside a suspicious vehicle in the area.
Police investigators and forensic teams were expected to enter the village under IDF protection to collect evidence and testimony.
“The security establishment strongly condemns any harm to security personnel while carrying out their duties, as well as acts of vandalism and damage to property,” the IDF said. “Such incidents divert attention, undermine stability and hinder the security forces’ defensive and counterterrorism activities.”
Family says months of harassment drove them out
The Tubasi family had lived in Jalud, in the Nablus area, until leaving in July. Earlier this month, family patriarch Mahmoud Tubasi told Ynet that the family had spent nearly three months effectively trapped in its home before finally leaving.
“For almost three months we were besieged in our house, and in the end they drove us out,” he said.
Tubasi said the harassment began in early April and targeted two adjacent houses built by members of his family.
“On the night of April 3, settlers came and set fire to the doors of the houses. We woke up in panic and managed to put out the fire,” he said.
“On April 19, settlers came again and put up a sukkah next to our houses, right beside them, and from then on they didn’t leave. They threw stones at our homes day and night and played loud music at night so we couldn’t sleep.”
Tubasi said the family was also threatened with being burned “like the Dawabshe family,” referring to the Palestinian family attacked in an arson attack in the West Bank village of Duma.
He said that on April 27, settlers broke through a wall on the ground floor of one of the houses and set fire to a storage area.
“The violence continued every day and we had no life,” he said. “After two months, at the end of June, the settlers took over a house between us and the village and blocked the only road we had to reach the village with spikes and rocks. They also cut off our water and electricity.”
The family remained until July 22 before deciding to leave, Tubasi said.
“We realized it was hopeless. We had no strength left,” he said.
‘The houses of my brothers were burned’
During the overnight violence, Palestinian reports said the Tubasi family home was set on fire along with other property in Jalud. Mahmoud Tubasi later said his family’s vehicle had also been torched and that Israeli soldiers moved family members to safety.
His daughter, Mayar Abad, wrote on social media: “My father’s car was burned. My brothers’ houses were burned. God, show us the wonders of Your power against the settlers. God, take revenge on them, reward us for our disaster and replace it with something better. Give patience to our hearts.”
Palestinians also reported violence elsewhere in the West Bank overnight. In al-Mughayyir, northeast of Ramallah, vehicles were reportedly torched and graffiti sprayed. Palestinians in Qaryut, not far from Jalud, said a woman was injured after being attacked by extremists.
Herzog calls violence a ‘moral stain’
President Isaac Herzog condemned the Jalud violence as an extremely serious incident and called for those responsible to face the full force of the law.
“This is a moral stain, an attack on the rule of law and our most basic values as a people and a state,” Herzog said, adding that arson, stone-throwing and attacks on IDF and Border Police personnel had “no justification whatsoever.”
“The violence is deeply contradictory to the values of Judaism,” he said.
Foreign Minister Gideon Sa’ar also condemned the riot, calling it “serious and abhorrent.”
“Anyone who commits these criminal offenses and assaults Border Police fighters and IDF soldiers, and even harms them, are criminals who must be dealt with to the full severity of the law,” Sa’ar said. “They harm our values. They harm Jewish settlement. They harm Israel.”
Yashar party chairman Gadi Eisenkot described the events as “revolting” and condemned the violence, arguing that attacks involving arson, stone-throwing and assaults on security forces harmed both residents’ security and the work of the security establishment.

Nato's top figures focus on pushing back against Russia's attempt to undermine support for Ukraine - snap analysis
Jakub Krupa
Rutte’s comments there are (perhaps not surprisingly) very much aligned with what Nato’s top commander Alexus Grynkewich told EU lawmakers last night.
In a rare appearance at the European parliament, Grynkewich warned that “the goal of the Russian activity right now is primarily to break our will to continue supporting Ukraine.”
“The logic of this is if we make the security situation seem dire enough, populations will want nations to withhold from Ukraine for their own protection. …
If there is a hybrid attack on your country, reinforcing the will to support Ukraine will show the Russians that their strategy isn’t working, and maybe have them back off that strategy.”
Top Nato figures appear to be focused on very publicly calling Russia’s tactics out in a bid to stop Moscow from succeeding and having any impact on social attitudes towards helping Ukraine – particularly ahead of 2027, with big elections coming up in France, Italy, Poland and Spain.
Rutte, Sinkevičius warn against Russia's 'campaign of hostile actions' to test Nato's resolve - summary
Nato secretary general Mark Rutte has urged allies to keep calm and carry on supporting Ukraine, saying Russia is “failing to undermine” the alliance’s support for Kyiv despite growing number of sabotage, drone incidents against Nato(11:07).
Rutte warned that Russia “continues its reckless campaign of hostile actions against Nato allies,” trying to “weaken our resolve and stop our support for Ukraine” (10:57).
His comments came at a press conference with Lithuania’s prime minister Mindaugas Sinkevičius who warned that Russia’s actions are “becoming increasingly hostile and less restrained” (10:59).
But Sinkevičius pushed back against recent warnings from Denmark, Poland and Germany about a potential imminent threat, saying there is no evidence of Russia “getting ready” (11:10).
Rutte says Nato has 'options' when responding to hybrid attacks
Pushed a bit further on hybrid attacks, Rutte acknowledges they “are having an impact,” but repeats his point that Nato has “all the response options: sometimes visible, sometimes not.”
He also says it’s important to, whenever possible on the basis of available evidence, publicly attribute these incidents to Russia, as Estonia did today.
“I applaud it,” he says.
He says Nato is acting “in the spirit of staying calm, carrying on.”
Lithuania's PM pushes back against warnings of imminent threat from Russia
Lithuania’s Sinkevičius says Russia “seeks to spread fear, to bring division … but it will not succeed.”
“We are not shaking [with fear]; we are doing what is meant to be done,” he says.
He says countries also do a lot of work in the background that is not publicly seen.
He says it’s important to be open about the challenges posed by Russia, but pushes back against “exaggerations” that something could happen within “upcoming months of weeks.”
“Is there any proof, real proof, that our intelligence services are providing … that Russia is getting ready or something? There is actually none,” he says, stressing “the risk remains,” but it’s not deemed to be escalating at the moment.
He adds “we have to … calmly do our work and we are doing that.”
Keep calm and carry on supporting Ukraine, Rutte tells allies
Rutte gets asked about various recent sabotage actions against Nato allies, including the UK, Germany, and Lithuania.
Should we stop calling them hybrid threats and call them what they are, he is asked. And does he agree with warnings coming from several countries about “decisive weeks and months” ahead?
Rutte says he agrees with the criticism of the phrase “hybrid threat,” as “it sounds a bit cuddly,” and does not reflect the severity of the threat.
But he says the key thing is that Nato “has all the response options we need,” even if “you will not always see them publicly.”
He says allies do a lot to counter the Russian threat.
“I would urge some calm, because we are investing in our defence [and] Russia is not in a good place,” he says.
He adds allies should “carry on, keep the support for Ukraine going, because the best response to any action in this grey zone of what Russia is doing is more support for Ukraine.”
Rutte says “we should not be naive about Russia,” but adds “they know we are stronger and we have to make sure by carrying on with our investments that we are also stronger in two, three, five years from now.”
'Russia’s actions are becoming increasingly hostile and less restrained,' Lithuanian PM warns
Sinkevičius is up next, as he thanks Rutte for today’s talks.
He warns that “the security [situation] in Europe is challenging,” as Russia’s actions are becoming increasingly hostile and less restrained.”
“We see the hybrid attacks: in Lithuania, Poland, Germany, elsewhere. And it’s not a question of proximity now; it’s a question of Russia’s actions.”
He says Lithuania leads the way in Nato as one of the top defence spenders, above 5% of GDP, and invites Rutte to a formal ceremony marking the permanent deployment of a German brigade to Lithuania in 2027.
'Russia continues its reckless campaign of hostile actions against Nato allies,' Rutte warns
Rutte continues saying that “Russia continues its reckless campaign of hostile actions against Nato allies.”
He says:
“[Russia] is trying to weaken our resolve and stop our support for Ukraine. But Russia is failing. It is failing on a battlefield in Ukraine, and it is failing to undermine our unity and support for Ukraine.
Our message to Moscow is clear: we will do even more for Ukraine and not less.”

Faisal Mahmud
29 September 2026•Update: 29 September 2026
Japan’s elderly population reached a record high as the country’s overall population declined for a third consecutive census, Kyodo News reported Tuesday, citing finalized 2025 census results.
People aged 65 and above accounted for 29.4% of Japan’s population in 2025, up 0.9% from the previous census in 2020.
Japan’s population, including foreign residents, fell by 3.17 million, or 2.5%, from 2020 to 122,972,528 as of Oct. 1, 2025.
The census, conducted every five years since 1920, showed the population declining for a third consecutive survey.
Meanwhile, 30.1% of the population was concentrated in the Tokyo metropolitan area, crossing the 30% threshold for the first time.
Japan’s demographic decline has been accompanied by persistently low births.
The country recorded 671,236 births among Japanese residents in 2025, down 14,937 from the previous year and the lowest since comparable records began in 1899, according to Health Ministry data.
The total fertility rate also fell to a record-low 1.14 from 1.15 in 2024.
However, preliminary Health Ministry data showed 342,068 births in the first half of 2026, including foreign nationals, up 0.8% year-on-year and marking the first increase for the January-June period in 11 years.
Deaths stood at 778,982 during the same period, resulting in a natural population decline of 436,914.

TAIPEI (Taiwan News) — Outstanding credit extended by Taiwan banks to New Southbound countries reached NT$2.46 trillion (US$77.27 billion) at the end of August, an increase of NT$464.8 billion in the first eight months of the year, according to Financial Supervisory Commission data.
The eight-month increase was 5.8 times the FSC’s full-year target of NT$80 billion and had already surpassed the previous record annual increase of NT$265.7 billion, set in 2022, per UDN. The year-end balance target of NT$2.08 trillion was reached in February.
Australia recorded the largest increase in outstanding credit through August at NT$168.5 billion, followed by Vietnam at NT$90.4 billion, Singapore at NT$81.6 billion, and India at NT$76.6 billion. Bankers attributed the growth mainly to strong economic activity in those markets, which boosted corporate demand for credit.
The FSC has set New Southbound lending targets since 2017 as part of the government’s New Southbound Policy, per CNA. Australia has become a particular focus for banks, with two representative offices and seven branches operated by Taiwan lenders in Sydney.
Taipei Fubon Bank recently opened a Sydney branch focused on corporate and institutional banking, with plans to participate in infrastructure and renewable energy projects. The bank said Australia’s stable economy, mature financial markets, and industrial resources continue to attract international capital.
CTBC Bank recorded the largest increase in outstanding credit among Taiwan banks through August at NT$54.1 billion, followed by Cathay United Bank at NT$52.9 billion, Taipei Fubon Bank at NT$50 billion, E.Sun Bank at NT$48.5 billion, and Mega International Commercial Bank at NT$39.7 billion.

Taiwan’s AIDC demonstrates anti-drone system at prison drill
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-29
07:47:11 UTC
16:47:11 KST

TAIPEI (Taiwan News) — Aerospace Industrial Development Corporation said Monday that it provided an anti-drone system for a recent safety drill held by the Ministry of Justice’s Agency of Corrections, according to a press release.
AIDC supported the Corrections Agency’s 15th Ching An safety drill on Sept. 19 with its domestically developed anti-drone system. The system uses no Chinese components and can detect, identify, track, and drive away drones.
The agency included drone countermeasures in this year’s exercise as increasing drone use raised security concerns. Justice Minister Cheng Ming-chien (鄭銘謙) inspected the event, joined by Corrections Agency Director Lin Hsien-ming (林憲銘), AIDC President Chuang Hsiu-mei (莊秀美), and Senior Vice President Alex Tsai (蔡明晃).
AIDC said the system uses layered defenses, intelligent detection, and multiple countermeasures. It can identify several intruding drones simultaneously and alert operators, allowing them to assess the situation and respond appropriately.
During the drill, the system transmitted live tracking data and used signal jamming to drive away intruding drones. AIDC said the response followed the Corrections Agency’s zoned joint-defense mechanism.
AIDC said the system has a maximum defensive range of 5 kilometers, making it suitable for protecting critical infrastructure, VIPs, and airspace during large events.
Chuang said the system’s open architecture allows different functions, sensors, and equipment to be incorporated according to the customer’s needs. Tsai said the drill provided a valuable opportunity to identify areas for further improvement.
Drone countermeasures are generally categorized as soft or hard kills. Soft-kill measures use jamming, spoofing, or signal hijacking to disrupt or take control of a drone, while hard-kill measures physically destroy it using projectiles, missiles, or other weapons.

TAIPEI (Taiwan News) — The Taiwan-US-developed Mighty Hornet IV attack drone was prominently featured Monday as President Lai Ching-te (賴清德) inaugurated a military drone facility in Chiayi County.
Lai presided over the opening of the eastern campus and the groundbreaking for the western campus of the National Chung-Shan Institute of Science and Technology’s (NCSIST) drone industrial park in Minxiong Township, per Liberty Times. Images of the Mighty Hornet IV appeared on large displays at the venue and roadside banners nearby.
The park’s eastern campus was built with more than NT1.1billion(US34.5 million) in government funding to support military drone development and production. NCSIST said the facility would focus on research, testing, and manufacturing, with a research building and integration hangar designed for testing medium and large drones.
Liberty Times suggested the eastern campus could become a production base for the Taiwan-US-developed drone. However, the report did not confirm that mass production had begun.
The Mighty Hornet IV is based on the US-made MQM-178 Firejet target drone developed by Kratos Defense & Security Solutions, with NCSIST contributing payload and mission systems. The two organizations are collaborating on the attack drone, which is designed as a lower-cost alternative to cruise missiles.
The drone reportedly has a maximum cruising speed of Mach 0.69, approaches the speed of sound during its final dive, and carries a 30-kilogram high-explosive warhead. Its reported range is 1,000 kilometers.
Liberty Times reported that the drone could eventually operate alongside Taiwan’s Hsiung Feng IIE cruise missiles in coordinated attacks designed to overwhelm enemy air defenses and deplete their interceptor missile supplies. It could also be adapted for reconnaissance or electronic warfare, depending on its configuration.
During the ceremony, Lai said Taiwan’s drone industry was accelerating and urged the Legislative Yuan to pass additional defense spending proposed by the Ministry of National Defense. The park’s western campus is expected to attract private-sector manufacturers and help Taiwan become a regional hub for a drone supply chain involving democratic partners.

- On the night of 28-29 September, Romania tracked an aerial asset near its airspace and scrambled fighter jets to monitor the situation. However, no airspace violation was officially reported at that time.
- On the night of 25-26 September, an unidentified object violated Romanian airspace, leading to the scrambling of Allied fighter jets.

Hamas has yet to issue a statement confirming al-Beik's death or his position within the Qassam Brigades as of Tuesday morning.

EBA urges Ukraine to keep scrap export ban in 2027
Ukraine
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-29
10:44:14 EEST
16:44:14 KST

The European Business Association (EBA) urged the government to keep the zero quota on ferrous scrap exports, which effectively bans scrap exports in 2027, or, if it is scrapped, to set an export duty of EUR 180 per tonne for all destinations, taking into account Ukraine's international obligations, the association said in a statement.
"Domestic processing of scrap metal in Ukraine allows value added to be created, jobs and tax revenue to be supported, and steel and finished metal products to be supplied with raw material. Using scrap also helps reduce energy costs and CO₂ emissions in steelmaking, which takes on added importance with the EU's application of CBAM," it said.
EBA member companies appealed to the Cabinet of Ministers and the Economy Ministry, it said.
Recently, after most Ukrainian steelworks stopped because of massive Russian attacks, scrap collection companies called on the government to review the restrictions on scrap exports. Scrap collectors had earlier advocated abolishing the de facto export ban and introducing quotas of 200,000 tonnes a year for supplies to EU countries.
The Cabinet of Ministers set a zero quota on scrap exports effective January 1, 2026, to ensure that Ukrainian enterprises have this raw material.
Ferrous scrap exports from Ukraine grew 53% in 2025 from 2024 to 448,680 tonnes, the EBA said. It said easing the current restrictions could lead to higher exports and a raw material shortage for Ukrainian producers.
Ukraine produced 4.3 million tonnes of steel in January-August 2026, compared with 7.41 million tonnes in 2025, UAVtormet said. Steelworks received 925,400 tonnes of scrap, compared with 1.56 million tonnes in 2025, and scrap procurement totaled 971,700 tonnes, compared with 2.11 million tonnes, it said. Preliminary forecasts call for steel production of 6.4-6.5 million tonnes in 2026, scrap supplies to steelworks of 1.2-1.25 million tonnes and scrap procurement of 1.22-1.25 million tonnes, it said.
Ukrainian enterprises cut ferrous scrap exports by 95.1% year-on-year in January-August to 13,860 tonnes from 283,060 tonnes, and to $3.93 million from $85.4 million in monetary terms. January exports of 9,310 tonnes, made because of the completion of last year's contracts, compared with 68,520 tonnes in December 2025. There were no exports in February-May, 4,080 tonnes were sold abroad in June, 315 tonnes in July and 157 tonnes in August.
The Cabinet of Ministers amended Annex 1 to its Resolution No. 1795 of December 31, 2025, by Resolution No. 563 of April 29, 2026, allowing scrap exports under licenses issued by the Economy Ministry to foreign trade entities that won electronic auctions for the sale of such goods held in December 2025. The auctions were held under the Procedure for the Alienation and Leasing of Property of Business Entities in which the state or a legal entity wholly owned by the state holds more than 50% of the charter capital.

Israel’s West Bank road closures turn routine journeys into long ordeals
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-29
07:44:06 UTC
16:44:06 KST

Israel’s West Bank road closures turn routine journeys into long ordeals
Palestinians face delayed medical care and long journeys as Israel tightens movement restrictions across the West Bank.
Mohammed Abu Hijleh still finds it hard to believe that his mother passed away just over a week ago; she had suffered from nothing more than diabetes. But the restrictions Israel imposes on various cities, towns, and villages in the occupied West Bank can alter a Palestinian’s life in an instant.
Zahriya Abu Hijleh, 66, was attending her niece’s wedding reception in her hometown of Deir Istiya, northwest of Salfit, on September 20, when she suddenly felt dizzy and collapsed.
Recommended Stories
list of 3 items
- list 1 of 3Israel revokes Dutch diplomats’ status over sanctions on settlements
- list 2 of 3Israel’s Smotrich calls for ‘war’ in West Bank: Rhetoric or real threat?
- list 3 of 3Mapping Israel’s 300 checkpoints: Where they are and how they work
After she was taken to the town’s medical centre, the doctor immediately ordered her transfer to Salfit Governmental Hospital, a facility just an eight-minute drive from Deir Istiya.
Mohammed requested an ambulance, but the vehicle could not enter the town because the iron gate operated by Israeli forces at the entrance was closed. Instead, an ambulance from the medical centre transported her to the gate, and from there, she was taken off the stretcher, carried past the gate on foot, and transferred to a second ambulance waiting on the other side.
It is a scenario that happens repeatedly in the occupied West Bank, Mohammed told Al Jazeera.
“My mother was breathing her last; had the gate been open, we wouldn’t have lost her on the way,” he said.
Medics later determined that Zahriya had suffered a pulmonary embolism and required urgent treatment, according to her family.
“Sadly, she died due to the delay,” Mohammed said. “She had no prior health issues other than diabetes.”
Comprehensive closures
The military checkpoints and iron gates erected by Israel in the West Bank have become a significant source of misery for Palestinians.
They disrupt daily life, causing delays for people trying to reach work, schools, and universities, while also posing a daily threat to the lives of the sick.
Israel periodically imposes closures on the West Bank for various reasons, including Jewish holidays. The current closure runs from September 27 to October 3, coinciding with the Jewish festival of Sukkot.
While Israeli settlers move freely between West Bank cities, and even storm Palestinian villages and towns under Israeli army protection, Palestinians are forced to wait for hours at closed checkpoints.
Ibtihal Mansour from Nablus endured such an ordeal last Friday while visiting her in-laws’ home in the village of al-Janiya, near Ramallah.
The family left the village at 10am, hoping to reach Nablus within 45 minutes. But they encountered closures at the Atara and Ein Siniya checkpoints north of Ramallah, effectively trapping them in the area.
“We tried taking alternative routes west of Ramallah, but were surprised to find the road between Ramallah and Nablus blocked by settlers, with all vehicle traffic completely halted. We remained on the roads, trying to find any way through, until midnight, a span of more than 14 hours,” she told Al Jazeera.
Her children were crying, exhausted after spending so long confined in the vehicle. Passing through one roadblock near Nablus, in an area called al-Lubban Asharqiya, a soldier forced Ibtihal to wake the children. When her 11-year-old son did not wake up, she said that the soldier punched him in the head, causing him to jolt awake crying.
“The scene was heartbreaking; I felt a deep lump in my throat and profound sorrow. Long hours of waiting in the vehicle ended with an assault like this, and the ordeal didn’t even end there,” she said, explaining that they had to turn back. “We were forced to spend the night at my sister-in-law’s home in Ramallah before setting out early the next morning for Nablus.”
Like Ibtihal’s family, many Palestinians travelling between cities and villages are forced to stay overnight in hotels or at relatives’ homes. Some municipalities have converted wedding halls and mosques into shelters for those stranded, providing meals donated by residents of towns near the checkpoints.
The Colonization and Wall Resistance Commission (CRRC) recorded 942 checkpoints, closure points, and obstacles across the occupied West Bank as of September 25, up from 793 in March 2024.
The total length of the obstacles amounts to approximately 107.7km (70 miles), according to data from the UN Office for the Coordination of Humanitarian Affairs.
The CRRC says the closures effectively fragment Palestinian communities, making access to workplaces, schools, medical facilities, and agricultural land dependent on whether roads and crossings are open.
Al Jazeera has reached out to Israeli authorities for comment on the road closures and the allegations from Palestinians in this article, but has yet to receive a response.
Strangling Hebron and Jerusalem
In Hebron – which has an Israeli settler presence in the centre of the Old City – the Israeli army has closed the Ibrahimi Mosque to Palestinians and tightened restrictions at checkpoints and gates leading to the site until Wednesday, all while securing access for settlers to celebrate Jewish holidays.
Issa Amro, coordinator of the Youth Against Settlements group, told Al Jazeera that soldiers have closed checkpoints and imposed curfews in several city neighbourhoods, restricting resident movement and making it increasingly difficult to reach the Old City and the Ibrahimi Mosque.
“The area west of the mosque contains settlements and closed zones, while access from the east is limited to a few roads. These measures make reaching the site both more difficult and more dangerous,” he explained.
The situation in occupied East Jerusalem is also fraught, as Israel imposes strict restrictions on Palestinian movement and access to the Al-Aqsa Mosque, while thousands of Israeli settlers enter the site and move about unhindered under heavy security escort.
Activist Fakhri Abu Diab told Al Jazeera that Israel’s closures in occupied East Jerusalem during the Jewish holidays are part of attempts to impose religious sovereignty over the city.
Abu Diab explained that Israeli settlers and hardliners head either to storm the Al-Aqsa Mosque or to synagogues to perform religious rituals, while Palestinians are forced to remain at home.
He described how the closures disrupt daily life in East Jerusalem, shutting shops, schools, and workplaces, and halting movement.
“Israeli police restrict the movement of Jerusalemites. Families and vehicles attempting to move about risk being attacked by extremists and settlers, while the latter are permitted to roam freely and dominate the streets,” he said.
