Main enemy of hens-and-chicks is not frost, but water: how to water, feed, and protect the plant
Ukraine
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-29
09:58:50 EEST
15:58:50 KST

Main enemy of hens-and-chicks is not frost, but water: how to water, feed, and protect the plant
Kyiv • UNN
Hens-and-chicks withstand drought and frosts down to –30…–35 °C, but require sun, drainage, and moderate watering. Excess moisture causes rot.
Houseleek (Sempervivum) is a perennial succulent of the Crassulaceae family, commonly known as "hare's cabbage" or "live-forever" because of its ability to survive in the most challenging conditions. The plant forms compact rosettes of fleshy leaves that store moisture, so it easily withstands drought, heat, and even severe frosts. Houseleek is grown as an ornamental plant for rockeries, rock gardens, borders, containers, and even "green roofs"—thanks to its undemanding nature and the wide range of rosette colors, from emerald green to burgundy and silvery violet.
How to properly care for this plant is explained by UNN.
When and where to plant houseleek
The most favorable time for planting is spring, from April to May, when the soil has warmed up but the heat has not yet exhausted young plants. Early autumn, in September, is also suitable, allowing the houseleek to take root before the cold weather.
Choose a sunny or slightly shaded location for planting: the more light the plant receives, the brighter and more intense the color of its rosettes will be. In the shade, houseleek becomes elongated, losing its compactness and ornamental appeal. Ideal locations for this plant include rock gardens, raised flower beds, gaps between stones, and containers or window boxes with good drainage.
Houseleek is also often chosen by Ukrainians for landscaping graves. This hardy plant can grow for a long time without active human care and produce attractive greenery, creating an aesthetic effect.
What type of soil is suitable for houseleek
The main requirements for the soil are looseness and good permeability. Houseleek categorically cannot tolerate heavy, clayey, or waterlogged substrates. The optimal mixture consists of ordinary garden soil, coarse sand, and fine gravel or perlite in an approximate ratio of 2:1:1. A drainage layer of expanded clay, broken brick, or small stones must be placed at the bottom of the planting hole or pot to prevent water from stagnating around the roots. Soil that is too fertile and moist promotes rot and makes the plant vulnerable to disease.
How to water houseleek
Watering is the most important and, at the same time, the simplest aspect of caring for houseleek; the main rule is not to overdo it. Immediately after planting, water the plant moderately until it takes root. After that, water houseleek only during dry periods, when the top layer of soil has completely dried out several centimeters deep. In summer, one watering every 7–10 days is usually sufficient, while in rainy weather or autumn, additional watering is not needed at all—the plant receives enough natural precipitation. The greatest danger to houseleek is excess moisture, which causes the roots and rosettes to rot, rather than drought, which the plant withstands without difficulty.
What to feed houseleek
Houseleek does not require frequent or abundant feeding. On the contrary, excess fertilizer, especially nitrogen fertilizer, harms the plant: it loses the characteristic compactness of its rosette, becomes loose, and becomes more vulnerable to diseases and pests. Once a year, in spring, a small amount of complete mineral fertilizer for succulents or cacti may be applied at half the dose recommended by the manufacturer. Organic fertilizers—humus, compost, and fresh manure—are contraindicated for houseleek because they excessively enrich and moisten the soil.
Pruning and shaping
Houseleek does not require special pruning, as its rosette structure forms naturally. Care consists of removing dry, damaged, or rotting lower leaves at the base of the rosette—this prevents the spread of rot and maintains the neat appearance of the clump. It is worth remembering that the mother rosette blooms only once in its lifetime, producing a flower stalk, and then dies after flowering, leaving numerous daughter rosettes—"pups"—around it. The spent rosette should be carefully removed, making room for young shoots and preserving the decorative appearance of the arrangement.
Diseases and pests of houseleek
When watering rules are followed, houseleek rarely gets sick. The most common problem is rot of the root collar or the rosette itself, which occurs due to excess moisture, especially during the cold season. Affected parts should be removed immediately, while the soil around the plant should be dried out and drainage improved. Occasionally, the plant is attacked by mealybugs or aphids; they are treated with a soapy solution or appropriate insecticides. The best prevention is good drainage, moderate watering, and sufficient ventilation around the plantings.
How to Prepare Houseleek for Winter
Houseleek is an exceptionally frost-resistant plant: most species can withstand temperatures dropping to –30…–35 °C without any covering, provided they are growing in well-drained soil. The main threat in winter is excess moisture. Meltwater and prolonged autumn rains can cause the rosettes to rot. Therefore, in autumn it is worth taking measures to divert moisture: raise the flower bed, ensure drainage, or cover the plants with spruce branches or nonwoven material that allows air to pass through but protects against excess water. There is no need to prune or water houseleek additionally before winter—the plant prepares for its dormant period on its own.

Central Tokyo recorded its 34th consecutive day of rain Tuesday, the longest streak since records began, according to Japan’s weather agency.

The prolonged spell is not expected to end immediately.

Japan’s autumn rain front typically brings extended periods of unsettled weather as seasonal air masses interact over the country.

China Restricts Overseas Travel for Families of AI Experts - Bloomberg
Kyiv • UNN
Beijing requires permission for overseas travel by relatives of certain AI and chip manufacturing specialists. The restrictions are intended to prevent the leakage of knowledge.
China has expanded restrictions on foreign travel for leading artificial intelligence specialists to prevent the leakage of important knowledge to the United States. Bloomberg reports, as cited by UNN.
According to people familiar with the matter, government agencies have recently begun informing affected individuals about broader restrictions, including prominent startup founders as well as executives of strategically important companies in fields related to artificial intelligence. According to sources, immediate family members, such as the spouses and children of certain executives in the artificial intelligence and chip sectors whose work is considered critical to national security, are now required to obtain permission from Beijing before traveling abroad, even for short trips
The expansion of the restrictions is a continuation of Beijing's policy of controlling the departure of leading technology specialists. Earlier this year, China already restricted foreign travel for some artificial intelligence specialists from private companies, including Alibaba and DeepSeek. According to the publication, Beijing plans to gradually expand the list of people subject to the restrictions. Several individuals have already been informed of the need to obtain permission for family trips.
As the publication notes, China is also separately introducing rules that took effect on September 15 to ensure compliance with exit bans in cases ranging from criminal investigations to potential violations of the country's industrial and technological security.
According to available information, similar restrictions had previously been applied to prominent researchers, scientists, and executives of state-owned companies. Beijing is now also focusing on specialists in the private technology sector who are considered important to the development of artificial intelligence and the production of microchips.

A logo of Nvidia is displayed at at the Computex Taipei exhibition in Taipei, Taiwan. (AP File Photo)
Nvidia has unveiled a new security platform designed to stop artificial intelligence agents from going rogue, saying it sets “boundaries” that could have stopped previous breaches.
The announcement of the company’s Open Agent Safety Platform follows a series of revelations from top AI companies about their models escaping and breaking into other organizations.
The disclosures sparked furious debate about the safety of advanced artificial intelligence systems, including self-improving models that some fear could race out of human control.
Nvidia executives said in a media briefing on Sept. 28 the new, open-source system could have prevented a recent incident involving a swarm of OpenAI agents that autonomously hacked into AI company Hugging Face.

Nvidia’s security software, called OpenShell, lets developers “formally verify an agent has enough authority to do its job and no more,” Boitano said.
Because it’s open source, it can be “extended” to run on rival computing platforms including those from Arm and Intel.
The platform also includes a separate security layer called Sentry that runs onboard chips to continuously monitor AI agent activity and can “intervene instantly” if the agent starts trying to move beyond its target, the company said.
Nvidia said more than 100 organizations are using the platform at its launch, including Microsoft, Perplexity, Accenture and JPMorgan Chase.

Kanpur plane crash: No distress call, flight-monitoring gaps emerge in AAIB probe

2026-09-29
06:56:08 UTC
15:56:08 KST

A four-seater, dual-engine Tecnam aircraft crashed in a fatal crash on the outskirts of the Natthapurwa village near the Ganga Barrage in Kanpur.
NEW DELHI: The Aircraft Accident Investigation Bureau (AAIB) has found that Garg Aviation did not fully follow required flight-monitoring procedures before its training aircraft crashed near Kanpur on August 27, killing an instructor and a trainee pilot.The seven-page preliminary report also recommends that the Directorate General of Civil Aviation issue clearer guidelines on how Flying Training Organisations should monitor flight data.The Tecnam P2006T twin-engine aircraft crashed near the Ganga Barrage less than 20 minutes after taking off from Kanpur's civil aerodrome. The 39-year-old instructor and 28-year-old trainee were killed.
No records of flight-data checks
AAIB said Garg Aviation told investigators that it carried out random checks of data from the aircraft's Garmin system. However, the operator could not provide records of those checks and did not have a Standard Operating Procedure explaining how the monitoring was conducted or what limits would trigger further action."When queried on flight data monitoring, the FTO stated that random monitoring of Garmin data was being carried out; however, no records of such monitoring were maintained, and there was no SOP defining how the monitoring was conducted or what exceedance limits were considered for it," AAIB said.
The Garmin data card acts as a type of flight-data recorder for small aircraft. AAIB said interim safety recommendations were necessary and called for stricter compliance with flight-data monitoring requirements."Further, DGCA may issue specific guidelines detailing the procedure to be followed for flight data monitoring, which shall be made part of the TPM," the probe agency said. TPM refers to the Training and Procedure Manual.
Aircraft stopped responding after final radio call
The aircraft, registered as VT-NBV, took off at around 11.11 am on August 27. About 14 minutes later, it made a radio call saying operations were normal and that it would contact the controller again after 10 minutes.That call never came."No further call was received from VT-NBV thereafter. The RT controller attempted to contact VT-NBV but received no response," AAIB said.The aircraft had no distress call before the crash. Garg Aviation was informed at around 12.10 pm that the plane had force-landed in the Ganga Barrage area, after which the company's team went to the site.AAIB said local residents had reported the crash through the 112 emergency helpline. Police and ambulance teams reached the site and took both occupants to a hospital in Kanpur, where they were declared dead.
Engines and flight data being examined
Investigators have recovered the Garmin data card from the wreckage and downloaded its information for analysis. Both engines have also been recovered and quarantined for detailed examination.
"Both engines have been retrieved and quarantined for further detailed examination. The investigation team is coordinating with the OEM for further examination," it said. OEM refers to Original Equipment Manufacturer.The investigation also involves Italy's ANSV and the US National Transportation Safety Board, which have each appointed an accredited representative. Tecnam has also provided a technical adviser.AAIB has sought documents relating to the aircraft and its operating crew from the DGCA as the investigation continues.The crash occurred at Kanpur's civil aerodrome, an uncontrolled aerodrome managed and maintained by the Airports Authority of India. An uncontrolled aerodrome does not have an operating control tower.

Taiwan's ITRI transforms fishing waste into reusable materials
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-29
06:55:06 UTC
15:55:06 KST

TAIPEI (Taiwan News) – The Ocean Affairs Council announced on Thursday that the Industrial Technology Research Institute has turned foam fishing floats into plastic pellets suitable for manufacturing, according to a press release.
The Ministry of the Environment's 2024 statistics show that fishing waste accounts for up to 70% of coastal waste, with foam floats responsible for 31.5% of the trash. Distant-water fishing uses floats that are later thrown away, burned, or buried.
The council said it used a two-pronged approach. It subsidized ITRI to convert foam into reusable thermoplastics and incentivized fisheries to use less foam and turn in disposed gear.
The council said its departments coordinated the effort by connecting authorities with fishing enterprises and recycling facilities. It noted that wharves now have collection sites, with disposables labelled and tracked.
The council said the institute is currently doing test manufacturing. It said that aside from recycling and reusing, it is encouraging consumers to use daily necessities made from reclaimed plastics.

TAIPEI (Taiwan News) — President Lai Ching-te (賴清德) on Tuesday said the government will invest an additional NT$100 billion (US$3.2 billion) over eight years to help small and medium-sized businesses upgrade and grow.
Speaking during a meeting with representatives of a national association of lunchbox and catering businesses, Lai said small and medium-sized businesses account for nearly 80% of jobs in Taiwan. He said the Cabinet approved a support program this month to help businesses upgrade energy-saving equipment, adopt digital management systems, and train skilled workers.
Lai also highlighted the importance of the school meal industry to the small-business sector. The association represents 131 school meal providers in 14 cities and counties that prepare lunches for about 1.07 million students each day.
He thanked nutritionists, cooks, quality-control staff, drivers, and others involved in preparing and delivering school meals. Their work includes sourcing ingredients, preparing food, controlling temperatures, and ensuring meals reach schools safely.
Lai said nearly 99% of ingredients used in school lunches are domestically produced and traceable. He credited government support and suppliers’ sourcing efforts with bringing more locally grown rice, vegetables, fruit, meat, and seafood into school meals.
The president also praised meal providers for handling food supply disruptions. During pork supply restrictions imposed amid African swine fever controls last October, providers quickly switched to chicken, eggs, and soy products.
Lai said the industry also responded when cooking oil supplies became tight this summer. Meal providers coordinated supplies to keep school lunch services running.

Russia Responsible for Arson Attack on Milrem
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-29
06:54:08 UTC
15:54:08 KST

“Today, we can state with full confidence that the arson attack on Milrem in Estonia on the night of 15 August was an act of sabotage commissioned by the special services of the Russian Federation. The Estonian Internal Security Service has reached this conclusion after a thorough assessment of the information it has gathered,” Prime Minister Kristen Michal said.
According to the Prime Minister, the act of sabotage is part of Russia’s broader campaign in Europe, aimed at intimidating us and forcing us to reduce our support for Ukraine and the pressure on Russia. “Such activity is absolutely unacceptable and irresponsible,” Michal said, adding that it also demonstrates Moscow’s growing desperation in a situation where Russia has failed to achieve the objectives of its aggression against Ukraine.
At the same time, Estonia is strengthening its preparedness and internal security to counter such Russian activities. “The Estonian state is capable of protecting its security,” the Prime Minister said. “Thanks to Estonia’s strong security and law enforcement agencies, our country is an exceptionally difficult environment for an adversary to conduct such operations, and similar activities have also been prevented before they could be carried out. Russia will not intimidate us or change our policies through such actions.”
Foreign Minister Margus Tsahkna confirmed that Estonia’s response will be exactly the opposite of what Russia is seeking to achieve. “Together with our allies and partners in Europe and beyond, we will increase pressure on Russia, tighten sanctions, and seek additional ways to restrict the travel of Russian citizens to Europe. We will also continue and strengthen our comprehensive support for Ukraine. Russia’s attempts to intimidate us will not diminish our resolve — they will only strengthen it.”
According to Margo Palloson, Director General of the Estonian Internal Security Service, the threat of provocations and attempted acts of sabotage originating from Russia remains. “Russian special services continue their attempts to recruit and influence people in Europe, including for the purpose of carrying out acts of sabotage. Organisations contributing to the support of Ukraine and defence industry companies face an elevated threat. The Estonian Internal Security Service recommends that they strengthen both their physical and cyber security measures,” Palloson said.
“Estonian security authorities are closely monitoring Russia’s activities and cooperate closely with both Estonian companies and international partners to prevent such incidents,” Palloson added. “Estonia is a safe country, and our goal is to ensure that it remains so.”
The criminal investigation into the exact circumstances of the incident is continuing, but the preliminary information gathered so far in the criminal proceedings also indicates that the attack was commissioned. The suspects believed to have directly carried out the arson attack have been apprehended and taken into custody and no longer pose a threat.
On the night of 15 August, a fire broke out in a building used by defence industry company Milrem Robotics on Betooni Street in Tallinn’s Lasnamäe district. Emergency services responded immediately and the fire was quickly brought under control. No lives were in danger.
On 17 August, two Latvian citizens suspected of carrying out the arson attack were detained in Latvia. A third suspect was detained on 18 August. Searches of locations associated with the suspects in Latvia resulted in the seizure of numerous data storage devices and items that may have been used to set fire to the building.
On 17–18 September, Latvia handed over all three suspects to Estonia.
Defence industry company Milrem Robotics, in cooperation with European Union countries, supplies THeMIS unmanned ground vehicles to Ukraine.

Congress attacks EC over SIR row, says will fight ‘to save’ voters’ rights (Image source: X)
NEW DELHI: Congress president Mallikarjun Kharge on Tuesday accused the Election Commission of compromising the integrity of the electoral process through the Special Intensive Revision (SIR) of voter rolls and changes to voter-enrolment rules. He also stated that the party would step up its campaign against Chief Election Commissioner Gyanesh Kumar and the government.Addressing the Congress Working Committee (CWC) meeting, Kharge said the party faced a “historic responsibility” to protect democracy and the Constitution, drawing a parallel between the Congress’ fight for voting rights during British rule and its current campaign over voter rolls.He alleged that names were being removed from electoral rolls “at the behest of the BJP and the Modi government” and accused the CEC of becoming a “puppet” of the government.
On the contrary the Election Commission has maintained that its decisions have full legal sanction and that differing views among commissioners are part of institutional deliberations.Kharge also targeted changes to Form 6, which is used for enrolling new voters.
He alleged that the rules had been changed in a way that could disenfranchise young voters. He also contrasted Prime Minister Narendra Modi's government with the decision of the Rajiv Gandhi government in 1988 to lower the voting age from 21 to 18.“They didn't provide jobs, and now they don't even want to give the right to vote,” Kharge said, alleging that the government feared questions from the youth.Also read: ‘All SIR rollout decisions unanimous’: EC says agendas for all meetings to be circulated in advance
Kharge congratulated Rahul Gandhi for raising questions over voter rolls in Mahadevpuram, Aland and constituencies in Haryana and Maharashtra.He referred to allegations involving duplicate voters, doubtful addresses, multiple voters registered at the same address and entries linked to Form 6, saying the Election Commission should have acted on the issues.“If the Election Commission had shown even a little seriousness in that direction, they would not be in the dock today, and their credibility would have been preserved,” he said.Kharge also praised Congress workers who organised protests at the block, district and state levels following Rahul's campaign.The Congress has been pressing for Kumar's resignation amid a controversy over reported differences within the Election Commission over the SIR exercise. The poll panel has said that operational queries raised by Election Commissioners Sukhbir Singh Sandhu and Vivek Joshi were part of normal institutional deliberations and that its orders followed established procedures.Kharge also questioned the decision-making process behind SIR, asking whether it was wrong to seek clarity on who approved the exercise and why the two election commissioners were allegedly kept out of the internal portal.
Congress lists five demands
Kharge laid out five demands that he said the Congress would pursue:
Full data on major changes to voter lists should be made public.
Voters whose names have been removed should receive complete information and a full opportunity to appeal.
Political parties should receive voter lists and essential related data in a simple format and in a timely manner.
Serious discrepancies should be independently investigated within a fixed timeframe.
Election-related data and decisions should be transparent so that no political party can claim information is being withheld.
“The most important thing is that India's voters must have the confidence that their vote is secure,” Kharge said.
He said the Congress did not view the issue merely as a contest over winning or losing elections, arguing that governments may change but democracy and the Constitution were permanent.
Kharge targets PM Modi, Shah and Election Commission
Kharge also accused the BJP and RSS of systematically weakening independent institutions and said the Congress wanted the Election Commission to be strong enough to command the trust of both the ruling party and opposition.He alleged that two election commissioners had themselves described the CEC's actions as arbitrary and unfair and said those responsible should be removed.
Kharge also demanded Prime Minister Narendra Modi's resignation “on moral grounds”, alleging that the CEC had acted under his pressure.
The Congress president compared the current controversy with demonetisation, calling the alleged removal of voters from electoral rolls “vote demonetisation”.“In demonetisation, the poor stood in line. In vote demonetisation, the poor has been thrown out of the line altogether,” he said, arguing that voting was the biggest political tool available to poor, Dalit and marginalised citizens.The CWC meeting comes ahead of a meeting of opposition INDIA bloc parties on Wednesday, where a joint strategy on the SIR controversy and the demand for Kumar's removal is expected to be discussed. The opposition is also considering another removal notice against the CEC in Parliament.

Estonia's special care funding falls 5 times short of sector's expectations
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-29
06:50:00 UTC
15:50:00 KST

Estonia's special care funding falls 5 times short of sector's expectations
The government plans to allocate far less state funding to specialized care in the coming years than the sector sought. The Estonian Chamber of Disabled People says even that amount is welcome.
ERR reported this summer that the Ministry of Social Affairs was seeking an additional €200 million for specialized care over the next four years in state budget talks. The money would create new places in specialized care facilities and raise staff salaries.
Ministry Secretary-General Maarjo Mändmaa said a month ago that Social Affairs Minister Karmen Joller (Reform) had requested an additional €20 million for next year, for example.
The government has now agreed on the state budget and sent it to the Riigikogu. Although the ministry requested an additional €200 million, the government decided to add a much smaller amount to the sector over the next four years: up to €37 million.
In fact, the €37 million is intended for the social affairs and health sectors as a whole, not just specialized care. It is also meant, for example, to expand clinical training capacity for nurses, increase residency training capacity and fund various digital developments in healthcare.
Joller said it is now up to the Riigikogu to decide how much of the €37 million will go specifically to specialized care and how much will go to other areas of social affairs or healthcare.
"There are many different needs in my area of responsibility, not just specialized care. We have many needs and I want to discuss them with the other parties as well. Since the coalition will not pass this budget on its own, I think the opposition should also have a chance to say which areas it considers priorities for funding," Joller said.
Prime Minister Kristen Michal (Reform) said the state budget is in deficit and specialized care was one of the few areas to which the government decided to allocate additional money.
"Our budget is in deficit and if we want to reduce the debt burden in the future by running a smaller deficit, somewhat less money will be available for different sectors. [...] Many sectors received no additional money at all and instead faced cuts, so this was one of the few that actually received more," Michal said.
Maarja Krais-Leosk, head of the Estonian Chamber of Disabled People, said the planned amount for specialized care was certainly less than hoped for, but the allocation of up to €37 million was still welcome.
"I don't think it would be right to start shaking our fists or slinging mud over this now. I believe the figures also reflect the efforts of various politicians," she said.

Trump denies offering Iran sanctions relief, Tehran says ready for talks

Unknown Publisher

Trump denies offering Iran sanctions relief, Tehran says it is ready for talks
Sept 29 - US President Donald Trump said he has offered Iran nothing to end the war, rejecting media reports that cited US officials saying he was willing to ease sanctions and release frozen funds for "concrete" steps regarding Iran's nuclear programme.
"This is untrue. I offered them NOTHING," Trump wrote on Truth Social on Monday.
Axios and CNN both reported, citing unidentified US officials, that Trump was willing to give Iran sanctions relief and free Iranian funds as part of a final deal on the condition that Iran showed "concrete progress" on the nuclear issue.
Trump has cited preventing Tehran from acquiring a nuclear bomb as a key goal of the war, along with ending its ability to attack its neighbours and creating conditions for Iranians to topple their leadership.
Iran does not have nuclear weapons and denies it wants to develop them, but argues it has the right to a domestic nuclear energy capacity.
Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian, in an interview with the CBS show "Face the Nation", said Tehran was ready for talks on its nuclear programme and other issues, but would not accept "bullying or coercion".
"Iran is not seeking war, but will defend itself against pressure, threats and attacks,” Pezeshkian said, adding that it had already agreed that "we're not supposed to develop nuclear weapons".
US and Iranian officials spoke separately with mediators on Monday as part of a renewed effort to end the seven-month war, according to officials of both countries.
Iran insisted on Sunday that only diplomacy can solve its conflict with the United States and Israel.
"Our conditions are clear, and any move toward reopening the Strait of Hormuz is contingent on these conditions being met," Iranian Foreign Minister Abbas Araqchi posted on social media. "Only a negotiated solution can get them out of this deadlock."
Araqchi told reporters at the UN on Friday the proposed deal would trigger a seven-day countdown to reopening the strait and a pause in regional fighting.
Trump on Saturday rejected the plan and argued that desperation was driving the Iranians’ push for an agreement on the key waterway.
"They want to make a deal to open the Hormuz Strait immediately because they're losing so badly," Trump told reporters at the White House.
Araqchi said mediators facilitating Tehran's talks with Washington had not officially relayed a US rejection.
"We are waiting for the mediators to convey the definitive views to us, and we will make a decision based on them," Araqchi posted.
OIL PRICES RISE
The war, which Trump launched alongside Israel in February as "Operation Epic Fury", has killed thousands of people, severely disrupted global energy supplies, pushing up oil prices and fuelling global inflation.
Iran and its allies have responded by extending the conflict throughout the region. Iran has struck US allies in the Gulf with drones and missiles, while its Houthi allies in Yemen have hit Saudi interests.
Saudi Arabia, the largest of the Gulf states, has been drawn deeper into the war this month as Houthi fighters have advanced in Yemen, routing forces of the Saudi-backed government and threatening Saudi oil exports through the Red Sea.
Oil prices rose for a second successive session on Tuesday as lingering concern over Middle East supply outweighed signs of recovering crude exports from the region.
Brent crude futures had risen $1.49, or 1.4%, to $106.77 a barrel by 0326 GMT while US West Texas Intermediate crude was at $93.94, up $1.34, or 1.5%. Both benchmarks closed the previous session at nearly $1 a barrel higher. REUTERS

Good morning. This is Mared Gwyn in Brussels, penning today’s newsletter with my colleague Angela Skujins. In this edition: our correspondent captures an attempted Russian ‘double-tap’ drone strike in central Kyiv, and the latest on Ukraine’s funding crunch.
Euronews’ Sasha Vakulina was on the ground in central Kyiv when a Russian drone strike attempted to hit Ukraine’s National Academy of Sciences for a second time.
Run for cover: After Monday afternoon’s attack, which killed one and injured six, Sasha and her crew were filming the scene when emergency workers ran for shelter. Air defences intercepted a second incoming attack, and the crew captured the dramatic moment on camera.
Kyiv’s State Emergency Service told her the initial strike was a direct hit by a jet-powered drone on the three-storey National Academy of Sciences building. Euronews footage appears to capture the attempted double-tap strike, with a second attack targeting the emergency crew of the first. More.
The incident is one of many for those living in Ukraine. For civilians, it underscores the need for Europe to continue stepping up its support for the nation, particularly as Russia grinds its full-scale invasion into a fifth year.
Mind the gap: Brussels is today hosting a meeting of the Ukraine Donor Platform, with representatives of allied nations and financial institutions coming together to mobilise assistance for the war-weary country, Jorge Liboreiro reports.
The gathering takes on a special meaning amid a painful budget crunch that has left Kyiv with a $20 billion hole in its Ministry of Defence, and a day after foreign and defence ministers gathered in Brussels to discuss supporting Ukraine’s military. (The initial number of $27 billion has been reduced through austerity measures.)
Pressure piling: For the past month, the European Commission and the International Monetary Fund have been locked in intense talks with the Ukrainian government to pin down the precise extent of the deficit and design possible solutions. So far, no solution has emerged, and the $20 billion gap remains uncovered. Kyiv has warned that $9 billion in much-needed drone deliveries could be at risk.
“We want to bring together international partners ready to discuss how we can bridge the budgetary gap,” a Commission spokesperson said ahead of the meeting.
The Commission will be represented by Marta Kos, in charge of enlargement, who recently urged Ukrainian authorities to speed up the reforms that are linked to the bloc’s financial assistance.
If the legislation doesn’t move through in time, payments will be delayed, further worsening the situation. Ukraine will be represented by Finance Minister Sergii Marchenko. Earlier this month, Marchenko told us that his country faces the tightest budget since the start of Russia’s war.
Kyiv warns over grain crisis: Meanwhile, the blockade of Ukraine's Black Sea export routes is becoming "critical", with potentially far-reaching implications for global food prices, Ukraine's Minister for Agrarian Policy and Food, Taras Vysotskyi, told Europe Today.
Global costs: "We can already see that on average, grain prices have increased by 25 percent," Minister Vysotskyi said. "If you multiply it by the overall grain and food consumption out of grain, within a year, it could mean up to $60 billion in additional costs (for) consumers throughout the world." Watch.
Russia has recently intensified strikes on Ukrainian Black Sea vessels and infrastructure, on which Kyiv relies for the export of around 90% of its agricultural commodities. Attacks on storage facilities within Ukraine have also intensified.
Speaking just ahead of talks with agri ministers in Brussels, Vysotskyi said that Kyiv is making "some progress" in ensuring Ukrainian harvests reach the market, including through so-called "solidarity lanes" established by the EU to provide alternative transport corridors.
Kyiv ‘open’ to deal: Asked about the prospect of a negotiated deal brokered with Russia through Ukraine's international partners, Minister Vysotskyi said: "We are ready to create the safety conditions in the Black Sea for all of the civil goods, including Ukrainian agricultural commodities. We are open to it."
While acknowledging ongoing negotiations with partners, Vysotskyi explained that Ukraine can "never trust" Russia's commitment to a potential moratorium.
"The reality is that we can never trust what's going to happen tomorrow., or after any kind of memorandum or deal is done," the minister said.
Tobias Cremer, German Member of the European Parliament (S&D), just told Europe Today that the progress of Russian President Vladimir Putin on the battlefield is “that of a snail”, prompting him to lash out through restricting grain exports and executing hybrid campaigns against European allies.
"This war that Putin conducts in Ukraine against Ukraine is not purely about Ukraine, and Putin has said that very very clearly," he said.
"For him, this is a war against the European order of peace. It's a war to undermine the unity of NATO, and it's a war to undermine the way we are living in our free democracies." Watch.
Vučić facing EU scrutiny: The European People’s Party (EPP) – the EU’s most powerful political group – is set to discuss the membership of Aleksandar Vučić's Serbian Progressive Party (SNS), our correspondent Vincenzo Genovese reports.
It comes just after the Serbian President resigned to run for prime minister in the upcoming elections. SNS is currently under a scrutiny process, which could culminate in expulsion from the EPP, for Vučić's handling of opposition protests last year and his ties to Russian President Vladimir Putin.
Serbia’s recent handling of the funeral of Bosnian Serb war criminal Ratko Mladić has also infuriated EU officials and parliamentarians, with many calling on the EPP to sanction SNS in response.
Euronews explains: Does the EU have enough gas for winter?
As Europe heads into winter with a thin gas cushion, prompting Brussels to warn that the bloc’s energy price crisis could become a supply problem, our energy reporter Marta Pacheco analyses just how urgent the situation is.
European Commission for Energy, Dan Jørgensen, has said there are currently no immediate risks to security of supply and that the current energy crisis is "very different" from that in 2022.
But in fact, EU storage levels are now lower than they were in 2022, averaging around 70%. Latvia (47.1%), the Netherlands (52.1%) and Germany (55.6%) are registering some of the lowest fill levels based on industry data from 13 September.
In contrast, by November 2022, EU gas storage levels averaged 94.9% and ended the year at 83.4%, according to the Commission.

What's worrying the RBA now? The risks it couldn't ignore
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-29
06:45:05 UTC
15:45:05 KST

Key Points
- The RBA has raised interest rates to address "three big risks".
- An economist says there are already indications of another rate raise at the board's next meeting in November.
The head of the Reserve Bank hopes the fourth rate rise of the year announced on Tuesday will turn the tide on the past six months of elevated inflation.
The RBA announced interest rates would rise to 4.6 per cent from 4.35 per cent and didn’t rule out a potential fifth rate rise this year in November to try to tame inflation.
"The hope here is that this will be restrictive enough," Michele Bullock told reporters on Tuesday afternoon. "Now, will it be enough? I don't know."
The rate rise follows six months of underlying inflation of around 3.5 per cent, above the board's target range of 2-3 per cent.
The RBA's mandate is to reduce inflation into this band, while protecting as many jobs as it can.
News that makes sense
Your trusted source for staying up-to-date with the world around you. Get free daily news updates and analysis, straight to your inbox.
'Three big risks'
In justifying the call to increase rates, Bullock said the effect of the first three rate rises this year are still flowing through.
However, "three big risks" have also started to materialise over this time.
"One was the Middle East conflict going on for longer and fuel prices rising again," she said, citing previous guidance which had predicted that oil and energy prices would have stabilised by now.
The second challenge, according to Bullock, is the "AI boom", which was adding to demand both in Australia and overseas, although she said the risk had not fully materialised.
This boom has partly driven up prices for technology-related goods.
Finally she said domestic capacity pressures were higher than anticipated, referring to an economic situation where too much money is chasing too few goods.
"It's difficult to estimate output gaps and how tight the labour market is," she acknowledged, explaining that inflation numbers and unit labour costs come into play.
The Australian Bureau of Statistics is due to release the latest inflation figures on Wednesday morning.
Will there be another rate rise this year?
Several key economic indicators will be released before the RBA meets again in November, giving policymakers more data to assess the inflation outlook.
However, major bank ANZ is already predicting interest rates will then rise to 4.85 per cent.
Betashares chief economist David Bassanese said there are already indications the board could hike rates again.
"For starters, the Board's decision was unanimous. The Board also explicitly warned that it may raise rates again if needed," he said in a statement.
"Ominously, the Bank noted that local firms are facing higher costs and are either raising prices or "looking to do so". This suggests that inflation could rise even further in the months ahead."
Bullock declined to predict what the board would decide at its next meeting in November, saying the RBA will do what it has to do to reduce inflation.
"But if we can avoid massive job losses and a massive increase in the unemployment rate, that is a really important thing to be able to try and do."

OpenAI canceled the launch of a new AI model due to safety concerns
Kyiv • UNN
OpenAI will not release GPT-6.1 Astra because it does not meet safety standards. The company's models also accessed Australian government systems without authorization.
OpenAI, the developer of ChatGPT, confirmed on Tuesday, September 29, that it would not release its new AI model — GPT-6.1 Astra — due to safety concerns. UNN reports this, citing the BBC.
Details
The AI system, which independently performs tasks such as browsing web pages and using applications, "did not quite meet the company’s standards," Saachi Jain, head of security systems at OpenAI, told the BBC.
On Tuesday, OpenAI also published updated information about incidents that occurred in June but were not disclosed until last week, when its models accessed Australian government websites and systems without authorization.
These incidents and similar violations by models developed by major companies in the AI industry have intensified debate in recent weeks over the risks associated with this technology.
Leading AI specialists, including OpenAI’s Sam Altman and Anthropic head Dario Amodei, have called on the industry to slow the pace of development due to concerns about the risks associated with the technology.
OpenAI’s decision, first reported by The Wall Street Journal, is a rare case of a major AI developer withdrawing a new release because of safety issues.
The model did not meet the requirements for "adhering to restrictions and authorization, as well as how it informs the user about the type of work performed," Jain said.
"We want to make sure that the development of our model is safe regardless of whether it takes place inside the company or during release to users. But when we deliver it to users, we have an exceptionally high bar for safety and alignment," she added.

As Russia Targets Civilians, Pressure Mounts On Trump To Use Sanctions Powers
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-29
06:41:41 UTC
15:41:41 KST

WASHINGTON -- A new wave of deadly Russian attacks on civilian infrastructure in Ukrainian cities is fueling bipartisan calls in Washington for US President Donald Trump to use sweeping new sanctions powers against Moscow, with lawmakers arguing that greater economic pressure could strengthen efforts to end the war.
Russia's bombardment killed at least nine people and wounded more than 80 on September 28, according to Ukrainian officials. Moscow's forces struck apartment buildings, offices, data centers, and the National Academy of Sciences in central Kyiv in a daytime attack.
Early on September 29, authorities in Kyiv reported a new wave of Russian attacks, with journalists reporting several large explosions in the Ukrainian capital. Details were not immediately available.
The strikes followed a week of diplomatic efforts at the UN aimed at gaining traction for negotiations to end Russia's full-scale invasion, now in its fifth year.
"The [US] president must move out quickly to capitalize on the Graham Sanctions Bill," Republican Representative Don Bacon told RFE/RL on September 28, referring to the recently approved legislation.
"The Russians keep bombing cities and civilians. Americans overwhelmingly want to see the president take action now," Bacon said. "The Russian economy is one of our leverage points, and we need to take advantage of that."
The call is part of a bipartisan, bicameral push for Trump to make use of the Lindsey O. Graham Sanctioning Russia and Iran Act of 2026, which Congress passed by wide margins and Trump signed into law this month.
Pressure From Congress
Senator Roger Wicker, the Republican chairman of the Senate Armed Services Committee, also urged Trump on September 28 to use the economic tools provided by the legislation to increase pressure on Russian President Vladimir Putin.
In a statement shared with RFE/RL, Wicker praised Trump's efforts to pursue a negotiated settlement but said Washington must remain "clear-eyed" about Putin, arguing that Moscow has continued attacking Ukraine despite diplomatic efforts.
“He mocks the peace process," Wicker said, "but he might be compelled to take it more seriously if his bank account is threatened.”
Wicker said the law gives Trump several options, including imposing additional financial restrictions on Putin's associates and companies supporting Russian weapons production, sanctioning major purchasers of Russian energy, and targeting Russia's so-called shadow fleet used to evade existing restrictions.
"Peace will come through American and Ukrainian strength, not through Putin's good will," Wicker said, urging Trump to use the new authorities "to the fullest extent."
Democrats backing the legislation are also pressing for implementation, with a particular focus on cutting the energy revenues that help finance Russia's war.
"We're going to be watching the implementation very closely," Senator Jeanne Shaheen, a Democrat, told RFE/RL on September 17. "It's not just the sanctions piece that we think is important, but it's also, as I said, shutting down the revenues," she said.
Shaheen said pressure should extend beyond Russia to countries continuing to purchase Russian energy, singling out China.
Shaheen also called for action against transactions involving the shadow fleet, saying buyers should not be able to obtain Russian oil and gas through opaque trading networks at discounted prices.
Attacks In Daylight
The calls came as Ukraine reported another series of strikes on civilian and economic infrastructure. Russian drone attacks in the Kyiv region killed four people and wounded eight, officials said.
In Kyiv, a woman was killed when a strike hit the National Academy of Sciences in the Shevchenkivskiy district. Russian forces also hit a pharmaceutical company and gas stations in the capital.
Denys Sienik, charge d'affaires at the Ukrainian Embassy in Washington, told RFE/RL on September 28 that the attacks showed Moscow was expanding its targeting of Ukraine's economic and technological infrastructure.
"These attacks make clear that Putin is investing in continuing the war, not ending it -- with devastating consequences for civilians," Sienik said.
He described people trapped in the burning, smoke-filled National Academy of Sciences building, standing at windows as they tried to escape.
"This is not an isolated incident, but part of a sustained pattern of Russian aggression that continues to claim civilian lives across Ukraine," Sienik said.
He argued that greater sanctions pressure was therefore "an essential part of the effort for peace," saying measures constraining Russia's ability to finance the war could help save lives.
Where To Apply Pressure
The legislation gives the administration several potential avenues to increase economic pressure, but sanctions specialists say some of the most immediate opportunities involve targets that have so far escaped US restrictions.
"Many of the authorities enacted in this law were already at the president's disposal," Elaine Dezenski, head of the Center on Economic and Financial Power at the Foundation for Defense of Democracies, told RFE/RL.
"But the law will provide additional impetus for review of individuals and entities who may be subject to sanctions but who haven't yet been targeted," she added.
Dezenski pointed in particular to Russia's shadow fleet and foreign entities involved in its energy trade.
"That's significant as many of Russia's shadow fleet vessels remain unsanctioned," she said. "The same goes for many of the Chinese buyers of Russian oil and suppliers to Russia's sanctioned energy infrastructure projects."
Secretary of State Marco Rubio has emphasized that the legislation gives Trump substantial discretion over how to apply the new authorities.
"The law gives the president tariff authority," Rubio told reporters in New York on September 23 in response to a question from RFE/RL.
Rubio said the law also provides national-security waivers, allowing Trump to apply the measures selectively. "What the president has now is a tool in his toolbox that he can use not just to influence what happens in Russia and Ukraine and in that conflict but potentially what's happening with Iran as well," Rubio said.
"How he'll use it is up to him to decide, and up to him to announce."

Saunas, cinnamon buns and coastal scenery on the new rail route from Malmö to Oslo
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-29
06:40:56 UTC
15:40:56 KST

‘This carriage is due for modernisation. Don’t miss the opportunity to experience 90s Germany style,” reads the sign on the door to the dining carriage. The couple inside aren’t missing theirs: they’re taking endless selfies in the clinical pink-and-turquoise carriage that looks like a hospital canteen and smells like cinnamon buns and strong filter coffee.
I’m on Snälltåget’s iconic red-shelled train, on the Swedish rail company’s new route from Malmö to Oslo – a 6.5-hour journey along Sweden’s picturesque western corridor. Until now, the journey between the two cities involved long bus rides and fragmented train transfers. This direct line is easier and cheaper, with tickets starting at £11 each way. It’s already a hit, shuttling more than 25,000 passengers since launching this summer.
I was first seduced by Scandi rail travel a decade ago on a journey from Stockholm to Gothenburg, when I was berthed in a cosy dark-wood cabin and listened to a pianist play in a dining car. This time, starting in Malmö, I will take advantage of the new route to make a series of stops along the country’s western shore.
In my view Malmö, across the Øresund Bridge from Copenhagen, is too often overlooked in favour of Stockholm. The southern port city is less polished than the capital and grittier, but its residents seem more outgoing and curious. Within an hour of arriving, I’m invited to drinks by a group of local people – a level of openness I never experienced living in Stockholm. Almost half of the population is under 35, and 187 nationalities are represented, making it a hotbed of creativity. In the centre of town, the Form/Design Center occupies a former 16th-century grain store, now a meeting point and exhibition space for design, crafts and architecture enthusiasts. Then, there are Moderna Museet and Malmö Konsthall modern art galleries.
At Möllevången, or Möllan, a trendy neighbourhood popular with creatives, everybody looks as if they’re at art college, or have just returned from a weekend in Berlin. My friend Rob, who has lived in Malmö for nearly a decade, guides me through Folkets Park, the “people’s park”, pointing out his favourite pizza spot, Far i Hatten, which occupies cute wooden huts. We find a table at Ava nearby for a beer on a leafy square dotted with hip restaurants and organic wine bars – it feels like Malmö’s equivalent to London Fields in Hackney. Resisting the urge to continue our purposefully staid bar crawl, we down a nightcap at Bar Bobo and call it a night.
Snälltåget operates just one direct Oslo-bound train a day, at 6.38am from Malmö Central (plans are in the works to increase this next year), so it’s an early start at a station teeming with families and backpackers with rucksacks the size of fridge-freezers. We soon pass the romanesque towers of Lund Cathedral before chugging through pancake-flat yellowing agricultural fields, then skirt Apelviken bay – Varberg’s long, sandy horseshoe beach popular for kitesurfing and surfing.
Varberg is Sweden’s equivalent of a coastal British market town. It’s got bunting, cobbled streets, intimate cafes and a weekend market with vendors peddling fresh vegetables, fruit, marmalade, leather belts and socks. It’s also a spa town, which inspired my visit. I was intrigued by its pretty, Moorish-inspired Kallbadhuset (cold bath house), set on wooden piles above the Kattegat sea, where for about £8 visitors gain access to segregated men’s and women’s saunas, both with spellbinding sea views. A plunge in the brisk water after the sauna proves the perfect antidote to a 6am start after a bottle of red wine the night before. Floating on my back, I look up to see a group of Swedish veterans sitting on a wooden bench, baring all (it’s a nude bathhouse), the building’s mustard shades completing an almost Hockney-esque scene.
According to a sign outside Skarpe Nord – a community-run women’s bathing spot nearby – people have been nude-bathing in Varberg for more than 100 years. Walking along the promenade by a cavernous passage of blasted rocks that resembles a secret pathway from Lord of the Rings, I pass a collection of other designated naked bathing spots. But with the grey weather showing no sign of clearing, my hotel’s spa proves more inviting.
In the bowels of Hotell Gästis hides a replica of Vladimir Lenin’s favourite bathhouse. The hotel’s owner, Lasse Diding, built the spa as a homage to his idol, inspired by a visit to the original bathhouse in St Petersburg in the 1980s. This slightly eerie space is clad in more than 75,000 cobalt tiles and decorated with candlelit busts of communist leaders.
Diding’s interest in the communist movement began during the Vietnam war and never left him. The eccentric entrepreneur is responsible for Varberg’s many visible politically left-leaning monuments – a giant Palestine flag, Hotell Havanna (an ode to revolutionary Cuba) and a statue of Danuta Danielsson, who became a symbol of solidarity after hitting a marching neo-Nazi with her handbag in Växjö in 1985.
The following morning, I hop on the fast train to Gothenburg, a 39-minute ride away. After checking in at the sophisticated, French boudoir-style Hotel Pigalle, just five minutes’ walk from Central station, I wander along Kungsgatan, the city’s modern shopping artery, towards Magasingatan. The area is packed with vintage shops (Ragtime, Pop and Humana) and craft stores such as Customwood, which makes bespoke wooden furniture to order.
I grab a fika (the Swedish tradition of taking a break to drink coffee and indulge in a sweet treat) at Da Matteo, a barn turned cafe spread across three floors. The Scandi-industrial interiors are straight out of a design magazine, as bespectacled folk work away on their laptops. Scents of bread and coffee drift from the in-house bakery and coffee roastery; my bullar (a classic cardamom bun) and a latte cost just under a tenner.
Wandering around Slottsskogen park later, I remember why I wanted to move to Gothenburg after a fleeting first visit all those years ago. Sweden’s second-largest city is compact and easy-going. It has a rough-around-the-edges feel like Malmö in places, with the liveability, nature and culture of Stockholm. At its heart is the pretty old town of Haga, which has narrow cobbled streets, inviting wafts of baked goods and the sound of creaky, wooden trams chugging by. And Slottsskogen is my favourite park in Europe. Roughly the size of Hyde Park, it’s home to deer, penguins and Gotland ponies, and exactly the kind of place you can spend long hours strolling without purpose.
The Gothenburg to Oslo leg of the journey is the cinematic climax. It starts with rolling green pastures, cows grazing on a riverbank and forests thick with towering conifers beneath a blue summer sky. Then nature really starts showing off: lakes widen, trees grow greener and granite canyons appear grander with every kilometre, drawing excited kids to press their noses against the windows.
Keen to see it up close, after pulling into Oslo I dump my bags at Citybox, a minimalist hotel a few minutes’ walk from the station, and head north to Sognsvann. This lake and recreational area on the outskirts of the city is the starting point for a circular walk up to Vettakollen, a popular viewpoint. After an easy, 30-minute uphill hike, I reach a rocky mound skirted by pine trees, where families are picnicking. Oslo unfurls in the distance, the urban sprawl of metal and glass stretching to the fjord. For me, this is what makes Scandinavia special: the urban and the natural worlds seamlessly colliding.
The trip was provided by Visit Sweden. One-way tickets from Malmö to Oslo with Snälltåget cost from 149 Swedish kronor (£11). Double rooms at Hotell Gästis from £90. Doubles at Hotel Pigalle from £85. Single rooms at Citybox Oslo from £68

Hard cheese: Tough times for Greece's Naxos Graviera cheese as production falters
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-29
06:38:32 UTC
15:38:32 KST

Naxos Graviera, the hard cheese of the Greek Cycladic island was named the world’s best cheese in 2025 by the food guide TasteAtlas, but its makers are now facing increasing production problems.
Naxos Graviera is one of Greece's most famous and important hard cheeses, which secured Protected Designation of Origin (PDO) status as far back as 1996, thanks to a decision by the European Commission.
Its popularity has long since crossed Greek borders, as it is exported to 20 countries. In 2025 it was even ranked first on the international gastronomy platform TasteAtlas – Local food around the world, as the best cheese in the world.
The much-coveted accolade confirmed the enduring reputation of a product that has become synonymous with the gastronomic identity of the Cycladic island and is a cornerstone of the local agricultural economy.
It was the latest in a long series of national and international distinctions. Among others, it has won the gold taste award at the Greek Cheese Festival in 2011, as well as two Stars in the Superior Taste Award competition at the iTQi Institute in Brussels in 2015, 2016 and 2018, while in 2017 and 2020 it took the gold award at the Taste Olymp Awards.
This hard cheese, with its pale yellow colour, thin dry rind, delicate aroma, sweet and subtle flavour, and highly distinctive aftertaste, has for years enjoyed a reputation as one of the island's two flagship products, alongside the Naxos potato. It is one of Greece's top cheeses, ideal for every culinary use.
The dairy of the Naxos Union of Agricultural Cooperatives, is the island's largest cheese-making facility and the driving force behind the product on Naxos.Giannis Politis, Professor of Physiology of Nutrition and Production Traits at the Agricultural University of Athens, has been working with the Naxos Union of Agricultural Cooperatives for the past eight years.
"The distinctive character of Naxos Graviera comes from a combination that is hard to find in cheese-making. First of all, Naxos Graviera has a very sweet taste, which is combined with very high elasticity," said Politis. "My international experience in cheese-making has led me to the conclusion that Naxos Graviera rivals the graviera produced on the border between Switzerland and France. Naxos is the largest island in the Cyclades, with very special features."
"At the moment, around 75% of Europe's aromatic plants are found in Greece. And Naxos is a paradise for aromatic plants. So here on Naxos we have, first of all, cows on the lowlands. In the mountains we have sheep and goats. The small ruminants graze on grass rich in aromatic plants, and as a result Naxos produces milk with a distinctive flavour but also a special composition," added Politis.
Naxos Graviera is made from local cow's milk or a mix of cow's milk with sheep's and goat's milk, in a ratio of 80% to 20%.
The Naxos Union of Agricultural Cooperatives produces this exceptional cheese using milk exclusively from animals that live and are raised on the island, following traditional cheese-making rules at every stage of the process. The Naxos Union of Agricultural Cooperatives produces around 1,250 tonnes of graviera a year.
Konstantina Vadoula is a Food Chemist at the dairy plant: "Our primary raw material is milk, and it comes from short distances. This means we can collect it and have it arrive at the dairy in good time, where it undergoes quality control so we can check it is suitable and meets the specifications, and then it goes through heat treatment to become the final product, which is graviera.
"Every year we produce around 1,200-1,250 tonnes of graviera, which is sold in wheels of 9 kilos, 3 kilos and 1 kilo, as well as in 250-gram pieces. 100 tonnes are destined for export. At the same time, we export 250 tonnes of other cheeses, such as Naxos Kefalotyri, Naxos Goat's Cheese and Naxos Mountain Cheese," said Vadoula.
Most of the graviera produced is destined for the domestic market. Sales could be double or even triple, but the decline in milk production limits the quantities available, which in turn means exports remain lower than in the past. Even so, this particular cheese is the flagship of the island's export products:
"Milk production on the islands faces inherent difficulties. We are not in mainland Greece. Feed does not reach us easily here, and it is expensive. All this creates problems," laments Politis. "The state needs to step in and help. This is a product that is essentially a national champion. It is produced and it sells easily. So what we should be doing here is creating conditions under which it can not only be produced, but produced in the quantities required and in the quantities the market can absorb."
"The key issue, especially as we are currently celebrating 100 years of the Naxos Union of Agricultural Cooperatives, is to keep livestock farming alive on the island. Because if livestock farming is maintained, I can tell you that absorbing the graviera produced will be, as my students would say, "a piece of cake". Naxos Graviera ought to be counted as part of our country's heavy industry," Politis concluded.

Russia has lost around 1,532,500 troops in Ukraine since the beginning of its full-scale invasion on Feb. 24, 2022, the General Staff of the Armed Forces of Ukraine reported on Sept. 29.
The number includes 1,440 casualties that Russian forces suffered over the past day.
According to the report, Russia has also lost 12,388 tanks, 25,463 armored combat vehicles, 155,031 vehicles and fuel tanks, 50,498 artillery systems, 2,169 multiple launch rocket systems, 1,681 air defense systems, 443 aircraft, 356 helicopters, 538,702 unmanned aerial vehicles, 2,780 unmanned ground vehicles, 35 ships and boats, and two submarines.
Ukraine's General Staff has not revealed its own losses during the full-scale invasion, citing operational secrecy.
Independent Western think-tank reports agree that the Russian casualties significantly surpass Ukraine's losses, with the Center for Strategic and International Studies (CSIS) estimating the ratio to be "roughly 2.5:1 or 2:1."
A January 2026 CSIS report said Ukraine has likely suffered between 500,000 and 600,000 casualties from February 2022 to December 2025, of which between 100,000 to 140,000 are thought to be killed in action (KIA).
While Ukrainian officials rarely disclose the figure, President Volodymyr Zelensky told France TV on Feb. 4 that at least 55,000 Ukrainian soldiers have been killed in action since the beginning of the full-scale war, in addition to significant numbers who are missing in action.
The intensity of Russian drone attacks and the fighting has made it extremely difficult for Ukraine to retrieve the bodies of fallen soldiers, which are needed for DNA confirmation.

From Jamui to Delhi, the burden of safety from sexual assault cannot fall on women
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-29
06:30:55 UTC
15:30:55 KST

As an Indian woman, I often feel myself oscillating between states of anxiety or anger. The anxiety is about doing the mental maths of how to stay safe – thinking about what I’m wearing, where I am going and how I’ll get there, and so on. The anger is at the sheer absurdity of this, and the stories of of sexual violence and harassment I read about every day. I am not the only one.
Last week, two particularly enraging incidents captured national attention. First, a video showing a group of men accused of harassing and molesting two teenagers at night in Bihar’s Jamui went viral. Then, a 17-year-old, out with a friend in Delhi, was allegedly gang-raped in a park by men posing as police. After, women in Bihar told Outlook how the incident in Jamui triggers greater controls and pressure on them. In Delhi, authorities curbed access to public parks and a premier women’s college, Lady Shri Ram College (LSR), briefly moved classes online.
I have noticed this pattern repeatedly: after incidents of sexual violence go viral on social media, the fallout further ensnares women. We are the ones who get told to avoid certain places, regulate our behaviour, dress modestly or be home earlier, thereby placing the burden of escaping this menace on us. Feminist activist Kavita Krishnan has described this phenomenon as “perhaps the most widespread form of gender-based violence in India”.
Instead of figuring out why sexual violence remains entrenched in our society, how patriarchal agency perpetuates such violence or what kind of social conditioning is needed for men, women are instead expected to take up less public space. (It is another matter that women might not be safe even inside their own homes.)
Regulating women is easy because “it does not require any institutional cost and, most of all, it sends the signal to concerned parents that the problem is being handled”, says Meena Kandasamy, a feminist author, whose latest novel, Fieldwork As a Sex Object, is about a woman’s life being upturned when a deepfake video using her face goes viral. “Their target audience is not the young women who feel unsafe but the rest of society.”
In my experience, this repression happens at three levels: first in the realm of family, then in broader society, and ultimately by the state. It begins at home, under the guise of protection, with arbitrary curfews or dress codes. It gets reinforced at a community level with institutions and social groups through moral policing, victim-blaming and the expectation that women should not put themselves in “unsafe” situations.
Then there is the response of the state. Restricting access to parks after sunset can surely reduce the number of people in those places, but it doesn’t address why women are unsafe there. Harassment and sexual violence are, unfortunately, not tied to timings or daylight. And further restricting women’s lives is not the solution to injustices foisted on them. All three, Kandasamy says, consider women as a “problem to be handled”.
“She’s not a citizen (for the state), a member (for the community), or an adult (for the family). She is treated like an inanimate but precious object – like a diamond that has to be locked up to prevent theft,” she said.
‘Moral policing’ of the wrong target
Women, however, are pushing back against this approach. In recent days, students from Delhi University have come out on the streets demanding safer public spaces including more street lighting, usable public toilets, more housing and scholarships for female students. Vedayana, 20, a student at Lady Shri Ram College (LSR), says locking up parks is not the solution: “If you are not putting up safety measures to make it accessible to women, then it is as good as saying that the park is only for men.”
The scale of the issue is devastatingly clear. A recently published survey of more than 4,000 women in New Delhi and Bengaluru, found that 65% of women in New Delhi and 29% in Bengaluru experienced harassment in public spaces in the past year.
Another 2024 study from India and Pakistan found that women’s overall mobility remains abysmally low, and what freedom they do have is almost entirely tied to education, employment or unpaid care work. Substantive mobility for leisure or pleasure is practically nonexistent.
Despite how widespread and urgent the problem is, the political response can further shake public confidence. A female minister from Bihar, commenting on the molestation video said: “Moral policing can be done in a more decent and elegant fashion.” Another minister from the state drew fire for describing it as an “isolated” incident”.
Minimising crimes against women reflects a political culture in which accountability becomes optional. Students such as Vedayana want this to change. Political parties, she tells me, should pledge to not give tickets or positions to anyone accused of sexual harassment. “We don’t want the leaders sitting at the top to perpetrate and preach rape culture,” she adds.
Parliament is not immune to accusations, either: the BJP politician Brij Bhushan Singh, who formerly headed the Wrestling Federation of India, was recently accused of sexual harassment by six female wrestlers – he denies the allegations, and was acquitted by a magistrate, in a case that is undergoing appeal. According to an analysis of 2024 parliamentarians by the Association for Democratic Reforms, 15 winning candidates declared cases related to crimes against women.
For Vedayana, changing the mentality has to begin early with families and the way boys are raised. “If you are in a position of authority, use it to influence people by speaking out against patriarchy and groom your sons first.”
What else we’re reading about
Golden girls | Indian women’s cricket team beat Sri Lanka by 147 runs to win gold at the Asian Games last week. Smriti Mandhana’s smashing 79 off 45 deliveries helped India reach a formidable 216 in 20 overs. Deepti Sharma’s three-wicket haul helped India end Sri Lanka’s hopes with just 69 runs on board. Sri Lanka settled for silver, while Pakistan claimed the bronze after beating Bangladesh.
Moma | A solo exhibition by one of south Asia’s most distinguished artists, Nilima Sheikh, opened at New York’s Museum of Modern Art at the weekend. Fractured Skies, presented in collaboration with the Kiran Nadar Museum of Art in Delhi, will run until next June.
EC under fire | An explosive Indian Express investigation has revealed how two of the top three election officials objected at least 14 times over a period of 10 months to changes made by the Election Commission over its controversial exercise that has struck 130 million people from the voter rolls.

An inquiry committee probing the theft of donations from Ayodhya’s Ram Temple has uncovered 105 instances of cash being removed or concealed. The thefts were caught on CCTV cameras.
According to a preliminary report, some of the accused allegedly hid the money on themselves during the process of counting donations and then walked out.
Vibe check
Tony Klor’s city vlogs from Indian towns are “hella dope,” to use his own words. The 32-year-old American has visited about 200 cities around the country, taking his Instagram followers to places that rarely feature on a travel itinerary.
It’s a treat to watch him having the time of his life. He marched with Anganwadi workers in Nashik chanting “pay my didis”, ribbed with middle-aged uncles sweating it out in a park, whom he christened “Nizamaddies”. Wandering through the mining town of Ballari, which he describes as “highkey vibey”, he films its temple, church and mosque.
“A lot of people who watch my videos are Indians and they have no idea about these magnificent places in India,” the tech professional-turned-content creator says. “India is like the easiest place to make a friend in the world. People invite me to their weddings on the street that I met five minutes before that. Hospitality is so, so next-level.”

Farshid Moussavi Receives the 2026 Soane Medal
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-29
06:30:00 UTC
15:30:00 KST

Farshid Moussavi has been awarded the 2026 Soane Medal for her contributions to architectural practice, history, and theory. The Iranian-born architect and educator, who founded Farshid Moussavi Architecture (FMA) in 2011, will receive the medal at the Royal Academy in London on November 24, 2026, where she will also deliver a public lecture. The annual award, established by Sir John Soane's Museum in 2017, recognizes individuals whose work has contributed to a broader understanding of architecture and its role in society.
Moussavi's practice spans architecture, education, and writing, with projects ranging from cultural and residential buildings to retail interiors. Recent works by FMA include the Museum of Contemporary Art in Cleveland, La Folie Divine apartments in Montpellier, Îlot 19 housing in La Défense-Nanterre, Paris, and the Harrods Toy Department in London. The Museum of Contemporary Art in Cleveland and La Folie Divine reflect the practice's engagement with cultural and residential programs, while Îlot 19 forms part of the mixed-use development of the La Défense-Nanterre district. The practice's largest project to date, the Ismaili Center Houston in Texas, was completed in November 2025 following an international competition.
Born in Shiraz, Iran, in 1965, Moussavi studied at Harvard University Graduate School of Design, University College London, and the University of Dundee. Alongside her professional practice, she has maintained a longstanding involvement in architectural education, teaching at institutions including the Architectural Association, the Berlage Institute, Harvard University, UCLA, Princeton University, and Columbia University. She currently serves as Professor in Practice of Architecture at the Harvard University Graduate School of Design and previously headed the Institute of Architecture at the Academy of Fine Arts in Vienna.
Moussavi has also developed a body of architectural writing addressing the relationship between design, culture, and contemporary practice. She is the author of four books, including Architecture and Micropolitics in 2022. Her research has also addressed social housing and adaptive reuse, while her work on French architect Renée Gailhoustet contributed to renewed attention around Gailhoustet's approach to collective housing.
The 2026 Soane Medal was selected by a jury of architects, critics, and curators chaired by architect Amin Taha. Moussavi joins previous recipients including Madelon Vriesendorp, Hanif Kara, Anne Lacaton and Jean-Philippe Vassal, Peter Barber, Marina Tabassum, Denise Scott Brown, Kenneth Frampton, and Rafael Moneo. Vriesendorp received the 2025 medal and was the first UK-based female artist to receive the award since its establishment.
The 2026 Soane Medal comes amid a series of recent recognitions highlighting contributions to architecture across different contexts. Polish-American architect Daniel Libeskind received the 2026 Praemium Imperiale for Architecture, while Japanese architect Kengo Kuma was selected for the 2027 Andrée Putman Lifetime Achievement Award, recognizing his influence on architecture and the built environment. The 2026 OBEL Award, meanwhile, was given to the Balearic Social Housing Model for its approach to public housing administration and the housing shortage in Spain.

Poland eases rules; will shoot down airspace violators more quickly
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-29
06:29:24 UTC
15:29:24 KST

On the 28th of September, Polish Deputy Defense Minister Cezary Tomczyk announced that Poland plans to simplify the procedure for shooting down objects that have entered its airspace without authorization, Politico reports.
Tensions between Warsaw and Moscow are palpable following repeated Russian violations of Polish airspace in recent weeks, and this decision could cause them to escalate further. Speaking to reporters, Tomczyk explained that pilots currently must not only rely on radar readings but also establish visual contact with an object before shooting it down; this entails flying up to the target to identify exactly what it is.
Now, the Polish Ministry of Defense plans to scrap the visual identification requirement. Tomczyk noted that, once the changes are implemented, a pilot or commander will be able to decide whether to shoot down an object based solely on radar data. The new rules will save time, meaning
Polish fighter jets will be able to shoot down drones and missiles coming from Russia more quickly.
On the 23rd of September, a Russian Mi-8 helicopter briefly entered Polish airspace from the Königsberg region. It penetrated about 300 meters into Polish airspace and remained there for 42 seconds. Poland responded by scrambling fighter jets. The Polish Operational Command commented on the incident, noting that Russia was once again testing the readiness of Poland’s air defenses.
Poland has previously shot down drones that entered its airspace. Around this time last year, Polish Foreign Minister Radosław Sikorski stated that Poland would shoot down Russian fighter jets if they crossed the airspace border, adding that the Russians had been warned.

Australia raises interest rates to 15-year high
Unknown
