Adana food festival targets over 1 million visitors for 10th edition
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-29
06:06:43 UTC
15:06:43 KST

Freshly baked simit and traditional turnip juice are displayed at an Adana food festival stall.
Türkiye’s southern city of Adana is aiming to attract more than 1 million visitors to the 10th International Adana Taste Festival, which will take place from Oct. 9 to 11 at Merkez Park, Governor Mustafa Yavuz said.
The festival welcomed around 800,000 visitors in 2024. Organizers expect attendance to surpass the one-million mark this year as the event marks its 10th anniversary with an expanded international program.
Speaking about preparations, Yavuz said planning has been underway for months through consultations with industry representatives, municipalities, chambers of commerce and commodity exchanges. He noted that the festival, launched in 2017 as a local event, has evolved into an internationally recognized gathering after hosting participants from 12 countries in 2019.
The three-day event will bring together Turkish and foreign chefs, with flavors from countries including India, Mexico and Egypt. The central Anatolian province of Kayseri and the southwestern province of Muğla will participate as guest regions, showcasing their local cuisines.
Yavuz described the festival as a form of “gastro-diplomacy,” saying it promotes Adana’s history, culture, agricultural products and culinary traditions to international audiences.
Known internationally for its spicy kebab dishes, Adana plans to broaden the festival’s culinary focus this year by highlighting desserts, street food and seafood, an area less commonly associated with the city.
The program will include concerts, cooking competitions, harvest tours and workshops. Authorities expect the festival to generate significant economic activity not only in Adana, a city of around 2.3 million people, but also in neighboring provinces, where accommodation facilities are expected to see high occupancy rates during the event.
Organizers are also placing a strong emphasis on sustainability. The 2026 festival will be held under a zero-waste theme, with biodegradable and recyclable products replacing conventional packaging materials, plastic bags and straws. Officials said waste management and environmentally friendly practices would be integrated throughout the event.

Bolat holds talks in Brussels on ‘Made in EU’ initiative
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-29
06:04:52 UTC
15:04:52 KST

Trade Minister Ömer Bolat discussed the potential impact of the European Union’s proposed “Made in EU” approach on Turkish industry during meetings with senior EU officials in Brussels.
Bolat told Anadolu Agency that he met with Stephane Sejourne, the European Commission’s executive vice president for industrial strategy; Marta Kos, commissioner for enlargement, and deputy leaders of the liberal group in the European Parliament.
Discussions focused on the EU’s proposed Industrial Acceleration Act and its “Made in EU” initiative, he added.
The minister said the proposed measures could have significant implications for foreign trade and investment, adding that Türkiye has been regularly conveying its position, expectations and assessments of the possible effects to EU institutions and member states.
He noted that when the issue first emerged on the EU agenda about a year ago, proposals were largely focused on protecting European industry and paid limited attention to their impact on external trade relations.
However, he said the European Commission’s proposal published on March 4 included Türkiye and the EU-Türkiye Customs Union within the scope of the “Made in EU” framework.
He added that restrictive provisions remained in the annexes of the proposal, particularly for the automotive sector, and said Türkiye had communicated its concerns to European Commission officials, members of the European Parliament and ministers from EU member states.
Bolat noted that the Türkiye-EU Business Summit and the third High-Level Trade Dialogue meeting will be held in Brussels in two weeks.
Following the meeting with Kos, Bolat said in a post on X that the EU’s new industrial, competition and trade policies, particularly the Industrial Acceleration Act, should be compatible with the functioning of the Customs Union.
He said both sides agreed to work on a concrete and positive trade agenda, identifying public procurement, technical regulations and connectivity as priority areas for deeper cooperation.

Oil prices rise as bond sell-off hits global markets
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-29
06:03:49 UTC
15:03:49 KST

Oil prices climbed further on Tuesday as uncertainty over US-Iran talks fuelled inflation fears. Government bond yields rose to multi-year highs, putting pressure on stocks.
International crude oil prices climbed further on Tuesday morning amid uncertainty over US-Iran talks, as hopes of reopening the Strait of Hormuz, a waterway crucial to oil shipments, faded.
Hopes that Middle East tensions would ease were dashed at the weekend when Donald Trump rejected Iran’s offer of a seven-day truce.
Mediators are working with the US and Iran on a deal to end the fighting and reopen the Strait of Hormuz, officials told the Associated Press. The disruption to shipping through the waterway has affected global trade and added to inflation.
Iran has proposed reopening the strait if the US lifts its blockade of Iranian ports and eases sanctions, among other conditions. Washington says any deal must also address Iran’s nuclear programme. Officials said the two sides disagree over the timing of concessions and who should act first.
Brent crude, the international benchmark, gained nearly 2% and traded above $107 a barrel early Tuesday, well above its price of roughly $72 a barrel in late February before the Iran war.
US West Texas Intermediate crude rose 1.8% to more than $94 a barrel.
High oil prices have renewed inflation concerns and expectations that the Federal Reserve will raise interest rates again next month. Government bond prices have fallen as a result, pushing yields to multi-year highs.
The benchmark 10-year US Treasury yield rose above 5.27% on Monday, its highest level in 19 years, following a rise of nearly half a percentage point through September. Yields rise when bond prices fall, and this month’s sell-off is the heaviest in two years.
The US two-year yield has risen even further, climbing by more than 0.57 percentage points this month to nearly 5%. In Europe, Germany’s benchmark 10-year bond yield reached 3.62%, its highest level since June 2009.
Government bond yields help set borrowing costs across the economy, from mortgages to company loans. As yields rise, governments, businesses and households face higher costs, while stocks can become less attractive to investors.
In Japan, a 40-year government bond auction drew its strongest demand since 2020 as relatively high yields attracted investors, according to Bloomberg.
Stock markets also struggled after all three main Wall Street indexes fell on Monday.
In Europe, Tuesday's open showed a mixed reaction.
The Euro Stoxx 50 was flat in early trading while the broader pan-European Stoxx 600 traded 0.2% higher.
The UK's FTSE 100, Italy’s FTSE MIB, Spain's IBEX 35 and the Netherlands' AEX all traded between 0.1% and 0.2% higher than their Monday close.
However, France's CAC 40 and Germany's DAX 30 both dropped about 0.5%.
Over in Asia, Japan’s Nikkei 225 lost 1.3%, South Korea’s Kospi declined 0.9% and Hong Kong’s Hang Seng dropped 0.6%. Hong Kong-traded shares of Shein fell 11.7% after the online retailer reported a 67% fall in quarterly adjusted net profit from a year earlier.
The Shanghai Composite was little changed following a report from China’s official Xinhua News Agency late Monday that its State Council had discussed ways to make economic policies more effective.
Australia’s S&P/ASX 200 was down more than 0.1% by early morning in Europe.
Australia’s central bank raised its key interest rate by 0.25 percentage points to 4.6% on Tuesday, a 15-year high, as rising oil prices fuelled inflation. The Reserve Bank said higher fuel costs were pushing up prices across the economy, while growth and inflation had been stronger than expected.
The US dollar edged up to 157.42 Japanese yen from 157.39 yen. The euro fell to $1.1362 from $1.1371.
Gold remained near $4,160 after steep losses on Monday, as expectations of further rate rises weighed on the metal, which pays no interest.
Investors are also awaiting key US inflation and jobs data this week that could influence the Fed’s next decision. Markets are pricing in another rate rise at the end of October.

Euronews Travel & Tourism Summit 2026: Watch live from Brussels
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-29
06:00:58 UTC
15:00:58 KST

The Euronews Travel & Tourism Summit 2026 is taking place in Brussels, bringing together political leaders, policymakers and industry experts to debate the biggest issues shaping the future of travel.
Europe’s travel industry is in the spotlight today at the Euronews Travel & Tourism Summit 2026 at the Albert Hall in Brussels.
Throughout the day, Euronews will be live from the Belgian capital with interviews, panels and debates exploring how tourism is responding to a year marked by geopolitical disruption, airspace closures and extreme weather.
Follow this page for live updates and highlights from the Euronews Travel & Tourism Summit 2026 in Brussels
‘We have to put our money where our mouth is’
Members of the European Parliament must work to ensure that under-the-radar destinations are able to grow their tourism sectors, while hotspots need "room to breathe”, according to Daniel Attard MEP, S&D.
Speaking during the panel “Managing visitor flows and shaping tomorrow’s destinations”, he said that there is no use in encouraging travellers to venture beyond the beaten path, especially if there are no means to be able to connect them to those destinations.
As such, “we have to put the money where our mouth is at the European level”, he said, adding that “we have to create better connections, invest in new connections”, as well as bolster aviation services.
Attard was joined by Ourania Georgoutsakou, Managing Director of Airlines for Europe (A4E), who added that air connectivity is equally as important. She also noted that the trend over the past few years has seen the shoulder season extend and steadily grow by upwards of 30%.
“People are choosing to go longer and that kind of collaboration with the local hospitality sector, with the authorities, allows an offering of an extended season, which is an important way of going forward,” she said.
While when it comes to destinations experimenting with tourist taxes to manage demand, Marta Machado, Deputy Director General of HOTREC - Hotels, Restaurants, Bars & Cafés in Europe, highlighted the need for better data, especially on the continent's short-term holiday homes to enact better decisions "on the management of the completion capacity of the visitor flows".
Edi Rama speaks exclusively to Euronews
Speaking exclusively to Maria Tadeo at the Euronews Travel & Tourism Summit, Albanian Prime Minister Edi Rama explained that his country is making significant leaps and strides in the tourism world.
He explained that Albania used to be the “most isolated country in Europe and the North Korea of Europe” and that, after it had emerged, it was “confronted with very, very disturbing stereotypes”.
Rama added that the country plans to target the world in terms of tourism. He admitted that the country’s infrastructure is somewhat lacking, but that it’s improving significantly.
He claimed that it has an airport that is “the fastest growing airport of Europe”, and there are plans in place to open a new airport in Vlorë, and another seasonal hub in the country’s south.
“We have a fourth up in the mountains, but it’s not yet working as we wish,” he added.
‘The South Caucasus is completely underrated’: Azerbaijan calls for more visitors
Azerbaijan is looking to expand its tourism offer beyond Baku, with the country’s tourism chief highlighting its natural diversity, cultural heritage and growing connectivity as it seeks to attract more international visitors.
Speaking to moderator Jane Witherspoon, Florian Sengstschmid, CEO of the Azerbaijan Tourism Board, said the wider South Caucasus region remains largely overlooked by international travellers.
“The South Caucasus is completely underrated,” he said, adding that Azerbaijan had “much more to come and much more to offer”.
He urged visitors to venture beyond the capital and explore the country’s Silk Road heritage, ancient villages, UNESCO sites and mountain landscapes.
“It really is to travel beyond Baku, to travel along the Silk Road through side valleys, ancient heritage villages, UNESCO World Heritage sites,” he said.
Azerbaijan is also working to improve international connectivity, with Brussels set to gain four weekly flights to Baku from May 2027.
Schmid said tourism development should also benefit local communities, pointing to villages where investment had helped create businesses and revive traditional crafts.
But he said growth should not simply be measured by visitor numbers.
“Is it all about the numbers? No, it’s not all about the numbers,” Sengstschmid said.
“It’s about how you really increase the length of stay. How do you make people enjoy more of the country during their journey?”
His ambition, he added, was for “a few more travellers, but a higher impact”.
Romania invites travellers to explore beyond Bucharest
Dan-Adrian Pop, Romania’s Secretary of State at the Ministry of Economy, Digitalisation, Entrepreneurship and Tourism, spoke to moderator Evi Kiorri about one of the most exciting emerging destinations in Europe.
Despite Romania’s proximity to Ukraine and the ongoing conflict, Pop urged visitors to come and see the nation for themselves.
“Overall, I would say that we are safe as any other European country. The whole country is very well protected, and from internal security for the citizens and for the travellers, I think we are one of the safest countries in Europe,” he said.
Bucharest as a destination has long been popular with European travellers, but Pop explained that Romania has so much more to offer than just the charms of its capital.
“We focus very much on rural tourism, spa tourism, and adventure and active tourism,” he said.
“They have a lot of options to be out in nature and close to the citizens, to the people who live there, who know the places, and who guide them through this experience.”
He also praised the vast amount of walking routes in the country, some “1,000 kilometres from north to south, through the Carpathian Mountains”.
While he admitted that infrastructure is lacking in some places, and the summer season isn’t as long as in other European nations, there’s still plenty to experience thanks, in part, to the country’s citizens.
“The people of Romania are one of our most valuable promoters, and they know the destinations, the local destinations that would fit for their friends. They are the first ones to invite their friends all over the world to Romania,” Pop said.
Cruise industry targeting younger travellers and greener future
Gianni Onorato, CEO of MSC Cruises, speaking to Hannah Brown as part of The Big Question, has said the sector is attracting a younger generation of travellers, while diversification and new technology could help it tackle concerns around overtourism and environmental impact.
The cruise executive also said the profile of passengers had changed significantly during his 40 years in the industry.
“While now there is a much younger demographic. The average age is 35 to 54. A lot of families, a lot of young people, and this is very good because this can ensure the future of this industry,” he said.
He also pushed back against the perception that cruise passengers simply arrive in a destination, spend little money and leave again, pointing to the industry's wider economic contribution.
“Cruises contribute to the European economy by €65 billion a year and with 445,000 permanent jobs,” he said.
He argued that cruise operators could also help spread tourism beyond Europe's busiest destinations by working with local authorities and promoting lesser-known ports.
“We are looking very much to diversify our destinations,” he said, highlighting the Greek island of Syros, close to the more famous Santorini and Mykonos.
“Syros is becoming more and more on the map of tourism, and we are very happy about it because it is also helping to respond to the [overtourism problem],” he added.
The executive also pointed to the potential for cruises to support tourism outside the traditional summer season, noting that ships can move between destinations as weather conditions change.
On sustainability, he said the industry was making progress but still had work to do. He said MSC had reduced its emissions by almost 42 per cent against its 2008 baseline, putting it “almost five years ahead of the checkpoint for 2030”.
But he said the availability of cleaner fuels remained a major challenge.
“The target is there. There is only one issue: the fuel availability. So that needs to be produced at large scale,” he said.
Looking ahead, he predicted that cruise holidays would continue to attract new audiences, including solo travellers and multigenerational families.
“More and more we will have a younger audience. By the way, we will have new segments: solo travellers. It’s a new segment, very important,” he said.
Onorato also suggested the industry could increasingly move away from measuring success simply by passenger numbers.
“I believe tourism in general will be much less measured on the quantity, on the volumes, but much more on the quality of the emotions that we are able to give to the travellers and also the quality of the contribution, not only economically, that we can give to the locals and local community,” he said.
Sustainability in focus
Sustainability, affordability and accessibility can work together, but tourism needs to balance environmental, social and economic considerations, panellists told the Euronews Travel & Tourism Summit.
Speaking to moderator Mike Starling, Andreea Stăjcu, Deputy Head of Unit, Head of Tourism Sector, DG MOVE at the European Commission, said travellers themselves were increasingly demanding more sustainable options.
“The travellers really want to travel in a sustainable way,” she said, pointing to cycling and night trains as examples.
MEP and former Croatian tourism minister Nikolina Brnjac said sustainability could not be reduced to environmental measures alone.
“It is achievable, but only if we approach it in three pillars: social, environmental and economical,” she said, adding that better rail and public transport connections were needed to reach rural and peripheral areas.
Managing visitor numbers was another key theme. “We must not be afraid of the numbers,” Brnjac said.
“It’s bad management of the tourist flows.”
István Ujhelyi, former MEP and UN Tourism official, similarly stressed that tourism growth cannot simply be stopped.
“You can’t stop this growing,” he said, noting that international tourist numbers had risen from 25 million in 1950 to more than 1.5 billion last year.
Sven Wiltink of Radisson Hotel Group said sustainability needed to become part of the industry’s core business, rather than an optional extra.
“Sustainability is not a bolt-on element,” he said.
Central Europe as 'one destination'
Olivér Csendes, President, Hungarian Tourism Agency and Sandrine Buffenoir, Director, Netherlands, Belgium & Luxembourg, Atout France, sat down with moderator Mared Gwyn-Jones to talk about looking at Central Europe as one destination and the inextricable link between nature and tourism.
Oliver Cndish, representing the Hungarian Tourism Agency, said tourism should be used to promote Central Europe as a single, interconnected destination rather than being constrained by national borders.
“I would love to see more international collaborations where we position the way we live and our regions, basically as one destination,” he said.
“We don’t have to limit our thinking and the creation of experience spaces to national borders,” he added.
Cndish pointed to the relatively short distances between European countries as an opportunity to create multi-country experiences - part of the popular “trip-maxxing” trend, which has gained traction this year especially.
“If you look at it from the US or Asian perspective, the distances are very small in Europe. You can travel 100 kilometres, and you have already touched two or three Central European capitals,” he said.
He also highlighted the Danube as an example of an attraction that could be promoted across borders.
“We have treasures like the Danube, that’s found in a lot of countries in Europe, and has always been a connection, connecting cultures,” he said. “So why not use this as an active part of the experience that people will have, enriching their lives and the way they see and experience Europe.”
Cndish also praised cooperation within the EU, saying: “I believe Europe is doing an amazing job collaborating.”
He pointed to the European data space for tourism as one example, saying it could help countries work together on issues including visitor flows and extreme weather.
“Think about all the discussions we had about visitor flow, protecting visitors, warning them in case there is a danger, whether it’s wildfire, whether it’s whatever different extreme weather conditions. This is only possible if we have the right data at the right places,” he said.
He also stressed the importance of protecting the natural environment, saying: “There is no tourism without nature.”
“Tourism needs to be a force for good and needs to also support the resilience of the living areas,” he added.
Atout France’s Benelux director Sandrine Buffeno also highlighted tourism’s role in bringing Europeans together.
“Tourism is a key aspect of connection between all European people. It’s a key factor in knowing each other better, in working together better, living with each other,” she said.
“It’s a classroom to learn about each other,” she added.
'Climate change the biggest threat to tourism'
Eduardo Santander, the CEO of the European Travel Commission, sat down with moderator Mared Gwyn-Jones to speak about the impact of the threat of climate change on global tourism and the role of Europe as a destination.
The CEO explained that “climate change is the biggest threat to tourism right now, by far.”
He was speaking following a summer of record heat and related travel chaos across the continent.
“We see that trains cannot run sometimes because the rails are expanded because of the heat. We saw this at the cruise lines on the European rivers - they couldn’t run because it was too dry,” Santander said.
“We have to prepare for that in a much more coordinated and comprehensive way,” he added.
“We see resilience becoming one of the engines of European tourism. We have to become even more resilient to whatever is next.”
Santander explained that, due to the impact of climate change, travel and tourism is getting less affordable.
“Travelling is becoming much more expensive, and you all have travelled this summer, I guess, and you notice it in your pockets.”
He also spoke about the trend for “coolcations”, which have gained plenty of traction this year, especially: “We see a lot of people from southern European destinations looking for what we call ‘cool locations’ — places that are cooler in summer and where you can enjoy the weather in a more predictable way.”
Santander also emphasised the economic importance of tourism, which makes up some 10% of the European economy, a figure that rises to between 15% and 20% of some nation’s GDP.
He also sang the praises of Europe as a tourism destination.
“Europe is becoming the playground, some people call it. It’s becoming a museum, an attraction park,” he said, asking, “what’s wrong with that?”
“An attraction park or a museum is a perfect place to be. Normally it’s well organised, well managed, they have a nice restaurant, they have clean toilets, so there’s nothing wrong.”
US Global Entry for Belgians by end of 2026?
Bill White, the Ambassador of the United States of America to the Kingdom of Belgium, sat down with summit host Jane Witherspoon to speak about the special relationship between the two nations.
While the Ambassador praised Belgium for having so much more to offer than “waffles, chocolate and beer”, he did criticise the lines at the airport in Brussels, saying they “suck”.
“They’re really bad. One of the things we have to do in our transatlantic alliance and relationship is to recognise that if we want people to come to Belgium, we have to fix this problem. It must get better immediately,” he added.
Nevertheless, White announced that he has received approval from President Donald Trump to allow Belgian citizens to apply for the US Global Entry programme, which is designed to speed up entry at US airports. Global Entry is a DHS programme for pre-approved international travellers.
In practical terms, he explained, that means: “you’ll register, you pay your fee, get vetted, and then you fly to the United States, and you look at the kiosk at JFK or wherever it is, you smile, don’t smile, you get ‘whoop!’ right through, and then you go get your bags and spend money”.
He urged Belgian citizens to “write to your congressman or your parliament person, let’s go, get the paperwork done, because when you travel, it’ll be seamless. One, two, three.”

UN warns of ‘narrowing window’ to restore world’s forests
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-29
06:00:56 UTC
15:00:56 KST

The world faces a “narrowing window” to restore forests essential for food security and resistance to the climate emergency, a United Nations report has warned.
More than 489m hectares (1.2bn acres) of forests have been cleared since 1990, while an even greater area is degraded, the world body said in a call for governments to make forest restoration a national priority.
The State of the World’s Forests report acknowledges recent steps forward in protection and tree planting around the globe but says action has not kept pace with commitments.
Over the past two decades, national, regional and global initiatives have promised to place more than 1bn hectares of land under restoration, but barely a fifth of that is actually being restored, the report by the UN Food and Agriculture Organization (FAO) notes, saying: “Progress is uneven, and it is insufficient to meet growing global needs.”
Forests, which cover 4.14bn hectares (about a third of Earth’s land surface), store 714 gigatonnes of carbon and host up to 80% of the world’s terrestrial biodiversity. They also play an important role in regulating rainfall and in reducing hunger, with nearly one-third of the global population depending on them for livelihoods.
Threats are intensifying. Every year, about 127m hectares of forest are affected by fires, with further damage caused by insects, diseases and severe weather events. This is making forests ever more vulnerable, as it comes on top of pressure from farm expansion, the climate crisis, pollution and the extraction of fossil fuels and other resources.
“This widening gap between demand and sustainable supply highlights a structural imbalance that threatens both ecological integrity and the long-term viability of forest-based economies,” the report states.
It says remedial action on forests and other degraded ecosystems would benefit people, food security and the economy – with restoration of 1bn hectares estimated to generate $1.8tn in benefits each year.
Qu Dongyu, the FAO director general, said the report “makes clear that forest and landscape restoration is more than an environmental priority – it is a strategic investment in resilient agrifood systems and rural development”.
He said: “The window for action is narrowing, and delayed or poorly designed restoration will increase long-term costs, exacerbate inequalities and risk locking landscapes into unsustainable trajectories. Given the continued loss and degradation of forest ecosystems, as well as growing global demand for land-based products and services, there is an urgent need to scale up effective restoration.”

KT, London

An independent surveyor, commissioned by you in May – when you had reached an impasse with the company – concluded that the damaged extension needed underpinning or rebuilding. There was no obvious progress in the case, however.

Hospitals in England hit by shortages of common drugs such as paracetamol
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-29
06:00:56 UTC
15:00:56 KST

Hospitals are being hit by shortages of key drugs used to provide pain relief, prevent blood clots and tackle high blood pressure.
Dozens of NHS trusts in England have encountered scarcities of aspirin, the painkiller co-codamol – a combination of paracetamol and codeine – and ramipril, a blood pressure tablet.
Nine trusts have had problems getting enough supplies of two of those three common medications, while one – Kent community health NHS trust – ran short of all three.
The shortages underline how precarious the health service’s supply chains for basic medicines have become in recent years as a result of trade disputes, global conflict and manufacturing problems.
Pharmacists have said supply problems have become a “national crisis” and in some cases have left patients unable to access their usual medications for weeks at a time.
Hospitals’ drug supply problems have emerged in freedom of information requests by Dr Rodolfo Catena, an expert in global health supplies at University College London, about stock levels of the three drugs. Sixty of the 184 trusts from which he sought figures responded.
The most widespread shortage involved aspirin, which is used to reduce pain and the risk of blood clots. Twenty-six (62%) of the 42 trusts that responded about it had experienced disruption to their supplies between last December and March this year.
Thirteen (31%) of the 42 trusts that replied on co-codamol had run short of that drug, which helps relieve muscle pain, period pain and toothache. York and Scarborough NHS trust’s supplies had been disrupted since May 2025, and Royal Wolverhampton NHS trust had trouble getting enough co-codamol for the 10 months between October 2025 and August this year.
Seven (16%) of the 43 trusts that answered Catena’s question about ramipril had been unable to get as much of it as they needed. More than a third of adults in England are thought to have dangerously high blood pressure, which heightens the risk of a heart attack or stroke, but 59% are unaware they have it, research showed last week.
Frimley Health NHS trust, which cares for people in Surrey, Berkshire and Buckinghamshire, resorted to paying higher prices for ramipril to ensure uninterrupted supply of it, rather than risk supply problems that would affect patients, Catena found.
His findings tally with National Pharmacy Association analysis. It has found that although shortages in recent years have mainly been of specialist drugs, for example to treat ADHD and epilepsy, supply problems now often involve generic medicines, which are much cheaper to produce.
Catena, an associate professor in operations and supply chain management in UCL’s Global Business School for Health, believes the shortages he found show that NHS England is wrong to classify drug scarcities in its operational risk register as only a “medium” risk to the provision of care.
NHS England has given drug shortages a score of 16 out of 25 on its risk assessment scale. But the widespread nature of shortages makes it unlikely that it will be able to fulfil its ambition to reduce that score to nine by next month, Catena added.
Improving supply chain resilience is also a key priority for the Department of Health and Social Care. Catena called on it to change the current system whereby only drug companies are obliged to warn it about any impending shortages. He said NHS trusts should be put under the same obligation so that service bosses were more aware of disruption to drug supplies and could act to minimise them.
Almost all (92%) of the trusts that responded said they had no contingency plan to tackle supply problems and 82% said they had not reported the scarcities they were facing to NHS England.
A spokesperson for the Society for Acute Medicine, which represents hospital doctors, said: “Medicine shortages can disrupt treatment and create additional pressure for clinical and pharmacy teams. The key is ensuring resilient supply chains, timely communication and access to suitable alternatives so patient care is not delayed.”
A health department spokesperson said: “We regularly speak to NHS trusts and national clinical leads about medicine availability and are aware that ramipril is in limited supply, which is why we issued serious shortage protocols so patients in the UK can still get the medication they need. We are working closely with relevant suppliers to resolve this and issues with co-codamol and aspirin to ensure continuity of supply.
“The vast majority of the UK’s licensed medicines are in good supply, and we have robust measures in place to mitigate disruption for patients. This government is investing in the UK medicine manufacturing industry to manage supply disruptions where they occur.”

Mac mini M6 review: truly mighty but now more pricey
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-29
06:00:55 UTC
15:00:55 KST

Apple’s latest Mac mini brings real speed and power for far more than everyday tasks in a practically pocketable form you can fit almost anywhere.
The impressive new desktop machine is the first to receive an update to Apple’s latest M6 chip while remaining smaller than a headphones box. It is the cheapest computer Apple sells with an M-series chip, but like every other memory-containing piece of electronics, it has been hit by RAMageddon, driving up the starting price to £899 (€1,049/$899/A$1,449) from the £599 or equivalent of its M4 predecessor.
Apple introduced the Mac mini’s dainty form with 2024’s M4 model, which remains the same for the new M6 version. A lot has changed since the M2 Mac mini, which was pretty compact. The current mini measures just 12.7cm square and 5cm thick, with rounded corners and a solid aluminium body. It’s happy to sit on a desk, but is small and light enough to mount behind a monitor to turn any screen into a DIY iMac.
The machine is fairly minimalist. A small LED on the front shows you when it’s on. The back has three Thunderbolt 4 (USB4) ports, a 2.5Gb ethernet socket, an HDMI 2.1 port, and a figure-eight power cable. It lacks any USB-A ports, but adapters are readily available for legacy devices not yet converted to USB-C, such as flash drives or printers.
It has basic speakers built in, which are good enough for macOS’s notification sounds.
The mini runs the latest macOS 27 Golden Gate, which brings welcome refinements to Apple’s Liquid Glass design that was introduced last year. But the big update is a relaunch of Apple’s Siri assistant and AI tools. Siri AI, as it is now known, is vastly superior at understanding and performing tasks, such as finding information on your Mac or the web, and has a dedicated app to see previous interactions. It can read what’s on your screen, so you can ask it to track parcels from just a code in your email or find an object from an image with the CMD+Shift+Space keyboard shortcut.
Siri is integrated into Spotlight search, which is handy but sometimes results in it trying to search the web instead of launching an app or a file on your Mac if you mistype, which can be frustrating.
Apple Intelligence is smarter too. Writing, proofing and summarising tools are built in and accessible from most apps, along with a collection of other features. The most surprisingly useful tool I found was file and folder naming suggestions, which made matching long file-naming schemes a doddle. Boring but very useful.
Specifications
- 
  Processor: Apple M6
- 
  RAM: 16, 24 or 32GB
- 
  Storage: 256, 512GB, 1 or 2TB SSD
- 
  Operating system: macOS 27 Golden Gate
- 
  Ports back: 3x Thunderbolt/USB 4, HDMI 2.1, 2.5Gb Ethernet
- 
  Ports front: 2x USB-C (USB3), headphones
- 
  Connectivity: wifi 7, Bluetooth 6, Thread
- 
  Dimensions: 127 x 127 x 50mm
- 
  Weight: 670g
Serious M6 speed
The Mac mini is offered with the newest Apple Silicon chip, the M6 (as tested) or with an M5 Pro, which has greater performance in multicore or graphics applications.
For most people the M6 is more than enough, with the fastest single core performance of any of Apple’s chips by about 8.5% in testing. That means it absolutely flies along with apps launching near instantly and tasks just flying by. Compared with the previous generation M4 Mac mini, the new machine is about 25% faster in single core tasks, 50% faster in multicore tasks with graphics performance about 75% faster. That makes it a giant leap over older machines coming to the end of their useful lives.
The machine is also power efficient and runs silently unless pushed to the limit, and even then is very quiet.
Sustainability
The Mac mini is made with 50% recycled materials. Apple breaks down the computer’s environmental impact in its report. Apple offers trade-in and free recycling schemes, including for non-Apple products.
Price
The Mac mini M6 costs from £899 (€1,049/$899/A$1,449) with 16GB of RAM and 256GB of storage.
For comparison, the A18 Pro MacBook Neo costs from £699, the M5 MacBook Air starts at £1,299, the M4 iMac starts at £1,499 and the Mac Studio costs from £2,499.
Verdict
The Mac mini is a fantastic general computer squeezed into a tiny box that fits just about anywhere. The new M6 chip has buckets of power and performance for practically anything. If you know you need more graphics performance the M5 Pro chip is also available, but at a significant cost.
The port selection is very good for a machine of this size, only lacking traditional USB-A ports of those commonly needed. With three Thunderbolt 4 (USB4) ports it’s easy to add a dock or hub if you really need more connectivity.
The only downside is the RAMageddon-linked price hike that makes the Mac mini M6 slightly less of an instant recommendation than its predecessor. At £899 (€1,049/$899/A$1,449), it is still a lot of Mac for the money, just not the total bargain the M4 version used to be.
 Pros: very fast M6 chip, quiet and cool running, plenty of ports, headphones socket, 2.5GbE, wifi 7, Bluetooth 6 and Thread support.
Cons: price hike, no expandable/replaceable storage or memory, no USB-A ports, no SD card slot, only 256GB of storage in base model, power button on base is difficult to reach.

British and US forces obliterate target off Scottish coast
United Kingdom
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-29
07:00:45 BST
15:00:45 KST

Ships, aircraft and a submarine from the United States and the United Kingdom have concluded Exercise Atlantic Thunder 2026 in the North Atlantic, a multi-domain sinking exercise that ended with the destruction of the decommissioned guided missile frigate ex-USS Klakring, according to United States Sixth Fleet, which led it.
Captain Kelechi Ndukwe, commander of Task Force 65, told the UK Defence Journal that the exercise ran from 14 to 25 September, with the sinking itself carried out on 21 September some 150 nautical miles offshore of the Hebrides range. Forces assigned to five American task forces took part, numbered 65, 67, 68, 69 and 1060, alongside the Royal Navy and the United States Air Force.
Asked by this publication what the objectives behind the joint targeting had been, whether they were met, and what an exercise of this kind signals to those who might be watching, Ndukwe said: “We used national technical means to be able to put this together, and I think what it really highlights is the strong bond between the U.S. and the U.K. Our ability to trust each other, to share information, and to show that we are a joint and strong and united force. Peace through strength is really what it shows. Our ability to reach out and touch at the longest distance possible is what we displayed, and you know I think it just shows our ability to be able to work together and interact and really push the limits here.”
In his formal statement on the exercise he put the same argument more bluntly. “Atlantic Thunder demonstrates the unmatched lethality and interoperability of the United States and United Kingdom,” he said. “This sinking exercise not only validated the power behind U.S.-UK offensive weapons but delivers a clear message to adversaries that the U.S. Navy and Royal Navy remain a ready allied force.”
Asked by the UK Defence Journal how much had changed since the previous Atlantic Thunder, held off the same range in 2022, the captain identified reach as the difference. “In past iterations of Atlantic Thunder, we weren’t able to test at the longest range, and I think that’s the biggest change from previous exercises,” he said. “This one, we really were able to test the multi-domain, multi-axis, incorporating the Air Force into it, and really test the boundaries of range for this one, and the new technologies over the past four years that we’re able to bring into play here.”
The guided missile destroyer USS Paul Ignatius demonstrated what Sixth Fleet called the maximum damage and range capability of an anti-surface variant of the Standard Missile 6, and the submarine USS Massachusetts then engaged the target with the Mark 48 Advanced Capability Torpedo, which Sixth Fleet said resulted in the final hit and ultimately sank the frigate. Ndukwe said the sequence had been worked out in advance so the sensors recorded each impact in turn. “We started with the longest range ordnance, which is why we were going with SM-6 first, and then moved in to shorter range,” he said, adding that the SM-6 shot was testing the surface-to-surface engagement at the furthest range available, a figure he said could not be shared.
Britain confirmed both of its newest ship-busting missiles during the same serial, firing the Naval Strike Missile from HMS Portland and Sea Venom from a Wildcat helicopter of 815 Naval Air Squadron. Ndukwe confirmed at the briefing that the Sea Venom shot was the missile’s first live firing since it reached initial operating capability, and that it hit the target.
Lieutenant Commander Louise Kirkaldy, Portland’s principal warfare officer, said: “The successful firing of NSM marks a significant milestone for the Royal Navy, demonstrating our ability to deliver credible, modern maritime strike capability. This achievement reflects the professionalism, dedication and teamwork of all those involved, whose hard work has ensured we remain ready to meet the challenges of today and tomorrow.” Petty Officer James Kenyon, the above water warfare specialist who fired it, called it “the culmination of over a year’s effort in planning and bringing the drills into service.”
No uncrewed systems took part at any stage, the captain confirmed when the question was put to him directly, which sets the exercise apart from much of the trials work now running in British waters.
Four years went into the preparation, involving serving personnel alongside civilian counterparts. On the American side Ndukwe named the portfolio acquisition executive organisation, the Navy Information Warfare Command and the Naval Surface Warfare Center as having worked jointly on it, “ensuring that sensors were properly installed on the frigate to be able to take that data back, inform future capabilities, and really push the envelope on what we’re able to do with future weapons designs.” Sixth Fleet has since said the sensors were placed by Naval Surface Warfare Center Carderock and Naval Information Warfare Center Pacific, and that the data will be used to identify system failures rapidly, determine repair needs and strengthen the navy’s response in a real engagement.
Communications were the part the commander said he was proudest of, and the link architecture was built out by United States Sixth Fleet and run from its headquarters, then shared with HMS Portland, and he said there were no difficulties with it during the exercise. “We were really proud of the ability to communicate throughout the entirety of the exercise,” he said, adding that shared battle damage assessment “will ensure that the Navy and our navies will continue to be capable and lethal fighting forces.”
The units involved covered Paul Ignatius, Massachusetts, HMS Portland, P-8 maritime patrol aircraft flown by both the United States Navy and the Royal Air Force, a Royal Navy Wildcat helicopter, United States Air Force F-15E Strike Eagles, and personnel from Explosive Ordnance Disposal Mobile Unit 8.
On why an American hull was brought across the Atlantic rather than a British one used, Ndukwe described a cost-sharing arrangement between the two governments. “That was part of the agreement between the two navies and the departments of defense, was that we would pay for the tow of the ship across, and then the Royal Navy or the UK would pay for the range,” he said. Klakring entered service on 20 August 1983 and was decommissioned on 22 March 2013, and was named for Rear Admiral Thomas B. Klakring, who won three Navy Crosses commanding the submarine USS Guardfish in the Second World War, as we reported.
What remains of her will stay on the seabed off the Hebrides. “For the environmental side, it was all done during the course of the planning. It was approved by the EPA in advance, and it’ll become a natural reef. It’s sunk in a deep, deep valley there, right off the Hebrides,” the captain said. Sixth Fleet added that in line with Ministry of Defence environmental policy, monitoring was carried out above and below the surface by trained personnel to reduce the risk of harm to the marine environment and to marine mammals.
North Atlantic weather presented obstacles during the serial, Ndukwe said, though all the primary objectives were met and nothing the team had wanted to test failed. Asked by the UK Defence Journal whether work had begun on a follow-on, he confirmed that it had. “Planning has started with the goal of execution in 2028,” he said.

Modular House with a Sloping Facade / Papundekl Architects

This single-story family home in a South Bohemian village navigates a dual context: it respects local rural heritage on one side while completely opening up to nature on the other. Designed for a couple in their 60s who wish to spend their time cycling and living closer to nature, the building blurs the boundary between interior and exterior by turning its back to the village road and facing a secluded forest with a stream.

He also stressed that the EU’s new budget should respond to the current security situation and the threats posed by Russia.
Cohesion policy and the common agricultural policy remain key instruments for achieving the EU’s objectives. At the same time, they help to strengthen Europe’s competitiveness, resilience, and food security,
underlined Deputy Minister Ignacy Niemczycki.
On the EU’s budgetary income, he said that Poland is ready to continue talks about new sources for financing the EU budget and noted that they should not lead to increased financial burden on the less-developed member states.
The ministers also discussed the agenda for the European Council’s October session. Deputy Minister Ignacy Niemczycki highlighted Poland’s unchanged stance on Russia’s aggression against Ukraine, solidarity with Ukraine, and the need to resume debate on the use of the frozen Russian assets. Besides, he spoke for the need to devise innovative solutions regarding Russia’s hybrid operations and migration pressure.
While discussing the rule of law, the secretary of state said that Poland supports the objectives of the dialogue within the Council of the European Council, such as: promoting and safeguarding the rule of law and exchanging best practices in a spirit of mutual respect. Greater consideration of the views of the business community and a more in-depth analysis of the activities of regulatory bodies, including public procurement and competition authorities, should help to increase legal certainty for small and medium-sized enterprises, strengthen the EU’s competitiveness, and improve the functioning of the internal market.

NATO commander warns EU defense efforts must not rival alliance
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-29
05:56:05 UTC
14:56:05 KST

Gen. Alexus Grynkewich, NATO Supreme Allied Commander Europe, left, and Gen. Nick Perry, commander of Joint Force Command Norfolk, right, speak to the media after an assumption of command ceremony aboard the USS Nimitz at Naval Station Norfolk in Norfolk, Va., Sept. 24, 2026. (Peter Casey/The Virginian-Pilot via AP)
Any defense structure developed by the European Union should complement NATO rather than compete with the alliance, NATO’s top military commander in Europe has said, warning that parallel structures could strain limited resources.
Gen. Alexus G. Grynkewich, NATO’s Supreme Allied Commander Europe, made the remarks on Sept. 28 during a meeting of the European Parliament’s Security and Defence Committee and its delegation for relations with the NATO Parliamentary Assembly.
“Whatever it is that the EU does with its member states and how it structures, should not be in competition with NATO,” Grynkewich said.
He said separate structures would be costly and risk duplicating capabilities already available through NATO.
Grynkewich also called for closer EU-NATO cooperation on defense procurement, pointing to European initiatives that give preference to EU-made products in strategic sectors.
Such policies are particularly important for defense companies from the United States, Canada, Britain, Norway and Türkiye, he said.
Grynkewich cautioned against rigid rules based on where military equipment is manufactured, arguing that battlefield performance should take precedence over its country of origin.
The ultimate goal should be for NATO and the EU to work in coordination to provide military personnel with the best available equipment, he said.
Grynkewich also pointed to the NATO Summit Defence Industry Forum held in Ankara in July, where more than 50 billion euros in new procurement deals were announced, including projects involving strategic airlift, surveillance and intelligence capabilities.
He said the EU’s financial and regulatory tools and NATO’s military requirements could reinforce each other, calling for deeper cooperation between the two organizations.

RAF Fairford bomb plot 'clearly involves' foreign actor, US secretary of state says
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-29
05:53:32 UTC
14:53:32 KST

Iran's embassy in London has said it "categorically rejects and strongly condemns" speculation that Tehran was involved in the incident.
A UK probe into a suspected bomb plot at an airbase used by the United States was mired in confusion on Tuesday, after media reported no explosives were detected in the vehicles seized nearby.
As armed guards maintained a cordon around a nearby village, Washington questioned the decision to release on bail five men arrested near the Royal Air Force Fairford base in southwest England.
Three white vans were discovered near the base on Sunday and the men, all London-based Britons in their mid-20s, were detained.
Armed police were also visible on Tuesday patrolling around the airfield used by US planes to bomb some targets in Iran.
Police have said officers conducted an extensive examination of the vehicles with the help of "military assets" and forensic experts.
They did not disclose their findings. But The Times newspaper and several other UK media outlets have reported that police found no traces of explosives, easing fears that an attack had been foiled but leaving many questions unanswered.
A resident in the neighbouring village of Kempsford, Patricia told the AFP news agency it was "very embarrassing that people around the world thought it was a terrorist attack but in the end no, it's a lot of noise for nothing."
Announcing the release of the five suspects on Monday, the head of UK Counter Terrorism Policing, Assistant Commissioner Laurence Taylor, said the men "absolutely remain under investigation."
He insisted his officers were keeping an "open mind" and considering "every possible angle" in the security scare, including the possible role of "proxies" working knowingly or unknowingly for a foreign state.
Iran's embassy in London has said it "categorically rejects and strongly condemns" speculation that Tehran was involved.
'Serious situation'
Adding to the hazy picture, US President Donald Trump told reporters on Monday he was "surprised" that British police had released the five, adding: "I wouldn't have done that."
Hours later, US Secretary of State Marco Rubio called the incident "a very serious situation...that clearly involves the hand of a foreign actor" but declined to provide further details.
On Sunday, Trump had said the UK and US were investigating the suspects "for a long time" and that they "were looking to do big damage to our fort."
The security scare became public after a farmer living in the village of Whelford near the airbase rang police after seeing the three vans blocking a road and a group of masked men fleeing the scene.
Armed officers arrested the five men on suspicion of explosives offences and, later, "suspicion of preparing a terrorist act" under anti-terror laws.
Security at the base had reportedly been heightened recently.
Britain gave Washington permission in March to use Fairford for "specific defensive operations into Iran" to destroy Iranian missiles at source.
US bombers and other planes have since been seen taking off and landing from the base, the only one on Britain's mainland used for this purpose.
The lack of clarity over the weekend incident has sparked different unverified theories, with some media reporting allegations that the men could even be fuel thieves.
"It's a bit odd they were here in the middle of the night," one local told AFP as she did some gardening in the nearby village of Kempsford.
"If they were true terrorists they wouldn't have released them," she added, asking not to give her name.
Aerial footage of the vans showed they appeared to contain barrels, and at least one was marked with a fake logo and phone number giving the false impression that it was owned by a legitimate diesel delivery firm.
The legitimate firm said in a statement on its website that "neither the vehicle nor any of the individuals involved has any connection whatsoever with Fuel2U", adding it was cooperating with the police.
Iran linked to series of attacks in Europe
Britain didn't join the US and Israel in the Iran war, which began on 28 February, and initially denied Trump’s request to use bases in the UK to strike the country.
But then-Prime Minister Keir Starmer agreed in March to let the US use bases in Britain for what he called “defensive” operations against Iran’s missiles and their launch sites following Iranian attacks on UK interests and Britain’s allies in the Gulf.
American B-1 and B-52 bombers have taken off from Fairford, 160 kilometres west of London, for operations during the Iran conflict.
Iran has said that it considers any base used to attack its territory a legitimate target.
British security officials say proxies linked to Iran have been behind a string of arsons and other attacks in the UK and other countries, many of them targeting the Jewish community and intended to sow fear.
They have previously warned that Tehran could expand its targets in the UK if conflicts in the Middle East continue.
UK Foreign Secretary Ed Miliband said on Monday that the incident is a “reminder of the threats our country faces.”

Norway to provide €2.3 million to find Ukrainian children deported by Russia and help prisoners
Norway will allocate 25 million kroner (€2.3 million) to help find and bring back Ukrainian children deported by Russia and assist prisoners of war and civilians held in detention. The funds will be channelled through UNICEF and the International Committee of the Red Cross.
Source: European Pravda, citing the Norwegian government
Details: The new aid will be allocated to UNICEF and the International Committee of the Red Cross.
These funds are intended to help find missing people, bring more people home and support the rehabilitation and reintegration of those affected by the war.
Fifteen million kroner (€1.4 million) will be allocated to UNICEF's work on the reintegration of deported children who have returned to Ukraine and on searching for missing children. This is part of a new, larger contribution of 132 million kroner (€12.2 million) to UNICEF's humanitarian programme in Ukraine.
Another 10 million kroner (€921,506) will be allocated to the Central Tracing Agency of the International Committee of the Red Cross. The agency aims to prevent people from going missing and ease the suffering of families who receive no news about their loved ones – whether because they have been taken prisoner or killed, or because they fled their homes due to the war and lost contact.
Meanwhile, Norway is co-hosting a conference in Toronto on 28-29 September aimed at drawing international attention to the issue.
"Russia's illegal war of aggression against Ukraine has resulted in serious violations of international humanitarian law and human rights. We must continue to draw attention to these violations and do what we can to support Ukrainians affected by the war," said Norwegian Foreign Minister Espen Barth Eide.
Background:
- On 28 September, the Council of the EU sanctioned another 10 individuals and 17 entities for their involvement in the illegal deportation of Ukrainian children to Russia and forced displacement within Russian-occupied territories.
- In September, the Canadian government added eight more Russians to its sanctions list over their involvement in the illegal deportation and forced displacement of Ukrainian children to Russia as well as their indoctrination and militarisation.

US, Iran resume indirect talks through Qatar
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-29
05:50:13 UTC
14:50:13 KST

Iranian Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi (C) listens as President of Iran Masoud Pezeshkian speaks during the General Debate of the 81st session of the United Nations General Assembly at United Nations Headquarters in New York, New York, Sept. 23 2026. EPA/SARAH YENESEL
The United States and Iran have resumed indirect contacts through Qatari mediators, with Tehran saying it expects Washington’s formal response as early as Sept. 29 to proposals aimed at reopening the Strait of Hormuz and reviving negotiations.
Iranian Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi met Qatari mediators in New York on Sept. 28, while U.S. officials held separate contacts with the mediators. No face-to-face meeting between the two sides took place.
“They had ideas, and we discussed how a way could be found to meet Iran’s conditions and how those conditions could be fulfilled,” Araghchi told Iranian reporters.
He said the proposals would now be presented to the U.S. side and Washington’s response relayed back to Tehran.
“I hope this will happen by tomorrow,” he said before leaving New York for Tehran.
The renewed contacts came after U.S. President Donald Trump said he had rejected Iran’s proposal for a seven-day process to reopen the Strait of Hormuz.
Under Tehran’s plan, Washington would take steps including ending its naval blockade, lifting oil sanctions and releasing frozen Iranian assets. Iran would then reopen the strait and resume negotiations on its nuclear program and a broader agreement.
Despite Trump’s rejection, mediated contacts have continued.
A U.S. official described the discussions as positive and constructive but said there would be no agreement unless Iran’s nuclear program was addressed.
Trump on Sept. 28 also denied a report that his administration was prepared to offer sanctions relief and the release of frozen Iranian funds in exchange for nuclear concessions.
“This is untrue. I offered them NOTHING!” Trump wrote on Truth Social.
U.S. Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent, meanwhile, argued that Washington’s economic pressure was pushing Tehran toward negotiations.
Bessent told Fox News that about 15 million barrels of Iranian oil remained in transit, largely to China, and claimed Iran could have “nothing left to trade” within roughly two weeks once those shipments were completed.
He said the pressure campaign was intended to ensure that Tehran complied with the terms of any future agreement.

Oil prices rise amid risks of supply disruptions from the Middle East
Ukraine
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-29
08:46:15 EEST
14:46:15 KST

Oil prices rise amid risks of supply disruptions from the Middle East
Kyiv • UNN
Brent rose to $106.77, while WTI rose to $93.94 per barrel. Markets are assessing the risks posed by the U.S.-Iran conflict to supplies through the Strait of Hormuz.
Oil prices rose on September 29 for a second consecutive session. This came as concerns about supply disruptions from the Middle East caused by the conflict between the United States and Iran outweighed signs of recovering oil exports from the region. UNN reports, citing Reuters.
Details
Brent crude futures rose by $1.49, or 1.4%, to $106.77 per barrel by 3:26 GMT (6:26 a.m. Kyiv time), while U.S. West Texas Intermediate crude rose by $1.34, or 1.5%, to $93.94. Both grades closed the previous session nearly $1 per barrel higher.
"A clearer picture is emerging of increased oil export volumes from the Persian Gulf, but most of this increase still depends on workarounds such as ship-to-ship transfers. These methods are less efficient and more expensive than standard operations, so oil prices remain high," said KCM Trade Chief Analyst Tim Waterer.
Oil exports from the largest Middle Eastern producers rose to 12.8 million barrels per day in September, reaching their highest level since February, preliminary data from analytics firm Kpler showed on Monday, driven by increased shipments from Saudi Arabia and the United Arab Emirates.
According to officials from both countries, the United States and Iran held separate talks with intermediaries as part of renewed efforts to end the seven-month war. Further negotiations are expected to focus on a revised version of the seven-day proposal submitted by Iran on the sidelines of the United Nations General Assembly.
What risks oil prices face
"The main risk remains the confrontation between the United States and Iran and its consequences for energy prices and inflation expectations," UOB said in a research note to clients.
"Iranian officials are reportedly pessimistic about reaching an agreement before the situation in the Strait of Hormuz escalates further, which supports a high level of uncertainty over oil supplies."
The war, which began in late February with U.S. and Israeli attacks on Iran, has drawn attention to the Strait of Hormuz, the most important shipping route for oil and gas supplies, disruption of which has upended energy markets.
Meanwhile, the United States is considering easing regulations to allow broader sales of red-dyed diesel fuel to help lower prices, which could allow some buyers to avoid the federal fuel tax, people familiar with the discussions told Reuters. The proposal emerged after several days of discussions as one of the main alternatives to a ban on diesel fuel exports.

A U.N. panel organized by Türkiye called for stronger international standards to protect children from online risks, as speakers warned that rapid advances in artificial intelligence were outpacing existing safeguards.
The event, titled “The Invisible Architecture: Building Safe Digital Systems for Children – Advancing International Standards and Shared Responsibility,” was held at U.N. headquarters in New York on Sept. 21 on the sidelines of the 81st U.N. General Assembly.
Organized under the auspices of first lady Emine Erdoğan, the panel was held by Türkiye’s Family and Social Services Ministry in cooperation with UNICEF and the Office of the U.N. Special Representative of the Secretary-General on Violence against Children.
Belgium’s Queen Mathilde warned that children should not bear the risks of rapidly developing technologies.
“Children cannot be the subjects of a global technology experiment or guinea pigs for business models based on data collection and attention,” she said.
Mathilde said child safety should be a central objective of AI governance, extending beyond parental controls, content moderation and data protection.
Serbian first lady Tamara Vučić stressed the need to prepare children for both physical and digital environments through education and responsible technology use.
The first ladies of Gambia, Kenya and Sierra Leone also called for stronger regulation and greater accountability from technology companies, particularly over personal data, online exploitation, cyberbullying and privacy.
Sahar Salam, the wife of Lebanese Prime Minister Nawaf Salam, urged greater oversight of AI systems, citing the case of a 15-year-old in Lebanon who died by suicide and was found to have been communicating with an AI system.
“We cannot expect children to understand the commercial logic of algorithms or assess whether an AI response is psychologically appropriate,” she said.
UNICEF Child Protection Director Sheema Sen Gupta said protecting children online required action beyond the national level, while U.N. Special Representative on Violence against Children Najat Maalla M’jid called for greater accountability from governments, technology companies and the wider digital sector.

Media executives: Foreign-language dubbing ban harms economy, security
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-29
05:39:00 UTC
14:39:00 KST

Media executives: Foreign-language dubbing ban harms economy, security
ERR and private media outlets in Estonia have called for a reversal of the ban on foreign-language dubbing.
Content in languages other than Estonian is generally subtitled rather than dubbed for TV and film, save for children's shows and films, which are often dubbed.
Media leaders say leaving Russian un-dubbed poses a security threat and, partly due to Estonia's small size, an economic one. The executives want the Language Act amended to lift the ban.
In a letter to Education Minister Kristina Kallas (Eesti 200), the media chiefs say the ban does not serve the stated aim of protecting Estonian and harms the common information space and media accessibility.
The issue also affected shows subtitled in Russian for Russian-speaking audiences.
"Banning dubbing/voice-overs in foreign languages does not automatically mean viewers will be amenable to subtitles. The experience of Estonian public broadcaster ERR's ETV+ (Russian language – ed.) TV channel shows that the absence of Russian-language voice-over/dubbing diminished audiences for television series in other foreign languages by more than 50 percent," the executives wrote.
They noted Russian is Estonia's second most widely spoken language and the Russian-language media space is a key environment for non-Estonian media, so restricting dubbing runs counter to the consumption habits of a significant share of viewers.
"It is obvious that if the way Estonian television channels provide media content changes, Russian-speaking viewers will leave our information space, piracy will increase and hostile information influence activities will become more effective," the appeal said.
Beyond security, the ban would cut television audiences, subscription and advertising revenues, and investment in audiovisual content, the executives say. Estonian audiovisual companies would also become less competitive against foreign platforms, which the state cannot restrict equally — creating absurd cross-border situations.
"For example, in addition to content available in Estonia, [TV channel] Go3's on-demand audiovisual media service catalog also offers Latvian- and Lithuanian-language overdubbed translation options intended for audiences in Latvia and Lithuania, as this is the official translation method in Latvia and Lithuania. [...] As a result of the adopted amendment to the Language Act, however, Go3 will also have to restrict the provision in Estonia of content with Latvian- and Lithuanian-language voice-over, even though such content has no connection whatsoever with the aim stated in the explanatory memorandum of reducing the influence of the Russian-language information space or language-based segregation in Estonia," the appeal noted.
The media concerns proposed amending the Language Act to restore providers' ability to use foreign-language dubbing and voice-over for foreign-language audiovisual works.
"Instead of restricting the use of foreign-language audio translation, the guiding principle should be that the primary obligation is to ensure an Estonian-language translation of audiovisual content. Once an Estonian-language translation has been provided, the service provider should have the right to decide whether and which additional language versions or translation methods it offers as part of its service," the authors wrote.
The framers say such an amendment would fulfil the law's original objective without harming society or the economy.
The appeal was signed by ERR board chair Erik Roose; Jüri Pihel, CEO of Duo Media Networks; Toomas Luhats of TV3 Group's Estonian operation; and Risto Rosimannus, representing V World North Europe.
A copy was sent to Culture Minister Heidy Purga (Reform) and MP Liina Kersna (Reform), who chairs the Riigikogu Cultural Affairs Committee.

Column: A new journey of win-win cooperation between Macao SAR and Southeast Asia
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-29
13:37:42 CST
14:37:42 KST

by Xing Zhiyuan
Chief Executive of the Macao Special Administrative Region (SAR) Sam Hou Fai recently concluded a successful visit to Singapore, Indonesia, Malaysia and ASEAN. Thirty-seven official events were held and 189 cooperation agreements were signed during the eight-day visit, a packed itinerary that yielded fruitful results.
This visit not only raised the profile of Macao's successful practice of "one country, two systems," but also injected new momentum into Macao's efforts to build a higher-level platform for opening up and to better integrate into and serve the country's overall development.
This visit marked the first time a chief executive of the Macao SAR had visited Indonesia and the ASEAN Secretariat, and the first return visit to Singapore in 15 years and to Malaysia in 19 years. Mr. Sam Hou Fai held in-depth exchanges with leaders of the three countries, the ASEAN secretary-general and senior officials, comprehensively enhancing strategic mutual trust and understanding between Macao, the three countries and ASEAN, laying a solid political foundation for long-term cooperation.
People from various sectors in the visited countries expressed confidence in Macao's development prospects, with many also voicing a strong desire to deepen cooperation with Macao and Hengqin.
The Singapore side said that both sides can deepen cooperation in tourism and urban development, and unlock new development opportunities in areas such as digitalization, innovation, sustainable development and elderly care services. Indonesia noted broad prospects for cooperation with Macao in halal products, traditional Chinese medicine and connectivity. Malaysia expressed its desire to promote cooperation in healthcare, education, science and technology, as well as tourism.
The ASEAN Secretariat, for its part, said it is confident that ASEAN member states and Macao can fully complement each other's advantages, strengthen collaboration in investment, trade, tourism, people-to-people and cultural exchanges.
Chief Executive Sam Hou Fai made full use of meetings, speeches, receptions and interviews to present a comprehensive picture of Macao's distinctive practice of "one country, two systems" and explain its rich connotations. A video specially produced for the occasion, titled "The Successful Practice of 'One Country, Two Systems', The Third Five-Year Plan for Economic and Social Development of the Macao SAR (2026-2030) Embarks on a New Journey," highlighted the key arrangements of the Third Five-Year Plan as well as new opportunities arising from Macao-Hengqin integration. The figures cited -- a 3.7 percent year-on-year increase in GDP in the first half of the year, a 9 percent rise in visitor arrivals and a 6 percent increase in international visitors -- made it clear to all that "one country, two systems" is not an abstract concept, but the fundamental reason behind Macao's profound transformation.
Political leaders in the visited countries praised Macao's successful practice of "one country, two systems," noting that Macao has long enjoyed social stability and rapid economic growth and has become a highly open, globally renowned city and a bridge connecting China with the rest of the world, serving as a model for the international community.
Macao's tourism sector signed 75 cooperation agreements with the three countries. Indonesia, in particular, said that building on the restoration of visa-free access for Macao, it would promote the resumption of direct flights between Macao and Jakarta.
Macao and Indonesia jointly held the exhibition "Splendor of the Mirrored Sea: Macao's Symphony of Civilizations on the Maritime Silk Road." It helped audiences appreciate the deep cultural ties between Macao and Southeast Asia and their shared heritage as key hubs along the Maritime Silk Road. The event built a bridge of mutual understanding between the people of China and Southeast Asia.
Chief Executive Sam Hou Fai delivered a speech at the National University of Singapore, where he encouraged Singapore to take part in developing the Macao-Hengqin International Education (University) City. He also introduced the Belt and Road Scholarship to Indonesia and Malaysia. Macao's higher education institutions signed 16 cooperation agreements with leading universities in Singapore and Malaysia.
The Macao SAR government continued its government-enterprise approach of "joining forces to go global," putting together a delegation of more than 120 business representatives from Macao, Hengqin and 15 provinces and municipalities from the Chinese mainland. With a focus on Macao's "1+4" industrial development, the government arranged three promotion sessions, 370 business-matching meetings and nearly 30 field visits. It also facilitated the signing of more than 100 cooperation documents.
Officials and business communities in the visited countries were optimistic about Macao's unique advantages, which link the Guangdong-Hong Kong-Macao Greater Bay Area and the Chinese mainland with Portuguese- and Spanish-speaking countries. The business-matching sessions were lively. Clearly, Macao is small, but it is not a simple "transit station." It is a "Precise Connector" that understands rules and markets.
Looking ahead, Macao will make every effort to turn the outcomes of the visit into action, which will further enrich the successful practice of "one country, two systems" with Macao characteristics.
Editor's note: The author is a commentator on Macao affairs, writing regularly for Xinhua News, Global Times, China Daily etc.
The views expressed in this article are those of the author and do not necessarily reflect the positions of Xinhua News Agency.
