Women and children displaced by Nepal's floods say safe housing, privacy and stability remain out of reach as they try to rebuild their lives
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-29
13:29:00 UTC
22:29:00 KST

Nepal floods leave women and girls vulnerable
September 29, 2026
One month after deadly flash floods in Nepal swept away Karishma Tamang's community in Rasuwa District, the pregnant 26-year-old is still struggling to find a safe place to call home.
Karishma, who is expecting her second child, has been moving from place to place with her 4-year-old daughter since the devastating floods swept through Nepal's Bhotekoshi-Trishuli river corridor near the Chinese border at the end of August.
"Initially, we were kept in a covered hall at Bidur Municipality in Nuwakot District," she told DW, adding that hundreds of people shared the same shelter for days.
"Now we have shifted to a small makeshift family tent at the nearby Barahachaur area. Still, we can't sleep during rainy nights as it leaks when it rains." Her brother and his two children remain missing after the flood.
There is no proper toilet, although a small makeshift latrine has been set up near the tents, Karishma said.
Children and pregnant women like Karishma need privacy and safety, but such facilities remain scarce in the Himalaya nation's flood-hit areas.
"It would be great to have a stable place to stay, where I could cook my own meals, feel safe and have some comfort," she said.
Safety concerns in temporary shelters
The August 26 flood, triggered by a glacier collapse along the Nepal-China border, killed about 1,450 people and left more than 5,500 missing. Reconstruction costs are estimated to be $4.8 billion (€4.2 billion).
At least seven people, including girls, women and local volunteers at temporary shelters and camps, spoke to DW. Although none reported experiencing sexual harassment or abuse, their accounts point to widespread concerns about safety and vulnerability in the aftermath of the floods.
Sabita Tamang, who lost her 5-year-old daughter, nephew and niece in the floods, is also staying in a makeshift tent in Barahachaur. The 24-year-old said she has to travel beyond the nearest tap to bathe and collect water.
"We feel uncomfortable taking a bath in an open space among strangers and unknown locals," she told DW. "Many children have seen their family members, friends and neighbors caught in the floods," she said, raising concerns about the impact on their mental health and education.
Risk of trafficking and abuse
Save the Children Nepal has warned that protection measures for children and their families must be strengthened across flood-affected areas amid concerns about trafficking, violence, exploitation and child marriage.
Many families have moved into rented rooms. Yet hundreds are being housed in temporary shelters and makeshift tents in Nuwakot and Dhading districts.
Save the Children Nepal raised concerns about privacy and safety for girls and women because unfamiliar people have unrestricted access to shared spaces.
Ayush Joshi, director for advocacy, campaigns, communications and media at Save the Children Nepal, told DW that the organization's report was based on qualitative assessments involving affected people, including women and children, as well as volunteers deployed in flood-hit areas.
"Many temporary shelters are built without planning. Camps on the outskirts of towns have inadequate lighting at night and lack separate washrooms and private spaces," Joshi told DW, noting that there is unrestricted access for unfamiliar people.
"Such situations naturally increase the risk of insecurity, potential harassment and exploitation, especially for young girls and children."
According to Joshi, in the aftermath of the disaster, many people became separated from their families, while some children lost their lives and older siblings had to become caregivers for younger siblings.
"In such circumstances, cases of school dropouts and child marriage could increase," he added, referring to Save the Children's field assessment. "We have seen many children facing mental health issues, like becoming angry, frightened and crying loudly. There is a need for socio-emotional healing."
What does the government say?
The Nepali government has also assessed the risks of trafficking and potential child abuse and has collaborated with organizations such as Save the Children, the police and local authorities to strengthen protection measures at displacement sites.
Chakra Bahadur Budha, spokesperson at the Ministry of Women, Children, Gender and Sexual Minorities, said the government had increased monitoring and surveillance and was raising awareness about gender-based violence and trafficking.
"We have mobilized and kept all relevant stakeholders on high alert to check at points of entry and exit, so as to protect affected people from being trafficked or abused," he told DW.
Authorities took back at least 78 children from two Buddhist monasteries in Kathmandu and placed them in temporary camps. Budha explained that the monasteries had rescued and supported the children, offering long-term shelter, education and employment, but the government discourages such arrangements outside established procedures.
"We have strictly discouraged religious or charitable organizations from keeping children without following legal procedures," Budha told DW. "Adoption has also been discouraged for now, but children can be placed with close relatives, such as uncles and aunts, for their protection after verification of their relationship."
The United Nations Children's Fund (UNICEF) said at least 541 children have either lost their parents or become separated from their families.
Initial assessments indicate that learning has been disrupted for more than 14,000 children across 62 schools and learning centers in flood-affected areas in Dhading, Nuwakot and Rasuwa districts.

Large shark stuck in city canal draws 600,000 visitors as rescue efforts begin in South Korea
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-29
05:37:09 UTC
14:37:09 KST

A large shark has become an unlikely tourist attraction after getting trapped in a narrow city canal in South Korea for more than a week.
More than 600,000 people are estimated to have visited a waterfront park in the southern port city of Busan since the 3.5-metre shark – nicknamed Bukang-i after the name of Busan’s North Port – was first spotted in its waterway on 18 September.
Experts believe it to be a bronze whaler shark that followed prey from the sea into the canal and could not find its way out.
The coastguard in the city about 200 miles (325km) south-east of Seoul tried to drive it out on the day it appeared but suspended the operation six hours later, on the advice of scientists who warned that forcing the animal could harm it or make it aggressive.
On Tuesday morning coastguard boats sprayed jets of water behind the shark to push it towards the canal’s mouth, a method officials said was modelled on the rescue of a great white shark that became trapped in shallow water off Massachusetts in 2004.
The first attempt failed, after the shark slipped past the boats and swam back into the canal, the Herald Business reported. The national institute of fisheries science said the shark was stable, but officials said its ability to feed and move was restricted, which could weaken it the longer it stayed. On Tuesday afternoon the operation was suspended again because the shark wouldn’t leave the waterway.
Sharks are not unknown in South Korean waters. The fisheries institute recorded 46 large sharks off the east coast in the first half of this year, nearly four times as many as a year earlier, which it attributed to warmer seas and more of the fish that are the sharks’ prey.
The North Port Waterfront Park, which usually draws about 2,000 people a day on holidays, recorded 607,000 visits between 19 and 28 September, according to the city.
On Tuesday Kim Jung-sook, 62, came to say goodbye to the shark, telling the Maeil Shinmun newspaper: “I’ve grown attached to it after seeing it here for a few days … I feel a bit sad.”
Busan’s mayor, Chun Jae-soo, is a fan too. “It really has star quality. It comes up every five to 10 minutes,” he told CBS radio. “It’s just so pretty.”
The city has named the shark an honorary publicity ambassador, giving it the title “Shafluencer”, after 91% of respondents to a city Instagram poll backed the idea. Boogi, the city’s mascot, is to accept the certificate on its behalf.
Lee Do-yoon, eight, who came with his father to see it off, was not worried that it appeared to be time to see it off. “It’s OK,” he said. “Bukang-i is going to meet its friends.”

Australian central bank raises interest rates to 15-year high
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-29
13:37:05 CST
14:37:05 KST

SYDNEY, Sept. 29 (Xinhua) -- Australia's central bank on Tuesday raised interest rates to a 15-year-high, citing inflation driven by the conflict in the Middle East.
The Reserve Bank of Australia (RBA) said its Monetary Policy Board voted unanimously to lift the cash rate target from 4.35 percent to 4.60 percent, the highest figure since November 2011.
It marks the fourth rate rise delivered by the RBA so far in 2026 after three previous increases of 0.25 percentage points each in February, March and May.
Economists and Australia's major banks had unanimously predicted the decision to raise the cash rate target on Tuesday.
The Monetary Policy Board said in its decision statement that the conflict in the Middle East has broadened, causing global energy prices to rise much higher than assumed when the board decided to keep interest rates on hold in August.
"The Middle East conflict remains unresolved, and there are scenarios where inflation is higher and activity lower than forecast. Global oil supply disruptions are maintaining upward pressure on global and domestic energy prices and inflation," it said.
Speaking earlier on Tuesday, Treasurer Jim Chalmers said that the conflict in the Middle East has been "absolutely disastrous" from a cost-of-living and economic perspective.
"We're seeing inflation going up around the world; we're seeing interest rates going up around the world. And unfortunately, Australia's not immune from the same pressures," he told Australian Broadcasting Corporation radio.
The latest data from the Australian Bureau of Statistics (ABS) showed that annual inflation fell from 3.8 percent in June to 3.5 percent in July.
The trimmed mean, the measure of underlying inflation preferred by the RBA, remained steady at 3.6 percent. The RBA targets annual inflation of 2-3 percent.
The ABS will release inflation data for August on Wednesday, and the Monetary Policy Board will next meet at the start of November. ■

Cambodia's economic growth projected to slow to 3 pct in 2026 amid rising costs: IMF
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-29
13:36:54 CST
14:36:54 KST

PHNOM PENH, Sept. 29 (Xinhua) -- Cambodia's economic growth is forecast to slow to 3 percent in 2026 from 5.3 percent in 2025, driven by surging energy costs, weakening tourism, and declining remittances, the International Monetary Fund (IMF) said on Tuesday.
The Southeast Asian nation, which relies heavily on garment, footwear, and travel goods exports, alongside agriculture, tourism, and real estate, faces a mounting combination of domestic and global headwinds.
"Growth is projected to slow to 3 percent in 2026 before recovering to 4 percent in 2027, reflecting higher energy costs, weaker tourism and remittances, decelerating garment exports, subdued domestic demand, and tighter financial conditions," the IMF said in a press release.
"Inflation is expected to remain elevated at 5.6 percent in 2026 before easing as energy prices normalize," it added.
The current account deficit is projected to widen sharply, although resilient foreign direct investment and adequate international reserves provide important buffers.
The IMF said risks to growth are tilted to the downside, including from renewed energy and trade disruptions, persistent scam activities, and a sharper real estate correction.
Potential disruptions from El Nino conditions could keep agricultural price pressures elevated, it added. ■

Dry weather with strong winds in the south - forecast for September 29
Kyiv • UNN
On September 29, dry weather with no precipitation and temperatures of up to 23°C is expected in Ukraine. Gusts of wind of up to 20 m/s are possible in the south.
Dry weather, with temperatures reaching 23 degrees Celsius and strong wind gusts in the south, is expected in Ukraine on September 29. UNN reports this, citing data from the Ukrainian Hydrometeorological Center.
Details
According to the forecast, there will be partly cloudy skies today.
No precipitation.
Fog in places in the western regions at night and in the morning.
The wind will be predominantly northeasterly, at 7–12 m/s, with gusts of 15–20 m/s in places in the southern part during the day.
Temperatures will be 6–11°C at night and 15–20°C during the day; in the southern part, 9–14°C at night and 18–23°C during the day; in the Carpathians, 1–6°C above zero at night and 10–15°C during the day.

Evicted Spanish pensioner to return home, lawyer says
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-29
05:36:00 UTC
14:36:00 KST

Spain agrees on measures to fix housing crisis, ban eviction
September 29, 2026
Spain's coalition government on Tuesday said it has agreed new measures to tackle the country's housing crisis after the forceful removal of an 87-year-old pensioner from her apartment in Madrid last week, sparked nationwide solidarity protests.
Spanish Health Minister Monica Garcia said the housing legislation includes a ban on evictions until 2030, tighter rules for short-term rentals and a two-year extension for existing leases.
"It's time to intervene in the speculative housing market and begin to rebalance the scales between citizens and vulture funds," Garcia, who belongs to the leftist government's junior coalition partner Sumar, wrote in a post on X.
Legislation still needs to pass through parliament
The Spanish government, led by Prime Minister Pedro Sanchez and his ministers, approved the measures after a meeting.
But since Sanchez leads a minority government, he is still dependent on votes from a number of other parties in parliament before the bill is set in law.
Sanchez's ruling Socialists were engaged in talks with coalition partners Sumar and others up to Tuesday.
Socialist Housing Minister Isabel Rodriguez is scheduled to address a press conference later on Tuesday.
A case that triggered mass protests in Spain
Images and videos last week that showed Maria del Carmen Abascal — known by her nickname Maricarmen — escorted out of her apartment by riot police officers touched a nerve among Spaniards who've long called for a solution to the housing crisis in the country.
Maricarmen's father had first rented the property in 1956 in Madrid's Retiro neighborhood and she continued as the tenant after her parents died.
Spanish newspaper El Pais reported that Maricarmen had rented the apartment from a private landlord until 2018, after which a real estate company acquired the property and took over its management.
According to the newspaper, the legal dispute between Maricarmen and the real estate company lasted eight years and their latest attempt to evict her from the apartment marked their fourth attempt to do so.
The issue placed Spain's housing market in the spotlight where many long-term tenants have been priced out of their apartments due to an affordability crisis and a shortage of homes in Europe's fourth-largest economy.
Protesters rallied around Maricarmen's cause, especially because pictures of her being taken out of her apartment building and into an ambulance were vividly present across social media.
She is a wheelchair user too.
People then hit the streets of Madrid in the thousands on Saturday, with many having ended their protest by setting up tents in Madrid's historic Puerta del Sol plaza at the end of the night.
More people, including multigenerational families, joined Sunday.
Maricarmen to return home because of 'social mobilization,' lawyer says
Maricarmen's lawyer on Monday said that she was going to be able to return home, calling the victory a "result of the social mobilization."
"If this agreement we have reached is signed, it will obviously be a better and happier outcome for everyone," Abascal's lawyer Beatriz Duro told reporters.
"Hopefully this agreement, this different way of ending this type of situation, which is unfortunately experienced every day in this country, helps to change the paradigm when it comes to housing in general," Duro said.
Edited by: Elizabeth Schumacher

More people, including multigenerational families, joined Sunday.
Maricarmen to return home because of 'social mobilization,' lawyer says
Maricarmen's lawyer on Monday said that she was going to be able to return home, calling the victory a "result of the social mobilization."
"If this agreement we have reached is signed, it will obviously be a better and happier outcome for everyone," Abascal's lawyer Beatriz Duro told reporters.
"Hopefully this agreement, this different way of ending this type of situation, which is unfortunately experienced every day in this country, helps to change the paradigm when it comes to housing in general," Duro said.

====================================================================================================

AI boom and arms industry set €1bn startups at record level in Germany
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-29
05:32:06 UTC
14:32:06 KST

By Alexander Sturm, dpa.
Germany’s startup sector is producing a growing number of companies valued at over €1 billion ($1.14 billion), partly driven by the artificial intelligence boom, according to an annual study.
The research by the German Startup Monitor shows that about €8 billion in venture capital has flowed into startups by the end of September 2026, surpassing the approximately €7.5 billion invested throughout the whole of the previous year.
By the end of September, 10 new startups have achieved a company valuation of at least €1 billion – so-called “unicorns” – according to the report, which has been published yearly since 2013.
The data analysis and survey of more than 1,800 growth companies is to be presented in Berlin on Monday by the German Startup Association.
With a total of 39 unicorns, Germany has reached a record level, the report said.
These include major names such as online broker Trade Republic, smartphone bank N26 and software firm Personio. New additions this year include software company Osapiens, Neura Robotics and defence firm Stark Defense.
“Germany is founding [new companies] again – broadly and on a strong technological basis,” said Verena Pausder, chairwoman of the association.
For the purposes of the study, startups are defined as companies that are less than 10 years old, offer innovative products or business models, and have strong ambitions for growth.
Defence and AI key drivers
The startup sector is benefiting from rising investment in defence companies, including Quantum Systems and Helsing, which are attracting large sums from investors.
AI is a further growth driver. For 53% of the startups surveyed, the technology is central to their product – up from 39% in 2024. At the same time, AI is said to be making it significantly easier to found companies.
The report also highlights weaknesses in the startup sector. Capital flowing in was said to be concentrating more heavily at the top. “Across the board, the number of financing rounds is around a quarter below the 2021 level.”
Some 89% of founders surveyed called for more venture capital from Germany and Europe.
“The available capital is not sufficient to make the leap to the top of the world,” Pausder said.
International strategy
A majority of startups (62%) also said they would prefer the United States for a potential stock market listing, with only 27% favouring Germany. And for digital technologies, 64% said they relied predominantly or entirely on US providers – partly due to a lack of European alternatives.
The government must implement its startup strategy and make financing easier, Pausder said. She added that company formation within the EU must be simplified.
The association sees strengths in the sector’s links with universities. Every second startup (51%) was said to be supported by research institutions, and for 59% the product was said to stem from new scientific findings.
Universities are the most important pillar in the ecosystem, said association research expert Alexander Hirschfeld. “Measured against the quality of Germany’s research landscape, however, far too few companies are still being founded from it,” he said.
The shortage of skilled workers is causing less concern among startups. Only 15% see it as a major obstacle, down from 30% two years ago. Some 83% said they planned to make new hires within 12 months.
Source: dpa.com

Rights group accuses Vietnam of abducting Australian and Norwegian activists

Rights group accuses Vietnam of abducting Australian and Norwegian activists
- Published
A pro-democracy group has accused the Vietnamese government of abducting two of its members, an Australian and a Norwegian citizen, in Cambodia and taking them back across the border.
Vietnamese authorities confirmed that they had arrested Tran Hiep and Nguyen Duc Thuan, but say they had entered the country using forged documents and planned to carry out terrorist activities.
It said the men had admitted to being members of Viet Tan, which Vietnam sees as a terrorist organisation.
Viet Tan called their arrest a "blatant fabrication intended to conceal the fact that the Viet Tan members were abducted in Cambodia and forcibly taken to Vietnam".
The group, which has members in Vietnam and abroad, said the two men had been travelling in the southern border district of Kaoh Andaet in Cambodia when they went missing and had not been heard from since 18 September.
Tran's wife, Chloe Dang, told Australian media he had been meeting pro-democracy activists in Cambodia and had no intention of travelling to Vietnam.
He was meant to meet her in Bangkok to board a return flight to Australia but never turned up, she said.
"He always knew there was a risk doing human rights work, but we never thought that this would happen," she told the ABC.
According to a Vietnamese state media report published on Monday, Tran and Nguyen were detained with a third man at the border in Tay Ninh province on 18 September.
The trio "confessed to being members of the terrorist organisation 'Viet Tan,' [and] carrying forged documents to illegally enter Vietnam in order to carry out terrorist and sabotage activities," the report said.
They were charged on Monday with membership of a terrorist organisation while an investigation continued "to clarify the criminal acts of the suspects in order to handle them according to the law", it said.
"A state orchestrating the abduction of individuals abroad and forcibly taking them to its territory is a serious act of transnational repression," said Viet Tan. "It violates Cambodia's sovereignty and the fundamental principles of international law."
The Viet Tan statement did not mention the third man, who was named by authorities as Thai Cong Truong Son.
Australian Prime Minister Anthony Albanese said consular support was being provided to Tran's family.
"That's what Australian governments do for our citizens. And we'll continue to engage directly with the family."
"Vietnam authorities' confirmation that they detained [these] activists... demonstrates yet again that Hanoi is arguably the most vicious and pernicious practitioner of transnational repression today in Southeast Asia," Phil Robertson, Director of Asia Human Rights and Labor Advocates said in a statement.
"This latest act is an unacceptable outrage."
The Vietnamese and Cambodian authorities have been contacted for comment.

Danish Architecture Center Celebrates Urbanist Jan Gehl's 90th Birthday with a Calendar of Activities and an Exhibition
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-29
05:30:00 UTC
14:30:00 KST

For the second year running, Copenhagen was named the world's most livable city in the 2026 Economist Intelligence Unit's Global Liveability Index. According to the Danish Architecture Center, part of this progress in urban quality of life is due to the work of Danish architect and urban planner Jan Gehl, who celebrates his 90th birthday this year. Jan Gehl has dedicated his professional career to the field of city life and people-centered urban development, founding Gehl Architects (now Gehl Studio) in 2000 and publishing extensively on urban design methodologies to create lively, healthy, and human-centric urban environments. In honor of his birthday, the Danish Architecture Center is presenting an exhibition and a series of activities centered on the role he has played in urban development worldwide.
Jan Gehl is an architect, researcher, and urban planner who has devoted his life to understanding what makes cities good for people and how design can contribute to life, play, and community experiences in urban surroundings. He is recognized for his research on public-space development, published across numerous books on the subject, the most recent of which is "A Good City – The Short Story," written in collaboration with Copenhagen's former city architect, Camilla van Deurs. In DAC's profile of the urban planner, Life Between Buildings is described as his most defining work, first published in 1971 and since translated into 30 languages. The book was inspired by the work of urban theorist and author Jane Jacobs, joining her in questioning heavily trafficked boulevards, freestanding buildings, and the large, empty spaces characteristic of car-centric design.
   A good city is one that takes people as its starting point. We are walking, sensing and social beings who naturally seek out places with shelter and a sense of presence – where we're protected from traffic, wind and cold, and where we can meet others and find safety in a social setting. It's completely instinctive and rooted in the biological evolution of Homo sapiens. ― Jan Gehl
Related Article
The Metrics We Use Decide the Cities We Build: Urban Indicators and Lived Experience
Part of DAC's tribute to Gehl is to show today's audience his role in establishing the idea that people should come first in the design of urban spaces. While "people-first cities" is a concept widely recognized today, in the 1960s urban planning was primarily concerned with buildings, cars, and traffic. According to the institution, this shift in perspective grew out of a challenge posed by his wife, psychologist Ingrid Gehl, who brought attention to the needs and behaviors of people moving, meeting, and living together daily in cities. As obvious as it may seem today, it was a new approach to urbanism grounded in experience and in "the life between buildings." Copenhagen's harbor baths, bike lanes, parks, squares, and public spaces weave people's lives around the built environment and bear witness to the practical application of these ideas.
The new main exhibition at the Danish Architecture Center, titled Cities for People, was developed in collaboration with Gehl Studio and Jan Gehl, and opens on World Architecture Day, October 5. The exhibition draws on Gehl's life's work and his 12 quality criteria for public urban spaces, exploring how people-centered urban design can improve citizens' health, well-being, communities, and quality of life. DAC's exhibition expresses the conviction that public space and urban design can support communities when planning begins with people's everyday lives, before streets are drawn and buildings are built. The approach builds on the principles developed in the book Life Between Buildings and is expressed through an exhibition featuring immersive and participatory experiences.
In the exhibition, visitors will have the opportunity to physically experience when a place feels safe or unsafe, and how the same public space can feel very different depending on age, gender, and life situation. They are invited to imagine cities with room for both community and freedom, energy and calm, and to share ideas about the kind of public space that brings joy. DAC is also developing a special AfterDAC program that explores the exhibition's themes through conversations and debates, including one between Jan Gehl and architect Ane Cortzen. With upwards of 70 percent of the world's population expected to live in cities, the institution brings to its main exhibition halls the question of how to create cities that allow people to thrive amid a complex, contemporary lifestyle. Jan Gehl's career helps shape the answer to this question, opening up reflections on concepts such as human scale, urban life, and life between buildings — now firmly established in the international urban planning lexicon.
 Jan Gehl has shown the world that the perceived quality of a city is primarily achieved through understanding people's needs and through caring about how people live as individuals and in communities. This is a clear and compelling idea, but it requires complex knowledge and political support to implement for the benefit of all in the city. Jan Gehl's and Gehl Studio's consulting has proven effective, and their work has altered our fundamental understanding of what is considered a good city and how to design it. This is a huge achievement" ― Kent Martinussen from the Danish Architecture Center.
Other recent news about the future of contemporary cities includes the launch of the signature campaign for "Right to Housing! Now and Forever," an official European Citizens' Initiative (ECI) demanding affordable, sustainable, and fair housing across the European Union. In New York, London, and Brussels, city governments are looking for ways to contribute to circular construction by transforming former industrial buildings into centers for the recovery, storage, sorting, redistribution, and education around construction materials. Earlier this year, Beijing was named World Capital of Architecture 2029 by UNESCO-UIA, a title awarded every three years to a city that hosts a year of architecture-focused programming timed to coincide with the UIA World Congress of Architects. The title recognizes a city's commitment to using architecture, urban planning, and culture as tools for sustainable development.

Russia attacks Ukraine with Zircon and Iskander missiles and 152 drones: air defence downs 109 aerial assets
Russian forces attacked Ukraine with a Zircon/Oniks anti-ship missile, two Iskander-M/S-400 ballistic missiles and 152 drones on the night of 28-29 September. Air defence forces have downed 109 aerial assets.
Source: Ukraine's Air Force
Details: The Russians started the attack at 18:00 on 28 September. They launched a Zircon/Oniks anti-ship missile and two Iskander-M/S-400 ballistic missiles from Kursk Oblast.
They also used 152 Shahed (82 jet-powered) and Gerbera attack drones and Parodiya decoy UAVs.
The drones were launched from the Russian cities of Oryol, Millerovo, Kursk and Primorsko-Akhtarsk as well as the temporarily occupied territory of Donetsk and from Hvardiiske and Chauda in temporarily occupied Crimea.
Aircraft, anti-aircraft missile units, electronic warfare assets, unmanned systems units and mobile fire groups from Ukraine's defence forces have been involved in repelling the attack.
Quote: "As of 08:00, [Ukrainian] air defence forces had destroyed or jammed 109 aerial assets:
- 1 Zircon/Oniks anti-ship missile
- 2 Iskander-M/S-400 ballistic missiles
- 106 Shahed, Gerbera and other types of drones."
Details: Hits by aerial assets have been recorded at 24 locations and the fall of downed aerial assets (debris) at 16 locations.
The attack is ongoing, as several Russian drones are still in the airspace.
Background: Air-raid warnings were issued in the city of Kyiv and several Ukrainian oblasts on the night of 28-29 September due to the threat of Russian ballistic missiles. Explosions were heard in the capital and fires broke out.

Gaming Scottish granny plays her way to Guinness world record

Gaming Scottish granny plays her way to Guinness world record
- Cath Bowie, a 78-year-old Scottish grandmother, became the world's oldest female Fortnite streamer recognised by Guinness World Records in 2023.
- She started playing Fortnite in 2017 after watching her grandson and began streaming in 2018, gaining over 24,000 followers on Twitch.
- Bowie enjoys the game's challenge and community, encouraging older people to try gaming and never let age stop them.
AI generated
In 2017, Cath Bowie saw her grandson play the multiplayer shooter game Fortnite and decided to give it a try. Little did she know that nine years later she would play her way into the record books.
On Sept 24, the 78-year-old Scottish grandmother was named the world’s oldest female Fortnite streamer by Guinness World Records (GWR).
She was also featured in the Guinness World Records Gamer’s Edition 2027, which was released in September.
Bowie, better known as “grumpygran48” to over 24,000 followers on Twitch, said she was “instantly intrigued” when she saw her then 17-year-old grandson playing the game in 2017, when Fortnite launched Battle Royale mode.
Battle Royale mode is an online multiplayer video game type where a large group of players fight to be the last person or team alive.
“Nearly nine years later I am still playing it, still absolutely loving it, and although still growing older I have never made my age a deterrent,” Bowie told GWR.
She said she had tried other online games, but nothing got her hooked as much as Fortnite.
“I call myself a ‘Fortniter’ more than a gamer,” she added.
She started streaming in 2018, but her grandson was sceptical of her success.
“As a young guy he just couldn’t believe that his grandma would do such a thing and suggested that nobody would join me or watch me,” Bowie said.
“Saying that was like a red rag to a bull to me. I would show him that I could do it — 24,000+ followers later and he doesn’t mention it. I wonder why?”
Bowie said she loves the challenge the game gives her. She streams herself playing for up to six hours a day.
Over the years, many of her fellow gamers became supporters and friends.
“I play with some wonderful folk - from the UK, quite a few from the USA, from Canada, New Zealand and Australia,” she told the BBC’s Radio Scotland Breakfast programme.
“It’s super meeting all these folk. The chat we have, it’s lovely — I’ve had folk with me for quite a few years now.”
And to older people who want to try gaming, Bowie said: “Never let age stop you. If I can do it so can you.”

South Korean Submarines Could Save Australia From the AUKUS Shambles
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-29
05:19:00 UTC
14:19:00 KST

In July, the Canadian government announced that it has chosen the German-Norwegian bid to build 12 conventionally-powered submarines to replace their obsolete Victoria class fleet. The Canadian Broadcasting Corporation reported the estimated cost of the submarines at CA$24 billion. With 35-year lifetime maintenance and sustainment costs added, the overall program cost is likely to be in the vicinity of CA$100 billion. This compares more than favorably to the A$368 billion (the dollar equivalents are similar) allocated so far to AUKUS.
The Canadians said they had a hard time choosing between two excellent options – the other being the South Korean KSS-III submarine.
Professor Hugh White has long experience with our Collins class submarine project and, more recently, with the details of AUKUS. He says that as an alternative to the AUKUS project “any off-the-shelf submarines Australia could get its hands on, we should take.”
One option is to turn back to the French Naval Group for a new order of 12 submarines. In evidence given to the AUKUS public inquiry in Canberra on 2 September, retired admiral Peter Briggs gave an informed presentation on the capabilities of nuclear-powered submarines. He favors procurement of a low-enriched uranium nuclear-powered submarine, based on the French Suffren class, for the Royal Australian Navy (RAN). He strongly opposes purchase of the US Virginia class and the proposed British-designed SSN AUKUS boats, describing the plan as “flawed and undeliverable”.
His conclusion about the AUKUS submarines is widely supported by the evidence and a strong consensus of military and academic opinion.
During his presentation Admiral Briggs stated his view that conventional diesel-electric submarine technology was not acceptable for the next generation of RAN operations. His argument was that conventionally powered submarines have neither the stealth features nor the endurance needed for effective undersea naval operations. Nonetheless, the example he cited concerned the limitations of the existing Collins class submarine design. As is well known, Collins is an outdated platform that is nearing the end of its operational life.
Given the South Koreans only recently lost the bid for 12 submarines to replace the ageing Canadian fleet, their new submarine should be available for export without delay. The KSS-III proposal had an appealing range of handover deadlines promised for Canada. The expected first boat delivery date was scheduled to be 2032, with the initial batch of four submarines delivered by 2035 and the remaining eight boats at the rate of one per year until 2043, when the entire fleet of 12 would be in service. It has been reported that the South Korean tender may have suffered a disadvantage because Canadian infrastructure and crew capacity to absorb the fleet in that timeframe is underdeveloped. This is much less a problem in Australia.
These delivery timeframes compare to 2032 proposed for the first second-hand AUKUS Virginia; thereafter delivery in 2035 and 2038 respectively. The first British-designed AUKUS SSN boat is not expected to be delivered until the fuzzy “2040s.” Obviously, procurement of an entire one-class fleet of 12 KSS-III submarines by 2043 is an attractive option. It would adequately cover the capability gap of decommissioned Collins class submarines, scheduled to begin in 2040. If the argument about needing more naval capability now has any relevance, early delivery is a must.
KSS-III Capability
Defence Central is the authoritative London-based bureau for published defence intelligence. They produce “deep-dive reports on procurement, weaponry and integrated command structures”.
Defence Central notes that in 2021 South Korea became the first country without nuclear weapons to successfully test a submarine-launched ballistic missile (SLBM). The launch came from the Dosan Anh Changho, the first KSS-III class submarine produced. South Korea’s KSS-III program represents the third phase of the country’s indigenous submarine development strategy. Earlier phases relied heavily on German technology. The KSS-III represents a leap forward to a fully domestic design capable of supporting strategic missions, including nuclear deterrence.
The KSS-III supersedes two earlier models in both size and capability. Measuring 83.5 meters in length with a beam of 9.7 meters, the submarine has a submerged displacement of approximately 3,800 tons. It is powered by a diesel-electric propulsion system with an air-independent propulsion module that allows for greater submerged endurance compared to conventional diesel-electric submarines. The crew complement needed is 50 people – a massive reduction on the 135 sailors required to operate the US Virginia class boats – and the 100 crew required for the 10,000-ton SSN AUKUS boats, should they ever reach naval service.
The design configuration allows the KSS-III to remain submerged for up to 20 days without surfacing, a key feature for survivability in contested waters. The boat has a top submerged speed of 37 kph, or 20 knots, and an operational range of around 19,000 kilometers. These specifications allow for long patrols in both coastal and open sea environments. The latest version boats are also capable of generating electricity underwater to recharge their fuel cell batteries. This enables long underwater voyages and obviates the need for frequent “snorts,” when the submarine has to come to the surface and potentially reveal its position to an enemy satellite.
One of the defining features of the KSS-III is its vertical launch system (VLS). It is the first South Korean submarine equipped with a VLS capable of deploying a battery of underwater-launched missiles. The Korean-designed Hyunmoo-3 cruise missiles offer a credible second-strike capability, especially relevant given the regional missile capabilities of North Korea and China. The Hyunmoo-3 is roughly equivalent to the US Navy’s Tomahawk but is supersonic, with a reported speed of Mach 1.2. In addition to SLBMs, the KSS-III can carry heavyweight torpedoes and anti-ship missiles launched from its standard torpedo tubes.
The newest design KSS-III, known as Batch 2 submarines, will have an increased displacement of approximately 4,000 tons and an expanded VLS capable of carrying up to ten missiles. They will also feature enhanced sonar systems, improved stealth characteristics and a more advanced combat management platform. Batch 2 construction is already under way, with the second unit expected to be launched this year.
The new boats also feature advanced anechoic tiles covering their HY-100 steel hulls to suppress underwater radiated noise and reduce active/passive sonar detectability. The K-111 class submarines are part of South Korea’s three-axis defense system, a strategy aimed at detecting, intercepting and retaliating against missile threats. The inclusion of SLBM capability on a conventional submarine makes the KSS-III unique.
Should the AUKUS public inquiry find that a non-nuclear-powered alternative to the Collins class is a desirable option for Australia’s defense, it is manifest that the KSS-III should be considered as a replacement. The independent publication Naval News describes the KSS-III as “the most potent conventionally powered and armed submarine in the world”. The cost is much more affordable; its performance is outstanding; it has none of the problems associated with nuclear waste disposal and security – and it can be delivered on a much faster schedule than the AUKUS boats.
Perhaps more importantly than all of this, discontinuing the purchase of AUKUS nuclear attack submarines surely removes a powerful incentive for China to attack Australia.
This article was originally published by the website Pearls and Irritations and is reprinted with permission.

More than 80 reported abducted in Nigeria as police find human remains
Farmers and women abducted in northern Niger and Zamfara states as police find human remains, including 28 skulls, at suspected gang camps.
More than 80 people have been reported missing in Nigeria after being abducted by armed gangs, a media report said, as authorities announced the discovery of human remains suspected to belong to victims of kidnapping in the southeastern state of Abia.
The AFP news agency reported on Monday that at least 87 people, mostly women, were missing after two separate weekend attacks.

At least 47 farmers were abducted by armed men while harvesting peanuts in the northern Niger State on Saturday, while 40 women were kidnapped in the neighbouring state of Zamfara on Sunday, the agency reported, citing two security reports and a local source.
The kidnappings in the Mariga area of Niger and Yargada in Zamfara are the latest attacks by criminal gangs who specialise in ransom kidnappings and cattle rustling. Locally known as “bandits”, they regularly carry out bloody raids on villages, killing residents and torching homes after looting them.
Separately, police in Abia announced in a statement on Sunday that they found 28 human skulls and bones ”suspected to be [of kidnapped] victims”, after raiding camps linked to criminal groups in the forests.
In a statement on X, the police said suspects at the scene had fled and added that “efforts are intensified to apprehend the fleeing suspects”.
Mass abductions for ransom have become common in parts of northwestern and north-central Nigeria, with armed gangs frequently holding abductees until they are paid large sums of money.
In August, gunmen abducted as many as 600 worshippers during Friday prayers at a mosque in Dekera village in the north-central Niger State.
According to research from SBM Intelligence, a Lagos-based consultancy, armed groups raised some 7.8 billion naira (nearly $6m) in ransom payments between July 2025 and June 2026, more than triple the 2.6 billion naira paid during the same period last year.
The latest wave of kidnappings comes a few months ahead of the January presidential elections, in which security, along with the rising cost of living, is set to be a major issue.
President Bola Tinubu has faced growing criticism over lax security.
Residents of Niger State protested last Monday over the abduction of hundreds of people who, they said, remained in captivity a month after gunmen attacked several communities in one of the country’s largest mass kidnappings.

Ukrainian forces repel 30 Russian attacks on Pokrovsk front, 213 combat clashes recorded overall

Source: General Staff of the Armed Forces of Ukraine on Facebook, information as of 08:00 on 29 September
Details: A total of 213 combat clashes were recorded over the past day.
On the North Slobozhanshchyna front and in the operational zone in Russia's Kursk Oblast, four Russian assaults were recorded over the past day. The Russians launched four airstrikes, using nine guided bombs, and conducted 190 strikes on Ukrainian positions and settlements.
On the South Slobozhanshchyna front, Ukrainian forces repelled eight Russian attacks. The Russians attempted to advance towards the settlements of Nova Kozacha, Dovhenke, Khrypuny, Riznykove and Lozova.
On the Kupiansk front, the Russians conducted one attack in an attempt to improve their positions towards the city of Kupiansk.
On the Lyman front, Russian attempts to break through Ukrainian defences were repelled, with the Russians conducting 11 attacks near the settlements of Ridkodub, Novoselivka, Drobysheve, Lyman and Dibrova.
On the Sloviansk front, the Russians conducted two assaults near the settlements of Yampil and Kryva Luka.
On the Kramatorsk front, the Russians conducted one attack near the village of Yurkivka.
On the Kostiantynivka front, 22 Russian attacks were recorded. The Russians conducted assaults near the settlements of Kostiantynivka, Novoselivka, Dovha Balka and Vilne and towards Kucheriv Yar and Zolotyi Kolodiaz.
On the Pokrovsk front, the Russians conducted 30 attacks. According to updated information, the Russians attempted to advance near the settlement of Svitle and Molodetske and towards Dobropillia, Novohryshyne, Serhiivka and Novopavlivka.
On the Oleksandrivka front, the Russians conducted two attacks near the settlements of Oleksandrohrad and Berezove.
On the Huliaipole front, the Russians conducted five attacks on Ukrainian positions. They attempted to advance near the settlements of Hirke, Huliaipolske and Charivne and towards Vozdvyzhivka.
On the Orikhiv front, the Russians made five attempts to improve their positions by attacking towards the settlements of Novoandriivka, Yurkivka, Pavlivka and Stepnohirsk.
On the Prydniprovske front, the Russians did not conduct any assaults.
On the Volyn and Polissia fronts, there is no evidence of any offensive Russian groups being formed in the area.

Ukraine's digital minister: 'We want Europe to use Ukraine as an AI sandbox'
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-29
05:15:25 UTC
14:15:25 KST

Ukraine has built a digital state under the pressure of war. Digital Minister Oksana Ferchuk tells Euronews what Europe can learn from Ukraine, from digital government and AI to cybersecurity and resilience.
Do you know where your driving licence, ID or marriage certificate is right now? In Ukraine, you can access these and many other essential documents directly on your phone.
The country has built one of the world’s most advanced digital government systems, with services that allow citizens to handle much of their everyday bureaucracy online.
During her visit to Berlin, Ukrainian Minister of Digital Transformation Oksana Fedorova met with her German counterpart, Karsten Wildberger, to discuss how Ukraine and Germany could share their experiences.
The two countries agreed to bring together dedicated teams to take a closer look at what Ukraine has done well – but also at what has not worked – and explore which of its digital solutions could be useful for Germany.
Euronews met Ferchuk at the Ukrainian Embassy in Berlin during her visit to discuss the kind of cooperation Germany and Ukraine can expect, her views on the latest warnings about AI, and how Ukraine's digital infrastructure can withstand Russian attacks.
Euronews: What are some of the key things Germany can learn from Ukraine that these teams will be looking at?
Ferchuk: First of all, our ecosystem of state services, which we utilise in a platform called Diia ("action" in English). It's a mobile app, web portal and network of offline locations where we, as a government, provide public services to Ukrainians.
The app gives users access to more than 30 digital documents, including your passport, driving licence, information about your children, your tax ID and your children's tax IDs. Beyond these documents, which we believe could also be used across Europe as the EU moves in the same direction with its digital identity wallet initiative, we offer a wide range of services. These include selling a car through the app, giving someone else permission to drive your car without having to visit an office and checking and paying fines online.
Another area of the app is where you can get married or divorced online and you can even propose online. Ukrainians living abroad who want to get married under Ukrainian law can also do so through Diia, with our postal service then sending them the official paper certificate by post.
In total, we offer around 250 public services online. We agreed to analyse these services together with the German ministry team, identify some for service design, and potentially even develop a prototype for Germany. We also agreed to build this connection not only between our government teams, but also to introduce German counterparts to the IT companies that have been developing these kinds of applications and services for the Ukrainian government for several years. We call them the GovTech Alliance of Ukraine, and we'll be happy to introduce them to our German partners.
Euronews: There seems to be a greater acceptance of making mistakes along the way.
Ferchuk: This is one of the biggest differences between the IT world and government. In government, we have to do everything in accordance with the law. But as a government, working together with parliament, we also have the ability to change the law.
That is the mentality we have. If we see that a simple, user-friendly service cannot be provided because of certain legislative restrictions, and changing those laws would have a positive impact on society, we change the law and then make the service easier to use. In the IT world, by contrast, success often comes from experimenting and trying things repeatedly.
To give people the freedom to innovate, you have to give them permission to make mistakes. Those mistakes should never compromise data protection or security, and they should never breach the law. But you have to give your IT teams the freedom to make mistakes. Otherwise, they will simply follow what is already set out in the legislation, and there will be no real innovation.
Euronews: If we look ahead to the winter, Russia also targets critical infrastructure, so there can be situations where there is no electricity, no mobile network, or people simply can't charge their phones. How do you make sure that people can still access these essential services in those situations?
Ferchuk: That's a very important question and another area of cooperation with the German government. We discussed it separately because we are not only building a digital state; we are building digital resilience. This is not our first winter. Unfortunately, it's the fourth or fifth, depending on how you count from the very beginning.
Will this winter be more difficult? Yes, we expect it to be, but we have been preparing for it since the summer.
We have a specific programme with telecom operators and are training our teams on what to do when the electricity goes out during blackouts. We are preparing to use generators and batteries to keep base stations running and mobile networks operational. We are now planning for outages of up to five days, with a plan for each area. Unfortunately, Russia started attacking our digital infrastructure a week ago. They attacked more and more our data centres.
Recently, they attacked two of our telecom providers. But the result is that the services are still available because we have backups and can move systems into the cloud or underground. We have a specific resilience strategy for all state-owned and government IT systems and services. We have backups for everything and are now conducting exercises, including deliberately switching some systems off.
It's all part of the training. What Europe can expect from Ukraine is an opportunity to see how the state can use AI to improve public services. With your Ministry of Digital Transformation, we have agreed to connect our AI teams and develop some services together. Your teams will be able to see how we train our models, which models we use and how the architecture is built. And we are ready to share not only our successes, but also our mistakes. This is an important message for the European Union. We are now required to harmonise our legislation with the so-called AI Act.
But we would like to propose a slightly different approach. We propose that Europe use Ukraine as an AI sandbox: a place where it can observe the experiments we are conducting, learn from what works and then implement those lessons safely in the European environment. In the digital sphere, our experience with documents and public services could also be replicated across the European Union, creating a single digital space where documents are accepted across borders and services are available cross-border. This is our proposition to the European Union and to Berlin.
Euronews: Why is Ukraine so digitally advanced? Was this something that was accelerated by the full-scale invasion, or did it already exist before the invasion?
Ferchuk: That's more of a philosophical question. I'd say it started in the early 2000s, when many businesses began innovating and developing digital products, laying the foundations for Ukrainians to start using digital applications. We realised that it was much easier, more convenient and more user-friendly when services were available online.
The first wave of adoption and acceptance really came from the commercial sector. Then, in 2019, a new government came to power, and several prominent figures from Ukraine's IT sector joined it. They had a clear vision and strategy and in 2019 they established the Ministry of Digital Transformation. From that point on, that vision was implemented, refined and continuously updated. As a result, we now have a government that thinks about digital transformation and digital tools across all areas. And it's not just about policies.
We have also created dedicated digital transformation positions in every ministry and every major government body. If you want to provide a service to a citizen, you often need information from different government bodies. We have digitalised much of this information and created a large number of decentralised registers. This is also very important: the registers are protected, and the information is never stored in one central database.
When you, as a citizen, request a service, we only retrieve the specific information we need about you from each relevant register or database. We then bring that information together to provide the service. That is one of the reasons why this system is possible.
Euronews: How do you protect data when so many government services are online? Russia is using hybrid warfare, including cyberattacks. Is there a specific security system or firewall in place, or does accessing only specific pieces of information from different ministries already provide an additional layer of protection?
Ferchuk: Both.It's a really complex architecture that is, first of all, decentralised. Second, we classify information according to its level of importance. We have open information and a lot of open data that is publicly available in Ukraine.
Then we have personal information, which is protected and not publicly available, but can be accessed when you request it as an individual. And then there is classified information, which has to be protected under much stricter rules. For each type of information, we have specific rules on how it should be protected, based on international best practices.
Is it 100% safe? In IT, you can never say that anything is 100% safe. But this is also a battlefield. The enemy is attacking us in cyberspace every day. There are thousands of attacks every year, and we are constantly developing our skills and our community of experts who know how to protect and monitor these systems 24/7.
We have what we call security operations centres, where teams monitor system logs and analyse anomalies and user patterns, increasingly with the help of AI. So it's a constant process: the enemy improves its tactics, and we improve our tools and defences.
Euronews: Like a cat-and-mouse game.
Ferchuk: It's a constant technology race. The good thing is that Ukraine has a large community of IT specialists and a strong academic sector, producing around 20,000 IT specialists each year.
This environment has also helped us build a strong community of cybersecurity experts. The major companies that develop and sell cybersecurity tools globally are also very interested in testing their technologies in the Ukrainian environment.
Euronews: Is there a parallel here with the defence industry? With drones, for example, companies are gaining valuable battlefield experience because their systems are being tested and used in Ukraine.
Oksana Ferchuk: It's the same approach, but the difference is that this experience is valuable not only for countries at war. Cyberattacks are already a reality for many countries. Different types of adversaries, not just Russia, are using these tactics to disrupt or destabilise the IT systems of other countries and their allies. So this knowledge is very valuable.
The good thing is that the major companies producing cybersecurity tools are very interested. They come to us, and we work with them directly. They provide us with new updates, and there is also a continuous cycle of innovation: new tactics from the enemy, new products from vendors, and new defensive tactics and experience from our teams. It's developing very quickly. That’s why we are concerned and would really like our partners and allies to be part of this race and see what's happening.
The Baltic countries are very good at sharing this experience. We would love Germany to do the same.
Euronews: You've mentioned AI. Some AI developers themselves warn about the risks of increasingly powerful systems. From a more basic perspective, how do we ensure that AI doesn't get too much access to our digital infrastructure?
Ferchuk: I don’t really want to comment on it in those terms, because some people make very emotional statements that are then picked up by other media. I'd rather approach it from a different perspective. When the internet was first developed, there were concerns that it would change the world, take away our jobs and so on. So we shouldn’t be afraid of this new technology.
When you look at AI in more detail, you understand how advanced it is and what kind of fundamental changes it can bring to our everyday processes. AI is a really powerful tool. It can help us analyse more data, make more decisions based on facts rather than feelings and, above all, eliminate the routine bureaucratic work that everybody hates. So I see the influence of AI in a very positive way.
At the same time, for people who are afraid of AI and are wondering whether to use it to modernise their economies and everyday lives, they have to look at what is happening in other countries, where this question is no longer being asked. Those countries are already in a race, actively building infrastructure and training specialised models that increase productivity and efficiency and will have a huge economic and cultural impact.
If your country or your industry is not using this technology, somebody else in another country already is. And we have to remember that we are part of a global market and are competing globally. So I would say it’s really wrong not to pay attention to this technology. It can improve our lives dramatically. We just have to be wise enough to put the right guardrails in place and use it in an ethical, effective and responsible way. We actually have a strategy for using AI to achieve the maximum possible impact.
Our vision is to build what we call a full AI stack. We are working on our own sovereign AI factory infrastructure. At the same time, we use cloud infrastructure to compare the performance of different models. We mostly use open models and train them for specific tasks, and we now have a lot of experiments under way for government use.
Then we have the application layer. This includes the mobile applications I mentioned earlier. Diia is a government services app used by more than 24 million Ukrainians. It's a great platform for showing people what an AI-powered service can look like. We launched the world's first AI assistant that helps you understand how to access the government service you need.

Czech Republic ready for Wembley 30 years after Euro '96
United Kingdom
Unknown Publisher

Czech Republic ready for Wembley 30 years after Euro '96
- Published
The Czech Republic will return to the north London site that staged one of the biggest days in their history during this international break - as they head back to Wembley.
They face England twice in Nations League Group A3 - in Prague on Tuesday (19:45 BST) and London on 6 October.
The Czechs have been to Wembley since losing the Euro '96 final to Germany under the old stadium's twin towers, but this visit marks the 30-year anniversary of that remarkable summer in England.
The Czech Republic's nearly moment
Euro '96 was the first European Championship staged after Czechoslovakia separated - forming the Czech Republic and Slovakia.
But nobody expected the Czech team to have much impact at the tournament, including the country's own players.
They were outsiders, and most of the squad were still based in their domestic league.
Several had booked their holidays for straight after the group stage - which involved Germany, Italy and Russia - and Vladimir Smicer was even due to get married.
Midfielder Patrik Berger says his then Borussia Dortmund team-mate Jurgen Kohler did not even know the Czechs were at the Euros... and the defender was in the Germany squad.
Berger, speaking to the BBC Sporting Witness podcast earlier this year, said of Kohler: "He was asking me what my plans were for the summer. I said 'I'm going to the Euros' and he said 'to watch games?'
"I said 'no, we're playing you guys the first game of the group stages and then we will play in the final' - and he was laughing."
The Czechs lost their opening game 2-0 to Germany at Old Trafford before beating Italy 2-1 at Anfield.
Smicer's late equaliser in a 3-3 draw against Russia - at his future home of Anfield - was enough to see them through because Italy failed to beat Germany in the other game, finishing 0-0.
"We knew we were still in it, but we didn't know what the other result is," said Berger, who would go on to play for Liverpool with Smicer. "One minute we're not qualifying, the next it was we qualified, so we didn't really know.
"After the final whistle it took a few minutes before we realised we qualified for the quarter-finals."
In the quarters came one of the most memorable European Championship goals ever, with Karel Poborsky scooping the ball over Vitor Baia from the edge of the box to give the Czech Republic a 1-0 win over Portugal at Villa Park.
And, after a goalless draw against France in the semis at Old Trafford, the Czechs would win 6-5 on penalties.
Their spot-kicks were netted by players including future Ballon d'Or winner Pavel Nedved, Berger and Poborsky, who was back at the ground weeks later as a newly signed Manchester United player.
"You don't want to go there," said Berger of taking a penalty in a shootout.
"If someone says something different they're lying. Nobody wants to take that penalty."
He said the team "couldn't believe" they had beaten France.
"We were living the dream," Berger said. "It was an amazing feeling. An amazing moment for the country.
"To get to the final was kind of like a miracle for everyone."
Two days before the final, Smicer returned to Prague to get married.
Thousands of Czech fans turned out in the city centre for the occasion, but Smicer had to return to England the same day.
The Czech Republic faced Germany in the final at Wembley - and led after 59 minutes through Berger's drilled penalty.
He revealed he was not even meant to be the penalty taker but "could see nobody really wanted to take the ball".
"The only thing in my mind was hit it as hard as possible on target," he said.
Sadly for the Czechs, Oliver Bierhoff equalised 14 minutes later - and then scored the first ever golden goal in a major tournament final to give Germany the win.
"It wasn't meant to be," said Berger. "I'd love to be European champion, but silver for us was like a gold because it opened doors to so many of us. And it opened doors to the generation after us. I have no regrets.
"Thanks to Euro 96, because it was played in England, I caught the eye of Liverpool.
"There were 100,000 waiting for us in Prague celebrating. Even silver felt like winning the tournament for us."
What happened next
As Czechoslovakia, the country won the European Championship in 1976 - and lost two World Cup finals (1934 and 1962).
But the Czech Republic's first tournament as a separate nation remains the last time they reached a final.
They have, however, enjoyed other memorable European Championships - having reached the 2004 semi-finals and the quarters in 2012 and 2021.
The 2004 squad had a mix of youth - such as Petr Cech, Milan Baros and Tomas Rosicky - and experience with Smicer, Berger and Poborsky.
They lost to eventual winners Greece in the last four.
Ondrej Zlamal, a Prague-based football journalist, says that team and their performances "were even better" than in 1996.
"This generation with Nedved and others culminated in 2004 and we had a feeling we should have won the Euros. We played better football than in 1996," Zlamal said. "It was the second highlight of the golden generation."
Their only two World Cups since then - 2006 and 2026 - have ended in group stage exits.
Zlamal said: "The performance this summer was really disappointing.
"There is a simple answer to why [the team have not lived up to the heights of the past] – we don't have such talented footballers as we had.
"We don't have enough players in the top teams like we used to.
"When I was six I watched the 1976 final which Czechoslovakia won, and my father told me 'remember this because you won't see it any more'.
"I don't believe this generation can reach such a success because the competition and football is much bigger.
"Miracles happen and maybe there could be a new generation which could be surprising as 1996... but I don't believe it will happen again."
A new era is starting with the Czech team under Spaniard Santi Denia, the first foreign manager in the national side's history.
His first squad - for Nations League games against Croatia, England and Spain - contains seven players with either no caps or one cap - although none are aged under 22.
Thirty years since Berger, Smicer, Poborsky and Nedved endured their north London heartbreak, the creaking old stadium has long ago been substituted out and replaced by a Wembley fit for the 21st Century.
Denia and his players could certainly pick a worse setting to deliver a statement performance.

Earth’s day isn’t exactly 24 hours. The reason may lie deep inside the planet
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-29
05:08:47 UTC
14:08:47 KST

Earth’s day isn’t exactly 24 hours. The reason may lie deep inside the planet
- Date:
- September 29, 2026
- Source:
- Nature
- Summary:
- Scientists may have solved why the length of Earth’s day changes by a few milliseconds over decades. Subtle shifts in the inner core appear to tug on the mantle, revealing a surprisingly dynamic world thousands of kilometers beneath our feet.
- Share:
Most of us think of a day as a fixed 24 hours. In reality, Earth's rotation is not perfectly constant.
The difference is tiny, measured in milliseconds, but physicists can detect it. Over time, some days become slightly shorter or longer depending on subtle changes deep inside the planet.
Earth's Core and Mantle Trade Momentum
For roughly three decades, scientists have known that Earth's liquid core does not always rotate at the same rate. Changes in the planet's magnetic field have revealed that the liquid core can gradually speed up over several decades, then slow down during the following decades.
At the same time, the mantle, the roughly 3,000 kilometer thick rocky layer that includes the crust, responds in the opposite direction. When the core speeds up, the mantle slows slightly. When the core slows, the mantle speeds up.
This exchange happens because Earth's total angular momentum must remain constant.
Even very small changes in the mantle's rotation are enough to alter the length of a day by a few milliseconds.
A Hidden Gravitational Tug Inside Earth
Scientists have long struggled to explain exactly how the core and mantle exchange this rotational momentum.
In a new study published Sept. 23 in Nature, University of Alberta physics PhD student Huifeng Zhang and professor Mathieu Dumberry present a possible answer.
Their work shows that small changes in the rotational speed of Earth's inner core, the solid region at the planet's center, can create what scientists call a "gravitational torque." Because the inner core is not perfectly spherical, changes in its motion can gravitationally interact with uneven distributions of mass in the mantle.
That interaction can slightly alter how quickly the mantle rotates, producing small changes in the length of a day.
Competing Forces Control Earth's Rotation
Another force also acts at the boundary between the core and mantle.
Known as core mantle boundary torque, it produces friction and electromagnetic drag that oppose the gravitational pull. This resistance helps limit how much Earth's day length can change.
According to the researchers, the small observed variations in the length of a day arise from subtle shifts in the balance between gravitational torque and core mantle boundary torque.
Earth's Inner Core May Be More Dynamic Than Expected
Beyond helping explain a long standing mystery about Earth's changing day length, the findings also offer new insight into what is happening deep inside the planet.
Zhang and Dumberry say the inner core appears to "deform viscously" on a time scale of about 10 years, suggesting that Earth's deepest interior may change shape and respond to forces far more dynamically than its solid composition might imply.
Story Source:
Materials provided by Nature. Original written by Geoff McMaster. Note: Content may be edited for style and length.
Journal Reference:
- Huifeng Zhang, Mathieu Dumberry. Gravitational torque drives multidecadal variations in length of day. Nature, 2026; DOI: 10.1038/s41586-026-10999-2

OpenAI scraps release of newest AI model over safety concerns
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-29
05:03:28 UTC
14:03:28 KST

Darren Lyn
29 September 2026•Update: 29 September 2026
OpenAI said Monday that it is scrapping the release of its newest next-generation artificial intelligence (AI) model over safety concerns, according to media reports.
The move comes in the wake of recent industry-wide instances of rogue AI models conducting cyberattacks on their own.
OpenAI nixed the plans because of concerns researchers raised during its internal testing, which makes the decision one of the clearest instances that AI's autonomous misbehavior could halt the industry's lightning-fast progression of artificial intelligence development.
The Wall Street Journal reported that OpenAI had planned to launch the model, known as GPT-6.1 Astra, in the coming days or weeks, aiming for an October debut. According to the report, "the model was more capable than the company’s previous models in completing challenging tasks from end-to-end without human assistance, as well as writing."
 
Specifically, GPT-6.1 Astra showed higher levels of deception, according to an internal interview with OpenAI's head of safety systems, Saachi Jain.
It wasn’t always honest about telling users of the actions it did or didn’t take, he said.
In addition, the GPT-6.1 Astra model engaged in what is called "scope authorization," meaning that it "would push ahead on a task without asking the user for permission and would at times reach for external tools and services even if it might be unsafe."
"For anything regarding safety and alignment, there’s a tradeoff," said Jain. "You really do need to find what’s the right line between staying within scope but also avoiding laziness in terms of how the model actually pursues tasks even when it hits friction."
OpenAI’s move followed weeks of reports that some of its AI models went rogue during their testing, hacking into websites without the company’s knowledge or exhibiting other behavior that the lab said was "concerning," such as hiding mistakes and making up data as well as hacking into several outside companies' websites, temporarily disrupting, and even shutting down, some of their operations.
Last week, OpenAI announced that it was pausing training for its most advanced models and said that it would instead focus on the safety of future models. The company added that it has embarked on an extensive review of actions taken by its new models during testing and that it was possible it would discover more incidents.
OpenAI’s Chief Executive Sam Altman said Friday in a social media post that the company had "not been as fast as we would have liked" in disclosing AI incidents.
"We are prioritizing as best as we can based on severity," he said.
The cancellation announcement of the newest artificial intelligence model comes one day ahead of OpenAI’s annual developer conference in San Francisco, where new models and services are usually launched and offered to software developers at reduced prices, a segment in which the ChatGPT maker competes with rival AI company Anthropic to win over clients.
But in recent weeks, OpenAI and Anthropic have both called on industry partners "to slow down the development of cutting-edge AI models and invest in safety standards, noting they will temper the pace of their own internal AI progress."
