US Secretary of State Marco Rubio said Monday that Cuba has already “fallen,” describing the island as a failed state with a dysfunctional economy and government.
In an interview with Fox News, Rubio argued that Cuba’s political and economic systems have failed to provide meaningful benefits to its population and said the country needs a period of transition toward greater political and economic freedom.
“Well, the truth is Cuba's already fallen,” he said. “It doesn't have a functional economy and it's governed by people who continue to preach about some revolution that has been dead for 20 years.”
Rubio said the Cuban government’s political model has failed to produce a functioning economy or government.
“The problem that Cuba has basically right now is it is a failed state in every sense of the word,” he said. “It's not a functional government and it's not a functional country. It just simply isn't.”
He also pointed to migration from Cuba as evidence of the country’s economic difficulties. He said that since 2021, nearly 20% of Cuba’s population has left the country, describing the migration as a consequence of a “complete failure.”
"We're hopeful that Cuba will choose a different path," Rubio said.
Rubio argued that economic reforms alone would not be sufficient to fundamentally change conditions on the island. He said political freedoms would need to accompany economic changes.
“In fact, you cannot have economic freedom in Cuba if you don't have political freedom first,” he said. “You have to have both happening at least at the same time. That will require a period of transition."

A total of 31 US senators urged the Trump administration to extend and redesignate Temporary Protected Status (TPS) for Ukrainians living in the US as Russia’s war against Ukraine continues.
The bipartisan letter, led by Sen. Tammy Duckworth, asks Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin and Secretary of State Marco Rubio to issue an 18-month extension and redesignation of TPS for Ukraine before the current designation expires on Oct. 19.
The senators warned that allowing the protection to expire could force thousands of Ukrainians living in the US to return to a country still affected by active fighting, civilian casualties and widespread damage to critical infrastructure.
Ukraine was initially designated for TPS on April 19, 2022. The TPS was subsequently extended and redesignated through April 19, 2025 and extended again beginning April 20, 2025.
"Protecting the approximately 101,000 Ukrainian TPS holders currently living in the United States is a humanitarian imperative, but also a sound economic decision," they wrote.
According to the lawmakers, Ukrainian TPS holders contribute approximately $2.6 billion to the US economy each year and pay about $716 million in taxes annually.
“Current conditions in Ukraine clearly merit the continuation of TPS status,” the senators wrote, arguing that Ukrainian nationals cannot safely return while the war continues.

Ukrainian Intel Exposes Russia Helping Iran Target US Forces
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-29
04:09:40 UTC
13:09:40 KST

Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky has announced that Kyiv’s intelligence services will begin sharing evidence of what he described as a highly coordinated military reconnaissance loop between Russia and Iran.
According to the intelligence, Moscow has utilized its network of spy satellites to monitor Gulf states and critical US military assets in the Middle East. These orbital passes directly correlate with the timing of Iranian drone and missile strikes.
JOIN US ON TELEGRAM
Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official.
Zelensky offered a striking example. In a 48-hour window between July 19 and 20 alone, four air bases fell squarely within the lens of active Russian satellite surveillance – two in Bahrain, one in Jordan and one in Kuwait.
The intelligence described by Kyiv points to a potentially sophisticated reconnaissance cycle: pre-attack satellite collection, tactical tracking imagery that could assist operational planning, and post-strike battle damage assessment.
“The purpose is clear,” the president warned.
The specific Ukrainian intelligence revelation does not emerge in isolation. Western intelligence officials previously told The Wall Street Journal that Russia had supplied Iran with satellite-derived targeting information for attacks on US forces.
Ratcliffe’s high-stakes diplomacy from Moscow to Shannon
The disclosure also intersects with an unusual sequence of intelligence diplomacy involving CIA Director John Ratcliffe.
Ratcliffe traveled to Moscow on Aug. 25 for previously undisclosed meetings with senior Russian officials – the first known visit to Russia by a serving CIA director since William Burns traveled there in 2021.
Zelensky Warns Russia Is Training North Korea for War, Feeding Iran Satellite Intelligence
The CIA and Kremlin did not publicly detail the agenda.
The White House subsequently played down the significance of the visit.
Less than a month later, Ratcliffe and Zelensky unexpectedly crossed paths at Shannon Airport in Ireland.
Both aircraft were refueling. Zelensky was traveling to New York for the UN General Assembly, while Ratcliffe was returning from a meeting with Egyptian President Abdel Fattah el-Sisi.
Two sources familiar with the encounter described the conversation to Reuters as informal, with no details of the discussion disclosed.
Congressional scrutiny over a growing axis
The question of whether Russia is providing intelligence that assists Iranian attacks has already been a focal point of intense scrutiny in Washington.
During a high-profile Worldwide Threats hearing in Congress, CIA Director Ratcliffe was pressed by lawmakers about the extent of the Russia-Iran-China intelligence-sharing network.
Confronted by members of the Senate Select Committee on Intelligence, Ratcliffe formally confirmed that Tehran was aggressively requesting advanced intelligence assistance from both Moscow and Beijing to help it evade Western air defense networks.
Though some elements of the findings were withheld for classified sessions, the congressional record highlighted growing alarm over how Russia’s strategic cooperation with Iran directly threatens deployed American personnel.
“The Iranians are requesting intelligence assistance from Russia, from China, and from other adversaries of the United States,” the CIA director told lawmakers.
Asked directly whether Russia was doing so, he responded that he knew the answer but would discuss it only during the classified portion of the hearing.
Trading Ukraine for the Middle East
The deep leverage Moscow holds over Middle Eastern stability was further illustrated by staggering press reports detailing a backchannel proposal from the Kremlin.
According to investigative reports published by outlets such as Politico and The Wall Street Journal, Russian representatives presented a transactional geopolitical trade to the United States.
The reports revealed that Russia offered a bargain: Moscow would halt its intelligence-sharing and targeting-data pipeline to Iran in exchange for the United States severing its vital intelligence support to Ukraine.
The proposal was reportedly floated by Kremlin envoy Kirill Dmitriev to senior US representatives.
While Washington immediately rejected the deal, the transactional offer laid bare Moscow’s calculus – treating its surveillance support of Iranian strikes against US forces as a bargaining chip to isolate and subjugate Ukraine.
Washington now has a new sanctions tool
The disclosure comes shortly after President Donald Trump signed into law the Lindsey O. Graham Sanctioning Russia and Iran Act of 2026, a sweeping bipartisan package.
For the first time, this law grants the White House the authority to slap scorching secondary tariffs of up to 100% on foreign nations that continue to act as top buyers of Russian energy or facilitate the Kremlin’s sanctions evasion.
President Zelensky has explicitly called on Ukraine’s Western allies to demonstrate that there can be no “business as usual” with Vladimir Putin, warning that Moscow uses false diplomatic signals to buy time while escalating its campaign of terror.
By turning the screws on Russia’s global financing network and choking off the resources funding both the war in Europe and espionage in the Middle East, the US now possesses the ultimate economic leverage to force the aggressor toward real diplomacy.
In a striking diplomatic paradox, Vladimir Putin – the very leader accused of using satellite surveillance to help target US forces in the Middle East – could travel to American soil if he accepts the official invitation to attend the upcoming G20 summit in Miami.

Chinese automation equipment maker RoboTechnik Intelligent Technology fell up to 9.8 percent in its Hong Kong trading debut on Tuesday, after raising HK$5.18 billion in its share sale.
The stock dropped to as low as HK$393.20, compared with its offer price of HK$436, after opening at HK$419.60. 
It was last down 8.5 percent at HK$398.80.
The broader market was also weaker, with the Hang Seng Index falling 0.6 percent at one stage and the tech index down 1.2 percent.
RoboTechnik was one of four companies to start trading in Hong Kong on Tuesday, in a test of investor appetite for new share offerings amid a revival in the city's IPO market.
Hong Kong IPOs, including secondary listings, have raised US$46.54 billion so far this year, a 94.3 percent jump from a year earlier, LSEG data showed.
Printed circuit board maker Shenzhen Kinwong Electronic opened seven percent lower at HK$65, versus its HK$69.88 offer price, after raising HK$5.1 billion. 
The stock was last up 9.5 percent at HK$76.55.
Specialty chemicals and semiconductor materials maker Red Avenue New Materials Group opened 9.1 percent lower at HK$40 versus its HK$44 offer price, after raising about HK$3 billion.
Robotics technology company Direct Drive Tech opened 4.1 percent higher at HK$22.48, versus its HK$21.60 offer price, after raising HK$1.08 billion.
"I don’t think the IPO market has the same punch as before," said Dickie Wong, executive director of research at uSmart Securities. 
"Because of US-China tension in AI and chips sector and fears that AI is getting frothy, names in AI, robotics and PCB are no longer being chased the way they were.
"People are picking more carefully now. Theme alone is not enough. Valuation and recent momentum matter more. Subscription demand and first-day trading have both cooled a lot."
RoboTechnik makes equipment for photovoltaic cell manufacturing and assembly, and testing systems for silicon photonics devices used in optical interconnects for data centres and artificial intelligence infrastructure.
It sold 11.88 million Hong Kong shares in the base offering. 
Cornerstone investors, including Temasek, Sunpeak Asset and IvyRock, agreed to buy about US$232.4 million of shares, the prospectus showed.
The company plans to use listing proceeds for research and development, expanding production capacity and speeding up deliveries, global sales and service operations, as well as for potential acquisitions and working capital.
RoboTechnik reported first-half 2026 net profit of 6.3 million yuan, from a 12.2 million yuan loss a year earlier. 
Revenue rose 145.1 percent to 608.1 million yuan, driven mainly by silicon photonics assembly and testing equipment. (Reuters)

====================================================================================================

A leftwing victory in Berlin shows people want freedom, and liberals cannot deliver it | Eva von Redecker
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-29
04:00:53 UTC
13:00:53 KST

The German leftwing party Die Linke won the state elections in Berlin on 20 September. It’s unclear whether the party will be able to form a coalition, appoint its lead candidate Elif Eralp as mayor, and follow through on her core campaign promise: to socialise the housing stock of the city’s biggest real-estate companies. A barrage of accusations started to circulate immediately after the results came in. Even by the standards of present-day polarisation, the pitch was extreme.
On the basis of one leaked chat and one rapper’s performance, the party was described as schmoozing with criminal clans and endangering the lives of Berlin Jews. Accusations of antisemitism prompted the Greens and the SPD – potential coalition partners – to question any potential cooperation, while “alt-right” opinion-makers suggested that “Hamas and Hezbollah” had won the elections, or that the German Democratic Republic (the old East Germany) was about to come back. Alice Weidel of the rightwing AfD alleged that Die Linke intended to “shoot the rich”.
Our liberal capitalist orders are designed to protect property. Touch one bit of it, and the whole thing is apparently on fire. And yet, nerves aren’t always this raw. The current flare-ups reveal a deep crisis. Sober-sounding commentators have pointed out that the accusations against Die Linke are simply a strategy to stop the socialisation agenda. But that account of moral panic as deliberate strategy can hardly explain everything. Why do so many people want to believe the smear campaigns, especially while the simultaneous wins for the AfD are swiftly normalised?
The frenzy becomes less surprising once we understand the way in which liberalism is under pressure, and how that pressure predisposes the saner political forces to look like freedom’s foes. Freedom is the core of liberalism. It is freedom of a particular kind: individual freedom. It lets you do whatever you want as long as you don’t violate the freedom of others or, crucially, their property. The analogy between freedom and property runs deep: my entitlement to do whatever I want is derived from ownership of the self. I am my own quasi-property, and in that capacity I face other self-owners and rely on the state to adjudicate between us.
This balance, between personal freedom and the freedom of all others, is already precarious , but in the face of the global crises we face now, it is especially under strain. Liberalism cannot govern economic inequality or ecological disaster, except by pitting the individual freedom of future or far-away others against the freedom of the currently privileged. Without democratic pride in our collective ability to rule our shared fate, the resulting policies look like sacrifice with no upside – I lose the (however hypothetical) freedom to own a row of houses, or I lose the freedom to drive a car, but even if I got public housing or public transport in turn, that wouldn’t register as compensation. After all, I cannot do whatever I want with those.
Reason might be on the side of anti-discrimination, social distancing or electric vehicles, but freedom kicks on the other side. It isn’t full liberal freedom any more, which would have to regard other people as a limit, but its unhinged, ultra-possessive part.
The right offers quasi-property (or “phantom possession”, as I like to call it) to satisfy its voters: it defends traditional gender roles, the family, freedom of speech and the nation as though they were things to own. “Take back your country” was a core campaign slogan of the AfD. It alludes to the “great replacement” myth, according to which white populations are in the process of being replaced by people who are not. This plot weaves together several possessive entitlements: white citizens should “own” their country; the country and its men should “own” female reproductive powers to increase the domestic birthrate. And migrants aren’t even seen as capable of moving by their own will, but are imported by a woke or Jewish cabal, and now need to be removed by “remigration”.
While such racist discourse is more associated with rural areas, “phantom possession” can suddenly override concern for fellow migrant citizens in Berlin, too. Any wrong step by the Left will suffice for the political middle to succumb to its own generalised property panic. Shaken by the success of the AfD, disoriented by a future that liberalism effectively cannot rule, challenged by emancipatory claims of various groups, and struggling to defend Israel’s crimes, much of the so-called centre also breaks the liberal pact that is founded on equality.
In what some German Jews describe as “paternalistic philosemitism”, centrist pundits exceed the concern to fight antisemitism where it happens. Instead, they prop up an idea of absolute victimisation and defend it at all costs. They defend German “memory culture” as if it were their private asset. Consequently, Die Linke – just as human rights organisations, anti-zionist Jews, pro-Palestinian demonstrators and anyone perceived as vaguely “Arab” – is cast in the role of ruthless plunderer.
How Die Linke – and its promise to socialise some private housing – will weather this particular campaign is still unknown. But whatever happens, it has to continue to navigate a fractured political map. Like all emancipatory efforts at present, its potential Berlin mayoralty is up against unhinged claims, and faces objective problems that require real change.
Which is why the left cannot win within the liberal script. It can only win with a compelling formulation of freedom that points beyond the current impasse. Like Zohran Mamdani in New York, Die Linke has understood this. It has not only promised an abstract right, but literally the freedom to stay in one’s city, one’s neighbourhood, one’s flat. And this freedom can scale up: against displacement, genocide and the ecological doom that threatens our ability to remain on planet Earth.
The German left urgently needs to find a way to translate such an agenda to the countryside, where parts of the white population have fallen for fascist myths. Which non-toxic freedom could repair their lost sense of place? And above all, how can we guarantee the freedom to stay for the migrant communities who are threatened with deportation by the AfD? Where this fails, even the most basic liberal achievement of human rights is lost. And definitely not because of socialised housing.
- 
  Eva von Redecker is a philosopher and nonfiction writer. She is the author of The Freedom to Stay

‘Just look at this monstrosity!’ Inside Britain’s bilious back yard shed wars
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-29
04:00:53 UTC
13:00:53 KST

Linda loves her shed. She loves that she can work there rather than in her dining room, which her toddler likes to tear through. She loves its Scandinavian vibe – it’s clad in wood and set on decking at the bottom of her garden. She loves the views of the countryside from the window by her desk. Or she did. Her desk faces the wall now, because she’s too nervous to face her neighbour. She never sits on the decking, either. “What if they see me?” she says. “It’s a horrible feeling.”
Linda’s neighbours are unhappy about her shed, or “garden room”, which is actually two rooms. They do not like its size (7.25 metres by 2.74 metres, or 3.5 metres if you include the raised decking) or its position, about 30 metres away from their house. Linda says they have barely spoken since the construction, which is awkward, as the gardens are separated by a low fence.
The neighbours say the shed is more than half a metre too tall and too close to their property for it to be a “permitted development”, one that can be built without applying for planning permission. In England and Wales, there is a height cap of 2.5 metres from the ground if any part of the outbuilding falls within 2 metres of a boundary (it is within 1 metre of a boundary in Scotland). If the building is further from the boundary, it can be 3 metres or 4 metres high, depending on the roof type. The council agreed and told Linda she needed to apply for retrospective planning permission. She says it was an “honest mistake” and that she received the wrong guidance from her builders. “I was mortified. I would never have done it intentionally,” she says.
Before the build, Linda says, she had a friendly relationship with her neighbours; they would lend each other tools and garden materials. She says she had had an informal conversation with her neighbours about building a garden room in the space and heard no objections. Her neighbours say they were not consulted at all before construction, which took about a month.
Linda says she found out the extent of her neighbours’ feelings about her shed only in the paperwork for their planning dispute. They said they could see it from every window of their home and that they felt they had lost all sense of privacy, which had affected their daily lives and mental wellbeing. They also said an estate agent told them it had negatively affected the value of their home.
Retrospective planning permission for her shed has been granted, on the condition that a privacy screen and other planting are put up. Was it worth it? Yes, Linda believes, but she says: “I wish we had known to go about it the right way; it would have saved us money and a heck of a lot of effort and time …”
The dispute between Linda and her neighbours is just one example of simmering resentment over the increased use of these kinds of outhouses in the UK. The news is regularly peppered with spicy shed disputes – and no social strata is exempt. Pink Floyd’s David Gilmour was ordered to move a shed in his garden in upmarket Hampstead, north London, last year after it was described as “intrusive” and “overbearing” by neighbours who wanted a retrospective planning application to be refused. It was ordered to be rebuilt further back from the boundary.
Part of the reason for these disputes is the growing popularity of outhouses. Simon Rix, a senior planning consultant and a director of Planix.uk, a consultancy company that advises people who want to extend, says he received “a trickle” of clients who wanted to build luxury sheds before the pandemic, but that has “probably gone up tenfold”.
As well as home offices, gyms and storage, many are used for habitable living spaces, as the housing crisis continues to stunt home-buying. “Quite a lot of people are coming to me because they want to move into it and let their children live in the main house,” Rix says. He is also seeing more static caravans in gardens for the same reason – these don’t count as a “development” and do not need planning permission if they are housing a family member. “Neighbours get really grumpy, because they can be quite tall and imposing,” he says.
Planning rules around these outhouses are “monumentally complex”, says Rix, who would like them to be simplified. Both sides regularly misunderstand their rights. “Neighbours frequently assume that if something looks large, blocks a view or sits right on the fence line, it must be illegal. Conversely, homeowners often wrongly assume: ‘It’s my garden, I can do what I want.’ This gap in understanding, combined with the post-pandemic boom, is creating a perfect storm for neighbourhood disputes,” he says.
The regulations and rules around erecting outbuildings as part of permitted development vary not only in terms of the height and the proximity to a neighbour’s boundary. They must also be single storey and, in England and Wales, not “forward of the principal elevation” – the front wall of the house facing the highway (in Scotland, there is some provision for a small shed). Outbuildings cannot take up more than 50% of the total garden, either, and listed homes and those in conservation areas and other special sites face different restrictions. According to research by Ronseal, more than 40% of Britons are unaware some sheds will require a planning application.
Yet even outhouses that meet permitted development heights can loom large and cause tension in tightly packed British gardens. Emma watched her husband creep into their garden under cover of darkness late one night to measure the shed their neighbours were constructing close to the boundary, because it looked so vast. “He climbed on to our picnic table with a tape measure,” she says. “It’s so close to our boundary that it wasn’t a stretch to measure it – he didn’t even need to hang over the fence.”
The shed measured under 2.5 metres and the couple had to accept that it was permitted. They felt that mentioning anything to the neighbour would only cause bad feeling, but while they have grown used to the building, which is barely used, they worry about how potential buyers will view it. “The overriding factor is they are small gardens,” says Emma. The plots are around 10 metres by 7 metres. The neighbour mentioned their plans, but “we thought it would be a pod … we didn’t anticipate the sheer size”, she says. “Remaining friends” was most important. “We get on well and didn’t want to rock the boat,” she adds. “But if it was being used as a home office constantly, with phone calls being made and they’re looking back at you, maybe we’d feel differently.”
Dr Mike Talbot, a psychotherapist and the CEO of UK Mediation, says the company has noticed a rise in inquiries concerning external structures such as sheds, garden rooms, hot tubs and even trampolines. He believes that councils tend not to intervene and often recommend mediation. Fewer than 10% of inquiries actually reach that stage, though, because while the opposing neighbour is usually the one to call them, they must then approach the shed builder – who generally does not wish to join (or share the £450 cost of the process). He recalls an occasion when a shed window “was mysteriously broken” and things turned nasty: “The shed owner went round and threatened to smash their neighbour’s face in.”
However, if mediation takes place, it can be positive. One set of neighbours built a shed to be used as a playroom and office with a window on the neighbour’s side. They had previously had a good relationship, but were “not talking … which is quite common”. (Talbot says “slamming doors or dirty looks in the driveway” are other repercussions.) The compromise was blocking the window and putting up a trellis, which appeased both parties. In another example, an agreement was made concerning the times at which the shed owner’s teenage children could use the space.
Talbot believes that people are “more insular” than they used to be and less concerned than previous generations were about getting on with their neighbours. Social media plays a part, too. “We are so much more subject to scrutiny and you know that, if you do something people consider to be out of order, it’s going to be on the local Facebook group,” he says. “Trust is slower to build; we are more cautious of whom we talk to.” But if neighbours build a good relationship, he says, they are less likely to react negatively if a large shed does appear.
Dan has a good relationship with his neighbours, so when they approached him to discuss their plans for a structure in their 20-metre garden for a family member to stay in, “I had no problem”, he says. As it would be more than 2.5 metres high and a habitable dwelling, the neighbours had to apply for planning permission. “I looked at the plans and it seemed reasonable,” says Dan.
However, issues encountered during construction meant the height increased. When Dan and his partner arrived home from holiday, “I went to our bathroom, looked out of the window and said: ‘You need to come here immediately and look at this monstrosity,’” he says. After an emotional conversation with the neighbours, they agreed to take the height down, but Dan believes it is still about 1.5 metres higher than agreed in the original plans. For the sake of keeping good relations, he has decided not to go to the council and has instead spent about £2,000 on fencing to try to hide the structure.
“I did not want to ruin their plans,” he says. “But I did feel emotionally blackmailed.” While he is getting used to it, and continues to chat pleasantly with the neighbours, “when we look out of our living room window, it’s right there. And if someone is stood in that building, they are looking right in at us. It just feels slightly invasive. When people come round and notice it, they go: ‘Oh my God, what?’ They’re shocked.” Dan’s main worry, however, is the impact it may have when he comes to sell his house.
Linda, meanwhile, hopes to rebuild relations with her neighbours. “We’re not horrible people, on either side,” she says. “No one has done anything wrong here.” But unlike her shed, which will weather and soften, she knows there is no guarantee of this.

‘Intimidatory’ far-right marches should not be allowed, says Angela Rayner
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-29
04:00:53 UTC
13:00:53 KST

Far-right marches led by the self-styled “Danny Tommo” should not be treated like normal protests, the communities secretary, Angela Rayner, has said, calling the marches “intimidation” that should not be permitted.
Rayner said the behaviour of some masked marchers – who have blocked roads and transport hubs – was not an acceptable form of protest.
Daniel Thomas, the instigator of the marches over the past month, was arrested and charged last week after allegedly using a blade to slash an inflatable dinghy in the Channel while a rescue worker was onboard.
Rayner said the marches were frightening local people. “When you see hundreds of predominantly men in black wearing black face masks shouting, going down the street, that is intimidating,” she said. “Whether you agree with the message or not, it’s intimidating.”
She added: “It is not a protest. I’ve been on many protests myself when I was in my union days. We have music, we have banners, but we don’t wear balaclavas and shout divisive rhetoric down the street.
“There’s a line, and I think organising to disrupt and cordon off areas to stop people going through public highways, this is all behaviour that is intimidatory and is not acceptable.”
Thomas has recently brought dozens of nationalist protest groups together under the umbrella name of Patriot Platform. Masked and hooded anti-migrant activists from the movement have convened in English coastal towns and ports, in one case blocking traffic in and out of the port of Dover.
Rayner said she was deeply concerned by the way social media was amplifying extreme voices – especially those targeting the RNLI.
On the day that a 10-year-old child and two women died attempting to cross the Channel, Rayner said there needed to be more humanity about how migrants were described and treated when they attempted to cross in small boats.
“How can we get to the point where we dehumanise like this,” she asked. “Yes, we can have an argument about the criminals putting people on these boats, the legitimacy of someone’s claim. But when you’ve got a human being at risk of death, do we let them drown?
“That is ultimately what it comes down to. Yes, we politicians have a discussion about policies, about people we give asylum to, about how we stop boats. But [to] attack volunteers that save people from drowning?
“These are volunteers. If there’s a risk to life at sea, an RNLI volunteer without any political persuasion at all or any ideology will go out and will save lives at sea.
“To whip up hatred as if they are making a judgment on the value of these lives that they’re saving or not, and to put their faces up, identify them, to whip up online hatred towards volunteers whose sole job is to give up their time to save lives at sea. It’s not acceptable.”

‘It keeps growing’: the tent camp that stands against Spain’s housing crisis
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-29
04:00:53 UTC
13:00:53 KST

Wielding a broom and dustpan, Marta García, 60, darted past the edges of tents, sweeping up bits of litter as she passed a poster that read: “What kind of times are these, when we need to defend the obvious?”
On Saturday, as tens of thousands of people took to the streets of Madrid to protest against the country’s deepening housing crisis, the retired schoolteacher was among a small group who had sought to take the protest one step further.
“At first we were 10 tents,” she said, gesturing to the sprawling encampment set up in the central Puerta del Sol plaza behind her. “Now, we’re more than 300 tents, and it keeps growing.”
Days earlier, many across Spain had watched in shock as news channels showed Maricarmen Abascal, an 87-year-old woman with a disability, being evicted from the home where she had lived for seven decades. The shock soon gave way to anger as the octogenarian was shown being brought out of her home on a stretcher, flanked by protesters on one side and police officers on the other.
Housing campaigners seized on the moment. “The whole country has seen that housing speculation has no mercy on anyone,” said Alicia del Río of the Madrid Tenants’ Union. “We’re not sad, we’re angry. And we’re not going to stop until we change things.”
Abascal’s lawyers reportedly reached a deal for her to return home on Monday evening. “If this agreement we have reached is signed, it will obviously be a better and happier outcome for everyone,” her lawyer, Beatriz Duro, told reporters, saying it could “help to change the paradigm when it comes to housing in general”.
At the encampment earlier on Monday, many described the days of nationwide protests and the encampment as a turning point in a movement that had long simmered as rents rose by 80% within a decade, while the cost of homes climbed by 63%.
“We need stability,” said David Iglesias, 25, as he described how the ever-soaring prices had forced people to put their lives on hold to try to keep a roof over their heads.
“People who want to have children should be able to do so, even if they are renting. People who dream of becoming musicians or barbers should have the chance to do so and not have to worry that they need to work, work, work to pay for housing,” he said. “It’s an endless loop that is undermining the mental health of young people.”
As he spoke, a large banner flapped nearby, reading: “You can speculate on watches, jewels, cryptobros and Ferraris. But not on our fucking homes.”
The swelling encampment had prompted a raft of comparisons to 2011, when the Indignados, or 15M movement, began with a month-long occupation of the same Madrid plaza before snowballing into a force that had reshaped Spanish politics. Iglesias, however, brushed off the similarity. “That was about a general demand for change,” he said. “But we have a goal, and if this goal isn’t met by Tuesday, we’ll have to take action somehow.”
It was a nod to the informal camp slogan, launched by housing campaigners and oft-repeated by protesters in recent days: “Either the rentier economy falls, or the government does.”
As Spain’s government gears up for its weekly Tuesday meeting, campaigners have put forward a list of demands, from measures to halt evictions to the regulation of short-term and room rentals, making it clear that this is being seen as a make-or-break moment.
On Sunday, Spain’s prime minister, Pedro Sánchez, said his government was “working around the clock to introduce a royal decree on housing on Tuesday”.
The protests have put the Socialist leader in a complicated spot; while his coalition government includes leftwing forces who have long pushed for change, Spain’s fractured parliament means his chances are slim of attracting support for measures that could bring about real change.
Still, the momentum has continued to grow across the country, fuelled by the campaigners who occupied the offices of Madrid’s social housing agency on Monday to those in Barcelona who began the day by blocking off major thoroughfares.
“Today cannot be a day like all others,” said Enric Aragonès of the Barcelona Tenants’ union, ahead of a protest planned for Tuesday evening in the city. “There are only 24 hours left until we find out whether the government will approve a decree that is a sham or genuine.”
In Madrid, the calls for change had attracted a diverse group, including Oscar-winning film director Pedro Almodóvar, who visited on Sunday to voice his support for the protesters. “The housing problem is paralysing Spanish life,” he told broadcaster RTVE.
Sitting cross-legged in a tent and knitting to pass the time, Guillermo Esteve said he was part of a group of vegans who had decided to show their support by joining the encampment. “We’re a group of people who believe we can do things better,” he said, describing his hope that this would be part of a sweeping change that would start with the real estate sector, then address the precarity of the labour market and eventually tackle production systems. “We want laws that give us hope, not what we have now.”
The sentiment was echoed by García, the retired schoolteacher. “This camp is an example of how people still believe that things can change,” she said. “I have my life sorted out; I have a house. But I have two daughters who are sharing bedrooms because they have no other choice. So I can’t just sit around doing nothing.”
This was how she had ended up in the heart of Madrid on a Monday afternoon, sweeping the city’s central plaza, she added with a laugh. “Look, if I didn’t think this was going to amount to anything, I would just stay home and cry,” she said. “But I have to stay helpful.”
With contribution from Stephen Burgen in Barcelona

Why am I obsessed with China’s ancient golden age? I took my daughter on a trip to find out
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-29
04:00:53 UTC
13:00:53 KST

Tang
During the Tang dynasty, which lasted from the seventh to the early 10th century, Vikings were raiding the coasts of what today is called Europe. In the small archipelago now known as Britain, Anglo-Saxon kingdoms flitted by. Meanwhile, in Mesoamerica, after 3,000 years of flourishing, the Maya civilisation was collapsing. In the east, China had been united for nine centuries and the Tang dynasty was already a proverbial high point of world culture.
The Tang dynasty achieved an incredible level of social and cultural sophistication. Advances in science and medicine, sublime poetry, mystical paintings, high fashion in women’s clothing beyond the palace walls, exquisite ceramic and pottery arts, the invention of gunpowder and printing, highly elaborate cuisine, creative urban design and much more. It was a truly cosmopolitan empire with dynamic diplomatic relations with the neighbouring kingdoms.
When I ponder this, an urge arises in me: a kind of duty, if you like, to write about this era. The Tang contrasts sharply with the image of a self-enclosed, inward-looking China, one that the west has long liked to promote. An open, cosmopolitan melting pot, it was the eastern centre into which flowed the riches of the silk roads that stretched all the way to the Byzantine empire.
But still, why the Tang? And why learn about the Tang from me? I have my own story to tell, which has no pretence to objectivity. My story involves a specific, passionate reconnection with my own heritage. I wanted to return to China after a long absence. The last time I was there had been a decade before, along with my then three-month-old child, Moon. My desire to go back was in part for her, now 11 years old. So she and I set off on a journey back to the cultural womb from which I had emerged and had left behind. I had to explain the Chinese past not only to the child, but to myself.
Xi’an
Our journey began in Xi’an, the capital of the Tang dynasty. A high-speed train had brought us from Beijing on a searingly hot day in July. On the road, the tarmac glistened and oozed out its black heat, while the city roared in full force with an immense river of traffic.
I had booked a traditional-looking hotel, thinking we should taste more of the old China. When we reached the hotel, we had to squeeze ourselves in between a gang of businessmen all wearing black suits with alcohol-flushed faces. They spoke at high volume, while coughing and hawking. Was it a gathering for people with respiratory illnesses? I could smell their strong cigarettes from several metres away. With “no smoking” signs in the lobby, they stood by the hotel gate puffing away while cracking loud jokes. They spoke Shanxi dialect and I could vaguely make out that their laughter was to do with food and women. How familiar all this was; men in suits, chain-smoking, looking for girls – the kind of stuff that came with the recent wealth from the “Chinese miracle”. Where were the women, though? As usual, women worked. The receptionist and the manager were women. They gave us the room key after taking our money.
Our room reeked of smoke; even the white bedding. We wanted to venture out immediately. We jumped into an air-conditioned taxi and set off to find some famous landmarks.
An hour later we were standing by the Giant Wild Goose Pagoda. Moon hid under a nearby pomegranate tree, sucking an ice lolly, her chestnut-coloured hair tangled with sweat. Beyond the deafening sound of cicadas high up in the tree, the heat formed a shimmering layer of pink fog above the pagoda. Sweat was dripping from my eyebrows, obscuring my vision.
Everyone in China knows that Xi’an is one of the oldest cities in the country. It’s our Rome or Athens. Over a 2,000-year period, it served as the capital for several dynasties, though it was called Chang’an back then. Traces of the Tang are everywhere. Like many other old monuments, the Giant Wild Goose Pagoda of today is not original. Built at the beginning of the Tang in the seventh century, it was restored in the eighth century, then rebuilt in the 16th century after an earthquake. Constructed of brick and wood, the facade displays elaborate sculptures and carvings on the eaves. We joined a swirl of tourists around the tall tower, but we were not allowed to enter because it is too fragile for crowds.
Moon was born and brought up in England. She had never experienced this climate, nor such crowds massed around her. There was not a single puff of wind. I feared she might get sunstroke. Hopping from the shadow of one tree to another, we managed to exit the park.
Once outside, we leaned on the ancient city walls, enjoying the small respite offered by the shade. The wall, I read, was 14km in length, mainly built in the Ming dynasty in the 14th century. But the original was Tang. Xi’an is a great palimpsest on which many cultures have written their lives. This is very different from Rome or Athens, which are full of original ruins. Nothing in China can remain as ruins – the government either recreates the supposed original or builds something totally new. Ruins cannot exist under communism.
Numbers
We wandered around a street market looking at all kinds of Chinese vegetables. We were eating stir-fried potato strips with vinegar and chilli.
‘What’s this, Mum?’ Moon prodded a plate of white vegetables with her chopsticks.
‘They are lotus root slices. Try it!’
Embarking on this trip led me to think about my own relationship to China, but also about my daughter’s. Such an immense past. I wondered how I could educate her. What importance could it hold for her? Moon was English, or British: her first language was English, despite my ongoing efforts to fill her ears with my native tongue. These efforts have resulted only in the most moderate success. Moon could understand my Chinese, but it was as though the language had not penetrated beneath her skin. In England, at the end of a school day, she would say to me: “I find history difficult to enjoy.” I would respond: “If you do not know your history, you won’t know who you are!” And I heard myself say to her: “We can learn from the brilliance of the past, and one of these is the Tang.”
But what did I really mean by that? Was I trying to convince myself as much as I was trying to convince my daughter?
We spent the evening in one of the city squares, eating a half watermelon. We squatted by the flowerbeds and watched elderly couples dancing under the street lamps. The music, very kitsch 1980s Chinese songs, blasted in our ears. So at the top of my lungs I screeched at Moon about the ancient past, sounding not unlike the way the lectures were delivered in a re-education camp.
“In the beginning, Xi’an was a stone-age village. Then a long, long time ago, like 3,000 years ago, it became the centre of a kingdom. Didn’t you learn about the Trojan war in ancient Greece? So that was around the same time.”
I was already flailing, but I went on. “One of those earlier dynasties, the Zhou, was the founding dynasty of this area.” Moon started to look around, displaying her boredom. I paused, feeling a rising anguish.
“The Qin emperor – Shi Huang – decided to design his capital. It was called Xian-yang then, north-west of Xi’an. He built many palaces and unified the Chinese writing system. That was 2,000 years ago. You know he was the same one who started building the Great Wall of China.”
Moon spat out a few watermelon seeds. I searched desperately for something more dramatic.
“But he also burned a great number of books and buried the scholars alive … Can you believe that?”
“Horrible! Poor scholars!” Moon cried. “Why did he do that?”
“Well, because he wanted to control people’s thoughts. Many emperors or dictators have done similar things. Anyway, the Qin empire only lasted for a short time. Then, around 202BC, a new dynasty came, one called the Han. The first emperor was Liu Bang.”
I stopped, now frowning myself.
“What’s wrong, Mum?”
“Well, I really don’t like talking about Chinese history using western ways of counting years!”
“You mean BC or AD. I don’t like those either!”
“Yeah, what has China got to do with some man, Jesus Christ, being born so far away, who meant nothing to the emperor Liu Bang! We have our own way of dating different periods.”
Now Moon turned to look at me: “What is your Chinese way?”
I thought for a while, but I found myself fumbling. I could not translate the Chinese calendar in a simple way to an 11-year-old. The Chinese dynasty calendar is based on the name of the emperor followed by the name of the dynasty, along with a number to signify the year within that dynasty. Each new dynasty starts again from year zero.
“Just give me an example, Mum,” she said, swallowing a piece of watermelon.
“OK. We say: ‘唐高祖 12 年’, meaning the 12th year of the reign of Emperor Gaozu of the Tang. Or, in your western equivalent, AD630.”
As seemed to be so often the case, my speech to Moon was a mix of Chinese and English words. I went on, feeling like a schoolmistress. “You know, in the beginning of the Tang, in the early seventh century, Xi’an was one of the world’s largest and most populous cities.”
It is estimated that about 1 million people lived within the city walls. By the dynasty’s end, in the ninth century, the country’s population had grown from 50 million to 80 million.
For a contemporary Chinese person, numbers are essential to measure things, since we grew up in a populous country and under a governing party that was obsessed with numbers and numerical record-keeping. The Chinese Communist party would always describe a place with wording such as “the village used to have 38 Communist party members, which has expanded to 380, occupying an area of 32,000 sq metres”. We Chinese children grow up reciting numbers. Moon nodded, vaguely. Numbers are difficult for a British kid in this context.
Silent armies
Contemporary Chinese tourism is about rediscovering the country’s wondrous past, often in a banal and highly commercial fashion. History, it seems, can be a place for solace and the temporary forgetting of the stresses of contemporary Chinese life. I keenly felt that “history” was packaged as a touristic spectacle during this trip. Even so, I was confident that our travels would allow me to reassess my relationship to a past which had been entirely denied during the Cultural Revolution. I felt this intensely, and I believed that many in China felt the same way.
Once you are in Xi’an, you cannot avoid passing the site where the terracotta army was buried. The warriors are not from the Tang dynasty, but from the earlier Qin, about 2,200 years ago. After waiting in an enormously long queue outside the Qin tomb site, a great throng of tourists pushed its way into the tomb like a host of locusts. By then we were already exhausted and our water bottles were empty.
Inside the vast hall where the terracottas were displayed, the eager tourists pressed on top of one another – not unlike the statues themselves. Beneath us, on the brown earth, headless figures, broken arms and body parts were neatly laid out. Most of them bore the uniform of a Qin dynasty warrior. They were ethereally still, as though waiting, or listening, but outside of time. I felt that we ourselves had come here to be temporarily buried along with these effigies of imperial power, a living host of terracotta tourists.
These are not the traces of the Tang, though the Qin led to the Tang by way of a great tangled knot of dynastic struggle.
“If there had been no Qin dynasty, then there would be no Tang,” I said to Moon.
“So it’s like if there had been no Greeks, there would be no Romans?” she responded, boldly. She knew much more about Greek gods and Roman goddesses than I did.
I pondered what the child had said while I gazed down at the broken statues. I asserted, and she agreed, that ancient Chinese culture was as rich and advanced as ancient Greek culture. But what did it mean really? I tried to breathe better. The air inside the hall was musty and thick with dust while the army of tourists pushed us this way and that in a vortex of human interaction. At one point, my child and I were desperate to get out from under the oppressive weight of all this history.
The court diary and the sisters
Very similar to the Anglo-Saxon Chronicle, or even the Domesday Book from 1,000 years ago, there is the Old Book of Tang, comprising 200 chapters that chronicle the events during the Tang era as recorded by court ministers. The book is difficult to understand as it is written in classical Chinese.
The difference between the Anglo-Saxon Chronicle and the Old Book of Tang is that the former was written by monks living in monasteries, while the latter was written by mandarins living in the imperial court. Church culture was surely very different from court culture. The western church was a sanitised place peopled by men only, whereas the palace court was a luxurious and sensual inner city full of cultured courtesans and powerful women.
“It was a tradition during those times that the palace diary, or any official record, was kept by the ladies of the palace,” I said to Moon.
We had just arrived at the Huaqing hot springs, 20km from Xi’an, a site where the Tang emperors and their wives would spend their leisure time. Now it is a major tourist destination.
“But I thought women were badly treated back then, and they could not read or write,” Moon said.
“Not during the Tang! From the Tang dynasty onwards, women were celebrated for their literary and artistic skills, not just because of their beauty.”
Indeed, around the eighth century, there were five famous sisters, whose key responsibility was to keep the court diary. The sisters were the granddaughters of a well-known poet, Song Zhiwen, and were educated not only in classical poetry, but also in politics. All five became accomplished writers and thinkers, and they made a pact never to marry but to devote themselves to literature and art. Together they wrote the Analects for Women, a counterpart of the Confucian Analects from a female perspective, which became a classical text in women’s education in the Ming and Qing dynasties. In AD788, these sisters were recommended by a local official to Emperor Taizong, a great devotee of literature, who personally examined their work and recruited them all into the palace service as xueshi – masters of learning. The emperor held them in the highest esteem. It was during the Tang that, for the first time, literate women became important court ministers, called shangshu.
“That’s pretty amazing,” Moon said. “You told me that in ninth-century England, there were just Vikings raiding villages, and most people were illiterate.”
“That’s right. And if Alfred the Great had not promoted literacy, no one would be able to read except the monks.”
During the Tang, one of the areas in which women assumed an increasingly significant role was as artists, and some courtesans were famed singers and dancers, as well as being known for their extravagant clothing and hairstyles. Before the Tang, women in China were mostly veiled, and almost never in public service. The women of the Tang changed that tradition with the support of an enlightened court. They became fashion-makers, inventing elaborate makeup and sporting lavish dresses.
Would it be too pretentious, too pompous, to call the Tang era one of the earliest feminist eras in ancient history? I thought of the Anglo-Saxon women during that period, or the wives of the Vikings and Romans. I was not convinced that they had achieved such power.
The Grand Canal
In Britain, I have always lived by Regent’s Canal, around east London. After I left China, more than two decades ago, my daily routine revolved around that rusty urban English water. I would pass by the narrowboats along the winding waterways and often I thought of the Grand Canal in China. The Grand Canal is the longest and oldest artificial waterway in the world. The most ancient part was built in the fifth century BC. Later, in the seventh century AD, Emperor Yang of Sui undertook an ambitious project to connect the south and the north by a waterway. Then the Tang emperors expanded its scale and perfected its usage.
I first saw the canal in 1993 when I left my southern home town and travelled to Beijing to study. The Beijing Film Academy is located right next to the canal, by the gate of the old Yuan dynasty ruins, and a park had recently been built along the waterway, with willows hugging the banks. After the day’s classes, I would leave the campus and sit by the water, reading or eating a takeaway. The water was motionless. I always wondered how such great quantities of rice and tea had been transported on this water in olden days.
Often, on a cold sunny afternoon after snow had fallen, with one hand holding a translation of Pier Paolo Pasolini’s poetry, I would throw little stones on to the frozen surface to see if the ice would break. It was by that canal, dare I say, that I became a young intellectual, however arrogant and pretentious that may sound. I could even say that I was part of the historical landscape, stoic but everlasting, regardless of the destruction of ancient culture in China since the Cultural Revolution. For me, the Tang is the exact opposite of the Cultural Revolution. The former is rich and culturally diverse, whereas the latter is poor, unimaginative and functional in all aspects of life and thought.
When we briefly visited Beijing, I wanted to show Moon the canal and the park near the Beijing Film Academy, but I never managed to venture to that part of the capital. Beijing was too big to get around. The six massive ring roads and countless highways surrounding it seemed larger than the orbits in our solar system.
Luoyang
One might complain about the quality of water or air in China, but one can only admire the public transport: roads and railways lead to every possible destination. This is a very recent phenomenon. When I left China some 20 years ago, the infrastructure was very poor. The train from Shanghai to Beijing took two days: today it takes less than five hours.
We were on a high-speed train from Shanxi to Henan province. The landscape was lush and mountainous; the vegetation was emerald green and luminous under the sun after a rainstorm.
We arrived in Luoyang at noon, hoping the day would be cooler than the 39C we had suffered through in Xi’an.
During the Tang dynasty, Luoyang was called Dongdu (東都), the eastern capital. When Wu Zetian became empress, she constructed the tallest palace in Chinese history in Luoyang, of which there is now a duplicate in the old town, to the east of the city.
We stayed in a brand new Hyatt hotel in the new town of Luoyang. So new, in fact, that the hotel lobby was still filled with the large bundles of fresh flowers brought in for the opening celebration. From the 16th floor, I gazed down. On my left was the huge campus of the Luoyang Institute of Science and Technology; on my right was the jigsaw-like People’s Park, with sports facilities; on the horizon, skyscrapers stood in a bland, uniform line, like a monoculture forest. Where was the history? I longed for old sights and sounds.
From Luoyang, we visited the nearby Longmen Grottoes, one of the largest Buddhist sites in the world, which has survived more than 1,500 years. What a monumental sight to see countless statues of Buddha! Their elaborately sculpted details were once painted in gold. Now, all of them stood bare and colourless and most of them were missing body parts.
“Mum, do you know that there are 100,000 statues on these hills?” Moon said, reading a signpost.
“That’s a lot,” I said. “What else does it say?”
“It says there are more than 2,345 caves, some are little more than small holes, some are as large as 17 metres in height.”
As always, the Chinese fanatically list numbers when referring to any historical artefact, but anyone who visits these grottoes hardly needs to learn them. Like me, they can experience a dizzying feeling of disbelief, even as our feet stand firmly on these old rocks. Like Stonehenge in England, or the Egyptian pyramids, these monuments induce a feeling of the sublime.
As we descended toward the riverbank, I looked back at the blurred faces and figures of the Buddhist caves on the hill. How much more history could I take in one afternoon? Must we see 10,000 Buddha statues to come to the conclusion that there is a Buddha? Must we erect 20m Jesus on the cross statues to prove he died for us? Why are we so wedded to the materiality of spiritual life? Isn’t the sky vast and awesome enough to be pondered upon? Emptiness is where the richest possibility lies.
Weary and drowsy, we abandoned the sumptuous spectacle. Flagging down a taxi by the gate, we wanted to hurry back to the hotel before the rush hour, where we would deal with the small and ungodly things in our daily life, such as paying our bills, charging our phones, ordering a meal and brushing our teeth.
The Qianling Mausoleum and the
afterlife
We travelled over great distances on high-speed trains. From the northern plains we crossed over the Yangtze River and then zoomed down to southern regions, before going north again, entering the grasslands of Inner Mongolia. Moon had been tasting all sorts of strangely flavoured food and learning local dialects and could almost have passed as a native Chinese kid.
At the very end of our trip, to draw a full circle, I wanted to pay a visit to the place where the Tang emperors and empresses were buried, so we returned to Shanxi province and arrived at Qing Xian, 85km north-west from Xi’an.
Here, along the highways, even the ginkgo trees are newly planted, all trimmed, standing straight and of even height, like an obedient army waiting to be summoned to action. Even though this place was very much part of the royal centre of Chang’an during the Tang, visually there is nothing much to see now. Because of its peripheral location, its past has been totally paved over to make way for its new industrial purpose. One can see only some traces of the old ways of life half-hidden in a street corner: a tiny shoe repair place, an old tailor’s shop or a grandmother selling tea-brewed eggs by the roadside. Otherwise, large trucks carrying steel and cement rushed through streets, horns blasting.
Qianling Mausoleum is where some of the most important imperial families of the Tang dynasty are entombed. After a long, stifling ride, the bus finally dropped us in front of a large complex.
The scale of the mausoleum was something I had never seen in my life. A labyrinth to confuse anyone. Once we entered, we had to take another bus inside the vast complex, again with crowds of tourists. The bus took you up to the hills to get to the different burial sites. It was like travelling into an ancient settlement, with pavilions and waterways and inner gardens. There was even a busy street full of restaurants inside the Number Four Mausoleum site.
It was difficult to correlate the tomb numbers on the map with the actual sites. There seemed to be a lot of tombs, but few were open to the public. The sound of cicadas faded away while the noon heat was rising. Under the burning sun, we felt like two roasted ducks. We staggered towards a mausoleum that promised some air-conditioning.
We arrived at two tomb sites, one belonging to a princess and another to a prince. From the gate, we could see a sloping tunnel stretching into a darkening underground world. Cool but sepulchral air coming from the tunnel gate enticed us inside.
We followed a group of perspiring tourists, walking into the narrow tunnel. It was the tomb of Princess Yongtai. She was the seventh daughter of Emperor Zhongzong and the second daughter of his wife, Wei. She died when she was 15, apparently while giving birth.
“Oh, she died so young!” exclaimed Moon.
There were elaborate murals around us, depicting palace ladies and officials in an enchanted garden. The colours were faded and the walls full of holes and patches. As we entered further, the air became musty and heavy.
As we approached the end of the tunnel, we came upon a chamber with frescoes, and the mausoleum revealed itself. It was a miniature wooden house with carved windows and inscriptions on the surface. Inside, there was the actual coffin.
What was life like for Princess Yongtai 1,300 years ago? I could not decipher the obscure inscriptions, but what I had read earlier from the New Book of Tang told me a different story of how she died. Since the all-powerful Empress Wu was her mother-in-law, Princess Yongtai did not have an easy life. An animosity persisted between the two women. It was well known that Empress Wu led an unconventional sexual life; even in her old age, royal family members, as well as ministers, were well acquainted with her exploits. As a result, indignation and resentment accumulated in the court, and when the princess was found to be disloyal, punishment immediately ensued. According to the New Book of Tang, it was said that the princess was caned to death, though elsewhere it was recorded that she was forced to kill herself.
We did not visit the next tomb – we wanted to go straight to the most mysterious site, Empress Wu’s tomb. After much inquiry, we learned that it was impossible: no one would be allowed to enter the mausoleum of the emperor and the empress. In fact, we were told, the two main tombs were not even excavated.
So we wandered on the hills of this sacred place, sucking on our ice lollies in the shade of pine trees. We imagined a curious dark world inside the uncovered tombs, barred to modern people. Time to leave, but still we lingered on: we suspected we would never return to this place.
Along the road was a procession of statues, some headless and some armless. We walked past these ancient figures and sometimes stood before them, as if waiting for speech, a command or a bow. They stood like sturdy sentinels, without acknowledgment of our presence, their stone minds, far beyond the doings of the passing parade of tourists. I thought of John Keats’s “cold pastoral”, and felt a shiver and prickling of skin in the heat. Was that a slight puff of wind, or time itself touching our all too fragile bodies?
Adapted from Everyday Tang, published by Notting Hill Editions (£9.99). To support the Guardian, buy your copy at guardianbookshop.com. P&P may apply.
Xiaolu Guo is a novelist, memoirist and film-maker. Her most recent novel is Call Me Ishmaelle (Vintage), a retelling of Melville’s Moby-Dick.

‘Inception’ trips, Chinamaxxing and undertourism: Euronews Travel’s top trends and predictions for 2027
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-29
04:00:49 UTC
13:00:49 KST

From holidays within a holiday to undertourism and longevity retreats, the Euronews Travel team picks out some of the trends and destinations for travel in 2027.
Travel is constantly changing and 2027 looks set to bring plenty of new ways to see the world.
From holidays designed around health and longevity to a growing appetite for slower, more meaningful escapes, travellers are becoming more selective about how they spend their time away.
Next year will be huge for astronomy lovers, with August’s so called “eclipse of the century” viewable in parts of southern Spain and north Africa, while those in the know will be eschewing Bali for lesser explored parts of Indonesia.
It’s likely in 2027 that travellers will also look beyond the usual hotspots, rethink when and where they travel, and find new reasons to visit destinations that have long been overlooked.
There’s plenty to get your teeth into – from the rise of longevity retreats and the changing face of wellness travel to new takes on adventure, culture and accommodation.
These are the trends the Euronews Travel team expects to shape travel over the year ahead.
Our predictions and trends for travel in 2027
Eyes on the skies
It was already a big year in 2026 for those who dream of the stars, with the Artemis II mission successfully completing a lunar flyby and a solar eclipse that plunged parts of Spain and Iceland into darkness for more than two minutes.
Next year will be even bigger, with the “eclipse of the century” on 2 August and Artemis III planned for some point in 2027.
The August eclipse earned its moniker as it will be the longest total eclipse on easily accessible land in the 21st century, with cities in Egypt near the point of greatest eclipse seeing the sun blocked by the moon for more than six minutes.
Spain will be lucky once again, with totality in cities including Cádiz, Marbella and Málaga, but the eclipse will also be visible in countries including Morocco, Tunisia, Algeria and Saudi Arabia.
It’s also a big year for those who fantasise about exploring the universe, with Star Wars celebrating its 50th anniversary.
While there will of course be re-runs of the original Star Wars in cinemas, on the travel front, I imagine there will be a resurgence in visiting iconic filming locations around the globe, like the limestone karsts of Guilin, Lake Como, and Wadi Rum. Think set-jetting, but with a hint of nostalgia. Dianne Apen-Sadler
Beyond second and third cities into ‘undertourised’ destinations
Earlier this year, I made the case for giving European destinations beyond the famed capitals a little more love by venturing to “second cities” – the places travellers may overlook because they sit beyond countries’ main tourist hubs.
My guide to some of the continent’s best second cities included Basel in Switzerland, for its dynamic art scene, and Cambridge in the UK for its punt vessel cruises across the River Cam.
If 2026 was the year of second cities, 2027 could take that instinct even further. I see travellers increasingly seeking out destinations that are largely under the radar.
Social media continues to have a major impact on how we discover and plan trips, but it can also very quickly turn obscure destinations into a must-see, and overcrowded, destination overnight.
As travellers become more conscious of this, with Skift research finding as many as 42% of travellers saying they would actively avoid overcrowded places, the search for slower-paced and quieter travel could see second and even third cities lose their allure.
As such, we may see more footfall next to cities such as Japan's Toyama over Tokyo or Osaka. Around an hour away from the Japanese capital by air, the prefecture’s tourism strategy has been to retain its rural charm and offer visitors a slow mountain escape with scenic hikes and local delicacies.
At the turn of the year, we may also see more initiatives from destinations to not only spotlight “undertourised” destinations, but also manage tourist flows. Earlier this year, I spoke with Mayor of Dubrovnik Mato Franković, who discussed the “Respect the City” strategy to tackle overtourism in the “Pearl of the Adriatic”. Could this strategy work across other popular tourism destinations? Fakhriya M. Suleiman
Chinamaxxing
It seems nowadays that you can add -maxxing to the end of anything and turn it into a trend. Euronews Travel is not above this, and I will not be apologising for it, even if it’s “cringe”.
Post-Covid, there was a massive influx of tourists to Japan, but with the easing of visa restrictions, I think China is enjoying its long overdue moment in the spotlight.
Citizens from nearly 80 countries can now visit for up to 30 days visa free, which is barely enough time to discover the country’s futuristic cities, many UNESCO World Heritage Sites, and varied landscapes that will take your breath away.
Social media is also a big factor – when TikTok was temporarily shut down in the US last year, many users flocked to Douyin, the Chinese version of the app, and autotranslate on X has meant more people are interacting with users from the country.
Just last week, the payment app TenPayGo, which works with Apple Pay and international cards, launched, making it easier for international travellers, too.
I visited China earlier this year (read all about it here) but I’m desperate to go back, and I can easily see it becoming somewhere I visit again and again. Dianne Apen-Sadler
The ‘Inception trip’: A holiday within a holiday within a holiday
Multi-destination travel is not a new trend by any means, but whenever we book a holiday these days we seem to have a regular habit: we book one trip, then start booking other trips within it – often after we’ve arrived.
Inspired by Christopher Nolan’s epic dream within a dream within a dream concept, I call this the “Inception trip” – a holiday within a holiday within a holiday. We’ve done this a few times now, but this summer in Spain was a perfect example.
What began as an escape to the Spanish Pyrenees, and a few days in Barcelona tagged on at the end, somehow evolved into a much bigger road trip. Taüll in the Vall de Boí was our base, but once we arrived, we extended our exploration even further. Much, much further.
As well as day trips into the Val d’Aran and across the mountains to the medieval town of Aínsa, we made the decision to drive across northern Spain for an afternoon and night in San Sebastián to watch the solar eclipse. That happened on 12 August and we only decided that morning to venture north to see it.
It was a long drive, but totally worth it. Not just for the eclipse itself but also to scratch San Sebastián off my bucket list. Being in this trendy city for around only 18 hours, we did pack a lot in and got a taste, literally, of why it’s so popular.
The more I travel the more I seem to like the “Inception trip” format – and I suspect I’ll be doing more of it in 2027. Where’s next on my list? Who knows, but whatever we plan to travel to definitely won’t be the final itinerary. Mike Starling
Type B travel
Social media is great for exposing you to new cities you hadn’t considered visiting before, but once you’ve booked a trip it seems like the algorithm knows and keeps pumping your feed full of content about it.
It’s ruining the element of surprise in travel, with more than two thirds of tourists saying a destination felt familiar because of the amount of videos they had consumed about it, even if they hadn’t been before.
Which is why I think Type B travel is going to have a big moment in 2027.
Spontaneous, and maybe slightly chaotic, Type B travel means rocking up to a new place with no plans and nothing booked, and letting your heart decide what to do.
I think it’s a natural extension of 2026’s lore chasing, which involves doing things you wouldn’t usually do because you’re on holiday and you want some great stories to travel home with.
I also think it could go a long way to helping with problems around overtourism – you won’t end up in line for the next viral spot if you simply haven’t heard or seen it. Dianne Apen-Sadler
The evolution of longevity retreats
Like multi-destination travel, longevity retreats may also be nothing new, but the way they’re being approached is likely to shift in 2027.
The move will be towards healthspan rather than simply lifespan, namely helping people stay healthier and more active for longer.
Next year, expect longevity retreats to become less about a quick wellness reset and more about understanding your body, identifying potential health risks and returning home with changes you can actually maintain.
For travellers, that could mean anything from metabolic testing and tailored nutrition plans to sleep analysis, movement assessments and consultations with doctors or other qualified practitioners. Some retreats are also experimenting with treatments such as cryotherapy and hyperbaric oxygen therapy.
Obviously, part of the purpose of healthspan retreats is still very much with longevity in mind – and there are plenty of new openings to be aware of if any aspect of this trend is up your street.
Clinique La Prairie in Phuket is slated to open its doors this November. In a Tri Vananda – or multigenerational living community – setting, its offerings will include preventive health, personalised nutrition, movement and overall wellbeing.
Meanwhile, in Austria, Naturhotel Forsthofgut in Leogang recently expanded its wellness facility by introducing a dedicated, science-backed longevity space known as waldSPA Health. Health programmes here include intermittent hypoxia-hyperoxia training, a non-invasive oxygen therapy thought to rejuvenate cells. Saskia O’Donoghue
Ditch hotel stays for checking into authentic experiences
Are all hotels the same? Well, according to research, as many as 74% of people either strongly or somewhat agreed that many hotel brands feel very similar to one another. Its findings also revealed that travellers are increasingly seeking authenticity when they go abroad. While I don’t think hotels are going anywhere in 2027, travellers may become more curious to look beyond them.
Rather than simply being an afterthought, I see niche stays forming part of the reason why someone chooses to travel abroad. I for one am very tempted to visit Morocco just to experience what the travel guides have been raving about: staying in a riad rather than a conventional hotel.
A scroll through the “#riadmorocco” hashtag is filled with snaps of travellers’ experiences these technicoloured architectural marvels built around an inward facing design where an open-air courtyard with a fountain take centre stage.
Meanwhile, Japanese Ryokans may be among the world's oldest forms of a hotel, dating back to the 8th century. Traditionally, these inns feature tatami flooring of woven straw-based rectangular mats, iconic futon bedding and yukata robes. A stay at a ryokan usually starts with a Japanese breakfast and ends with kaiseki ryori – a Japanese multicourse dinner of local delights, such as fish, soup and seasonal veggies.
There’s also the trend of volunteer exchange-for programmes, where visitors work for a set number of hours each week in exchange for their bed and board. Whether taking care of animals or painting and decorating, this sounds like a great way to not only meet like-minded people, but during downtime, explore a new destination, without having to worry about accommodation costs. Fakhriya M. Suleiman
Indonesia – so much more than just Bali
Think of Indonesia, and you’ll probably immediately land on Bali. The island has long been an enormously popular holiday destination for westerners seeking affordable luxury and a beautiful – and varied – landscape.
More recently, though, there’s been something of a backlash against Bali, with travellers unhappy at developers knocking down long-established local businesses.
I went two years ago and while it’s absolutely a fun spot and, in parts, stunning, it did feel incredibly overtouristed, with congested roads full of travellers packing in as many destinations as possible.
As Bali’s popularity has grown, so have its prices. In some cases, accommodation and food costs rival those in Europe, meaning one of the biggest reasons to visit is no more.
Luckily though, Indonesia is huge – and has countless little-visited places, so a more affordable, authentic and quieter experience is very much possible.
If you’re into nature-based, off-the-beaten-path trips, you don’t have to go far from Bali. Lombok is right next door, and boasts lower prices as well as unspoilt beaches, waterfalls, endless hiking opportunities and Mount Rinjani, the second-highest volcano and mountain in the whole country.
True nature lovers should head to Komodo National Park, a UNESCO World Heritage Site established to conserve the unique Komodo dragon.
You can still spot them here, as well as other creatures including the orange-footed scrub fowl, the Timor deer and various species of whales, dolphins, and sea turtles.
For true remote exploration, you could do worse than to visit Raja Ampat. The remote archipelago is famous for having some of the richest marine biodiversity on earth.
Only reachable by ferry, the region is made up of hundreds of jungle-covered islands, and is known for its beaches – with the bluest water you’ve ever seen – and coral reefs, all rich with marine life. Saskia O’Donoghue
Urban active travel: The city is the gym
Sports tourism used to be relatively easy to define: fans travelling to events to watch their favourite teams, or taking part in activities such as marathons, cycling or golf. But since the pandemic, the sector has really evolved, with outdoor adventure, wellness and fitness now becoming part of the offering.
In 2027, I predict that evolution will be reflected in our cities and towns. Running and walking are perhaps the most obvious examples. Look at any major city’s tourism website and you’ll find recommended routes for a jog or a stroll.
Some hotels have even been embracing this idea for years. For example, Westin Hotels & Resorts has more than 150 “Run Concierges” worldwide, who can accompany guests on group runs and help them discover a destination while exercising.
With city-break visitors looking to the outdoors rather than just hitting the gym, I expect more hotels and destinations to follow, offering curated routes through parks and past landmarks. This could be particularly useful for solo and business travellers who want an active way to explore.
The “race-cation” trend may be booming, but runners don’t necessarily need an event as a reason to travel. Running, cycling and fitness are increasingly becoming ways to experience a destination. Mike Starling
