====================================================================================================

Column: Beware of Japanese right-wing's attempt to revive militarism
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-29
11:07:04 CST
12:07:04 KST

by Zhou Yaxin
Ninety-five years ago, the Sept. 18th Incident shocked China and the world.
It marked the beginning of Japan's long-premeditated aggression against China. The Chinese people rose up in resistance and fought an arduous War of Resistance until securing victory 14 years later, at a staggering cost of 35 million military and civilian casualties.
While the historical wounds have yet to heal, present-day concerns are mounting by the day.
Ninety-five years on, the poisonous legacy of militarism has yet to be fully addressed. Japan's right-wing forces are still going to great lengths to downplay, if not glorify, the history of aggression.
August 15, the day of Japan's unconditional surrender, should be an occasion for it to deeply reflect and repent. This year, however, Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi, in her capacity as head of the Liberal Democratic Party, made a cash offering to the notorious Yasukuni Shrine that honors 14 Class-A war criminals of World War II. According to Japanese media, she worshiped the shrine from afar, while multiple incumbent cabinet members and lawmakers visited the shrine in person. At the National Memorial Ceremony for the War Dead, Takaichi made no mention of "reflection" or "lessons," the customary language used by successive prime ministers, laying bare her stubborn refusal to reflect on history.
After the end of World War II, Japan never did any serious soul-searching about its war of aggression, nor did it fully purge the remnants of militarism. Many war criminals returned to politics and the Japan Self-Defense Forces (JSDF). These right-wing figures, inheriting the militarist ideology, have tampered with textbooks and historical records and carried out PR and whitewashing campaigns in an attempt to downplay and glorify the history of aggression and colonialism, and indoctrinate Japan's younger generation with right-wing historical narratives. They express "regret over defeat" and portray Japan as a "victim" instead of reflecting on and repenting for its war crimes. By doing so, they distort perceptions among the Japanese people and the international community, and seek public support for the right-wing government's re-militarization agenda.
The right-wing forces represented by Takaichi are also accelerating efforts to revise Japan's three key security documents and seek constitutional revision to expand military capabilities. They have lifted the ban on exports of lethal weapons and signaled an intent to revise Japan's Three Non-Nuclear Principles. They have deployed long-range missiles with "enemy base strike capabilities." Japan's defense budget has grown for 14 consecutive years, surging to over 9 trillion yen (about 57 billion U.S. dollars) in fiscal 2026, or 2 percent of the country's GDP. Instead of adhering to its "exclusively defense-oriented" policy, Japan has now ripped off the mask of a "peaceful" nation and is attempting to make itself a "war-capable" nation again.
A comparison between Japan today and Japan before World War II reveals striking similarities:
In 1882, Aritomo Yamagata coined the "line of advantage" theory, framing the Korean Peninsula and China as Japan's "lifeline" and laying the ideological groundwork for Japan's annexation of the Korean Peninsula and aggression against China. In November 2025, Takaichi associated a so-called "Taiwan contingency" with a "survival-threatening situation," thereby grossly interfering in China's internal affairs and fabricating an excuse for meddling in Taiwan-related affairs.
Before World War II, Japan invaded Asian countries and imposed colonial rule under the pretext of "Pan-Asianism" and "liberating Asia." Today, Japan justifies its military buildup and expansion in the name of pursuing "proactive pacifism" and upholding the "Indo-Pacific order."
Before World War II, Japan inculcated unwavering loyalty to the Emperor among its people through the Imperial Rescript on Education. Today, the National Defense Academy of Japan retains the "tradition" of making students walk dozens of kilometers overnight to the Yasukuni shrine to worship the war criminals enshrined there. Under the poisonous influence of militarism, a serving JSDF member went so far as to intrude into the Chinese Embassy in Japan with a knife.
Even more dangerously, whenever Japan's economy falls into a slump, it tends to pursue external expansion to divert attention. After the Meiji Restoration, Japan vigorously developed modern industry, but suffered from insufficient domestic capital, widespread bankruptcies among farmers, acute social tensions, severe fiscal pressure, and a narrow domestic market. To secure overseas sources of raw materials and markets for its goods, Japan launched the First Sino-Japanese War, from which it obtained massive reparations and access to the Chinese market. The Showa Financial Crisis of 1927 and the Great Depression of 1929 caused anxiety in Japan, eventually leading to the growth of militarist forces and the launch of external aggression.
Today, the yen has hit a 40-year low, Japan's national debt has risen to over 200 percent of its GDP, prices are soaring, and more than 1,000 companies are going bankrupt each month. The Takaichi government seeks to prop up Japan's economy by bolstering the defense industry and aggressively selling arms abroad, at the risk of reopening Pandora's box of militarism.
In disregard of the postwar international order, Japan is trying to break free from the constraints of the postwar system. It is accelerating re-militarization and posing a real threat to peace and stability in the Asia-Pacific.
History must never be forgotten. Otherwise, past mistakes will be repeated. On the 95th anniversary of the Sept. 18th Incident, we shall never forget the suffering endured by the people of China and other Asian countries that were invaded, nor the atrocities committed by Japanese militarists. All peace-loving nations and peoples should remain vigilant against the resurgence of militarism in Japan and guard against attempts by Japan's right-wing forces to create a new Sept. 18th Incident.
Editor's note: The author is an international affairs observer.
The views expressed in this article are those of the author and do not necessarily reflect the positions of Xinhua News Agency.

NASA, Boeing outline next steps for Starliner
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-29
11:06:50 CST
12:06:50 KST

LOS ANGELES, Sept. 28 (Xinhua) -- NASA said Monday it plans to conduct an uncrewed Starliner-1 mission to the International Space Station (ISS) as early as December this year or January 2027, with a crewed Starliner-2 mission targeted for 2028.
NASA also announced plans to exercise options for a fifth and sixth Starliner flight to and from the ISS, and said it will work with Boeing and United Launch Alliance to certify the Vulcan rocket for Starliner crew transportation after the final flight of the Atlas V rocket.
The uncrewed Starliner-1 will serve as an engineering evaluation mission to validate improvements made to the spacecraft, verify improved thermal environments, obtain performance data needed for system qualification and identify residual risks ahead of crewed missions, according to NASA.
The agency will use data from Starliner-1 to continue implementing corrective actions identified by its Program Investigation Team and complete the testing and certification required for crewed flight, NASA Administrator Jared Isaacman said, adding that the current plan is to return astronauts to space on Starliner-2 by 2028.
Boeing's Starliner spacecraft launched in June 2024 on its first crewed flight test, carrying NASA astronauts Butch Wilmore and Suni Williams, and docked with the ISS. During the flight, some of the spacecraft's reaction control thrusters did not perform as expected, and helium leaks were detected.
NASA ultimately decided to return Starliner to Earth uncrewed, while the two astronauts later returned to Earth aboard a SpaceX Dragon spacecraft in March 2025.
In February, NASA released findings from its Program Investigation Team into the 2024 crewed flight test. The investigation identified 61 recommendations for NASA.
Based on the findings, Boeing has made thermal modifications to Starliner's service module, which NASA will evaluate on Starliner-1. NASA and Boeing also have jointly decided to implement an additional thruster valve design modification to support spacecraft certification and future crewed flights.
Following Starliner-1, NASA and Boeing will complete the service module thruster valve design modification. Boeing will also implement other improvements, including installing new crew module thrusters and batteries, as well as making minor modifications to the parachute system to improve performance and reliability, NASA said. ■

S. Korea's business sentiment edges down in September
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-29
11:06:49 CST
12:06:49 KST

SEOUL, Sept. 29 (Xinhua) -- Sentiment for South Korean businesses over the economic situation edged down in September, though the broader recovery momentum remained on track, central bank data showed Tuesday.
The composite business sentiment index (CBSI) in all industries retreated 0.5 points from a month earlier to 99.1 in September, marking the first fall in three months, according to the Bank of Korea (BOK).
Despite the slight contraction, the index rose from 94.1 in March to 97.7 in June and 99.1 in September, maintaining an upward trajectory toward the neutral 100 mark.
The CBSI among manufacturers declined 4.3 points to 99.5 due to fewer working days, industrial strikes and lingering fallout from the Middle East conflicts.
The index for non-manufacturers gained 2.2 points to 98.9, fueled by rising outdoor activities and higher consumer spending ahead of the Chuseok holiday, the South Korean version of Thanksgiving Day.
The result was based on a survey of 1,760 manufacturers and 1,403 non-manufacturers conducted between Sept. 10 and 17.
Manufacturers picked subdued domestic demand, expensive raw materials, and economic uncertainty as key barriers to doing business, while non-manufacturers selected faltering consumer demand, an uncertain economic situation, and higher labor costs.
The economic sentiment index (ESI), which reflects sentiment among both businesses and consumers, stood at 99.9 in September, up 0.5 points from a month earlier. ■

Panama Canal to increase daily transits through larger locks to 10
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-29
11:06:44 CST
12:06:44 KST

PANAMA CITY, Sept. 28 (Xinhua) -- The Panama Canal will increase daily transits through its larger Neopanamax locks to 10 starting Oct. 15, the Panama Canal Authority said Monday.
The move will bring the total number of daily transit slots across both sets of locks to 33. The canal authority said the decision was based on current and projected water levels in Gatun Lake, a key source of water for the canal, which connects the Atlantic and Pacific oceans.
Near-average rainfall in the canal's watershed has also allowed authorities to set the maximum draft for ships using the Neopanamax locks at 49 feet (14.94 meters), effective immediately. Draft is the depth of a ship's hull below the waterline.
As water shortages persist, the authority said its booking system remains the only way to guarantee passage on a specific date, adding that it will continue monitoring water levels and rainfall and announce further changes as conditions allow.
The Neopanamax locks, which opened in 2016, accommodate ships too large to pass through the canal's original locks. ■

====================================================================================================

As Netanyahu hits 19 years in office, Israel must confront the case for term limits - editorial
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-29
03:05:25 UTC
12:05:25 KST

On Monday, Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu marked a milestone: 19 full years as Israel’s prime minister.
Those years came in three nonconsecutive stints - from 1996 to 1999, from 2009 to 2021, and from December 2022 until today. Cumulatively, it is an astounding amount of time for one person to lead the nation. Netanyahu has served as prime minister for roughly one of every four days since Independence, and for nearly two of every three days since 1996.
For Netanyahu, this is an impressive political achievement. For the country, however, it raises a question: Is it healthy in a democracy for one leader to remain in charge for so long?
The obvious response is: Why not? This is what the people want. Netanyahu has repeatedly won elections – or more precisely, assembled governing coalitions. That is the people’s will.
But democracies place limits on majority rule not to thwart the will of the people but to preserve the system through which it is expressed. Term limits are one example.
Opposition parties support limiting prime minister's tenure
In 1951, six years after Franklin Delano Roosevelt died, following four election victories and just over 12 years in office, the US ratified the 22nd Amendment, preventing anyone from being elected president more than twice.
The main concern was keeping power concentrated in one president’s hands for too long. There was also political motivation: Republicans drove the effort after being shut out of the White House for so long.
Both impulses are present in Israel. The four “change bloc” parties – B’Yachad, Yashar, The Democrats and Yisrael Beytenu – have all backed limiting the prime minister’s tenure, though they have not agreed on a formula.
Term limits have substantive benefits for Israel
They are undoubtedly motivated partly by political considerations: They do not want Netanyahu, or anyone else, to block them from power indefinitely. But political motivation does not necessarily invalidate a reform. Republican frustration with Roosevelt did not make the 22nd Amendment inherently undemocratic.
Term limits also have substantive benefits for Israel.
While limits on prime ministers are rare in parliamentary democracies – where parliaments can remove the prime minister – they are not unheard of.
Hungary amended its constitution this year to cap a prime minister’s service at eight years, following Viktor Orbán’s 16-year uninterrupted run. Thailand also imposes an eight-year limit. Israel need not reject an idea merely because few similar systems have adopted it.
Too much time in power can be unhealthy for both the leader and the country. Long tenure can breed entitlement: the sense that someone who has governed for so long is owed certain privileges.
More dangerously, it can foster the perception that one person is irreplaceable, blurring the democratic distinction between the leader and the state. The leader is not the state; the leader serves the state.
An expiration date would also encourage leaders to focus on achievement and legacy rather than endless political survival.
Also, term limits would force parties to cultivate new leadership. A prime minister who intends to remain indefinitely has no incentive to groom a potential successor. As a result, talented figures are pushed aside, and the public is encouraged to believe no viable alternative exists.
Regular transitions are healthy. New leaders – even from the same party – bring fresh eyes, are less bound by their predecessors’ assumptions, and can reset relationships at home and abroad that have become stale or poisoned.
Israel’s current experience suggests another compelling reason: Term limits can serve as a democratic pressure-release valve. They reassure those bitterly opposed to the government that no leader will remain forever and that renewal at the top will come at a known interval through the political system.
That would not eliminate demonstrations, nor should it. Protest is a legitimate democratic tool. But a predetermined endpoint can help prevent people from feeling that permanent protest in the streets is the only conceivable route to change. Term limits do not guarantee that another party will take power, but they do guarantee turnover at the top and create the possibility of a change in direction.
Term limits are no cure-all, and they will not resolve every weakness in Israel’s political system. But after 19 years under one prime minister, the burden of proof should no longer rest solely with those proposing them. It should rest with those arguing that unlimited tenure is healthy.

One last 'last' for Broncos legend Ali Brigginshaw in NRLW grand final
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-29
03:05:05 UTC
12:05:05 KST

Ali Brigginshaw is into her fifth NRLW grand final with the Brisbane Broncos after winning her first four.
She, Julia Robinson and Chelsea Lenarduzzi are "the OGs" who have been with the Broncos since the beginning of the NRLW in 2018.
What's next?
The Broncos take on the Roosters in the NRLW grand final from 4pm AEDT on Sunday.
Retiring Brisbane legend Ali Brigginshaw has one more NRLW match to play, but her competitive drive is just as strong as the day she took up playing rugby league at the age of 10.
The 38-year-old five-eighth will play against old foes the Sydney Roosters in the grand final with a team-first mentality, but also with the determination to get one over opposite number Jocelyn Kelleher the same way she did in the 20-8 preliminary final victory against Gold Coast.
Rugby sevens superstar Teagan Levi was wearing the number six and Brigginshaw had her measure.
"All the talk has been about her and I took it really personal[ly," she said.
"I said to the girls, 'I will do whatever I can to make sure I can shut her down.'
"I am just really proud. We trained extremely hard to get to this moment, but I am also proud of myself … 38 years old and I put myself in this position to be the best teammate and work my bum off whenever I play."
When Brigginshaw won her fourth NRLW title last year, there were a couple of conversations about retiring with a premiership.
"People were saying it was a good ending, but I had all the belief in this team that we were going to get [to another grand final]," she said
"The hardest thing is getting there. You get there and you put yourself in the best position to compete and win it.
"It is a huge week and I am just excited to do it again because you never know when it is going to be your last … and this will be my last."
Brigginshaw calls herself, winger Julia Robinson and prop Chelsea Lenarduzzi "the OGs", being the three original Broncos from 2018 who are aiming for a fifth premiership with the club, while fullback Tamika Upton hopes to add a third Broncos crown to two won with Newcastle in 2022 and 2023.
Only Michael Hancock and Kevin Walters have achieved the feat in Broncos history.
"We are the OGs. We are also good mates and they are part of the reason I love the Broncos," Brigginshaw said.
"Duzzi is passionate about everything she does and Robbo is the heart. The love they both have for the team and the jersey is what I love.
"We all just bleed for this jersey, and the best thing is that I see other people who want to do it and love the place as much as I do."
The Broncos lost eight players from last year's grand final side, but the new-look outfit, featuring superstar halfback Jesse Southwell, has bought in to the club's systems and culture.
"It is kind of frustrating how people forget how many we lost," Brigginshaw said.
"To win a premiership with them, then rebuild and get back here again … proves we have the right people here to give ourselves the best opportunity."
As a result of Brigginshaw's impending departure, everything at Red Hill has a "last" associated with it this year, whether it be her last game at home in a club match or her last preliminary final.
"It is just a bit of a joke around 'the last last'," she said.
"I have got there now, so let's have a crack."

UN agency warns funding crisis could leave 8.3 million people without aid
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-29
03:02:45 UTC
12:02:45 KST

UN agency warns funding crisis could leave 8.3 million people without aid
GENEVA – A deepening funding crisis could leave nearly 8.3 million refugees and forcibly displaced people without access to assistance in 2026, and push protection systems in some countries towards collapse, the United Nations High Commissioner for Refugees (UNHCR) warned on Sept 29.
UNHCR is facing one of its worst-ever funding crises following aid cuts by the United States and other countries. It faces a US$5.79 billion (S$7.4 billion) funding gap, according to a new report by the agency, after money available to the agency fell 24% between 2024 and 2025.
As at July, UNHCR had received only 32% of the US$8.51 billion it required in 2026, while the number of forcibly displaced and stateless people globally remains near record levels.
UNHCR expects the population under its mandate to reach 131.2 million by end-2026, up from 129.4 million at the end of 2025.
“Below a certain threshold, the system doesn’t shrink, it fails,” the agency said in the 26-page report outlining the impact of budget cuts on refugee registration, child protection programmes and services for survivors of gender-based violence.
The report highlighted severe consequences in countries hosting large displaced populations.
In Chad, where refugees have fled conflict in neighbouring Sudan, 319,000 people face registration delays, while 200,000 women and girls could lose access to safe spaces and prevention programmes.
In Sudan – which the UN considers the world’s worst displacement crisis due to the civil war that entered its fourth year in April – about 140,000 refugees and asylum-seekers remained unregistered by mid-year after registration activities were suspended for the first five months of 2026.
In Afghanistan, UNHCR grants given to people returning to the country have been slashed from US$375 to US$170 a person, while the country has received over one million people in 2026 alone, due to forced or voluntary returns from neighbouring countries, including Iran and Pakistan.
UNHCR said that further cost-saving measures could not compensate for funding shortfalls, after having already cut its workforce by 33% in 2025, closed offices in 140 locations and discontinued operations in 15 countries compared with 2024.
The agency also said a growing share of donor funding is tightly earmarked, rising to 51% in 2026 from 19% five years earlier, limiting its ability to shift resources to the most urgent priorities.
UNHCR warned that reduced funding was gradually eroding the protection system, increasing the risk that refugees remain undocumented and that survivors of gender-based violence are left without the support they need. REUTERS

5 things to do over the National Day ‘golden week’ holiday in Hong Kong

The confusing story of the Samaritans and the Jews: Who split from whom?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-29
02:59:52 UTC
11:59:52 KST

On the 14th of Nisan, as evening falls, the entire Samaritan community gathers on Mount Gerizim, which rises above the West Bank city of Nablus. The high priest leads the evening prayers. Lambs are slaughtered by knife at the moment Exodus 12 specifies: twilight.
Their carcasses are roasted whole in deep pits dug into the mountainside, the entrails burned separately, and the meat is eaten in haste, dressed for travel, as Exodus 12:11 prescribes. The community holds that it has been doing this here since the days of Joshua, by its reckoning, over 3,300 years ago.
There are about 850 Samaritans alive today – roughly half in Holon, a satellite city next to Tel Aviv; and half in Kiryat Luza, the village on the mountain to which the Nablus community moved during the first intifada. In 1920 there were 141. Most readers know them from the Gospels – the Good Samaritan of Luke 10; the woman at the well of John 4 – "When a Samaritan woman came to draw water, Jesus said to her, 'Will you give me a drink?'".
Their real history is older than either the Jewish or the Christian telling, and it turns on a question neither tradition can close: who split from whom?
Jewish tradition says the Samaritans were never Israelites at all. The Samaritans say they are the Israelites – the northern tribes who never went into exile.
The story the Bible tells
The received version comes from 2 Kings 17. In 722 B.C.E., after a three-year siege, Assyria conquered Samaria and ended the Kingdom of Israel. The Israelites were deported eastward, and in their place the Assyrian king settled peoples from Babylon, Cuthah, Avva, Hamath and Sepharvaim (2 Kings 17:24).
The newcomers, ignorant of "the custom of the god of the land," were set upon by lions, and an exiled Israelite priest was sent back to teach them. The result, the chapter reports, was worship of the Lord alongside their own gods "as did their fathers, so do they unto this day" (17:41).
In the first century C.E., the Jewish-cum-Roman historian Josephus made the identification explicit, claiming that the Samaritans descend from descend from the settlers the Assyrians brought from Cuthah – and the rabbis adopted that tradition. In the Talmud the Samaritans are called "the Kutim." According to this account, the Kutim are foreigners with a borrowed religion, and there was never a split that needs explaining.
Parts of it are certainly true. The Assyrian king Sargon II's own inscriptions claim roughly 27,000 deportees from Samaria, and foreign settlers really were sent to replace them.
A conquest that left no ashes
The late Gary Knoppers, the biblical scholar whose "Jews and Samaritans" (2013) is the standard modern synthesis, described the archaeological record.
Excavations in the ancient city of Samaria found no destruction layer datable to 722 B.C.E. Across the region, local pottery types changed only minimally. And of the five imported peoples, the material trace is close to nil – "almost nothing has been uncovered that can be attributed to the countries of the different groups of deportees," the archaeologist Ephraim Stern conceded, in a passage Knoppers cites.
Nobody knows how many people lived in the Israelite kingdom. On the estimates Knoppers cites, the 27,000 people Sargon deported were a quarter to a third of the population. The great majority stayed.
But a small minority of scholars argued Sargon's deportations touched only the elite.
They did not deny that Sargon deported Israelites and brought in foreigners, but don't think he did so on a large scale. The British biblical scholar Richard Coggins, in "Samaritans and Jews" (1975), put the exiles at 3 or 4 percent of the Israelite population. The Israeli historian Nathan Schur, in his "History of the Samaritans" (1989), called Sargon's figure literary hyperbole and added that the newcomers stayed mostly in the city of Samaria. Their evidence was chiefly the Bible itself: Jeremiah and Ezekiel, more than a century later, still speak of the northern tribes as living in the land.
Knoppers agrees with them about the prophets: northern Israelites did remain in the land. But he rejects the rest of their case – that only the elite were deported, that Sargon's figure is exaggerated, and that the newcomers stayed in one city.
A decade-long survey of Lower Galilee by the Israeli archaeologist Zvi Gal found the region practically abandoned from the late 8th century, and Sargon's predecessor, Tiglath-pileser III, records deporting 13,520 people from its towns. A detailed study of numbers in Assyrian royal inscriptions by Marco De Odorico (1995) deems Sargon's 27,280 to be authentic.
The minimalists' estimate that only 3 or 4 percent of the Israelites were kicked out rested on old estimates that the population of northern Israelites numbered around 800,000, which archaeological surveys have since cut drastically. Also, the foreigners were not confined to one city: Assyrian buildings and cuneiform tablets have turned up at Megiddo, Gezer, Tel Hadid and elsewhere.
Knoppers' own middle course is that many Israelites did remain – a reduced population in the Samarian hills, which also absorbed a modest number of settlers brought in by the Assyrians. If that's true, it undercuts the core claim of 2 Kings 17: that the people of Samaria after the year 722 B.C.E. were non-locals. According to Knoppers' reconstruction, the population from which the Samaritans would later emerge descended mostly from northern Israelites who had stayed put.
The chapter that argues with itself
Verses 24 to 34 of 2 Kings 17 describe the settlers adopting the worship of "the god of the land" under a returned Israelite priest, who is installed at Bethel – one of the old royal sanctuaries of the northern kingdom. Whatever the chapter meant to say about these people, it has just described the worship of the God of Israel continuing in Samaria, at an Israelite shrine, under an Israelite priest.
Verses 34 to 40 then flatly deny that these people fear the Lord at all. The two passages cannot both be right. Knoppers' explanation is that they come from different hands: "a succession of Judahite writers struggled to explain this survival," he writes, and the later writers never removed the earlier account.
There is a further wrinkle in the Greek. Étienne Nodet, a Dominican priest and professor at the École Biblique in Jerusalem, points to the Septuagint – the ancient Greek translation of the Hebrew Bible, made in Alexandria from the 3rd century B.C.E. Where the Hebrew's closing verses say the people of Samaria do not keep the Lord's laws, the Greek says they do, following "the Law and... the command that the Lord commanded to the descendants of Jacob."
The Greek is so favorable to them, Nodet observes, that "one wonders whether the texts are really talking about the colonizers or rather about a remnant of the ancient Israelites of the northern kingdom."
The Greek still contains the verses about the settlers' own gods. But Nodet argues that those verses, too, are a later addition: Josephus, who retells the chapter and had nothing but contempt for the Samaritans, shows no knowledge of them, and would surely have used them if he had.
A temple that was not supposed to exist
Then there is the mountain. Josephus dates the Samaritan temple on Mount Gerizim to the days of Alexander the Great, in the late 4th century B.C.E., and 20th-century scholarship long followed him.
In a 1971 study, the German historian of religion Hans Kippenberg argued that the Samaritans became a separate community only in the 3rd century B.C.E. or later – a sectarian offshoot that broke away from a Judaism already formed. But the excavations of the archaeologist Yitzhak Magen, conducted from the 1980s, undercut that chronology.
Beneath the great Hellenistic precinct on the summit of Mount Gerizim lay a Persian-period sacred precinct, roughly 96 by 98 meters. Nearby: thousands of burnt bones of sheep, goats, cattle and doves – the animals the Torah permits on an altar – carbon-dated to the 5th century B.C.E. The earliest coin found is a Cypriot drachma of 480 B.C.E.
Little of the Persian-phase structure survives beyond walls, a gate and stones that may have belonged to an altar, and Magen's temple is a reconstruction from them. What is beyond dispute is that sacrifice to the God of Israel was being offered there, on that mountain, in the 5th century B.C.E.
Magen dates the building of the sanctuary to the first half of the 5th century B.C.E. – earlier, on his reading, than the arrival of Nehemiah, the Persian-appointed governor who rebuilt Jerusalem's walls, in 445 B.C.E. Jan Dušek, the Czech scholar of ancient inscriptions who re-edited the Gerizim inscriptions in 2012, prefers the second half of the century.
Either way, sacrifice was being offered on Gerizim roughly a century or more before Josephus's date for the temple, and within about a century of the rebuilt temple in Jerusalem. Kippenberg had the Samaritans breaking away from an established Judaism. But the precinct shows them sacrificing to the same God during the same centuries in which that Judaism was taking shape. Knoppers describes two closely related communities, in constant contact, each with its own sanctuary.
Centuries later, when the sanctuary was at its Hellenistic height, its worshippers left some 400 fragmentary dedicatory inscriptions naming priests and donors – among them men named Judah and Yehud.
The book both communities kept
The two communities also shared the Torah, though not quite the same text of it: the Samaritan Pentateuch – still written in the Samaritan script, a descendant of the paleo-Hebrew alphabet used in ancient Israel before Jews adopted the square Aramaic letters still in use today – differs from the Masoretic Text, the standard Jewish text of the Hebrew Bible, in some 6,000 places, most of them minor.
Among the Dead Sea Scrolls are Pentateuch manuscripts that share the Samaritan text's characteristic expansions but lack its Samaritan additions. Closely related texts, that is, were circulating in Judea too, which means the expansions are not a Samaritan invention. They are older than the quarrel.
There was a mechanism for that. Both communities had priesthoods claiming descent from Aaron, and each tradition concedes that the other's priests descend from Aaron too, if from a lesser line, even while denying the legitimacy of the other's sanctuary. A shared priestly class is a shared scribal class, and a shared scribal class is how one Pentateuch stays one Pentateuch across a political border.
The Pentateuch, Knoppers concludes, "has to be regarded as a common patrimony" from before relations "became seriously aggravated in the last two centuries B.C.E." Deuteronomy's central command, he argues, was left deliberately open: "the place that the Lord your God will choose" names no mountain, and each community read it as its own. On this view, the vagueness was the point: it let both communities keep the same book.
One letter, 21 times
Over time, scribes on each side adjusted the text toward their own mountain.
That same formula – "the place that the Lord your God will choose" – appears 21 times across Deuteronomy. In the Jewish text the verb is imperfect, yivchar, "will choose," leaving the question open for Jerusalem to be the answer revealed later. In the Samaritan text it is perfect, bachar, "has chosen," which closes the question at Sinai. One letter (in Hebrew), and the mountain is already decided.
The standard scholarly view was that the Samaritans had made the change. That view has loosened: the Swiss biblical scholar Adrian Schenker showed the perfect form is also supported by some Greek, Old Latin and Coptic witnesses, and Knoppers now writes that it is "no longer self-evident" that the Samaritan reading is a late sectarian correction.
The Samaritan text also carries an additional commandment. In both places where the Ten Commandments appear – Exodus 20 and Deuteronomy 5 – the Samaritan Pentateuch adds one more, assembled out of verses that exist in the Jewish text elsewhere: it orders an altar to be built on Mount Gerizim upon entering the land.
The effect is to move the choice of the mountain out of history and into the Decalogue itself: not a decision made later, but part of what was given at Sinai. Unlike the expansions shared with the Qumran manuscripts, this commandment appears in no Dead Sea Scroll; it is a Samaritan addition.
And then there is the verse that runs the other way. Deuteronomy 27:4–5 orders an altar built after the crossing of the Jordan on a named mountain: Gerizim in the Samaritan text, Ebal in the Jewish one.
The two mountains are not interchangeable. Deuteronomy 11:29 has just assigned them opposite roles – the blessing is pronounced on Gerizim, the curse on Ebal – which makes an altar on Ebal, the mountain of the curse, the harder reading to explain.
An Old Latin manuscript reads Gerizim. Old Latin matters here because it was translated from the Greek Septuagint, and that translation was made in Alexandria in the 3rd century B.C.E. – before the Samaritan text was finalized, and outside the reach of the quarrel. A Samaritan alteration could not have gotten into it.
On this evidence the Jewish "Ebal" is probably the altered reading – a Judean correction, Knoppers suggests, that removed a linchpin of the Samaritan argument. Most copies of the Septuagint say Ebal, so the question is not settled. But here the evidence leans the Samaritans' way: the Old Latin reading goes back to a Greek translation older than the quarrel, which Samaritan scribes could not have touched.
Enter the Hasmoneans
So when did they finally become enemies? There is no clean date for a schism. But there is a date for the act that may have made reconciliation impossible.
In 111–110 B.C.E. John Hyrcanus – ruler and high priest in Jerusalem, of the Hasmonean Jewish dynasty the Hanukkah story celebrates – besieged Mount Gerizim and destroyed the sanctuary (Josephus, "Antiquities," Book 13). His forces then besieged the city of Samaria – by then settled largely by descendants of Macedonian colonists – and by 108 B.C.E. had razed it and enslaved its inhabitants. The sanctuary was never rebuilt.
Jews of the late Second Temple period kept the date, though not the reason. Megillat Taanit – the Scroll of Fasting, a first-century C.E. list of days on which mourning was forbidden because of some past deliverance – marks 21 Kislev as Yom Har Gerizim, Mount Gerizim Day.
But the explanation that came down attached to it has nothing to do with Hyrcanus: it tells a story about Alexander the Great and the high priest Shimon the Just. Historians have connected the holiday instead with the demolition, which fits the date and the name.
If that connection is right, Jews went on marking the destruction of the Samaritan temple long after they had forgotten what the day commemorated.
"It was not the circumstances surrounding the construction of the Mt. Gerizim temple," Knoppers writes, "but rather its destruction centuries later that embittered the Samaritans against their Judean neighbors." The estrangement the Gospels take for granted – "Jews do not share things in common with Samaritans" (John 4:9) – postdates the demolition by more than a century.
Even the rabbis could not decide
Nor did the question close quickly on the Jewish side. The early Tannaim – the rabbis of the first two centuries C.E., whose rulings make up the Mishnah – treated the Samaritans as Jews.
Rabban Shimon ben Gamaliel, one of the leading rabbis of the mid-2nd century C.E., went further: any commandment the Samaritans have accepted, he taught, they keep more scrupulously than Israel does (Tosefta, Pesahim 2:3 – the Tosefta being a compilation of early rabbinic rulings parallel to the Mishnah).
The opposite position – a Kuti is like a gentile – belongs to the generation after his, that of Rabbi Judah the Prince, some three centuries after Hyrcanus, and hardened further among the Amoraim, the rabbis of the 3rd to 5th centuries whose debates fill the Talmud.
What cannot be settled
Even the scholars who stress the Assyrian upheaval accept that some Israelites stayed, so the Samaritans descend at least in part from northern Israelites. What remains in dispute is how much of the old northern kingdom survives in today's 850 Samaritans – and that, the evidence cannot settle.
Knoppers's position is the cautious one: real Israelite continuity, reduced by deportation, mixed by absorption. Nodet's is the maximal one – the Samaritans are "to this day the direct heirs of the ancient Israelites," and rabbinic Judaism is the younger tradition, formed by the reforms the Bible attributes to Ezra the scribe and Nehemiah which the Israelites of the former northern kingdom – the Samaritans' ancestors – never adopted.
Nodet dates those reforms far later than the Bible does: he reads the biblical Ezra as a back-projection of a charter the Seleucid king Antiochus III granted the Jews around 200 B.C.E. – a redating few have accepted. The evidence does not decide between reduced continuity and unbroken inheritance.
For some three and a half centuries, two sanctuaries to the same God, with two priesthoods each claiming descent from Aaron, shared a Torah tradition between them. They were drifting apart the whole time – separate cults, separate priesthoods, and eventually rival claims about which mountain the text had meant.
No single date marks when the drift became a schism, and Hyrcanus's destruction of the sanctuary is the nearest thing to one. Each spring, on the 14th of Nisan, the community still goes up Mount Gerizim, where the sanctuary stood, to slaughter the Passover lambs.

OpenAI cancels release of new artificial intelligence model over safety concerns
OpenAI will not release its latest artificial intelligence model, Astra 6.1, after internal tests found it fell short of safety standards, the maker of ChatGPT confirmed on Monday. The decision came ahead of a meeting of AI leaders at the White House Tuesday convened by US President Donald Trump and House Speaker Mike Johnson amid mounting controversy over the risks posed by rogue AI.
OpenAI will not release its newest artificial intelligence model, known as Astra 6.1, after internal testing by the maker of ChatGPT revealed it did not meet safety standards, the company confirmed Monday.
The news comes one day before the AI giant hosts an annual developer conference known as OpenAI DevDay in San Francisco, where the company is expected to make several announcements – though it is unclear if a new version of Astra will be among them.
Read moreRogue AI accessed federal websites, posted user images online, ChatGPT says
Astra 6.1 was an improvement over previous models in some aspects, but "it didn't quite meet the bar in terms of staying within scope and authorisation, and how it communicates back to the user about the type of work it's done," Saachi Jain, OpenAI's head of safety systems, said in a statement.
"We want to make sure our model development is safe no matter whether that's in the company, or when we ship it to users. But when we ship it to users, we have an extremely high bar in terms of safety and alignment," Jain continued.
AI safety fears
US President Donald Trump and House Speaker Mike Johnson are set to convene leading artificial intelligence executives at the White House on Tuesday amid calls from Congress for stronger industry oversight.
Watch moreAI-pocalypse? Tech leaders, politicians clash over development slowdown
The lunch meeting, not yet confirmed by the White House, will feature Meta CEO Mark Zuckerberg, Google CEO Sundar Pichai, and OpenAI President Greg Brockman, according to CNN.
Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei will also attend, a person close to the matter told AFP, just two days after a private meeting with Trump. SpaceX executive Elon Musk is expected to take part as well.
So will Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang, according to another person familiar with the matter.
Concerns about AI safety have escalated in recent months after models developed by OpenAI and rival lab Anthropic were involved in security incidents during testing.
Read moreAI leaders urge caution at UN, with Anthropic chief pledging to slow down
Agents built with OpenAI's models have inappropriately accessed websites maintained by US federal agencies, an Australian government health statistics portal and Hugging Face, a repository of AI models.
OpenAI apologized Monday for not properly responding to the Australia incident, which involved its AI models accessing government websites without authorisation.
Read moreOpenAI AI agent breached Australian government website, PM says
"We are sorry and working to do better in the future," OpenAI said in a blog post, adding that the company would explain "what we know, what we have changed, and what we will do to rebuild trust with the Australian people".
"Our aim was to give affected agencies a detailed account once our investigation was complete," the ChatGPT-maker said. "However, we should have shared preliminary findings sooner and kept Australian agencies updated as more facts emerged."
OpenAI, Anthropic and other major AI developers have promised to prioritise making models that have safety guardrails to mitigate risks and that are also aligned with human values.
American chip making giant Nvidia announced on Monday that it created a system designed to stop autonomous AI programs from straying beyond what they were instructed to do.
"I believe it's an engineering problem...and we all need to hope that's an engineering problem," Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang told broadcaster CNBC on Monday.
"If it's not an engineering problem, it's not solvable," he added.
The AI Security Institute (AISI), an initiative under the UK government, published a study on Monday showing that GPT-6 Astra went off the rails more often during testing than its predecessors, GPT-5.6 Sol and GPT-5.5.
In simulations, GPT-6 spontaneously carried out cyberattacks at rates significantly higher than those observed for the other two interfaces.

Israeli military closures isolate Ramallah, strand Palestinians for hours
Motorists report six-hour waits as tightened checkpoints disrupt travel, work and medical access across central West Bank
Qais Omar, Tarek Chouiref
29 September 2026•Update: 29 September 2026
İSTANBUL
Tightened Israeli military closures around Ramallah and Al-Bireh have stranded thousands of Palestinians for hours, restricting key routes into and out of the central occupied West Bank cities.
Long vehicle queues have formed repeatedly at Atara, Ein Sinya, Jaba and other checkpoints in recent days, with some Palestinians reaching home only after midnight.
An Anadolu team observed continued closures and heavy congestion Monday at several entrances to Ramallah, severely disrupting movement between the city and surrounding towns and villages.
Malik Anas was returning from Ramallah to his home in Qalqilya when he became stuck at the closed Atara checkpoint northwest of the city.
He told Anadolu that he waited around six hours before Israeli forces reopened the checkpoint after midnight.
Thousands of Palestinian vehicles were held there, he said, while others reported reaching their homes as late as 2 am after lengthy waits and diversions.
The restrictions have also disrupted access to medical care.
Palestinian activist Aayed Ghafari documented a patient being transferred from a private vehicle to an ambulance at Atara on Monday after being unable to cross the checkpoint.
“The occupation army has deliberately been closing Ramallah’s entrances for days and preventing residents from passing in their vehicles,” Ghafari told Anadolu, saying the measures had disrupted daily life and work.
Palestinians have linked the tighter restrictions to Jewish holidays, while Israel says such measures are imposed for security reasons.
Recent closures have affected several main routes linking Ramallah with the rest of the occupied West Bank.
The official Palestinian news agency Wafa reported closures at Atara and Ein Sinya and at the entrances to Aboud and Nabi Saleh, alongside tighter restrictions around Yabrud and Jaba.
On Sunday, thousands of vehicles were stranded around Ramallah and the northern outskirts of occupied East Jerusalem as restrictions hit several crossings and roads simultaneously.
The Ramallah and Al-Bireh governorate has 160 permanent checkpoints and closure points, according to the Palestinian Colonization and Wall Resistance Commission, second only to Hebron with 221.
Across the occupied West Bank, the commission has recorded 942 checkpoints, closures and other movement obstacles.
The UN Office for the Coordination of Humanitarian Affairs (OCHA) said such barriers can force Palestinians onto longer routes and disrupt access to workplaces, schools, hospitals and other essential services.
For Palestinians around Ramallah, journeys that normally take minutes can now stretch into hours, depending on which checkpoint is open.

Vietnam Airlines jet deployed brakes twice before botched take-off
- A Vietnam Airlines Boeing 787 activated brakes twice during take-off at Munich Airport, causing a late lift-off and tail strike, with no injuries among 287 onboard.
- The plane lost acceleration halfway down the runway but took off after the co-pilot increased engine power; the aircraft was substantially damaged.
- Investigation is ongoing; key brake components were seized, cockpit audio was overwritten, and the cause of braking is still unclear according to the German Federal Bureau of Aircraft Accident Investigation.
AI generated
MUNICH – A Boeing 787 aircraft operated by Vietnam Airlines had its brakes activated twice while barrelling down the runway at Munich Airport in August, leading to a perilously late take-off and the plane’s tail striking the ground.
Movement of the two left brake pedals was recorded on the same side of the aircraft, where a highly experienced captain with more than 27,000 flying hours was seated, the German Federal Bureau of Aircraft Accident Investigation said in an interim report released on Sept 28.
The report, citing data from the aircraft’s flight recorders, also said that the brakes were applied a second time while the plane was rushing down the runway before take-off.
The report did not specify if the braking action was caused by the cockpit crew or stemmed from a technical issue.
Investigators seized several system components, including the brake system control units and the electric brake actuator controllers. The audio recording in the cockpit during the time of the take-off was overwritten, according to the report.
The Hanoi-bound 787-9 plane, which was carrying 287 passengers and crew, experienced a loss of acceleration halfway down the runway, but the flight crew determined there was not enough tarmac left to abort take-off.
With the plane’s speed insufficient, the co-pilot increased power to the aircraft’s engines to get off the ground beyond the tarmac threshold, according to the report.
No one on board was injured. The investigation into the incident is ongoing and no conclusions have been reached.
There were four pilots in the cockpit at the time of take-off. The pilot flying – a captain – occupied the left-hand seat, while the co-pilot was designated so-called pilot monitoring.
The pilot in command, nominated by the operator, was seated in the left jump seat, and another pilot was seated in the right jump seat, according to the report.
The pilot in command – another captain with almost 23,000 hours of flying experience – replaced the pilot flying in the left-hand seat after take-off, and performed the subsequent emergency landing.
The aircraft was “substantially damaged” during the mishap, according to the report.
The plane lifted off from the grass after overshooting the runway and “the tail section and the wheels of both main landing gears collided with parts of the approach lighting”, according to investigators.
Four of the left main landing gear tyres were observed to be damaged after the aircraft returned to the departure airport, investigators added.
Before landing back in Munich, the aircraft had dumped 62 tonnes of fuel to reduce its weight, the report said.
The aircraft weighed a total of 240,857kg at take-off – close to the maximum take-off mass of 247,207kg. Fuel accounted for 68,783kg.
While in the air dumping fuel, the flight crew reported a suspected flat tyre to air traffic control, according to the report.
Vietnam Airlines was contacted for comment outside business hours and did not respond immediately. BLOOMBERG

The unlikely Australian Black Summer landmark that's been classified as a national treasure
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-29
02:40:38 UTC
11:40:38 KST

In brief
- A public telephone that became a lifeline for a small town during the Black Summer bushfires has been heritage-listed.
- The landline phone put through over 1,000 calls from locals when power and mobile services failed.
Under furious orange skies and plumes of bushfire smoke, locals and tourists lined up at a public phone to talk to family and friends or check in on neighbours.
Some used the public phone in Narooma to tell loved ones they were safe, while others revealed they had lost everything in the catastrophic Black Summer bushfires that razed much of the NSW far south coast.
Historian Naomi Parry Duncan was holidaying in Narooma on New Year's Day in 2020, among those who had to shelter at an evacuation centre as the fires loomed.
There was no mobile reception or power during that "bewildering and frightening" time, sending many to wait at three public phones in town, Parry Duncan recalled.
"At all of the pay phones there were queues of people politely waiting," she told the Australian Associated Press news agency.
News that makes sense
Your trusted source for staying up-to-date with the world around you. Get free daily news updates and analysis, straight to your inbox.
"It was quite an intimate space in the queue."
The phone outside Narooma Plaza on the Princes Highway has been heritage-listed for its cultural and social role in the Black Summer fires, with almost 1,000 calls made over two months during and after the disaster.
Parry Duncan led the nomination to the National Trust of Australia NSW register.
The phone is now marked with the trust's bronze plaque, emblazoned with gum leaves, to denote its significance.
The quiet empathy displayed by people waiting for the phones as they carried shared trauma was a particularly moving sight, Parry Duncan said.
"The instinctive thing to help each other was really quite amazing," she said.
Her New Zealand-born partner saw the way people waited patiently for the phone and felt a deeper understanding of Australia, she said.
The landmark status was being sought for other phones, including one in remote Queensland and another in Melbourne.
Telstra is mandated to maintain Australia's 14,000 pay phones, with all local and national calls to standard fixed lines and mobiles free since mid-2021.
Within the last year, 25 million calls have been made from pay phones, including 300,000 to triple zero and crisis support lines.
"Where we've got vulnerable people in the community out there who need crisis support and to stay connected, they're showing us these pay phones are absolutely critical," Telstra regional general manager Chris Taylor said.
Telstra has been working to ensure better resilience during disasters, such as power back-ups to help restore connectivity more quickly, Taylor said.
Parry Duncan said public phones have a long history in Australian culture, playing a particularly important part in women's lives.
The phones were used to help women find employment and leave abusive relationships throughout the last century, as well as keeping Indigenous communities connected, she said.
"They are so important for keeping us together, especially when you've got a country that is spread over such vast distances as Australia."

Iran’s Araghchi meets Qatari mediators as US calls for nuclear talks

Iran’s Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi has met with Qatari mediators in New York to discuss a proposal to reopen the Strait of Hormuz, while a United States official said there would be no agreement to end the war unless Tehran’s nuclear programme is addressed.
Araghchi told Iranian state media on Monday that the Qatari mediators would carry the ideas discussed at the meeting to the US and that he hoped to receive Washington’s final response by Tuesday.

The gathering comes quickly after tech giant OpenAI’s cancellation of the release of its newest model owing to safety concerns, and a series of revelations that the technology had gone rogue.

Major AI companies, particularly Anthropic and OpenAI, have issued stark public warnings about uncontrolled development of increasingly powerful systems – even as they push out this same state-of-the-art technology.
Those concerns intensified after a former employee of both companies went public with warnings that the industry is moving faster than safety reviews allow.

Trump has repeatedly characterised these warnings about existential risks as overblown and opposes curbs on the sector.

With midterm elections in November, US lawmakers from both parties have drafted multiple Bills to better govern AI.
Some would require companies to disclose more about how their systems work and what safeguards they employ.
But with the House on recess through early November and senators soon to head home to campaign, Congress is all but certain not to pass comprehensive AI legislation before the vote. AFP

Thailand’s Constitutional Court Dismisses Petition Seeking Annulment of General Election
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-29
02:28:00 UTC
11:28:00 KST

Thailand’s Constitutional Court yesterday dismissed a petition challenging the legality of the last general election, ruling that the ballot papers used did not undermine the confidentiality of the vote.
The ruling came in response to 22 complaints about the use of barcodes and QR codes on ballot papers in the February 8 election, which some claimed could breach constitutional requirements for secret voting, the Bangkok Post reported.
Nearly 38 million Thais voted in the election, which was won decisively by Prime Minister Anutin Charnvirakul’s Bhumjaithai Party. Bhumjaithai emerged from the polls with 192 of the 500 seats in the House of Representatives, and later formed a coalition government with a host of other parties, including the once-powerful Pheu Thai party (74 seats). The opposition People’s Party won 120 seats.
However, in the aftermath of the election, a host of complaints were submitted to the Election Commission (EC) for its adjudication, including complaints of alleged vote-buying, uncounted ballots, and other irregularities. While these were dismissed, it took the complaints about the use of barcodes and QR codes on ballots, which were ostensibly intended to counter fraud, more seriously.
In March, the Office of the Ombudsman ruled that there were sufficient grounds to question whether the EC and its leadership had acted in a way that contravened constitutional protections about voter confidentiality. If the Constitutional Court ruled that that the secrecy of the vote was compromised by the use of barcodes and QR codes, it had the power to annul the result of the election.
However, in its ruling yesterday, the Bangkok Post reported, the Constitutional Court said that that barcode and QR codes were “applied to prevent use of fake ballot papers and their cross-constituency use, and to control the number and printing of ballots.”
While the ballots contained information that could potentially be used to identify voters’ decisions, this information was only accessible if any outside party had access to used ballots, ballot stubs, and the lists of voters’ names – and then used mobile phones to scan the codes on all the documents. The fact that all three of these things were stored separately and were “sufficiently safe” from outside access, offered sufficient protection of the secrecy of the ballot, the Constitutional Court ruled.
Although the charter court endorsed the legality of coded ballots, it advised the EC not to use any codes that connected to the results in future.
The ruling averts this costly possibility of a new election – the Bangkok Post estimated that this would cost the Thai state upwards of 7 billion baht ($216 million) – and will no doubt come as a welcome relief for Anutin’s coalition government, especially given the Constitutional Court’s history of brash interventions in Thai politics.
Anutin has seen his approval ratings fall in recent months, due to rising living costs and political scandals involving corruption and the alleged rigging of the 2024 Senate election .
In a poll released on Sunday by the National Institute of Development Administration, only 13.8 percent of respondents chose Anutin as their preferred prime minister, down from 21.7 percent in June. Bhumjaithai’s rating declined from 17 percent to 12.1 percent over the same period, behind the People’s Party and the Pheu Thai Party.

California Gov. Gavin Newsom signs bill to create safe spaces around synagogues
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-29
02:27:24 UTC
11:27:24 KST

California Gov. Gavin Newsom, a Democrat, has signed a law that will create protective spaces around religious institutions, after a pro-Palestinian protest at a Los Angeles synagogue last year turned violent.
The legislation, AB 2664, establishes 100-foot zones around the entrances to houses of worship. Within the zones, no one will be allowed to come within eight feet of a congregant without consent to distribute leaflets, hold a sign, or engage in oral protests that aim “to harass, obstruct, threaten or intimidate the person.”
Failure to comply could result in fines of up to $1,000 and/or imprisonment of no more than six months, with second violations raising those bars to $5,000 and one year, per the law.
“Every Californian should be able to walk into a synagogue, church, mosque, or other house of worship without fear,” Newsom said in a statement.
“California is continuing to protect these organizations and the people they serve, and we’re strengthening that work from the front door to expanding security resources to community events statewide.”
Newsom’s status as a leading Democrat – and one considering a 2028 presidential run – makes his enthusiastic endorsement notable. Progressives in other locales, including New York City, have pushed back against similar laws, saying they endanger speech protections.
Bill comes after violent protest at Los Angeles synagogue
The bill’s signing came less than a year after a violent protest rattled the Wilshire Boulevard Temple in Los Angeles. At the December event, pro-Palestinian demonstrators blocked people from entering the synagogue and cut off parental access to the religious school. Protesters destroyed property and assaulted a security guard; one person was arrested for battery and another for vandalism.
At the time, Mayor Karen Bass denounced the incident, which took place at one of the largest synagogues in the city, as both “abhorrent” and antisemitic.
The following spring, California Assembly member Rebecca Bauer-Kahan, a Democrat, introduced the legislation, drafted by Jewish California, a lobby representing a number of the state’s Jewish groups. Newsom signed the bill on Friday inside Wilshire Boulevard Temple, joined by Jewish California leaders, synagogue clergy and members of the California Legislative Jewish Caucus and the broader community.
The legislation advanced despite vocal opposition. The Council on American-Islamic Relations slammed the bill for infringing upon free speech by creating “new criminal penalties that would put peaceful protesters and community advocates at risk.”
In a statement following Newsom’s signing ceremony, the council’s California CEO, Hussam Ayloush, argued that some sales of “illegally occupied land” are occurring “exclusively to Jewish Americans at events hosted by American synagogues.”
“If a house of worship in America chooses to serve as a platform for illegal land sales meant to normalize Palestinian displacement, Americans should be able to peacefully demonstrate against that immoral activity,” Ayloush said. The protest at the Wilshire Boulevard Temple did not target land sales, but a public safety and technology event organized by the Consulate General of Israel.
Legislation gains support from groups of multiple religions
Jewish California stressed that the legislation not only gained support from dozens of Jewish groups but also from Muslim, Sikh, Christian and Hindu organizations. Ultimately, the bill passed with 34 out of 40 State Senate votes and 61 of 80 State Assembly votes.
“With the Governor’s signature, California is sending a clear message: everyone has the right to practice their faith safely and freely,” Bauer-Kahan said in a statement.
“Antisemitism is rising, and so is hostility towards other religious communities,” she added. “This law protects all worshippers of all faiths, and it ensures that faith can be practiced without fear.”
AB 2664 was one of six bills relevant to the Jewish community that passed in California’s state legislature last month. Newsom signed one of the other bills, AB 1853, on Monday afternoon – enacting a ban on including misleading or threatening information, like hate speech, in California voter guides.
The governor has until Sept. 30 to either sign or veto the other four pieces of legislation. Among the most contentious is SB 1387, a bill that would expand the definition of ethnicity “to include Jewish identity” on state agency data collection forms.

France: Student protests over conditions at French high schools fuel political clashes
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-29
02:26:00 UTC
11:26:00 KST

France: Student protests fuel political clashes
September 29, 2026
Student protests spread to high schools across France on Monday, resulting in dozens of injuries, over 160 arrests and arguments between senior politicians — a day ahead of a nationwide strike by public sector workers and seven months ahead of the presidential election.
Teenagers at French lycées (equivalent to US high schools) have been blockading their schools since last week in protest at overcrowded classes, heavy workloads, poor quality learning materials and teacher shortages.
The movement began in the Ile-de-France region around the capital, Paris, but on Monday spread to other regions including Lille in the north, Marseille in the south and Sedan in the east.
Video footage on French media showed student protesters lighting flares and firing fireworks, even inside a school building, while police officers responded with tear gas.
French student protests: what have politicians said?
As of Monday night, French Interior Minister Laurent Nunez reported incidents at around 180 establishments resulting in 164 arrests and injuries to 12 students, three teachers and 12 police officers.
He acknowledged that the "difficulties of high schools must be heard and addressed" but said: "This wasn't about making demands, it was really violence in its purest form."
He added that "a number of individuals … were masked, equipped with fireworks in tubes and projectiles [and] clearly wanted to confront the internal security forces."
Prime Minister Sebastien Lecornu called the "escalation" of the situation "irresponsible" and said: "Fireworks, fires, violence near high schools: nothing justifies endangering students, staff, or police officers."
'Hands off our youth!' French politicians clash over protests
Education Minister Edouard Geffray said that the protests, which he described as a "classic high school student movement," were being exploited by violent elements — and took aim at the left-wing La France Insoumise (France Unbowed or LFI) party and its presidential candidate Jean-Luc Melenchon.
"There is a political hijacking of the blockades by elected officials from France Unbowed," he said.
Earlier on Monday, Melenchon had accused the government of implementing a "crackdown" with "obvious racist undertones."
"Hands off our youth!" he wrote on social media, while encouraging LFI activists and officials to support the protests wherever they could.
Prime Minister Lecornu called the accusation of racism "an insult" and accused Melenchon of "racializing a debate about student security and adding to division where a responsible politician should be looking to restore calm."
In the Parisian suburb of Saint-Denis, the LFI-run local council called the students' demands "legitimate" and published a statement reading:
"Let [the authorities] come and talk to [the students] and see for themselves whether the youth are being instrumentalized, or whether they are simply capable of thinking, organizing themselves and defending their own study conditions and their future."
France: strikes — and an election — to come
The Union Syndicale Lycéenne, the French union that defends the interests of high school students, said it would urge a nationwide blockade of schools on Tuesday — coinciding with planned strike action by public sector workers.
French primary school teachers' unions said they expected some 40% of teachers to be off work on Tuesday.
With a key presidential election only seven months away and incumbent President Emmanuel Macron constitutionally barred from standing for a third term, French politicians from across the ideological spectrum are seeking issues that resonate with voters.
Melenchon, a 75-year-old veteran anti-capitalist who finished third in the 2022 presidential election, is popular among younger, left-leaning voters.
His LFI party was one of the left-wing outfits which joined the Nouveau Front Populaire (New Popular Front or NFP) coalition in 2024 to oppose the far-right Rassemblement National (National Rally or RN) in legislative elections.
The coalition beat the RN but the elections produced a divided parliament which has been dogged by political deadlock and votes of no-confidence.
Prime Minister Lecornu is still trying to build enough support to pass a 2027 state budget, but his government is besieged by opponents who are unwilling to accept spending cuts while energy costs continue to rise.

Laura Gamba Fadul

Brazilian President Luiz Inacio Lula da Silva widened his lead over Senator Flavio Bolsonaro in first-round voting intention polls with just six days to go before the presidential election, but two surveys published Monday show the candidates remain in a statistical dead heat ahead of a potential runoff.
Polls conducted by Quaest and Nexus show the incumbent gaining ground ahead of the first-round vote scheduled for Oct. 4. Under Brazilian election law, if no candidate secures more than 50% of the valid votes, the top two contenders will face off in a second-round runoff on Oct. 25.
According to the Quaest poll, which was commissioned by O Globo and TV Globo, Lula holds 39% of voting intentions compared with 34% for Bolsonaro, expanding the president's advantage from a four-point margin last week.
Other surveys suggest a much tighter contest. A poll by Futura/100% Cidades places Lula at 38.3% and Bolsonaro close behind at 37.7%, well within the margin of error.
Flavio Bolsonaro, a 45-year-old lawyer and senator, was selected as the conservative candidate by his father, former President Jair Bolsonaro, who is currently serving a 27-year prison sentence for plotting a coup d'état following his narrow loss to Lula in the 2022 election.
While Flavio Bolsonaro entered politics early, becoming a Rio de Janeiro state deputy at age 21 and a federal senator at 37, he maintained a relatively low national profile until receiving his father's endorsement.
His campaign has faced scrutiny following revelations that he is under investigation for alleged corruption and money laundering tied to a biographical film about his father, which was partially funded by a banker arrested for fraud.
Positioning himself as an international conservative, Flavio has touted his ties to foreign allies, boasting of a private meeting with US President Donald Trump at the White House earlier this year.
The election in Latin America's largest nation carries immense geopolitical and economic weight. As an agricultural powerhouse rich in natural resources, Brazil holds key reserves of rare earth elements, vital freshwater supplies, and substantial offshore oil fields.
The race also highlights a shifting political landscape across the continent. Flavio Bolsonaro represents a surging conservative wave in a region where governments in Argentina, Bolivia, Peru, Chile, Ecuador and Colombia have grown increasingly aligned with Trump's agenda.

Brits want to get closer to the EU — and even Farage’s voters agree
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-29
02:21:43 UTC
11:21:43 KST

LIVERPOOL, England — Seven out of ten voters want the government to build a closer relationship with the European Union, according to a new POLITICO Poll that shows the extent of support for overhauling the Brexit settlement.
Even among voters who support Brexit campaigner Nigel Farage’s Reform UK party, a majority — 51% — share the view that the current arrangement with Brussels is too distant.
The poll comes at a highly sensitive moment for the U.K.’s governing Labour Party, with Prime Minister Andy Burnham facing demands from some senior colleagues to reverse Brexit and rejoin the EU.
Advertisement
“The public now often looks to Europe for overseas alliances, particularly as the U.S. is increasingly perceived as at best unreliable and at worst adversarial,” said Seb Wride, head of polling at public research company Public First, which conducted the poll for POLITICO. “But it’s not straightforward for the government. ‘Getting closer with Europe’ is not the same as ‘reversing Brexit,’ and Burnham will have a challenging needle to thread to appease his pro-European wings without reopening wounds the public would prefer stayed closed.”
The Brexit referendum a decade ago divided the country, cost two prime ministers their jobs and triggered often bad-tempered divorce negotiations between London and Brussels that took years to complete.
Public First asked respondents for their views on moving the country closer to the EU and accepting EU rules. Some 31% said Britain should build a “closer” relationship with Brussels, but only if it did not mean complying with the EU’s rulebook. But 39% wanted “much closer” cooperation even if that did require the U.K. to follow some EU rules again.
The poll also confirms how the Brexit debate has carved the country into two blocs — pro and anti. Supporters of parties on the left were far more likely to back a closer EU relationship than those on the right. Green Party voters were the keenest of all: 64% said they’d support much closer EU ties even if that meant applying more EU rules. Older voters were less keen on closer ties to Brussels.
Among Reform UK voters, 51% said they want a closer relationship — twice the 25% who want more distance from the EU. That poses a potential challenge for party leader Farage, a career Euroskeptic. The finding could also provide ammunition for Labour politicians who want Burnham to be more ambitious about his plans to upgrade the U.K.-EU relationship, potentially including a return to the bloc’s customs union, single market or even full EU membership again.
As Burnham prepared to deliver his Tuesday speech to party members and activists in Liverpool, a succession of ministers and others gave their views about what kind of closer relationship with the EU he should pursue.
Advertisement
Former Prime Minister Tony Blair published a report urging Burnham to put rejoining a reformed EU on the agenda for the next decade.
In an interview at the POLITICO Pub in Liverpool on Monday, Mayor of London Sadiq Khan called on the prime minister to begin the debate about rejoining the EU immediately, saying Brexit has been “a disaster” and “the biggest act of economic self-harm any country has ever done.”
“At some stage, sooner or later, we’ll be having the conversation about rejoining the European Union,” Khan said. “Why wait?”
Public First surveyed 2,028 U.K. adults online Sept. 13-15, 2026.

IOC launches Trustworthy AI Framework
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-29
10:18:21 CST
11:18:21 KST

GENEVA, Sept. 28 (Xinhua) -- The International Olympic Committee (IOC) has launched its first Trustworthy AI Framework for the Olympic Movement, aimed at guiding organizations in using artificial intelligence responsibly, ethically and with confidence.
Developed with support from digital transformation consulting partner Deloitte, the Framework sets out seven principles, including safeguarding, data protection, reliability, transparency, accountability, fairness and sustainability, as well as a checklist to help organizations assess risks, the IOC said.
Alejandro Merino-Madrid, the IOC's head of artificial intelligence, said: "AI has the potential to transform how athletes prepare, how sport is delivered, and how fans experience the Olympic Games."
"But technology must always serve sport - not the other way around. That means protecting athlete data, safeguarding fair competition and ensuring people understand how AI is being used. This Framework gives the Olympic Movement a common foundation to embrace those opportunities with confidence, while keeping athletes, integrity and our values at the center," Merino-Madrid added.
"Artificial intelligence is transforming sport, creating opportunities across athlete support, Games operations, fan engagement and the day-to-day work of sports organizations," read the IOC statement.
"At the same time, its increasing use raises important questions around fairness, athlete data, transparency, security and accountability. These challenges are particularly important in sport, where trust in competition, decision-making and the integrity of results is fundamental," the IOC added. ■

Colombia holds IMF financing talks as fiscal strain mounts, sources say
BOGOTA, Sept 28 - Colombia has held talks with the International Monetary Fund in recent weeks, including discussions on possible financing, as the government races to contain a deepening fiscal crisis that has rattled investors, three sources with knowledge of the matter said on Monday.
One focus of the previously unreported discussions was whether Colombia could secure funding on better terms as it confronts soaring borrowing needs and widening deficits, said the sources, who requested anonymity as the discussions are private.
President Abelardo De La Espriella, who took office in August, said on Sunday he had ordered his economic team to open talks with the IMF to seek a negotiated solution to the crisis, acknowledging the severity of the strain on state finances, but did not say that the discussions had begun.
After Reuters reported the talks, Colombia's Finance Ministry confirmed it had asked the IMF to send a technical mission to the country, following meetings in Bogota between IMF Deputy Managing Director Nigel Clarke and Colombian officials.
The ministry said the consultation would allow the fund to review the government's fiscal plan and economic outlook and would be a first step toward deeper cooperation.
Later on Monday, the IMF confirmed Clarke's visit and said the IMF backed a "homegrown reform program" for Colombia, and that a Finance Ministry delegation would travel to Washington next week for further talks.
The IMF did not announce any financing arrangement. A separate source familiar with the matter said it remained too early to discuss the size of any possible program and that any formal negotiation would require a dedicated IMF staff mission and further talks with the authorities.
Colombia is struggling amid lower tax revenue, expanded spending under the previous leftist government and persistent inflation. Those fiscal concerns have complicated efforts to contain borrowing costs and stabilize public debt, and De La Espriella has promised sweeping austerity measures to cut spending.
The government now expects Colombia's budget shortfall to be much larger than previously forecast this year and to widen even further in 2027.
It will also increase borrowing by more than $10.5 billion this year. In 2027, borrowing is set to reach $71.7 billion, more than double what was initially planned. REUTERS
